Tacoma's weakest point is its optimism. Maybe it's me, I love desperation, I love sadness and bleak, gloomy places so part of what I love in walking simulators is the absence of people which inevitably creates a tension.
But Tacoma, the new game from the makers of the wonderful Gone Home, found a way to put people back in the formula and while the result is certainly interesting from at least a couple of angles, it makes me pine for the missing humanity of most of the other games in the genre. Not only your character speaks, but you will get to spend time with the crew of the Tacoma in a much more physical way than in the hybrid way of Everybody's Gone to the Rapture, or the radio fleshless friendship of Firewatch.
I was mentioning the optimism. The story, without spoilers, is about a space station where 6 not particularly cool characters end up stranded and with no oxygen. You are the contractor tasked with recovering the AI files and basically what are VR tapes of what happened. The VR tapes idea is awesome: you "play" VR recordings of past events and have to move around following certain characters or some others to hear what they say or see what they do. Rewinding or Fastforwarding is made very easy and so the whole thing flows really well. Having to re-play a recording is not a chore considering you can move around as you please and rewatch the whole thing, or parts of it, from wherever you like and across different rooms. It's neat. I am not sure if it has been done before but it works really well as a device to advance the plot as opposed to the usual note-fiding or playing of disembodied audio snippets.
But the biggest problem is that there is never any intensity in what is going on. You are on an abandoned ship where it is easy to imagine everybody died and yet you can't grasp the gravity of the situation in the environment nor in the actual scenes and interactions of the crews you get to watch. It looks like everyone is really cool and prepared to die, so efficient, so wise. Don't get me wrong, I don't miss stereotypical freak outs or someone grabbing a weapon and threatening to blast the hull or whatever. But as storytellers the people at Fullbright failed to convey emotions in the story they were trying to tell. Not everything has to be about desperation and pain, and I can appreciate a group of developers that make a point to stay away from tropes of violence and aggression, yet the whole story ended up for me as too light, too delicate, a bit tasteless as you would tailor a serious story if you had to make sure even children could watch it without parental guidance.
Eventually, the ship looks only OK (if barely). Gone is the extra detailed Home of Gone Home, and while you can still pick up every single thing and manipulate it to look at all labels, posters, business cards, or bottom of a cup in the game, the sterile, metallic plates of a modern space station simply can't have the same charisma of a mansion. They are duller by definition.
What I liked the most, all things considered, is the ending. Once again Fullbright skillfully misdirects you only to deliver a cute plot twist that, given the soft and gentle paradigm of this game, I couldn't help but appreciate, but I walked away not completely satisfied. This is a short [s]game[/s] story that suffers by a literal lack of punch. As a result, it's harder to care too much about it.
But is it fun? Toothlessly maybe.

Does a 2D Dark Souls Super Metroid sound good to you?   Enter Hollow Knight.
The game is close to perfect.  The mysterious atmosphere is there, the combat is pretty tight, and there are secrets all over the place.  The amount of content in Hollow Knight is impressive, and due to the map mechanics, the sense of exploration when discovering that content is very real.
I feel like I should comment on the difficulty, because it seemed somewhat inconsistent.  I should note that I'm a completionist and that I missed a crucial ability (picking it up way later than intended), so maybe that colored my experience.  But I found some of the main quest bosses to be on the easy side, where I'd show up and tank my way through them on the first try.  The optional bosses, as well as the lategame bosses, were more difficult, and a couple gave me that gamer's high after I beat them, as if I had finally downed a difficult Dark Souls boss.  I never unintentionally lost my souls by dying before I could collect my shade...I guess that's a consequence of the rather forgiving healing system.
The free DLC has not been anything that exceptional, but I don't care because the base game has so much optional content already in it.
I'm not singing Hollow Knight's praises enough.  Seriously, is it the best game ever to come out of a Kickstarter?  I wish I could go back in time and help fund it.

BIT.TRIP BEAT is actually a really cool rhythm game.  I wasn't expecting much  with this title, but I'm pleasantly surprised.  It's quite addictive, and the difficulty is there as well.  The basic concept is kind of like pong, where you hit little dots with your pattle as they come flying toward you, but as the level progresses and the beat gets more intense the patterns the dots come at you increase in difficulty.  There are all sorts of neat effects, like disappearing, dots that freeze your pattle, double time, pattle shrink, bouncing dots, etc.  It's a lot of fun; however, the levels are extremely long, and if you end up losing, it takes forever to get back to the position you were at when you "died".  This is unfortunate, because it really discourages you from playing again.  So, although it's addictive, it's really only good for pick up and play gaming.
That said, the sound quality and gameplay this game offers is extremely high, just try the "Test" level on the main menu (which is a Portal reference) and you'll see what I mean.  But, while we're on that topic, the menus are needlessly complex and quirky. When you click on an item, a dot crosses the screen and you have to bounce it off your pattle to enter that submenu.  It's eye rolling, but that's really the only complaint, besides the length of the levels, that I have.
Pros:
Addictive and fun gameplay
High sound quality
Good as far as rhythm games go
"Test" level is awesome
Cons:
Soundtrack and level design can get lengthy and repetitive
Stupid main menu design

Stanley sat at his desk, ready for another day of work.  He looked at his messages, and saw that his boss wanted a meeting about the new project in the company.  Specifically he wanted Stanley to find the test results of this new product.  So, Stanley opened his browser and set to work.
Stanley is often easily confused.  Like now, where he confused the word 'product' with 'game', and the words 'find the test results' and 'play'.  Stanley moved closer and closer to his monitor as he continued 'finding the test results' on this 'product'.
Stanley could swear he heard his boss walking behind his desk, looking over his shoulder, but when he turned around, no one was there.  Of course he could never realize that this was all in his head, and that if he only looked and listened more carefully, all would eventually be revealed.
Stanley continued playing.  What, you want me to say something more?  I don't think you deserve any more.  Seriously, Stanley, I spend all this time narrating for you, and do I get an ounce of respect, or a pat on the back, or a thank you donut?  No, I just get stuck sitting here, watching you play.  It would be seriously depressing if your stupid repetition were not so entertaining.
Stanley looked up from the screen momentarily.  "Did someone say 'stupid?'" he asked.  But when he heard no answer, not even me, even though I am here all the time watching him, the ungrateful little... oh, and there he is, playing the game again.
Stanley, I seriously think you need to start working now.  You understand that games like this are something you pay to play, right?  And that you need money to pay, right?  Money you earn by working?  Right.  So, let's go back to work, and earn some money, so we can buy and play this game.
Stanley continued ignoring the advise of his closest friends and coworkers.  Maybe because he had headphones that blocked everyone out.  Maybe because he kept ignoring the email alerts telling him to get back to work.  Maybe because no one pays attention to text on a screen in a game anymore.  Maybe, just maybe, because this game, and my voice for filling in and regally, royally, maybe even divinely, telling the story and making such an immersive experience, drew Stanley into a depth of play not unlike that other game, oh, what is it called... Globe of Glue?  Land of Colonialism? What, really?  World of Warcraft?  Oh, no.  Not that one.  Something more realistic.  Oh, what is it?  Does it involve babies and puppies?  Then maybe that.
What was that?  Stanley?
Oh right.
Stanley was fired later that day.  But all was well.  He used his severance pay to purchase the game.  I would say that everything went alright for him, but honestly, when is that ever the case?  It doesn't help that he doesn't call, or write, or even tweet to say how he is doing.

Early Access - For anyone still not familiar, it means you are buying a game that is not yet finished, but in at least playable state. You are supporting the development of hte game, reporting bugs, and ideas for new featuers or enhancements.
While neither complete nor perfect, what Novus Inceptio has so far is quite nice.
Story - Well, there's not really much at all at the moment in the game itself.... you wake up as a clone, get a tutorial on how to gather food, materials, and released into the world to survive and explore.
No idea why, what happened to the world, or why you have a little robot satelite following you acting as a backpack.
This is fairly common for survival/crafting games, but hopefully it gets explained a bit as development continues.
There are hints about future lore, a few ruined buildings to find...
Exploration - Good environment with a hand-crafted "island". . While it's mostly a "forest / grassland" environment, the variety of trees, brush, and varrying terrain levels make each major forested area not feel exactly the same.
Some parts feel too empty, with very little points of interest - but the developer has stated they will be adding more points of interest in future updates.
Unlike many games, you have an ability that lets you climb hills too steep to normally walk across, in a limited fashion.
This does not have a different animation, so you slowly "walk" up a steep cliff - but remember this is Early Access.
Controls - Overall functional, but sometimes laggy on inputs. UI is still under development, and sometimes if you click an item in Inventory window, the click "goes through" the window and clicks the item behind it. This has lead to me accidentally picking up an entire cabinent in my house, instead of a single branch in inventory.
Combat - Fairly simple, mostly functional. Hold Mouse 1 to attack, Mouse 2 to defend. If you time it right, you can easily defend against a monster's attack and take zero damage for a fight. With only 1 real weapon type (Sword/Dagger + Shield), and very simple "stand in place and hit every 1.5 seconds" enemy AI, each fight turns into a timed "click to earn Meat and Leather" minigame.... Not a bad system, but deperately needs some variety in monster AI and abilities. (Wolves jump back+lunge, or try to jump to one side, forcing you to reposition; Bears that stand up on back legs and can knock you down if you dont evade, etc.)
Early Access, so hoping this improves further down the line.
Crafting - I've actually been very impressed with the crafting system. A good variety of crafting types (Woodcutting, Stonemasonry for building housing, Leatherworking & Blacksmithing for weapons and armor, Tailoring for thread used in most everything and decorative flags/curtains. For most crafts, you have to make "usable materials" before just magically sticking things together. For example, carving a branch into a shaft, then a refined Handle + smelting ore into an ingot, then making it into a Blade + refining plant fibers into usable thread material to make Twine - Handle + Blade + Twine to make a Knife.
Leveling (The RPG element) - While you do not have an "experience bar" per se, every crafting action and statistic (Str/Vit, etc) has it's own individual skill level. The more you use actions tied to it, the more it levels up. Blacksmithing, Weaponsmithing, Metalurgy, Farming, Stonecutting, Fighting, Defensive Fighting.
As primary statistics increase, you get more health, or inventory carry weight, stamina, etc.
Building (aka, making your own House) - This is the biggest item that reminds me this is Early Access. While there is a "functional" building system, and I have built two moderate sized houses with it - the system needs some work. It's buggy, sometimes randomly resets your viewpoint, and some items do not connect well together. Torches or Lamps mounted on a wall "float" about 5 inches away from the wall they are connected to. If you start creating a brick pathway, and there is any sort of incline in the ground, your bricks will either "float" above or "sink" down into the ground. Grass and flowers will show through any sort of pathway you lay down.
Even with these complaints, i have generally enjoyed building each base, it just takes patience...
The developer has noted that the current building system will be re-worked, so i look forward to future changes.
Farming - Another system with planned future overhauls, but the existing version is fairly reasonable. You do not have to micro-manage plants to get a moderate crop. Lay down the seeds, give them some water, and walk away for a while. After a time, you can harvest. You can put more work into it for a larger harvest, but it's not required.
Developer - Why am I making a note about the developer when reviewing the game? For an Early Access title, it makes a huge difference. The developer actively reviews amd replies on the Steam forums for bug reports and suggestions. Since the major "New World" patch (v0.50), they have been releasing patches and enhancements on a reasonably fast basis.
Overall - 7 / 10. I think I paid $15 on a sale a while back, and feel like I got my money's worth.

This game provides such a wonderful single player experience. There are no objectives, no requirements, purely open ended sandbox. You don't even have to eat if you don't want to. Its like there is specifically nothing required to do. You could just load up the game and watch the environment. From a game perspective, this could be good or bad. Some players don't know how to react to a game with no clear cut goals, and they feel a lack of achievement. Others find that it is great, and can build, craft, fish, garden, or gather to their hearts content. If you don't enjoy playing in an environment with no expectations, find something else. If your dream game is to be wild and free, experimenting and learning at your own pace, creating and destroying as you see fit, then I highly recommend this game for you.

In a world culture saturated with violence and games of mass death and destruction, we've been starving for games of mass construction or production. The Farming Simulator series has delivered and satisfies the need.
With 2015, the ante has been raised and now you can choose to do forestry additional to or instead of, your normal farming grind. While the farming aspect of the game is largely autonomous with little micro-management, the forestry aspect is hands on entirely. You'll enjoy the variety of ways to make money, but you may not find the game challenging even on hard. The difficulty levels simply determine how long your grind is going to be.
If you're into machinery and would rather build up than tear down, this is the game for you.
That being said, as you start to master the game, you will also start to feel disappointed in Giants for their seemingly lack of vision in their game design. There is so much potential they seem to be missing and the DLCs are mostly redundant equipment. Nothing that really changes or enhances one's strategy. I don't know if it's the project leadership or the team's budget, but they publish a mediocre new release every two years.
It is exciting that 2015 ushered in the very popular forestry aspect we saw growing in the mods. It's sad that no DLCs were forestry oriented. Not even the new Gold Edition.
Not enough variety of missions, maps don't take fully advantage of available machines. No need for the more expensive equipment. Though, I do like that they implemented a horsepower measurement to match  implements with their proper tractors.
Hirelings are basically nobodys. They should have profiles with faces, skills, certifications. You should be able to hire and fire as you need them. Kinda like EuroTruck.
There needs to be more options to what you can do with your logs. If you have them processed for lumber, you should be able to get the lumber, and either sell it or use it to build something.
Though in a way, I do recommend this game to new people who at least have a mild interest in this genre, unless Giants pulls up their socks, some other gaming company is going to sneak up and deliver what the real farming simmers want in a farming sim game.

+1080p and several other graphical updates such as CSAA and better shadows using GeDoSaTo.
-Pacing is at a snails pace which I can forgive if the story is actually moving along. But chapters 2-10 (game has 13 chapters) can be summed up as such:

.
-Character motivation is pretty non exsistant for the most part so it's hard to know why characters do things when they do them.
-Story is filled with plot convenience. Example:

-You can only control one character in battle. If he/she dies it's game over. This is maybe the games worst sin, next to not being able to switch out characters during battle. The reason this is bad is because, well lets imagine this:
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
But wait, the game forces you to control the character with the least health.
Why doesn't the game let me switch control to the surviving members once the character I'm controlling dies?

Hunting quests, because you haven't been killing things the entire game or anything.

I was asked to write a honest review of this game. So here I am.
As usual I will start describing the gameplay/game feel. I was expecting a jrpg similiar to any other FF game I've played. Story, party, exploring the word, kinda linear but open world style of gameplay, turn-based battle system.
It's really hard to say if I'm happy with that. A lot of people are mad about the part when you get a really extended introduction part where you can't really adjust your gameplay and that really is annoying I have to admit. Game drags you through a lot of tutorials, some of them are helpful, other are completely redundant. This could've been done in a much simplier way, or via a seperate tutorial system. So be wary, you will not feel "freedom" for a lot of time.
Let's talk about the battle system/leveling system. It really is different from what I've seen. You're pretty much controlling the leader and the other guys in your party simply follow the AI schema. I'm not saying it's totally wrong since you can just control them with "Paradigms" (AI schemas?), but sometimes it's more of an annoyance. Normally if you wanted to heal a party member using a Cure spell you would just queue a command, choose a target. Here you kinda have to switch your paradigm so your party member actually behaves like a healer and not a damage dealer. He might also just not heal the party member you'd like to heal, which is kind of a problem. Keep in mind: being inefficient about this (letting one follower be a medic 100% of the time) will result in lower battle rating, which is quite crucial as the higher it is, the more of your Technical Points are regenerated (points used to use some special abilities). This enforces a lot of switching, and strategizing as characters may have different roles. You can also setup your own paradigms so that eg. 2 of your fighters will deal damage and 1 will heal, etc.
There's a minor issue with leveling I guess. The good ol' "you leveled up!" system was removed. Instead you get Crystarium Points (correct me if I'm wrong), which allow you to get more stats or new abilities. The character development is not linear so you don't get a warning "hey, you can unlock this!", and sometimes checking your Crystarium page so often might be a good (and annoying) idea.
The story is a story, it's quite hard to follow, but unveils after a while and you really get the feeling of immersion, which is... good? I mean, usually at the beginning of Final Fantasy games you don't really know what's going on, and then you find out. I think the game is ok in that departament. Some moments and dialogues are pretty cheesy, but well whatever, it's a Final Fantasy game. If you're an anime fan you will be wondering "what the ♥♥♥♥ is he talking about, it's perfectly ok", provided that you play through the game of course.
Time to talk about the audio/visual stuff. I will also talk about the PC port here.
Music and voice acting are good. Audio fits the atmosphere/area, it's dynamic or slow and calm when it needs to (dialogues/drama/battle). Nothing to worry about here. As mentioned before some of the voice lines are cheesy but it's not like it ruins the game for you.
As for the visuals I'll be honest with you: it doesn't really seem that bad to me, though I understand people's concerns about game being run in 720p out of the box (there are some fixes I believe). The areas are very detailed, there's a lot of variety regarding enemies/allies. It's all beautiful. I'm running the game on my laptop and all I was worried about is the performance. I was shocked when I found out THERE ARE NO VIDEO PREFERENCES.
Quick rant about the port here: Well I've played older FF games, DMC3, and many other games just butchered by Japanese devs (talking about ports here). This is no different, I could be mad, but I'm not anymore after these years. Game will close if you press ESC (as in quit do desktop without asking). There are no video settings as mentioned before. There's a lot of checkpoints/savepoints in game though so at least you won't be losing much of progress if you accidently quit the game. Also you pause the game with 0 key. Yea, to skip the cutscene you've already seen you need to press 0 on your keyboard, then 1 on your keyboard. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ were they high?
After all playing the game feels good. It's certainly no GOTY. It's just... good. I would rate it at 7.5/10, maybe even higher. It's not exactly addictive but you don't quit the game raging after a while, it's totally playable and considering the low price I'd recommend it even more, if you just love the FF beautiful stories, turn-based system games. Well actually, if you don't have a console this is most probably your best bet when it comes to jrpgs (or other FF games released for PC). It's so much better than Last Remnant, that's for sure.

Pac-Man Championship and its DX sequel set the standard on how classic 80's arcade games should be remade.  Q*Bert: Rebooted unfortunately misses that mark by a wide margin.
Q*Bert: Rebooted comes with two modes: Q*Bert: Classic, which is an emulation of the original arcade game, and Q*Bert: Rebooted, which is an enhanced remake of the original.  Rebooted gameplay is similar to the original, except movement can made in six different directions instead of four, making it much easier to evade enemies.  Along with a couple new enemies and the omission of Ugg and Wrong Way, the difficulty progression is very slight and very repetitive, as the same five maps are used in the progression track.  It gets only somewhat difficult near the end of the game, and when you do finish the last level, it bugs out and does not go to either an ending or credit scene.
Q*Bert: Classic is still the better game, but this emulation is quite bad.  The controls are not very responsive.  The sound effects for Ugg and Wrong Way are missing. The behaviors of Sam and Slick are also incorrect.  They do not reverse the color changes that Q*Bert makes; instead they actually help Q*Bert by changing cubes to the target color.
Q*Bert: Rebooted is recommended for arcade game nostalgics who don't care about quality or accuracy in their games.  You are better off finding a Q*Bert ROM to play on an arcade emulator.

Civ Beyond Earth
If you are new to Civ, theres no doubt in my mind that you'll enjoy this game. For experienced players who have had played previous Civ games you'll find that Civ Beyond Earth is like Civ 5 but it forces you to think differnetly. Civilization Beyond Earth uses a Affinity system as a specialization of sorts for your Civ so not one Civ has an advantage over the other. Long story short, there are no intances of any civ being OP.
In previous Civ games a linear tech progression system was key to success. IF you have nukes before everyone else thats good, right? In Beyond Earth, the Tech web forces you to throw that out the window because there is no such thing as a Technologically advanced Civ in a Future Setting. The AI does need improvement however the the subtle changes they go through as the game progresses was nice. For instance as you progress through the game and one of your opponents chooses a majority in a certain affinity that leader starts to look like how that affinity presents and it ideas. Unlike Civ 5 cities are not instant, instead outposts are created and over a period of time they become cities. The difficulty has been dumbed down a bit. Normal (Mercury) difficulty is similar to cheiftain or warlord in Civ 5. A hint for anyone wanting that perfect difficulty setting, try Vostok or Gemini. The pre-start game choices was also a nice implement letting players actually choose what they start out with(while this is limited you can bet there'll be more choices in future DLC) instead of no choice and no clear advantage over anyone else early on like in previous games. Last but not least the Aliens. The Aliens do not behave like the Barbarians in Civ 5 but instead like creatures. Leave them alone and they'll leave you alone however as the difficulty progresses they become more and more hostile to the point where you cant let anything out of your territory without a military escort. Also unlike Barbarians the aliens do not progress in tech over time(thank goodness because a laser toting siege worm would be terrifying) instead you have different types of aliens you encounter, one being the siege worm that can and will kill you if you aggrovate it enough.
Long story short Beyond Earth is a game of Great potential that has its shortcomings but with no doubt they'll be fixed with time. Is it worth the buy? Yes.

Tempest:
~~~~~~~
Being a pirate can have its ups and downs, you know! For you it will start on the 26th October 1743 when you lose your ship “The Genriett” to a brutal and mysterious creature after an epic sea battle. Doesn’t sound like you and your crew will start on a high, but deep down you know that your faithful friends are still alive somewhere close by. After all, they are strong as a rock and light as a feather (better to be a feather than a rock if you have to swim ashore).

Tempest is an action/RPG game set in the charming Pirate era, where you take control of a ship and its crew. You will explore the sea and battle with or against pirates and other factions (9 in total). Gather as many goods and gold as you can because your journey will not be easy, and you will not be without a scratch to you.
Reach ports and you will be able to repair your ship in case you could not dodge effectively those small projectiles named “Cannonballs”, “Bar shots”, “Shrapnel’s”, “Mortars” and others. Buy well-needed medicines for your wounded crew, ammunition, hire new pirate to your crew or even give them a bit of training (you need experience points which you earn in battle) so they can be a little bit more efficient during battle. Upgrade your vessel hull (can’t upgrade everywhere though) or add an artefact to it but first you have to earn it in battle. Another aspect I really like is the customisation of your boat, add signs on your sails and flags, defence structure, skull and others on your bow… Fabulous, I reckon I was a pirate in my previous life.
Movements in battle are really simple, you just use WASD on your keyboard. W and S are for the speed of your ship: you can choose to have your sail fully open (100%), half open (50%) or just stand still and get probably get hammered! A and D will be the keys to steer your boat either left or right.  You will be able to choose the precision of your shots, but it will take you longer to reload your cannon. If you prefer to get 80% chance of hitting your enemies it will take you 4.9 seconds to reload against 2.2 seconds if you choose 30% chance of hitting your target. Sometimes, it is only a couple of seconds that determine success or defeat. The targeting system is like a V on each side of your ship. The point of the V will be on each side of your ship and that will give you the angle of your firing range. Keep your enemies in sight within the V and all you have to do is fire your cannons. The closer you are from your enemies, the better chance to hit them hard! Oh.. I nearly forgot, you might even encounter interesting sea creatures like the “Mighty Kraken” or other small sea beasts.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	Good and easy combat system
-	Good ship customisation
-	Good  management content in port (trading, hiring, etc)
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Don’t have an option to start a new game. You will have reset and exit the game.
-	No achievement / Trading cards (early access)
Well, I am very impressed with this game so far. I truly can’t wait to see the final version! This game is a jewel in the making!
8.9/10

As a gamer who was around to play this game when it first hit arcades in the 80's, I was expecting Q*bert Rebooted to be a fun, modern take on the original. How wrong I was.
The problems begin with the classic version. Why they didn't just emulate the original ROMs when they hold the rights to the game is bewildering. Instead what we're given is a poorly programmed mess of a port that gets many things wrong. Two-thirds of the sound effects are missing. Ugg and Wrong Way are completely silent, as are Slick and Sam, who also don't revert the colours on the cubes (and sometimes change the cubes to the RIGHT colour instead). No ditty plays when you collect the green ball that freezes the board. The game sometimes continues to move enemies after you've cleared a stage. The unused discs don't score any bonus points when you clear a level, instead of the 50 bonus points x level you should get.
As for the Rebooted part, it is one huge cluster as well. The hexagon pattern removes the difficulty and strategy of trying to clear the bottom corners of the level. Other than the resolution, nothing graphically stands out. The level music and the map music often play at the same time. Q*bert only has the one voice sample and it seems to play randomly instead of when he gets hit. The music is MIDI quality at best and elevator quality at worst.
Steer well clear of this reboot. Not even nostalgia goggles can protect you from this crummy game.

A great-looking, touchingly written and brilliantly executed take on the (terribly named) "walking simulator" genre, where you explore an environment to reveal a story-- admittedly, without much in the way of gameplay challenge. In this case, you are a subcontractor assigned to collect data from a space station that was recently hit by a terrible accident. So while you're waiting for those downloads to finish, why not poke around the few remaining scraps of surveillance video (presented in an augmented reality format that projects the past events all around you into the "real" 3D environment of the station) to learn a bit more about what happened?
All you really have to do to move the story forward is interact with the AR video of the right crew members at the right moments to extract a bit of extra data here and there about what they were looking at in their own "AR desktop" (and by extension, what they were thinking about) at each of those moments-- about 6-8 of these moments for each "act" of the story. But the characters are written so compellingly, and with such specific voices and stories, that you're naturally drawn to explore more of the ship and more of the crew's history, right down to inspecting various "insignificant" objects that nevertheless flesh out the world and make the core stories feel that much more real. Even as you follow the different crew members around trying to catch them at the right moment to extract their data, they weave in and out of conversations with each other, with themselves, and with the ship's AI that provide a fascinating portrait of each person's private life and public persona, and how those two aspects support, conflict with, and flow into one another as they deal with the crisis on the ship.
Of course, it's clear from early on that not everything is as it seems in this scenario. You may figure out some of what's going on before it's officially revealed, but there are definitely still some surprises in store for the shocking, thrilling ending. The game is over in less than 4 hours (unless you go for 100% achievements), but it's a really exciting and emotional ride through a brilliantly imagined future. Highly recommended.

The first 100 turns or so hooked me.  The next couple hundred made me wish I could relive the first 100.  Becomes grindy and repetitive due to simplification and stripping down the Civ formula, especially if your a vet of Civ5 w/expansions.
Brief +/- based on my playthrough
+ The aliens.  In the beginning they're tough customers.  Honeymoon ends early...
+ Great art style from units to cities to map
+ The tech tree/map takes some getting use to but is interesting, but...
+ The three affinities, but...
- - Civilization "Health".  Mine was beyond -100 for the last 60 turns and it didn't hinder my ability to continue on.  Maybe, someday I'll go back and learn more...maybe.
- ...how the three affinities are unlocked in the tech tree actually take away from replayability.  You're going to want to     go all in with any one of the three affinities to unlock their full potential thus limiting the paths you take for each tech/affinity.
- ZERO improvemnets on Diplomacy and AI (my biggest Civ gripe)
- Legacy performance issues.
- The aliens.  Once you start teching up you'll start to see how one dimensional they are.  I was really intrigued initially to see what part they'd play in the long run, unfortunately they become little green barbarians.
- Unit levelups totally underwhelming.  One option only: +% to ranged/melee strength.  Really lame.
- City interface bare bones.  (why are building, construction, details all default "off"?)
- Mini map is way too small
- No map overlay toggle like CIV5 so I can add resource icons to the map?
- No great people
- Wonders.  They don't provide a large bonus, but they're also not difficult to build.  Not very "wonderful".
Overall, it feels like a WIP total conversion Civ5 mod.  A missed opportunity as the mid-late game really just feels like a feature-trimmed Civ5 with a graphics and names swap.  At best, this should have been a $15 mini expansion to Civ5.  Very disappointing.

Tempest is a lovingly-crafted, charming addition to the insufficiently-populated
genre. At the time of writing, some aspects are more polished than others, but there's some solid buccaneering to be had, with the potential to be a real gem upon final release.
Your adventure begins in a second-rate vessel, your prized ship having been destroyed by a monstrous sea creature. This is a fitting way to begin because it stokes your anticipation of the ship upgrades to come and hints at some glorious kracken-cracking retribution (I hope). Gameplay is essentially split into 3 distinctly different, but complimentary forms:
The overall presentation really stands out as a stylish, extremely well crafted piece of work that oozes a dark, yet jolly "piratey" atmosphere. Text is presented on dark canvas backgrounds, adornments are used to emphazise the era and super-slick overlays slide and pop in and out of view. It all blends together very well and if this level of polish can be extended to the rest of the game, it would amount to something very special.
The 3D battlefields have a unique look to them. Moonlight bounces a wonderful glow across the ebbing and crashing waves, natrual rock formations and towns offer really nice backdrops for the action and some scenery (i.e said rocks) are not super-smoothed, but every-so-slightly rough around the edges, which for my tastes is perfectly befitting of the theme and enhances the appeal of the presentation.
The customization, upgrading and crew leveling looks really promising. A good deal of cosmetic choices can be made from the beginning, with gems and weapons hopefully opening up more interesting options later on.
At the time of writing, I feel that the steep learning curve and punishing difficulty needs a lot of attention. You are simply dumped into the deep end without any idea of the controls or what any of the icons do. It's not very intuitive, but you will figure out the icons soon enough. Help with controls either pops up after you've figured it out yourself or disappeared before you can assimilate it. I'm still confused about the controls and how to line up an effective barrage of cannon fire. I almost always run out of cannon balls or health before the battle is over.
If you lose a battle, your gold and resources take a huge hit. Once or twice is enough to leave you in a situation where you cannot afford any repairs or ammunition. As far as I can figure, your only option at that point is to start the whole game again, as neither manual saves or multiple profiles are currently supported.
Worth mentioning is that the game is very well optimized already and looks really nice even on older machines.
I feel that Tempest will one day mature into a unqiue priate game with a ton of charm, so I'd recommend keeping your good eye on this as it develops.

As of writing this review i've played the game for a little bit under a half hour and less than 30 levels in, and I'm absolutely in love with it.
This game has an incredibly simple premise and so far it executes it exceedingly well. You're a white square that leaves trails of paint on an invisible world wherever you touch, and when you die or do an air jump paint sprays all around to help you discover where you may need to go next. Its an incredibly simple yet genius mechanic. The controls for getting around, doing jumps and sliding down walls feel very tight, very much like super meat boy (which I bet this game took a lot of inspiration from). Any mistakes I made felt like they were entirely my fault, not the game's.
The game doesn't penalize you much at all for dying, you just start at the beginning of the level (each one of which is not very large at all). In fact, dying is most likely required in order to reveal new areas of the level you can't see or reach from where you may happen to be. The paint trails you leave are all of the colors of the rainbow, which means when you've revealed most of the level it's a beautiful splash of color contrasted against the dark purple background.
The game reveals new mechanics at a very nice pace too. You are able to get the hang of basic movement before you encounter enemies, and other elements like spikes and moving platforms/walls are also introduced at a very good pace. I can't wait to see what else is in store as I make it farther in.
The music is amazing too, it sets and complements the mood of the game perfectly. If you like downtempo electronic music you'll love playing the game just to listen to the soundtrack. The calmness of the music may help temper any frustrations you encounter on a particularly hard level as well. It really ties together the entire experience into a well-executed, beautiful aesthetic.
The last thing so far that I love about the game is the "hidden" heart tokens you can collect in some levels. I encountered one early on by accident when a splash of paint revealed it and I had to go back to make sure I didn't miss any any time I discovered a new one but died or finished the level without grabbing it. As far as I can tell they're optional (I have 8 so far, no idea if they unlock anything yet) but finding them and collecting them is another nice challenge, often involving some more difficult platforming maneuvers but they're very rewarding to find. It's also fun if you discover them entirely by accident like I did once or twice.
In short, you need this game if you like platformers like super meat boy. It doesn't feel nearly as punishing so far, so if you get intimidated by those harder platforms, this one is still worth a shot (even when it isn't on sale, which is still an absolute steal).

I feel like when reviewing games, especially Early Access ones, I have to think "hey this game is new, so I shouldn't expect much?"
Wrong!
If a game is developed enough to arrive on steam, they should have enough of a base to draw in MORE customers based on how great it IS and can BECOME. But loads of early access games come out and loads of them are garbage, not all. But a fair amount. I think the game should have better textures, it should also really feel like a sandbox. It to me feels like a "free" singleplayer game, I have freedom to do what I wish, but the game for now just makes it seem like I am doing something apart of a linear storyline. I hate that, esp in a game where freedom is a must have. I believe the game can be improved but as it just came out on steam a week ago, it isn't worth it for now.
Some people may hate me for this review, or just refuse to read all of this and give me a thumbs down, but the thing is. If a game has been in development long enough to be considered worthy of SAIL, then it should have much more to offer instead of going on steam to pick up little speed, then they use some of the cash to make the game better over a course of 2 years, and then later have the game die and be horrible. This happens all the time with steam games, and people should wait before releasing their games to die so fast.
That being said...
- PROS -
Combat - as it is still early, there can be a lot more, however they seem to have many tools a ship would need with a week of release time.
Maps - As promised there will be more maps, or at least an upscale.
Multiplayer - Something intended to be added later I assume based on what I read before purchase. I think it would be and interesting feature. Not sure how it would work but then again I am not the devs.
----------------
- CONS -
Lack of freedom - Currently as I said, I just feel like a man with a ship, and there is some story I am not being told I am partaking in.
UI -  I am not a huge fan of the interface, it seems slightly clunky.
Ship "Upgrades" - Really more customization, I am not immpressed with having FREE stuff to start out with on my ship, I like to earn it, and if I have freedom to do what I wish, I should be well able to start slow, and pick up speed with customization options. That being said, I also don't really enjoy the accessories your ship can have, like the side add-ons. Spikes, Guardes, etc.
Graphics - As stated before, the graphics aren't too great, the water looks amazing but when you zoom in to dry land when talking to someone on a quest, it is horribly blobby and blurry. I am sure this could be adjusted early on but not too sure how they want to take a stab at it.
I would say after all this I would pay 5 dollars for the game. But at 10. Nah.

- Supports content creating among the community

There are some cons, which are to be ignored for the review, because they are not related to the quality of the game but I thought I'd mention them anyways, please dont get rejected by them:
- not enough people are playing for a multiplayer shooter
- servers are empty very often, clicking on the "quick match" option results in joining an empty server

conclusion:
It is a fun, entertaining and refreshing game. Content is constantly flowing into the game, so there is no repetetive maps or gameplay, but the controls are not as responsive as they could be.
Overall I do recommend this game, because a larger community will help to improve the game to a point where I have nothing to complain about anymore.

Final Fantasy has been around for a while, but this is the Final Fantasy game that introduced me into the series. In my opinion, Final Fantasy XIII is an incredibly
game. From the storyline to the dynamic characters, from the picturesque settings to the beautifully orchestrated music, this game is an easy favorite for me. As a fan of RPGs, I've never really tried a "JRPG" before, but Final Fantasy XIII has shown me a new sub-genre of gaming to love.
Only one thing I found that slightly irked me about the game is the post-game or end-game Gil (the in-game currency) and item farming to get the coveted 100% completion. It can become mundane, but I've been able to push myself through. Another common complaint I've seen online is people are upset this PC remake of the PS3/XBOX 360 doesn't use 1080p but 720p for the graphics. Personally, I don't find it a concern big enough to
buy the game. Could it look more polished up, sure, but what couldn't? It still plays well and looks stunning.
One of my favorite things about this game is the fact that it's incredibly easy to get the hang of battling monster (which is the main game-play mechanic). As you progress, combating enemies goes from something easy-breezy to moderately challenging to downright complex. The game does an incredible job though of introducing each new character, skill, ability, and game-play mechanic in a timely fashion which makes it easy to adapt to. Some battles will literally last you six seconds while others can have a "target time" of 30 or more.
The characters are another thing I fell in love with for this game. The cutscenes that develop the plot further with well-spoken dialogue and an amazing array of people. Along the journey of Final Fantasy XIII you'll meet people ranging from the stoic "Lightning" Farron to the overly optimistic Oerba dia Vanille. It's an incredible array or personalities that collide due to fate, and how they interact is beautifully done.
In summary, Final Fantasy XIII is a wonderful game. It offers a challenging game-play with easy-to-use controls, scenic locations, all wrapped up with an amazing storyline.

Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth is the latest installment of this popular long running series.  Now after a few games in this highly addictive turn based game I feel comfortable writing this review.  So a lot of chattering about this game is its going to a predecessor to one of my favorite Sid Meier's game of all time Alpha Centauri and probably my first 4x strategy game.  The other chatter was all about how this is just a new skinned Civilization 5 and how its just Civilization in space.  They both couldn't have more wrong in my opinion.  This game is definitely no SMAC (Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri)  and other then the hexagon squares is all the feel I get about Civilization 5 even though they used the same engine used for Civilization 5.  This truly is a stand alone game I look forward to the DLC's as they get released because the game does seem lacking in some a few areas and I'm hoping for more substance more of the just one more turn mentality many of us Civ fans want and have that holy schnikes its 4am moment all of Civ fans desire and experience only so well and often more then we would like to.  Alright the game introduces some new mechanics the affinity tree similar to the ideologies in Civilization 5 but at the same time completely different.  Love the concept of this but its one of the area's lacking wish it had substance the three affinities are harmony living in peace with the planet and adapting to the planet in contrast to the purity affinity.  Purity is all about the desire to keep/preserve the human race and save the people of earth.  Then there is  the Supremacy the ideology behind this is all about technological advancement and liberating the people of earth.  Each one affinity affects how your game plays out and how your civilization looks and feels even  how the cities grow and the appearance they take.  But there is no way to truly combine them they even affect the upgraded soldiers, tanks, and advanced military units later in the game.  Would like to make a side note saying one of these late game military units looks (stolen) from Stargate SG-1 and is a Replicator in appearance .  Also the technology tree has a distinct feel like that was stolen as well the layout and colors are eerily similar to another 4x strategy game Endless Space.  Also the technology tree is confusing and no easy way to navigate it it basically it starts in the middle of a circle and branches out in all directions.  Then each tech  has main tech then two below it then it branches out again very confusing  but you don't have to research it all.  Should of just been a spider web all the way if that was the idea but then you could really tell the idea was stolen from Endless Space in my opinion.  Now the Virtues seems from culture seem really secondary with all the emphasis on the affinity branches.  All though really useful as you advance your civilization.  Also there are four virtue trees (culture) military, growth, science, and money (energy in the game).  Now they want you to pick one and follow the three with bonuses going down the columns but also to branch out with bonuses on the row but are most costly because you need to advance across all branches  to achieve those bonuses instead of straight down a row so choose wisely.  Now these three combined affinity, research, and culture add a very distinct feel of play not seen in any of the Sid Meier's Civilization games before if you ask me.  That is why I recommend this game and say its not a successor to SMAC or Civilization 5 in space.  To many it was truly astonishing how many people want SMAC to return and how many people hate a new Civilization coming out (this always happens remember the loud cry from Civilization 4 to Civilization 5) We have to admire a game that in six franchise releases still has so many die hard fans for each one.  And for Sid Meier his idea that brought us 4x turn based strategy games on such a monolithic scale.  This game has its flaws instead of creating such a vivid intro video they should of spent more time on the game and design of units and affinity tree because I would be surprised if they say it turned out like they envisioned.  Now one of one of the more interesting features is the quest the game assigns to you. For affinity points, production, tech points, food, and all the other aspects in the game.  Really a nice feature gives you something to try to achieve why playing other then the end game of winning.  Also the planets are rich with alien life that is passive aggressive but levels with you as you play unlike the barbarians in Civilization 5.  These aliens get other creatures/units on the map as the turns progress also they are hostile if you attack and hostile if you don't  but will leave you alone if you can work it.  So what else is there about this newest installment I haven't covered .  The characters there are are only eight playable factions from all over the world and don't belong to just one nation which is an interesting idea.  Because honestly this is the first Civilization game that is in the future not using historical characters.  They do seem a little lackluster and I would like to see my own faction character as they progress down the affinities.  And they don't seem to have set traits/affinities they go down just seem to do the opposite of there neighbor but I’m not 100% sure on this one yet.  Sometimes they get along sometimes they don't.  Also the spying in the game gives you more options which is a warmly welcome.  Need to setup a spy network in the designated city, and steal tech, science, maybe search for defectors, or drop a dirty bomb to name a few of the choices in the covert actions you can perform and maybe get a quest in to entertain you why spying.  But this is such an impressive game and can't be reviewed completely to do it justice.  Like any game and new installment it has its pros/cons but I would recommend buying and trying it out.  If you are a SMAC fan it will want you wanting more like colonizing on water creating your own units and the videos for your advancing tech  nothing will be SMAC till they release SMAC 2 no matter how much the developers try or say its the spiritual successor to SMAC that’s a marketing ploy that got me and its not even close to SMAC once you play.  This is also not Civilization in space for one it's (going obvious) on a alien planet not in space.  Its just a futuristic Sid Meier's Civilization game.  So if your a 4x lover and/or a Civilization fan GET THE GAME.  Cause you know you will eventually anyways.

Amazing Game.  Want details why?  Well, its best experienced by playing the game, but I will give it a shot.  Here are my top eight reasons (Not nessisarily in order):
1:  Its not Alpha Centauri.  Its not Civ V with Alien face paint.  Its much more, and much better.  I don't want a carbon copy game, I want something new.  Something interesting.  Civ BE delivers.
2:  Tech Web.  No more do we have to research every damn thing to progress.  Now, we progress technology as we want, not as we are told.  You want to focus in just one area?  Go ahead!  You want to go everywhere?  Go ahead!   You think one technology is useless and want to avoid it till a later date when you can get it quickly?  Sure!  The Tech Web itself is an unspoken method of customization and choice.
3:  Affinities:  They make sense, give you various unit customization, and offers an RPG element if you want it, or just a way to determine how you want to play the game if you don't.  You can use any tactic with any affinity, but some do work better with certain affinities and upgrades.  Plus, the way it changes your units in game is actually interesting and unique.
4:  Unit Upgrades are much better.  You have a wider variety of upgrades in total, even if there are less upgrade choices each time you upgrade.  Also, certain Affinity based upgrades are very theme accurate and are different from what we have seen in the past.  Also, the upgrades physically change the units in ways that were both asteticly appeasing and fit my inner Nerd/your chosen affinity.
5:  Wonders are powerful, but not game changing.  Some have very useful abilities, yet don't break the game.  Granted, maybe some swing on the underpowered side, but overall its balanced.  And if you are smart, you can still use wonders into your stratagies.
6:  Aliens are not Barbarians.  They are more dangerous.  More deadly.  And more interesting.  They will defend their homes from the human invasion, destroy your trade routes (without the right tech quest upgrade), and screw with your people, especially if you aggro them.  YOu can pass off with a peaceful existence though, provided a siege worm doesn't nest next to your city.  But overall, much better then those bland auto aggroed barbarians we are used to.
7:  Starting Customization is much better.  More options, and instead of having it all set you can mix and match different starting options for your own playstyle.  Plus, it lets you play whatever faction you want without worrying if its starting ability sucks as much.
8:  Victories:  Now, this is important, because it adds so much difficulty to this.  The AI players can and will go for WCs.  They will build the Emancipation Gate, the Mind Flower, the Contact Beacon, ect.  And if they see you getting close to Victory, expect an all out assault and be ready to defend yourself.  Because they will bring a force to take your capital, and everything else.

This is more about great story-telling than exciting gameplay. This gem combines solid environment design, an interesting near-future world that is relatable and a bit disturbing, top-notch voice acting, and the best elements of storytelling derived from classic games. For example, backstory is often revealed in games like System Shock2, when you watch ghosts loop through moments of their lives before they became the corpses you see on the floor. Tacoma blends Augmented Reality recordings in just this way, layering everyone's perspectives in the storytelling to let you uncover a compelling mystery. A gaming experience like this doesn't have to be extremely original, or even long to get my thumbs up. It just has to be well done. Tacoma is very well done, indeed.

TLDR: INK is a very unique platformer that is worth playing. It is rather short and not very difficult so expirenced platformers beat it in around 3 hours. 8/10.
First off, the whole charm of INK is the unique mechanic of painting the level as you play. If that does not intrest you do not buy it looking for another Super Meat Boy.
Painting the levels as you play is a lot of fun and looks incredible with colorful paint dashing the level's surfaces. I found the graphics to be very well done. The painting also adds a new unique stage of each level's progression as you go from revealing the level -> dying while learning the timing -> perfecting it.
The level design is well done with fresh level design ideas being cycled constantly. Every 10 levels or so a new level mechanic is introduced such a projectiles then tracking projectiles etc.
I found the difficulty curve to be okay, with two exceptions of easy levels towards the end. I really enjoyed the second boss but I felt like final boss level could have used the painting mechanic more since the whole game is based around it instead of being a platforming challenge. An example of this would be something like moving platforms where the boss erases the paint periodically.
This is a short game, but I found it to be just the correct length. I think any longer and the painting mechanic, while unique, would have gotten stale. It also doesn't have any boring or uninteresting levels so I think the devs cut a lot of the bad levels out which is a huge plus for me. The game doesn't waste your time with filler levels.
The soundtrack to INK is fantastic.  I felt it fits right in with the creativeness and uniqueness of the game and I never noticed any annoying repetition.
The only real negative I found with INK is the 30 fps engine cap.  Unfortunately the devs said this is an engine problem so it would not be easily fixed. I barely noticed the 30 fps cap during gameplay and only realized that I had a cap when reading the steam forums after completing the game.  The 30 fps cap does not hinder gameplay much at all.
Overall, I really enjoyed INK and recommend it. 8/10

Tacoma might be the first game which truly captures a great blend of storytelling through gameplay. You are on a desolate space station on a mission to retrieve the AI of the ship and as you go about your business you get to see how the events on the ship played out. There are some minor puzzle solving elements with you interacting with the objects left behind by the crew during their time on board. The way you go about getting relevant information is incredibly engrossing as you get to act as a sentient observer to events recorded by the ship's AI in a 3-D space.
The core mechanic is not completely novel (the first example which comes to mind is the crime scene mechanics in Batman Arkham Origins) but the developers' take on this mechanic feels very intuitive and futuristic. It feels like using AR to scrub videos that play out in 3-D space which isn't just confined to a small rectangular patch in the room. It isn't even confined to one or two characters at a time. You see how events unfold as characters split off and interact in seperate ways and it gives a real glimpse into how people really interact with and without the pressures of group dynamics.
The game is a strong character study of a cast of well fleshed out characters in a setting that portrays a futuristic setting in a very grounded manner. There's strong themes of family, seperation and the tricky nature of human relationships. The difficulty in forming those bonds and then maintaining them are touched upon throughout the character moments. The fancy tech that is involved is just treated as something which is normal in that particular world with the main focus being on the characters' actions and reactions to a traumatic event that the game bases itself on.
The world outside the space station is well realized in a subtle manner. You can piece together the state of the world through information gleaned off of ID cards, conversations, pictures and even a crossword puzzle (which feels like an incredibly creative way to give out information without it being in the form of exposition). One thing which I would deem as a negative is that it feels too contrived that the ship's AI has a strong majority of the recordings of only the bits relevant to the crew's reactions and motivations to the event which sets of the game and I would have liked some more pieces of interaction between characters which is not related to any station related work. It is present but I feel like there could have been more of it.
The voice acting is great and the lack of a musical score for the most part fits with the isolation felt in this setting but some ambient music to set the mood during particular scenes could have elevated the overall experience.
I understand that this genre of games isn't for everyone, but if you are looking for a more involved "walking sim" then I would highly recommend Tacoma.

I find myself sitting down wanting to play a game of Civ: BE, but deciding not to because I think it'll play out exactly the same way as my last few games: a bland time countdown victory quest and a little "you won!" popup. Frankly, Civ BE's endgames are boring to play, and further undermined by not being very interesting in general.
It pains me to say this because overall, Civ: BE is so damn cool. It has the seeds of everything I and others have ever wanted from a contemporary Sci-Fi Civ. The super powerful abilities/upgrades/buildings, the intriguing aliens and resources, and general feeling of optimism and discovery makes for a super appealing game environment. While promising, the game we have today is disappointing, with poor replay value. It's fun to play and look at, yet deeply unrewarding.
Most of the flaws in the actual game have been well described by other reviews -- the mechanics that have been added to (what is more or less) Civ V are at best shallow, and at worst broken and cheesy. Affinities are undifferentiated score-based research paths rather than defining philosophical differences. Trade is *extremely* overpowered but amounts to boring micromanagement. Quests are repetitive interruptions that don't vary much per game, and the storytelling is rather bland. The orbital layer seems very cool, but after playing with it a while, it tends to just amount to another repetitive micro situation, combined with the fact that it's annoyingly difficult to shoot down other satelites (which creates the incentive for everyone to spam cheap sats -- you'll never be able to actually fit in that planet carver usefully). Add in the standard Civ V issues (abuseable AI, weird diplomacy) and even the wins feel kind of hollow.
I did have some fun "un-terraforming" the planet as Harmony affinity for a while (since the miasma becomes a buff rather than a penalty), but the orbital layer is cumbersome and the AIs didn't do anything intelligent about it.
Overall, the biggest flaw IMHO is that the endgame is dominated by research / planetary wonder quests, and there is very little I've been able to do to stop one of the 5 other players from completing these if they're decently underway. Because of this, you have to rush the science win every time (and sometimes due to random chance you'll get a really unbalanced early quest win off the bat) and then build your military.  My typical game ending is a time-countdown win with little interaction with half the civs, or a loss on the other side of the planet that I can't do anything about. It makes the whole thing feel rather inconsequential.
Perhaps in 6 months this game will live up to the promise it deserved, but for now, I wish I had my hours and excitement back.

At first glance it might be a good game, and it is. Unlike most games of the genre (that I know of), this game has a plot, and a new system which is basically you use items from one stage to complete another. It adds more playtime because you'll be wondering where should you use the items. Also, there's voice-acting, but that's just about it. The plot and voice-acting was overall mediocre, though that isn't the main problem. The main problem, and perhaps the biggest reason this game isn't good, is that you can't lose. There's no time limit in your search for hidden items. Yes there's a penalty for continuously clicking incorrectly, but it's not a game over/ restart/ something horrible. The screen just cracks for a while, and then you can resume your search again. The hints and helps are also unlimited, e.g. in a single stage you can just click on the hints and after waiting for a while, click on it again. Rinse and repeat for an easy way of clearing the game. Where's the fun in that? Overall it's not a very satisfying game. You can just ignore the helps, but with unlimited time it's just a matter of time before you grow bored and clicked on the helps. Recommended for those who doesn't want to lose in a video game, otherwise, stay clear.

TL; DR:
If you enjoy crafting/survival/sandbox gameplay with a unique crafting system and level system, and want to help influence a potentially great game, then please support the developers. If not, don’t even look at early access games.
Early Access Review: Single Player Only:
Despite the mixed reviews, I feel this is actually a quite enjoyable game in its current state.
With other 56 hours in game, I’ve built a lot and seen a lot. Made it to gen 8, will have to get back in and make it to gen 10 for the achievement.
There is a lot to do and explore, some of it takes a bit of actual thinking to figure out. And some things aren’t as obvious as others, but that might be why I enjoyed it so much.
Figuring things out on my own has always made a game feel more satisfying when you finally manage to build something that you have been trying to figure out how to construct for a while. As time goes on, it seems people are expecting more and more to be taught exactly how everything should work, and what they can do, and how to do it. If it doesn’t clearly explain that, then they feel it’s terrible.
There is so much potential for this game.
Yes there are bugs, yes there is a lack of content and really a lack of story of what is even going on.
But the Developers are working away at releasing new content and bug fixes.
So if you want a perfect, bug free, content and feature rich game with an amazing story and phenomenal graphics and audio, then you shouldn’t be looking at any Early Access Game.
These reviews should be to let others know what you think about the current state, is it even playable? Is there more than just running in a small field and building two items? Are the devs actively updating the game? Adding new content? Interested in the community feedback?
I think the ones who give a negative review because "swing and a miss" or "Honestly, waste of time" should be stealized.
Your pointless negative review leaves a permanent impression on a game that is constantly being developed.  I’m not talking about the ones who have (at the time) valid gripes, or ones who update their review the next time a patch is released.
Don’t support an early access game because you expect a polished top notch game, support an early access game because you think the game has potential, and want to show the developers that you want them to continue to make it better.
And if you really feel that the hours they have put into building the game, were a waste of time, then please by all means, I would love to see the game you develop, I mean with the expectations you have, it must have be a true GOTY and I’d love to criticize...I mean review it.

Final Fantasy has been around for a while, but this is the Final Fantasy game that introduced me into the series. In my opinion, Final Fantasy XIII is an incredibly
game. From the storyline to the dynamic characters, from the picturesque settings to the beautifully orchestrated music, this game is an easy favorite for me. As a fan of RPGs, I've never really tried a "JRPG" before, but Final Fantasy XIII has shown me a new sub-genre of gaming to love.
Only one thing I found that slightly irked me about the game is the post-game or end-game Gil (the in-game currency) and item farming to get the coveted 100% completion. It can become mundane, but I've been able to push myself through. Another common complaint I've seen online is people are upset this PC remake of the PS3/XBOX 360 doesn't use 1080p but 720p for the graphics. Personally, I don't find it a concern big enough to
buy the game. Could it look more polished up, sure, but what couldn't? It still plays well and looks stunning.
One of my favorite things about this game is the fact that it's incredibly easy to get the hang of battling monster (which is the main game-play mechanic). As you progress, combating enemies goes from something easy-breezy to moderately challenging to downright complex. The game does an incredible job though of introducing each new character, skill, ability, and game-play mechanic in a timely fashion which makes it easy to adapt to. Some battles will literally last you six seconds while others can have a "target time" of 30 or more.
The characters are another thing I fell in love with for this game. The cutscenes that develop the plot further with well-spoken dialogue and an amazing array of people. Along the journey of Final Fantasy XIII you'll meet people ranging from the stoic "Lightning" Farron to the overly optimistic Oerba dia Vanille. This is probably my favorite game of all time. I never played a game more than this one and I will say why in this review.
Back in 2011 or 2012 I remember being bored and looking for new games to play since I was new to PC gaming and always played on Consoles before this. I remember coming across a YouTube video about Arma 2 realism shooting. I thought it was interesting since I grew up playing Halo and COD when I was a kid. I seen this was something new so I thought to give it a go. I came for the realism but stayed when I noticed a server called "Cherno life". I had no idea what it was but it sounded interesting.
--- My RP Experience ---
I load into the server and I see there are Cops and Civilians. I learned that day what a online RP game was like back then. It was the funniest thing I have ever seen. People playing as Cops and chasing people who would rob a bank or gas station or commit murder. Even things like speeding got you pulled over. I never seen anything like it and I just loved it. I remember one day I got tired of some people playing as Cops just doing stupid things like killing civs for no reason and it annoyed me but I was in luck. I came across a video that had "City Life RPG" as the title. It was a mod and the very first I went and downloaded. It had things like sports cars and even ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 1979 Honda Civics in the game and if you couldn't afford that than I guess you could test your luck on stealing a car but the cops could find out and you could be put in jail and that isn't fun.
There was just so much to do in that mod, you could grow drugs and run a business doing it. You could do the boring legal route to and sell olives which hardly made money but it wasn't illegal. Fishing and illegal fishing (shark hunting) was a thing and if you wanted to just be clean you could even become a cop which was hard as hell to do in this server. Robbing banks was even a choice but usually a stupid one unless you had snipers or were good at tricking the cops otherwise it wasn't worth it. It was pretty much GTA but with real people instead of A.I
I put at least 1000+ hours into that mod because it was so different and niche that it just appealed to me. I even met people on there who I still talk to today 5 years later. The mod just had one of the best communites ever and nothing comes close to it for me. Like I said in the beginning, I came for the realism side of the game but the RP side I accidently came across kept me playing it for a very long time.
--- DayZ Mod ---
When I started playing Arma 2, I remember there being 4 DayZ servers. They weren't that popular either but I tried it one day and I loved the idea and the game itself. It was something that has never been done back then. I remember this mod just blowing up and 4 servers became a 1000 in 2 months. Arma 2 went from a niche game with 4,000 people playing at most to one of the top PC games out there all thanks to this mod. Survival games have been changed forever because of the success of this mod that was made into a full standalone years later and is still one of the biggest Early Access titles in history. DayZ was fun with friends but after a few months of playing it and things like Overpoch, EPoch started coming out and all the hackers started joining it kind of going annoying. Combat logging was huge back then to which ruined the mod for me but in the beginning I think it was one of the best mods ever to release.
--- Realism Mods ---
Played some realism mods for a bit because that is what I was looking for in Arma 2 in the first place. Mods made it so fun to play and for awhile I enjoyed it. I did this for around 3 months and just got tired of the ego some people had. The community kind of ruined it for me but overall I still enjoyed it. Some of the best mods I have ever seen in a game like DayZ so this was nothing short of incredible.
I said this before and I will say it again. My favorite game of all time. One of the best communites (in some mods, DayZ was pretty bad after awhile.) and the best mods I have ever seen created in any game.
I would recommend this game in 2012 but not 2016. Its kind of dead these days because its such an old game. It might still be worth playing for DayZ mod though since this game goes on sell for as cheap as $2 sometimes. Otherwise just wait for a sell.

An unsure "Yes" with some hope.
Now, with about 14 hours of gameplay, it's time to tell community what I think of Civilization: Beyond Earth (BE).
In a phrase, a big disappointment, but with a healthy expectation. A triple-A title from triple-A producers and publishers, and, yet, an unpolished experience. Maybe it's human nature to expect past performance as future behaviour.
I felt the same thing when Civilization V went out. After dozens of hours on its predecessor, it was a underwhelming experience. After Gods and Kings and Brave New World, though, it was a prime experience that got 1/4th of all my gameplay hours last year. This is the base for my good feelings about this unfinished game.
When I have a new game on library, I wait friday, buy a bag of chips and some sodas and, after work, experience it. This time, I was out of chips and drinking the soda disappointed with the game that cost me 1/3rd of weekly pay.
The familiar systems of Civ V were there: policies, research and gold (energy), happiness (health). Not a big change on those. The nice advisor was a good thing, but on second play, you'll want that he shut up for good. The voiceovers are poor, and sometimes, glitched. There is no variety.
UI and colors are dull. For a genre that has a tradition of long hours of gameplay, it's difficult to get attached to "endless gray". The cities are nice, but the wonders... are just blueprints. I expected nice videos, or even beautiful and meaningful slides, but all that I get is a unfinished project. An idea? Get blueprints when starting a wonder, and a marvelous image of it when it's done. With my soda, I built the Stellar Codex, and my reaction was... take another sip and cry. Of boredom.
Same thing when my civilization went Purity; an advertised feature, but too much cosmetic, too little immersion. The quests are great, but they will need updates so we don't get used, and bored, for a feature. Say the same for the aliens: I expected different aliens and behaviour for different planets. So, even a fungi world is teemed with buglike creatures? I was amazed with the first contacts, but after some hours, it was only "that scorpion-shaped ranged alien, again".
Aliens are just glorified barbarians. I expected then to act as a global city-state, with objectives and intelligence. AI and diplomacy are also the same, with poor decisions: after all, how much 1 science is worth in energy? I have no clue, and don't want to do the math. I do math at my work all week.
The background history is there, but you'll have to carve it out of the Civilopedia. It's something that was great to read, but is almost a secret. It's okay that in a game like Civ V we know human history, and on Civ BE, we are making something new, but I would like to see more of it at questlines.
It just begs for some big expansion - DLC's won't do any magic here. It's a great engine, we all know it from Civ V, but is was put in a coma state. Enemy Within, the expansion for XCOM is a nice remainder of what Firaxis can do: 48 maps! Sidequests! New systems!
I'll continue to play, after all, it's a mixture of sci-fi with future history, something that I've waited for a long time. But I expect changes, and believe that producers and publishers will hear us. Don't mess up the franchise, boys and girls! Just give us, long-time and devoted players, the experience as it was meant to be.

Review: Tacoma (PC Game)
I've enjoyed Walking Simulators since Dear Esther. My favorites include The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Firewatch, Everybody's Gone to the Rapture, and Soma. Done well, Walking Simulators present an interactive fictional reflection on human experience. I look for strong, believable, nuanced characters and engrossing, surprising mysteries revealed in craftsman-like fashion.
Tacoma succeeds on all counts.
Not long for a game though respectable for a novel or movie, I started Tacoma twice to re-enjoy the initial sequence, explored thoroughly, and achieved a running-time of under 5 hours. A determined player could probably complete the game in under 3 hrs.
Tacoma delivers a compelling story that will make you laugh and cry and cheer.
If you enjoy fiction and walking simulators you will enjoy Tacoma.
If you're price-insensitive (e.g. you buy hardbacks vs paperback or prefer to see movies on opening night rather than on second-run), Tacoma is well worth full-price. But if you're more of a value-shopper, purchase Tacoma when it costs roughly $10 and you'll certainly perceive entertainment value + running time > cost.
Five Stars.
