Pros: Graphics are out of this world, best I've seen. Adds features that you really missed - insta-kill from short distance with more weapons(not only melee ones), body storage boxes double as hiding spots for 47, etc. Social stealth and sneaking stealth are more or less equally possible. Social stealth doesn't make you unrecognizable - those of the same job/rank will see through the disguise at close range, adding tension. Unarmed melee is possible, and it's done like 47 is Jason Bourne(which is how it should go, given the whole stronger, faster killer clone thing). Instinct Mode reinvigorates the growing-stale game mechanics of the series; predict patrol paths, blend in/trick with disguise(for those of the same job/rank), see enemies before they can see you(through walls and such). Contracts Mode allows creation and sharing of "levels", you use one of the story levels  to set up the kill(s): who, how, how fast, dressed as who/what and where to escape to. Challenging, especially on higher difficulty settings, culminating in Purist, that takes away nearly all feedback you receive, and your HUD!
Cons: Linear progression through tiny levels(several put together now make up one "hit", so you don't get to approach it how you want to, except planning the hits themselves). Far too story-driven for the franchise, and the plot doesn't follow the threads set up over Contracts and Blood Money; it ret-cons things and is unappealing to long-time fans, and frankly not satisfying. 47 spends this as a protector, when this kind of emotional and straight-forward story doesn't fit his character. Broadened appeal means losing some of the freedom. Locations, with admittedly strong atmosphere, are US-centric, without even using that to bring forth the rich flavor of America, like Blood Money does... there, it's the South, Vegas, Rocky Mountains, etc., here, it's the Midwest and Chicago.
My recommendation: If you love the first four games and the core concept, you will probably do better to skip this one. I do recommend it to those who either want their games, or don't care if this is, story-driven, linear, and so forgiving of the player making mistakes and/or getting caught that you can play this as an action/shooting game just as much as a stealth game.

Man, I hate when people give crap to 'walking simulator' type games - like hey, sometimes I just want a nice atmospheric game with a great narrative and world I can explore, where I don't have to worry about something trying to kill me. Anyway, I really liked Tacoma. It was immediately immersive, the story was intriguing, and the characters felt like real people - all of them had strong personalities and their reactions felt genuine for someone in their situation. Loved having the ability to replay 'memories', to be able to watch the same scene play out from multiple perspectives depending on who you were following. I also enjoyed looking through everyone's stuff and listening in on their calls, which is a simple but fun mechanic, and was another thing that helped the characters feel less like pixels and more like someone I could have met walking down the street. And have I mentioned the silhouette aspect yet? I think it was a good choice to portray the characters in that manner - you grow closer to them as you learn more about who they are, but for all your eavesdropping and involvement in the situation, they remain just out of reach. It's a reminder that you're still an outside party, still detached, only watching shadows. It was eerie in just the right way.
My only complaint that's not really a complaint was that I wish it could have been longer. And I wouldn't have been opposed to having something happen at the end that put some pressure on the player - wouldn't have had to be combat-related in any way though; there could've been a timed event, or maybe a tough choice to make. But overall the focus of this game was the people and the story, and I feel that it delivered spectacularly on that. I'm still interested in the world of Tacoma and, though it's probably unlikely to happen, I would be happy to play through another game set in this same universe.

An extremely competent and well put together dark souls inspired metroid vania game that is heavily focused on combat with plenty of platforming as well. Progression is frequent and sastifying, however a bit slow paced at the start. The primary progression is through finding items and abilities, but you will mostly just be getting money which isn't limiting throughout the game, so it doesn't feel great. However, I was still compelled to explore every nook and cranny which isn't something I normally do.
The combat and controls are extremely tight and feel great, however, you get abilities later that require you to charge your attack which, on the default key, makes jumping difficult while charging. Probably a good idea to switch attack to a different button before getting too used to it. The only REAL problem I had with the combat were the particle effects. While the game is completely fair, the tells for many boss attacks are very difficult to see against the backdrop. I often found myself tanking hits because I just couldn't see a tell or projectile against a white lit background. Outside of that, I found the game a slight bit too easy for my tastes. Never once did I die and lose my money, and I don't ever remember dying to a normal enemy. The main story bosses felt a bit easy as well, but the optional bosses were more challenging. Based on this game's reputation, it's probably just an issue with me and I have an edge from my ample time on rogue legacy which has very similar gameplay. The game is also well polished, as I had almost no bugs occur all the way through, and none of them were bad. One time the camera glitched out till I left the screen. I know from the speedrun that the game has ample glitches, but I never came across any but that in a casual play through.
The story is very inspired by dark souls, setting you in a bleak and decaying world with story primarily told by the setting around you rather than cutscenes. I liked the story more than Dark Souls, however, because the story telling elements weren't quite as obscure and I got enough to invest me in it without digging through item descriptions. The environment and art style is a perfect compliment to the story, and is eerie and gorgeous all the way through. Overall though, the story isn't extremely compelling, but it certainly isn't a point against the game.
Finally, we have the quite good soundtrack. I didn't LOVE it, but it certainly was effective and well done. I don't remember any of the tracks and won't be listening to it in my free time like I would for Transistor or Undertale, but each song was good and did an excellent job of enhacing the mood and presenting the environment of each area and boss.
Overall, I highly recommend this game for anyone who likes metroid-vania games, combat platformers, or dark souls styles story. If you just want a nice dose of a focused and well crafted gameplay that only indie games seem to provide, it's perfect for that. It's a steal at $15, and I got about 30 hours of gameplay out of it without normally being a completionist.

For some reason I like this little hidden objects game enough to have played it all the way through three times. The thing is, it's not even a good HOG -- the graphics are dated, the story is lame, and it's nowhere near as sophisticated as the recent HOGs by Artifex Mundi or Silverback. So why do I like it? Let's see if we can figure this out:
- It's short; you can finish it in under two hours. Some people would say this is a negative, but I appreciate the fact that you can complete it in one sitting.
- It's easy; the graphics are big and cartoonish, and you can find most of the hidden objects just by clicking on anything that looks out of place. Again, this could be viewed as a negative, but when I choose to play a HOG I am not looking to be mentally taxed, at all.
- You see pictures of the objects you are supposed to find, rather than a word list. Not only does this make the game even easier, but you don't have to waste any time trying to figure out if a 'nut' is supposed to be an almond or a piece of hardware.
- The hidden object scenes are logical. That is, they're not just random collections of weird items that have nothing to do with each other. The objects all belong in the scene, but they are out of place. For example, a typical task is to find some buttons scattered around the room and sew them back on to a jacket, or find all the pieces of a broken stone column and then repair it. You actually feel like you are accomplishing something as you work on each scene and restore it to order.
- The game doesn't do anything especially well, but it doesn't do anything especially wrong, either. The music is decent (or at least not annoying), the voice acting is decent (or at least not annoying), and the heroine is nice to look at.
So there you have it. Mirror Mysteries is not going to make anyone's top ten list, but if you can get it cheap on sale, and if you have a mindless hour or two to kill before bedtime on a Thursday night, it fits the bill perfectly.

I really enjoyed playing Battlerite when it released. However after hours of playing the game many of the flaws started to show themselves and became more and more apparent.
BUY IT OR NOT:
Don't buy it, get it for free when it becomes free-to-play early/mid Q1 2017
Pros:
-No RNG on the damage, everything has a set damage values so you won't randomly get killed by a lucky crit.
-Just about everything is a skillshot (no clicking on an enemy and having your character auto-attack, you need to aim everything)
-Lots of characters to choose from, and some still being added.
-Balance between the characters feels good for the most part.
-No talent trees or "gemming"
-Matches don't last very long, so if you end up with an inexperienced team mate, you don't need to wait long before a new game.
-Community is slightly better than other MOBA's (I don't think it will last)
-Developers seem to still be vested in the development of the game, however I don't think many of them play their own game very often.
Cons:
-Matches don't last very long, not much excitement from winning a 5-10 minute game.
-The report player system is a complete joke, purely placebo at the moment
-Many character abilities seem to not work as intended, such as invincibility not blocking silence/root. Being feared into the circle of death does not break fear. (incapacitate/petrify is broken by it)
-Community is relatively small, you could queue against a team, wait 4-6 minutes so you don't fight the same people, and still get queued into the same team.
-Community feels as if it's getting more and more toxic.
-While individual characters feel balanced against each other, some team compositions certainly don't feel balanced.
-Double healer in 2v2 queue is viable against any other team comp, and in some cases overpowered.
-Ranked play is currently not worth the grind. You get 0-15 points for beating a team, most often you gain 1-7 points. Ranking up takes 500 points, I believe the max rank is 15 or 20.
-No ranked tokens to spend on cool ranked skins/titles/weapons.
It's a good game, but it shouldn't be a Hitman game, it's more in line with something like Splinter Cell, if you like stealth games this might be for you.

BACKGROUND:
This game was gifted to me from someone I had once played Team Fortress 2 with. I never imagined I would have had so many hours of entertainment. I've met a lot of amazing people through this game that I've kept in touch with for years.
Although labeled as a tower defense, its unique playstyle sets it apart from many other tower defense games in my opinion.
PROS:
-character variety (4 core builders; the rest are DLC)
-maps offer diffferent amounts of difficulty
-loot is satisfying as hell (especially when you get your first Ultimate++)
-incredibly fun with a group of friends
-you can still solo if you prefer
-achievements are actually worth going for as they reward you with characters skins that boost DPS
-lots of old players that are still around that are eager to guide new players
CONS:
-if you're not a student athlete, this game isn't for you
-late game (Nightmare mode) "requires" DLC heroes such as the Summoner and EV
-unfortunate lack of popularity therefore not as active community wise as it used to be

Once you get past the feel that its "just civ 5 with a sci fi skin" you start to see how amazing the game really is.
A lot of people only seem to comment on the similarities (only one military unit per tile. I don't think this is a bad thing though) but very few comment on the difference.
Looking at the tech web for example. I no longer go though the same steps of getting code of laws and then having court houses everywhere, now I have to think. If I want to get rid of the horrid misma (which is everywhere!) then I need alien genetics, but then I open myself up to spies for not having computing (NOTE: get spies. Lost my capital to an faction I wasen't even at war with, and I had to declare war to force my way back. A spy in the city would of prevented this).
Things like this, and the fact that the aliens (your barbarians) get stronger as game goes on, making them not the push over once you get on in the game, makes this game amazing in the civ line. I love these games, and I see no bad in this game, early days yet, but its a defo go on the demo (as Fraxis are lovely enough to give one) and take it from there.

Since no one else is jumping to review this game, i suppose I will. It's solid. It's not the best and it clearly needs some work, primarily in the graphical portions of the game (water clips through ships and the waves can be higher than towns sometimes. It's odd watching a wall of water pass through your ship without the ship reacting to it). Gameplay on the other hand is very similar to games like Sid Meier's Pirates or Windward just with more focus on questing and you sailing back and forth throughout the world for reasons I'll not spoil here. There is a heavy focus on Sea Combat so you won't have any boarding actions or land battles like in Sid Meier's Pirates. You sail the boat using WASD and your cannons are fired automatically. Basically, you have a certain firing arc on your ship which you need to keep on the enemy ship and then they will fire after a few seconds. Theoretically, you could fire both sides of your ship as long as you keep both within the firing arc. So gameplay is pretty simple from what I've seen so far.
You've also got some pretty intense customization in the game and as you pick up bigger and better ships, you'll also be able to get more things to customize your ship with (Flags, Sail colors/designs, hull designs or color patterns etc). Your crew can also get injured and gain experience which affects the efficiency of your ship and how you perform in combat. You can hire new crewman by sailing into port, going to a "tavern" and dragging them onto your ship for a nominal fee. It's all pretty standard stuff for the "Pirate" Genre but it does do some pretty cool things with passive bonuses (Artifacts, skilled crewmen etc) that you might not see in other Pirate games. And I think that's what sets Tempest apart from games like Windward, you can really make your Pirate ship your own... think Pirates of the Burning Sea levels of customization, which is cool. For an early access game, this one is looking pretty good. Honestly my main complain is just the water clipping through stuff, it's crazy distracting.
Also, watch out for freaking Krakens. They are definitely out there.

Quick review from the perspective of someone that's played every Civ game (like most of us) for a few hundred hours each.
Three games in I'm really enjoy it but then again I just love the Civ formula. I like the way the tech tree is set up, more versatile in that it's a big web with fewer timeline-esque dependencies. I like what they're doing with the affinity system and how other nations react to it. The unit level up system is cool that as you gain affinity you permanently alter your troop specialization, sadly the difference between harmony (getting along with aliens) and purity (rejecting alien stuff) is materially not very different in practice. I would have liked bigger consequences for the paths you took. As it is if your game lasts long enough you can be 12 harmony, 12 purity, 12 supremacy which doesn't really make sense. The addition of satellites that have AOE attack, defense and passive effects is neat and can be used to a solid advantage but I didn't find them to be integral part of the game. I would have liked to see this play a bigger role. Have more emphasis on the fact that after you've mastered space travel you're no longer restricted to a 2D battlefield of land and sea. I think that was a big missed opportunity.
It obviously doesn't have the depth of Civ 5 so going from Civ 5 with both expansions to this feels like a let down. "oh there are only 7 nations to choose from... lame" "oh the government options aren't there, sigh" but I'm sure that will change. I would expect to see the aliens as a fully playable faction in the future (currently you can learn, domesticate and eventually create their units but can't play specifically as them) Although it begs the question, why buy now if you know in 8-12 months there will likely be more to do with exapansions, patches and with steam sales it'll be the same price.
On the whole it's not the revelation Alpha Centauri was when it came out. This isn't an entirely new game. I don't agree with sentiments that it's nothing but a Civ 5 skin, I certainly wouldn't go that far. The buildings and upgrades aren't blatantly just reskinned Civ 5 buildings and units but it's certainly not that far removed and the analogues to familiar buildings and units are apparent. If you like Civ 5 that's not a bad thing and given the iteration style of Civ over the years it's sort of to be expected. There are new and interesting units inspired by the alien technologies but on the whole it all feels very familiar. To throw out an arbitrary number it's like a 15-20% different game in terms of changes and iteration they would have likely done with Civ 6 but set in an alien world. It's good, I'm enjoying my playthroughs and I'm going to keep playing, I just wish the whole experience felt a little more alien (pun a little intended)

I'm saddened by the general consensus on this game. A "Mixed" rating on the steam page is fairly disheartening. However, I understand, in almost every aspect, the concerns and point given by those who have reviewed it in its current state. It is a click fest, the diplomacy is basic, and the trade system is a bit ridiculous.
The game, as it stands, is unfortunate. The replayability is low and my games are usually short. I love a long game, with interesting diplomatic exchanges, usually in the form of major relationships forming or major wars. In this game, neither really ever appear. In Civ 5, I could do all of that. In this game, it's the only thing I feel is VERY difficult to do. Diplomacy takes a hit with this one.
The rest of the game is just fantastic. Many have said it, but I feel the trade system is a bit overpowered and I don't think it's a problem. Trade facilitates positive relationships, something I feel Civ 5 glossed over. I don't actually ever remember another nation say " I'm glad we're trading." The tutorial is really helpful and after one playthrough I learned I all needed to be successful in all other playthroughs. The unit progession is nice and I'm quite happy with the late game variety. The affinities are nice approach to ideology, changing the look of your cities and troops. I also REALLY love how the leaders change in accordance to their own affinities.
Some will complain about the leaders. I think they're alright. They have great animation, different personalities (as I can tell), and a good aesthetic other than Elodie. I'm not a huge fan of the direction they took her. I'm not just poking at the French here, I just feel like she is the least developed.
The game stands alone as a great title. There's not a whole lot wrong with it other than replayability. There really is no reason to play it after seeing the different landcapes and playing through the affinities. That's probably where I draw a line.
I agree with what TB said in his Youtube video. It suffers from its thematic. It's a great game as is, just not what we had hoped it to be.  After some expansions, I'm sure it'll be even better.
I recommend it. $50 is a bit steep, but I think Firaxis has earned something for this. They wanted to make this work and fell short of expectations.

As a fan of most and any Sid Meier Civ game, you probably know what you're getting yourself into. As for someone interested in a turn-based sci-fi strategy game, there are a plethora of countless games to jump into and Civ: Beyond Earth could be, might be, exactly what you're looking for. However, for the seasoned Civilization player, Beyond Earth is both rewarding, but restricting.
At first glance, and within the first few minutes of the game, it feels and acts alot more like the last iteration of Civilization, Civ V. As you progress in the game however, you start to notice certain things that are missing; for better or for worse, these become the core differences in Beyond Earth compared to any other Civ game in the franchise. First off, there is a progress of time as indicated in most of the Civilization games, where you literally rewrite the history of any said fictitious civilization you choose to excel with. In Beyond Earth, that isn't the case as this is essentially the future, on an alien planet, where you can choose to win in a multiple of ways, except the result starts to feel familiar in every way.
As far as I can tell, the game seems to end at 330 turns. This can become problematic as some victories take much longer than anticipated unless you focus like a laser on the objective on how to win and when to get started. There is a work around to this: unless you go into the Advanced Setup option for setting up a game and change the Max Turns to a much higher integer, say 999, otherwise the game will always end at turn 330. I've yet to see a way to turn this feature OFF completely, and the max amount of turn option seems to be the only way to remedy that. Not even checking it and marking the integer at zero seems to affect it, the game will still end at turn 330. What I've discovered however is that if you use the Max Turn feature to a much higher value than the allotted turn 330, and win, you will not be credited with a Steam Achievement for whatever Victory you hope to achieve. In order for you to win those achievements, you MUST win by whatever means BEFORE turn 330.
The introduction of the Affinity system is also curious. It works, it gives a diversity of gameplay mechanics depending on which affinity to choose from (there are three, Harmony, Purity and Supremacy.) And certain technologies you unlock throughout the game level that affinity but only affect in leveling those particular affinities. They indirectly level and affect the other affinities, but not as much as boosting ONE particular affinity outright. The problem I've faced with the Affinity system is that even if you happen to come across being technologically advanced, even going as far as to complete several Wonders and many other advancements ahead of your opposition, if you do not max out a particular affinity at a given point and time, you will be outmatched by other factions who have leveled up one of these three affinities before you do. In this regard, being a "jack of all trades", or hodgepodging what seem like great set ideas for your civilization, will not benefit you and you will be sorely punished for trying to do this. It would seem then that the only way to avoid being overwhelmed by superior firepower, is to max out an affinity level sooner than your opponents will, and believe me, you WILL learn to choose one affinity over the other for the sake of survival and dominance. When you watch a single outranking enemy unit of a particularly high Affinity level literally steamrolling through your armies, the game ends very quickly, very painfully.
If you've never played a Civilization game then it'll be hard for anyone to miss what exactly is missing, and what new features are present. So far, there is very little new added into Beyond Earth as opposed to the past titles in the franchise, and once again, the game feels like a lesser iteration of its former self--I akin this feeling to Beyond Earth feeling like a reskinned, withdrawn standalone expansion to Civilization V, where the game continues after you've finished the Science victory and send a portion of your population into space, thus bringing us to this newest chapter of Beyond Earth... cuz... it's literally BEYOND EARTH.
The game is still rather enjoyable, but if I had to draw some similarities and conclusions, it's that Beyond Earth is NOT Civilization 5, and definitely not a true successor to be regarded as Civilization 6... maybe Civilization 5.1, but definitely not 6. And I'm pretty glad that it isn't. It's another direction in the franchise to interest those more inclined to Sci-Fi aspects of a turn-based game, and it does its job very well in that regard, it does after all hold Sid Meier's name on the title.
Lastly, there is one more thing I wish the game was done better on: The Trading system. In the beginning, with less cities and a few outposts you can manage trade routes with, it's a manageable task. Later on however, if and when you settle over a dozen cities and want to link them all up with trade routes for purposes of improved productivity, culture, energy, food and science, it becomes a mess. What ends up happening is that if you manage to link trade routes to your cities and allied outposts, the game instantly becomes a tiresome responsibility of having to micromanage EACH AND EVERY SINGLE trade convoy and vessel you own. To put this in perspective, presuming you improve the Autoplant in your cities to allow one more trade route with your Trade Outpost, that allows you to have 3 convoy/vessels at your disposal for each city routed to wherever you wish them to make trade with. As mentioned before, this scales miserably. If and when you amass over a dozen cities, you then have the responsibility of having to redirect each and every one of those trading units to where they're supposed to go after their trade cycle is due. That alone is an extra 36 actions you must attend to displaced across an amount of turns it takes for each trade unit to reach their destination. The problem here is that at this point, you spend more time managing your trade routes than you do actually playing the game.
Believe me, try and set up a truly maxed out trade system across ALL your cities and trade outposts and you'll see exactly what I'm talking about...
To remedy this, it would have been so much easier if you could send your trade units out and they instantly become autonomous to infinitely return themselves to that one destination until they are either plundered, killed or rerouted yourself via the Trade Overview menu. If it's the ONE thing I have a gripe over with this game is, it's the trading system, which becomes VERY messy the longer the game goes on. This is not a game breaking or review ruining factor, just something I noticed very astutely and wish was much more simpler, and not so painfully demanding or inefficient to the point that I often think about NOT wanting to set up trade routes--but in refusing to do so, the game becomes that much harder without the boost in all around productivity and benefits you can amass from trade!
In time, there may come expansions to address certain things (like trade...) or add new features into this title as seen in the past with Civilization 5, utterly changing the game's mechanics and gameplay significantly. But as it is, Beyond Earth stands on its own two feet as a great game with familiarity to past, experienced Civ players, and definitely something new, challenging and rewarding for newcomers. Get yourself caught in another case of "One... More... Turn..." syndrome and step into a brave new world; Civilization: Beyond Earth will have you covered.

At first I hated this game, thinking that it "ruined" the Hitman series, so I left it after the first missions (probably the third one); fortunately, one day I tried it again and I completed it, discovering how cool it actally is.
The first half part of the game was pretty boring to me, but then it began really interesting. Sure, there were still some missions which annoyed me (they're the ones where you have to get behind a cover and stay there for a long time in order to escape from a place and reach a new one, without having any targets to kill), but 90% of the rest was really amazing and I felt like playing on older Hitmans. If you're looking for some old-like "silent" action, missions such as Streets of Hope or The King of Chinatown are the ones which you're looking for.
Except for the exaggerated amount of bloom and lens flares which can be very annoying, the rest of the graphics is amazing. Performance is pretty bad, so I wouldn't suggest this game if you have a bad PC and you aren't going to buy a high-end one. Plot is ok/good, but what really surprised me is the longevity. It took me 30+ hours to complete it, even without having done all "additional objectives" (although I've repeated many times some missions in order to get SA rating).
Now, I can say that I'm disappointed for some aspects of the rating system (no penalties for found bodies? What? No timer? Too bad), for the disguise system (they're useless if you don't use instinct), for the exaggeration in the use of covers and for the cover system itself.
Recommended!

Hitman Absolution is the fifth entry in Io Interactive's Hitman series of stealth assassination games. Since the series began, the developers have always iterated heavily with each instalment, never being content to leave game elements as they are when improvements can be found. Absolution is no exception, and feels smoother, more attractive, and more compelling than even 2006's superb Blood Money.
Players that see the Hitman series purely as a series of largely unconnected, discrete challenges always focused on assassination may be disappointed with the new approach, but for everyone else Absolution is probably the ultimate Hitman game yet. Agent 47 is as deadly as ever, but he is now both hunter and hunted, reliant on his wits and what he can scavenge from the environment to succeed. This time around it isn't just duty that drives 47, but a strong and coherent plot that makes every hair-raising infiltration and carefully-planned kill feel personal and important.
Gripping from start to finish and polished until it shines, Hitman: Absolution is a truly brilliant game and a must for any fan of stealth and third-person action games.

Absolution draws a hard line between itself and the previous 4 installments of the game without alienating die hard fans of this franchise. Absolution is far more cerebral than it's predecessors. The storyline is multifaceted and weaves together a plot that focuses on exposing 47's ambitions, strengths, and flaws without making him appear weak or whiny; he is still the ultimate badass, but much more human and believable. Absolution shows a more realistic and approachable 47; one I, and I assume others, can easily identify with. This game really develops Hitman's character on a much deeper level than previously attempted.
The movements of 47 are very swift and responsive. In fact, many of 47's movements can be compared to how Sam Fisher's movements are in the Splinter Cell games, which means players can now access cover and look around at a 360 angle. I would also compare the sneaking around to the Metal Gear games, as well. In this game, there are just SO many ways to go about taking out a primary target. On one level, I was given the option to take out a target in 12 different ways. That way could be by taking him out, wearing various disguises, taken him out quietly, poisoning his food, blowing his car up or taking him out with guns blazing. Not to mention, players can get reward for doing so, which enhances the replay value of this game.
The AI has been greatly improved. Characters interact with their environment, situations, and the actions of 47 in many fascinating ways now. Characters generally still have predetermined paths but they can now be interrupted, altered, redirected, and distracted to allow 47 to accomplish his objectives. This really makes a difference in the game play. You no longer have to memorize guards paths or actions, rather you can now change the course of events by affecting the characters in any given situation to gain access to your targets.
All in all this game is by far the best adaptation of Hitman yet. I highly recommend it. You can play this game and still feel comfortable without having ever played any previous versions.

The game has an interesting idea, but poor execution.
Good:
This game is unique in having you uncover the level as you move through it.
The ambient music fits the game well, and I personally don't mind the simple graphics.
There's a steady difficulty curve, gradually going from easy (teaching the player) to hard.
Bad:
This game's premise mixed with  fast-paced play doesn't fit well together. The game will force you to move fast, but you'll end up dying a lot because of spikes or other obstacles that you couldn't see coming.
While the controls are tight, I found them to be irresponsive at some points, as well as having next to no control while in mid-air, leading to even more unavoidable deaths.
When the level scrolls from side to side, or top to bottom, or both, the camera lags behind, obscuring anything in your path as you're moving. This also doesn't fit with the fast-paced gameplay.
Overall, while the idea of the game is interesting, everything else around it besides the graphics and audio falls flat due to poor design. I enjoy challenging games, but I couldn't help but feel that the entire time I was playing, I died too many times to what I mentioned above, which in turn put me through arbitrary trial and error.
If you have a lot of patience, and can adjust to the controls, maybe give it a try. Otherwise, you won't be missing much.

If you like games such as League of Legends but dislike long matches, you'll most likely love this game. Considering the short length of the matches it feels way less frustrating when you lose compared to some other games. It has a good variety with its champions and has a good system for customization. However the matchmaking is not very balanced. This is probably due to the fact that the game does not have that big of a player base yet.
Also, buying the game during early access is probably worth it since you will get all the existing champions as well as the champions that will get released in the future for the price you pay, as well as a founder icon and title. The full price is 20 euro at the moment, which I personally see as a completely reasonable price considering what you get. You won't have to spend your in-game currency on champions and instead you can spend it on chests and gear for the champions you like.
I highly recommend this game if you're a fan of MOBAs, if you like games with a competitive scene, games with a ranked mode and games with fairly short matches.
Keep in mind that these are my personal opinions based on my experiences with the game.

I'd had my eye on this one for a while and finally decided to grab it when it came on sale.  Glad I did.
You're sent to the station to recover the AI core, clipping on some AR equipment so you can interact with the station's systems.  While you're waiting for various bits and pieces to download to your ship, you go exploring.  That's when the story starts getting interesting.  Fragments of the AR recordings made by the station are stuck in the system, and it's these that you use to piece together the lives of the crew in their time on board.  You can - and should - keep replaying the recordings to pick up the perspectives of each person.  The candid parts where one or two of the crew are on their own are quite touching.
It's not the longest game ever, but then it isn't one really intended to be rushed through.  It's one to take your time and explore.

Going to review with a description of my first game.
The game has that Civ feel to it. Landing on an alien planet and settling down after making your intial choices has that overwhelming sense of urgency that it should. Within a matter of moments you see aliens probing your landing zone, various resources that you have no idea what they are for and new terrain features that exist only to hurt and kill your units. It is in this moment that I am thinking to myself "Hell yes, lets play"
I no doubt fumble through my first 5-20 turns with no serious plan in mind other then what previous civ games have taught me. I need to expand, I need to centralize my power and I need to be ready. Ready for what, I have no idea but its a good plan so I run with it. I take a serious 20 minutes inside of the tech web to launch, atleast a mid-term plan and I come up with something. I happen to have an abundance of a resource called Fyraxite (sp) and there is a late game unit called an "angel" that requires it, sign me up.
It is at this point that I have now commited to one of the three affinities in the game, Supremacy. The others being Harmony and Purity, I have decided that I want robots to fight my battles while my people tinker at home in the comforts of their fortified cities, what could go wrong...
Well the tech takes some time, so for now my soldiers are still my frontline fighters against the alien menace, but I have recruited some new mechanized combat vehicles. I obtain the required tech and get my first colony unit in play, now to get it where I want it. The game now has an AI like assistant to help guide you and since this is my first game I left all functionality on, if just to hear him explain the aspects that I am unsure of.
The AI suggested that I build my new colony in an area ripe with resources but just enough out of reach of what I want my territory to be (at this stage in the game) to be uncomfortable. I make my next significant choice, I play it safe and keep it just a few hexes closer to my comfort zone. Each choice you make seems impactful, I often found myself thinking "could I have pushed the limits and made it work?" Furthermore, naerly each building you complete for the first time presents itself with a little mini-choice. You read a paragraph of a story and determine what best works for your civ. For example, I build a trade depot and something occurs that is causing it to use less power then anticipated. Do I re-focus this excess power into enhancing my trade ability (+1 trade route) or send the power back to the grid (+2 energy)
Anyway, I start mowing down alien bugs and flying drones to clear the way for my next colony unit. I start to think ok, this isnt so bad...then I see it. A Siege Wurm. I cannot deal with it with my current force and I sacrifice one unit to gauge the strengh of the wurm. So I settle for a different location in a different direction, meanwhile the siege wurm probes my territory and I take pot shots at it with my city defenses as I can. These are no barbarian pushovers.
It is at about this time that the politics start to kick in. The other civs are carving out their own respective areas and trading and building. I happen to be near the Slavik federation and the Brazilian civ. I have the southern portion of our small continent, Brazil has the Northwest and the Slav's the Northeast. War breaks out, the Slavs want to take over Brazilian territory and they march over and take the first city. (after approx 5 turns of battle) Furthermore the Slav's decide that they  can push the Brazilians off of our continent altogether and leave them with 1 puny island just off the coast. It is at this junction that I make my next major decision of the game, I declare war on the Slavs and move to assist Brazil. Now I want to point out the fact that I weighed this choice for about 10 minutes prior to making the commitment, as this was my first game and I want to win.
I enter the war and I have 1 obvious motive and 3 ulterior ones. I want to not allow the Slavs to be the dominant power on my continent. I want to test out my newly formed robot combat units. I want to be the dominant power on my continent. Lastly, I want to test out the orbital layer system and use this satelite that buffs the combat capability of my units. We fight off the Slav's and in no time I am laying siege to the once Brazilian and now Slavic city. I conquer the city and am faced with another huge decision. I can give it back to Brazil or keep it for myself. Giving it to Brazil gives me huge brownie points but resets the balance of power to a more Romance of the Three Kingdoms era of stagnation. Where as keeping it clearly asserts me as the dominant power and alienates me from my new ally Brazil who would clearly see my joining the war as a power play. Naturally, I keep it. If Brazil wanted it they should have defended it better.
I opt to not send any delegates to the Slavic federation and await theirs. I fortify my borders and probe into their territory with raids on units or light siege activity. I have the stronger force as well as a satelite that buffs my units in play but not the numbers to assault along the entire broad borders that we share. Within 5-8 turns I am greeted by a delegate suing for peace. He offers me resources, energy and....a city! I review the treaty to make sure I am reading it correctly and sure enough, he is offering me his 2nd most productive city. I accept and we shall have peace.
My plan could not have gone any better. I lost a single military unit, gained 2 cities and stifled the growth of 2 neighbors. I had planned to win this game through a peaceful means and now I have the peace of mind to put that in motion. I begin to build a giant teleportation gate back to earth. Meanwhile, the other leaders that have landed on various continents are becomming less happy with me lately...
Perhaps it was the balance of power shift. Perhaps it is the fact that my people no longer die in needless battles (because I send robots now!) Perhaps it is because I have begun construction on a game ending wonder.
Right now, alot of things happen. My robots have devoloped sentience and have requested to have their own city (aww crap)
Every other civ, except Brazil hates me (which is ok because I am trading with Brazil exclusively anyway)
I have a solid defense force of robots and upgraded infanty units around my borders as well as hovering combat vehicles and giant siege tank walker things (oh yea)
I grant my robots their own city, half out of fear (about 1/3 of my military is 100% robotic, 1/3 is mechanical and the remaining third is augmented human/cyborg, so worst case senario is I lose control of 2/3 of my force) and half out of curiousity. I place my new city via a colony unit as usual but I tactically place it near no significant resources and fortify the area with humanoid troopers. The city is under my direct control like any other city but it has gone silent for a few turns. Suddenly I get a robot delegate who wants to open trade lanes, I sent a transport of goods and the robots seem content to have their freedom, under my guidance of course and all goes well. (I have no idea what to expect at this point so I never remove the 3 humanoid solders from the area for the remainder of the game, alas nothing happens. But was it because I kept a human presense or...)
I complete my teleportation gateway to earth. The game is not over. I now need to send over a military presence to earth to show them that my civ can be trusted with their future. After about 15-20 turns of churning out various unit types (mostly humanoid, sending my robots through the gate, still out of fear of rebellion and attempting to even the ratio of robot to human forces on the alien world) the game ends and I have won, an Emancipation Victory.
After all this joy, fear and wonder however, I find it hard to finish a second game...

Pros:
- Massive, vibrant open world.
- Visually stunning
- Great setting
- Sea Shanties!
- Plenty to do for completionists
- Naval combat / sea adventures
- Crafting / Hunting / Diving / Looting / upgrading and outfitting!
- 18th Century characters brought to life
- 18th Century story part of the game
Cons:
- Tail missions (that almost all end in a scripted blood battle, thus removing the need for stealth)
- Follow missions. You would think that by 2013, the ability to force NPCs to run to the next objective would have been established in the series.
- Abstergo - everything. Pulling the player out of the 18th Century West Indies to remind them that they are in a game with condescending puns and euphemism really breaks the immersion.
- Controls sometimes fiddly, Edward would occasionally jump in the opposite direction that I was intending, but this is rare.
Conclusion:
AS4BF is easily the best game in the series. The 18th century world of the West Indies has been brought to life with all of the swashbuckling adventures you would expect in a fairy tale. The only thing that stops AS4BF from being a truly fantastic game are the same hangovers from previous games that the developers have failed to iron out. Tail missions and Abstergo ‘present day’ activities are tedious and immersion killing. Even still, AS4BF is probably my favourite game of 2013. 9/10.

I gotta do it, it pains me but I have to write a negative review.
I can sum this game up in one sentence: Re-textured Civ 5 vanilla.
I defy anyone who doesn't think so to prove otherwise.
Basics:
1) Energy is gold.
2) Health is Happiness (and no, saying they're different because you only get a -10% productivity at -20 health instead of your people rebelling is not making your point for you).
3) Virtue is [culture].
They function literally the same. Virtue increases your borders, just like culture. Resources, strategic resources, etc.. all of it is just re-skinned.
AI? I played on Apollo, not once did the AI attack me, even when I was buying land all up on their border. You get a passive aggressive message saying "I see what you're doing", but that's it. I spied nonstop on people and got caught many times, blew up their satellites, made units defect, etc... yet all I got, again, was "I see what you're doing". You want to know what BE is like? Load up Civ 5 vanilla and play it on the easiest difficulty with no AI and that's BE.
Wonders? When you can figure out where they are (hint, it's the smooth hemisphere icon with something under it on the tech web) are just like regular buildings with n+1 modifiers. Oh this increases the virtue in said city by 5% AND counts as a node? Why then did I spend 1200+ production on it? No wonder movies. It's an aesthetic thing, but when you grew up with AC busting out with wonder movies that made you FEEL in wonder, it's kind of lacking.
Same thing with the tech. Uninspiring. There is no race to get gunpowder, or friction-less surfaces (AC), it's just clicking for a marginal improvement. And the reason for that is that buildings in the bases are underdeveloped. It's like the wonders are the regular buildings, and they just didn't do the wonders.
Affinities? Good concept, atrocious execution. You get them by default for researching things. You want to play harmony but really want that gene tech? Guess what, you're bootstrapped into going purity as well (some people would call this "strategy" as I would have to balance tech with affinity. good point, Unfortunatly, it is irrelevant when I can simply research all the tech and have max affinity. So, I call it lazy execution of another layer of gameplay). Like wonders, affinities do almost nothing for the bulk of the game but give your units a different skin. Sure, there are SOME benefits per affinity. Harmony level 6 heals in miasma, but by the time you reach that level, getting +5 health from miasma is worthless. Same with all other affinities. The only purpose for their being in the game is to trigger some of the end games.
Units? SIX (I'm ignoring worker/colony). Rover, Missile, Soldier, Boat, Air, Super. That's it. Sure, you can upgrade them for a marginal improvement based on your affinity level (and you get one or two new ones based on your affinity...yaaaayyyy, but they are, again, virtually identical to what you have already), but Civ 5 at least has the common decency to give you units that vary in skill and use. Better still, AC let you design them. Here, you get SIX. Unacceptable.
End games. Too easy. You build gates/flower and then you wait X number of turns or put X number of units through them and you win. There's no race for tech and components. There's no launching with a 1/3 complete spaceship hoping it'll make it, it's either all or nothing.
Gameplay: The only other time I've felt like playing a game was a job was when I was going for gold in GT and missing it by .0001 seconds. THAT is work and yet, somehow, clicking the "next turn" in this game felt eerily like that. I've never been as bored playing a Civ game as I felt playing this.
The basic problem with the game is this: Like with recent releases this game suffers from one major drawback: oversimplification. X-com did the same (but it pulled it off WAY better), Simcity 5 did it, Deus Ex Invisible war (and to a certain extent Human Revolution) etc... They all did. It seems that now days companies just want to move product. However, because they've gotten so big, they have to move a LOT of product and they are so afraid that mouth-breathers aren't going to be able to handle complex computations and thinking ahead. So, in order to appeal to the broadest base, like Fouchet in Bad Boys, they cut their product with something. In these cases it's with "stupidity". What you get then is Civ 5 in space. Literally.
In the context of complicated games being good, Civ 4 took the cake on that. But Civ 5 was a massive simplification. It's like they thought they'd streamline it and people were like WTF is this, and then they took it back to 4 with the expansions. Same thing with BE, but this time it doesn't feel like an honest mistake, it's almost like they knew from the start what they were doing.
It's unfortunate. This game could have been so much better, and what is even more galling is that it is GOING to be so much better....five months and 30$ later when the expansion comes out.
Save your money and wait till this is either on sale for at MOST 30$ or they do some GOTY edition (obviously with the expansions) for 60$.

I feel terrible for having to not recommend any game in my favorite 4x franchise. Unfortunately, I have to take some of my time to warn others against something they may not like. By this time, most other reviews have hammered in the idea of waiting for expansion packs or DLC, but that is atrocious behavior by the industry. I'd told myself never to preorder anything, but did so with this because I honestly thought I couldn't go wrong. I couldn't have been MORE wrong.
After 500 hours into civ 5 BNW, this is a massive downgrade. I won't reiterate the small technical problems that most people have, but rather give an overall objective opinion based on things that are done more poorly than civ 5 BNW.
I can't recommend this game as of now, but maybe in the future. The UI is a massive block of grays and any shades of gray imaginable. This combined with the tiny map make it almost impossible to use the minimap. For whatever reason, everyone seems to have this mass suspicion that everything in the future is uniform, dull, gray, and has no color in life whatsoever. This particularly annoys me because it detracts from the visual aspect, but also from the playability of using certain interfaces. The tech web is all gray/purple with white buildings/units. This makes is so difficult to figure out if research gives you a unit or building, and especially what building it gives you and what it does. Wonders are impossible to tell the difference against a normal building. The only hint is that it has much more production cost.
When looking at the city screen, your "civ" color is almost indistinguishable against the background, and tiles worked are so massive that they cover the tiles that it corresponds to so you can move workers around. On the normal view, your unit icons are so dull in color that they mostly match the tile colors as well, so it's almost impossible to tell where units are. Think as if the whole game, no matter what faction you are, it's like playing in civ 5 in 100% jungle tiles as Brazil (with green borders). You can't tell anything apart.
I've had no crashes, but I did try to start it up once, only to have steam just kick me out every time without launching or asking me to stop the process. Had to restart steam to solve that one.
Now subjectively,
I hear many many references to SMAC, which I never played. From what I have been reading, however, I can gather that it was truly amazing. I've also heard this was supposed to be a spiritual successor. I specifically remembering Firaxis saying it wasn't, and that we would be disappointed to look at it that way. That said, I still think they shouldn't have gone the way they did. They tried two contradicting things and didn't pick one, so the end result was being bad at both. They tried to keep civ 5 mechanics, such as trade routes and spying, but also tried new things by taking this on other planets. Too close of ties to civ 5 made for bad planet design -- too humanlike for being so-called "alien." Since it was so much like civ 5, we required it to at least be on par with that game, but it was too dumbed down. We liked the locations and atmosphere, but it was too contained to civ 5 to really take off. It either needed to stick 100% to civ 5 mechanics or it needed to go somewhere completely new. Neither of which it did.
Overall, I put 15 or so hours into the game, but I only won one game. It didn't even feel good. The other games, and especially the first game, I had to deal with mentally handicapped AI that only wanted peace for every single city I owned outside my capital. First game I played, I ignored streamlining down the affinity point research so I could bolster my units. The result was one civ annihilating every single city I had singlehandedly with ONE battlesuit. One unit. Destroyed. 5. cities. alone. Not one type, one single unit. The game just lacks balance in anything. Other reviews can tie all this together much better than I can, but please stay away from this if you love BNW. This is just 100% a disappointment as it is now.

If this game was made out to be Dune 3 this game would have received epic positive reviews, but as it stands it has to live up to one of the biggest Turn Based Strategy names in the business. While some of the points that are raised about the UI and the not always logical AI and more of these little things, I do feel that despite it's flaws it is a solid stand alone game, it is not a classical Civilization like we are used to. You start off after a points based win, in a different galaxy, lord knows how many lightyears away. And you land on an alien world.
Here it takes Three distinctive paths towards one of three victories, although all victories are possible to achieve regardless of which path you choose. There are two extra victory conditions with Dominance and Contact, which are not tied to either Purity, Emancipation or Harmony. Each needing different approaches. Again it is possible to have all 5 victory conditions running alongside of eachother simultaneously, though that is only really possible on the lower settings in difficulty.
The quests add a little spice to the mix giving you options to make your expedition slightly stronger or more versatile. I do believe the upgrades that are given to all units is a great feature, though this does mean that military players will continue to overrun you even with 'old' units as they get an upgrade with the rest of em.
I see why people can be very critical about this game, I too see flaws in terms of balance and gameplay. But I must admit that it has a very high replay value and does manage to keep me quite entertained. This game just has to live up to the Civ series and does not quite manage that just yet, regardless I fully reccommend it.

Hidden object games are a guilty pleasure for me. I've played way more than I care to admit, and this game is among the worse ones I've played. It's very short, for one, and is also by far the easiest I've ever played. The hidden object scenes can often be completed without even looking at the items you need to find because they just don't blend in. I don't know if there's some kind of drop shadow or what exactly makes it obvious, but I could just easily pick them out. There's also way too much hand-holding with a pop-up telling you when you're out of things to do at that scene. There's no logic involved at all. I never had to ask myself, "Okay, so I found this item. What scene had a problem I haven't solved where I might need something like this?" You're given numbers telling you which scenes still need actions and if you pick the wrong scene, a popup tells you you've already done all you can there, instantly narrowing down your choices. I really didn't like that at all. There are also maybe 3 actual puzzles at most. I should mention I always play these games on Casual difficulty, as I enjoy them only to mindlessly pass time when I'm stressed, and even so I found this too easy.
The graphics were also very pixelated when set to fullscreen. This is my first time playing a hidden object game on a PC instead of my phone, though, so I don't know if perhaps that is the standard.
The only real upside is that the music was enjoyable. It's the first time I've ever noticed the music while playing, though that may be due in part to the fact that I wasn't mentally engaged.
Bottom line: don't pay full price. My rule of thumb is to try and get 1 hour of gameplay per dollar. I got this on sale, so I came out close to even, but don't buy this for $5.

When making a game, it is obvious that your past experiences will influence your game. In this case, I think it's good! It has obvious influenced from Wurm Online and Black Desert.
I love Wurm Online and I have been waiting for it's "spiritual successor", so to speak, for a long time.
The complicated, in-depth crafting, the slow gathering of resources, the multiple stats that govern so much of the game, such as quality of items and fail chance. I love all those things.
What's more, I feel that they've successfully managed to take those core concepts and improve on them, removing some of the less fun aspects and introducing some new interesting ones.
The influences I see from Black Desert is mostly the fishing.
The problem right now is that there's not enough to do. I have played this game for 11 hours and I feel like I've experienced all that there is to experience in this game. It has very interesting ideas and concepts going for it, but they need to be built upon as they feel a bit shallow and unfinished at the moment. This is not a criticism of the game, but more of a note on the early access status.

Extra note on the comparison to Wurm Online:
There is one thing that I felt when I played Wurm Online for the first time that is missing from this game. The sense of real progression. I spent hours just figuring out how to play Wurm Online and once I managed to make my first, crappy, iron tools I felt so good about myself because I really had to work for it. Novus Inceptio is too abundant with "rare" resources and I can make ingots of them immediately. Wurm Online had amazing, deep, game mechanics that are unrivaled by any game I have seen to date and I truly feel that this game has the potential to be that game.
This all depends on the target audience, of course, as I don't imagine everyone enjoying the mechanics of Wurm Online as much as I do.

Having never played this game before and only hearing about all the crap people give it. (legit crap though...see later)  I enjoy this game a lot.  Once you get past the first few areas, the combat picks up a lot and you really start to get a feel for the flawed characters, how they mesh together...or not, at times.  Back to the combat though.  Yes you control 1 character, and yes if s/he gets down'ed it's game over, but that adds to the sense of urgency in some battles that you need to control the game very carefully.  Yes there's that silly auto-battle function, but you literally will not have fun with this game at all if you just rely on that.  Paradigm shifting and having good setups is essential to winning mid-late game fights.
Yes the "exploration" is quite linear, but once you realize that, it makes you want to see every nook, cranny, horizon, etc. for what it is.  And some places are just plain gorgeous, nearly on par with top level pc games.  Also that linear'ness means you can't go back to any areas at all, on Cocoon at least, so find every treasure chest/orb you can.  But yeah this is a beautiful game and stop and smell the roses sometimes.
The story?  People say it's confusing or convoluted or whatnot.  ...I found it fairly simple.  You just have to pay attention to what's happening, read the bits of dialogue presented to you, don't skip the cutscenes. (lol telling this generation of gamers that is folly, i know).  Don't let your ideas of a "perfect story" cloud what's going on.  Listen to the character's plight, how they interact with each other and the world around them.  Let the characters grow on you.  ...Yes even Vanille, though if you use her in the party after a certain point, try to keep the volume down.  Otherwise it'll sound like you're watching an adult film.  Not sure what her voice actress was thinking in that regard.
You don't "level up" in a traditional sense.  You gain points every battle you use to advance on the crystarium and increase the power of your roles and characters.  The crystarium itself levels up though almost every time you face a major boss.  The enemies do respawn in some areas, so grinding is possible.  though early in the game if you want to grind you have to save/quit/load.  Your weapons and accessories gain experience through using items gained by defeating enemies or buying at the conveniently placed shop consoles.  (there are no "town hubs" to go to like other Final Fantasy games)  Also your HP is restored after every battle.
The visuals, sound effects and music/soundtrack?  All excellent.  Areas that Square/Square-Enix never fail to deliver.
In short, i'm only halfway through the game, and I enjoy the crap out of it.  Final Fantasy 13 has a reputation for being a polarizing entry in the series.  People love it, or they hate it.  ...I'm on the side of the fence that loves it for what it is.  A charming adventure with a cast of quirky characters in a desperate situation trying to survive and get to know each other and grow as people.  ...Who happen to have super powers.
My only gripes with this game are the quality of the port.  No grapics options?  Locked to 1 resolution?  Alt-tabbing breaks some of the visual functionality and sometimes crashes the game.  I wish i could go back to visit areas.  Vanille's battle sounds reminding me of "adult content".  The lack of being able to get gil without farming specific enemies in specific areas for sellable items.  ...The lack of use for gil until the endgame.  The game does lose framerate in high stress/action areas, even though my pc blows a PS4's specs out of the water. (this is a playstation 3 game, so...).
Right though.  Give the game a chance.  You'll either kick yourself for not playing this fantastic game sooner, or you'll hate it.  It's fairly cheap as well, so, yeah.

I really enjoyed playing Battlerite when it released. However after hours of playing the game many of the flaws started to show themselves and became more and more apparent.
BUY IT OR NOT:
Don't buy it, get it for free when it becomes free-to-play early/mid Q1 2017
Pros:
-No RNG on the damage, everything has a set damage values so you won't randomly get killed by a lucky crit.
-Just about everything is a skillshot (no clicking on an enemy and having your character auto-attack, you need to aim everything)
-Lots of characters to choose from, and some still being added.
-Balance between the characters feels good for the most part.
-No talent trees or "gemming"
-Matches don't last very long, so if you end up with an inexperienced team mate, you don't need to wait long before a new game.
-Community is slightly better than other MOBA's (I don't think it will last)
-Developers seem to still be vested in the development of the game, however I don't think many of them play their own game very often.
Cons:
-Matches don't last very long, not much excitement from winning a 5-10 minute game.
-The report player system is a complete joke, purely placebo at the moment
-Many character abilities seem to not work as intended, such as invincibility not blocking silence/root. Being feared into the circle of death does not break fear. (incapacitate/petrify is broken by it)
-Community is relatively small, you could queue against a team, wait 4-6 minutes so you don't fight the same people, and still get queued into the same team.
-Community feels as if it's getting more and more toxic.
-While individual characters feel balanced against each other, some team compositions certainly don't feel balanced.
-Double healer in 2v2 queue is viable against any other team comp, and in some cases overpowered.
-Ranked play is currently not worth the grind. You get 0-15 points for beating a team, most often you gain 1-7 points. Ranking up takes 500 points, I believe the max rank is 15 or 20.
-No ranked tokens to spend on cool ranked skins/titles/weapons.

SImply put, if you want to play Civilization V or Alpha Centauri, go play Civilization V or Alpha Centauri. It clearly takes a lot from each game (Civ V for the engine, AC for the general idea), but is, at the end of the day, its own game. ANd, in my humble opinion, it is a fine addition to Sid Meier's legacy.
There are a few minor issues, mainly with the UI. Lack of information, or even a simple inclusion of the current date were somewhat disappointing, but the UI was never clunky or difficult to use. It simply would benefit from a few additions, such as demographics. In my experience thus far, the AI could benefit from being a little more aggressive on higher difficulties as well.
Overall, Beyond Earth can be summarized as having options. The tech web is interesting and well-implemented, and it truly feels as though you are exploring possible avenues of human advancement, instead of following the rigid path laid out for us in prior Civs (albeit by necessity). The virtues system offers more real choice than policies, as there are clear benefits for going deep on one category, or broad across several. Effectively, to have a focused but specialized civilization, or a more versatile one.
The amount of choices does mean that each individual aspect lacks the same level of personality and emotive connection when compared to prior Civs, but not only is this an acceptable tradeoff, it is better for the affective feel of the game. The future, and the world, is meant to feel cold and alien, not warm and familiar.
It is a fine game, for fans of the turn based genre. However, don't view it as a sequel to Civ V, but, rather, a new (but similar) game. There is also likely to be more content coming by way of expansions in the future; it pays to remember that Civ V itself was quite low on content prior to the release of G&K and BNW.

It's more of Civ 5 in a scfi skin with a couple smaller details that differentiate it from Civ 5 but the game play is pretty much the same. This is exactly what I was looking for though so I am not disapointed in this new addition to the franchise. Sure SMAC was and is a better game but SMAC is arguably one of the best turn based strategy games of all time. If Firaxis had acheived a game on the level of SMAC on day one release I would have been stunned.
Look at the Civ 5 vanilla release and compare it to this release. So far I have not encountered many bugs and this is a far better game than vanilla Civ 5. In my opinion, Civ 5 did not really become that fantastic amazing game we all know and love until Gods and Kings was released and then made even better by Brave New World. My point is that this is already a solid entry and can only be made better with DLC/expansions much like Civ 5 was. I can speculate that the future DLC will add alien races much like the SMAC expansion did.
Gameplay wise there are noticable differences between Beyond Earth and Civ 5. Wonders are farrrrr less powerful in Beyond Earth and in my opinion are a waste of time to build. Trade routes are a lot more powerful and the more you have the better (Polystralia FTW). Affinities take the role of idealogies but also upgrade your units as you progress through your chosen affinity so you dont have to spend money upgrading your military units after they become obsolete. It happens automatically. Diplomacy is pretty much the exact same with the minor difference that you can exhange "favors" for resources now. The aliens seem agressive compared to barbariens but only if you go near their nests or show hostility first. Early game the aliens will be everywhere and it is wise to leave them be if you dont have a strong military (♥♥♥♥ing seige worms). Happiness in Beyond Earth has been changed to Healthiness. It is difficult early on to maintain a positive health rating but the system works differently than in Civ 5. When your civ is unhealthy, your cities can continue to grow at normal rates you just get debuffs (-10% culture, -10% science is the first one) and they become more and more severe as you continue further and further into unhealthiness. The Tech web is not linear like the technology tree was in Civ 5. It is a giant web that starts with basic technologies that will have smaller leaf technologies that become available as you research the base tech. Certain technologies unlock affinity points and others unlock new buildings and units. There are also Orbital units in Beyond Earth now. You can clear miasma, boost your energy intake, buff your military units or even shoot laser beams to destroy opposing forces depending on the sattelite type.
All in all I love this game and think it is a great addition to the series. I cannot wait to see what they do with the DLC. I realize that my opinion is subjective however so this is my recomendation : If you absolutly LOVED civ 5, like im talking +500 hours of in game time, you will like this game and you should pick it up. If you're more casual with Civ and turnbased strategy games in general then I recommend you wait for a sale or wait for the inevitable Civ: Beyond Earth Complete Edition with all the DLC. Hopefully my review has helped. Thanks for reading.

If you loved Gone Home, it's a no brainer. If you didn't... it's still not much of a brainer. Look, read this and decide if it appeals to you:
You enter a space station, in orbit between the Moon and the rest of space. Your task is to retrieve the station AI per your contract with the operating company, as well as any and all personal logs, desktop and holographic conversation records. You do this by passing around the station, playing through the recorded holograms, scrubbing back and forth to get the info you need to proceed. It'll take you 2+ hours to do, and by the end you'll have had a narrative experience you got to interact with and review. The world is dense, there's plenty of hints at a bigger picture for the universe of the game, and you get to reunite two robotic cleaner lovebirds in the process, should you wish.
Now, if you read that and think "this is dumb, where are the guns"... Avoid this game.

The game experiments with a a lot of new systems which is good, I don't want Civ5 in space. But a lot of them still need some work. The best of these is the affinity system which selects and upgrades your unique units.  There is also a quest system for introducing the player to various game mechanics and customizing their buildings. The orbital layer for sattalite units that can affect the ground units/tiles in various ways. And lastly you start in the middle of a tech web instead of one end of a tree which is pretty neat.
The new systems are promising but the implementation is a little lacking. With an expansion or two the game could be amazing but at the moment it is both overwhelming for the new player and tedius for the experienced. It hits you with a lot of relatively significant choices right at the beginning and by the end a huge number of pointless ones.
New players are hit with everything right from the beginning, a foreign tech tree, unknown personalities, and a strange new map. The tech tree is a difficult problem for every science fiction world. Mostly civ5 does this well but for instance researching "Alien Ethics" allows you to build a "mind stem". Do I want that or not? And because you start in the middle of the web it can be quite confusing which way to go. Diplomatically the new factions still have personalities, but they aren't easily recognizable like their historic counterparts. And the very terrain is hard to read with fictional resources used for unknown purposes. Within a play through or two these are all tackleable but for a newbie it's quite unforgiving.
For the expereinced player there are three primary sources of tedium. Trade routes, workers, and building quest decisions. The first two are known to civ5 players but are a little worse here. Trades routes are no longer limited by faction but by city so you can have (and need) a lot of them. And since they don't last as long as they did in civ5 you have to constantly refresh them, several a turn by the end of the game. Automated workers are still pants on head stupid but now some tiles now have very high maintainence costs and they like to build these everywhere which can bankrupt your economy. So you should probably manage every worker every turn but doing so is agony by the end of the game.
And lastly the first time you build any new building you get a choice of two upgrades for that type of building. But these upgrades don't appear in the tech tree mouse over. So it can be very difficult to to know whether you want something or not. Some of these choice are so good you don't know why they even bother making it a choice. For instance the first ultrasonic fence can protect all your trade vessles from aliens or it can not. And others of these choices are so pointless that you don't know why they wanted to bother the player. Does x building provide +1 coin or +1 production? And by the end of the game with lots of science you can unlock building almost as fast as you can build them and you get bombarded by these dumb questions.
So the game needs a lot of work but it's not all bad news. The graphics are pretty, the engine is relatively stable, and the setting is fantastic. Where else in a civilization game can you have super soldiers in power armor fighting autonomous death machines and genetically engineered zeno-titans? The factions seem to play to win, and are willing to go to war for it if there is a chance. The diplomacy model is quite improved by the addition of IOUs for the inevitable AI demands and the game is much better at telling you why you are being denounced or befriended. And the satallite layer feels less tacked on than say tourism in Civ5, even if the espionage system hasn't really changed.
There is a lot of promising stuff in here, especially the affinities which are new and very cool. The social policies offer interesting synergies, different factions can have dramatically different units. And it is a civilization game, it kept me up late into the night playing because I was having fun and just wanted one more turn. But I think I might stick with Civ5 for now.

Tacoma
by Fullbright
Genre: Environmental Narrative
Release: August 1, 2017
-----
From the creators of the enjoyable Environmental Narrative Gone Home comes another one, this time set aboard a failing space station rather than a dark house in the middle of a storm.
Space Station Tacoma, a cargo-processing point, has seen better days. A recent meteor collision has forced the evacuation of the six personnel, and Venturis, the megacorp who runs the station, has sent you, a lowly subcontractor much like those six, to retrieve the station’s onboard AI, ODIN, who ran the station’s systems. Along the way you have the chance to retrieve augmented-reality recordings which show life on the station, both long before and just before the incident, and rewind and view them from any angle. Many times they show multiple characters conversing in small groups, so this is to your benefit!
The personalities you encounter are colorful and memorable. They each have individual experiences on the station, and feelings about being posted there, and reactions to suddenly being displaced due to the incident. You can also access their AR Desktops, which contain messages and logs which further flesh out their characters.
I’m not saying anything else, so that you may experience the story as thoroughly as possible. Check it out if you love stories like this!

Brought this game because I originally had it on the xbox 360 with 400+ hours on Dungeon Defenders. Brings back so many memories with friends that I met on their. Happy too see this game still getting updated and for £9.99 is 100% worth every penny. This game is a tower defence game like 'Bloons Tower Defense' but in 3rd person where you stop the goblins from reaching the eternia crystal. In newer versions there are gamemodes like PVP which has recently been added. There are 4 calles that you can pick from, a Apprentice (Uses a staff), a Squire (Uses a sword), a Huntress (Uses a crossbow/gun) and a Monk (Uses a spear/aura energy). These classes can be leveled (Max level being 100 as of making this review) but keep in mind that this will not be an easy task too do on your own. Apon opening the game you will be greeted with 4 tabs, Online play (Up to 4 players can play tower defence or PVP), Local play (Single player/splitscreen), Credits (People who created the game) and Options (The config for your game NOTE: I would suggest putting 'Push to talk' on because it is obnoxious when a 12 year old kid joines the game with a potato mic). Clicking on Online play (Which most people would do) will bring you too a screen where it will say 'Ranked' (People take this mode seriously and cheating will result in a perm-ban on this mode) and 'Open' (Cheating is allowed and no-one takes this seriously on this mode).
Runs on medium end devices / Single player / Online play / Comic graphics
Overall I would rate this game a 9/10 - May, 2017
