A decent HOG in my opinion.
I wouldn’t say that this is the most popular of genres when it comes to games and I would say they are usually rated pretty low because of that fact.
The genre within itself is pretty cheesy. The stories are usually quite silly, making excuses as to why you have to find a load of junk amongst more junk and generally being pretty lame. But I amongst a lot of other people actually enjoy these games. They are a guilty pleasure for me I must admit. I used to sit and play them with my mum, seeing as they really are the middle aged woman’s kind of game.
With all that said when it comes to playing and rating hidden object games, I usually tend to just rate them by how bearably cheesy they are. This one being pretty bearable.
The story is interesting and compared to what I have seen of other HOGs, is a bit more logical.
I guess?
Most HOGs, you’re a detective or investigator of some sort looking for clues to solve a case, at least that’s a popular one, but even then in those cases you are just collecting random bits of crap. You know, a tooth brush, some hamster hair, a spade and a packet of hobnobs, calling them “clues” and wah-la! We’ve found the killer!
No, no. In Mirror Mysteries you’re searching for pieces of a mirror, scattered through different worlds and realms. There is of course the obligatory point and click “I’m not going to just straight up give you what you are looking for, first YOU need to do something for ME” so you end up solving a lot of other people’s problems to. But still, as far as HOGs go… at least it makes more sense. Which was nice!
The whole find/place mechanic in this game is something I liked also. You can jump in and out of scenes easily and in some cases need to jump back and forth to proceed. It’s not at all tedious, it’s actually a bit of fresh air. HOGs usually have a set screen, you solve that screen entirely before moving on. This at least gives you a bit of freedom to do more than one thing at once. Or at least, it feels that way. It’s nice this genre of game not being so linear for once! I like it!
Like many HOGs the resolution for this game is a bit low. It’s never been an issue for me, the genre itself just looks old and dated so low res has never bothered me. But I have noticed in reviews that a lot of other people take this very seriously! So just to warn ya!
Apart from that and the game being fairly short (which I sometimes, especially with HOGs, I actually like) all in all I would say this is a decent game. If you are a fan of the genre I would say definitely give this a try. Although I haven’t played the second one yet. Should be interesting!
TL;DR: As far as HOGs go, decent story, nice mechanics, bit short (I completed it in an hour), low res but generally a good game. Go for it.

At the preset time Novus Inceptio is in need a lot of work. Combat leaves a lot to be desired and survival is trivial. But allow me to expand of those two points. I should in opder to be fair preface this portion of my review by saying this game is very much in early release. The current state of Novus Inceptio is buggy to say the least. From trees that are transparent when viewing from the botttome after being cut down, to wolves that fight in super slow motion. Survial is a simple matter of standing in water and fishing for everything you need. A little disapointing, but not all doom and gloom. What do I mean? After the last update the Devs anounced they had some major issues. My first thought was, "Oh really you think?" But I read further... They plan to go back to core of the game rebuild / fix all the problems they are facing before they move on. I actually had to read that several times before I believed it as truth. It brought me back to another game ( I will not mention it's name) where the developer said mistakes were made in the begining and he's not going back and fix them. Sorry, the game is broken. I am dropping the project. Thanks for your money. The team behind Novus Inceptio brought hope back to my belief that an indie team could make a great game. They are going to core of the game reworking it till it's right, then moving forward with their plans to farther develop the game. It's not often you find a team that is not getting a large salary who does a total fix from the bottem up on a game. Kudos to you guys. While not a total game as of yet, it's worth the price of admission. If they continue along this path I have no doubt the value of this game will increase. OH, I almost forgot, they have to make this an MMO. Don't know how they are going to work it into the game, but I plan on being there for the journey. This game is certianly worth the money.

It's a good game for just chilling out in, crafting, gathering... Building rudimentary bases etc. Now I'll admit I got this in a Humble sale for like a fiver or like $6-ish
Also - Lore on the game, is contained in the store page, just read through the large description on the games page
Has huge potential, I'm getting Wurm Online / Life is Fuedal / Xsyon prelude, vibes from it which I am absoloutely okay with it, hunger and thirst don't decrease drastically and don't really distract you unless left for a considerable (possibly more realistic than most games) time.
Pros :
-Crafting is pretty easy, simple to grasp but does have a decent amount of depth and realism.
-Base building is the classic and easy to grasp "snap to" system where pieces snap to foundations you place.
-Buildings you buils are shown as blueprints and need to have materials added to them which is a nice change and let's you see how a building looks before wasting resources. Resources may also be salvaged from the buildings if they aren't needed any more.
-For a survival game it's more realistic than others in terms of you're not starving after 5 minutes of no food (in real time).
-Graphics are reasonably pretty, they're not the best but hey they're still damn pretty.
-Very.. almost Zen, due to the peaceful nature of the game atm - may change with some big combat update (Early access will be early access :P)
-Has a wide array of Graphical options available (for those interested in sliders and menus)
-Regular(ish) updates.
-Patience is required to play which is very reqarding over the usual instant gratification (personal tastes)
Cons :
-Building camera is more than a little wonky.. like Hold RMB and move using W/A/S/D or arrows but my camera when it go to move it after staying still to lay my blueprint bulding snaps to the point I started building at.
-Real time procedural generation causes stutters at times, not horribly but bad enough to cause yo uto become disorientated when you roll the mouse only for a stutter to occur and you end up facing backwards from your intended location.
-Requires patience to progress, this is a very... Good and bad point, for many the need to just jump and speed run and power level to a point of supremity is not catered to.
-Game "feels" early access. Some polish is still required to certain aspects and a lot seems to be missing atm. But updates are regular.
-Translation is shaky at best though credit where credit is due, it is a small team behind this I believe so... I mean if non are experts on language, theres nothing they can do.

Operation Arrowhead is a standalone expansion to last year's ArmA II, and comes with a new story campaign, a number of standalone missions, and a big chunk of improvements and additional units and features to make for a more complete war experience. The action this time takes place around the fictional setting of Takistan, where you'll tangle with hostile forces while infiltrating facilities, eliminating guard patrols, and hopping into tanks and helicopters to power past enemy roadblocks and knock out convoys. In case you've never played a game like this before, all I can say is before you bother checking out any of the content included here, play through all of the tutorials. This isn't a product that allows you to jump right in and feel at home with the flight, vehicle, and on-foot controls. There's a lot to consider with each mode of transportation and combat, and a specific procedure for doing everything from telling your squad to stay put in a location to ordering missile strikes from your AH-64 Apache by way of a ULB helicopter's laser targeting system. That's not meant as a knock against the game, instead just a fair warning to anyone unfamiliar with the product.

Tacoma is a very short, but riviting experiance. The characters are engaging and the way the story is presented is incredibly novel, and brings to mind the immersive theater performance "Sleep No More", in which all of the audiance members are free to move about the multifloor "set" and follow the various characters around as they conduct their scenes. Each of the miniature stories in the game is actually several interlocking stories, featuring various members of the cast as they interact with eachother and with the Station's AI. The folks at Fullbright use this concept to it's greatest possible potential, and truely explore how to tell a story in this format. It's stunningly done, and my only regret is that I wish there were a little bit more of it. As it stands though, I would rather have a short and sweet experiance than sticks in my mind, than a long and overwraught one that goes stale part way through.
I recommend this game for anyone who prefers games as more of a medium for story rather than something that involves real "game play". If you were a fan of Gone Home, Life is Strange or Firewatch you will love this.

Hmm. This game has great potential to live up to what we've seen in pre-release panel presentations and so forth.
There's a lot of evidence that the publishers doubted its viability - not just in how it was not even announced until it was nearly "done", but also in the state in which it shipped.
I'm happy to say that there are very few really bad bugs in the game - I think only two that actually affect game progress have shown up at CivFanatics. However, there are also a couple of really annoying quality-of-life problems that need to be addressed in a patch ASAP. These problems strongly suggest to me that the game was only tested on really high-end hardware, and not across a broad spectrum of machines. Possibly, because of the AMD logo, they did not test adequately on NVidia graphics cards, but also they seem to have not looked at the overall UI on a broad enough variety of displays.
First, an outright bug - on middle-of-the-road NVidia hardware, something in the graphics updating slows down the processing of unit selections, manual or automatic, and sometimes freezes them entirely; the unit info and commands do not update to the new unit and the big end turn/deal with issue button doesn't update. This is probably in the graphics subsystems, because if you use the minimap to scroll to an unexplored area, or alt-tab out and back in, or save and reload, it snaps back to the proper state.
Second, overall graphics quality. The tech web icons are not thought through carefully - the difference between a building and a wonder is so non-obvious that I haven't figured it out yet on my good-sized screen. The graphic effect for miasma, a key game mechanic, is so badly done that many players, myself included, have to read the tooltips rather than look at it visually.
Less enjoyment-killing but still inexplicably cheap, there is only one voiceover actor for all the techs and wonders. They have different actors for each leader in diplomacy, but when any leader is speaking in a tech or wonder popup the voice is the same one - I think it's Kavitha.
With all that said, if they fix the UI update bug, and modders continue to fix the graphics problems, the game will be an excellent addition to the series.
Caveat - if you're one of the Civ5 haters who loathes the substantial changes from 4 to 5, you may well hate BE as well. Calling it a "reskin" of Civ5 is completely unjust (unless you want to call Civ 2 a "reskin" of the original too), but it continues in the vein of less macromanagement and more story.

In my honest opinion, this is a good game that grabs my attention and I enjoy playing, as will many I would hope and imagine. However let me try and summerize all that has been said, both good and bad and explain why this works for me. The game definitely needs an update or 2 but as it stands it's a fairly decent game.
For die hard Civ fans this game probably won't go down well, as some have said it will feel like a step back.
For Civ V players and newcomers this will look very familiar visually (the maps, unit stacking/non stacking) and the gameplay is practically identical but with a futuristic approach.
For newcomers to the franchise this is a great game that you will enjoy, especially if you are into sci-fi, and it is not a walk in the park either. First time around it will really get you thinking and working.
So why do I say this? Well the new details really stand out and work very well. The tech web for example, it branches off so much that every game can take a different approach and probably should. You can spend 100 turns taking a radically different scientific approach to every other player in the game. I love this, it really means you have to think about what you want and what your colony needs. The choices are much broader. Quests are a lovely addition as well since they further seperate your company/colony from everyone else. Most new buildings come with an option to further aid your cities in one of two ways which means that, again each choice really matters. And the affinities are also a lovely touch as the art work gets a wider range and your connection to the planet you are naming your new home begins to shift and change. These aspects are what I think makes this game a great choice and fun to play.
But that's also the problem. They are bold and interesting choices but there seems to have been a few setbacks that were ignored in place of these. As it stands there are some minor art glitches, nothing too intrusive. The wonders need a total overhaul - they are nigh impossible to notice in the tech web and aren't even labelled as wonders until you research them. Admittedly the Civ V version with all the art work is great and I think I prefer it but this game is a lot more about the science and discovering the undiscovered, the new and the fascinating. As such the wonder art work is basically a blue print which totally fits with the theme. So I don't think that should change but I do prefer the Civ V version. And honestly, the wonders feel a bit pointless. They do not add enough, they are simply there.
The leaders/companies to play as have no backstory UNLESS you read up on them on the website. I really dislike this and think it should be in the game a lot more. The affinities make up for a lack of unique units/buildings but I still feel we could learn more about the future colonies and how they came to be. This is the future, the script is a blank page, an open book (excuse the puns) but I'd rather it wasn't left like that.
Finally the UI and the trade system - both need looking at. Now I am not one for hand holding, I love a challenge, but the UI is extremely difficult to navigate at times. The City screen is not explained well and when you find your buildings they take up almost half the screen. It's simply not laid out very well. And the trade system has had too much weight placed on it. This is basically how you generate the essential items for your colony to thrive as otherwise your cities will go into stagnation and starve. In Civ V it was a brillaint addition. It feels like here they have ran with it and gone "That was the best part, shove it in" then neglected to balance it with the rest of the game.
This seems like a lot of negativity but honestly, I really enjoy playing this. Perhaps I am easily pleased but I can really see the potential. This game could work wonders, but it NEEDS updates and patches. As such I will recommend this game....but don't buy it yet. Wait for a while, see how it grows and pick it up then. Try out the demo and see what you think yourself, that's the best choice. Then, perhaps, one day we will all make planetfall.

Oozing awful writing (sub-Babylon 5), bad stereotyping and bugs, yet its still worth a look.  Read on for more:
You're shipped out to a random planet where you are to compete with other refugees/pioneers from Earth for supremacy.  So much for the background.  Could be interesting, but they've pinched off a turd to rival Babylon 5 as far as story is concerned.
The Space-theme is infinitely better than previous historically-themed Civilization titles (for one thing you don't need to suspend disbelief quite as much as Queen Elizabeth taking on Ghandi, etc.)  But it plays upon awkward, naive stereotypes.  So expect wicked South American generals and Corporate-minded Anglo-saxon spies.  So its hardly progress in terms of story, but the space setting takes away much of the anachronisms of the older titles and presents a clean slate.  And at least the South American general doesn't chew a Cuban cigar.  I bet they were itching to put one in, though.
The space theme presents a clean slate, but what's written on that slate is rather obscure and eclectic.  Technologies  give no real clue as to what they ultimately produce, so if a resource isn't appearing on your map or your workers aren't mining it there's a good chance you've not researched the necessary tech yet.  Good luck finding it, though.  The tech tree is pure pseudoscience gibberish.
The aliens are tedious stuff, clearly knocked out by jobbing artists hired cheap by Firaxis.  Predictable and dull, there's nothing here to excite the imagination (H,P. Lovecraft wouldn't be impressed.)  The whole thing has that horrible, tacky feel of Star Trek or - even worse - Babylon 5.  Okay, nothing is quite as bad as Babylon 5, but you get the idea.  A lack of imagination pervades all.  You get your worms copied out of Dune, your green monsters copied out of (insert just about any sci-fi book or TV series here).  You get the picture.
The characters you choose from and pit your wits against, apart from being woeful stereotypes, are also incredibly irritating.  At no point has anyone bothered to introduce real personality or character to the colonists.  Instead they are a mess of dodgy, middle-class travel show memes.  So the African leader quotes cod-wisdom that would embarrass a fortune cookie, and the Indian leader turns out a steaming pile of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to match (because poor, miserable, third-world countries  clearly must have wiser leaders than established, less corrupt, well-run Western democracies.  I mean, everyone knows that, right?)  And of course, the Western leaders are greedy, spying, untrustworthy asshats.  Expect a lot of the game to consist of enduring painful Political Correctness rammed down your throat.
Lets face it, the Beyond Earth could do with a decent set of writers on board.
The game is as moreish as any Civ title, but it doesn't quite hold up in terms of being free of bugs.  The automated workers do some really strange stuff, including looping between building two improvements on the same tile.  Its as if they can't figure out which of the two improvements they like best so they swap between both in a neverending loop.
The explorers are just as bad, deciding that automated exploration is best served by travelling to extreme lengths of the map while ignoring the area around your starting camp.
The AI has a weird, almost schizophrenic personality where one moment its helping you and sharing a pact, then suddenly turns on you without warning and starts a war.  It's not at all convincing, and doesn't feel like a 'natural' betrayal, made worse by a diplomacy system  so weak it needn't be there.
Finally, my worst gripe is the end-game.  Someone has to win, but unless its you, you'll never find out who did.  The game just ends with a message telling you your dead meat.  It doesn't see who of the AI won, or how.  It doesn't give statistics or even clues.  Get over it.
And yet I recommend it?  Why?  Well, I'm hoping that the bugs will be fixed.  Perhaps an end-game stat sheet will be included in time.  Obviously the writing isn't going to get any better, but there's always MODs and DLC to fix it in future.  But the game is sound, and the space setting feels a lot less damned weird than having Genghis Khan making secret pacts with Winston Churchill as in the older games.  Sure the stories bad, but its not as insultingly bad as past Civ games.
If you're enjoy watching sycophantic holiday shows and think  people living in third-world countries are cute and wise because of their self-induced poverty, then Beyond Earth is the destination for you.  But I'd suggest you wait til it drops in price before paying it a visit.

If you played "Gone Home," deciding to play this one is easy: if you liked "Gone Home," you'll like this, otherwise, not.
For those who have not played "Gone Home," it's hard to advise you. This is not a "game" in the traditional sense. You won't be solving a lot of puzzles or making a lot of choices that affect the evolution of the plot. What you will be doing is figuring out what happened on a space station before you got there, when a number of events forced the crew to deviate from their original (rather mundane) plans.
Piecing together the story will feel a bit like unraveling a mystery, but in a very interactive way that a book or movie cannot deliver. The better half here calls this, "an interactive graphic novel." Until I think of something better, that's what we're calling it.
For what it's worth, we loved this and we loved "Gone Home," but we'll hold off of a third one for a whlie (fortunately, Fullbright hasn't put out a third one as of this writing, so that's really not a decision of wisdom so much as of circumstance, but we'd hold off of a third one if there were a third one, so nanny nanny boo boo to anyone who was going to point out that there was no third one as of this writing :) ).

Civilization: Beyond Earth feels like a weird hybrid of RTS and 4X. It's got all the elements of a 4X game; a sprawling tech tree, complex cities, etc. but at the same time has the pacing and focus of an RTS game: In Beyond Earth, you do not play to experience.  You play to win.
Perhaps that's what leaves a sour taste when I win a game here.  In older Civ titles, I feel like I've watched thousands of years of history unfold even as I've shaped and guided the people to prosper.  In Beyond Earth, I feel like I could have changed my build order to have one more worker instead of one more soldier by turn 50 and won perhaps 8 turns earlier. I don't feel like I'm building mighty wonders or influential great works; I don't feel like there is a living, breathing world of rivalries and intrigues.
Instead, I feel like I should look at my surroundings, beeline Transgenics again anyway while plopping out 7 cities and 21 trade routes, then setup internal routes to rush build the Mind Flower.  Game over.
Perhaps the victory conditions simply come too early.  Perhaps they're too easy to get; research a tech, get 13 affinity, win. Perhaps it's just that the imbalances of the game break the intended pacing; my civilization can easily produce 40 Science from its cities and 150 Science from trade routes.  My wonder city can go from 60 production to 120 with internal trade routes. There's no diplomacy; there's no war.  The AI (Civs and aliens) are passive to the point of apathy.  Abysmal health is meaningless. There's nothing to slow you down on your sprint to victory, and there's nothing to do but sprint.
Beyond Earth has great potential, but in its release state, fails to live up to it. Whereas Civ V could make an epic history into a quick game with the Quick game speed and yet still feel epic, Beyond Earth feels like a rush to the finish line.  The unique flavors of a faction go almost unnoticed. The affinity system feels like an extra little bit of something to do along the way, instead of defining HOW you play; your civilization is not shaped by the choices you make and the actions you take, but rather by arbitrary bits of research here and there when it should be front and center and core to the gameplay.
For a die-hard Civ fanatic, it's worth a play.  And it's worth keeping an eye on as it invariably undergoes changes through patches and balance updates.  There's a lot that can be done with Beyond Earth, especially because it breaks away from the historical nature of the 'main' Civ franchise: They can do, literally, anything within the realm of their imagination. And we've seen Civ V grow -- over time -- from its vanilla release to BNW; we know what Firaxis can do and the evolution of policies to virtues, of a tech tree to a web and other changes are all steps in the right direction here. But if you're looking at whether it's worth it in the here and now or are just a casual Civ fan, or just a 4X fan in general, you may be better off getting (Or just sticking with) Civ V for the time being.

Before I started to play, I read the dismal reviews and I went ahead and prepared myself for profound disappointment. I don't have a great system; I'm playing on integrated graphics with a processor that barely exceeds the minimum requirements. I've had a few FPS drops, but whatever. I was expecting an ugly mess, and I got a game that looks a little dated, but hey, it's five years old and still really pretty. The controls for keyboard were well mapped (except the notorious ESC key that exits the game immediately), and I didn't have any issues getting my Logitech F310 to work. Technically, I haven't had any major issues with the game.
Next comes the reviled linearity. Personally, I adored Final Fantasy X in all its linear glory, and I'm not finding this any more restricting. There's even a later game area (I'm not sure how late; I'm not finished with the game) with vast areas for open exploration and many side quests. Where it's linear, I haven't felt uncomfortable or boxed in. Rather, where it's opened up, I've felt a little agoraphobic even.
The story is perfectly sensible. If you pay attention, things will make sense when they're supposed to (and they won't make sense when they aren't, but rest assured that everything so far has been given a perfectly reasonable explanation). You're dropped into the middle of a confusing situation, the narrative is nonlinear, things are explained very slowly and only when it's necessary, and that's all fine and good storytelling. I personally have not felt confused except where I knew I was supposed to be, and anything that felt out of place or like some ridiculous deus ex machina device has been explained in a totally believable way.
I expected the characters to be annoying. I heard that Lightning was intolerably selfish, that Snow was basically a cross between Seifer and Zell from FFVIII, that Hope hopelessly whined all the time, and that Vanille was just utterly obnoxious. I haven't gotten that impression yet. I'm spellbound by the characterization because it's all about how the protagonists are processing traumatic events. Every ostensibly annoying thing each character does is a perfectly realistic response to trauma and the narrative does nothing to hide that. In that sense, it's carrying on the tradition of characterization in nearly every Final Fantasy game since IV -- creating strong characters out of their responses to past and present trauma.
I know I haven't really covered everything about this game, but I can definitely give it my highest recommendation despite not having played all the way through yet. If you're hesitating because of negative reviews, I say give it a try -- it's very inexpensive compared to the original price on the PS3. If the graphics bother you, there are apparently unofficial fixes, though I haven't even thought to look them up yet. It's a great game with good pacing, compelling characters, and a fast-paced though expansive storyline.

A depature from the dark humour of Hitman bloodmoney or the expansive environments of Silent Assassin/ Contracts.Absolution takes a bold step on its own and carries little resemblance to the Hitman series.

In creating a new take on Agent 47, new mechanisms are introduced and widesweeping changes are made to gameplay.
Pros-
* Graphics improved from Blood Money
* New story arc, memorable characters and excellent voice acting
* Greater polish to the appearance of the game, in game menus and ui
Cons-
* Environments of a map are now divided into choke/exit points that load to the next level. In prior games the mission starts with the entire map accessible, the level is now broken down into smaller checkpoints,
* Persistance is vastly reduced, player actions from a previous checkpoint in the map have no effect on the ai of the next level
* The use of disguises are made relatively redunant, enemy ai are almost always certain to see through disguises at the higher diffculties, leading to prolonged and unavoidable firefights
* Greater emphasis on an aggressive playstyle because of the new checkpoint system and changes to disguises, the only way to get through level transistion chokepoints is by run and gunning
* New point shooting system can be a detraction from the purist type of play and by introducing this mechanic the game is comparable to metal gear solid/splinter cell
* Reduced replayability, a high number of missions can only be completed by taking out all the enemies on the level, there is less room for softer approaches.
* Weapons loadouts can no longer be customised before the mission, players start each mission with fibre wire and ballers.
In summary, heavy emphasis on scripted missions and cutscenes. While occasionally this packs a punch, the effect wears off, and gameplay of the player is vastly funnled. Worth a buy if on sale.
Hitman Absolution sets a new benchmark in gameplay but in many other ways it does not surpass the standard of Blood money.

Final Hallway XIII - The greatest casual auto-pilot JRPG in the entire Final Fantasy library.
Well this game is a million years old now [obvious hyperbole]... let's talk about it.
On to the game play:
The first 20-25 hours of the game, depending on how much you love upgrading weapons and accessories, is basically a tutorial that eases you in to the battle system and crafting features.... Once you realize how easy it is, you'll wonder why they even bothered pacing you.
It's a FF game catering to mainstream JRPG casuals, just like FFX did years before it... flash some graphical T & A and the bro's come a running. Then they claim to think they know stuff about RPG's and believe they're diverse because they're playing a game outside of their realm of EA sports titles... *sigh* whatever... let them have their piece of candy.
This game basically combines the story telling and gameplay progression elements of Final Fantasy IV and the graphical boner inducing glory that was FFX, put them both in a blender and yeah, you get this... a great looking FF game with autism.
For the first 25 hours or so you are introducted to our motley crew of characters, their backgrounds, obnoxious personalities and how to set the game on auto-battle and leave it there until you gain some kind of control over your party.
The game also introduces the crafting system, albiet a bit briefly and never really explains much other than telling you that you can upgrade your gear and dismantle it or sell it for gil... Bringing me to my next gripe, you never earn gil in this game, only components and computer parts that you can sell for gil... kind of ridiculous in a FF title, no? So needless to say this game is artificially extended by the GRIND. Seriously the game is only about 50 hours long but you'll be grinding materials for over 80+ hours if you expect to get everything in the game maxed out... be warned.
The game's maps consist of linear hallways for roughly 80% of the game with only a few area's giving you some room to explore. Nothing is really hidden either, there are literally zero secrets in this game, everything is incredibly obvious and in your face. The map never lies to you either, every area is mapped out properly so once you hit the edge of a map, that's it... there are no hidden path ways... It doesn't leave much to the imagination unfortunately but at least you know you're not going to need a guide book to hit 100% completion.
FF13 sets out to tell a story, and that's exactly what it does, it's like the Metal Gear Solid 2 of Final Fantasy games... The game consists of very little game play and mostly cutscenes moving along the drama and unfolding the convoluted and confusing plot. At some point you'll just start disregarding everything everyone is saying so you can auto battle the next colossal, gorgeously rendered monster.
It's a great looking game, I'll give it that, it's just not a great Final Fantasy title... they stopped being great after FF6... it's just a sad fact. They all have way to many flaws in them to be considered great additions to the franchise and this is just another one added in to the mix of mixed bag RPG titles. Although I must admit, after playing FFXIII-2... it makes this game seem incredible in comparison.
I recommend this game for someone looking for a story to just disappear in to for a few hours a day but as a gamer who enjoys to actually play their games and delve in to things rather than just run back and forth grinding out materials... I'd have to say meh.
Thankfully I've already beaten this game years ago and felt like experiencing it again, so I'm in a good mood... other wise I would of just trashed it but in retrospect the game does look beautiful... and I think that's what SquareEnix's original intensions were... to just show case how powerful the new generation of consoles could be.
Either way, "bad ports" aside (what did you expect? I mean really?) It's like a 6.5/10 overall.

This game should be reclassified as a 'tidying up simulator'. The narrative feels as if written by an 8 year old... Lady with two children park outside abandoned house (I don't know why, they just like the look of it). Lady wakes up to find kids have disappeared into house. Turns out a talking mirror has somehow trapped them in his 'mirror world'.
To save your idiot children, you have to visit several different 'mirror worlds' (I don't know the exact terminology) and tidy up random junk. Each room is a still image - most items you can find without even knowing what it is you're looking for because they stand out like a sore testicle. Others are more difficult just because they're in a dark corner on the very edge of the screen. So you'll want to straighten back up to avoid unfavorable glare during your physical slump into boredom.
The 'puzzles' are equally as basic. You just need to click everything the game tells you. Even if you can't find them, the Hint button will glow every now and then, pointing out the exact location of an unfound item. Expect weak dialogue, for example: "I should've been a plumber, these pipes are broken" (even though she fixes several pipes and alike throughout the prior chapters). Most of the 'interactive' parts will be: find a locked box in area 1, you have no key. Go to area 2 - sure enough you will find the key - treat yourself to the previous area's elusive items.
You fix the broken mirror (did I mention the your children broke the mirror?... Mirror's crime was justified) and then (SPOILERS)... In the end, it was all a dream... Honest truth. Shocking.
I've played a few dire creations by this point, but I did complete this one, though I'm not sure why.

A very short, but nice fragmented hidden object game with a pleasant design and minimal plot. Definitely recommended, but only at a discount price.
The premise of Mirror Mysteries is fairly simple: the main protagonist’s children get trapped in a mirror and she has to visit seven fairytale-like worlds to get them back. The small stories featured in the levels are simple but charming, which is also reflected in the clear and friendly visual design.
The game is part of the fragmented object sub-genre, so expect a lot of tiny and well-hidden parts– luckily there is a built-in magnifying glass and the game does not resort to cheap tricks. The constructed items need to be placed in various scenes, but this is just a way to prolong game time, not a new puzzle element.
Still, the game is incredibly short, probably under two hours even for an inexperienced player, therefore it is only recommended to buy if you find it in a bundle or on sale (which happens frequently).

This game isn't terrible, but has a few fatal flaws that keep me from recommending it.
1: The movement is terrible, which is a game changer with platformers. You're too fast, you jump too low, and everything is too floaty.
2: The design. The level design isn't terrible, but by no means good, and they doesn't take advantage of the ink mechanic much. Some levels are just: Kill all the enemies, which coupled with the bad movement, makes them extremely frustrating. Some are fine, but don't take advantage of the ink mechanic.
3: Bad implementation of the ink mechanic. As I said before, they're not implemented into the game much, and some levels get split into 2 parts. The inking part, and the playing part. It feels like a marketing gimmick, rather than an integral part of the game.
4: Lack of variety. For it's price INK has a good amount of levels, but there is nothing else to add a bit of variety. Collectibles are in random levels, so finding them is a chore, and there's nothing else to do.
Other nitpicks: Hitting the level end kills you, which makes for very cheap deaths. Difficulty doesn't scale very well. Bosses are too easy. 30 fps, I don't care, but I'm sure some graphics snobs will.
Overall I'd give in a 6.8/10. Not terrible, but not quite good.
You'll like it if you want a challenging platformer that doesn't have cheap deaths, and are willing to put up with the things I stated above.
DON'T buy it for the ink gimmick.

Honestly, the game doesn't age well. The game design is about as simple as can be while checking off all the "necessary" checkboxes of the time:
Progression: Simplistic
Shooter: Obviously
Story: Barely
Katana: Yeah, but not as deep as you'd imagine.
It uses the same old tropes from all shooters: Introduce new "tough" mob by itself as a "boss" then later on make you face them more and more often until they're regular enemies. The AI will swarm you and body block you leaving you with no way to get out. The boss fights are long and tedious as well, often times following the "Do A until B happens and repeat 3 times" mantra. The swordplay, which is supposed to be a huge selling point, is about as simplistic as can be. It doesn't make a lick of difference which direction your going when you attack, it's just an animation and doesn't change how you really connect. You'll find yourself spamming your attack button with it mindlessly. As for the special moves, they all consist of double-tap a direction and hold left click. 1 heal, 1 straight line, 1 360 AoE, 1 wave. The progression system leaves a lot to be desired, namely it takes too long to upgrade things and the difference it makes is negligible for the most part.
If you want a very simplistic shooter, then sure, but if you want something more deep and satisfying? Look elsewhere. The graphics 4 years later already look 8 years old with muddy textures, absurd amounts of bloom, and blocky models.
Maybe worth $5-10 now, not the $40 it currently is as of this review. Best of all, from my understanding, the second one is viewed as worse as the progression system went the way of a very grindy Borderlands, but with less flavor.

Originally released in 4 parts, Aldorlea now brings Arvale to Steam as a full game ---- and it's a very good presentation.
Opening at the castle of Entoque we find our main character, Duncan, who is a gardener for the king but has apparently been at the center of world saving activities in years gone by. The problem is that he has no memory of what transpired. And so the story begins as the king sends him on a simple mission, and Duncan slowly learns more about his past, and how to uncover the details ---- which is critical because dark forces are gathering once again.
There are a ton of things to do (with a good number of side quests), things to find, people to recruit and interact with, dungeons/mazes to explore, monsters to deal with, weapons and spells to master, and a narrator to interact with as you move through the land. The narrator is full of good humor, and adds an interesting perspective to the events of the game, as well as being very helpful to the beginning player.
There is as much interaction with non playing characters as I've seen in this type of game in a very long time ---- but it all adds to the exploring aspect. And this is a game where anything and everything needs to be examined for clues and information.
The artwork is beautiful throughout with battle scenes being especially well done.
Music is excellent without being obtrusive.
And there are plenty of cut scenes adding to the story.
The care and attention to detail in Arvale are easy to see and certainly enjoy throughout this well crafted game that would be a fine choice for any player of any age, of any experience. A first-rate and engaging rpg adventure.

I have no experience with any of the other "Assassin's Creed" games, so I can not compare those with this one. I was curious about his game since in recent history with Johnny Depp and "Pirates of the Carribean" and also the the Starz movie channel series "Black Sails" I thought I would give this game a chance.
The game has a good story. A very involved one with some good twists and turns as you go along.
The game handles well. The main character has those Parkour skills of the other Creed games and can climb while running and jumping almost anything you come across. I was not used to playing a game like this but got into it real easy.
If you are mature enough to have seen "Black Sails" you will see the same characters of the real history of pirates. These people were real and that kind of makes the game more cool. It also follows the similar plot lines about keeping Nassau free.
All the things pirates do you get to enjoy also. Gun fights, sword fights and even fist fights. You get a ship and go and plunder all the big and little ships you want. You get upgrades and find upgrades with pirate maps you find on dead pirates. Earing money through missions, plundering ships, ,wharehouses and even pick pocketing. You also can hunt sea creatures and sell skins from them. Lots of different ways to make money.
A couple of things I did not like. Not to give away to much of the story here but you play 90+ percent of the game as Edward Kenway. That is the good part. But you are a person in the here and now as Edwards decedent. You hook up to a computer and download memories. That is the bad part. You get taken out of the Edward part of the game and have to play a slow moving FPS person that gets told what to do by a guy. That is the second story and you have to do some not so fun things before you get back to playing as Edward. There is not much time involved in that but it takes the rythm out of the game.
Another part I got tired of is that you collect Animus shards which have nothing to do with pirating but with the lame part of the game. You can skip that if you want to. You also stop at every little island and grab loot. Fun at first but the constant swimming gets old as you are getting tons of stuff. Later in the game you can stand near a row boat and instantly get back to your ship. I would have liked that for the loot collecting.
The game has great story telling. It has stealth and action. It gives you many ways to accomplish your missions. You can go guns blazing or sneak your way in, what ever you choose. I liked the freedom of that. You even get to manage your own navy. How cool is that. Lots more that I have not revealed so if you want to be a pirate then get this game. Only a few short lame parts to suffer through and the rest is high seas adventure.

I love Farming Simulator 2013 and so I really want to love FS15.  And there are things to really love about this game, especially the attention to graphical detail.  This is a much 'prettier' game than FS13, no question.
Given how much time and money they obviously spent on the aesthetics of this game, I'm forced to shake my head on how they managed to so completely screw up the physics, the most fundamental gameplay element.  The trucks slide around corners like they're greased in buttermilk.  The tractors and wagons act like Bambi first walking across the frozen pond behind Thumper. The whole game feels like an extended viewing of Olympic ice dancing and I half expect a French judge to give me a '6' on my routine.
I guess part of the issue is that I came from FS2013 using the More Realistic mod which, combined with the Soil Management Mod, actually caused FS2013 to approach the status of 'simulator'.  But this is just a huge step backward.  I can only beg them to quickly release a patch to both restore the physics to the FS2013 standard or, at the very least, release the Developer specs so that those more intelligent than I can do it themselves.  It's just a travesty that they haven't fixed this yet and I check my steam account every night waiting for them to finally get off their butts and fix this game.  As it stands I won't even let my 7 year old son play it, I just point him toward fs2013.  "The game is still broken and it's not worth the aggravation, son."
When the physics is fixed this game has the potential to far exceed the experience of older FS versions (and any other farming simulator).  Right now it feels like a half-baked developer version.

Gotta say, when i thought of a Farm Simulator, i didnt think of all the outside stuff too. Quick over view (may contain spoilers).
Main menu is easy to navigate, and the tutorials are definatly worth the time, if your new to farming completely i suggest the first map. Following all the tutorials gives you a good starting idea and point to get going. Start simple, not that there are many other options.
You always start a new game a with couple tractors a Tipper trailer and a Combine, cultivator and sower. Simple things you need to get your farm going. The physical limits on the different tractors are real (--99hp 78kwh can't deal with the work load of a trailer or sewer that a requires 150hp and 110kwh, it will still hook up and you can move and use the equipment still but it is very very slow going and it may stall it self out (stop moving)).
There are collectables scattered around the world "Gold coins" after collecting all of them all you get an increase in resources at your Silos. which ends up being turned into money, (after delivering them). The price of selling resources ranges throughout the game, Special deals pop-up now and than, allowing you to sell for double, or more at times, and the "message board" is a great way to help your bank acount in the begining.
Couple of Cons about this game, the AI for the hired workers could use some work, they can and do run into trouble, if a building or another hired worker is in the way (fertalizer just keeps pumping out the Fertalizer till empty and wont stop using it if they are jammed up). having said that they will try to shift postions to get around the obstical but wont move very far. The traffic are on set paths and don't react to your tractors or vehicles (they turn infront of you and crash into your stuff if its in the way while in a corner). They will stop but not quickly and they cant be moved either (if you run into them and you bump back or spin out without causing them to do anything except stop.
Hired workers also continue to sew and fertilize despite being empty with can be irritating as you than have to re-do it.
Once you get a few fields going its can become difficult to keep everything going smoothly without some help. Even though your "hired workers" will sow and collect, fertilize and plow for you, unloading cant be automated and some things like baleing (hay/grass/silage) is not able to be automated either, so you end up losing out on a fair amount of time doing these tasks yourself.
It has good multiplayer fuctions, so you can start/load a saved farm up with some friends and play together. Easy to join and setup in that regard. can even set it up so that your "workers" (friends or other players joining your game) can have a seperate account from your main farm one, which allows you to pay them.
Ive throughly enjoyed this game and will continue to do so, Personaly i recomend this game to anyone that enjoys the Simulation of Farming, and Logging.
My rating 8/10 for Playablity, overall Fun and Varience.

I want to like this game, but in its current form I can't.
The leaders are bland and uninteresting, and are reduced to bonuses, they lack character and personality. Probably they wanted to make each leader work with all three affinities, but the end result is a bland mess of uninteresting characters who seem to repeat the same lines ad infinitum, no matter what they are asking you.
They should have given them distinct personalities and affinities that they lean to and let us add a randomizer to said personalities in the options menu.
on the other hand, the leaders change appearance as they transition towards an affinity, something that was sorely missed since Civ III.
The affinities, they are, well, carzy in their own way, the more you clim into an affinity, the more disconected with reality they seem. Purity seems fixated on earth's glory, Supremacy goes borg lite and Harmony takes the worst from the Na'vi. At least if you go by lore.
The lore is interesting, but it is hiden in the civpedia, and has no easy access from the main map. this is sad because, like I said, it tends to add details that would make the game more interesting.
And affinity clim is too dependant on tech, there are quests, but they get repetitive after a while.
Worse, some of the recompense for affinities make little sense, like purity level 1 making your explorers immune to fauna. Also the endgame level of affinity is 13, that is too low and allows people to win in the midgame (or rather this game has no real midgame).
The endings seem rather unfulfilling, much like CiV, you only get a still image and a small blurb. no recap, no score, no history and no why that is a victory condition and defeat? there is only one in game, so loosing? puzzling and strange. I mean it shows a ruined settlement with a short phrase "we thoguh we were invicible". that is neat, so why did I lose is the question and why is it a loose condition?
There is no diplo or cultural victory and I understand they cannot be cooperative either.
so in this end, it is worse than BNW.
The quotes that came with tech are uninspired and, worse, instead of taking a clue from SMAC and have each leader read its qoute they are all read by the same voice actress, making them uninteresting and blander.
Tech progression needs some work, the web is fine, but some techs are accessible too soon for my taste and too easily. protip: an oribtal layer is interesting, having use of that layer from day one, less so. keep in mind the first part of the game should have been player versus environment. you are trailbazing into a new planet! not just a reskin of CiV
There are no Terraform options, cut for some reason, leaving us with resource improvement, except sawmills, that we can do from day one. interesting, it is an alien world and we know, instantly how to build our structures there AND which food we can eat. no research needed (this is immersion breaking, imho).
Miasma is a poor man's xenofungus. it impedes units, cost health, but does nothing to cities exploiting those squares, which is inconsistent. Also it is difficult to see, specially in resource tiles. they should have gone with something orangeish or purplish or even iridicent.
The AI can't fight it's way out of a paper bag. I know 1upt was done to kill the stacks of doom, but the AI isn't up to using it effectively, they could use the stacks, though. my advice here would be to eiher go back to stacks or get rid of impassable terrain, we need to minimize obstacles for the AI, with open, larger maps and more movement points per unit so that the AI might be able to do something with its units other than getting slaughtered by the player.
I know this is no SMAC, hell calling it a SMAC successor would be insulting for the fifteen year old game, and I know the devs told us, repeatedly this was no SMAC 2. It Shows. If you consider they started with a mature engine (CiV + expansions) then it is inexcusable for the game to be such an unbalanced mess.
I tried to keep comparisions between BE and SMAC as short as possible, but no matter what the devs say, the comparision is easy and obvious: there aren't many colonize an alien planet games (SMAC/X, Pandora and this one)
Bottom line? I'd say wait and see, patches and expansions might change the game for the better.

Where to start with this title? Firstly I'll get it out of the way and say it's a good game, no question. It's far from perfect but if you like civilization then you will like this title.
I fear the single downfall of this game lies in the development. It's as if Firaxis did not have a large enough budget to fully complete this game to make it unique. There are a couple things that bother me with the game so far, the voice acting and it's oh-so-similar CIV 5 likeness. Maybe this was my own fault coming in to this game expecting something COMPLETELY different or something similar to Alpha Centauri. Not that any of these reasons are terrible but I think I worked it up in my head that this game was going to be the perfect blend of Alpha Centauri And Civ 5. It's not, it's good but far from a breakout series.
The sole thing I would say about the voice acting is that it needs more work. Each civ does have a unique voice actor but when wonders are complete or you're read a definition you get the voice actor who also voices the Kavithan Protectorate. Should this bother me? I think I was just spoiled with Civ 4 and Civ 5.
On to the good stuff - There were a few things I really liked almost immediately after starting. The futuristic theme lends more capabilities and options for the familiar civ player to start with. I love planetfall, this is basically the enactment of your ship touching down and establishing your first colony on the planet you choose. Before this you are allowed to tweak how you start and what starting benefits your sponsor and civilization get. These options range from scientific, cultural to militaristic benefits to help you mould your civ before you start planetfall, Pretty cool stuff.
The addition to upgrading your military was a very nice change. Depending on how you steer your civilization this can define what type of militaristic units you get. The 3 directions you can split in to are determined by how you research your technologies. Researching technologies can give you points towards an affinity which can affect your military in very unique ways. This is in addition to veterancy which was not removed but instead improved on.
Overall I would say this is a great title. I have been playing it since release and don't foresee stopping any time soon.

now that I've got that out of the way: Civilization: Beyond Earth is just that, Beyond Earth. it feels like any other Civ game, other than it started after a previous game's space race victory.
Pro's:
Affinity System: you get to choose how humanity adapts to a new planet. Do they terraform the planet into a new earth (purity), do they adapt their bodies and way of life to the planet(Harmony), or do the Modify themselves AND the planet to be perfect via technology(Supremacy).
Alien "Barbarians": aliens replace barbarians and feel relevent for the whole game. they just work better.
Awesome end game units: From Giant aliens attacking from the orbital layer to a giant robot which can't help but remind me of  the book/radio story "The War Of The Worlds"
Tech Web: you have control over where your technology goes, though you will usually end up following  the same pattern at the beginning so you can work the tiles/ access the units.
Con's:
The Harmony affinity never gets an "Ignored by aliens" or a "Aliens will never attack you", which they really should be getting.
Game just feels like Civilization "In Space": I can't put my finger on it, but something is just missing.
While previous games sometimes felt hard to avoid war, with 4 of the ways to win not even requiring you to go near other Civs you really just never seem to have interact with them unless you go for the domination victory, which is really hard to do before someone else wins (I had to turn off all other victory types to do it)
Hard to lose the Civ mindset: You are not some giant Civilization in this game, you are trying to preserve Humanity, if another "Colony" is offers you a deal that looks one-sided "Because things aren't that great over here" understand the difference in setting than that of previous game. Until you realize that difference, both in phrasing and in situation, all the deals are going to seem Mean and one-sided.
Summery:
This is a good entry into the Civilization series, but not the big jump you might think it would be by leaving earth. As long as you remember to adjust your mindset away from running a Civilization over to running a Colony, you can play it as you have all the previous games. It's still a good game, just not as big of a change you might have been expecting.

Freedom Fall is a short and quirky platformer. There are a few "descend the tower" games on Steam but this one in particular stood out for me as more well polished graphics wise. Freedom Fall is probably one of the easier ones once you get the hang of it but I enjoyed playing a few times. Despite the entire game being played out in a castle tower there was a lot of environment diversity. Each set of stages felt like a different location from the gardens to the aqueducts. Since you play through the stages quickly no stage ever gets stale.
The story is told by the princesses' writings on the walls. As you descend she'd leave you notes either berating you or talking about her family. It was all very lighthearted and funny to read as you descended the tower. For a character we race a few times and meet at the end of the game her personality really shone through her writing. And while the 3 endings aren't terribly different from each other the replay value that this game has is based on the layer challenges of time trial, no death count and most cogs collected.
Usually the game provides you with a 'hard' and 'easy' path to follow integrated into your journey so you only need to choose which path to travel. For an even easier play there are 3 accessories you can purchase This is also a game where achievements add a second layer of replay ability. Can you get through the game without buying anything, or how about no deaths ever? These are just a few of the challenges achievements that add value. I found this game to be interesting and a bit of a challenge that killed a few hours.

A great little game overall. If the story telling type games are your thing, I can recommend this for sure. The casting of the player as an investigator after an event on a space station, was a clever way to make a mostly hands off role have meaning. It is all done using a first person perspective, rather than the typical side on or 3rd person set up of say a telltale or a typical point and click.  I think this helped make the player feel there, as well as part of the story.
The graphic design is good, and at times captivating in its use of colour and window views of the spinning station. The humour is gentle, but effective. I thought the voice acting was also well chosen and done.  I really liked the flashbacks, that came in the form of walkng around the ship, while a 3D holographic playback of the now gone crew was left running, (Its not something I have seen before -- the closest perhaps for me being the memory editing in "Remember Me").
Its tempting to say it lacked puzzles. But having finished the game, I'd gladly play another of the same format. I think they got the pacing right, and adding more fetch and click puzzles could have jsut slowed that down into a griind. But maybe one or two more important decisions, or clever problems to solve would be welcome.
It had a relatively intelligent script. Like a lot of sci-fi, some modern political concerns are raised, but with a mostly subltle light touch. The influences from certain well known sci-fi films are there to be found.
I think Fullbright could set other stories in the same framework and 'universe'.

Espionage system - clearly not tested enough, anything beyond "steal tech" is too risky and too hard to execute.
Health system - not rewarding/punishing enough, when you are higher than -10, you are totally okay. Also makes Diplomacy nearly useless without luxury resourses.
Aliens - great replacement for barbarians, fun to fight with. Also, siege worm is amazing.
Virtues system - great.
Visual look - great.
New science "tree" (more like web) - confusing as hell and all the icons are poorly done.

New victories - seems kinda cool, but not tied in with gameplay at all. Emancipation victory is amazing.
New races (sponsors) - really basic bonuses, bland and dull characters.Only 8 leaders presented. Also - why the ♥♥♥♥ can you take artists as colonists and they apparently give you health bonus? Why? Who would do that? I dont get it.
Unit upgrading is amazing. Just need some work on affinity system.
AI sucks as much balls as in Civilization 5. Maybe even more.
No soundtrack. Almost.
Overall... meh. Needs some expansions and overall work. Not worth the money now.

It's hard not to recommend this, given that I made a 7 cent profit from buying the game then selling the cards... getting paid to play a game is never wrong. :-)
But even ignoring that, I had a surprisingly good time with it. Defy Gravity is your basic puzzle platformer where you have to use an unusual mechanic to navigate levels. In this case, you can shoot gravity fields that attract you or repel you and activate a shield that lets you ignore all gravity fields. By mixing these, you can sort of rocket-jump-grapple-hook your way through levels. Some timed jumping and obstacles that sometimes are and sometimes are not affected by the gravity are there to stop your progress.
In the words of a wise man, you're going to die. A lot. The game takes delight in throwing stuff in your way at just the wrong moment. But at the same time, it's surprisingly forgiving with how you swing around the level and you can often brute force your way through tight spots. "Hectic" is not a word you usually associate with puzzlers, but Defy Gravity can get pretty hectic -- and that's when it's arguably at its most fun. For me it hits just the right balance between frustration and challenge.
The graphics and sound are absolutely nothing special, but in terms of pure gameplay, this is value for money even when it's not 90% off. When it is, of course, it's a no-brainer, just get it. :-)

While this game may have a few sligh flaws (which may just be preference anyhow) I would say that it was fairly well designed, and captivating until the end.
The art style is very unique and well drawn, though I did find myself yearning for a bit more color and variation somehow... The game is trying to invoke a rustic, old and somewhat dreary look, and it succeeds in doing this...however, a little more color might have been a nice addition.
I found the lore and mythos of the world in Oknytt to be especially interesting, and the voice actor (whom I believe portrays all the voices in the game) does a very good job of emoting and providing enough soul to each character... I do have a minor gripe with the main character's voice, who is obnoxiously meek and apologetic, on the verge of sounding kind of saccharine...I understand this is to help portray the character as being a small, weak creature, but still...something about the main character's voice kind of bothered me.
Most of the puzzles and problem solving is fun, save for a few puzzles which seemed a little too abstract to really feel like "problem solving". Aside from these few subjective gripes, I would definitely say that this is a game worth checking out if you're into point and click adventures and have an interest in Norse lore and other cultures.
It's not a perfect game, but it's certainly a good game, and I feel like I got my moneys worth.
I would play it again, and if you've got a few dollars to spend and want to try a relaxing (albiet, kinda gloomy) game with an interesting world and cast, I would suggest that you give Okyntt a go.

I think this game is decent for the price. It's a unique concept, but gets difficult fast.
In the game, you play as a white square that spreads ink across the level. Walls, enemies, etc. don't show until you spread your ink onto them (I know that sounds weird, but there isn't very many other ways to put it). I think it's a really interesting concept, and the ink constantly changing colour made the game look really nice, but it can be annoying when the only way to uncover some parts of the level are to kill yourself.
Now, let's talk about difficulty. Make no mistake, this game is EXTREMELY difficullt. I'm talking N++ and Super Meat Boy grade frustration. Many other reviews complain about the homing missiles being far to accurate, however it's still possible to beat them, so I don't think it's fair to complain about that.
One issue I found is that double jumping only works half the time. This can be quite frustrating when you rely on it to complete hard levels. Many of the other reviews document this, and I think the developer needs to fix that ASAP. Failing a frustrating game is bad enough, but failing it because of the control mechanism will quickly get on your nerves.
I've completed the game (Man, that final boss is annoying) and, while it was difficult, I feel like it could have been longer. This is the kind of length you expect in a $1.99 game, not a $4.99 game.
TL;DR:
Pros:
-Looks great
-Music suits the aesthetic of the game
-Will keep you hooked for a couple of hours
Cons:
-Concept is unique, but doesn't work well in a platformer.
-Double jump, one of the most crucial moves, doesn't work half the time
8/10

Honestly, the game doesn't age well. The game design is about as simple as can be while checking off all the "necessary" checkboxes of the time:
Progression: Simplistic
Shooter: Obviously
Story: Barely
Katana: Yeah, but not as deep as you'd imagine.
It uses the same old tropes from all shooters: Introduce new "tough" mob by itself as a "boss" then later on make you face them more and more often until they're regular enemies. The AI will swarm you and body block you leaving you with no way to get out. The boss fights are long and tedious as well, often times following the "Do A until B happens and repeat 3 times" mantra. The swordplay, which is supposed to be a huge selling point, is about as simplistic as can be. It doesn't make a lick of difference which direction your going when you attack, it's just an animation and doesn't change how you really connect. You'll find yourself spamming your attack button with it mindlessly. As for the special moves, they all consist of double-tap a direction and hold left click. 1 heal, 1 straight line, 1 360 AoE, 1 wave. The progression system leaves a lot to be desired, namely it takes too long to upgrade things and the difference it makes is negligible for the most part.
If you want a very simplistic shooter, then sure, but if you want something more deep and satisfying? Look elsewhere. The graphics 4 years later already look 8 years old with muddy textures, absurd amounts of bloom, and blocky models.
Maybe worth $5-10 now, not the $40 it currently is as of this review. Best of all, from my understanding, the second one is viewed as worse as the progression system went the way of a very grindy Borderlands, but with less flavor.

This is a very nice little point and click adventure. Got ot on a whim because it's based on nordic folklore and was dirt cheep (seriously 0.49€ right now is a steal, It is quite possibly the best game you can get for < 0.5€ right now). And I'm really happy I did, the mood, aesthetics and music comes together to a really nice experience. The puzzles are for the most part pretty straight forward (with a few excptions) and the creatures you speak to usually tell you what they want or you will find contextal clues that will help you understand what you need to do, even if you don't know how to do it. It's not that long, took me around 7 hours to finish and was never really stuck for long periods of time, but well worth the time.
+
*A few really good puzzles that are not basic "use object X on Y".
* The atmosphere is fantastic
* The artwork is great, clearly inspired by John Bauer (swedish painter and illustrator)
* The music is stellar
* The use of the 4 runes to have various effects on each area was a pretty novel idea.
-
*I do think the narrator, while overall great, got a little anoying with some of the voices he makes and the pronounciation of the various creature names is pretty bad. This is probably the only game ever that I kind of wanted a Swedish voice as a option.
* The usual point and click problems by mashing together random objects to make a new one is pressent in a few puzzles.
Conclusion.
If you find it as cheep as it is right now, go for it even if you don't think you like point and click adventures that much. The mood and setting for the game might win you over. But even at the regular price it's still a solid recomendation.

Fullbright's sophomore entry into the narrative adventure genre presents a compelling look into a milestone era for humanity's endeavors in space exploration. Set in the year 2088, Tacoma depicts a world in which corporations both familiar and fictitious have succeeded in commercializing interplanetary travel and lunar colonization. Rapid advancements in augmented reality and artificial intelligence technologies are at the forefront of this revolution and also represent the basis for an unprecedented set of moral and ethical quandaries that have yet to be carefully considered. You're introduced to a uniquely diverse, nuanced cast of characters as you conduct your mission aboard an abandoned industrial space station. Exploring key moments in the lives and personal struggles of each of the crew members is done seamlessly through examination of three-dimensional augmented reality recordings that steadily reveal underlying motives and unexpected plot directions. Showcasing thoughtfully written storytelling and characters, Tacoma immerses you in a grounded sci-fi experience filled with engrossing moments of intrigue and introspection that doesn't feel all too far removed from reality we could expect to see in the coming decades.

I was looking for a calm game to enjoy when I bought Tacoma, and started playing the game somewhere around 2 am, planning to try it out quickly and then finish it after I got some sleep. One hour later I’m still awake, terribly tired but engulfed by the story and unable to stop playing. So yeah, I love this game.
Your job as a player is to find out what happened to the crew of Tacoma. To do so, you watch “digital representations” of the crew members as they interact with each other and their environment – kind of like a 3D movie you can walk around in.  You can watch these scenes multiple times – and you have to if you want to figure out what all of the characters were doing in each scene. Additional to these scenes, the player can also look through the characters messages, e-mails, chats and pictures to learn more about them, and explore their rooms in the “old-fashioned” way – by looking through drawers, for example.
Depending on how you play Tacoma, it can be a very short game. It doesn’t take much time to “watch” the story unfold, but there are a few Easter Eggs that are harder to find. (Plus there’s a dartboard and a billiard table you can use and waste time on, so yay.)
I know not everyone digs exploration games or “walking simulator”, but I personally greatly enjoyed the atmosphere of the abandoned Space Station. The characters are loveable and complex, the story is gripping, and there is so much to explore. If you enjoyed Gone Home or games like Blackwood Crossing or Her Story, you should give Tacoma a try.

Oknytt is a charming little adventure game that brings us to the strange world of Swedish folklore. Its traditional story structure and the excellent narration will surely captivate you too… assuming you can see anything in the unnecessarily dark scenery.
Once you start Oknytt, you find yourself in a gloomy forest, where a stranger offers you to tell a tale around the campfire about a small, insignificant creature and his adventures through a magical night. This sets up the perfect mood, because the entire narrative style is like that: a single person spinning the tale, imitating all the voices throughout the story.
Said story is like a folklore version of a road movie, where we accompany this small creature from the moment he emerges from his underground lair to the wide world above, only to follow the events that drag him around from place to place. His journey is about meeting the rich diversity of magical creatures the Swedish folklore can offer, each contributing their small or large part to the big picture.
Since the point of Oknytt lies in the journey and not the destination, its gameplay also follows a laid-back, easier approach. It is reminiscent of the old point ‘n’ click adventures, when games tried to captivate players not with action sequences but with narrative style and puzzles. Here, these puzzles are not exactly difficult because they use some weird moon logic, but because the player’s inventory is too crowded all the time to easily figure out the next step (prepare for some trial and error marathons). In addition, the game is dark as a moonless night, but a gamma slider can fix this to a large degree.
Oknytt will not change the world or the adventure game genre; but if you decide to play it, the soothing voice of its narrator and the overall innocent charm will captivate you for hours.
