I’m a long-standing fan of the Civ series and I’ve logged over 750 hours (!) playing Civ V. Needless to say I’ve been looking forward to this for quite some time. Unfortunately, while the new setting is welcome, I really feel that a lot of what makes Civ a charming and involving game has been stripped out – the core mechanics remain similar and the new tech web is a welcome departure – but it lacks the satisfying depth of its predecessors.
Something that you begin to realise playing Beyond Earth is how much the Civ series depends on a familiarity with its historical setting to give flavour and inform your decisions. You know that Atilla the Hun’s hordes rampaged across China and consequently what he might be like to deal with; you have an idea of who Ghandi is therefore what he might play like – their histories inform their game mechanics, but there are no such cultural touchstones here. Yes, the characters that lead each faction have certain traits, but they might as well be called “blue team” or “red team” – there’s no historical contextualisation or existing character to draw from and because of that it becomes difficult to care about them.
I’ve seen it argued that it’s actually the inverse of traditional Civ – that instead of having a pre-formed personality which eventually becomes more homogenised, leaders start out as blank canvasses which gradually develop personalities shaped by their tech. However, in practice I’ve seen little evidence in the writing that this is actually the case, merely that you mentally note that a faction is leaning towards one affinity and they might now shift their focus in one direction or another.
Additionally, because of the futuristic setting, it’s difficult to actually tell what you’re researching. Beyond providing stated bonuses to tiles or buildings, there’s no way to actually conceive of what the building looks like or its function.
That’s fine when it comes to basic buildings like the early trading posts and clinics but it really suffers when it comes to wonders. I know that a Bytegeist gives me a cultural and scientific bonus but what actually
it? The lengthy text descriptions do shed some light on this, but it’s hard to form an immediate connection with it in the same way that say, The Pyramids or The Statue of Liberty do. Wonders have been relegated to just expensive one-time buildings.
While you can argue that that’s all they ever were in Civ, a hallmark of the series is how well it hides the raw stats in each play-through behind charm and personality, something which is completely lacking here. This is actually where I really miss the little wonder cinematics which are also absent in Civ V – a little video could go a long way to showing what kind of effects that wonder has (something that Call to Power 2 did nicely way back in 2000).
This also extends to culture. Yes, a culture bar ticks up a few points every turn and yes you can build things to influence it but it’s hard to see what the culture is actually representative of. Culture implies a certain diversity and identity and that’s something that Beyond Earth really lacks, especially because there are no civ-unique units or buildings. That’s disappointing because the intro cinematic actually suggests a cultural dimension which is absent in gameplay.
The designers seem to be well aware that a lack of historical narrative is a problem and have introduced quests in order to give a bit of contextualisation and direction to gameplay. However, what these mostly amount to are just “choose one bonus, this or this” or “choose one action, find out what you get several turns later”, neither of which are particularly satisfying.
The aliens are a nice idea and welcome change to the usual barbarians, but they’re still more of an annoyance than anything else. They have rather unpredictable AI – they’ll ignore units and trade caravans one minute while decimating them the next – at least with barbarians you sort of knew where you stood. Also, once your Civ has reaches a certain tech level, they seem more of a chore than anything to deal with – all they really seem to do is pick off trade caravans which need to be tediously defended. I was disappointed that there wasn’t more interaction with them.
Even when you play towards the Harmony affinity which is ostensibly about integrating with the indigenous flora and fauna, there’s no obligation to keep the original aliens around and as they’re frequently in the way of valuable real estate, they just become cannon fodder. It’d be much more compelling to perhaps allow units to tame wild beasts with a certain affinity level and use them for more than just military units – then there’d be more of a trade-off between exterminating the bugs and keeping them around – and a narrative and gameplay reason to prevent other players from doing so.
Here I also think they missed an option to be really creative – different aliens for different worlds or even simply different habitats (curiously, all types of aliens seem to be found in every type of terrain) could lead you to assess if it was worth domesticating them.
The way that difficulty is implemented will be a familiar gripe to fans of the series. The AI has a base level and the way that the game is made harder is by giving the AI more stuff, not making the AI actually better at what it does. It’s no more cunning at higher difficulties; it just has more to throw against you. I’m not really sure if I expected this to change in a new Civ game, but it doesn’t require you to make more creative decisions, just more efficient ones. And the bizarre and unpredictable demands of the AI  - notably the “stop settling near us complaint” – which seems to occur at the drop of a hat, seem to have been intensified here.
That’s not to say that it’s not a solid enough game – the Civ franchise has had two decades to develop and the core 4x gameplay is decent, but the inherent charm, the soul of the game, seems curiously absent. It functions perfectly adequate as a collection of systems and numbers, but it doesn’t feel like more than the sum of its parts. All in all, in feels like a re-skinned and modded version of Civ V – but actually with some features removed; the religion stat added in the Gods & Kings expansion isn’t present here; you can’t win a cultural victory and the lack of diversity of units and buildings is disappointing.
That makes it hard to recommend even if it’s not actually
per se but it’s certainly a much shallower, homogenised game and a much less satisfying game experience.

I have owned dungeon defenders since it came out and i enjoyed the game alot. at first dungeon defenders was a fun game for me to play with friends and attempt to progress past the current level I was stuck on. However, as more and more DLC were added that were basically necassary to buy in order to have the best gear and fight the most powerful enemies, the game became progressively worse.
Nightmare difficulty, while a fun experience simply does not feel rewarding, as the gear that drops is almost never better than the gear you will already have. Another point here that could be good or bad depending on what kind of player you are is that at nightmare difficulty, it is nearly impossible to beat the levels solo. You almost always either need to have every character at max level with good gear or play with 2 or 3 other people who have the characters that you do not.
Possibly the biggest problem with dungeon defenders is the community. The community is teeming with hackers and pretentious high level players. There were many hackers who would hack gear and then sell this gear for real money to new players or young people who didn't know better. People who bought hacked gear by accident would not only be ousted by the community but would also be banned by Trendy Net from playing online multiplayer, while the people who sold the gear in the first place would almost never get banned.
If you are going to buy Dungeon Defenders, I would reccomend playing only by yourself or with friends, and I would also reccomend that you stop playing the game once you have gotten past the campaign on insane difficulty. The game is enjoyable enough until that point, with many different strategies and many different fun ways to play. Past insane difficulty, the game becomes a constant grind that almost never feels rewarding.
TLDR: The game is fun playing with friends until you defeat insane difficulty, past there the community is terrible, the game doesn't feel rewarding and the flood of DLC is a money grab that is basically essential to buy to get anywhere past mediocre gear.

As of writing this review, I have completed up to level 45.
You will die a lot in this game. This is in part due to the unreliable double jump and overall wobbly control experience of sliding on paint (the other part is that there aren't any in-level checkpoints, which can be painful at times ngl). Dying does leave you with a crucial advantage, however unfun it might be: the map that you have revealed with paint will stay revealed.
The game is also lacking some glaring settings options. This includes (sadly) a volume mixer.  Actually, if I am being more accurate, there isn't a settings button on the menu screen at all.
1)  The art is very unique (wonderfully pixel-y and rainbow in a charming way), and the music adds to the atmospheric effect. The levels get more challenging but not before you can master the crucial double jump and wall jump (to whatever extent possible, because as I mentioned above, they are somewhat unreliable).
2) When you expect to die a lot, it's a lot easier not to get salty. Also, playing in shorter spurts can help with this.
3) Most fundamentally, I generally enjoy puzzle-platformer games. I usually find myself drifting toward more story-driven puzzle-platformers, but this strictly puzzle game is still really fun to play. :)

"Hide in plain sight" - thats what they said in the trailer.
Boy I was excited about the game - the very first game I preordered, because it looked gorgeous and the delevopers seemed like they knew what people expect from a hitman game.
Like a child I didn't get to bed just to play it the second it was released. And for the first few seconds I was overwhelmed. It look good, the story didn't seem particulary well but interesting enough.
And then it all went down...
Lets go to the positives first:
- Beatiful! You have to give them credit for that
- Contracts seemed like a good idea
- Shooting mechanics are quite good, covering works well
- Some nice ways to eliminate your targets
- Kinda good stealth game
- Very good level design (visually)
CONS:
- An absolutely broken checkpoint system. It doesn't even save who you killed. Everything came back to live afterwards. Everything you tried to buid up to vanished.
- Disguise system is broken. Others have mentioned it. Hide in plain sight is only possible if the enemies are far away and you really really hurry up. Everyone wearing the same disguise can spot you. Like hundreds of cops would know each other on a personal level if they are hunting for a suspect. This was the point that killed it for me... Instead of thinking of clever ways of how to acquire a disguise that will get you through the next section they are utterly useless, you still have to hunker down in cover... Wait for painfully long periods of time until some NPC has finished the dialog to continue. Because, well, you wear the same clothes as him and the checkpoint is placed when they start talking, not when they are finished.
Wonderful!
Instinct lets you put your hand in front of your face for a short period of time because well... f***, thats why. Doesn't make any sense.
- Very restricted areas. There are magic doors that you close behind you and no one will come through the door - ever. The level is divided in independent sections that share nothing between them.
- The story gets really dumb and embarassing. They wanted to center it around our protagonist. And they could have made so much good with it, instead it turns quite obnoxious, weird and unbelievable...
- Killing in cut scenes. You might have heard that. It doesn't happen often, but it is odd enough that they even think about that. Worse than the killing in cut scene is that the enemy is being killed IN FRONT OF DOZENDS OF BYSTANDERS which is exactly what Hitman is NOT about. Ridiculous
Bottom line is:
If you expect a hitman like game, don't get this, not on sale, not ever. You are most likely going to be severly dissapointed. It is bad as a hitman game, they stripped it of almost everything that made it unique and interesting and not only dumbed down the gameplay to make it more accessible, but dumbed down the gameplay for no apparent reason because it actually makes it LESS accessible (other than perhaps lazyness when it comes to programming (I've been there)).
If you are looking for a stealth game where you can calmy time your next moves and know nothing about hitman, or hated the previous games, this might be a pleasant surprise for you.
Then you should get it. It's a catch for 5€..
I get that things need to change to keep a series interesting. And the previous games had their flaws. But changing all the central gameplay elements is not the way to go.
If it didn't say "Hitman" on the box, I might recommend it for being an 'okay' stealth game... But this is no Hitman, don't be fooled by it's looks. It's by far the worst Hitman game ever made.
Summary:
Hitman fans - Stay away
Stealth game fans - Give it a go. When it's on sale

21 hours into the game: Why didn´t I play this game earlier?
Finally a FF that tries something new!
Since I play games for the story in the first place, I love how many cutscenes and dialogue are used in this game compared to other FF titles I played before. All the characters get a lot of screentime so you get to know their personalities quite well. There have been some decision by characters I really couldn´t comprehend how they could do what they did, but until now all these strange decisions have been shown afterwards in a different light which made me understand their motivation. The story had some intersting twists up till now, wonder how it will all play out.
I played FF 1,4,7,8 and now 13 and up till now 13 is my favorite
(beware: I absolutely hated FF7, lame plot, lame chars imho, so if you loved FF7 I may not be the reviewer you want to trust)
The fight system takes a little getting used to, but once you get used to often switching, you will begin to see the potential and the fun increases dramatically. Be prepared to experiment a lot before you get a feeling which roles to combine and when to use which combinaton. Odin is the first enemy who will really test whether you understood the system (died a least 10 times before I could defeat him)
The music is typically SquareSoft. It´s elegant, complex and will help you immerge into the game world. A good friend of me misses the typical FF sounds, like the victory theme, but like I said before: finally a FF that does something new! Yeah many FF themes are brilliant, but after so many games they got very repetive for me.
For me this FF is much more an interactive Fiction than a game, which is why I love it.
Also it´s quite cheap. Squaresoft could have asked for the full price like many other companies want for their ports. The low price was what lead me to try this game and damn it would be worth a full price.
All in all it´s been a long time since a game got me hooked like FF13 did!

Ink has an interesting concept and a great musical ambiance.
Along with the colorful environment, it makes it a really relaxing game, that should be about 2 hours of moderately hard gameplay to finish for an average player.
The level design's clever, even though I've always felt like homing rockets are just wrong in platformers, but that's my personal opinion.
Controls are good, you just need to get the hang of them, just like in any platformer. I've seen a lot of people complaining about that, but before mentioning the completely off-topic Super Meat Boy, they should remember SMB also does require an adaptation period.
I loved playing through Ink the first few times, and I recommend it to just anyone, because even if you don't enjoy the gameplay in itself, it is still going to be a peaceful experience.
Finally, like every puzzle-platformer, Ink has huge replayability, and I highly recommend it to speedrunning enthusiasts, especially those who are new to the thing, because speedrunning Ink requires only perseverance and platforming execution, and you don't have to learn any glitches or daunting strategies.
It's a great game, well worth its price in my opinion.

text: It's a nice Diablo clone, but a little too much Diablo and not enough Diablo and definitely not enough Torchlight. You get gems and sockets, transmutation, unique item drops or rares with random stats, town portal and identify scrolls, waypoints, hordes of mindless monsters, randomly generated dungeons, and skill trees. Unfortunately you lose out on multiplayer, varied environments, and a demon filled story to paste it together. Torchlight is not unique enough to not just be Diablo 2 version 1.x. And Diablo 2 version 1.x may still be better at being Diablo 2 version 1.x. That said, if you're a bit bored of killing the classic baddies of the Diablo series, but don't want to do anything unique either, this can actually be a bit of fun as a diversion. If you are a big fan of the genre there is never enough to go around. I hear Torchlight 2 is a big improvement. Diablo 3 has fairly well righted the ship. If you just want to loot all the things maybe even try Borderlands instead. 4/5

This game is an interactive novel.  So if your looking for anything more than a story you will be disappointed.  However if you are looking for a story, this is a good one. Freedom Fall is a platformer game, in which you play with Marsh, a young boy who finds himself in the top rooms of a huge tower, in prison, but with the door opened - so he steps outside, and after getting through room after room he will finally escape.
Originally I wanted to write this section to the end as kind of a reward because I LOVED this aspect of the game, but as a recommendation, it serves it's purpose better at the start:
The game is a platformer with slight combat elements, and IT HAS A LEGIT, GOOD STORY. It sounds weird, but it's true. I don't want to spoiler too muc h - the princess who's taken you captive will communicate with you using paintings on the tower's wall - she tells about her life, family, best friend, while mocking you for being a prisoner who probably dies soon, has no friends (so she draws you a cockroach to have at least one pet :) ) - the princess actually has a great character - mix a naive, childish personality with the role of a princess - she kills the to-be-husbands she doesn't like without mercy, even joking about their attempts to escape the tower - while also writing things like she's having tea parties with her best friend (who happens to be a DRAGON).  And you're not invited.  Hmpf.   The game also features a checkpoint system, and this was a huge surprise - the game's story includes the checkpoints, the way you respawn at checkpoints are included in the game's narrative. The game's platforming is really fair and nicely done, but the story, and the way the game tells the backstory to the player is the most outstanding point of the game. If you're intrested in it and don't mind slight cute spoilers, check out the screenshots at the community hub, people created tons of screenies from the best paintings :)
The game consists 14 + 1 bonus levels, and plays like older platformer games - you collect bolts instead of coins, which can be used to buy a granades (can destroy some traps/objects to help progress )parachute, dragon wings to allow double jump and a hoverboard that's more like hoverboards should look like.  There are no enemies in the game besides two bossfights, but each and every level is filled to the brim with traps. Swinging axes, rotating spears, spikes, bladed wheels, bouncing huge explosive balls, mechanical venus fly traps, spiked chains and lightning. While this sounds overwhelming, the game really often divides the tower into an easy, and a hard side, so if you're not really up for a challenge or just want to finish the level in the fastest way, you can always choose the easy path every time. To balance things out, choosing the hard path will reward you more collectible bolts and ocassionally granades, if you want to collect the most possible bolts, choosing hard paths is kind of mandatory.
Speaking about shortest time and collectible bolts -The game is quite short, it can be completed under 2-3 hours for the first time.
But each and every level has a par value for shortest time, less deaths and most collected bolts. While all three can be done theoretically at the same time, it requires a lot of practice - but as it can be done one by one, it makes the challenge (and getting the perfect game achievement)  easier to get, while providing some extra gameplay time with distinctive goals. The game also has an achievement for finishing the story without dying - this is a little hasslework as you need to restart the actual level after dying (the game could use a hardcore mode which automatically restarts for you), this also requires a separate run. Every game can be speedrun in less than 3-3.5 minutes - considering one plays the game for fun, then for no death / collecting bolts / speedrunning (these can be done in level selection mode) - and the fact that there's three achievements which require three different ending of the story, the gameplay time can easily stretch into 5-10 hours for achievement hunters.
Personally I really enjoyed the game - I usually have low expectations, so I thought it will be an arcade-ish platformer with questionable platforming and randomgeneration, but instead got a solid platformer with great level design, easy and harder paths, a charming story and a really unique way to get to know that story - it may not be the greatest platformer of all times, but it's a really solid one, and I'm glad I picked this up in a bundle and played it.
Price-wise I would recommend it during a deeper sale (lowest price so far:5€) or from a bundle if you're not not into getting all achievements - while the story is good, 9€ is too much for a single gameplay's time and content. The multiple endings and collectible "on par" goals can create a lot more content and gameplay time for player who love collecting achievements - I can recommend getting it at full price only for them (or to users who wish to support the developer).

*Art-Really well done and sets the atmosphere of the game so well. The little cutscenes looked pretty low-res to me, which was disappointing considering everything else looked so good, but the overall artwork looks great to me and the cutscenes aren't a huge part of the gameplay. When you launch the game, it lets you choose 16-bit or 32-bit graphics; I was using 32-bit. If the game is too dark for you, there is a gamma option in the settings menu once you're in-game.
*Music-Overall, the music is very pleasant to listen to and I did not find it overwhelming nor too repetitive. There was one background sound that played in a couple of locations that got really annoying to me and detracted a little bit from the gameplay but not enough to make me dislike the game. At some point, I had turned the ambient sounds down a little bit but I don't recall if that helped with the annoying sound any; probably needed to turn it down more but it was my first play-through and I wanted to experience everything, which includes the background noises that add to the atmosphere (rain, thunder, crickets, etc.), so I didn't want it too low. You can adjust the volume of the music, the voice over, and the ambient sounds in the settings menu.
*VO-For the most part, I enjoyed listening to Brian Hall narrate; his voice just lends itself to storytelling and that is what this game is, someone telling a story. There were a few times that his voice got annoying as he was doing specific characters, but overall he did quite well (even if he didn't properly pronounce the Swedish words, according to others).
*Story-I found the story to be interesting, although I'm confused as to what the creature, the main character, was exactly. Then again, I don't know if the creature was meant to be anything specific or not. Some of the creatures were already familiar to me, although I don't think I had heard their Swedish names before so I got to learn while playing. The ending was a surprise to me, I don't know why because I know it was hinted at, but I was not expecting that to happen to the little creature. There is a lorebook that fills itself in as you meet the other creatures and as you come across certain objects; you can get to the lorebook via the game menu [ESC] and, once there, you can read about the creatures/objects and you can also listen to Brain Hall read the descriptions.
*Gameplay-Overall, I found the game to be fun. I got frustrated a few times trying to figure out what items I needed to combine or what I needed to give to who, but that could have been due to me being tired so I wasn't thinking as clearly rather than having to do with the game itself. I came across an old review on a website where the writer said the game doesn't give you any hints, but it does; almost everything is a hint so you just have to pay attention and think. After completing the parts I struggled with, most of them were "duh, I should have known that" moments; although a few weren't as obvious (make sure you play with the runes at the bottom of the screen, after interacting with all of the objects in the scene). Dealing with the Hag is probably the more obscure puzzle of the whole game, at least I think it was for me. The game has several save slots, and no auto-save so make sure you save every so often by opening the menu and clicking save.
In conclusion: I thought the game was really well done, I had fun playing it, and I have absolutely no regrets buying it. I'm not the greatest at putting my thoughts into words so I hope this review wasn't too horrible to read.

Freedom Fall has a great premise that lets you get right into the action. You're trapped in an enormous prison tower and need to work your way down to escape while avoiding all manner of traps and dangers. Along the way, you are taunted by very amusing taunts scrawled on the wall by your captor, a deranged princess.
The game controls wonderfully, and is extremely responsive. You can optionally get a few upgrades as you proceed, a double jump, glide, and a more controllable glide. And you can throw bombs to get past traps and barricades. They keep it simple, along the lines of an NES or SNES era title so you can play without being bogged down by the control scheme or number of options. The graphics are quite attractive as well, although perhaps more variety would have been nice.
The game is a bit on the short side, but for completionists, you can get a few different endings, play on a hard mode, and collect some in depth achievements. Definitely a pleasant surprise of a game.

This is an extremely charming game. It's a physics based platformer. The reason why it's so cheap is because it's a fairly short game (I have 100% on it, and I haven't been playing offline). You play as a sprite with the ability to shoot physics altering gravity and anti-gravity "wells". Think 2D Portal in which portals don't teleport you, they attract or repulse matter (including you). Apart from that theres a Bullet Bill jumping element to some puzzles, but imagine being able to influence their trajectory by shooting a well in the vicinity.
Now, you gotta understand that Defy Gravity hasn't been made to look outstanding. I don't know what it is about it, but I can tell the devs were doing this out of love for making a game.
Props to the music, it really clicks in with the puzzling around. There's no other notable sounds, the gun shooting is adequate.
Graphics-wise... well its a 2D sprite game. It's also very blocky, and I do regret the dev's choice of font for the menus, but this is me nitpicking.
The only true flaw this game has is how short it is. It's 24 levels with a hard mode for one more playthrough. It's arguably 48 levels long, but the difference between one half and the other is that you need to approach problems from a different perspective. A shame there is no climax to the game - it just abruptly ends.
I say it's worth the price. I mean come on, it's the price of a cookie. Develop your brain instead of acquiring calories ;p. Just be sure that you're fine with dying a lot to find the solution. Don't worry though for the longer levels - there are frequent checkpoints (in my opinion too frequent).

This is a nice, fairly short hidden object game.  Nothing particularly special IMO, but not a bad way to kill a few hours (it took me about 3 hours, in one sitting).  There are seven levels to clear, each with a few rooms, and you'll sometimes need to go back and forth between them to get everything you need and place objects where they belong.  For the most part, it wasn't too difficult to do this, but there were times when objects were particularly well hidden and I used the built-in hint system to help me get them.  There's a short delay between using hints, so you can't use them in a row quickly, and clicking on wrong objects a number of times in a row (semi-quickly) seems to active a similar cool-down period.  There's also a magnifying glass available to zoom in on the scenes, but that didn't seem helpful to me.  Besides simply finding objects and placing them, there are also a few puzzles to solve, which is nice because it adds some variety to the game play.  Only one of these puzzles stumped me:  the safe in the forest area, the 5th level, I think.  Rather than brute-force it, I went to a walkthrough for the solution.  The puzzle was to turn the dials on the safe until the symbols lined up correctly, but I didn't notice any clue to help me figure out what the correct symbol order was.  I did see clues for other puzzles though, so maybe I just missed them here, but this stood out to me as probably the main negative point.  Overall the game is generally fun and not too long, but there doesn't seem to be much replay value, since there are no achievements or anything.  And once you've seen the story (which is relatively basic, but helps move things along), I don't think there's anything really new to see in the game.  Given that and that it's $5 for ~3 hours of game play, maybe less because I wasn't fully concentrating on playing the whole time, I might suggest waiting for a sale, but if you like games of this type, you'll probably enjoy this one.
Worth it

I enjoyed this game because it's a very portal-esque platformer, except that it's much, much, much easier to die in this game than it is in Portal. In fact, dying is a good 70-90% of what you will do.
Basically you play as a gravity-mancer, which is a person who uses a gravity gun to create bubbles of gravity and antigravity. With these bubbles, you will redirect yourself, platforms, enemies, and platform-enemies to try to survive a series of increasingly difficult puzzles. This game requires as much skill in execution as problem-solving, and is more fun to play than most $15 platformers out there with better graphics. On top of all that, it's cheap. If you like puzzles, platforming and difficulty, you should definitely buy this game.

I went into this expecting a puzzle-driven game like Blocks That Matter, Trine, Gunpoint, Tetrobot and Co., or maybe even Limbo. Unfortunately for me, I was wrong: to me, Teslagrad ends up feeling much more like Super Meat Boy or VVVVVV.
The puzzle design is fine - I actually liked the magnetic puzzle mechanics themselves, and wish they were used a bit more interestingly. There's plenty of potential, with robots and enemies and all kinds of mechanisms scattered throughout the game. But the puzzles don't really get more interesting or clever as the game goes on - instead, the game increases its challenge by requiring increasingly precise timing and control to actually execute on the solution to each puzzle. Checkpoints are not particularly generous, either, which makes the many sections with deathtraps especially irritating.
I hate this kind of game. I'd much rather spend ten minutes of my time figuring out how to solve a puzzle than spend five minutes trying to execute the precise timing of a solution I figured a few seconds after encountering the puzzle. I persisted because the pacing of overall progress feels so quick - it feels like the kind of game you should be able to get through in an afternoon or two of practice.
Unfortunately, after completing four of the five boss fights, the game asks you to rerun through the entire game to find 15 of the previously-optional, hard-to-reach collectibles. Without them, you can't reach the final area. I already had 7 and this was still irritating to do, and the game smugly suggests you really ought to collect all 36 collectibles in order to get the proper ending, though at least that's mercifully optional.
If you love platformers that require very good twitch skills and pattern-learning in order to succeed, you might enjoy this; for an indie game, it's decent if unremarkable in technical and artistic terms. But if you're looking for a puzzle-platformer where most of your effort goes into figuring out how the heck to solve a weird puzzle room, and you like that feeling of satisfaction after
the design, stay away from this.

So Square Enix never fixed this port and still suffers 30fps and below framerate issues in combat because for some reason every HUD element of this game messes up the frame pacing sigh... so I'm putting my review to not recommended.

[Original review]
yes it's true, the port is sloppy due to resolution locked at 1280x720, framerate fluctuates depending on the HUD and USB devices and some cinematics are poorly rendered despite the steep download size due to pre-rendered cinematics (39GB of the 50GB download is cinematics).
As for the game itself? It's still amazing. A fun experience with a good, albeit confusing storyline still shines... even at 720P the game still looks gorejous.
I'm sure there will be patches (official or not) that will help resolve the issues mentioned above. The game runs on "Crystal Tools" Engine which powers Dragon Quest X and Final Fantasy XIV A Realm Rebon so it has the potential to run perfectly with even just one GPU... so it's obvious that this was a console to PC port that didn't quite get the work it needed so hopefully Square Enix gives this game a good patch or two and help fix the release date's marred public view.
The game is quite linear compared to previous Final Fantasy games but there's so much storyline that it didn't use a lot of filler like old Final Fantasy games with the necessity of grinding or other methods to pad the gametime which was nice. There's also auto-heal after combat so you don't have to keep wasting mana or potions (speaking of mana, there isn't any, only Tech Points (TP) for special magic abilties / summons). So the game was built to not be slowed down by tedious tasks such as grinding which is something many jRPG's are critisized for anyways. Plus? you replenish TP by score-attack results screen at the end of combat which makes you feel challenged to defeat your enemies as efficiently as possible. So the game gets bonus points for a little modernization.
Keyboard and mouse controls? They work fantastic! It's compatible with QWERT and AZERTY keyboards off the bat which is great!!! The mouse is smooth and effective for combat-use too. Left Click is your confirm, Right-click is your cancel/decline and the scroll-wheel is for cycling menus if you don't feel like using W or S. My only complaint? 0 is your Pause menu and ESC is "Quit to Desktop" which can be an upsetting surprise if you're not careful or know about the dreaded action of the ESC button. :P
Overall? The gameplay is still solid despite the port not being properly optimized on PC (performance and graphics wise).

INK is a game with a decent premise, though one that would take expert delivery to be worth any amount of money, as it's a concept you could likely see in dozens of free newgrounds games. It doesnt help that the game has some (intentionally?) slippery controls that feel awkward and obnoxious to handle, simple puzzles and easy enemies combined with instant death on any failure. What becomes immediately apparent is there are two reasons you will die in this game: the unforseeable and the poor controls. The unforseeable is an inevitability with the concept and it was up to the devs to make that trial and error gameplay fun. They failed spectacularly. In a good platformer, the issue should lie in that your obstacles are hard to overcome, not that your controls are hard to overcome. This is the exact opposite of INK. Given the premise, it was apparent that trial and error would be quite a bit of this game due to its concept. In my opinion, what the devs should have done is balance out the obnoxious trial and error with tight controls, fun enemies, and creative levels. This game is lacking in those three departments. Every level and enemy revolves around the fact that you can't see and have trouble moving.
tl;dr this game feels like being a blind cripple in a street fight. It fundamentally fails to deliver almost anything beyond its concept, and suffers heavily for it. 3/10

This game has the potential to become one of the best survival games on Steam. One of the things that I love about this game is its crafting system. In other survival games like Ark, you can instantly create weapons out of sticks and fiber. in Novus Inceptio you need to harvest Leaves, craft Fiber from Leaves, craft Twine using Fiber, and then use that Twine along with other crafted materials in order to craft a weapon. This complex crafting system makes every crafted item in the game more valuable and every new item that you craft feels like an accomplishment. Right now I can see a good number of different weapons and armor to craft, and I'm sure more are coming in the future. The world of Novus Inceptio is also a lot of fun to explore and there are 'Anomalies' scattered around the world that transport you to another area where you can fight enemies and find loot. There is also a simple quest system that teaches you new stuff and keeps you occupied. It's also a lot easier to create buildings in this game because of the zoomed out view (like in The Sims). The graphics are also nice but not as nice as other survival games like Ark and its more closer to DayZ graphics. The survival aspects of the game are also more forgiving, unlike in other survival games where you have to eat/drink every 5 minutes to keep yourself from dying and you need to carry 10 axes in your inventory because 1 axe breaks after 10 hits.
As for the cons, obviously there are still bugs because this game is still in early access. There are times that I would get stuck on an object or get hit by an enemy even though I thought I avoided it. Optimization could also use some work because I encounter some stuttering and frame rate drops every now and then. There are also missing sound/graphics effects such as a hitting sound and blood/debris when I hit an enemy/object. Also, development time for this game is quite slow because they only have a small team.
Overall, this game is quite good for an Early Access and you can already have fun with its crafting and building system at this stage of its development. The cons that I have mentioned will surely be fixed once the game develops more and nears release. If you see this game on sale and you like survival games, GET IT.

Civ: Beyond Earth is a good game.  I've played 15 hours and I plan to play for many more.  It has a different feel than other Civ games, including Alpha Centuri, but that's not a bad thing.  I understand that it is natural to compare this game to its predecessors, but to claim that it is a bad game just because you look back on previous Firaxis titles fondly does not do Civilization:   Beyond Earth justice.
Beyond Earth (BE) is about surviving on a new and hostel planet.  It is not about taking a civilization from humble beginnings to vast empire like the other Civ games.  I agree that Civ V is more fleshed out than BE, but Civ V is a four year old game that had many issues when it was released, but was improved and expanded greatly after updates and two major expansions.  I started playing Civ with Civ III and I really like Civ IV, but Civ V is so complete that I have no need to go back to previous games.  Beyond Earth is great foundations for what I hope are amazing things to come.
Yes, energy is money, health is happiness, and production is...oh yeah, production, but the game works differently with all three things.  There seem to be more maintenance costs for buildings, that's because its energy and most things use energy.  You can't just keep building cities and expecting everyone to stay healthy because you're on an alien planet and resources are finite.  I like the idea of trying to survive and keep everyone health.  The only way humans would expand on another planet is slowly and deliberately.  I like having to approach BE in a different way than Civ V.  Also, if you get deep into a BE game, things do open up and it is easier to expand.  I think of it as your people have been on the new planet for so many decades that they now understand it and have the ever important infrastructure to expand as they would be able to on Earth.
As for Alpha Centuri, it certainly laid the foundation for this game.  I have played Alpha Centuri, but it was around the time Civ IV was out.  I did enjoy it, but the UI is a little obtuse at times, as one would expect of Civ games at the time and before.  Alpha Centuri is a great game, but you can't go back.  BE is similar, but it is nothing but a good thing that I can mix and match my virtues and ideologies so I can get where I want to go.
Civilization:  Beyond Earth is slower paced and forces the player to think about how to specialize cities over just building what you want in each one.  I love Civ V and I love BE I'll play them both because they're different games that give me a different experience.  If you're a Civ fan, give the demo a try, if not, try it anyway.  I can't wait to see what the first Beyond Earth expansion is going to be.

Ranger of the Jungle is a half-arsed mobile port and also a half-arsed Chinese to English translation.
I like my tower defense games and I particulary like Kingdom Rush.  Ranger looked to be a decent Kingdom Rush clone so I snapped it up pretty quickly, but sadly it's not.
The gameplay is slow which doesn't make things easy, it just makes it tedious to watch a mistake play out.  The larger-than-Kingdom-Rush characters and enemies make the game appear even slower.  The characters - particularly in the towers - aren't consitently sized either.
The art, whilst generally good, is also not entirely consistent.  Some of the sprites appear to be at lower resolutions than others and appear slightly blurry.  The heros too are not similar with some cartoony and others more realistic.
Slow gameplay and okay art are hardly reasons to not recommend a game but when coupled with tedious stages that need to be replayed to level heros, that recommendation starts to wane.  There's not a chance you'll beat a map on hard without significant grinding first.
Ranger of the Jungle is a skill based game that teeters on the edge of time-based / casual gameplay.  Unlike Kingdom Rush, where letting an enemy slip through was a huge failure, Ranger will still award three stars even if a mass of enemies make it through.
The music is servicable but gets repetitive.  The stage music is badly looped and ends abruptly before a starting again.  The long stage play times make this really obvious.  The sound effects are pretty minimal and utterly forgettable.  With one exception: the enemy escaped sound is copied straight from Kingdom Rush.
Ranger's greatest failing is that it's unfinished.  Clicks sometimes don't register on powers.  Buttons are grey'ed out even though they are not disabled.  Button text is sometimes in Chinese.  English paragraphs just stop mid sentence.  There are no graphics options, including fullscreen or resizable windows.  There isn't even an exit button as, obvisouly, the mobile version didn't need one.  Keys can't be rebound and the only actual keyboard shortcuts are for selecting heros and powers.  There are no shortcuts to start the next wave, pause, navigate menus or skip tutorials.
Lastly some of the stages are copies of Kingdom Rush's, though generally mirrored horizontally.  The towers are replicas of Kingdom Rush's with only the dwarven bombard tower replaced by a tree called The Ancient of War.  The upgrade progession is identical with three general upgrades followed by a specialist choice.
All the similarities - and I'm being generous with the term - only serve show just how mediocre Ranger of the Jungle is when compared to Kingdom Rush.  It didn't scratch my tower defense itch.  Play Defense Grid instead.

I personally loved this game.
It had flaws (i.e. the last two bosses) but the good certainly outweighed the bad. It has a very hand drawn sort of feel, and I'm not sure if that comes from the fact that it WAS hand drawn(?) or the very aesthetically pleasing smooth lines and paint look. It's a 2.5D (of sorts) game that features 2D environments but 3D backgrounds and scenery. It's a really really well done Metroidvania, you will get powerups, and you will want to backtrack (If you're 100% it for the true ending like I did). The game has some few flaws thankfully though they're minor.
Pros
+Beautiful Art
+Smooth Gameplay from platforming to puzzling and boss fights in between
+The bosses are all rule of 3, so you shouldn't have to worry about them being too long
+The music is phenominal, every track (despite being sometimes a short loop) feels alive and doesn't really get repetitive
+Getting upgrades/abilities feels rewarding and solving a puzzle feels the same
Cons
-The final 2 bosses are very annoying when it comes to the general strategy of 'trial and error' this game adopts with them
-The story (while beautiful) is pretty lackluster, you're forced to piece it together by collecting the scrolls and watching little puppet shows littered around
-The final boss is the WORST boss. You can get cornered pretty easily if you're not playing it safe enough or if you're playing it too safe
-Some characters just really aren't fleshed out
very much and when the game reveals something about them it doesn't seem as impactful, as you don't know much about them.
I nabbed it for 99Cents cause of the sale, and god damnit it is well worth every penny, if you can, buy it full price and support the devs. 12 Hours is a good 'not too long not too short' gauge for this game.

Defy Gravity is a platformer with a simple concept:  Get from point A to point B by creating attraction/repulsion areas.  The game is simple but fun, and provides a good challenge during the second half of the game.  It can be tricky but the checkpoints are placed in such a way that you're willing to take risks and try new ideas to get past some obstacle - a very important attribute for puzzle games.
The only thing that is sub par is the animation (or lack of).  It isn't really needed, but the game has the GameMaker feel, a bunch of sprites just moving around the screen with a short walking animation, which I find kind of off putting.  It isn't important, but it should be mentioned.
If you like physics manipulation games or platformers, then I recommend buying this.  The game is $3 at the time of this writing, more than worth it.

"Gone Home" set the bar very high for this team. "Tacoma" does not clear that bar. If you can get that expectation out of the way, "Tacoma" is a clever and amazing experience. The plot is hokey and contrived as hell, but so was the plot of "Gone Home." The mechanic of following AR recordings around a stylish space station is very unique, as are the characters. Yes, there are 3 gay characters out of a crew of 6, so the game feels like it's pushing a fantasy a bit hard, but I think it follows in the grand Star Trek tradition of exploring contemporary social issues through a less judgy lens. Also, 4 of of the 6 crewmembers are paired up in romantic relationships, making you wonder if the Tacoma space station has a shortage of professionalism, as well as oxygen. But that contrivance allows for a richer exploration of themes with a smaller number of characters, so I let it slide. The good v evil tale is also a bit harder to swallow when the game itself suggests opportunities for a more subtle and foggy approach to the morality of its universe.

Mirror Mysteries is a rather mediocre FROG. Personally, I prefer FROGs over HOGs, so I might be a little biased in recommending the game. If you really like the genre, you may give this a try. If not, look elsewhere.
In any case, don't buy this at full price. It isn't worth it. I bought it at a big discount, and I feel I got my money's worth.
The game in detail:
# It has only one game mode. It's fairly easy, and the hint button recharges quickly. There's a random clicking penalty, that doesn't really do much (you can still click; it just makes the screen harder to see).
# The graphics are decent, but not amazing. The HO scenes are clear, and the objects are big enough to be spotted. There's a magnifying glass feature, that I didn't use at all.
# It's quite short. It took me just 1.5 hours to finish it, and I read all the dialogues.
# I've encountered one bug: Whenever a steam message (like "Friend X did Y") popped up, the screen went black. The game didn't crash, though. Minimizing the game and maximizing it again fixed the issue - until the next message showed up.
# The story isn't very engaging. Some evil mirror trapped your kids, and you have to save them by retrieving missing mirror pieces. It felt quite bland to me, but it wasn't too bad. Overall, there isn't much of a story, anyway.
(Note: I can't say anything about sound or VOs, as I played it muted.)

Nice little puzzle game going with the theme of physics based utility guns. In Defy Gravity this gun is a device that creates gravity and anti-gravity fields. Player can also issue a shield against these special fields, which renders him (her?) immune to the fields but not the "ordinary" gravity. Strangely enough, some objects (it turns out they're the
) are affected by the fields while none of the others are.
This makes for adequate puzzles: in any level you have to reach the end, while juggling between platforms and deadly blades. Dying is not a big issue: you'll respawn at a close-by platform and can continue right away. However, there are a couple of rather difficult spots, that might turn to be frustrating to get past.
Then again the game is rather short. In mere 2.5 hours I completed both the base game and the hardmode that comes after, has more difficult levels and slightly different rules.
If you like punishing puzzle platformers like Super Meat Boy or Adventures of Shuggy, this game is a nice snack (it even costs almost nothing). Musics are nice, and while there's no actual story, you will probably find it fun to be one of the universe's magnificent "gravitomancers".
Regretfully, I encountered a couple of bad bugs along the way. First, the game freezes if you try to start a new game without having Windows Media Player installed. So, you have two options: install that or disable music (by -nomusic command line option). Another one was even more annoying: apparently some video cards (ATI Radeons) have a bug that the screen black-outs every once in a while. Very annoying issue. It would have been game-breaking, but it turns out at least I could work around it by doing double jumps (jumping in the air... so yeah) or going to Steam Overlay, both that repaint the screen. It does seem that the developers are looking into the issue, so hopefully it'll be fixed sometime in the future. It turns out the game was entirely completable and enjoyable despite these bugs though.

Oknytt is a pleasantly looking point and click adventure game that I finished in about 7 hours. I purchased it on sale.
Pros:
- Long playtime. I didn't expect it to be as long as it was.
- Beautiful artwork. Every setting looked unique in its own way, and everything looked ominous even though this isn't a 'scary' game.
- The sound effects immersed me enough.
Cons:
- Too much loading between events, especially some of the effects of pressing the runes.
- The narrator's voice is borderline cheesy, and it sounds like he is trying too hard. And, was the narrator even necessary beyond the beginning, end, and chapter breaks? Also, most of the voice actors spoke way too slowly.
- Several puzzles are very obscure or cryptic, and there were moments where I simply could not figure out how to move forward.
- There isn't an autosave option.
- The rune elemental effects were too random to allow for any strategy in pressing them. I would just press them at random to see what they did. Was this the intention?
Overal, Oknytt is a game that you'll love or hate. I didn't particularly enjoy playing through this game, and the ending was a bit disappointing. I feel like this game could have benefitted from some kind of hint system as well as 1080p resolution given when it was released.

Let me first note that I'm not a Civilization super-veteran. I've played some of Civ 5 but not a bunch (I had to stop because it was so addicting LOL) and I don't have any expansions for 5 (yet). I'm coming to this game without a ton of background experience and therefore without a lot to compare it to. I view that as a plus in my favor because I can enjoy the game more for what it is, not for what my imaginative fantasy vision of what it "should" be. Moving on...
Experience to-date: played and won two separate playthroughs. The first was as ARC (normal speed, largest map possible, regular difficulty - I believe this difficulty level is called Mercury?, Purity affinity) and I achieved a Promised Land victory. The second time I played as Polystrailia (fast speed, 8-sponsor map, Mercury difficulty, Supremacy affinity) and achieved a contact victory.
Pros and cons will be stated for each noteworthy point as I don't think I have enough space to go into all the detail I want:
- Tech web. If you've ever played this other 4X game called "Endless Space" (dev name escapes me atm), you'll be familiar with a tech web. But this one is better. Here you have one single web, with different technologies interpersed here and there that are connected to their neighbors in a logical fasion. Each technology also has an optional "leaf" you can research. It's a bit tedious to work with if you want to get your hands on a specific unit, but it does its job very well.
- Units.
PURITY: The Purity LEV tank feels powerful. A hovering monstrosity, able to take and give a punishing beating. The SABR looks, sounds, and acts awesome. It will pulverize anything you tell it to. I'm looking forward to conducting a domination victory just to relish in every unit's power and majestic glory. The higher-tier units are somewhat- to very-OP, but on the other hand, OP units are the most fun to play with. Resources can be problematic, so I recommend going with large maps and abundant resources if you want to conquer the world, as other sponsors will gouge you for resources and will only trade favors when asking you for resources. As time goes on animations or sounds won't play, but that is probably just my mediocre PC struggling to handle all the awesome.
- Gameplay:
It's a lot of fun. In my first playthrough (as ARC), I formed an alliance with the African Union and PAC and declared war on        Brasillia because I felt they threatened my chances at victory. After knocking them out of first place and putting them in 5th, I carried on business as usual. As you get closer to end game, tensions with other sponsors that have a different affinity - even friendly ones - will heat up. So build that Victory Wonder ASAP before war sends all your lovely plans to pot. Second time I played through and got a contact victory I nearly lost. If the other sponsors had been more dedicated towards achieving victory, then I would have definitely lost. Also, if you form an alliance, choose your partner wisely. I made peace with Franco-Iberia after helping defend Kavithan Protectorate only to have one of my alliance partners (PAC) declare war on them TWO TURNS LATER. That hurt...
- Diplomacy:
Not bad. Flawed, but not bad. A couple of times a sponsor would offer a trade - eg, a favor for some Firaxite. The deal didn't benefit me, but I decided to play nice guy. When I hit "accept", they REFUSED, saying that *I* had to offer better. Screw that... only happened to me twice, so it's not recurring or game-breaking. Also most of the time the AI only wanted to give me favors while I gave them valueable resources - petroleum, Firaxite, etc, or most audaciously, HALF my science income (that really offended me). and wanted appalling amounts of things from me in exchange for just a few science. On top of all this, many won't give you jack when you call up a favor. This makes the AI, even friendly ones, feel unfair and almost impossible to work with. I guess being on a new planet is stressful for everyone else.
Overall, the game is worth playing. I preordered and got the map pack, which isn't bad. Is it worth $50? It can be. If you're expecting another Alpha Centauri (and you SHOULDN'T BE) or something glorious and pivotal, then wait for a sale. Because it is neither of those. It is a step in a new direction. A step Beyond Earth and what we are familiar with. Stop looking for the soul of your favorite game in here, because you won't find it. Enjoy it for what it is. And have fun!

I will lead this off with a caveat: I understand this is an early access game, and as such it is not feature complete or polished.
I wanted to give this game a chance, because I have played enough early access games to know that occasionally a few get through that are decent, but this game bears all the hallmarks of a game that is going to rest on its laurels, and over-sells itself in its marketing. Very rarely do I abandon a game, especially an early access one, unless it simply does not work. Novus Inceptio, in its current form, is now the exception to that rule.
Even before I started playing my eyebrow was raised when it informed me that I had to choose my fullscreen/windowed setting, and level of overall detail in a loader before the game started. Not a great start, but hey, they might buck the trend and actually integrate something into the main game ui at a later date.
Then I am greeted with a very unwieldy UI and control system, that makes me think twice about the original dark souls PC ports control scheme. It has been a LONG time (read: star wars galaxies) since I've seen a dedicated alt cursor mode in a game, since most games have contextual cursors, or just flat out do not lock your camera to your mouse (because I mean, what the heck?).
Speaking of the camera.. It has this annoying habit of zooming in to first person whenever you get within arms reach of anything, especially resources. Time again I would cut down a tree only to be instantly zoomed in to first person view. The same goes for combat, especially when there are no sounds or animations for creature death, you just hit something, its bar goes down, you hit it again then its on the ground and you're zoomed into it, obscuring the ui and disorienting you.
As I progressed through the VERY basic and confusingly laid out tutorial, I was confronted with many of the unpolished animations that I would encounter, as well as the frankly awful pathing issues and terrain naviation issues that plagued my time testing, including such issues as having to jump to avoid being sucked into the void of the skybox below the terrain due to terrible pathing and glitches, to having to actually jump over a small (and I mean like 2 inches high) mound because my character was unable to simply step over it.
The inventory system is something worth noting too. Currently, I can load my inventory up with as much stuff as I want (both my regular and A2 inventories), without any kind of penalties whatsoever. I think in my entire travels i was carrying about 3/4 of a ton of resources with no drawbacks at all. I'm sure they'll get that fixed too eventually.
And then we get to the elephant in the room; The crafting and resource system.
Holy hell, the crafting and resource system.
I understand they wanted to make it a bit more involved and realistic than most games.. but there is realistic and there is convoluted nonsense, and the crafting and resource system fall well into the latter category. Some people may find the idea of having to craft ridiculous amounts of components in order to make one functional object.. I mean, I used to have multiple crafters in Star Wars Galaxies, so I enjoyed that kind of thing.. But this is just ridiculous. Let me give you a brief summary of how to craft a hammer in game. Yes, a hammer.
First, you have to forage for resources (using two skills, mind you. not just one). You will need several stacks of vegetative resources, like leaves. some branches, and a bunch more leaves. Then you have to turn 3 bundles of leaves into a fiber. You will need 2 batches of those. Then you will need to make a shaft from two branches. You will need to repeat that twice for a grand total of 3 shafts. Then you will need to craft a Twine (despite the tutorial asking specifically for rope, so thats another thing), using the two fibers. Then you need to create a handle out of one of those shafts. Then you will need to turn the other two shafts into a hammer head. Then finally, you can assemble all the items into your finished hammer.
Oh, did I mention that crafting has a success rate, so that depending on your skill during any point of that process above, you can fail and lose ALL of the components you put into the craft. So if you fail on the final assembly step, you have to go back and do it ALL AGAIN. I do mean do it all again, because there is no means to construct the components automatically, other than processing multiple at the same time. In an age were we have games like factorio that allow you to automatically assemble components to save time, we are reduced to doing it one step at a time.
Honestly, it feels like inflation of the early game to prevent people from being able to refund, but that is just a conspiracy theory of mine, and is unlikely.
In short, the game feels like an attempt to cash in on the current survival game craze, but the devs spent more time and effort on their promotion and licensing speed tree than they did testing. Then again, that's what we're for, I guess?
As I said at the start, I would not recommend this game in its current state to anybody, unless you want a very unpolished and clunky 3rd person clone of ark:se
Also, if it does not show that I own the game, it is because I refunded it.

If you haven't played large scale turn based strategy games before, '4x' is the phrase most important to these titles for your research purposes, and I have no words to help you. Try the demo, it might be for you. I won't judge. Enjoy.
SINGLE PLAYER ftw! I like civ. I like civ games, generally speaking. 4x is awesome! Strategy and all that, good stuff. This game has very little. Much like Civ 5, which is the exact same game with different graphics and too much religion, the strategy is barely more than trying to research things faster than others and keeping your units on hills. In the same way that most RTS games are a rush to a stronger unit or to the enemies main base with a mob of weak ones, every Civ game has one thing in common. It's a race to a technology that never ends until, well, it ends.
The game play is slow paced at standard speed. Rather boring but as expected in a 4x. Single city turns go by quickly, giving the impression of progress while very little is being made. Before you know it, you are in control of 5 cities and can knock down an entire branch of technologies in the same time it took to research the very first from your lone starting point. Wonders can be built, the land covered in sci-fi strip malls with monorails connecting them for easy transportation, and a massive army of choose-your-own-adventure-bots can quickly be at your disposal for squishing those pesky aliens that won't stay off your lawn. All of this can be yours, AND MORE! Aircraft carriers with space ships on their decks. Soldiers riding giant beetles into battle. They even added an orbital layer to allow the use of AOE satellites that not only give you better coverage than Sprint, but also increase your gains and other cool little things.
All that being said, this is nothing more than a reskin of Civ 5. Sure, many game companies use a previously successful framework to build a new game around it's bones but this one is so obviously the same that it could have been a dlc. SHOULD have been a dlc.
You've got the same unit options from the most basic melee fighter (which oddly uses guns that will only reach the next hex) to the heavier tank like units. The upgrades for each unit are there, although shifted and moved around to appear different. Gaining a veteran status as a military unit grants far less than the previous game, giving only the option between healing the unit or increasing it's lethality by %10. This can be done a number of times, each giving the same options, until.. what? No more? Oh. Must be maxed out. Guess I'll make another one EXACTLY like the last.
Unlike Civ 5 where a unit can gain bonuses than make it different from the rest, allowing for a group of soldiers able to fight amazingly well under certain circumstances, Civ:BE strips this away with the affinities. Gaining a certain amount of the 3 options gives you a chance to customize the way each unit of the same type works, taking away the need for each unit to evolve to it's surroundings through combat, and giving them all uniform strengths that need not be trained. You don't even have to pay to upgrade the old ones, they instantly become a cookie cutter army. Sounds good on paper but in practice it makes everything you own the same. A choice made that can never (unless I missed something) be retraced. From now on, all of your tanks are this way. Forever. Simple. Effective. Easy. Lazy. This nearly prevents change of military tactics. Bruce Lee says "Be like water." Civ:BE prefers mud.
They come free, these affinities, with your choice of technologies researched and a few other small decisions. No, choosing one affinity does not close off the other two. With enough research, and an idiot opponent, you can learn every tech and raise every affinity to it's highest point to give your armies the most options available without them ever being battle tested. Ever. Sure, they are missing the veteran status and a few %10 bonuses from never lifting a hand but, in reality, this game (like Civ 5) has little use for military tactics.
Other than a few small things like the military unit upgrades and the lack of religion, this is a copy with new skins and new names. Every unit type in this game has a counter-part from the previous. Every technology and resource is the same scramble for location as it was before, only with a different look.
The only difference in units, aside from aesthetics, is the giant "ultimate affinity units". Oh, and they're all roughly the same as the next. Ignore terrain features, capable of taking cities, cost alot, hit hard, etc.
-Religion doesn't exist outside of affinities. They don't spread. They just make people like or hate you, depending.
-Culture spreads your city's reach and gains virtues that can be chosen, giving bonuses like.. well.. religion. No! Social policies! Yeah, that's it. All rolled into one. Easier, better the further you invest, and kinda cool. I dig it. Hate religion.
-Happiness has been replaced with.. health? OK. Sure. How's it work? Oh, it's the same thing? Nevermind.
-Barbarian camps become alien nests. They act differently, usually waaay more enemies. And there's 7 different types. Kinda cool. The fact that the exact same species of non-space faring xeno critters can be found on every planet of every game you will ever play is kinda.. yeah. From the lush jungles of [generic name] to the arid deserts of [generic name], you can expect to see the same 7.
-Cities start as outposts. They can't do anything yet. Give it a few turns and your town will be just like the rest.
-City-states become Stations. They trade the most basic things, like culture and energy.
-Energy? Oh, that's money. You can put down reactors (markets) for more if you like.
-Food is still there. Not wheat though. It's fruit and tubers. Yep. Space taters. Great with xenobacon and star butter.
-Quests! These are new! They give you options for your tile improvements and stuff, giving the opportunity to customize your expansion a little bit. Actually pretty cool. I like this. Too bad each quest is identical with every playthrough, with identical circumstances, and identical choices. But still. I like customization. We all do. These work well. Good job.
-Tech web. No tree, it's a web. Way better. Again, well done. It's not original but it's a nice change.
-Natural wonders. Appearently only Earth has cool places to visit. There are none featured in this game.
-Resources. They are fewer, thank Cthulu, but do the same thing. You get only so many from each spot, like horses.
-We love you day. Whatever that's called. It's not here. Cities don't want anything. No pearls. No.. whatever. Simple. You tell them what to do, they do it, and care not even the slightest if you are at war or the enemy is at their steps.
-Taking cities. Still reduces your happi.. health. What? Annex? Puppet.. space city? Seriously?
-Colonists! Yay! It's a tank thing that folds out into a city! Metroplex? Is that you?!
-Trade. Man did they make trade important. Seriously. It's insane how important this is.
Play the demo. It does not get better after 100 turns. I honestly hate to say it, really. I was looking forward to this.
And don't hope for a cool movie or anything at the end. Just don't. It's better this way.

Late to the party with a review.
I recommend the game, with caveats...
STORY
It will catch you off guard, in a good way. You think it's going to be another generic plot to give you an excuse to blow stuff up with attitude. But, before you know it you're involved in a mystery that turns into a traditional Japanese folklore tragedy.
However, the greatness of the story mostly unfolds during long movie cut-scenes, which sort of distances you from your participation in it all.
COMBAT
Combat is fun at first, but as others have said it gets repetetive. Slinging your katana around is fun, but mostly boils down to nothing more then a circle-strafe slash-fest with a few special moves thrown in.
The pacing of combat in the game is also stop-n-go. You will wander around an area uninterupted, then suddenly an arrene-combat-fest shows up with tons of enemies. So, you either have nothing to do but find the next place to go, or you're absolutely swarmed with enemies and trying to keep your head above water. With all the Serious Sam posters in-game, I guess the devs for Shadow Warrior wanted to capture that same frantic pace of swarming arena combat.
But... a lot of the tools Lo Wang gets are lackluster. The weapons feel sluggish, I guess to entice you to use the sword. The pistol is a single-action revolver that requires you to manually♥♥♥♥♥♥the hammer after each shot... unless you buy an expensive upgrade for it which lets you fan the hammer for fast shooting... that has horrendous accuracy. The uzi eats ammo like popcorn, and requires you to buy an "akimbo" (dual-wield) mode to use 2 at once to really be effective. The crossbow feels like a sniper rifle wannabe, but you don't get too many chances to really use it effectively unless you use it's (you guessed it) expensive explosive arrow upgrade. The shotgun is a double-barrell (upgradeable to quad), and it's so slow to reload (even upgraded) that you avoid using it. (It does a good job of mangling lots of minions, but is a bit of a pain to use on large bosses due to reload time). There's a flamethrower that burns up minions, but seems useless against anything bigger. A rocket launcher is good, but takes forever to fire the next shot.
Basically... all the weapons are the usuals from other games... but sluggish and not as useful. Certain ones seem geared towards chewing through minion enemies, but it's hard to find a favorite. It's not like "oh, here comes this big bad-a**, time to whip out the (specific weapon that works great on them)". Nope. I felt like I was always bungling around trying to find a decent weapon in fights, so most of the time I just stuck with the sword.
They give you two other demon weapons, but one is a demon heart that rarely shows up after killing minions, and you can only carry one, and it only insta-kills 1 minion demon... whoopee. The other is a demon boss head that tears through things... but you can only carry one and it gets used up fast. So, you only use it when you have to.
So, on to sword fighting... it was fun... but they added in a bunch of weird skills and abilities to use with it that are just awkward to use. You can upgrade "skills" that are passive things (that don't seem like they really make that much difference, so seem pretty pointless). Then you have "ki" (chi, life force) skills that you have to manually activate in awkward button-combinations: healing (whcih is useful), a shield (which can be useful, but trying to defend doesn't help you eliminate enemies), a "trap" that's supposed to hold up enemies (but when you have tons around it's a pain trapping enemies when you can simply just kill them instead), and a stun skill that's like the trap in that it's more useful to use your time killing enemies then wasting time geting a ki maneuver setup up that merely stuns things.
So... you have these matgic powers that seem about as useful as a tick on a dog's behind.. save for the healing, which comes in handy a lot... b/c you get your butt kicked a lot.
There is a branch of skills to learn for sword fighting that let you do power moves. Like ki moves, these are a pain in the rear of button combos to get going, but are far more useful ... and make sword fighting more entertaining. Plus, you can get other skills that compliment them, like healing some health everytime you connect with a sword power move.
The problem is that there's 3 RPG-like things you have to manage... weapon upgrades, passive skills, and magic ki powers. Weapons take cash that you find to upgrade. Passive Skills take karma (basically xp you get from fighting). Ki take crystals that you find.
I don't mind the weapon upgrade system. The ki system is annoying, b/c you don't know how many you will get, and you don't know what is useful until you waste ki on it ... and then you're stuck with what you unlocked if you don't like it.
The karma / xp / passive skill system is baffling, though. The game rewards you more karma / xp if you make combat more flourished. IE: if you just beat on things with your sword, you get less bonus karma then if you switch to a different weapon, add in special moves, etc.
This is baffling, b/c it essentially rewards players that are already awesome at the game with more xp to get more skills that make it easier for them... and it punishes players that suck; they flail around just trying to get by, and don't get much bonus xp and thus can't unlock as many skills which would help them.
They're trying to entice you to use the wide-range of skills and tools provided, but when you're just treading water in the combats it seems insulting to have the end of combat go "you know what, you didn't impress us much, you only get 2/5 stars, and a low karma bonus". Hey, screw you! I'm killing enemies. I'm sorry I didn't impress you with my survival skills!
Plus, I wanted to mostly use the sword... but I'm punished for JUST using the sword.
Likewise, how this bonus ranking is figured is bipolar. In one combat I used tons of skills and weapons. I got a 2/5 stars (low rating). In another combat I kill some enemies with a demon head laser, then killed the rest with the uzi... just 2 weapons. I got a 4/5 rating. What the...?! So, there seems like no rhyme or reason to why you get bonuses. So, eventually  you just ignore the gimmick, but it's still a bit of a slap in the face when you busted your hump during a combat and the game insults you with a low karma bonus score.
I think my only other beef with the game is that you may like using the sword, but you can only upgrade it by going through the story. And it's only towards the end that it gets completely upgraded... and OP. You can shoot shuriken while holding the sword, but they are so underpowered and there's no way to upgrade them that they just turn into ways to blow up distant traps.
WRAP UP
Overall, I like the game. It's a "summer movie popcorn" kind of game you switch your brain off to. I do recommend it, for the mindless combat fun as well as the story. But, I feel like there's balance issues when it comes to the weapons, the sword, combat needs better pacing, etc, etc.

The Stanley Parable is one of my favorite games of all time. I played the original mod lots and then bought this when it was released as its own entity on Steam. This game is the less of a "game" and more of an interactive story or "walking sim".
It's incredibly funny, really absurd, got lots of depth, makes you think, and keeps you really engaged. These qualities are the overarching reason why so many absolutely love The Stanley Parable. The narratror is great and the sound quality is fantastic. This game made me think a lot about myself and my existence, while at the same time it also made me laugh so hard I almost crapped my pants.
Simply put, The Stanley Parable (like other games such as Shadow of the Colossus, Journey, ABZU, Antichamber, etc.) bridge the gap between video games and other fine art forms like books and theater and art. You will not regret this game if you buy it. You will never forget your original feelings and experiences of playing it. It's a cult classic.
As an added bonus, there's also some really silly and weird achievements to get which make you think outside the box and boost the replayability of this game (which is probably its weakest attribute).
