This game has a tremendous polarizing effect on gamers. Either you love it, or you hate it. Hence I'm not surprised to see such mixed reviews. (Of course, the poor port is adding fuel to the negative flames, but I'll address my views on that later on).
So here is where I am coming from; I have NEVER played a Final Fantasy game. This is my entry point into the franchise. I have played JRPGs but not on the PC, PS3 or Xbox; only old-school stuff like Sword of Mana on the Gameboy.
I did not expect much from the game, as whilst I patiently waited for it to download, I read almost exclusively negative feedback on steam and on the internet. I tried to ignore it, yet it did leave a sour taste. I launched the game expecting the PC to practically burst into flames. Hence my extreme surprise at how much I am genuinely enjoying myself.
I expected the game to be "unplayable". Touch wood, but the game has not yet crashed/stuttered/glitched whilst I have been playing it. I have not needed to tweak Nvidia settings besides fiddling with V-sync; I did this after I had some lag in one battle with 6 or so enemies. After switching it off, the lag didn't happen again (I don't know if that was conicidence or not). My computer is not state of the art. I could list the specs but, really, it's not the newest nor the best. However, it does exceed the minimum and recommended specs listed below. I think that perhaps one should bear that in mind when buying this game; I don't know how well it will run on either listed specs. Perhaps ensure that you either hit recommended or exceed it.
Now, about the port. Yes, I wish the resolution wasn't fixed/I could adjust graphics or sound in game/the file size wasn't so damn large. But honestly? I am really captivated by this game. Perhaps this is due to me being fresh-faced. Perhaps I don't have preconceived standards for JRPGs and SE and FF. But, to me, the game looks magnificent and beautiful. I haven't even bothered to download the resolution fix because I'm enjoying the game as it is. Just as a side note, I am using a controller but I played for a bit with the keyboard and it was highly manageable. I prefer using the controller simply because I think the buttons have been mapped appropriately.
Now the actual game itself. The issues I saw on the internet about the game mainly revolved around A) a confusing story B) linearity C) rubbish characters. Here is what I think; The story really isn't that confusing. I have spent a bit of time reading the in-game datalog but I'm following it just fine. The game is linear at the beginning, but it hasn't exactly irked me up to this point like I expected it to. In fact, I needed the slow, linear, tutorialized start because I am completely new to the game style. In terms of characters, they all are fantastic. Yes, the infamous Vanille is poorly English voice acted and makes, um, extremely strange sighs and moans. At one point I turned to my sister and said, "This sounds like a dodgy adult film." But she is overshadowed by the incredible Lightning Farron and Sazh. Lightning is a badass, yet her pain and inner conflict is so evident and tangible. Sazh is just great. Plus he has an afro with a chocobo chick just chilling inside it, try and not find that adorable.
The combat is REALLY great. I was worried it would bore me, but it has not as of yet. With the tougher enemies you need to micro-manage the fights intently; using Paradigm Shift has been a really interesting strategy and I'm starting to use it to my advantage. Combat is rewarding and I feel as though this game hits just the right difficulty; not too hard, not too easy. Just right for you to enjoy yourself yet still be challenged, without getting frustrated. This is so rare to find in a game.
I know my views conflict with others, yet I reiterate again; I come from a fresh-faced point of view. I had low expectations that were exceeded by this game. If you are a first timer to the franchise, I hope your experience will be similar and as engaging as mine.

I had no idea farming could be so much fun.
Try to pitch this game to someone who doesn't know what it is about:
I just realized how boring that sounds. But that's the funny thing about this game; it sounds SO boring and bland, but in reality it is surprisingly fun. I don't know why. The youtubers I've watched playing the game also don't know why. It just is.
But.. once you've passed the 10-20 hour mark and start making real progress, have to manage multiple fields and do your best to come up with the most efficient flow, you start to get a little frustrated by the lack of automation in the game. Basically you have one option and one option only: when you have aligned your machine with the field, you can "hire worker" to get the stuff done. That's fine and works as intended, for the most part..
But the workers are pretty stupid. They get stuck very easily, and you won't notice until you happen to tab into the worker's machine, only to discover that the entire proces has been halted for 30 minutes because he ran into a tree while he was turning, and apparently he hasn't heard of this thing called "to reverse".
The game does not give you any feedback on workers AT ALL, so you have to constantly tab through all your stuff to make sure everything is running smoothly. You also can't make workers do "passive" stuff, like wait for a harvester to get full and then drive up to it with a tipper, or tell them to unload crops from the silo and drive it off to a sell point. In other words, once you have a handful of fields, you'll be quite busy monitoring the progress, giving work orders, driving equipment from one field to another, helping stuck workers get unstuck and so on. And that's where the tediousness kicks in and the fun factor starts to decline.
The extreme lack of automation drives most people to use mods, or, well, one mod in particular, called Courseplay. Obviously this is a review of the vanilla game, so I will just say this: while Courseplay does offer a lot more automation features, it is very far from perfect. Courseplay will have you curse at the screen repeatedly, because the AI is basically still extremely poor. Even though you can make workers do more things, especially the "passive" stuff, you still have to sort out stuck workers all. the. time. So don't expect any wonders, only a little help. And more frustration.

Defy Gravity is an action platformer that is a mix between classic platforming and gravity based puzzle solving. Kara, our heroine, has access to a unique gameplay mechanic that she uses to manipulate the world around her. She has a gun that is able to alter the laws of physics through the creation of pockets of gravity and anti-gravity. By mastering the use of these abilities Kara is able to augment her jump in order to almost fly past obstacles. These powers can also be utilized to move objects that block her path and platforms that Kara stands on in order to traverse the levels.

An Assassin's Creed game where you are a pirate. Do I need to say anything else? Probably the best pirate game ever. 15 hours and only 25%, this game is massive. You can play it the Assassin way, use your hidden blades and hide in bushes, or the savage, pirate way, using your swords as your main weapon, attacking without thinking.
Pros:
- Massive world: 50 major locations with over 70 minor locations and islands to explore
- Great story and TONS of side-activities will keep you busy for at least 50 hours, and if you want to explore everything, it would take you at least twice that time
- Freedom Cry DLC, where you play as Adewhale (you'll meet him in the main game, no spoilers), around 5-10 more hours of gameplay
- Amazing graphics - Even today the graphics are amazing
- Hidden locations
- You can take over templar bases
- Abstergo missions and side-activities
Cons:
- Really poor optimization, at least GTX 950/960 recommended
- Glitches - there are only a few of them and none of them are game breaking, but in really adrenaline-pumping missions, killing a templar and watching them fly across the sky kinda ruins the atmosphere
- Grinding - you have to constantly grind and upgrade your ship if you want to complete the game which, in my opinion, can get really annoying when you travel 30km just to realize that you have to upgrade your ship and don't have enough money to do it
- Somewhat repetitive - Tail, Eavesdrop, Kill, Repeat
That's all I have to say about this game. Don't worry about the cons too much because I can guarantee that you will enjoy the game if you like Assassin's Creed and open world games.

Nailing that feeling of satisfaction when you’ve figured out a solution to the task at hand is very difficult. Not all mechanics allow it and not all games offer more than one route from point A to point B. I believe gravity manipulation and physics-based gameplay is one of the greatest things gaming has bothered exploring. When done well, it is logical, intuitive and rewarding. It’s like pulling out that second to last piece of Jenga.
This is what Defy Gravity Extended is: an extremely satisfying game. You play as Kara, following the Samus school of power armour where you couldn’t tell the gender were it not for the game description. She has to prove herself as a Gravitymancer in the Gauntlet, using her sassy gravity gun (which looks a bit like a Super Soaker). The gun can set two kinds of fields: one that attracts and one that repels. This is the basic premise, and the levels are variations upon previously-set rules. You might encounter enemies who are also affected by the gravity fields, a level may turn your anti-gravity shield permanently on, or you’ll have to use platforms affected by your gravity gun as well.
The graphics are really basic, and I admit I was a tad skeptical when I saw some screenshots, but after 5 minutes into the game all my doubts were washed away. The levels are very well-made and reward smart thinking. The first few stages give you hints where to place the respective gravity fields, but you will soon realize that you can use even less resources than recommended.
The music is also really good. Now, I’m not a music reviewer and I lack the capacity to translate how music feels using words, but Defy Gravity’s soundtrack took me off-guard in a very pleasant way.
The only complaint I can think of is a lack of level editor, which seems extremely appropriate for a game like this.

Pros:
- mechanics are unique and fun to play around with, especially as you progress. This game had me going "wow, that's cool" at every progression.
- fun plot, world-building overall
- unique map that becomes more interactable overtime
- physics is generally solid
- every new section or boss is unique and reminds me a lot of both Zelda games in how you use new powers to fight or progress in an interesting way, and Souls games in that literally everything kills you (except fall damage apparently).
Cons:
- once you get to a certain point in the game, the rest of the content is hidden behind a fetch quest that I just couldn't get behind. It would've been fine if it were to fetch things in a new location, and that would've been both doable and unique, but instead you end up going through the same area you've been through before, and it's not very enticing.
- there were a few gameplay ticks that I had trouble with. For example. if you bait one of the bosses to a certain spot and don't move too much, the boss just doesn't do anything.
- Some of the controls weren't pre-mapped to my controller, which I only found out because I spent 5-10 minutes after getting the first item learning how to use it. To be fair, it shouldn't have taken me that long to realise that none of my buttons aren't working, but it was a little strange that they weren't. The only reason I could come up with is that the game's controls are fairly unique, so they should be mapped to what the user likes the best, but if that was the case it should've been explained that way.

Tacoma is a relatively short game (you'll play it through in about six hours, tops), but it is utterly excellent IF you're the kind of gamer who doesn't mind a purely investigative game every now and again.
There are no lurking xenomorphs here; no gun-toting badguys. You play an AI specialist sent to recover a dormant AI from a damaged near-Earth space station so that the corporate owners can determine what happened. You're told up-front that the crew has already evacuated the station.
While you wait for the sections of the AI to download, you begin to explore the station and to piece together for yourself what might have actually happened, and that's the basic gameplay.
You find "virtual reality" fragment clips of the Tacoma station's crew as you investigate -- corrupted excerpts left unsecured when the AI shut down -- and these provide interactive clues to past events.
You can also examine and handle many of the objects aboard the richly-detailed, entirely immersive environment of Tacoma station itself as you seek to interpret what exactly happened aboard.
The game never explicitly explains the science-fiction setting of Tacoma station in 2088, but through inhabiting and investigating the station, you will get an acute sense of the immersive future world your character now inhabits.
Perhaps best of all, as your investigation progresses, the question becomes not so much "What actually happened here?" as "Which of many possibilities actually happened here?"
The clues you find suggest various possibilities. Will you guess at the correct answer? Very likely, near the end, but only as a number of equally-plausible scenarios competing in your mind as you explore Tacoma station.
An excellent change of pace from what we usually see in science-fiction games.
Absolutely, utterly  recommended if this sounds like a style of gameplay which would interest you.

Tacoma is the not-at-all related followup to the critically acclaimed Gone Home and Fullbright's second game. The sophomore game stereotypes suffer the same problems as a sophomore album from a band. Can they repeat success? Will they try to strike out in a different direction and potentially lose their fans with a bold change, or will they try to recapture and build upon the success of their first release? In Tacoma, you will find less of the former and more of the latter.
You are Amy Ferrier, a contractor for Venturis Corporation. Your task is to retrieve the AI named ODIN from Lunar Transfer Station Tacoma. While you're there, you can also learn the fates of the crew who are mysteriously absent. It doesn't take long to find out that a disaster aboard Tacoma is the cause of their disappearance.
Playing Tacoma is going to feel extremely familiar to fans of Gone Home. You're in space, on a space station, but you're still largely picking through other people's stuff and listening to their stories as you collect data on ODIN. The mechanical twist to Tacoma is that the stories are told mostly through wireframe mannequins of the crew presented in an alternate reality (AR) interface. ODIN was recording these scenes and allows you to view some of them. You can fast-forward, rewind, interact with physical objects and AR interfaces as you follow the crew through these scenes. The way these scenes play out is easily the most natural feeling presentation of video game cutscenes I've ever seen. A scene may start with half of the crew present, but some will walk in, others will walk out, and you can follow them through the scene to catch different conversations. It's really cool to watch in motion, and allows the game to present multiple storylines in an extremely seamless way.
Tacoma is packed with little side stories. If you were to solely follow the AR scenes or watch them only once, you'd absolutely get the gist of the main plot. However, in almost every drawer there's highly detailed notebook or tablet full of details that make Lunar Transfer Station Tacoma a place in the world, and make the wireframe cutouts into people. Tacoma accomplishes an incredible task of humanizing a seven person crew, in a video game, in a short amount of time.
The short play time is what will cause the most heartache for people. Like Gone Home, my personal playtime with Tacoma clocked in at a brief two and a half hours. I'm thorough too; I watched every AR cutscene multiple times to follow all of the characters in each scene, I read every AR interface, and I unlocked every locked door. A speedrun of Tacoma would only be limited to the amount of time it takes to watch each AR scene once, which is likely far less than 30 minutes total. If the short playtime doesn't discourage you, looking for anything more than a futuristic, AR-enhanced version of Gone Home might also bring disappointment. Make no mistake, for better or worse, Tacoma is very much a product of the team that made Gone Home. It didn't suddenly turn into System Shock or The Walking Dead. The puzzles to be solved are simple, and there is almost zero player input. In some ways, Tacoma would almost entirely complete itself without the player. In fact, you don't even need to watch the AR scenes. You can accomplish your mission by watching slow moving progress bars fill in over the course of three hours.
But you should watch those AR scenes, and interact with the objects around you, and get attached to these very human characters. Tacoma has some of the finest video game storytelling you will ever find. Just don't go looking for something more than that, because you won't find it. Tacoma is excellent, but it rides on the shoulders of Gone Home.

A fascinating slice of cyberpunk corporate dystopia, seen through the lived experiences of regular people. This perspective of the station’s average joe workers brings home the profoundly disturbing nature of this future, in way that your typical video game—where you play a supercool hacker or elite cyberagent, people with power who by their nature are removed from the system and able to disrupt it—can’t (but I still want to play the straight cyberpunk sequel on Tangier). Enough has been said about the AR interface of this walking/floating simulator and how effectively it uses every way you can experience a story in a video game that you can’t in another medium—rewinding, pausing, re-positioning yourself, following multiple simultaneous conversations. Instead I’ll say that, for a game in a genre that has a reputation for perceived interactivity, Tacoma had by the end defied all expectations.

Diablo is the obvious comparison you could draw with this combat-heavy RPG, but Torchlight is more than a clone. This is like a super-clone with psychic powers. Choose a character. Choose a companion cat or a dog. Enjoy a quaint cutscene, and then wonder where your evening went.
With Torchlight 2 on the horizon, and Diablo 3 even further down the line- enjoy this game as your go-to clicky-looty-action-rpg. The game just recently went on sale already, but perhaps we can see some deals when T2 releases.

Only played for a tiny amount, but it was plenty long enough to get a decent feel for how the game plays. That being said, my experience was half good and half bad.
The good:
1) The interface felt like it had a pretty solid foundation. With a bit of improvement, it can become something very impressive by today's standards.
2) It's pretty. While completing their little intro tutorial, I found myself constantly looking around the environment enjoing the view.
3) The crafting seems to have recieved alot of love from the devs. Very fulfilling.
4) Alot of the gameplay seemed to be fairly intuitive. Explore the UI a bit and you can pretty much figure everything out on your own. Even still, there was an intro tutorial to make sure you atleast understand the basics of needs, crafting and menu navigation.
The bad:
1) Mouse felt a little floaty. I never understand why game devs don't just use raw mouse input instead of mouse acceleration and differing X/Y sensitivities. Could potentially be a sign that they're not experience gamers, but too early to tell.
Solution for devs: Just use raw mouse input.
2) Controls in general were a bit clumsy. Four different keys for interacting with static objects is a bit much, and certain keybinds can be a bit awkward to use. This is especially frustrating when they're used fairly often. As an example, swapping cursor/mouse-lock modes would be better placed on the tab key.
Solution for devs: Consolidate entity interaction under one keybind, and expand from there. Maybe have the interaction key open up a context menu, sort of like right clicking things in the inventory?
3) Movement is locked into mouse-lock mode. This doesn't suit the game very well considering how many menus and contexts there are that require you to use the cursor.
Solution for devs: Consider allowing the user to control the camera by holding down the right mouse button and making it so that movement doesn't auto-swap you into mouse-lock mode. Maybe move combat toggle to ~, cursor toggle to tab and make it so that none of them auto-swap input mode.
TL;DR - Good game, but needs some polish. Definitely a game to keep on your radar, if not in your Steam library.

- You don't have a big map with targets and POI's anymore. Instead you get a small compass like map
- Disguises: It's now harder to fool other people into buying your disguise, especially if they have the same outfit on as one self. But this makes the game more challenging and fun.

All in all, Hitman: Absolution is a great game. But Die-hard Hitman fans need to be open-minded about the Gameplay changes and choose a difficulty that suits them best.

To cover the whole game, all changes, the good and the bad would require you to read far too much stuff. I will try to keep it nice and short. However, the most important bulletpoint first: This game on its own is not far as bad as some make you believe.
The biggest issue for many players seems to be the obvious similarities to the predecessor Civilizatin 5. While I agree that it is mechanically similar I don't think that the game has not evolved. The changes made are small but many and very distinctive. One might ask how those small changes justify such a long development time. I would answer with two things: This game runs super smooth and only has very minor bugs which can and will be patched soon. The balance of the game is good, not perfect, but sets a very nice foundation for things to come.
If we think back to Civilization 5, when it hit the shelves as a brand new product, a lot of the same complaints were made. A new offspring of the series can not, in my opinion, be as fleshed out as the previous parts with all addons. The first and most important thing is to set a working and balanced core game - which happened in this case. It is not the perfect game, I admit, but it is solid fun and has a lot of unleashed potential. So, let's get to the details, shall we?
The Tech Tree is now a Tech Web. You don't go from left to right but in the direction which benefits ther situation the most. The techs aren't as numerous as I would have wanted, but they are plenty. The balance in between them seems well done, some techs however are a little less impactful than others.
This new feature requires you to actually study the different pathes before you chose. Often, in midgame, you find out that you wasted time because you took a path which seemed beneficial but forgot to upgrade your infrastructure to actually build that stuff. I think that this is a great feature, which adds depth and more skill potential to the game. Many techs enhance the output of ressource tiles, the strength of units or allows you to even build new imporvements with your workers. Especially in the late game workers STILL are busy redesinging your entire layout, since new and more potent improvments are available.
The big downside is the UI of the Techweb. It is nearly impossible to actually see with one glance where what is. I even had a very hard time to distinuish wonders in it. So be prepared to actually spend a lot of your time in that web, finding the perfect path and wrtiting stuff on a piece of paper for later ;)
The combat and military system has been shrunk to the core parts and made more effective. I like the new impactful upgrades which come with the affinities you choose along the game. Counterunits are now even more effective and each unit type has it's own niche. Cities are easier to conquer and harder to hold, which requires you to build up in advance and not when the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan. So in general: Combat, and also the combat virtues, got a lot more powerful, rewarding and deadly.
Instead of releigion you now pursue an affinity. This has replaced religion and taken on a core role to victory. Through quests, which are remarkably boring and unsatisfactory, and tech brances you earn XP to a certain affinity. Whenever you level up you may chose a new upgrade to all of your exisiting units of one type in the game which gets applied immediatly. Certain thresholds also apply passive bonuses to your faction, like maintenance free roads and railways. The map has a couple, not very many, strategic ressources which require you to take one or another path over the other. Not only advanced units, but the most powerful buildings and even tile improvements of one affinity need a specific amount of those ressources. So planning and expanding early to those valuable sources is key! There are no luxury ressources anymore, since it is now your health which needs tending to. Ressources other than strategic ones ( and even those ) improve the tile they are on - and HOW thes improve. Though techs and affinity unlocks you will have tiles later on which produce lots and lots of energy ( money ), crop, science, culture. So, instead of many cities and valuable tiles in Civ 5 you now have to focus on few, pick the right upgrade, and improve the hell out of them. And better be quick about it, the opponents are doing the same.
The only way to keep your people healthy are specific buildings, virtues and tile improvments. So, if you want to expand quickly you need to dive into prosperity and get those health upgrades. With bonuses for thresholds for eacht virtue tree and for each virtue level it is quite intriguing and tricky to find the best possible path to advance. More than in Civ 5 those virtues shape your faction.
So, this about covers the best new parts of the game There also is a better espionage system, better ruin-focused early gameplay and a bit better loading performance during the rounds. If you look for a solid Civ game, which isn't yet ripe for  the ultimate challenge, with new concepts and different takes on victories and gameplay - go right ahead!

TLDR: I love this game, and its great fun. But there's a lot of bad with the crapton of good. Id recommend it to anyone who already loves the other Civ games!
Pros: More early game decisions that remove a lot of "next turn" turns. Awesome techweb that allows your people to actually BE different than other factions. The tech is diverse enough to where you can skip the "useless" tech you didnt want to bumrush what you DID want, and if someone makes a different choice then you then they dont suffer for it-their people just end up developing different strengths instead of exploitable weaknesses. Aliens that are a serious threat to your people. Affinity system lets you play how you want without gimping your military. Continued use of hexagonal grid and no unit stacking means 30 units cant hide and appear out of nowhere to come up your butt. Less unit types offer easy to pick up and easy to counter combat strats that let you focus on having more fun instead of remembering the 100+ different units and all their stats. They also always upgrade even on the go, so youre not holding onto troves of cash to upgrade them or even worse, keeping obselete ones around because you cant.
Cons: Why is the miasma so hard to see? It HURTS ME to stand in it so why does it camoflage to the ground? The end game spirals out of control, one moment youre making buildings and being nice to everyone then you hit affinity level 4 and suddenly youre out to kill everyone. It only gets faster as you continue to get affinity levels like no tomorrow. The game will "suddenly" end. Bam Promised Land ending, no victory screen no map no stats... just back to the main menu. EVen just hovering over the diplomacy screen will tell you just about EVERYTHING you need to know about someone, how advanced they are what wonders they have how much tech they have how much culture they have... and if you open a deal with them you get an exact amount of science and gold per turn too. There's also little deal making going on, without luxury resources Im not inclined to trade with anyone... if I give you Titanium youll just make Battlesuits with it! Why only 8 players? I loved huge brawls with my friends against the AI but if I bring 4 friends theres only 4 AI left. Speaking of AI, theyre ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They dont even know HOW to use the units they do make and theyre so passive I can literally stack Artillery outside their borders and they wont care. Even without my military, I was able to stage a coup d'etat in one of their capitals, apparently when spies are detected they dont care and wont station them defensively or use anti spy buildings/satellites. Why dont the Aliens get any tougher? For the first 150 turns youre almost completely at their mercy, building a fence to keep the siege worms out and sending military convoys (big ones) out with your colonists to fend off the alien hordes... but after that theyre a joke and your units will kill most of them in one attack. And the ones that dont die in one attack wont care what you do to them.
Travel brightly colored pasty areas and fight demons with a sword! And then realize you've been doing the same thing, over and over and over again, with little reward!
A truely  great game.

This game offers little when it comes to structured storytelling in lieu of having you walk to certain places and interact with certain objects to trigger a reaction from the narrator to understand what all of it is about. There are
endings (or
, depending on how you see it), in just over 1 hour I had seen close to half of them without rushing it one bit. I understand that The Stanley Parable isn't too bad if you're one to go all
looking for all the endings, but for me it got really tedious fast. You get to an ending, you have a giggle, restart the game and go click on every object to find the
which you can actually interact with, or go back and forth looking for something that you might have missed, thirsting to hear the narrator say something new. For a <$20 PC port, I have to say this was absolutely worth my money.
I've been wanting to play this game ever since its first release on the consoles. Unfortunately, I never did end up getting either of the consoles, and thus never ended up having a chance to play the game. I understood that a good bulk of the game consisted of cutscenes and movies (heck, if you add it all up, this is an 8-hour long movie with you moving the characters along with your controller), so I knew exactly what to expect. I'm a fan of story, music, and cutscenes, so this was perfect for me, since this game absolutely delivers on that front.
If you've ever been interested in the title and actually know what to expect, I'm not sure there's really any reason why you wouldn't get this game for the PC. The gameplay is not as interactive as you may expect (if you've played other RPGs), since you only get to control two things during combat: the party leader's actions, and paradigms. The other 2 party members are controlled by the AI and act according to the selected paradigm. You will, however, be switching paradigms a lot, and I'd say it makes up the majority of the gameplay in terms of combat.
I've had no issues with crashes, keyboard + mouse controls, or unbearable UI issues that others have mentioned before me. I was a little surprised that the Esc key brings up a prompt for you to quit the entire game, but at least it asks for confirmation (it would be quite an issue if this wasn't the case).
There are a few things to note, though:
- The game does not support 1080p, but there are temporary third-party solutions. On my 1920x1080, full screen causes the dreaded black bars to appear on the sides.
- There are very limited settings. What I mean is, there are limited video options (full screen or windowed. That's it), zero audio settings, and not ALL keys are remap-able. But for the majority of the keys can be modified to suit your preferences.
- I've experienced some tearing and occasional frame rate drops, although not to the point where I'd say it's crippling the experience.
- This is over 50gbs in size. Do keep in mind there were three discs for the consoles and still took up 20-40gbs (depending on console), but that isn't to say 50gbs isn't nothing.
All in all, this is definitely a "quick and cheap" port by most standards. But at the price of a dinner at a restuarant, there's only so much to be expected. Personally, I've gotten more than my money's worth, and I'm not even halfway through the game. I'd recommend this to those who know what to expect of FF13: a gorgeous game with plenty of cutscenes and movies, and one that doesn't exactly shine in the combat side of things-- but that isn't to say there isn't a good chunk of content to be played!

As it currently stands, running things stock this game is basically the console game running on a more powerful system then a PS3.  Like the PS3 version there's severe aliasing and shadow rendering issues associated with anything run in engine.  Note most of the "cutscenes" are actually rendered in engine, with cutscenes beyond the intro that are pre-rendered actually being kind of rare.  However, GeDoSaTo is compatible with the game, and can address both of these issues with a minimum of time spent modifying config files.  Antialiasing helps make the hair look right, and increasing shadow resolution helps with the quality of the shadows as one might expect.
Square Enix has provided the Japanese audio as an option as was requested prior to release.  So they might patch in proper graphics options, but GeDoSaTo will still probably look better as it is designed to allow rendering at 4k followed by downscaling to improve image quality over native rendering.
The Good:
The battle system on this game is basically involves taking role formulas and speeding them up.  So you have tank, buff, debuff, caster exploiting vulnerabilities via chain gauge, DPS, and healer roles.  Your job with this battlesystem is to strategically look at what's going on, and use these roles in an effective and dynamic fashion to win.  Associated with this you have a deck you set of role configurations, which you quick change during combat.
There's a lot of parallels between ideas and concepts in FF13 and FF3.  You have two worlds that are antagonistic towards each other, and the deeper background story this time around revolves a lot around information control.  Associated with that a lot of the story telling elements are done using subtle tools.  For instance when you hit the lake you may notice Vanille's brand isn't quite like the others, and you'll be able to put the pieces together around when Fang meets the rest of the party.
The Bad:
Eidolon fights can be annoying and counter intuitive.  There's a lot of stat stuff that's hidden with the item upgrade mechanics, and the upgrade curves of weapon and equipment is entirely opaque without looking things up.  The two of these can be dealt with by looking up a guide on the internet.  I'm left to assume that like with the sequence to unlock Tifa's Limit Break, this was intentionally obfuscated to sell guides, which the internet renders redundant at this point.
When full screen the Escape key automatically exits the program.  If windowed it brings up the prompt you'd normally expect, as will Alt-F4.  Chances are you will accidentally do this a few times, give Esc usually brings up the menu in computer games.  The main reason this can be annoying is that like the console version there is no autosave or arbitrary saving for that matter.  You must use the save points.
Addressing Critics:
This games is linear in the same way DooM 3 or CoD is linear.  There's usually side areas on the map to collect stuff, often directly behind where you start on a map for instance.  You however have no narrative control beyond choosing when to proceed and murderizing things in between you and continuing on.  So, yes it is more linear then KOTOR, Mass Effect, or Witcher but the major difference is in lack of narrative influence, like DooM 3.  There are a lot more detailed locales though, and quite a bit of variety between them.

Oknytt is a perfect example that it is not necessary to invent something new to create a good game. Oknytt offers classic gameplay, great art and simple but interesting story and, in my opinion, it is enough for point and click quest.
First of all, I want to mention art style. Game is beautiful, each screen and each character is carefully drawn. Oknytt looks dark, places and characters we encounter are quite unfriendly and sometimes even sinister, but the game itself is not scary. It is a kind of a mini-tour through scandinavian folklore, a short meeting with mysterious creatures that inhabit it. I really liked the bestiary, it was interesting and informative for me.
Plot is very simple and does not include unexpected twists. On the other hand, I must admit that I did not understand the ending. Why game ended this way? Perhaps I am not enough familiar with the scandinavian myths, so I can not see something important? Well, I do not know.
Puzzles are decent. Most of time, game is just about gathering and using weird stuff and junk here and there, but there is some actual puzzles. They are not too hard and can be easily solved, but these puzzles fit well in game, they seemed quite interesting for me, so I enjoyed them. I wish there was more puzzles and less "stuff-gathering"... well, alright, it is better than nothing and, of course, it is only my small insignificant opinion.
Well, and about narration... please, do not get me wrong, narrator did very good job, but... this voice, "no, this is not how it happened", now this words are stuck in my brain like nails! "Small insignificant creature", you say... well, nevermind.
So. I think, I can recommend Oknytt if you like point and click quests. It is not perfect, while art style is excellent, gameplay is only decent... but, in my opinion, for a short walk through fairy-tale it is more than enough.

Gone Home is one of my favorite games of all time, so I had high expectations going into Tacoma. I am also a hard science fiction nerd, so the abandoned space station setting is not new to me. But honestly, this game blew me away. The team at Fullbright has mastered the art of storytelling through environmental design and attention to detail. It's not necessary to discover the little hidden details--in fact, hardly anything in the game is "required;" the bulk of the game consists of waiting for files to download. If you choose, you could stand still and wait for the transfer to complete, but of course you are meant to explore and interact with the ship's AR (augmented reality) recordings of events leading up to the crew's exodus--but they help you better understand the game's small, but rich cast of characters. And these really are some of the most human characters ever seen in a video game. Each one has his or her own history, hopes, dreams, secrets, relationships, and all the rest.

I adore this game immensely. It tells the stories of multiple people, how they came to be on Lunar Transfer Station Tacoma, their lives on the ship, and the particular events that led to the members disappearing. It's up to you how much effort you want to put into the story - the more you search and discover and explore and experiment, the richer experience you receive. People crying "wah, £15 for 2 hours!" clearly cannot appreciate the amount of thought and care that went into such a game as this (also, it's longer than 2 hours if you make the effort to explore and not speedrun). The characters of Tacoma are diverse, endearing in their own ways, and so very human, and the world created is somehow familiar, almost unsettlingly so (space capitalism, it's capitalism but now in space), yet still futuristic and fascinating. I loved every second and will happily replay this game again in the future multiple times, to relive the experience of it. The ending still makes me giddy thinking about it.

A beautiful tale set in the Swedish mythos, you become the guide for a "small, in the scope of the world insignificant creature" who wanders about in the world on the longest, and darkest, night in many moons. On the journey, encounter and learn about other mythological creatures of Sweden, and explore the darkness as it comes to life in ways rarely seen. All of this, ultimately, is a campfire story, but a beautiful one at that.
The puzzles in this game, while not always intuitive, have a certain logic to them that makes sense. With the elemental runes of Earth, Water, Air, and Fire affecting every scene differently, some really interesting puzzles and solutions develop, along with some cute visuals and the more traditional inventory interaction system. And, if you really like storytelling, every interactable piece has an option to hear more narration, as well as the character's speech or just interacting with it.
I spent many hours contemplating what I experienced after finishing this game. It has a touching story and an art style I don't see often in games that I found quite pleasing, and the narrator does a great job at setting the tone.
If you like point and click puzzle adventures and campfire stories about mythology, then definitely pick this game up. If you like any one of those qualities I mentioned, pick this up. It's a gem.

The structural storytelling of "Tacoma" is neat, basically utilizing the "Detective Mode" from the Batman: Arkham series to allow players to, Rashomon-like, piece together various bits of narrative behind the tragic events that occurred aboard the space-station Tacoma. In a particularly trusting move, the game forces very little story upon players, allowing them to uncover as much (or as little) as they want about the ethically dubious Corporate culture of 2088, the Human Oversight Accord, and the growing sentience of AI.
Unfortunately, Tacoma does nothing more than introduce these concepts--it completely fails to follow through on them. You can discover intimate moments, like the desparate lovemaking of the married Roberta and Natalia, or the tender kiss and hug shared between the ship's captain and her botanist lover before the two voluntarily enter cryogenic sleep on the off-chance that this will allow the remaining crew members to help them all escape. None of this, ultimately, has any impact on what you're doing, especially since you're only watching events in retrospect.
[Spoilers follow.]
The crew does escape, and you've been sent by the corporation responsible for sabotaging them to clean up all the augmented reality logs and retrieve the AI--i.e., the evidence that would further implicate the company. But you don't have to choose between loyalty and betrayal; instead, you turn out to be a double-agent, actually sent there to liberate the AI, recognizing it as a sentient being. That's great, but also fairly off-course from what the game's presented thus far; it makes the game feel weightless. Fullbright's previous game, "Gone Home," similarly withheld information and forced players to discover things through flashbacks, as did "What Remains of Edith Finch," and yet both of those games acted directly on their narrators--it changed and impacted them. The stories they recalled had beginnings, middles, and ends. "Tacoma" is, at best, a science-fiction parable about corporate greed, one that has no consequence.

While the main story has it's difficult fights, it's not too hard to just complete the game on it's own. Going for 100% requires you to seek out every last item in every last corner of the world though; and thus far I've enjoyed the 39 hours (at this time of writing) I spent doing that. Definetely a single-player experience I'd recommend to all of you out there, best 15 bucks I've spent in a while.

Pros
+ Enjoyable story
+ Artwork is unique and beautiful
+ Has a "keep playing to finish the story" appeal (hard to find these day)
+ Fairly inexpensive
+ Easy steam achievments
+ Challenging enough without being frustrating
Cons
+ No real connection with characters (the story is nice but nothing jumps out as memorable)
+ Realatively short gameplay
+ Lacks a ramp up (do not need to be hand held, but starting game play is like fumbling around in the dark)
+ Absolutely no replay value

INK is a precision platformer where the box you control is not precise, nor are any of the platforms initially visible. This makes most of the platforming (especially in the later levels) nothing but frustrating.
The gimmick with this game is that you can reveal the platforms and walls by touching them or spraying ink by double jumping. While it is an interesting idea, its not always possible to know if you can make a jump or if there are instant death spikes (due to being unable to see the next platform or spikes without spraying ink first).
There are a few enemies you come across: boxes you have to jump on to kill and open the exit to the level, triangles that shoot a projectile in a line, and circles that shoot a homing projectile. The circles are simply frustrating and unfun to deal with whatsoever.
The game is also very short (I finished it in just over an hour and a half), but seems to be padded out with a lot of deaths. And you will be dying a lot in this game, not that most of your deaths will feel like your fault with the imprecise controls and frustrating mechanics.
2/10 Overall.

INK seams like it could have been an interesting platformer, but for me it quickly becomes frustrating.

At it's base, it's a precision platformer - where you control a soap. Ink part is quite interesting and maybe develops into many interesting things in later levels.
I'll just quickly add few annoying things that made me stop playing:
1) Controls are not precise (or tight) at all, you rarely feel like the death was your mistake.
2) When you are hugging any wall and jump, you bounce off that wall whether you want to or not, This mostly leads to death and happens all the time. You can probably learn to fight it ... if you want ...
3) When you kill and enemy you bounce off and keep the momentum but it doesn't refresh your mid-air jump. This forces you to "break" in air after almost every enemy and leads to a lot of stagnation (or death due to soap controls).
4) Edges of the screen are instakill. When a small ledge is near the edge and you slide just a bit, you're dead. No chance to recover, restart.
I don't mind hard games usually, this just might not be my type of hard. To me it just looks like they took some flawed and unfair control system and made it a feature.
Again, nothing to do with core concept of "painting the world".

Novus Inceptio is a very promising game. I have run one clone through a life, explored a lot of the starting planet (lots of running) and just started to think about building a base.
Pros:
I really like the idea and lore behind the game as I think that there are many possibilities for the devs to weave into the storyline. The robot companion is a good idea and hopefully will eventually have more uses in the future.
So far the different anomalies you can visit at the moment are all very different from each other and fit with the rest of the game.
The anomaly idea should allow the devs to keep adding content indefinitly to make exploration and resource gathering more interesting in the future.
I do like the crafting and the home planet although this has a few cons as well (see below).
I enjoy using skills to help level them as a feature.
Being able to swim could allow for underwater anomalies and exploration (please).
The Christmas event is fun and slightly addictive.
Cons - These may change as the game progresses
There is very little danger in the world so far. Enemies move in slow motion and stop chasing fairly quickly and the survival aspects are mostly ignorable.
You will quickly get to know the anomolies that exist so far but hopefully these will be added to in the future.
Starting planet has no real visual difference between level areas so no reason to move beyond the starting easy zone.
Crafting could do with a bit more of a tutorial as it is a bit unweildy at the moment with lots of different steps and ingredients. I like this but it may put some people off.
To conclude, this game has plenty of potential but it is a little lacking in challenge at the moment. There is no real point to progressing far as there is no danger and not enough to explore but I am hopeful that this will change as the game progresses. I did enjoy the time I spent in the game and I will keep checking back to see how things develop.

This game is incredibly frustrating. That's not to say it's not fun; it definitely is. It's the same fun as Dark Souls, where after cursing the devs to unending torture for half an hour, you _finally_ beat whatever you were hung up on, and feel like a friggin god. I didn't get that much, but that's just because I'm bad at the game. :(
I do have one big complaint, though: Where the ♥♥♥♥ is the options menu? I could not for the life of me find a way to lower the volume in-game, or set it to play in fullscreen windowed instead of plain fullscreen, so that it definitely won't crash when I tab back in, especially if I have a graphical simulation running in the background that also uses the GPU. It really doesn't need many options -- it's a simple game -- but that doesn't excuse the complete lack of an options menu with things that _are_ needed. The default (presumably full) volume at my computer's default volume is just loud enough to cause me actual, physical pain, and I couldn't find any way in-game to mute or even reduce the volume of anything, so I had to mute the entire machine while I went into the system volume settings and dropped INK's volume to half. That should be doable in-game.
All the same, the game itself is incredibly fun. I won't say I enjoyed every minute -- some jumps are incredibly frustrating because if you hold the jump button for just a moment too short, you'll miss it and fall to your death. This is especially frustrating when you think the thing you're jumping on to extends lower than it really does -- there's a reason why death and double-jumps splatter ink everywhere; it lets you see things on your next try.
In short, if you like challenging -- but not impossibly so -- platformers, INK delivers that with a great twist and beautiful graphics.

I heard high praise for Shadow Warrior since its release and always thought it had to be a mixture of nostalgia and the weird FPS /w swordplay fanbase. Boy was I wrong. Shadow Warrior might just be on the top 10 FPS games I've ever played up there with HL2, Bioshock and even Deus Ex.
The story starts off cheezy and predictable but by the end the complexity and otherworldy beauty of it got me by surprise. Not only does the story makes sense it is also moving and compeling. You WANT to know what happens next, you WANT to finish the game and reach that cathartic moment of you standing sadly victorious at halls of the gods.
The characters are rich and detailed. I genuinly loved the protagonist and sidekick and I was constantly feeling like a badass because for ONCE, you the player is the smart and all-powerful moving force. I am the one double crossing and outsmarting the enemy and with some very small insignificant exceptions there aren't any of the usual FPS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like having to sacrifice yourself or being powerless for 20 minutes. The one liners keep coming and the dialog feels fluid and smartassy at the same time. The other characters have a backstory and emotional depth that makes them feel real despite being gods or all powerful crime lords.
The meat of the game however is the gameplay and here the game is miles ahead of the competition. 9 weapons, available fairly soon in the game, combined with Gun, Talent and Skill upgrades makes you feel capable of meeting any challenge is style. And unlike the majority of titles with too many gun options, you'll actually use most in the same fight. The combat mechanics require you to figure out what option you should choose for each situation and by the game's midpoint you'll be switching between guns, sword and magic like a pro. The difficulty scales so beatifully that I rarely got stuck in a fight and the greatest moments are the ones where you are pushed to you limit, making microstrategic decisions on 10 HP which just makes winning all the more satisfying. Special mention goes to the Katana which can be your primary weapon and feels absolutely terrific to use. The swordplay is near perfect with a good mix of special abilities and brutally effective.
TLDR; Come for the gun/swordplay and cheezy oneliners, stay for the rich story and characters. 10/10 would Wang again.

For those who are new to the Hitman franchise, this is worth $5.00. Most definitely worth $5.00. This is a Splinter Cell-esque sneaker set in urban areas and a linear story. You should get at least 10 hours out of it.
For those who played the (in my opinion) far superior Hitman: Blood Money, don't expect a similar game. Sure, it's the same protagonist and killing people is still the primary goal. But instead of carefully planning your missions and equipment in outlandish and bizarre situations, you spend most of the game on the run and hiding. You're going to spend a lot of time hiding behind furniture throwing coffee mugs at walls and just standing totally still listening to NPC dialogue if you want to get through the missions "stealthily".
Towards the end of the campaign I just gave up sneaking and ran through it like an FPS because I was no longer motivated to avoid killing unnecessarily like in Blood Money. Essentially everyone wants to kill you or report you to someone who does, and there are large swaths of the game where you don't encounter anyone but gun-toting enemies and have no motivation to let them live other than the artificial challenge of sneaking - a system propped up by the ridiculous "hide your face with your hand" mechanic where you try not to get noticed by the janitors who think, "I know all the janitors in the world and you aren't one of them."
Finally, Absolution totally eschews the very interesting equipment mechanics of Blood Money. As mentioned earlier I eventually just shot my way through the campaign and the game essentially doesn't care. Blood Money allowed you to pick and choose your equipment for the challenge ahead and formulate a plan while watching the events of the game unfold with more money for more equipment being rewarded if you were more clever with your plan - Absolution essentially puts you on rails with whatever equipment you find lying around and it's extremely rare if your actions in a previous area have any effect on the next.

1. Most games that are trying to push the boundaries of narratives in gaming are just you walking for two hours while some story is revealed to you slowly. This is exactly like that only it's good.
2. The narrator, voiced by Kevan Brighting, is the star of the show. When a game has a small cast, it needs to be anchored by a truly excellent performance and that's just what his is.
3. This is that kind of humor that's truly funny but you don't laugh out loud at.
4. You play as Stanley, a distressingly mild mannered office worker. You start out in an empty office. The general goal as far as there is one is to figure out what's going on.
5. There is no one specific thing that is going on. A lot of things could be happening and at no point is the game ever like, "Okay, let's cut the crap. Here's what's been going on the whole time." You have to draw your own conclusions.
6. *the sound of minds blowing*
7. You can use your Googles to find how to get every possible one of the numerous endings but play through until you are stuck first and play some more before that. Google ruins everything. Or, actually, it only ruins some things. Self driving cars are going to be pretty awesome once they have that worked out but I don't much like the ever hanging temptation to cheat at every puzzle game on earth and I am pretty sure they've been showing my search results to Santa Claus.
8. Graphically, this looks pretty good but who cares.
9. The Steam achievements for this are pretty hilarious. Check them out even if you don't decide to play.
10. This game could be considered a Philosophy of Games 101 course but don't hold that against it. You will consider the relationship of player to character and player to developer quite a lot.
11. There's points where you wait around and do nothing and you are rewarded for that. There are also points where you wait around and do nothing and nothing happens at all.
12. My one small complaint is this doesn't have any really memorable music. I guess it didn't need it but I like music so I figure I had ought to mention that.
13. I think it is important to remember that just because a game pushes boundaries doesn't make it automatically good or worth playing. You have to get the other details right too and that's where
shines when so many games like it fail.

Infinity Wars is game with high complexity, interesting factions and unique and captivating art and world. To keep it short, I will just mention three mechanics that make this game so great to me.
First of all, the concept of simultaneous-turns brings greater depth to the game, as you do not have "free reign" during a turn as you would in other games.
Secondly, the setup of the battlefield into offense zone (where characters will attack the enemy fortress) defense zone (characters will defend against the enemy attackers), support zone (where they neither defend nor attack but are in play) and command zone (where you have three characters, which you can put into play or activate their abilities).
The first three, together with the simultaneous-turns, bring with it the question of where what characters go and in what order. For example you anticipate that the enemy is going to use a ability card that destroys all characters in the defense and offense zones, so you move your characters back into the support zone. But maybe it was a ruse to get a cheeky last hit on your low health fortress, so you move your most disposable unit to the defense zone just in case.
While the command zone reduces the random element of a deck, since you will always have three cards you can rely on.
Lastly, the moral cost associated to the loss of a character means that one must also take into account the losses suffered over the course of the game.
Unfortunately, it did not receive the great care and work it deserves. Notable bugs not being removed for ages, little communication with the player base and the devs have now in all but name abandoned the game, as not a single update from even community guides are published and the non-steam launcher was taken down.
It is a great game that had, and still has, a lot of potential. If only it would receive the care it deserves.

*UPDATE: MAY 2017*
Well, it's been about a year since I reviewed this game, so I figured I should update my review.
As the community currently stands, I've been playing more active than I have a year ago, and...
Well, a lot of players who were helpful, active, or high-ranked players, have seemed to completely abandoned this game by this point. It's pretty rare to see anybody above lvl 90 join a server, ever, except on weekends or during random games with 6 or more people. The majority of players are either lvl 1's, scattered levels between 2-50, and the lvl 70's. Although, this remaining small portion of the community can be divided into seperate groups.
Group 1: New players that are completely silent, either not knowing how to talk or choosing not to. This silent group also applies to some higher level players, who don't speak much.
Group 2: The remaining bad part of the community. Either people who spam gg ez in your face all the time or complain about other people being bad, they don't come up too often but you do see them in games. Most of these people will complain that it's a dead game, which in my opinion leads to the question: Then why are you even playing a game you don't believe in? Are you serious?
Group 3: The relatively ideal players, these players will chat occassionally, or often, possibly supply supportive information, or come up with some interesting chat topics as you stalk each other on the maps. Sometimes you can even arrange events between yourselves, such as limiting everybody to a certain weapon and providing some occassionally fun times. Although they are decently rare, you'll still see them, and they will provide some of the best times in this game. All of my good memories about this game come from these people, they MAKE the game realtively fun, absolutely.
Skins are still being made daily for this game, so the steam workshop support is still going strong. Overall, your purchase of this game is kind of relative. The times this game is most active will always be on the weekends, since the community likes to hold events during the weekend. That is, the active parts of the community. Ultimately, it depends on whether you can spare some money for this game. I would never reccomend buying the full price for this game, especially in its current state. $7 for this game would be an absolute bad deal for the experience you desire, just wait for a sale on this. This game goes on sale often, so you should be able to grab a copy if you don't already have one. For $1, I would reccomend this game as a cheap multiplayer alternative. However, if you want games with higher player counts, or playing with different people, I would not reccomend this game. Most likely with this game, you'll be playing mostly the same people, over and over again, with some newcomers inbetween. Overall, depends on your patience, whether you want to play with the literal same people only, and if you desire higher server counts.
(I'm biased from previous experiences, so I still give this game a reccomendation.)

I've bought alot of Indie Gala Bundles in the past and many of them allowed you donate part of your purchase to "Indie Gala Project X" - which was at the time, an unknown entity. A website? A special bundle? A game? Turns out that Blockstorm was project X. Considering the world was already over saturated with Minecraft style clones at the time, I wasn't impressed.
It's simple as it looks - a Call of Duty like shooter in a Minecraft-esque setting. Play typical FPS matches in a handful of prebuilt levels as well as the option to play in player made block levels. I could never get my aim quite right, and perhaps that will take some time and more sensitivity  adjustments, but I didn't enjoy the "gun feel" to feel like bothering further. I got some good kills here and there, but I got trashed while I was wailing my mouse around, or barely dragging it to hit a ducking, strafing target. There are Quick Match, Server Browser, and Editor modes.
I do like that changing your weapon and equipment loadout affects your speed, and the sniper rifle feels like a viable weapon instead of something that only pros will use. The neatest thing about Blockstorm is the ability to create custom maps, guns, and characters. You can't buy DLC, so make your own!
I don't like Blockstorm, but I feel this game does appear to do well with children and teens. With the few minutes I've played, the community seems friendly and non-toxic, so this is probably a good game to give to a child that you're not comfortable with them playing Call of Duty or Battlefield. The customization will keep them going, but this adult would rather play a more fufilling, competent shooter.

So far, I am not impressed. I play a lot of adventure games, and this one falls pretty low on my list. I like the story, and I will play through the whole game to see the story line completed, but it seems that in just about every aspect of this game the deveolpers took the easy way out.
The most obvious easy path they took is that there doesn't seem to be a single object interaction animation. Instead your character just stands there stupidly, the narator says what you did, and the newly altered object appears in your inventory. How lazy.
The game seems to have a single voice actor, which might add to the "reading a story" aspect of the plot, but comes of as cheap and ruins my immersion. His voice is fine as the narrator, but when he tries to do other characters, it's always the same, cheesy falseto.
Most frustratingly, tasks were not logical and did not give enough prompting. "I need tools" was the prompting for one task but despite having multiple things that pass for tools in my inventory, I made no progress. Finally through trial and error, I realised that he needed something else (no spoilers) not a tool at all!
In fact nearly half of the progress I made on this chapter was simple trial and error - just click every clickable point with every item from my inventory. No fun at all.
This was made worse by the fact that there is no "reveal hot spot" button for when you get stuck, so I had to resort to a walkthrough at one point just to learn that there was a hot spot that I didn't know existed.
But I think the worse part, and the most lazy choice on the part of the developers is that if you use the wrong item with anything, you get the same exact message every time "No that's not how it happened." This tells you nothing about how to proceed. How about "No I think I need something sharper for this job" or literally anything to point you in the right direction. So without that, when you get stuck, trial and error of every single item is your only option - expect no assistance.
So disappointing from a game with such a good storyline.

I've NEVER played a game that is more value for my money than this one. For a mere $15, I've had 50 hours of quality game time, easily more value than most AAA games.
This is an amazing game in most respects. The art is beautiful and the sounds and music are perfect for the game. The gameplay is VERY tight and precise. This is a metroidvania and a MASSIVE one so expect the usual trappings of such a type of game; areas locked off until you obtain abilities, secrets behind breakable walls and floors or events, respawning enemies and epic boss battles. This game has a very deliberate map mechanic where you will only obtain the map of an area once you buy it and even after you get it you will need to fill it out by exploring beyond what was drawn which fills out when you rest at benches. This promotes early game exploration of the world which makes for some GREAT moments. There is an area that truly makes you uncomfortable and you will feel VERY lost and hoping the map seller is right around the corner. There is also heavy inspiration from Dark Souls for the map design where there are multiple entrances and exits and gates that lead back to older more familiar areas. THERE IS SO MUCH TO DO IN THIS GAME and I will not spoil any of them. Explore the nest yourself and learn the secrets that lurk within.
The story is also VERY Souls-esque with a Bloodborne-type story where you, as a mysterious Hunter-bug come to an old civilization which has fallen into ruin and you try and piece together what happened. There are few cutscenes and majority of the actual plot will need to be understood through subtext and reading between the lines. Where it differs from the Soulsborne games is the characters. There are a LOT of them and some are funny, some are serious and brooding, some are neutral but have pasts that you figure out through exploration but all of them are compelling and wonderfully written.
This game is VERY good but there are definitely a few flaws. Backtracking is a real and present issue and fast travel points are a bit too spread out. There definitely needed to have at least one or two more such points. There is a lot of boss teasing going on with some great moments teasing a boss only to be let down. Boss quality is hit or miss with some bosses just being either cheese-fests or wars of attrition to see who whittles whose health to zero first. Story is at times deliberately overly vague and some straightforward dialog could have been helpful in establishing context and the plot.
But without a DOUBT, if you're a fan of platformers, metroidvanias or even just good games in general, GET THIS GAME

First, i am comparing this game to Alpha Centauri. Ruthlessly. Why, you ask? Because Beyond Earth was called „spiritual successor“ of that game. And because Alpha Centauri is truly a pearl of a game that sets the tone of every sci-fi Civ-like game in the future.
Second, I deleted my original review and added this more improved, more poisonous and better review instead.
Now, let us start.
-	The factions. Alpha Centauri had sever distinct factions. All of them were given proper personalities, they played different, they felt different, the AI treated them different. From fungus-covered territory of Lady Gaia to industrial lands of Chairman Yang, they were all different. And the quotes! People still quote the words of all of them and remember them. In CBE, the factions lack any personality. Previous Civs had the historic figures that would mean something to you, but in CBE, there are bland characters that add to nothing, are not really different and are completely forgettable.
-	The affinities. You can go for purity, harmony and supremacy- meaning staying human, becoming cyborg and hugging aliens. In theory. In practice, they are completely cosmetic and don’t matter much. You get some slight differences in units and cities use a bit different skin. That is all. And it is not logical- you can become purity without killing a single alien and you can become an alien-hugger harmony player and you can wipe out the entire alien population of the world without any penalty. Mostly- you can make a choice that does not matter.
-	The aliens. They were supposed to be different then barbarians in the Civ games- and they are. Unfortunately, they are more like neutered space-alien-barbarians. Never in my game had i had one attacking my cities. Especially when there is improvement that keeps them at least 2 squares away from the city. Even in the beginning, they are a no-threat. And even if you murder them by dozens, the aliens don’t seem to mind. Not more hostile reaction, aliens taking the offensive or something. Nothing. Even though there is first level harmony affinity that makes the alien hostility to come down easier and that does basically nothing.
-	The victories. Whatever victory you achieve doesn’t matter much. You get an uninspired pop-up text with a pretty picture saying basically „Congrats you won“ and voila, here comes the main screen. And all the victories except conquest one are basically science victories, where you have to build stuff and do some stuff as well.
-	The diplomacy. As bad as in Civ 5. Combine that with bland factions mentioned before and the diplomacy becomes a bore. Plus, no clear view on how one faction is feeling towards the other? Are the Polynesians and Africans close or do they hate each other’s guts? No way to tell? In addition, no Planetary Council or UN-like feature where you decide global things. And the city-states, now dubbed as “stations” are even less of a value then in Civ 5. You cannot interact with them diplomatically. You cannot warn other players who are attacking the station you are trading with stop, you cannot declare war on them. Or you can declare war on them by moving your melee troop (yes, the soldiers/marines are called melee troops) and attack the station. That is declaring war- no other way. And the AI is not aggressive. Wars are few and usually end up in status quo.
-	The planet. Looks like ye goode olde Earth, but perhaps with different skin and different kind of neutered barbarians roaming around. Terrain types are the same, terrain bonuses are the same, mountains have bluish skin. The resources are a bit different and occasionally, you see floating rocks or green goo. You feel right at home if you have played Civ 5- but is the point of Beyond Earth to feel right at home?
-	The military. Less units then in Civ 5. One type of ship and one type of aircraft. Oh, and a carrier. No choppers, no bombers, no fighters, no heavy battleships and light destroyers. Same with land units- one melee unit, one ranged, one tank or cavalry like things and one catapult with missiles. Plus some affinity-specific units. One unit per square, soldiers and tanks are referred as “melee” units. Guess they use the butts of their guns. They also upgrade automatically when you gain affinity level- that is kind of nice. But adds to confusion- suddenly all your soldiers are called Cobras or whatnot. And the combat is quite similar to Civ 5, only you see less, because AI is not very aggressive.
-	Quest system. Oh, the system that was going to bring the game to life! Really? Don’t hold your breath… Around 90% of the quest decisions are choosing what bonus to add to your building. So, do you want +1 health or +1 production to your new fancy clinic? Rest of them- you have to work really hard to fail and usually you get bonuses to your currently most advanced affinity. Sometimes you get to choose what affinity. And that is pretty much it.
In addition, there are minor nitpicks:
-	When the colony produces a construction, it does not tell you what building or unit it finished- just that project is complete. If you have 10+ colonies, you cannot remember what you built.
-	Wonder pop-ups- when someone else builds wonder, it does not tell you what it does. It makes sense when you get that someone build Sixtine Chapel, but less so when someone builds Archimedes Lever.
-	When you build Archimedes Lever, you get a nice boring blueprint nondescript wonder screen that tells you what bonuses you get, but does not answer the main question: the hell is Archimedes Lever?
-	Same applies to all techs and wonders and buildings. You get a name, not-half-as-good-quote as from Alpha Centauri and bonuses. To dig deeper, you have to look into Civilopaedia. Works fine for Civ 5, where for example “Gunpowder” and “Writing” or “Barracks” and “Temple” does not need further instruction, but when dealing with “Soma Distillery” and “Xeno Sanctuary” or “Alien Ethics” and “Dark Networks” in Beyond Earth.
There is still more, but the review is already two A4 pages long, so I’ll spare you. The conclusion- Beyond Earth is more like a badly done expansion pack of Civ 5 then a standalone game. It might get better with DLC/expansions, but at its current state I would suggest to wait with buying until the price drops about 75%. Or just do buy Alpha Centauri. If you manage to look behind aged graphics and terrible interface, you discover (or re-discover) a truly great game hidden behind it.
Thanks for reading!

Brings a refreshing twist to the Civilization franchise, but is definitely lacking in both polish and balance.
My experience with vanilla Beyond Earth is pretty much identical to my experience when vanilla Civilization 5 first came out: meh. Lots of flashy new features added to the core Civilization experience, but painfully long wait times along with glaring balance issues made vanilla Civ 5 less engrossing than earlier entries.
Then the expansions and optimization tweaks came out, and Civ 5 became the 4x turn-based strategy juggernaut that it is today.
Beyond Earth reminds me of that vanilla Civilization 5 experience: promising new features that will take a lot of tweaking and polish to get right.
An intricate tech web forces you to weigh what your faction needs right now while weighing it against your chosen end-game. Developing your chosen Affinity helps you better tailor your military, improvements and buildings the style of gameplay you are pursuing. Orbital satellites add a new layer of meta to help your faction while hindering your opponents. Aliens and miasma are challenging threats that add a layer of tension to the early and mid game.
It can be immensely satisfying to watch you choice of improvements drastically reshape the land around your cities, from lush green terrascapes to layers of generators and satellite arrays. Hunting for expedition sites with your explorers is particularly fun, especially when running around for progenitor ruins. Espionage got a major boost, from recruting a bunch of defecting military units to "flipping" the capital of your enemies and winning a domination victory this way.
On the other hand, wonders became nothing more than glorified city improvements that don't even have inspiring portraits - much less video animations to reward your efforts. Three trade routes per city that generate both energy *and* science when linked to foreign cities give way too many advantages to wide empires. Couple this with nearly unlimited health (or happiness in Civ 5 terms) that comes with the Prosperity virtue tree, and there is no way small, tall empires can compete with wide empires conducting infinite city sprawl. Faction leaders are bland, lifeless automatons that no longer impress after the first ten minutes of gameplay.
The limited AI still likes hitting your meatier tanks instead of bombing your softer rangers (archers) and artillery (catapults). The first few quests offer promising storylines to help you better determine your faction's future, but they quickly run out and are replaced by boring "quest decisions" that mechamnically force you choose between benefit A and benefit B for city improvements. Endings are anticlimactically and unceremoniously dumped upon you; creating a completely disappointing climax to the buildup you've been so working hard for. A poorly designed interface makes it very difficult to find the information you need at a glance; forcing you to spend a lot of time sifting through a lot of information - especially when it comes to the tech web and managing multiple trade routes.
At the end of the day, Beyond Earth offers a lot of promising new features offset by a range of significant balance issues as well as underwhelming aesthetic and narrative options. I believe that the new features of Beyond Earth coupled with solid gameplay offsets its many shortcomings, but it was a very close call.
What tips the scales in the game's favor, however, is Firaxis' track record with Civilization 5. This company turned a shaky new entry in the Civ franchise into one of its most successful entries in the span of four years. That's a shockingly long development time in the video game industry that ultimately paid off handsomely for the company.
Given enough time and support, we could see Firaxis repeat that success with Beyond Earth - something I am eagerly looking forward to given the promising array of new features introduced in this sci-fi reimagining of the Civilization franchise.
