Will preface this saying that it isn't a BAD port, but it is a bit of a lazy one. It operates almost indentically to the console version and for all intents and purposes works perfecly well, but the resolution lock and the bizarre rarity of framerates above 30fps let it down. You can do some manual tweaks via your GPU control panel to bump the framerate a bit, and GeDoSaTo can be easily applied to increase the resolution to your liking, but really options like this should be in the game's graphics settings already.
That being said, if we're to judge the game on its merits, whilst it's seen as a bit of a black sheep of the FF family, it IS a well made game with some properly stunning visuals and an interesting fast-paced combat system. The game world has some very intriguing lore and the story in general is quite good, but do keep in mind that it's quite a linear game and you don't really get to explore much.
So yeah, a good game that got a serviceable, if lacking, port.

Summary Recommendation: Do not buy. This is over priced demo ware.
Tacoma is fully fleshed out and realized. It's polished. The story is interesting but exceedingly linear. There are no choices. There are no puzzles. There are a couple of easter egg hunts, find a key or code, unlock a door to progress. But these are very simple. There are a few achievements attached to other egg hunts. The zero-g navigation is substandard but you don't spend a lot of time in zero-g so it hardly matters.
What does matter is that the world is well realized. Each character is beautifully rendered with their own personal motivations and objectives, including the motivation of the primary character, which is revealed in the final moments of Tacoma to bring the story to a satisfying conclusion.
However, even with the story being slowed down by the brilliant re-enactments of the crew history, the game takes less than 3 hours to complete. It took me 3 hours and I'm sure at least 30-60 minutes of that I was being distracted by real life.
In short, had I really pushed hard to complete the entire story and not stopped to look around, I probably could have finished the game in less time that Steam allows for a full refund.
I bought it on discount, and even at the discounted price I feel like I overpaid for 2-2.5 hours of linear story time. The developers of Tacoma have put themselves in the price category for a movie-- which is typically a multi-million dollar budget endeavor, and only grows to its price tag because of the traditional box office distribution method. (Direct to DVD or Direct to Streaming medium typically has a lower cost point.)
The game is filled with tons of objects that can be picked up and inspected, but only a handfull (less than 6) have any relevance to completing the story. Oknytt's tale starts with an unnamed, insignificant creature slowly emerging in a dark world: having no idea of its role in the big scheme of things the creature embarks on a journey to find its purpose.
Oknytt has alot going for it thanks to its charming art, creatures and lore coming from Swedish mythology and a pretty interesting story but it sadly becomes somewhat of a niche game due to its often cryptic, illogical puzzles that can easily stop your progress.
-good art style creates an appropriately dark world populated by mysterious creatures
-nice soundtrack
-the narrator does a good job both in telling the tale and voicing its various creatures
-interesting story
-puzzles go from unoriginal to downright obscure
-rune system is nice but too random in its actual operation
-a bit too reliant on pixel hunting
-lacking in animations
-FMVs look pixelated
Oknytt is decent and it has alot of charm in its art style and story but I sadly found it extremely lacking in its actual puzzles, hence the thumbs down despite the fact that this is not a bad game at all.
Puzzles suffer from a "try every object on everything" syndrome as I feel their directions are a tad too vague or they're based on abstruse item combinations. Said items are also often a bit too well hidden in the environment, something made worse by the mostly black and white graphics, or can be gathered through interacting with every single object in a scene, something that can get dull quickly. Last but not least some puzzles or items require you to use the four elemental runes at your disposal: sadly this also soon becomes a dull affair as you're basically forced to try each rune in every scene hoping for something to happen.
All things considered I feel the obtuse and somewhat badly designed puzzles are a bit too much for an adventure game to earn a recommendation as I think only seasoned fans of the genre will find the weird logic behind them easy enough to progress at a steady pace. Still, if you feel you can easily tackle hard puzzles or use a guide then you'll be able to properly enjoy its art and story, making it a decent purchase.

Telsagrad starts you off slowly. As you go room to room solving problems and collecting upgrades, it seems like this will be a puzzle game with some minor platforming; a light metroidvania with only a couple of upgrades but plenty of backtracking to use them. Then, about two-thirds into the game, the difficulty spikes dramatically and something becomes very clear. Just like its namesake, Teslagrad is in love with the scientific method. The setting – despite all of its electricity and wild inventions – is just a red herring. No, this game's appreciation of science goes deeper than simple aesthetics. At a fundamental level, the only way to best this game's challenges is through meticulous experimentation.
Death is instant from any source of damage and results in a respawn to the beginning of the room with no other penalty. In the early game this isn't really noticeable. If you were having any trouble making it through a room, it just meant you hadn't really learned the lesson it was trying to teach you yet. Once dangers start to appear more quickly than one can react, however, you're encouraged to die constantly and to use your mistakes to painstakingly memorize patterns rather than to use the cleverness or calm observation that suited the first two-thirds of the game. In this late game, you've gone from an eager student to a desperate researcher that will now earn his knowledge through blood, sweat, and tears.
Not a single word is ever written or spoken in Teslagrad. The plot instead must be interpreted through scenery, through silent puppet shows, and from the 36 scrolls scattered throughout the game. The scrolls themselves only provide a historical illustration of the tower you're struggling through and insight into motivations of the people who built it. Individually, none of these things make up a complete narrative; only when pieced together do they form something coherent. So just like the rest of the game, the story requires a careful analysis but promises great rewards to the persistent and the determined.

Storyline: On the darkest of nights when creatures and spirits rarely seen by man abound, a lost(?) traveler/wanderer is invited to join a campfire and listen to a tale.  The tale told by the invisible narrator is about a small insignificant nameless creature born out of darkness on the darkest of nights much like that night.  This epic journey of self-awareness and discovery turns into a magic strewn and danger filled quest which takes place in a single night full of magic and spirits taken from Swedish forklore.
Gameplay: This point and click game is divided into five distinct chapters, two of which are subdivided.  Each chapter is its own unique adventure quest with a build and use inventory,  Inventory items carry over from chapter to chapter, and all items are eventually used and have a purpose, generally logical.  (I note this only because some items found in chapter one are not used until chapter five.)  Look around carefully in each scene for other areas (found at the edges of the screen) and for items and locations to examine.  Nothing is hidden but lack of careful examination makes it easy to miss things.
The "examine" button is LEFT-CLICK.  (Please read the tutorial for mouse functions.  The way the game plays is a bit different functionally but easy once the player gets used to it.)  On the examination triangle is LORE (a scroll), SPEECH (conversation bubble), and TAKE (a hand).  I suggest clicking on all three.  LORE for the folk history of the spirit or place encountered and eventually for achievement completion.  SPEECH for the story narration, told as only an excellent verbal storyteller can tell it.   TAKE to gather the item.   Some inventory items are added automatically while others are not.  Some inventory items can be combined together to create something new while others are given to the spirits and creatures encountered.
The game is mostly mono-chrome in color, with dark blues, deep violets and shiny white to off-set this dark night shrouded world.
There are four elemental magics: earth, water, fire, and wind that the insignificant creatures has control over.  These magics are essential to game play, and certain tasks can not be completed without using the correct magic(s).  I suggest using all the magics on every scene just to see what happens because generally something happens when each elemental magic is used the first time.  (Nice detail to the game play.)
Each chapter (or sub-chapter in two cases) has its own set of tasks to complete and puzzles to solve.  The puzzles have no directions, and the clues to solving them must be sought out and inferred from environmental references or conservational text.  Most are head scratching brain twisters and CANNOT be skipped. (There is at least one excellent guide on Steam if the player gets stuck.)
There is no going back to previous areas once the game progresses, and there is little backtracking per se in each chapter.  Chapters three and five have sub-chapters.  Chapters one and five(part one) are set up in a circular fashion. Chapters two, three (part two) and four are back and forth travel along the central path which has branch paths off of it where tasks needed to be accomplished are.  Most tasks are logical and the player uses more or less what they think they need.  (Do not forget to combine inventory items.)
In the final analysis this is a story-rich narrated tale, and the game play takes a back seat to the tale being told.

Video review -
Ink is a fast pacing 2D action platform. In the game you play as a white square that splashes ink all over the level, an essential mechanic as the actual platforms of the level are not visible unless covered in paint. This adds a nice feeling discovery as you don’t know how the map really is and you need to unveil it. Ink is very challenging but has a great learning curve were the game slowly adds new elements like enemies, spikes and even bosses. The controls feel good and responsive but your white square sometimes start to go too fast making very hard to control.
Visually Ink is absolutely beautiful and that’s very impressive because the game’s graphics are simple geometrical shapes but the splatter of the ink is what really makes this game look so unique. The sound design is good, it doesn’t try to do much but the modest and calm background music offers a nice company through the game.
If you are looking for interesting characters and story development then Ink isn’t the right game for you, as the game relinquishes all of those elements in order to completely focus on it’s gameplay. But that doesn't mean that it is a lesser game, because the genuine fun platforming will provide for many hours of challenging fun.
• Final thoughts
With its humble price tag, Ink doesn’t ask much of you but what it does offer is quite amazing. This is a fun game for those who enjoy platforming, fast action and challenging games. Exploring the multiple levels while painting them is a unique mechanic that creates a unique aesthetic. There is no story here and overall the game doesn’t push its boundaries too far but instead focus itself in offering the best platforming experience it can. A fun addicting wonderful game.

You follow a little creature on his journey for fulfillment, wandering through nightly environments that are inspired by tales of folklore. Gameplay is quite standard to the point-and-click genre where you collect objects to interact with your surroundings and overcome puzzles. A nice addition though, is that you're equipped with four elemental runes (earth, water, air, fire) which activate and produce different outcomes depending on the scene. You can also interact with entities in a few different ways, such as touching, observing or talking to the person/object. Although not all interactions are entirely necessary, it can lead to some humerous/extra dialogue and is a nice feature nonetheless.
Environments and sounds reinforce your sense of vulnerability and isolation as the little creature; things that keep you immersed in the story and invested in the wellbeing of your character. I believe these aspects are key in turning a standard point and click experience into something more, and Oknytt pulls it off well.
Narrations are voice acted, delivered in a very... interesting mannerism that I haven't honestly heard before. The narrator also serves as the voice of the small creature, immitating what he might really sound like in all dialogue sequences. People have varied opinions, but I believe voice acting and sounds are some of Oknytt's fundamental strengths and a major part of what makes this game memorable, combined of course with an atmospheric beauty that is unique in its own right.
If I had to name an issue, it's that a few of the puzzles are a tad disconnected (hard to logically piece together) and your sense of direction can get confused at times. If, however, you take time to clear your head or use a walkthrough (I didn't, but maybe should have at those points), you can probably avoid these minor frustrations. I should stress that the majority of puzzles are fun to resolve, and you’ll enjoy the experience overall.
There's no time limit to the game, and thus the pacing is up to the player. I took my time to enjoy it and ended up with nine hours clocked, although even then the pleasure of the experience added value.
Overall, it's worth the money. It's emotional, captivating, and you needn't know a thing about Swedish folklore to enjoy it.

Oknytt is an almost monochromatic, dark and dreary point and click adventure that has you playing as "the small creature" in a world where hustomte trolls guard buildings. Like in most point and click adventures, you'll be walking around collecting objects and using those items to interact with the world around you. Where Oknytt deviates is you also have four rune stones at the bottom of the screen that can create fire, earth, wind and water. The fire will do things like light up a house or make the embers of a fire glow. Water will make it rain or a hustomte will drool. They all do something, even if its background stuff like a creature will appear or a dragonfly will buzz by.
These runes add another layer of complexity, because there are specific orders to them. Rain turns on and off, so do you need to have the rain on or off? Using common sense helps a lot, like you can't light a fire while its raining.
The game is simple to play, left click to walk somewhere, right click to open your inventory box, then left click to pick out an item and use it wherever. Seeing a foot icon lets you leave a screen once you've walked to it. For the most part, every area is one screen, but others with wide edges to the screen means that there's a larger area to explore.
Hovering your mouse over specific objects will show you text as to what they are. These objects are the ones that you can hold your left mouse button to interact with. You can talk, take or have the object described for you. Since I never bothered with the easy to read tutorial, it took me about 45 minutes before I realized to hold down the mouse. Most of the objects can be taken. You can intelligently figure out uses for them, unlike some point and click games, such as fill up a tea kettle at a spring of water. There are still times where you'll be left scratching your head like what exactly does a hustomte want in trade for a bolt of cloth or even to eat?
What makes Oknytt unique is the world that you're in. You play as "the small creature," a fat furry little guy that is still much larger than the mice or other mammals in the game. The art style is beautiful in its sort of colorless way, there's a lot of rich detail to each screen with dust partials wafting through the air and haze moving through the forever night sky. Its not all monochromatic though, there are punctuations of color. Dark blue skies, burning red embers in the fire, dark  streams that flow through caves and red eyed gnomes. It all adds to the beauty of the game.
Its not a happy place at all. These are humble settings, yet grandiose in its artistic detail. You'll visit corn fields, traverse humble graveyards with wooden crosses, crawl under the father's house and visit underground locales. While you're alone on your journey you'll meet plenty of well illustrated creatures like giant witches and arms that rise out from the grave.
The music is very ambient and fitting. There are long, slow string instruments. You'll hear nighttime birds, crawling under the father's house you'll hear the slow creeks of thick floorboards. In a way its all haunting and adds to the foreboding atmosphere.
Everything is voice acted as if someone alone is stilling a story. He'll use different voices for different characters and while its all admirably done, some of the voices are cringe worthy. Its more than some guy with a microphone, he feels like a professional voice actor and it helps lend credibility to the game. Plus, even if its him telling a story of what happened, I'd rather hear it than read through the text. You can click skip to stop the narration or turn it off. There are a few settings for sound, music and voice over. You can even turn off the subtitles. There's a save and load function along with a few extras to chronicle your journey.
If you're a fan of the point and click genre, you should be able to get into this game. I have a 3-minute review. The text is below, or you can watch the video in the link.
What’s so great about it is that you play as a white square thing filled with ink and all the levels are made up of invisible platforms. You can see those platforms by covering them with your ink. There are several ways for this to happen. You can simply slide along floor or walls to leave a trail of ink, double jump to splatter it all around you, or watch your ink splatter over the level when you die from any of the various obstacles. The latter will most likely be the case as this game gets hard. Although you can see the enemies which leave their own ink trails, you likely won’t see the spikes, or moving platforms in some stages until you bump into them.
On stages with these multicolored enemies, you’ll have to jump on all of them to activate the level’s exit. Some of the stages will have keys which will open these types of barriers. Sometimes there will be triangle-shaped projectiles you must dodge. Other times there will be player-homing bullets fired at you. And sometimes you may reveal one of the hidden coins in the game.
The music is very well implemented. Each of the three worlds has its own single music track which doesn’t stop playing when you die or beat the level. It plays continuously throughout its own world. But don’t worry that you’ll get annoyed by it. Each piece of music is longer than your normal platformer’s soundtrack piece, so you might not even notice when it eventually loops.
I’ll warn you it may take a while to get used to your momentum. When you jump in any direction, you will continue moving in that direction for as long as you are in the air. This means you won’t lose any momentum when you release the directional button. You will need to press back in the other direction to control your momentum. You also will jump off walls whenever you jump twice while next to a wall or sliding down one. This may sound normal, but while you must press against a wall to slowly slide down it, you don’t have to press against the wall to jump off it. Instead, just being next to it and jumping a second time will act as a wall-jump. This may be confusing when trying to jump up to another platform. Landing on top of enemies can sometimes appear inconsistent. You need to jump on top of enemies to kill them, but it may look like you landed on top of one when it killed you or you flew into the side of one when you killed it. It may have something to do with the fluctuating nature of the enemy’s shape, but I don’t know. These little nuances simply take some getting used to.
In total, there are 75 levels, split-up into three worlds, each with a boss at the end. There are 20 of those hidden coins to supply and extra challenge. If you just want to beat the game, most players will do so in two or three hours of play. Completing all the Steam achievements will take longer as the hardest three ask you to beat each world without dying at all: thee achievements I haven’t even attempted yet. I thought beating the game and getting all the coins was hard enough.

First of all, I think this game is great. It flows smoothly, great animations, its also very different - and there's one thing that's always fun: getting used to a new game.
However, I do feel like there are a couple things that impact the game negatively. The first is that the map sizes are way too small. I'm sorry to anyone who disagrees with me completely, but as someone who's been playing Civilization games since the first one, it feels too small. In II, and III (even IV) the maps were decently sized, and the biggest maps felt huge. In this one, the 'massive' size is about the size of a standard planet in Civ III or IV. I can zoom out a little and, even with only 3 other AIs, I can see them on my screen. That's too close (for me at least).
Since, I like to have lots of space to build big civilizations before going to war.
The second is that I feel the health system is a little misbalanced. With 10 cities each with three or four health related buildings, I'd still be struggling to keep my health score high enough. Considering that biowells take a while to get to, and its still somewhat difficult as occasionally I've had trouble getting workers to register that they CAN build biowells.
(A biowell is supposed to be buildable on any terrain by a worker after you unlock it, and it sometimes works, sometimes doesn't for me.)
Its difficult to manage health to get up to a big empire, and since this game favors bigger empires for more trade routes, I think that's a problem.
Still, the music is cool the upgrading units is pretty neat, and I like how AIs can stagger-start at the beginning of the game. It did take me a while to get used to which technology creates which wonder (its not exactly clear) though. I also like deciding to fight or live with the aliens on the planet. Though I feel like harmony should have more options to make peace with the wildlife than it does. Supremacy should have more emphasis on might than I think it does, but I appreciate that the developers wanted to make it so you can go as any affinity you want with any faction, and still make it work.
However, sometimes I feel like certain maps sort of force you to go toward a specific way, playing how the map wants instead of how you want...
I know there are a lot of negative points, but it doesn't take a whole lot of the fun away from playing it.  I'd definitely still recommend this game to anyone. Its not just a Civ V mod. Even with hexagons instead of squares, it still feels different. I certainly cant get enough of it :)

1. Most games that are trying to push the boundaries of narratives in gaming are just you walking for two hours while some story is revealed to you slowly. This is exactly like that only it's good.
2. The narrator, voiced by Kevan Brighting, is the star of the show. When a game has a small cast, it needs to be anchored by a truly excellent performance and that's just what his is.
3. This is that kind of humor that's truly funny but you don't laugh out loud at.
4. You play as Stanley, a distressingly mild mannered office worker. You start out in an empty office. The general goal as far as there is one is to figure out what's going on.
5. There is no one specific thing that is going on. A lot of things could be happening and at no point is the game ever like, "Okay, let's cut the crap. Here's what's been going on the whole time." You have to draw your own conclusions.
6. *the sound of minds blowing*
7. You can use your Googles to find how to get every possible one of the numerous endings but play through until you are stuck first and play some more before that. Google ruins everything. Or, actually, it only ruins some things. Self driving cars are going to be pretty awesome once they have that worked out but I don't much like the ever hanging temptation to cheat at every puzzle game on earth and I am pretty sure they've been showing my search results to Santa Claus.
8. Graphically, this looks pretty good but who cares.
9. The Steam achievements for this are pretty hilarious. Check them out even if you don't decide to play.
10. This game could be considered a Philosophy of Games 101 course but don't hold that against it. You will consider the relationship of player to character and player to developer quite a lot.
11. There's points where you wait around and do nothing and you are rewarded for that. There are also points where you wait around and do nothing and nothing happens at all.
12. My one small complaint is this doesn't have any really memorable music. I guess it didn't need it but I like music so I figure I had ought to mention that.
13. I think it is important to remember that just because a game pushes boundaries doesn't make it automatically good or worth playing. You have to get the other details right too and that's where
shines when so many games like it fail.

Updated Review: 13 had a very rough initial Steam port, and it took Square Enix longer than I would have liked for them to address it but they at least did, unlike with some other infamously bad ports of games. We got increased resolution, framerates, and controls over some things like shadow quality and anti aliasing. I still feel there is more work that could and should be done but this is probably the best it'll get, and it is good enough for me although the system requirements below are certainly underestimated, if you have a solid rig that can handle 2013-14 AAA games you should have a good experience, but if you have trouble running modern games, you probably will with this too despite it being a 5 year old game. That said, if you think your system can handle it and you love the Final Fantasy series, this is definitely one of the best in recent years.
Game plays very well and looks beautiful, but as I mentioned before, the system requirements underestimate what you really need greatly. I am running on a Radeon HD 6970 which well beyond what the PS3/360 were doing with this game and my CPU well exceeds what the game requirements ask for, yet I do still encounter some occassional framedrops, but the framerate is now 30+ about 95% of the time instead of 5% of the time like the initial release was, and battles do reach 60 frequently but it is a bit inconsistent. The stutter issue from the initial release is also gone, although you may see the framerate drop a bit here and there, it no longer has the issue with the pauses. I do still have some gripes with the port like the way you exit the game is clunky, there are no settings to tweak the audio, and a several missing graphical settings (Which would probably help out those that may have poor framerates) but it is serviceable enough to enjoy the game for what it is.
Final Fantasy 13 will often get criticized for things like the extreme linearity to the point where you're just running down corridors. Also there are criticisms regarding the lack of controlling your companions in combat and pressing A/X (on Xbox and Playsation controllers) constantly. People will also complain about its story being all over the place and not making any sense.
It is quite linear until you get to about the halfway point, which based on the Chapter system is actually near the end of the game, but at this point the game opens up quite a lot actually. The game takes on a broader scope at this point and give you a lot of side missions to do and at this point the battles get very challenging, so the mashing A/X is not even remotely accurate unless you want to find a quick death in the game (and for that matter is no longer accurate after the first few hours of the game).
The Paradigm system is easily one of the best Final Fantasy battle systems there has ever been imo. Paradigm is an excellent system for beginners to the series to get used to the mechanics, and it has a lot of depth in spite of its fast pace. The game does have a bit too long of a "tutorial" where it very slowly introduces the mechanics of the system, but by the time you get the full breadth of options, you will have a lot of fun with the battles.
The story is a excellent ride from start to finish. It does have some confusion in the beginning with a lot of weird terms like L'Cie and Fal'cie that can be hard to follow. However, the story is filled with action, intrigue, and struggle, and the characters show great emotion and depth with a well balanced party. Like all FF games though, this game does have its one or two characters which are annoying, particularly in the beginning, but said characters do grow a lot and become less annoying and more mature as the game progresses, stick with it and you'll enjoy the payoff.

Original Review: I recommend this game, but I don't recomend the Steam version at this time. The game is just running like crap. In spite of my PC exceeding all the recommended requirements, I've been lucky to get 30 FPS in most parts of the game, it usually averages around 18-25 with occasional stutters. The game does have excellent graphics, but it was a game released back in 2010 and ran on the consoles that were 4-5 years old without a hitch, there is just no excuse that a much superior PC cant handle it. I'd even argue in saying that it is a worse port than Dark Souls, since even basic things like Anti Aliasing are missing at least in some part unless you use Durante's mod.
People want Final Fantasy games on PC, but they also want games that look great and run great as well. If you want to buy a Final Fantasy game on your PC, skip on this until Square Enix fixes it and buy this on one of the consoles instead (PS3 version is the better version if you own both 360 and PS3), or buy a different Final Fantasy game like Final Fantasy 3, 4, 7, 8, or 14. I will update this if and when the game gets fixed for me. If it doesn't get fixed, I want Square Enix to know that I will not buy 13-2 or Lightning Returns when they come out, even if those games work properly.

When I downloaded this game, I expected to be a cool Voxel FPS, in the same genre as Block N' Load or Ace Of Spades.
The game started as well as my toaster laptop could do (around 20 fps), with some epic main menu music. All good here.
But it was here where I found my first issue:
I'd expected a tutorial for newcomers and oblivious players alike, but instead you're just "thrown to the wolves", i.e., you just join a random game, with no sort of matchmaking to even out the skill level. But that was okay by me (the lack of matchmaking, not the lack of tutorial), since not all companies can do a proper matchmaking and skill level matching system. (IMO it also depends on the size of the playerbase)

If you browse the serverlist (as a normal fella), you'll come across around 50, or perhaps even more servers. But when you apply the "hide empty servers" and optionally the "hide full servers" filters, you'll see that huge number was reduced up to, in the best scenarios I've seen so far, 6 servers.
Take note I've played and acquired a taste for the game during various open beta weekends, and in the beginning, that shocked me. Granted this game came out in 2014 or so, and I've only started playing around early 2016s, it was a no-brainer that it would lost a slice of its playerbase, but that got me investigating.
In the end, I stumbled across a good factor to this: lack of updates. A lil' more digging got me to discover one of developers' comment on the steam forums about it.
According to him, both Indiegala and Ghostshark had moved on to another projects. Recently, I've decided to take a trip to Ghostshark's website and I've seen Blockstorm advertised in their front page, loud and clear. To me, it does not seems like Ghostshark has forgotten this game. Nor did the remaining playerbase that still resists against the death of this voxel fps.
One of the things that made me come back to this game over and over again is the
It's very simple and user-friendly, so you don't need a degree in design or Photoshop like some other editors. (I look at you CSGO's workbench).
Another thing I liked, as I just mentioned it, is the playerbase. I'm sure this game had its activity peak, and now it's more empty than last year, but since this game has lasted some years with a low playerbase, I think it will never totally die.
And who knows, maybe IndieGala gives love to this game, because it certainly deserves it.

"Think of Portal where players can only shoot portal when they are in midair, and will be killed if they reach the ground"
Honestly this game is much more "re-action" than "action" because everything kill U in 1 hit and the game physic tend to catapult every object (enemy and U) in sonic speed around (and kill U in process cause U hit something U shouldn't).
The ratio of skill require to pass each challenge is around... 75% reaction skill / 25% puzzle solving skill. The hard part of the pzzle is not solving what player have to do, but if you can execute the 'solving process' or not.
Some level even go as far as 90% reaction skill.
For example, one of the puzzle require the plater to switch between 'push' and 'pull' on some rail. (Yeah, it's railgun that shoot the player to the door to next level). The problem about this level is that it requires superhuman precision 'push' and 'pull' (due to in-game physic and magnet simulation) or U will falldown on the way and have to do everything again.
Another problem is that some puzzle is 'memory maze puzzle that kill U if U go the wrong way cause respawn is faster' kind of puzzle. There's a level where U have to float up the tower and evade electrocuted barrier. The problem is that some 'path' lead U to deadend of eletrocuted barrier and player will be pushed to dead against it.
But except from these levels (around 10% of the level are like this), the rest of the levels are more reasonable and enjoyable.
All in all I will recommend it. This game have interesting concept of using magnet theme puzzle and reasonable physic to make it work (90% of the time anyway).
It also has very interesting boss battle that's more satisfying to fight/solve than most puzle game (the difficulty spike need some balance thought, it's so Dark Soul 1-hit-kill-mode).
The game is worth the price, especially on sale.

TL DR: Hollow Knight is seriously great. It's a beautiful game with great music and atmosphere, with a huge world to explore. Combat is fairly simple, but it's just dificult enough to be satisfying. If you like metroidvanias with great exploration and bosses to fight, this is a really great one!
Hollow Knight is a game about a sort of lone wanderer exploring a ruined kingdom. Hallownest was a great kingdom once, until a plague brought death and chaos to the realm. The world is divided into 17 locations with their own sub areas, most having a boss or two. The game starts out slow, but once you get wall-jumping and a dash it opens up a lot, having quite a lot of non-linearity. There's only one signposted goal in the game, which is to get to 3 locations, and you can pretty much get to those three in whatever order you like. There's tons of secrets to find once you get all the abilities, and the atmosphere's really good.
There's more than 150 enemies in the game, and they're mostly different besides some really basic ones. Sometimes the game will put you up against several of them on a confined space, leaving you to jump around slashing them with your nail. Hollow Knight's combat is fairly simple (you can attack, cast a spell or use a special attack in pretty much all 4 directions), but having to constantly be on the move and using downward slashes against ground foes to keep in the air, for example, is pretty satisfying. Some of the bosses are really well designed and have very good movesets, though none of them with too much variation.
It's a really beautiful game, and very satisfying to play. The amount of content is really good for the base price, and for the genre in general (from what I saw on HLTB, since I haven't played a great deal of metroidvanias). Simply put, if you enjoy 2D exploration and combat in a beautiful world with great music, this is your game.

The cut scenes are very well done and keeps me wanting to move the story along.
Combat is very fun and entertaining.
My friends won't even give this game a try because too many negative reviews on steam.  Reading the most recent positive reviews and they are all down rated with no feedback.  It looks like someone has a vendetta or an attempt to steer people to other free mmo games. This game is simple but pretty fun if you like platformers.  The concept is great, the mechanics seemed solid, and the level design was not bad for the levels I played in the game.  The idea of jumping out into space, painting anything you touch is pretty cool.  It is like Mario had a baby with one of the Splatoon characters.
It was a bit too fidgity for me when I got to a platform double the width of my character with an enemy on it that you had to jump up from below and stomp, but the wall against the platform killed you, so I quit at that point.  I don't have the patience, but it was likely on par with the original Super Mario Bros. for the NES, including the stomping of enemies.  In spite of me complaining about hard levels, if you like platformes like Mario, I guarantee this will not be difficult for you, and if you play Super Mario Maker, this will be a breeze most likely.

Hollow Knight gave me the same cold sweat, shaking hands and frayed nerves I got from Dark Souls.  The Trial of Fools is very, very hard but there's nothing so satisfying as beating it and not being able to sit still.  More than once I had to dry to controller before I had another go.
The world building is excellent and NPCs are very well characterised.  It's genuinely sad when you meet a ghost who doesn't realise they're dead, they're so excited about what's coming.
A tiny, insignificant little gem of a game.

Liked this. I can't say I would put it as my "Game Of The Year", but it was definitely a good time. This is also a whole more linear than Gone Home. I liked the story and characters though but your mileage may vary.

I won't deny this game has tedious moments where you need to memorise certain aspects or sequences - but that is also what makes this games so interesting. None of that quicksave/quickload bull, just hard work (and still, hard is relative).
The story that evolves in the background is simplistic and nothing new, yet collecting all achievements (in the form of scrolls in the game) will provide a few additional insights into what just transpired in the years before the game and how the situation came to be.
The mechanics are fair and as you continue playing, the logic behind the move sequences will become clearer.
All in all, I enjoyed playing (using a controller made it more pleasant), and 100%'ing almost doubled my playtime.
TL;DR
If you like a challenge that reminds you of some older games: go for it.
If you get tired of repetition and get frustrated easily by your own mistakes: stay away.

PROS:
- Artsy enough to be a real piece of art.
- Creepy artwork and character designs. But with a fairy tale vibe and dialgoues, creepiness is mitigated and thus not a horror game I assure you. Cute main character known as "the creature" and a small helpless fairy contrast all the dangerous environments and monsters they confront.
- Decent voice acting.
CONS:
- Actually the narrator's voice can get on your nerves if heard too much, he voices all other characters in the game and the problem is that the transition between narrating and mimicking characters' speeches can often get confusing, abrupt, and not really well-done.  Later chapters there are slight popping sounds when some of the characters angrily grunt. Quality also goes does down here and there and the pace the way narrator speaks feels uncomfortable and he seems to have some difficulty with breath control.  The voice actor must have had a hard time recording all the dialogues as he is the only person who speaks in the game. This probably will remind you that the game is developed by a small group of folks after all.
- Game pace; the creature's movement, animation, and pretty much everything is a bit too slow.
- Relatively long loading and saving time for such a little game.
Final Remarks:
The game is a typical point-and-click adventure genre, but its uniqueness in terms of being artsy alone is a good enough reason to warrant a fun and worthy playthrough.
. RECOMMENDED .

is a physics-based puzzle-platformer, tending towards a 'Metroidvania' in some respects. The game's puzzles are largely based around a magnetism mechanic and manipulation of attraction/repulsion of differently/similarly magnetised objects - including the player character himself - with a small range of tools. There are certainly some clever ideas here, but unfortunately my abiding feeling about
is of frustration, as I found many scenarios to be very fiddly, with behaviour not readily predictable - it was a case while it became clear what was needed, actually doing that was far from easy... but not for what felt like a lack of 'skill'.
Puzzle mechanics aside, while the game takes place almost all within a single building, there's a reasonably decent variety of environments. Graphics are simple but functional and the background music, while again simple, is catchy in a positive way.
is a short game - if you know what you're doing (and are able to pull it off!), it could be completed within a couple of hours or less, but I wouldn't see that specifically to be a negative here, especially as the games feels like it pretty much exhausts the types of puzzle scenario that the magnetism mechanic allows, without a significant shake-up.
Overall, while I wouldn't go as far as to call
a
game, I couldn't really rate it anywhere better than average given the feelings of frustration that it leads to.

1. Most games that are trying to push the boundaries of narratives in gaming are just you walking for two hours while some story is revealed to you slowly. This is exactly like that only it's good.
2. The narrator, voiced by Kevan Brighting, is the star of the show. When a game has a small cast, it needs to be anchored by a truly excellent performance and that's just what his is.
3. This is that kind of humor that's truly funny but you don't laugh out loud at.
4. You play as Stanley, a distressingly mild mannered office worker. You start out in an empty office. The general goal as far as there is one is to figure out what's going on.
5. There is no one specific thing that is going on. A lot of things could be happening and at no point is the game ever like, "Okay, let's cut the crap. Here's what's been going on the whole time." You have to draw your own conclusions.
6. *the sound of minds blowing*
7. You can use your Googles to find how to get every possible one of the numerous endings but play through until you are stuck first and play some more before that. Google ruins everything. Or, actually, it only ruins some things. Self driving cars are going to be pretty awesome once they have that worked out but I don't much like the ever hanging temptation to cheat at every puzzle game on earth and I am pretty sure they've been showing my search results to Santa Claus.
8. Graphically, this looks pretty good but who cares.
9. The Steam achievements for this are pretty hilarious. Check them out even if you don't decide to play.
10. This game could be considered a Philosophy of Games 101 course but don't hold that against it. You will consider the relationship of player to character and player to developer quite a lot.
11. There's points where you wait around and do nothing and you are rewarded for that. There are also points where you wait around and do nothing and nothing happens at all.
12. My one small complaint is this doesn't have any really memorable music. I guess it didn't need it but I like music so I figure I had ought to mention that.
13. I think it is important to remember that just because a game pushes boundaries doesn't make it automatically good or worth playing. You have to get the other details right too and that's where
shines when so many games like it fail.

Freedom fall is a short, simple, and very fun game.  It does pretty much what the trailer shows.  It's a brisk and often deadly platformer that usually scrolls downward.  It took me 92 minutes to finish the game once.  There are a lot of reasons to go back.
Grafiti from your character's captor is presented very often in small doses. The game's story unfolds through those messages, and made the first playthrough very much worth it.
There is also replay value, including at least one story branch, different solutions to the first boss fight, and a small wealth of achievements.
Yes, this is a platform game with a seemingly 16-bit inspired visual design. Yet it owes much to modern games.  There are ample checkpoints.  Death lurks around every corner. The player experiences the kind of slow-release narrative found more recent games such as the Portal series.
Although they seemed to draw inspiration from all over the last thirty years of gaming, Stirfire Studios cherry picked the best fits for the game they made.  The end result was fun on every level.
Very highly recommended.

A pure-blooded rouge-like from the original developers of the Diablo franchise. Torchlight blends a light-hearted, painterly visual style with hack-and-slash dungeon crawling. From a gameplay perspective it's almost too similar to it's spiritual predecessor Diablo, but it introduces a healthy collection of additions to make dungeon crawling smoother and easier for new players while still providing players seeking hardcore challenges a lot of meat to chew on. On top of that the game also has built-in support for a wealth of free community made mods that can add in new characters, classes, spells, items, pets, monsters, dungeon elements, and more at any time. You can even make your own mods if you're feeling industrious, the game comes with the same full featured mod making utility that the developers used to make the entire game.

This is another title in the Civ series. The simplest comparison between this and Civ: BNW is, this has the feel a better balanced game starting in a later era. That is the trade, water travel, and unit types become availble early and it seems to be quicker to approach victory.
It doesn not feel like it has the same length as civ: BNW and lacks some finishing touches. The most significant of these is simply the difficulty in just reading the tech web, wonders don't stand out from units or buildings and it is very easy to miss a significant thing if you aren't looking for it. A mod already exists to colour code this and hopefully this will become incorporated into the game. An inability to protect trading outposts is quite frustrating, they are worthwhile investments but do not pop up in the late game and the AI will quite likely destroy them.
It is still a long game, even if it does not have the obvious time periods of the previous game. The new social policy layout is an improvement. Units have been greatly simplified, which I find enjoyable. The basic types are researchable immediately and undergo improvements as your civilisation progress. There are more advanced auxiliary units to these, and once you know what to research to unlock them, they become interesting additions to late game warfare.
I would recommend this game to my fellow Australians but shortly after release this game was hit the the Australia tax. This meant an increase in price of almost 100% ($50 - $90), for no justifiable reason, beyond corporate greed screwing up the price at the release. It is honestly insulting that there is an additional $40 cost for late(ish) buyers in this region and completely unjustifiable. There is no hard copy to ship out, no anything and to Australians, New Zealanders and others in this region  I suggest playing civ 5 until the price drops or just getting $40 of cheap laptops / pcs, installing steam and smashing them all with a hammer. It would be satisfying.

Windows 7 64 bit

I'm a few hours in so far, I'll update my review once I'm further in, but here's my initial impression of this port:
Pros:
Price: $15, this seems about right, I wouldn't expect to pay much less and I wouldn't want to pay much more.
Audio: Japanese and English voices.  I liked the dubs of FF10 and 12, but found most of the FF13 characters fairly unlikable.  I'm preferring the original voices so far and I'm very glad they're an option.
Cons:
Resolution: 720p max.  I'm using a smaller 720p tv right now so it doesn't really bother me but I can see this being an issue.  I hear a fan-made patch fixes this, but it should have been resolved officially.
Framerate: I've noticed a few noticable framerate drops since I started playing.  Not sure what's up with that.
Size: Due to a rather sloppy implementation of dual audio, the game takes up almost 60 gigs of space.  It also takes about 35 minutes to install after downloading.  It's a relatively minor gripe but you probably ought to be aware of it.
I use a wired 360 controller and it works fine.  The game itself has its flaws, but I don't need to go into that too deeply.  Just expect to spend a lot of time reading the Datalog to find out what was supposed to have been conveyed in the scene you just watched that you might not have picked up on.  Overall, it's not one of my favorite Final Fantasy's, but it's a fun game and I think it was worth getting.

I am giving this game a "big thumbs up" because it is SOO much more than that...it was an experience.  First off, being of where it was made from then I do have to admit I came into it biased already determined to like it. (My grandfather hails from Sweden.  And parts of the game even contained folklore from a song sung to me as a child.)  However I still gave it a fair and open mind to let myself decide truthfully how I felt about it.  The graphics, for being simple as far as without a large color spectrum that is, were ABSOLUTELY amazing and fantastic!!  The understated colors did not distract in the least in my opinion from game play or the story...they placed them strategically and where they would matter most I felt.   The story line was very developed and complex. (When you get to the end then you will understand, and hopefully agree, why I say this.)  I was in complete surprise at the ending and also quite moved and left with a feeling of "WOW!"...speechless, as it were.  There are so many great things I could say about this game.  I very much liked the feature that when you need to combine items or give them to an NPC then you cannot make a mistake as the game will not let you pursue the wrong scenario.  The most of the puzzles were challenging, but not too much.  You do have an option to have either the voice or to have captions.  However certain small parts did require you to have just voice.  (I am guessing these were the areas that only the Swedish language was available and the Steam profile for the game does state this so it was not a surprise in the least for me.)  There were even a couple of more challenging achievements.  Also, in addition, the price is very reasonable and I would have even paid twice as much...it is that good.  So in closure, I highly reccomend this game to any one looking for unique game play, an original story (it is based on Swedish folklore), point and clicks, or even a calm and quicker game to experience.

Actually store page summarizes what this game is perfectly: it's from creators of Gone Home, game that put "Are walking simulators games?" discussion under spotlight. And yes, this is a "walking simulator" (i.e. adventure games with a modern approach) and it's set in a orbital station in year 2088 where our character walks around and gathers personal information of station's residents. In Gone Home we walked and read diaries of people we were investigating, here we're watching holographic recordings of certain past events. Personally I loved innovation that is "not reading diaries but watching puppet shows", not only it's easier to get engaged with, but also more expressive. Further comments on story would be in spoiler-territory, so I'll stop here.
Overall, if you liked Gone Home, give this a try. Definitely a refinement of that formula.

The game mechanics are easy to understand. There are items of interest on every screen, when you move your mouse around you'll get a pop-up with a name (shovel, lake, sky, etc), so you know it's something you can interact with.
You interact with objects/characters by holding down the left-mouse button to get a pop-up menu with three options:
- The narrator has some extra information about the object.
- The creature you are playing either says something about the object/character or actually starts a conversation.
- You try and take the object.
Basically you just use all three options on everything and everyone. If that doesn't do enough, at the bottom of the screen there are 4 rune stones (Earth, Water, Fire, Air). Clicking on those can make something happen, it all depends on the surroundings you are in. Don't forget to click on all 4 on every screen.
My progress is to get
, then
, then try and
something. Click on all 4 runes, if something happens, Lore/Talk/Take again and move to the next screen. Get an additional item? Try and combine it with EVERYTHING in your inventory, doesn't matter if it doesn't make sense at the time.
On the top left of the screen is a scroll icon, clicking it reveals the objectives that you still have to do for this particular chapter so you don't get completely lost.
At the top right is your inventory with items you can combine, give to others, or use on objects in the environment. Some puzzles and items you need to combine are a bit far-fetched. I would recommend using a walkthrough when you think you've tried everything. There is no hint system that gradually helps you along and there's no point in annoying yourself. Using a walkthrough at certain times keeps the game fun instead of becoming a bore.

Playing Oknytt can be an enjoyable experience even when using a walkthrough guide right from the very start, as I did. Using such a guide might in fact be recommended, as it helped me avoid the frustration and the tediousness typical to this kind of point-and-click puzzle games. Since there were no more headaches caused by having to find certain items, discover specific combinations, and so on, I could fully focus on the enjoyable parts of the game: the art style, the stories, the exploration (and the discovery of new characters, stories, levels), etc.
I'd say the gameplay isn't exactly Oknytt's strong point, but only unless you're not a fan of solving point-and-click challenges, as some of the item combinations are quite intuitive (unlike other similar games) and it's also got some gameplay originality in the addition of some "elemental runes".
Anyway, I personally enjoyed everything else about this little game, not the gameplay.
Its main theme is truly original, as it's inspired from the Swedish folklore. And not just barely, remotely inspired, but deeply rooted and connected to Swedish folklore, from the very start to the very ending.
The main story isn't very intricate but the many secondary characters that the main protagonist encounters during its journey are all interesting and unique. The ending was rather abrupt and quite ambiguous for my taste, but not bad enough to cause me any real disappointment.
The visuals aren't sophisticated, but they're charming. In a very dark tone at all times, the game feels immersive and captivating. The voice acting and the sounds are also top-notch. Even if there's one single voice actor for all characters, that guy is clearly hugely talented and does a great job.
As for the game's length and value for money, considering its low full price, Oknytt gets another plus in my book.
Pros:
- strongly inspired from Swedish folklore, making it original and even a bit educational
- nice visuals and art styles
- top notch voice acting and sound effects
- it's inexpensive, simple, lightweight, neat, and really enjoyable
Cons:
- gameplay based on typical point-and-click elements. Without a guide, it may take a lot more hours to complete, not to mention the unavoidable frustration coming along the way.

Zack Bell's INK is a hardcore platformer in which you play well designed stages, with many obstacles such as poor physics, and bad controls.
Each stage in INK is completely invisible to begin with, and the player will need to cover the stage in ink in order to see it- which is done by simply walking on the stage, double jumping, or being killed. Though this is a rather odd mechanic which does very little to add to the gameplay, it's not especially irritating; as a hardcore platformer, you die a lot anyways, and this is usually not because of invisible walls. The truly annoying feature of INK is its physics. There is NO friction in the air, which makes turning near impossible, and will account for many deaths on more difficult stages. The only way to slow down is to double jump. Double jumping, however, is only recharged through landing on the ground or a wall- not enemies, which means it's possible to be sent flying off the stage simply because you landed on an enemy instead of the ground.
Gameplay aside, INK is wonderful. It has an amazing ambient soundtrack, and pretty decent visuals, but these don't make up for the game's flaws.

Freedom Fall Review
What makes the Indie scene a competitor to the AAA market is truthfully a massive quantity of games.  I've seen this game in at least two bundles, and that's where I recommed you buy it, as Freedom Fall is simply too short for $10.  However, a massive quantity doesn't mean all the games are bad, in fact I'd argue Freedom Fall is one of the better games you can find in the Indie game scene.
I just beat it a few minutes ago so the game is still fresh in my mind.  Although I remember frustrating parts and an akward jump glitch in the beginning of the game, what really sticks out is the story.  Specifically the writing on the wall that you will be reading from the beginning of the game to the end - that's why I wanted to continue playing and ended up beating the game in one sitting.  Of course if you want to know what happens go and play the game, but basically your character is imprisoned in a castle for a supposed crime and the princess of the king and queen is a psychotic b!tch who installed all kinds of traps and spikes into an escape route.  If you can escape then you are granted freedom.
Gameplay is basic platforming, jumping, double jumping, hovering with use of tools you buy from collecting bolts and screws, Ratchet and Clank / Megaman and Bass style.  You'll find "shops" throughout and you'll buy the stuff you need early on in the game.  In fact I wonder what the point of the whole system is, you get the stuff so early that you won't need the currency bolts later on, it just seems kind of pointless, they may as well have started you with the tools.  You do have a weapon by using bombs (they're more like mini-grenades) that will destroy some traps if you so wish.  But, I'd advise against using it because there are parts where the bombs are mandatory and I don't remember them being on hand anywhere.  The levels do change up the style with you going through some watery levels, fire levels, and what was the most unique was a metallic-plant level, a "garden."  There are boss fights as well as an easy final boss fight with the aforementioned psychob!itch.
Every level has what I call the Angry Birds rating system, that is to say, three things you have to accomplish to fully beat every level.  I didn't three-star any of the levels but then again I played it on hard mode.  Although it does lenghen the game unquestionably, I still wish there were more levels as the game felt short on one playthrough.  You can beat it in like three hours, my time currently says four but that's because I left the computer on doing not nerdy things!
So anyway, yes, play this game, I will come back to it another time to try and complete the Angry Birds rating system!  But be warned, I COULD NOT get a controller to work with this game.  I do not have a Xbox 360 controller (I know, I must be stupid or crazy how dare I) and instead have a generic joypad.  That wasn't compatible so I tried Joy2Key and I swear the game just wants you to use a keyboard no matter what, the buttons responded but the directions, including the D-Pad and joysticks, just didn't do anything.  That's kind of a crime for a game that requires precision platforming, don't you think?  But it's a Friday, I don't feel like being a complainer.

Bit.Trip Beat is an awesome game that you can play while enjoying the music. It brings a bit of old school retro gaming to the table with a modern twist. Think of this game as one-player pong on steroids at a rave.
The game is played by controlling a paddle that slides up and down. You can use the keyboard, game controller or the best option which is the mouse. The goal of the game is to reflect all incoming 'beats' and every successful reflect makes a sound that goes along with the music. If you continue to do well, the music gets more intense but if you miss and do poorly, you'll eventually be taken to a black and white world with no music, reminiscent of PONG, until you do better.
There are several worlds to play and in each world there are several parts to play through and a boss at the end. The difficulty levels range from casual playing to challenging. There are in game powerups and challenges as well. Overall, a great aesthetically and musically pleasing game to pick up :)

I can't say I'm a hardcore Hitman fan but I enjoyed the previous installments and I enjoyed Absolution greatly. Yes, it's much more story driven then the previous parts, but the story is interesting to follow and it offers really interesting solutions to the concept of boss fights. Your enemies are humans, they can't withstand ten bullets in their heads, and garrote is quite enough to kill them, too. Well, almost, but that one little exception was in cinematic and doesn't count. The level design is nice, enemies behave relistically, stealth, both social and hiding, is crucial, especially on Professional difficulty levels. Of course, nobody forces you to do them all, and you can run through the game with blazing guns on Easy and complete it in like 10 hours or so, but, well, I don't think you can call it 'playing Hitman'. "Beat" takes an intriguing retro Atari 2600 visual identity and merges it with an evolved "Pong" style mechanic crossed with a musical rhythm game.  The game takes some getting used to because while the mechanics are dead simple the patterns sometimes give little warning and the background visuals are specifically designed to distract your attention.  Seriously, the distraction is so bad that the game literally can produce eye strain as you struggle to keep up with the flow patterns of incoming balls.  There are also elements of the game which aren't easily understood such as how the game penalizes you for missing beats (ball hits).  The music is entertaining and the visuals are exciting enough that this is probably a better game to watch someone else play than to actually *BE* the player.   In fact, Tracy's comment on watching me play was that this would be the perfect game to stone out to.

This game was everything I wanted and more. I expected some good puzzles and what it ended up being was lots of puzzles wrapped in a metroidvania way. Lots of variety, with physics, magnets, blinking, and more.

I will say that though the majority of the game is not too punishing, quick loads and saving every room, the bosses are definitely much moreso. As usual a boss will have 3 phases and if you die at any of them you have to do the whole fight over. Normally this wouldn't be too bad, but this is not a combat oriented game; it's puzzles and swiftness, and if you figure out the first but fail the latter, it can be frustrating to to go through everything you figured out again and again. The last boss and I suppose the 2nd to last boss to and extent feel very grindy.
I have to say despite all that I love, I find the true ending very...mediocre. I think the regular ending is better honestly. The true ending feels strange, and unrewarding of all the hard work you put in, and it ends abruptly, not even credits. I think the true ending could have been so much more or at least give you more lore or something, but it's worse than the regular one I'd say.

To those new to the RPG-scene, read the last line.
To those looking for familiarities and differences, pro's and con's compared to other games, read on.
Torchlight is a creative tongue-in-cheek mix of a few RPG's, the biggest influences being Dragonica and Fable (1.. ).
The graphics are 'chunky' which often invites thoughts of 'cheapness' and 'shortcuts', but was pleasantly surprised with the detail in customization it really goes. Spells are beautiful, the combat is amazing and the monsters are just hilarious sometimes. Those who've played Dragonica will understand the artistic style straight away.
The Fable-side of it is almost entirely the mechanics. Things just work.. well. There's no shortcuts taken, everything in it seems meant to be there from pets being able to take loot back to town for selling, to the myriad of mazes and routes possible for each (and every..) quest.
Buy it. Buy it now. It's not only a great first RPG, it's a great RPG to stand on it's own.

So the fight goes like this, I have to be able blink into the birds chest (after jumping so you don't just blink into the legs) hit the object in the chest, blink out, then you have to dodge this shockwave that you have blink right before it hits you otherwise you'll still be in its path & get knocked out of the arena, the bird then lays mini bird egg bombs that I've only managed to dodge by jumoing & blinking over them (though that doesn't always work) the main bird then moves to the side of the arena and sends a wall of electricty at you, which you get past the same way you get past the shockwave from earlier (though since it moves a bit slower & in a horizontal direction its much easier to dodge than the shockwave).

BIT.TRIP BEAT doesn't need nor demand perfection; ultimately it will be YOU who seeks a perfect run.  Every time you play, you'll always feel like you could have and truly SHOULD have done better.  Replaying stages is inevitable.  These songs will haunt your dreams.
Complicated rhythms.  Tricky targets.  And each song is ~15 minutes long, increasing the difficulty in order to make a perfect run.
Ultimately, this game should have been called BIT.TRIP ADDICTION

I'm a few hours in so far, I'll update my review once I'm further in, but here's my initial impression of this port:
Pros:
Price: $15, this seems about right, I wouldn't expect to pay much less and I wouldn't want to pay much more.
Audio: Japanese and English voices.  I liked the dubs of FF10 and 12, but found most of the FF13 characters fairly unlikable.  I'm preferring the original voices so far and I'm very glad they're an option.
Cons:
Resolution: 720p max.  I'm using a smaller 720p tv right now so it doesn't really bother me but I can see this being an issue.  I hear a fan-made patch fixes this, but it should have been resolved officially.
Framerate: I've noticed a few noticable framerate drops since I started playing.  Not sure what's up with that.
Size: Due to a rather sloppy implementation of dual audio, the game takes up almost 60 gigs of space.  It also takes about 35 minutes to install after downloading.  It's a relatively minor gripe but you probably ought to be aware of it.
I use a wired 360 controller and it works fine.  The game itself has its flaws, but I don't need to go into that too deeply.  Just expect to spend a lot of time reading the Datalog to find out what was supposed to have been conveyed in the scene you just watched that you might not have picked up on.  Overall, it's not one of my favorite Final Fantasy's, but it's a fun game and I think it was worth getting.

Shadow Warrior is a remake of the classic Shadow Warrior from the 90's. Played on an i5 4460 and a gtx 1060 I was able to run the game +60fps on Ultra using a 1080p resolution. Mouse and Keyboard are preferred however the game is programmed for gamepads as well. On a technical level this game is very well optimized.
You play as Lo Wang, an assassin who works for a Japanese millionaire business owner named Orochi Zilla. The setup is Zilla gives Wang a briefcase with 2 million dollars in it and sends him to go purchase a very special Katana called the Nobitsura Kage from a man named Mizayaki. Mizayaki refuses and knocks Wang out with the help of mysterious ghost-like entity. When Wang wakes up he discovers demons are roaming everywhere and this is where the game truly begins.
This is a first person shooter with arena encounters much like those in the Serious Sam and Painkiller games. Which means you go through the stage until you get locked in a big room and can't leave until you've defeated waves of enemies. Not just that but there are plenty of hidden secrets that can be found throughout the game by exploring each area. The rewards do make a difference in Lo Wangs power by being able to purchase upgrades earlier. Speaking of upgrades...
There's an upgrade system that lets you upgrade 3 different types of abilities; Weapons, which costs money. Skills, which costs Karma points and Powers which costs Ki Crystals. Weapons will be found at specific parts of the game and include things like a revolver, sub machine gun, shotgun, crossbow, flame thrower and rocket launcher. The money it takes to upgrade these things can be found in lootable containers or randomly on the ground or from hidden gold statue thingies. Skills enhance many things such as maximum hit points, stamina, the amount of money and bullets you find, extra damage to demons and stuff along those lines. You can also learn different Katana techniques which I talk a bit more about below. Skills are strictly upgraded through Karma Points which can be found from Karma Chalices placed throughout the game and also killing demons with combos & clearing full demon enounters quickly. Lastly, Powers are created through the use of Ki (pronounced chi in this game). There's no Ki meter or anything so Powers can be used infinitely. With Ki Powers you can do things such as heal yourself up to 60% of you main health (80% fully upgraded) or defend yourself with a Ki Shield. Ki Powers can only be upgraded using Ki Crystals which are hard to miss and found through natural game progression.
Certain skills and powers can used with the Katana by double clicking a movement direction and pressing attack or alternate attack keys/buttons provided you've purchased them via upgrade system. Guns can be upgraded to have an exceptionally powerful alternate fire but it'll cost you some major dosh. There's a stamina meter in this game and it is limited so you can not run and dash out of harm's way indefinitely. Don't fret just yet though, stamina automatically recharges! The recharge speed and maximum amount can be increased via upgrades, so there is that. There's an acceptable amount of enemy variety that includes lesser demons such the obligatory cannon fodder enemies. Ranged ones that shoot fireballs. Some flyers that shoot fireballs. Some annoying ones that teleport. Then you have greater demons which you may as well consider mini-bosses. Greater Demon Warlords have huge health pools, can pull you towards them or shoot beams at you (they do more than that, don't worry ;). With a specific skill upgrade you can actually turn their decapitated head into a devastating, room clearing weapon. There are a few very satisfying Boss fight encounters that I found fun, each with their own gimmick.
There are 17 chapters/stages and each stage is HUGE with lots to explore. There isn't a lot in the way of puzzle variety. It's usually press these switches or find this key or destroy those statues to break a seal on a door. The main focus is on combat, obviously, with some puzzles I've mentioned thrown in there along with the occasional cutscene. The game can take 10+ hours on average to complete. Highly recommend it, I'd put it right up there with modern remakes of other old FPS games like DOOM 2016 and Wolfenstein: The New Order. Great stuff here, we got a gem.

If you are expected something high energy and full of interactive characters you are going to be sadly disappointed. Farming Simulator isn't exciting, but it is relaxing. You are all alone in your chosen country farm (in Sweden or America) besides the random cars and people that walk by that you can not interact with. You start the game with a loan from the bank, several pieces of farming equipment (4 tractors, a harvestor, a tipper, a sower, a cultivator, and two small fields if you choose the Swedish town and one medium sized field if you chose the American town. The Swedish town starts with a tutorial to teach you how to use your new equipement.
There are a few options you can change in the game, you can increase the number of missions you get (mowing fields, delivering certain quanities of crops, using a forklift to deliver pallets of goods) by decreasing the amount of time it takes for a mission to appear. You can speed up or slow down your crop growth, speed or slow down time, toggle crop rot on or off (which means you won't have to scramble to harvest your fields before your crops die).
There are plenty of ways to make money in this game. You can grow a crop and sell it (hiring workers makes this easier), take up forestry, take missions, set up a wind turbine or solar panels, or raise livestock.
One thing about this game that really impresses me is the attention to detail. The machines in game are carbon copies of their real life counterparts. Nothing was spared in the replication. Every tiny sticker, bolt, or logo is in place and at the proper size. The side effect of this is that you get genuinely giddy when you can afford a new piece of equipment because of how gosh darn COOL they look.
Now, there is a multiplayer but it currently has a few issues. If you are playing together with a friend, forget about forestry for the time being. Due to both player seeing different limbs on the same tree, even if you cut them all off invisible ones will still somehow exist and this will make loading and transporting a tree to the lumber yard nigh impossible. Other than that though it seems to be golden. If you want to see multiplayer in action I suggest looking up Keralis and Docm's Farming Simulator 15 Derp Farm on Youtube. Look for the forestry episode and you will pee yourself laughing.
Also, if you like them, Farming Simulator does have Steam trading cards and achievments.
All in all I enjoy this game. It's very relaxing and like I said, you do genuinely get excited with each new machine you buy. It's not a game everyone would enjoy with it's slow paced simplicity but I still highly reccomend it to those people who just want a relaxing gaming experience.

I don't know how I actually got 200 hours in the game. It has a lot of things to add and fix, sometimes too easy, another time too difficult. In general, it's not ready (hint: Early Access). I first got it almost 2 years ago, and I must say that changes are already HUGE.
I can show a few reasons why this game is going to be great when finished:
1) This team is not only adds new content, they are refactoring old features! E.g. crafting system was rewritten completely in the recent update, while they could just leave it as it was and plug it with fixes. "Put some plugs and in push production" is often the trend. But not with this guys - they see when something's wrong, admit it and then fi.
2) There are submaps called "Anomalies". Some are really beautiful. And you know what they did? They temporarily removed half of them in order to fit in the current version of the world. Imagine some other game where creators say "Oh, you know, this part of the map doesn't make sense, so let's remove it until fixed." Nah, nobody does that, ending up with the large, but boring and dead world. Not with these guys.
3) User support. Authors are active on the steam forum, but also presented on skype and (discord?, not sure there). Bugs are fixed fast and features are added by requests. It's good to feel heard, knowing that your personal idea was accepted and implemented in the next update. Awesome!
Of course, there is more to come. From time to time user ask for a bow as weapon, making more conveniet gardening system and ability to capture animals making them domestic. But you know what? The skills for these activities existed in the game 2 years ago already, and everything is planned to be done, including online/cooperation mode! Plus, gardening is going to be updated in the next 1-2 updates. There is a Roadmap what to expect:
The game is not yet shiny, but getting polished constantly. I understand that lots of negative reviews critize the current state, but I see a vector of movement, and it is in positive direction. One day it might become a gem, and your support now can be helpful.

Great music, great gameplay, two button design is awesome.  Ruined entirely by one fatal flaw.
Roadblocks are the only real threat you face.  They pop out of the top of the screen with only a split second given to react.  You're supposed to push the boost button to break through them, but if you're too slow you will take damage.  The truck is supposed to help you by auto-steering around them, but you quickly discover that this gimmick is something you simply cannot rely on.  The view is very zoomed in, so you cannot see these hazards coming in advance.
The meat of the game, fighting enemies, is really easy.  You will effortlessly parry enemy fire, chew through bosses, but every run will end because of road hazards chipping away at your health one by one.
Yes, I have the reflexes to deal with the roadblocks.  No, I don't think it's fun, because that is the only challenge this game offers.  You're just trying to be vigilant about one small part of the gameplay while you utterly decimate all other threats.  It's very unbalanced game design, and I cannot recommend it.
