玩过万圣节DLC之后实在是忍不住了，来简单地反馈一下。
这游戏最大的特点对我来说就是，隐晦得毫无必要的剧情和硬核级的难度。且不说对难度的看法因人而异（某大仙干翻DLC的新BOSS之后轻描淡写地说难度适中殊不知这厮的梦境模式我打了半小时连BGM都没听完整），剧情这一点我个人觉得体验极差。很多人觉得游戏旁白/对白如诗的语言和深邃的意境使得剧情很有可挖掘性和美感，但是我觉得团队在所谓曲径通幽上算是矫枉过正了，简单粗暴地说，光看对白和旁白我几乎搞不明白游戏的世界观里这个KINGDOM到底发生过或者正在发生啥，主角又想要干啥，下一步我要去哪。可以说没有攻略的情况下玩得不明不白，何况难度上还要受苦。
这游戏的难度其实挺魔性的，受苦和死后跑尸的时候满脑子只想着给差评，但是撅着嘴干翻boss之后却意犹未尽甚至回头重玩。我觉得操作性和打击感上，这个游戏平衡得相当好，虽然仍有缺点，但起码让我很上瘾。没错，在刚刚被DLCboss梦境模式虐完的现在我依然满脑子差评，却昧着良心给了个推荐。
*******************************************************************
打败万圣节DLCboss格林梦境模式的分割线
可以说我本应该很高兴的，就像往常那样被虐完意犹未尽；
但是我的良心这次按捺不住了，我必须把评价改为不推荐。
我可以毫不客气地把梦魇格林列为全游戏最难BOSS，但是我差评的原因并不是难度，而是毫无必要、莫名其妙、让人很窝火的、纯粹是主角刻意被弱化/敌人刻意被强化创造出的♥♥♥♥♥♥难度。打败梦魇格林后我冷静地思考了一下，如果游戏难度正常，整个游戏的流程不会超过二十小时，那么我多出来的五十个小时的受虐流程未免也太可悲了一些。

Oknytt is a classic point & click adventure game, set against a background of swedish folklore.
A "small and seemingly insignificant creature" rises from a grave, having no clue as to where or who it is, or what his meaning in life may be, and decides to help a wingless fairie get a new set of wings. And with this starts a journey through the night, illuminated by the kindness of said creature.
The graphics reflect the dark tone of its encounters, with only a few occasional glimpses of colour. The animations resemble paper cuts more than actual animations, which fits the tone of the game quite well.
What really sets the mood though is the (english) narrator, a storyteller sitting by a campfire who invites you to listen to his tale. All narration and characters are voiced by him, making it very much resemble a radio play. His pronounciation is slow and accentuated, dragging one perfectly into the darkness of the tale, yet still capturing the optimism of the creature.
This is a perfect little tale for short days and long nights of winter. Just like its protagonist it seems small and insignificant at first, unfolding inwards to surprise again and again. As stars in the night sky looking small yet offering a light, this game may easily be overlooked.
It would be an excellent game if it weren't for its terribly slippery controls. They manage to be a game breaker, which makes me not recommend it, although I really like the concept.

Remove the portal gun from Portal, halve the budget, but retain the fun, speed, puzzles, and wit, and you have Freedom Fall.  It's a 2-d platformer that has you going down an impossibly large tower, run by a rather psychotic, but humorous, mute princess.  The puzzles and platforming are fun, often requiring good timeing and speed, but what will keep people playing is the hilarious and often dark commentary.  See, nothing is voiced in game, but the princess who runs the tower loves to write on the walls.  She will reveal her past, tease you, lie to you, or even joke and admire you, like in Portal, and the writing is often quite funny...and grim...but still funny.  They also do some intersting things with the idea of respawns and how it plays into the narrative.
Overall, a fun game.  It's only about 2-3 hours long if you just run through it without trying to get high scores, but still, I enjoyed it.  Fun and funny little title.

Just finished the "true" ending...felt it was time to go write my first review on Steam. I'm glad my first review here is for one of the greatest games I've ever played in my life. Buckle up--this'll be long ;)
Where to start...
THE WORLD: Incredible world with so many environments and creatures to find and interact with. Gorgeous, gorgeous art; each section of the giant world has its own themes and aesthetics and new enemies to fight. My experience with "Metroidvania"-style games is limited to Hollow Knight and Ori and the Blind Forest, but Hollow Knight's expansive environments each offer something unique and intriguing, making exploration a joy--more fun than exploring the big open-world RPG/FPS games I've played this year. The level of detail and care that Team Cherry put into the backdrop for this game is stunning. Individual rooms feel really well designed and the wealth of extra details that can be discovered upon later runs and backtracking makes the world feel like a living thing.
THE ART: This is basically a subnote to the previous point, but I HAVE to praise the sheer beauty of this game. Each new area had so much to see, and the handrawn style matched the feel of the world and the tone of the game SO WELL. I'm an art afficianado and even just traipsing through the world was amazing because every room had incredible visuals. The design of the allies and enemies constantly made me smile, and by the end of the main storyline I've taken almost 1500 screenshots of the game because it is simply one of the most incredibly lush worlds I've ever experienced.
THE LORE: Spinkled, often subtley, throught the world, I couldn't get enough of Hollow Knight's dark, brooding backstory. Learning bits and pieces from the many bugs you meet along the journey made me hungry to keep learning more, and in my opinion the rate and depth of these bits of lore was just right. Not getting too much at once means that a constant air of mystery surrounds your exploration, and once the pieces start to come together, the weight of what Hallownest once was starts to come to light. It was a thrill finding the Dreamers and learning about the King's deeds. The sequence in game related to the Void was a major highlight for me.
THE GAMEPLAY: This game was SO. MUCH. FUN. As I mentioned, my metroidvania experience is limited to this and one other game. I had no real platforming experience before playing Ori earlier this year--I never really played or enjoyed Mario, never played actual Metroid games, etc. Ori introduced me to the world of platforming, and while it had many great puzzles and challenges, I liked that game more for the world and the story than particular puzzles. It took me a while to get the hang of Hollow Knight's incredibly tight and responsive controls, but they eventually became second nature. Enemies have patterns to learn and you have skills and spells to learn, and it all flowed together really well for me. When I would make mistakes while fighting a boss, I knew those mistakes were on me, not some fluke of the controls.
It also took me a while to get used to the design of a game like this, where you fight smaller enemies throughout the world and then mini-bosses and bosses in specific areas. I was initially a bit flumoxed about save points, but then I devoted some time to exploring areas more thoroughly and discovered that benches (save points) are usually not too far away from a challenge, and going to save before tackling a bigger foe became straightforward. I've seen/heard some people complain about the backtracking involved in the game, and it's true that the game does essentially require a fair amount of backtracking to accomplish different objectives (many of which aren't entirely required, however). This never was a problem for me, given my love of simply experiencing the world and the luscious art style wherever I went.
There were several bosses that were very tough for me, and took me a long time to fully get their patterns down and be able to stand a chance. That was part of the fun, though :) It was nice to have a mix of relatively straightforward minor enemies through an area, and then some larger enemies and mini-bosses, and then a boss or two in each section of the world. It was a blast to find new areas, explore new sections of the world, find new enemies, find relics, learn about the world and the backstory of the kingdom, and face each new boss. My wife played her own savefile in parallel to me, and she's very new to the world of PC gaming, but even she's been able to learn the controls and master the gameplay, and has made it about 80% of the way through the game thus far.
Two things: that bloody Trial of the Fool...and the "true" ending....GOOD GRIEF. Very hard for me, but SO WORTH IT in the end. I'm still a bit shaky from the adrenaline and emotion of the ending!
THE MUSIC: I would be awfully remiss if I didn't mention Christopher Larkin's amazing soundtrack. Talk about supporting the world and its aesthetic with the perfect score--he really outdid himself here. Its a soundtrack unlike any I've heard before, and it's beautiful. I listened to snippets before buying the game, and knew I had to grab the soundtrack version. It's emotional, moody, mysterious, with plenty of variety but also a unity that made the whole game thread together so well. I loved it.
Finally, THE STORY: Blew me away. From humble beginnings to world-saving (or perhaps dooming, depending on choice?) consequnces. The choice at the end gave me a lot to think about before I attempted it. After hearing a few things about the different endings, I knew where I'd be headed. The journey down into the dark was so atmospheric and very very cool, and the revelation about the world and the King's actions was such an awesome reveal.
This game is easily one of the top 3 games I've ever played. I grew up on Age of Empires II, and have over 350 hours in Skyrim. Add Hollow Knight to these two...and dare I say: it takes my #1 spot. Its story made me feel so many emotions, it constantly amazed me with its art and world, and I grew close to the little Ghost, to Hornet, to Quirrel, to the Elderbug, and even to Zote. What more can you ask for? Seriously, this is a masterpiece. Team Cherry, many many thanks for such an awesome experience.

The third game in the F-22 series (the first was F-22 Lightning II and the second F-22 Raptor - weird naming I know). I spent countless hours playing Raptor (and the Comanche 3 and Armored Fist 2 demos on disc) when I was a kid. It was those games that made me fall in love with the military, particularly fighter jets. They taught me about military hardware (who said video games aren't educational?). I heard about this game but could never find it. Until today...
About 20 years later, I finally got a hold of this game. How does it play? Well, it plays almost like F-22 Raptor so I felt right at home. Not only was it nostalgic, but it is a good game even to this day. In terms of realism, this is somewhere between Ace Combat and DCS. You can easily learn how to fly and engage the enemy within the hour, but don't expect a walk in the park. Too bad they don't make them like this anymore.
Some of the problems from Raptor were solved. In Raptor, enemy missiles seem to hit you no matter what you do; you'd have to perform wacky manuevers to evade. Here, just make sure you're perpendicular to the missile's flight path. This may sound easy, but not when you're surrounded by enemy fighters who will fire simultaneously and/or you end up in an enemy SAM's radar (and usually that's your fault for not being aware). AI poses a challenge, both friendly and enemy. I lost count of the times my wingman saved my butt.
My favourite is the dynamic campaign like the last game. That means enemies that are destoryed in one level will remain destroyed throughout the campaign. This is where Bonus objectives come in; they require you to destroy optional targets. Of course you don't have to, but they may come back later in the campaign to haunt you, making future missions more difficult.
However, some problems remain. While your wingman AI is good, you still have to babysit him sometimes. One of the commands you can give him is "Evasive Manuevers". That's right, you need to order your wingman to preserve himself. The thing is the command isn't highlighted unless he's in danger. So you have to keep bringing up the interface to see if he's okay.
Also, try not to let enemy fighters get too close to you. They will superglue to your 6 o' clock and fire your machine guns till you're dead. You can evade them, but it's frustrating and difficult. The worst part? They can sometimes come so close that they collide into you, causing you to crash while they...ARE UNTOUCHED! Even MiG-31s (which can't really turn sharply) can glue to you! And they are fast too!
And...there are no cutscenes. I mean, I know that it's quite difficult to make a great story with a military game, but at least give some cutscenes which gets the ball rolling. There's no ending either; not even a "You defended freedom and democracy, yay!" cutscene. They had them in Raptor, why not here?
Lastly, the Mission Editor does not work. As in, every time you place your plane in, it crashes. Someone got it to work but he just needs to post a tutorial.
This review is longer than it should have been. Goes to show how much I love it. Wish I played this game sooner. My childhood self will be proud. I'm going to buy MiG-29 Fulcrum and F-16 MRF (also made by Novalogic) real soon...

The main premise of the game – jumping or dying releases ink that reveals the level for you – sounds really interesting in theory, but the problem is that it never gets used beyond that; there's no mechanic where the ink actively modifies the level or adds anything worthwhile to the gameplay besides just letting you see where to go in the first place. This means that every time you start one of the game's 75 levels you have to jump to your inevitable (and invisible) doom and die over and over and over again just to get around to see the entire thing – and by the end what could've been a good idea becomes little more than a chore and a frustrating gimmick. To make matters worse some of the game's mechanics work against the idea in the first place – e.g. there are moving platforms you might not hit and thus not realize they're there even after many retries. You could literally do away with the whole thing and turn the whole game monochrome (and visible) to make for a better experience.
In summary, bullet-point style:
👍Minimalistic design
👍Very fun boss fights - the true highlight of the game
👍Short, knew exactly when to stop
👎Frustrating gimmick
👎Floaty controls
👎Boring level design - obviously "inspired" by Super Meat Boy, but never tries to actually improve or innovate on its foundations
👎Performance issues when there are enemies on the screen; could be a bug - is the game using my integrated graphics card??
I wish I could give it a "meh", but Steam's binary system forces me to give this one a thumbs down. It's not a terrible game, it just could've been something better.

Freedom Fall is a short but extremely fun 2D action platformer where you play as Marsh, a prisoner in an enormously high tower. Your only chance to see the light of day again is to make your way down the tower while avoiding to die by the loads of flaming, spiking, buzzing and exploding traps and machineries, that the slightly crazy Princess has decorated the tower with.
The story is presented in a pretty cool way: There aren't any actual dialogues that distract you from the actual gameplay but instead the Princess communicates with you through writings on the tower walls (she is mute, anyway :p). The press describes it as a "reverse Rapunzel story" because you actually have to get away from the Princess instead of saving her. While fitting, there's also an inarguable similarity to Portal - if GlaDOS would be a medieval Princess who likes dragons. The basic idea of the "Escape-to-Freedom"-theme also reminded me a bit of the movie Running Man.
The game has an absolutely great sense of humour, which is both cute and cynical. It's subtle enough to not make you feel like you NEED to laugh or chuckle now - you just do because it's genuinely funny without trying to hard. Charming all the way through.
Visually, the game looks great and thankfully isn't another wannabe-retro 8-bit mess. All the art in the game is hand-drawn by concept artist Lisa Rye and has a colorful and vibrant feel to it. Especially Marsh and the Princess look absolutely awesome.
As a nice change from the typical sidescrolling platformers, the gameplay is all about getting to the bottom of the tower. To do so, you have to utilize gadgets like bombs, gliders, double jumps or hover boards, which you can unlock by purchasing them for cogs and bolts that you have to collect throughout the levels. Unfortunately, the levels don't really vary in terms of gadget utilization, so you can effectively beat the game with the glider gadget only without ever touching the double jump or hover board gadget. A missed opportunity.
It's also sort of a precision platformer but due the relatively slow pace of the game (there aren't any visible timers or such that put you under pressure), it's not even remotely as stressful as, say, Super Meat Boy, so you can actually take your time and plan out the safest or most rewarding path downwards. There also are a few "racing" sections where you need to be fast, but they never get to the point where you feel like you need to be inhuman to beat them.
Dying is part of the game (I did so 206 times during my playthrough), so you will definitely get squashed, smashed, sliced, spiked, burned, bombed and electrocuted a lot, but thanks to the frequently placed checkpoints, it's not much of an annoyance and instead actually motivates you to just be better on your next try.
With roughly 2 hours for my first playthrough, the game definitely is rather short and can be beaten in one sitting if you wish to do so. However, the game features multiple endings and while I don't know how much the story varies after the split points, this definitely adds quite a bit to the replayability because it gets you intrigued as to how the story unfolds towards another ending.
Additionally, if you're a fan of leaderboards, you can try to make it to the top by finishing levels under death/time or over cog par and unlock their respective achievements. A hard mode is also available, but I have yet to try it, so right now I can't really say what the difference between normal and hard is.

It's refreshing, fun and fairly casual, yet challenging enough to not get boring, but ultimately it's the humour and the writings and drawings that kept me going on until the end.

, Freedom Fall should be the game of your choice!

A good game, but there are a few significant problems, that affects the fun heavily.

This game was released in 1999, so I will not complain about the graphics or sound (which is actually still enjoyable).
What I want to talk about is the wingman controlling:
The wingman is behaving like a little child, you must always have an eye on him and tell him exactly what he has to do.
He gets often in the "hunted position" in a 1v1 dogfight and therefor you must help him out or he will get shot down. Sometimes he also do not want to shoot, although he is in a good firing position.
Something what happens seldom, but really sad and funny at the same time is, that your wingman is flying circles with his dog--fight-contrahent, where no one wins, because they cannot hit eachother .
This is maybe of tolerable, because you just have to carry him "little bit". The main problem is, the wingman-order-system itself!
I still do not understand why there is not always an "engage enemy"-order instead of "attack my target"?!
You must aim to the enemy plane, you want your wingman to destroy and THAN order it. Why can I not attack an enemy ship and tell my wingman by the way to attack (for example) the MIG-29 Charlie 2 (that keeps spamming missiles towards me)? This is 1000x easier than seeking for the enemy between tons of other planes and ground targets.
I am also wondering if the enemy planes have infinte ammo or if they just shoot anything they have to me.
All in all this is game ok, you can enjoy.
I had some good experiences, for example how fun it is to attack an enemy base or protect some friendlies or to dodge enemy missiles, outflank them and finally shoot multiple planes in the same time.
And yes, I think I can recommend this game, if you like military flight games, although there are some problems, which Novalogic could avoid, but this game is fun.

There's many comments flying around proclaiming this is an "old-school" shooter. People who say that, just like Jon Snow, know nothing.
This game is much closer to the school of Serious Sam/Painkiller arena shooters. Or Robotron in first person as I like to call them. Not that it is a bad thing, but don't try to find the intricate level design of Doom or Duke Nukem 3D because you won't find it here.
Even if the levels aren't very well design, they're arenas after arenas connected by some corridors after all, the game gets the most important thing in FPS's right. The combat. The guns just feel right (the crossbow is the spiritual sequel to Painkiller's Impaler) and enemies have this tendency to easily dismember.
While the combat is spectacular, it isn't a perfect game. The levels sometimes get repetitive, and there's not much variety of enemies. The boss fights aren't that interesting (all three are very much identical) and take too much time. Also, it's very common to get lost in the sameness of the levels, looking for that particular exit.
I still had lots of fun with this, mostly because there aren't that much games like this around. Or at least until Serious Sam 4 comes along, because Shadow Warrior 2 seemed to go into a slightly different route.

Shadow Warrior is a remake of the classic Shadow Warrior from the 90's. Played on an i5 4460 and a gtx 1060 I was able to run the game +60fps on Ultra using a 1080p resolution. Mouse and Keyboard are preferred however the game is programmed for gamepads as well. On a technical level this game is very well optimized.
You play as Lo Wang, an assassin who works for a Japanese millionaire business owner named Orochi Zilla. The setup is Zilla gives Wang a briefcase with 2 million dollars in it and sends him to go purchase a very special Katana called the Nobitsura Kage from a man named Mizayaki. Mizayaki refuses and knocks Wang out with the help of mysterious ghost-like entity. When Wang wakes up he discovers demons are roaming everywhere and this is where the game truly begins.
This is a first person shooter with arena encounters much like those in the Serious Sam and Painkiller games. Which means you go through the stage until you get locked in a big room and can't leave until you've defeated waves of enemies. Not just that but there are plenty of hidden secrets that can be found throughout the game by exploring each area. The rewards do make a difference in Lo Wangs power by being able to purchase upgrades earlier. Speaking of upgrades...
There's an upgrade system that lets you upgrade 3 different types of abilities; Weapons, which costs money. Skills, which costs Karma points and Powers which costs Ki Crystals. Weapons will be found at specific parts of the game and include things like a revolver, sub machine gun, shotgun, crossbow, flame thrower and rocket launcher. The money it takes to upgrade these things can be found in lootable containers or randomly on the ground or from hidden gold statue thingies. Skills enhance many things such as maximum hit points, stamina, the amount of money and bullets you find, extra damage to demons and stuff along those lines. You can also learn different Katana techniques which I talk a bit more about below. Skills are strictly upgraded through Karma Points which can be found from Karma Chalices placed throughout the game and also killing demons with combos & clearing full demon enounters quickly. Lastly, Powers are created through the use of Ki (pronounced chi in this game). There's no Ki meter or anything so Powers can be used infinitely. With Ki Powers you can do things such as heal yourself up to 60% of you main health (80% fully upgraded) or defend yourself with a Ki Shield. Ki Powers can only be upgraded using Ki Crystals which are hard to miss and found through natural game progression.
Certain skills and powers can used with the Katana by double clicking a movement direction and pressing attack or alternate attack keys/buttons provided you've purchased them via upgrade system. Guns can be upgraded to have an exceptionally powerful alternate fire but it'll cost you some major dosh. There's a stamina meter in this game and it is limited so you can not run and dash out of harm's way indefinitely. Don't fret just yet though, stamina automatically recharges! The recharge speed and maximum amount can be increased via upgrades, so there is that. There's an acceptable amount of enemy variety that includes lesser demons such the obligatory cannon fodder enemies. Ranged ones that shoot fireballs. Some flyers that shoot fireballs. Some annoying ones that teleport. Then you have greater demons which you may as well consider mini-bosses. Greater Demon Warlords have huge health pools, can pull you towards them or shoot beams at you (they do more than that, don't worry ;). With a specific skill upgrade you can actually turn their decapitated head into a devastating, room clearing weapon. There are a few very satisfying Boss fight encounters that I found fun, each with their own gimmick.
There are 17 chapters/stages and each stage is HUGE with lots to explore. There isn't a lot in the way of puzzle variety. It's usually press these switches or find this key or destroy those statues to break a seal on a door. The main focus is on combat, obviously, with some puzzles I've mentioned thrown in there along with the occasional cutscene. The game can take 10+ hours on average to complete. There are multiple levels of difficulty and even a New Game Plus mode they call EX mode.
The music and sound design are decent. The sound effects of the Katana were great however I did find the sound effects used for the guns kind of lackluster. They didn't feel like they had a lot of punch. As for the graphics, beautiful. They hold up very well and each stage looks like it was designed with a lot of care and thought. The bamboo forests and pagodas are great looking and some of the more industrial locations later on do too.
I was a big fan of the classic Shadow Warrior and I can say that Flying Wild Hog did a great job creating a similar theme as the original even if the tone might be a bit lighter. The story is a lot better than what you would expect from a limb filled gorefest like this. I quite enjoyed it and had a blast playing. The pacing seemed pretty dang good. The only time it seemed to really slow down and falter was in the last couple of chapters but by then the game is almost over. So by the time it got old I was about to finish anyway.
Highly recommend it, I'd put it right up there with modern remakes of other old FPS games like DOOM 2016 and Wolfenstein: The New Order. Great stuff here, we got a gem.

(Before writing this review, I've played 150 hours of Civ V and a small exposure to Civ IV, but none to Alpha Centauri, which many consider to be this game's predecessor and example to which it is judged.)
Civ: BE is very much suited to those fans of Civ V looking for a new spin on the same game you've played for a while, but not really to those looking for an entirely new game.
As of now, the game lacks some of the advancements that Civ V has made through BNW and Gods + Kings, a.k.a. religions, luxury resources, more civs, etc. However, its espionage system, for example, is much more diverse and interesting than Civ V's, adding different operations to perform and "support agents," who provide bonuses to field operatives from their espionage HQ.
Some may be disappointed by its apparent lack of unit diversity, as the unit types are limited to standard siege/melee/ranged/aerial/naval types, and their upgrades become progressively unlocked as you advance in the Affinities system, rather than through the tech tree as per Civ V. Though the progression appears drastically different at first, it mirrors the path one would take in an advance through the tech tree in Civ V, as more affinity points are unlocked while advancing through the new tech web, each point adding to your Supremacy (cyborgs and robots), Harmony (alien hybrids), or Purity (space racist) totals. The more affinity you gain, the more upgrades you earn in the various Unit Trees and special buildings, exclusive units, and affinity-specific buffs you'll unlock.
One other notable combat and unit change is the addition of the Orbital Layer, a secondary hex grid of satellites. Satellites can be launched onto the Orbital Layer and remain there for a set number of turns before de-orbiting, occupying tiles and providing bonuses to the land or units within them (ex: bonus combat strength, poison gas removal, bonus $$). 2 interesting satellite types are the orbital lasers and phase teleporters, which add a not-insignificant amount of strategy to be considered when placing satellites or de-orbiting enemy satellites and can lead to a half-ground half-orbital army.
Affinity is mainly earned through advancement in the tech web, which is a non-linear version of the tech tree from former Civ games. The web branches out from the base technologies of settlement in several different directions, with no clear or concise path appearing as "the best" for a given situation (ex: clicking on Mathematics to rush catapults as a military civ). This adds a large element of disorientation and choice to the game, which i feel is essential in differentiating it from other Civ games of the past. By throwing the player headfirst into a future environment in which they have no clue as to what technologies logically lead to what or which strategies are most viable (which one could rely on in past Civ games which mirrored humanity's history), Beyond Earth succeeds in creating an environment which satisfyingly mirrors the narrative told by the game, of a people thrown headfirst into a world of chaos and unknowns.
The above facts are the largest changes from Civ V to BE, and much of the rest remains the same. Basic gameplay and functionality remains the same as Civ V, but these added factors serve to differentiate it from Civ V and set it apart as its own game. What it lacks, however, is Civ V's years of polish through DLC, updates, and balancing. With only 8 civilizations, you'll be seeing the same faces in almost every game you play, but the Steam Workshop community and future DLC serve to alleviate that need. Contrary to previous Civ games, BE's civs are very similar to one another, with no massive playstyle changes evident only from their special abilities (ex: "Venice only builds one city." BE civs have bonuses such as: "+25% espionage strength and +25% intrigue from espionage operations", or "1 free technology from launching a satellite, +15% production to satellites"). This further opens up the user's choices, and along with Cargo, Citizen, and Landing Craft decisions makes for a much more diverse level of customization from the beginning of the game.
All of this, coupled with a great visual sci-fi vibe (other than occasional same-ish planet textures when randomly generating terrain colors and hard to see poison gas) and a stellar soundtrack creates a wonderful experience for the average Civ fan. I warn that hardcore fanatics may have a problem with BE because of its differences to Alpha Centauri and other Civ games before Civ V. Alpha Centauri featured a sprawling narrative and amount of storytelling, which BE lacks. An additional claim is that BE and Civ V have 'dumbed down' the Civ franchise by removing complex features such as unit-stacking. However, when treating BE as its own game, it is an extremely solid strategy title with lots of potential and room to grow.
My only advisories against buying Beyond Earth are if you're looking for a galactically different experience than Civ V, waiting for DLC or balancing, or are looking for the narrative depth found in Alpha Centauri. I would also advise against buying at full price (I bought at 30% off), but that goes without saying for any new releases on Steam.
TL;DR - Civ V in spaaaaace without some old mechanics but now featuring new hotness; hardcore Civ fans will be displeased with no leaps and bounds in functional changes from Civ V and a less compelling narrative than the history of the world, but BE stands on its own as a solid strategy experience with a great future outlook in updates and DLC.

There have been a ton of reviews on here expressing what I feel already, so I will mostly focus on the mechanics and UI situations that I find irritating.  To recap the sentiments that I agree with which I will not expand on:
- It is "decent" compared to where Civ5 was before its expansions
- It will most likely be much better after 1-2 expansion packs / DLC
- The leaders are indeed quite boring
Ok, onto the "new" stuff that I feel must be said:
SLOW GAMEPLAY: I'm on turn 281 and I can't say that anything interesting has happened.
HARD ON THE EYES: Maybe it's just the coloring of my particular world, but I find the tiles hard to distinguish from each other, and the semi-transparent mini-map is just flat-out weird.  And by weird I mean: what were they thinking.  For that matter, there is weird transparency all over the place.
WHAT DID I JUST DO?  Why in the holy prophets of Earth do they not tell you what you just completed in a city when you're selecting the next thing to produce?  Knowing this would increase investment in the gameplay by giving the player a sense of accomplishment.
MISSING TRADE FILTERS:  Why would anyone think it's fun to scroll through a list of a million cities to find the best yields?  Why would you copy so many other features of Civ5 and not the useful filters that allowed you to select things like "max gold" or "max science delta"?
WHERE ARE MY UNITS?  Again, we have an issue with totally bizarro choices in overlapping transparent iconography.  When a unit is sitting inside of a city, it's really hard to tell that it's there.
WHAT ARE THE YIELDS?  In the city screen, the icons used to assign a worker to a tile are so huge that they overlap the yields on the tile to the point where I honestly have no clue what the yield is beneath it.
HEALTH WEIRDNESS:  The Health/Happiness swap is "whatever."  But the health actually maxes out at the city population level - for example, if you construct buildings yielding 8 health, but you only have 3 population, you only add 3 health to your global total.  This is totally contrary to every single thing I've read in the Civopedia- so this is also an example of an incomplete and slightly misleading manual.
WHERE MY PEOPLE AT?  If I have units out and about, sometimes I completely lose them- this wouldn't be a problem if they hadn't removed the Military Overview which listed out all the units.  Another example of "why would you copy everything from Civ5 except this?"
Ok, I think that's most of my griping for now.  All this being said, I think this game will work out in the long run, but right now- I have to second everyone who said this feels like a mod to Civ5 that should cost $10-20 at most.  Actually, it's less than a mod because it removed so many of the features that improved Civ5 and lifted the player out of the weeds of micromanagement that plagued Civ2 - Civ4 (I never played 1).
MY CREDENTIALS: I have 900 hours logged on Civ5 and have been playing Civ pretty much constantly since Civ2.  I never played Alpha Centauri, but I think I might be the only person left alive who remembers playing and loving the non-Sid "Call to Power."  The rest of us were run out of town by the "true" Civ fans.
BOTTOM LINE: I think that this might actually be less annoying for someone who DIDN'T play Civ5, because they might not know what they're missing.  But for someone stepping down from Civ5 with all its expansions, it's actually almost unplayable.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
Novus Inceptio is a crafting, and survival game. It reminds me a bit of "Life is Feudal" or other games of that nature. The interesting thing about this game is that your character, as well as the world, can age. Your character is always accompanied by a robot (named; A2-A) that is supposed to log data as well as help you survive. The game has a unique background story as well as setting. The game plans on becoming an MMO and their "GHOST mode" within the game shows how the MMO mode would work.
The world is dynamic. Changes you make (or other players make) will affect the world. Even the game's lore shapes the world. Items you create in game, can be your own unique version, as there are many different ways, and combinations to make the
item.
--------

The graphic assets are decent. The terrain look good and although improvements can be made to some of the 3D models, the grass, trees, mountains, rocks, and most of the environmental visuals look good. The animation quality is good in some places, but a little bit weaker in others, specifically the character and animal animations.The game runs fine on a mid-tier graphics card and CPU. Playing around with the game's graphical settings is recommended.
There are a few glitches, such as the mouse disappearing and not being able to hit some targets in combat. Though the game mentions that there are some bugs, and even lists a few of them that are being worked on. As it's in early access, optimization and dealing with the glitches and bugs will progress until full release.
--------
The sound assets were decent. Birds can be heard chirping, the player's movements, and sounds from the environment/terrain. It wasn't annoying or repetitive and the audio meshes well with the setting. The background music is unfortunately kind of forgettable. Although the sound assets were all very standard, they do get the job done.
--------
The game is still in early access but there is still more to come. As in most games of this genre; you can build, craft, explore and survive. You can make many different tools and you also need certain tools in order to craft other items. You have some skills in the beginning such as foraging, cultivating, and even cooking. The game's mechanics are currently solid, though there isn't very much to do. The combat is also pretty lackluster at the moment. You can of course arm yourself with different types of armor, clothing and weapons.
There isn't currently much of a challenge to the game aside from trying not to die from hunger and thirst. The animals aren't really that aggressive, and the player is never in immediate danger. There's also an interface that shows the weather, time, and temperature, though it's not really relevant at this point in the game.
--------
The game might be a lot better upon full release. Though right now, I can't see myself playing it in it's current state, and I don't really find a challenge in it. Though it does look very promising. With some optimization and some more content added, the game could be the next big survival game. The game is in early access and it is expected to have bugs and a lack of content. The title should hopefully have all of these issues worked out upon full release.
Thanks to the devs for giving me the opportunity to review the game, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

Developed and published by McMagic Productions, Novus Inceptio (“New Beginning” in Latin) is an Early Access diamond in the rough. The game is planned as full-on MMO once it is completed but even for now, the Single Player experience is quite enjoyable.

Novus Inceptio features a large area to explore and futher develop. The game’s story has post-apocalyptic tones to it and it can surely be fleshed out even more in subsequent updates. In SP mode (also referred to as “GHOST” version) you find yourself with all the necessary tools to harvest, gather and build within the game world. A complex and fully functional crafting system that proves the dev team’s skill and further potential. It doesn’t contain too many in-game threats to your survival as you take relative little damage from the few enemies (mostly wildlife) present. This has to change, as weapons and fighting are as integral to surviving as the crafting tools are. A tutorial would be more than welcomed too as not all would-be players have sufficient crafting experience from similar titles.

From a graphical perspective, Novus is truly gorgeous. Despite using Unity Engine, the open world is filled with details, clearly showing the game’s two-year developent time and overall efforts into ironing out glitches. There are still some bugs here and there but as far as I could tell, none that may be game-breaking. Novus Inceptio has built-in weather pattern changes which along the day/night cycle, really offer a both beautiful and diverse scenery to explore and manipulate at will.

The sound department needs more attention but it certainly isn’t lackluster even in this Early Access version. Some voice acting would be apreciated too.

+ Gorgeous graphics
+ Complex crafting system
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements

- Still in Early Access (and consequently, no MP option)
What really impressed me about Novus Inceptio is how well simulated the inevitability of death is. You age (if diseases don’t shorten your lifespan prematurely) within the game and pass on what you have built to your offspring. That really motivates players to never stop seeking out areas with better shelter and resource pools. This is not meant to be a static game afterall and I do believe it can be continuously improved but I fear that once it reaches its MMO objective, survival will be less about witty crafting and more about defeating other human players that only care for combat. Countless films and games have proved that peaceful coexistence in a post-apocalyptic setting is just a pipe dream...

"Oknytt". It's a lovely, charming, and well-written story, inspired by Swedish folklore. You play as a small, insignificant creature, that meets many strange, magical and creepy beings during a very dark and special night. A warm narrator's voice will guide you through the complicated world of Swedish bestiary.
The small insignificant creature is very small and very insignificant indeed. It can't run, can't jump, can't fight, doesn't have claws or fangs, or amazing powers. But somehow, in the large scheme of things, the small insignificant creature turns out quite significant.
It's a short game, took me about 4 hours, I suppose you could do it within 3-5 hours, depending on how many times you get stuck. It's a typical point and click game, with a few puzzles, mostly quite logical and simple. Once in a while you have to use the classic "use everything on everything" move, when the tips are unclear, but in general, using your brain will get you through it. The interesting thing is the "elements" mechanic, where you can use an elemental power to see how it will affect your environment. You might summon an insect to sit on someone's head, rekindle a fireplace, or start rain. You never know until you try.
What is extremely outstanding is the artstyle. The story is very sweet, almost like a children's book, with a little innocent creature travelling an unknown world and helping others solve their problems. There's simple morals and a simple lesson to be learnt - even the most insignificant ones, can change a lot. The voice of the creature is just cute, and adorable.. like a children's story character's should be... And then you see the artstyle. It's dark. It's extremely dark, to the point of being malevolent. Most of the Swedish folklore creatures you meet look creepy, strange or even dangerous and scary. It's mostly black and white, with disturbing shiny eyes, and unsettling half-human faces. Each new room you explore is a whole new study on creepiness and hidden fears. It gave me chills a couple of times, and hypnotized me completely.
The sounds are very delicate, almost unnoticeable, but playing in with the dark, creepy artstyle perfectly.
As a whole it's a sweet children's story, with a terrifying almost horror-like environment. If you like sweet things, and creepy things alike - like I do, you will enjoy "Oknytt" in all of its splendor.

There are some farming games where you press 'H' to harvest your fields.
In Farming Simulator 15, you enter your combine [you start with a Comina C6], attach the header [if you haven't already], unfold the harverster, lower the pickup, and then drive as straight as you can --- or hire a driver to do it for you. As it fills up, you can offload into a trailer and drive it it to your grain silo. Playing this game I learned why farmers attach weights to their tractors, the difference between straw and hay, and that plows really aren't used as often as cultivating machines.
I will use "moderate" to describe the level of detail in the simulator. For someone who is not a farmer, I found the game to have a satisfying level of depth and detail -- but a purist might be disappointed that the controls you see in the cockpit view of the tractors are non-functional. Similarly, reversing a tractor connected to a dolly connected to a trailer was realistictly difficult -- but I think in the real world if I drove a semi off of an 8-foot drop, I would not be able to continue on my merry way with a full load of grain.
Recommended if for no other reason than it convinced me I do not want to be a farmer.

There's a certain incomparable magic to being told a story around a fire. Whether it's otherworldly or ordinary, the simple act of someone being there, repeating a narrative that may have been told to them in a similar fashion causes the tale to take on a new sense of substance, holding your attention through every tiny detail as they engross you in the whatever world they seek to create.
It's an experience that's almost intangible and unrepeatable, leaving a lasting impact that makes you wish to share it with others, most likely changing certain details and words to suit your own version which will then be transfigured and retold by those around you. This is what playing Oknytt feels like. It's an experience brought to life by its own brilliant storyteller, taking on the voices of the bizarre and frightening creatures that inhabit the sinister world you travel through. It's compelling precisely for how it's told than what it says, as though story formed out of Swedish folklore is indeed engaging, without the narrator there to guide you through it the spark would be lost and it would be rather worse off for it.
As a game, its classical adventure game formula is one of simple discovery and item utilization, though unfortunately one which is incredibly easy to lose your way in as you miss an obscured item or don't consider an abstract combination. It's unfortunate and rather frustratingly obtuse at times, often leaving me to the helping hand of a guide as I simply wished to continue a tale that was otherwise captivating.
For as convoluted it can at times become, Oknytt is so inherently enrapturing as to be worth exploring for however often you're forced to reach for the helping hand of a walkthrough. I feel personally required to again praise the narrator who for all intents and purposes makes the game what it is, though certainly helped along a good deal with the imaginative, eerie artwork that is strangely curious for how frightening much of it is. It's a game firmly grounded in its own lore, brilliantly imagined and executed, which left me entranced and maybe just a little bit anxious of what might be awaiting me next time I venture into the woods.

As of this posting I've been playing the game 14 days and have 149.5 hours played so far.
This game has a lot of good points, but just as many bad ones.
I'm going to list something good and then something bad, alternating back and forth.
-----
The in-game store credits (Ellunes) you can pay cash to get, are also regularly rewarded for achievements that you'll be getting without even trying, such as leveling up, killing monsters, taming creatures, etc.  You can even get them as login rewards, so while you can spend cash on this game, you don't need to do so in order to get items you would want from the store.  I've not spent money and yet I've had enough "Ellunes"to buy extra bags and several of the chance pet boxes and such already, with only two weeks played, and I still have hundreds extra.  Yes, many of those achievements are one time deals so you'll need to think ahead and plan wisely, because after you've leveled the amount you can get from just Daily/Weekly/Monthly achievements does diminish significantly.
----
"You Have Been Disconnected From The Server"
..I've never seen that message so many times in any game before this one, and I've played a heck of a lot of MMOs in the last decade.  It doesn't matter if you are trying to enter or exit (especially exit) a dungeon or instance, pass through a portal, or just use your recall/hearth stone.. you have like a 30% chance to be disconnected, which causes the game to crash, so you have to restart and wait five minutes for the game to load and all the logos to go by before you can get back in to play.
It's not just me either, I've played with my boyfriend almost all the time I've been playing Riders of Icarus, and it's random who gets the disconnect and at which points, I don't think it has ever been both of us at the same time and we are using the same internet connection so I can't blame my net.
Also when trying to close the game it crashes more often than not and Ctrl+Alt+Delete is your only option to actually get the game to close.
----
There is something like 145 different "Familiars" in the game that you can tame and use as mounts or combat pets, and there is an expansion just around the corner that will be bringing a lot more.  While the bonuses they give tend to be very melee heavy with less support for casters, they still offer a nice selection of different flying and ground mounts to collect.
----
Invisible Walls... the game is plagued with them, often randomly and/or awkwardly placed for no apparent reason.  You don't throw tons of invisible walls to block and often trap players, in a game with flying mounts that are supposed to be able to move around above the terrain.  So often you are forced to stick to the roads, even when flying, because there are invisible walls everywhere.  This is really an annoying and disappointing factor.  When I say invisible I do mean invisible, there are a few that have a slight particle effect so that you can see them, but most are completely invisible and it's so easy to get trapped in them and it's quite the hassle to get back out.
----
Pretty armor.  There are a lot of very nice armor sets in the game, and the level 25, 30, and 35 dungeon sets have animated energy and such flowing through/over them for a very nice effect (without being gaudy).
Overall the graphics are quite nice in this game and you have a decent amount of character customization, far more than a lot of other more popular MMOs out there.
----
Communication with the players... at times it seems like they are trying but then the simplest of things like changing the Pinned/Stickied post on Twitter to remove outdated/incorrect information that they later changed, is too much to expect from them.  If you want to use their Twitter to keep up to date you better be ready to ignore the top pinned posts and scroll down through all the silly posts about which animal is cuter, to find the actual information you need about events, maintenance, expansion delays, etc.
The music is soothing and the concept is nice but the gameplay's difficulty makes me contemplate suicide. I can't play it without wanting to smash my face into my keyboard.

When I began playin this game, i wasn't really sure of what to expect. This was supposedly a decent adventure, sure, but hardly could I expect it to be any different from most titles in the genre. Boy, was i wrong.
Whereas the game mechanics are the same as pretty much every other title in the  bunch, what really sets this out of the crowd is the setting: Swedish folklore is undoubtably something you don't come across much in games, or even everyday life, and I did enjoy learning a bit abouth its myths and lore, which the game seems to send you in endless waves of small curiosities and oddities you'll quite easily find yourself looking up either on the internet or the game's library.
Some puzzles are a little bit more complicated than others, but you'll rarely find anything that can escape a reasonable amount of thinking (sometimes linear, sometimes lateral) and the average playtime is well in the average. The story itself begins very slowly, and might sound and look rather dull, but give it a few minutes and the tune will change completely.
The narrator's voice is simply superb, and really adds that little "something" to both immersiveness and charm taht would have you go: "Yeah, you just gotta check this out", as it will lead you hand in hand with this tiny, pathethic little creature, with the warmest, tenderest heart you will encounter in a long while. I won't lie: I shed many a tear as the small creature progressed in its travel towards the ending of the game, and when the game did end... It did leave something behind. I wouldn't go as far as to compare this game to masterpieces of its genre, but it was certaintly an enjoyable, touching and tought provoking gameplay experience.
Summing it up:
If I were to give this game a mark, it'd be a solid 7.5/10, leaning heavily towards an 8.

TL DR: Hollow Knight is seriously great. It's a beautiful game with great music and atmosphere, with a huge world to explore. Combat is fairly simple, but it's just dificult enough to be satisfying. If you like metroidvanias with great exploration and bosses to fight, this is a really great one!
Hollow Knight is a game about a sort of lone wanderer exploring a ruined kingdom. Hallownest was a great kingdom once, until a plague brought death and chaos to the realm. The world is divided into 17 locations with their own sub areas, most having a boss or two. The game starts out slow, but once you get wall-jumping and a dash it opens up a lot, having quite a lot of non-linearity. There's only one signposted goal in the game, which is to get to 3 locations, and you can pretty much get to those three in whatever order you like. There's tons of secrets to find once you get all the abilities, and the atmosphere's really good.
There's more than 150 enemies in the game, and they're mostly different besides some really basic ones. Sometimes the game will put you up against several of them on a confined space, leaving you to jump around slashing them with your nail. Hollow Knight's combat is fairly simple (you can attack, cast a spell or use a special attack in pretty much all 4 directions), but having to constantly be on the move and using downward slashes against ground foes to keep in the air, for example, is pretty satisfying. Some of the bosses are really well designed and have very good movesets, though none of them with too much variation.
It's a really beautiful game, and very satisfying to play. The amount of content is really good for the base price, and for the genre in general (from what I saw on HLTB, since I haven't played a great deal of metroidvanias). Simply put, if you enjoy 2D exploration and combat in a beautiful world with great music, this is your game.

Fabulous game! Strong story line, voice acting, scripting, character development, world building, plot, graphics, and environment.
I bought and finished Tacoma in a day. Stats say I was at it 6 hours, but it needn't take that long. I didn't want it to end, and I am already itching for the next installment in this world.
This is a first-person, point-and-click adventure with a single story and ending, as far as I can tell. There are a couple of places you can explore in a different order, but these points of departure don't change the outcome.
I am in love with the crew of the Tacoma. There are no superheroes here, just regular people trying to do their jobs.  Most are trying to maintain connections with the important people in their lives; some are stuck in bad circumstances. All are victims of the system in ways many of us can relate to IRL. Great gender & racial diversity with background details that reveal ethnic and cultural differences with artful subtlety.
I loved the world building of "Tacoma." (Minor SPOILERS ensue)  Through private communications of the crew members, you learn about the larger world, controlled by corporations, split into new national conglomerates, and driven by a Loyalty Economy that reduces career freedom in most of the characters' lives.
Each character was fleshed out in detail with distinct personalities. For instance, I adored the Mechanical Engineer who creates pre-Raphaelite paintings with real paints and collects antique books on the TRS80, C64, and Amiga 500. Or the surgeon who graduated from Johns Hopkins and suffers from an anxiety disorder and has a skeleton in her closet. Or the communications specialist who is a fangirl of a Singapore band and has an addiction to Rubik's Cubes.
I recommend this to anyone who has wanted to live in space, loves slow walk-through adventures with solid scripting, and likes to be just a little on the edge of your seat about how the developers are going to close out the story.
Pros (besides what I mentioned above):
1. You can examine and pick up lots of objects, not only the items essential to the story. If you skip all the extra items (the people on this station are very messy!) you can probably finish the game very quickly, but I loved all those items--they help build the world and make the characters relatable. Great story enrichment.
2. Weightlessness!
3. The views. Good job, designers! I want to hang out up there after it's over.
4. Excellent use of the rewind technique to allow you to examine the various aspects of the mystery you are investigating.
5. You can drop something or "put it back." OCD folks, you can clean up the trash and straighten all the shoes to your heart's content!
6. Nice closure. I had tears.
Cons:
1. There is no inventory; you can hold only one item at a time. That means that you drop what you are holding if you try to pick another. (Okay, so that's a "pro," too, since you don't have a big, messy inventory--you usually need the important items somewhere nearby.)
2. Don't drop the key in the wrong place. It literally disappears under the carpet, and it's a pixel-by-pixel search to find it. You need it. This may be a glitch in one location, but I spent about 20 minutes and thought I'd have to start the game over.
3. Too short. Not for the money--just because I want there to be more.
I will definitely look for more from these developers and designers.

After playing two short four-civ games, I like it, but it definitely has problems.
Pros:
-The AI is sometimes more reasonable. Not so many 100-turn wars for no reason. Interestingly enough, I was actually attacked by a neighbor in order to delay me from winning.
-Combat is more fun than base Civ 5's though that may be the similarities to the DLC systems.
-There is still satisfaction in making super-cities, if you like doing that.
-Upgrading units with affinities is actually rather neat, IMO.
-Aliens are quite neat, and the xenomass is worth taking them out, but it is often too easy.
-Resources are spread more evenly.
-Trade routes are very useful, but annoying to work.
-Exploring can be a fun bit of time.
It's not easy to think of many more...
Cons:
-Poor AI battle strategies, but they will actually concede things more easily. Not surprising.
-It almost feels like an MMO with all the micromanaging you do clicking on this or that. Trade routes, spies, the evil helper, all those things.
-The help is poorly designed, Civ 5 is much more intuitive.
-Lack of advanced options in world creation. Civ 5 had some fun things you could change, but BE has just about none.
-Stations seem utterly pointless.
-Everything seems to go very slowly. Workers work super slowly and so do cities, the exception being some military unit types. Research and culture are okay.
-Wonders, save one or two, take too long to be of benefit as they give usually small yields.
-Orbital layer is not significant.
-Health is annoying. Either you put all your tech in it at first or you get penalized.
If you compare it to Civ 5, it's a disappointment. On its own, its not excellent but it's okay.

When playing a sequel to such a fine and creatively unique, niche series as HITMAN, one sets the expectations nigh immeasurably high;
Surely many had whined and complained like babes when the title was released and the gameplay was, on a few of the game's levels, limited to a degree at first glance as to how to eliminate targets and complete the murderous puzzles.
Being graded for one's performance so evidently (as opposed to being graded in the end of mission screen like in previous titles) was also apparently a big deal to many unable to ignore their score and be methodical and patient in constructing their way of performing, even the added abilities that are newly added in the game but not found in previous titles are optional, guaranteeing an á la carte selection in difficulty selections. but just like eating a previously new scrumptious food, the acquired taste blossoms after time, like a child disliking his greens.
The level of detail inserted into the game, the only in retrospect acquired realization that, yes, the motion capture for the cutscenes was worth every little penny in capturing the subtlety of the caracters and their narration, the level of appeasement and fanservice granted for the simple existance of the Contracts mode, source of fine competitive death-puzzling to heart's content.
A game that perhaps suffered from the typical hyped expectations being achieved in a way that was not expected by its fanbase; Such a non-issue fades over time, and thus leaves us with still one of the best HITMAN titles ever made, something for IO Interactive to be proud of and build on, both on polish, gameplay, and narration as well.
All these elements serve well to the pillars of what makes a game worthwhile; Context is given with a plot that allows the player to relate with the characters present, Challenge is present and selectable by the player to guarantee a Catharsis, a release of the load built up from the raised stakes in narrative. (and I again repeat how well-done the characters are done. Years from now I play other top titles and must shudder at the lifelessness still present in presentation.)
But even then, it is a game that still requires patience, attentiveness, and an open mind to appreciate at all, let alone in full.
Recommended for those with an ice cold sociopathic heart. A thinking man's stealth game.

These games are for deep and introspective thinkers. They make you feel less alone. How I came to find this game:
I ended up with "The Beginner's Guide" because of a humble bundle deal. I opened it up not knowing what to expect. When it was over I got the feeling that I didn't want it to be over. I was glad that I didn't pay full price for it, but it stayed in the forefront of my mind for days and I re-played it. It wasn't a game so much as an experience. I started reading about the developer and I came across another title they made called Dr. Langeskov, The Tiger, and The Terribly Cursed Emerald: A Whirlwind Heist which was free on steam so I played it.
Again, I really really enjoyed it, but I realized if I was expecting gameplay and got this instead, I wouldn't be thrilled. It is more of an interactive movie. A really enjoyable one.
After playing both of those titles, I couldn't resist but to buy the Stanley Parable. It is really a very deep game and I love it. You can replay it dozens of times and get different results evert time. I felt connected to the narrator and I don't regret it.
TLDR; these are interactive movies moreso than games but they will touch you in a strange way that will leave you fixated on it for quite a while after it's over.
I don't know how else to explain this, I'd reccomend all 3 games to any gamer or developer. They should be played by everybody at some point, but keep your eyes open for sales and bundles so you don't end up with buyers remorse if it's not for you.

Released in 2013, Teslagrad is a 2D puzzle platformer created by Norwegian developer, Rain Games. Set in a steampunk inspired vision of medieval Europe, players assume the role of a young boy who must uncover the secrets of the abandoned Tesla Tower and fulfil his destiny to become the last Teslamancer.
Gameplay is focused around the concept of using electromagnetism to solve puzzles and explore your surroundings. Players can charge environmental objects into one of two distinct magnetic poles (blue or red). Similarly charged objects will repel each other, while opposingly charged objects will attract each other. Players will also encounter oscillating electromagnetic fields which follow the same game mechanics, and can be used to propel players both horizontally and vertically in order to reach new areas or avoid hazards.
The gameplay is relatively linear, with each section of the tower needing to be completed before you can unlock the next. However, you will often find yourself gaining a new ability which can then be used to access previously unreachable areas or collectables. This backtracking is done with relative ease and does not normally feel too laborious.
Light combat elements are present, but for the most part you have little means of defending yourself. Instead, emphasis is placed on using your powers to avoid and outsmart enemies. Even the boss encounters have a heavy focus on evasion and retaliation through indirect means.
Teslagrad was developed using the Unity game engine. Graphically, it uses over 100 hand drawn illustrations as background artwork. These colourful environments are beautifully crafted and provide a charm that perfectly complements the steampunk setting. The 2D character sprites are decently animated as well. The soundtrack also deserves an honourable mention as the music has a whimsical tone that helps sell the concept of this fantastical world.
With regards to storyline, Teslagrad is fairly unique in that there is no written or audible dialogue in the entire game. The plot is conveyed purely visually in the form of short exposition theatres and collectable scrolls found throughout the game. As a result the story is quite simplistic, but it still provides an innovative and effective narrative that conveys all it needs to.
Teslagrad is a short game that can be fully completed in less than 10 hours. The later puzzles do become a bit more complex, and some of the optional collectables are quite well hidden, but there is nothing that cannot be solved without some patient experimentation or exploration.
The only main criticism I have is the boss encounters. All of the bosses follow set attack patterns which you need to avoid before you can retaliate. However, as the game instantly kills your character when hit, boss fights quickly devolve into a tedious process of trial and error as you slowly learn how to dodge each attack before promptly dying to the next one. It feels quite out of place when compared with the more logical puzzling encountered in the rest of the game.
Overall, Teslagrad is a decent puzzle platformer with intuitive controls, some innovative mechanics and engaging puzzles. It is a charming game with beautiful scenery and sound, all set in a fantastical world filled with interesting contraptions and strange creatures. It is a short diversion that manages to provide just enough entertaining gameplay before outstaying its welcome.

Very cool looking game BUT READ THIS!!  If you are in to survival game such as Rust or Ark or LiF or ANY \"REALEASED\" survival game, I strongly suggest you hold off unless you want to support the developers.
There\'s not a lot to it at this point(5/31/16), and it\'s very glitchy and buggy(It\'s in EA so obviously), so if you\'re looking to delve in to this sweet fantasy world, hit the pause button for a while.
Here comes the review of the game in it\'s current state.
Pros:
-Beautiful Landscapes
-Unique Twist on an Apocalypse Survival
-Little Robot Orb that Follows you around and carries your crap
-The building system is pretty intuitive and easy to use
-The survival gauges diminish at acceptable rates(Hunger, Thirst, etc)
-real time generation
The *In-between* (Kinda good but kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as well...)
-Crafting...  Literally everything.  Rough example.
You want to craft an ax to chop some wood?  Of course you do.  To make that ax you need, a handle, a blade, a head, and some rope.(Don\'t quote me on the exacts here I\'m just making an example)
To make the handle, you need to make a shaft, and for the shaft you need a branch.  Thank god you only need an ingot or some stone to make the blade, to make the head it was similar to the handle and rope was plant material to fiber to something else then finally to rope.  Crafting was such a chore, but the fact that you could crafting things out of different materials to get different strength items was really immersive and cool.
-Anomolies - These supposed rare floating light shows with a box in the middle take you to another \"world\" briefly and you get to explore next to nothing.  Granted they did mention they are quite useless at this point, but to be honest, the only thing I could see them being useful for would be to tell more of the story of what happened and such, but as of now they are just random places either a desert or a cave or something wherey ou run to the other side and get teleported back out.  But the cave one you can at least get iron and they do have little crates \"from the creators\" here and there that have resources and such but nothing really note worth.
Cons... The bad... The crap that will be fixed first most likely, but still it sucks...
-Combat  - even killing a little rabbit, albiet with a wodden sword, takes a long glitchy time.
-Movement - since everything is generated in real time it sometimes makes movement feel glitchy or laggy
Tie movement and combat together and it\'s pretty hard to play if you want to kill anything that\'s aggressive.
-Lack of Story
-Since survival is so easy there\'s no real driving force to the game.
TL;DR - Game has great potential.  Buy It or bookmark it and come back in 6-8 months when they are closer to their goal as a MMO.

Game Title: Novus Inceptio (EARLY ACCESS!)
Review Date: 01/03/2016
I can legitimately say that even from first glance that I've not played a game like this one. It has the same mechanics as some games but it definitely made them it's own.
I've been looking for new MMO for awhile now and it looked like it had enough potential to be something fun.
After about 3 hours spent on it, the game definitely earns "early access" or "alpha" status. In the most positive way possible.
My biggest gripes are with performance and the crafting and I can't see myself *playing* the game for fun at this stage of development.
It's definitely a game you should look forward to in the future and if you want to help it be as bug free as possible, pick up a copy ASAP.
The story *IS* there... However, it'll definitely need to be re-written in some parts.
It has a good mixture of sci-fi and fantasy, but it needs to be a bit more refined. Some parts sound interesting and others are awkward sounding when read.
It is written in English and since the company is based in Prague, (Czech Republic), some of it is in broken english. You can read it and still get the general concept for the backstory.
I will say that I loved everything you can do in the game. Most of my gripes for its gameplay are all based around performance issues and its UI.
I thought the crafting system was a bit overly complicated, not as in hard to understand but hard to navigate and use.
To craft an item you have to open your inventory, open your crafting menu, find a recipe, drag or double click each component to craft whatever you want, click on craft, wait 5-10 seconds, repeat.
I wouldn't have as many issues with the crafting, cause I do actually enjoy the concept, and since it involves higher quality items produced based on quality of components used, I don't really see a way around the way it's implemented now.
But it does get tedious when you try constructing buildings or anything that requires alot of parts.
Combat is about as basic as any other game. It uses actual aiming vs the "targeting" that most MMO's use. It's hard for me to personally test it since the only server at this time is based in Europe. From what I've experienced, I'll say it's definitely good enough.
It has a similar build system to "Life is Feudal: Your Own" and it's definitely improved upon it. You enter build mode and go into a free-cam state and place objects to build via the interface, really simple and efficient.
Also, unlike Life is Feudal: Your Own, building is balanced well enough to provide you something to work towards without dedicating the next two weeks of your life towards building a small cabin.
My only other gameplay gripe would probably be the death system. I haven't had the oppourtunity to actually test it but from what I've read you basically ghost-walk back to a safezone to respawn.
Though, it does feature something actually interesting. Your character ages and it tracks your generations of "clones" from your unfortunate accidents. You also won't lose your stats or gear you've gained from playing.
I'm going to say that the strong point for this games eye candy is going to be the world itself, aka the environment. It's a good mix between dense forests and open spaces to provide you with spots to build in without looking abnormal.
Models:
*Relatively* good, some need to be worked on more. It definitely isn't bad but it could clearly be better. I do get the feeling that this game is using too many polygons in its modeling for Unity 5, though.
Textures:
It's hard to judge the graphics in general since even people with god-tier computers will get low FPS in this game if they try turning the graphics up. Regardless, from what I've seen playing on "normal" and "very low", some textures DEFINITELY need to be redone. I'm fairly certain some are only 512x512 compared to your typical 1024x1024.
Environment:
The game shines here... sometimes literally... The world is randomly generated as you explore it, like minecraft, and it's actually pleasant to look at most of the time.
I haven't seen any terrain abnormalities or anything else you might see in some games as of yet, the only bad thing is that most objects emitting light glow ridiculously bright.
Nothing that can't be fixed by the developer, definitely not high priority.
I think this is actually a positive thing for the game, as weird as that sounds. I honestly don't recall anything bad or good about the audio, which means it does a good job of blending it in with everything else you're doing.
I did disable the music simply because I normally play all games without it. The little bits I did hear sounded *ok*, though.
Also, again, it is early access. *ALOT* of things are placeholder/thrown in just to get it started. It's the way game development works, especially on Unity.
As I said earlier, it's a game definitely deserving of the title "Early Access". Obviously right now there isn't going to be alot that'll make you stay and your main priority should be testing for bugs to help the developers release patches.
I'd love to give replay value a higher score, it's a issue with Early Access titles vs giving proper, professional reviews. I can't give higher ratings/recommendations based on what "might" be done in the future, or, what might just never be finished.
This game is a example of what Early Access titles should be during the "Early Access" stage. It's something too widely abused by no-name indie "companies" that dissolve after hitting the steam store.
I do sincerely hope that the developers don't become another part of *that* group. This game has significant potential as long as they find a way to put the effort and time it needs into it.
It definitely isn't getting the attention it deserves from the steam community, which is a serious disappointment. Playing this game partially reminded me of the first MMO I ever played, "Star Wars Galaxies". Twelve years later, I still want to go back and play that game some more...
Overall, it's early access and it's going to be early access for awhile. This is not a game you are going to buy, start up and be addicted to by any means in its current state. The only reason you should buy this game *RIGHT NOW* is to support its development with your money and your time by helping to find and report bugs to the development team.

I played this game back when it came out on the 360 and I originally hated it, I bought it full price and played it for about an hour (if even that). I had no desire to pick it up again because the 'Auto Battle' made the game incredibly boring.
Now that I've picked it up again I'm playing the game with the cursor option set to abilities by default and just flat out ignoring that the auto battle exists and I'm surprised that I'm actually really enjoying it! The combat is very satisfying, the characters are interesting, the plot is great, and the music is fantastic (as you'd expect from a FF game).
Yeah, the port isn't the best, but with the GeDoSaTo tool to fix the issues (it was recently updated so you can improve the shadows as well as the other fixes!) the game runs and looks great. I'm not minding the 'hallway-ness' so much either, I think that's because I've been craving a FF game for a few years and this is scratching that itch enough so that I can overlook that.
So yeah! Basically this is a long winded post to advise you guys to IGNORE AUTO BATTLE. Go into the options and set the default cursor mode to abilities, set the combat speed to slow, and pretend auto battle flat out doesn't exist. The combat is difficult and very satisfying (especially when you get 5 stars).
I can't see why they would add that feature when it detracts from the fun of the combat so much. At the very least it should have only been available in easy mode.
It's a good game, it's a fairly poor PC port, but at the same time it's certainly better than nothing, so I can't complain too much. Thanks Square for giving us PC gamers a chance to play this
