This game looked like it was made for me. I wanted to like this game. I TRIED to like this game. But in the end, I simply couldn't.
The graphics are good, the gameplay is good, everything's fine.... the whole problem comes down to a single issue - story design.
As far as I can tell, this game is not designed to be played as a game. Either that, or it's designed to be played with a spreadsheet, obsessively mapping out every single choice.
See, the way things work is that many of your options are controlled by events. What styles you have access to... who your friends are... whether you meet a brave warrior who will be your battle brother, or a dainty maiden who will be your love. And all of these events require you being in the right place, at the right time, usually multiple times... and there are no hints or anything that suggest this.
After giving this game a couple of playthroughs (hours on record seems bugged for some reason... maybe playing offline on my other computer?), I came to the conclusion that, if I wanted to do a specific thing or try a specific style or whatever, I would have to map the whole thing out in advance. What skills to train at what time to unlock the events, and then go to a specific place at a specific time to take part in the event to unlock the MacGuffin I'm after.
Basically, playing this game seems to mean either just rolling dice and hoping for the best, or planning out the entire campaign turn by turn so that you know exactly how everything's going to go, and then just grinding through the "gameplay" aspect of implementing your plan.
Either way, it doesn't appeal. Thumbs down.

The game has such a unique playstyle with a battleground consisting of four zones to put your cards in. Besides having to worry about your fortress' health, you also have to take the morale of your troops into account - losing too many valued troops will ensure defeat as much a the destruction of your fortress. Combined with the synchronised turn system this creates a tactical element and a mind-game that is unseen in other card games! The different factions have a truly unique playstyle and some of the animated cards are something to marvel at. The learning curve is rather steep but this just kept me coming back to the game to learn more about it and improve my playstyle and deckbuilding knowledge.
Give this game a try: play the campaign and some player matches with the free-to-play weekly decks and I'm sure you will be captivated by the experience.

I've been playing video games for 30 years so it is always a pleasure to find and play something with a truly original "feel" to it. I picked up Ink on a whim during a steam sale earlier this year and, to be completely honest, forgot all about it for 6+ months. I'm really glad I finally stumbled onto it again.
For all its visual simplicity Ink is a truly impressive little platformer. The music, while slightly repetitious by level 67+, is quite relaxing and a pleasure to listen to, the controls are simple and easy to pick up, and the difficulty scales at a gradual and natural pace.
The first few levels do a great job of easing players into the basic controls: moving, jumping, double jumping, wall jumping, and most importantly "painting" your surroundings. As your avatar, which is essentially just a small white square, moves across the game world it leaves a trail of paint which illuminates your otherwise pitch black surroundings. Double jumping causes your avatar to spray small globs of paint in a 360 degree radius which can also help you orient yourself in the blackness of your surroundings.
Each level contains a door which your character much reach to progress. Reaching the door involves painting your surroundings so you can navigate to it, defeating "enemies", dodging projectiles, avoiding spikes, finding keys and more (depending on the level) There are also "bosses" you'll need to defeat along the way which are significantly more difficult than the standard enemies you'll encounter more frequently.
As you can imagine based on the description above you're going to die... a lot! But, Ink gives you an infinite amount of lives so you won't really care or stress about it. By the time you reach the 60th level or so the difficulty will have ramped up significantly and you may find yourself thinking "How in the world can I get through this level?" but several quick deaths later you'll find yourself triumphantly moving on to the next level with a sigh of relief and some potentially sore thumbs from frantically mashing the buttons on your controller.
Summary: Ink is a ton of fun, especially for the price. GIve it a try! Chances are you're going to have a blast.

Fascinating evolution on the structure of Gone Home.  The central mechanic of watching a short series of events multiple times, from different perspectives, is a great fit for the vision of the game.  I never found myself getting bored or annoyed, but felt continuously stimulated as I scoured the environments.
The worldbuilding is engrossing and convincing.  The multicultural and LGBT representation in the cast deepens the characterization and presents an aspirational example of diversity.  Other issues and attitudes presented put up a mirror to the society we live in today and where we might end up in 70 years, especially the cruelty of unchecked capitalism.
A little twee hipsterdom sneaks in from time to time, but it's not obtrusive.  If I could change anything, I would probably loosen the linearity up a bit and give the player more freedom to experience events out-of-order, but the current design is very accessible and clear.
Maybe the biggest jump from Gone Home is the sheer fidelity on display.  Environments are just cluttered enough, and examining everything from notes to objects is greatly improved by sharp, detailed textures, where a lot of the assets in Gone Home didn't hold up well to inspection.  The music that's there is understated and pleasant.

Tacoma isn’t as great as Gone Home but as a sophomore effort it’s still quite good. It’s a little more linear in the sense that it doesn’t give you as much free reign to explore as Gone Home did and subplots aren’t as subtle and up to player exploration as Mr. Greenbriar’s story in Gone Home, but the writing is still solid and there is still some good exploration with stuff you can miss if you just blaze through.  The sci-fi elements are neat enough with a bit more grounded feel crossed with cyberpunk-esque megacorps. The AR stuff is good too, the voice-acting and animation really sell what’s otherwise a bunch of colored wireframes walking around. While it definitely won’t stick with me like Gone Home or this year’s Edith Finch, Tacoma is still a quality adventure game on its and definitely worth checking out.

A short but sweet space adventure, that's how I'd describe Tacoma in as few words as seem fit.
With a few words more, Tacoma is the second game made by the team at Fullbright, the makers of the absolutely fantastic, and very similar game, Gone Home. You find yourself exploring a space station where something seems to have gone wrong. Your objective is to piece together what happened and try to salvage what you can.
In a very similar way to Gone Home, Tacoma takes some very interesting turns in it's storytelling, and you are in for a few surprises and heartfelt emotions, especially if you take your time to fully explore the station and all its secrets. An interesting aspect of the game is that you find a lot of pre-recorded messages, recorded in the environment around you, that you can interact with and manipulate the playback of. It gives the environment a very believable atmosphere, and really lets you connect with the characters on-board the station.
While the game is very story focused, it has quite a few interactive elements strewn about that you can occupy your time with. Most of them are to get a few extra details in on the story, but others are simply there for fun and to add depth to the world around you. Opening up a dart-board, for example, reveals a picture of the CEO of the company the crew works for, and you are even able to toss darts at it yourself at your leisure.
Overall, if you enjoy the interactive narrative genre, call it a walking simulator if you will, this is another powerhouse experience by the people that helped get it started in the first place. Definitely give it a try!

Teslagrad is 2D puzzle-platformer released in December 2013. In an already saturated genre, Teslagrad aims to distinguish itself using the game's magnet mechanics. The protagonist can pull himself towards a faraway magnet and conversely force propulsion if he is standing on a magnet to leap large distances and heights in order to navigate and progress through the game world.
The biggest strength of Teslagrad is the balance between puzzle and platform aspects of the game. By using the tools the protagonist obtains as the player progresses in the game, both puzzle solving and quick platforming skills are required. The game does not have health and the protagonist dies instantly upon contact with the game's harmful obstacles. Thus the aspect of timing is crucial in many of the game's puzzles to progress to the next screen. The difficulty curve to progress is mild but it is raised for searching for the 36 collectables in the game, for both puzzle solving and platform skills. Speaking of difficulty there are handful of bosses in the game which the difficulty spikes for all of them. However those challenges are not impossible although for most players, it would take multiple attempts to take them down.
The controls are very crisp and responsive. Jumping feels good without being too floaty or limited. The default keybinding is slightly odd to get used to but it is fully rebindable with keyboard and gamepad.
The game's visuals are handdrawn in pencil and crayon. The art assets are relatively plain and unobtrusive to allow focus onto the gameplay. There are few instances of impressive art in the background. The game does not limit itself to certain colour palettes and various primary colours are used. This helps the player to distinguish what is in the foreground and interactable from the background art.
Music is mostly well-composed ambient with more intense orchestra coming in for the boss battles. Effects are well placed as it adds the steampunk nature of the tower atmosphere.
Overall, Teslagrad would be a worthy game for library of puzzle-platform fans.

Do you like survival games? RPG? MMOs?
Novus Inceptio is the answer to your question and preferences.
Alothough it's still in an early alpha stage, the developers are doing an amazing job, showing how an Early Access Game is meant to be.
The crafting system is simply splendid and well done. You have to gather a lot of materials, with an initial small weight capability. Every resource can be gathered in different ways, giving you different materials (for example a tree can be chopped if you have an axe, you can gather branches with a knife, or you can pick leaves or resin).
To craft items you need blueprints that can be found in chests around the vast (really really vast) world or in anomalies (myserious areas accessible via floating cubes). Crafting requires many materials that most of the time are the result of a previous refining.
Chopping and gathering around won't work, you need to plan your resource gathering in a very smart way if you want to survive this harsh world.
The graphic engine is superb, sometimes I stop to admire the landscape and its variety: for example trees aren't always the same, there are so many species. Specs aren't even that demanding considering the quality this game is offering.
Again, I am pointing out the Early Alpha stage of this game as I am reviewing it, just to let you notice how developed it already is..imagine in few months!
What are you waiting for? Add it to cart, you won't regret it!

[Early Access Review]
What a surprise this was.
While certainly there were early access 'annoyances' such as not being able to make a female avatar and a few odd translations, I must say I'm quite impressed with where this game is so far.
Graphics / UI
Are quite pretty and smooth, day/night transitions are realistic and the ambience and lighting is superb, particularly when approaching an anomaly and its glow illuminates the nearby landscape.  Animations are smooth, if a bit simple at this stage, and there was minimal glitchy/laggy experience with the graphics.  There are certain places where if you pitch the camera all the way forward, you can see 'beneath' the ground, but overall nothing that really interfered with gameplay.  The UI is smooth, responsive, and crisp looking with good functionality and is pretty intuitive the way it is laid out.  Hotkeys aren't tooltipped anywhere but with a bit of fiddling you work out that C is for character and I is for inventory, etc.  Overall very impressed with the level of polish.
Sound
The background/music ambience fits very well, and is engaging and immersing.
There seem to be some missing sound effects for things like mining, chopping trees, etc. but not really unexpected for an early access / alpha state.
Gameplay
Well, as it stands now, its a crafter/hoarder's paradise. While yes your character's inventory is limited, your trusted floating robot ball thing can carry whatever it likes, and it is easy to switch between the two.   You can happily forage/chop/mine and 'get stuff' to your heart's content and make it into other stuff.  The crafting has a good level of depth, involving quality levels and skill levels and particular materials.  At the moment I've only made the most basic of things, but I see the potential here for an exceptional system whereby different materials convey different quality/effects.
For example, I have the blueprint for a shirt, and I can either:
leaves -> fibers - > threads - > cloth
grass -> fibers - etc
or some combination of the two.
Everything is made out of its base components, so if you want to make a hammer, you'll need a head, a handle, and something to fasten them, and so forth.  The crafting UI has little mini icons indicating what is needed and they change color based on what you've got available in your inventory.
Anyway, needless to say, this game completely allowed me to stand there and make thread for 30 minutes, rewarded me with my tailoring level going up, and I was able to make something to wear.   Likewise with making tools, etc.
There is also a whole construction element (ie building a house) that I've not even gotten into yet.
Skills and stats go up slowly as you do things and the UI gives good feedback on success rates & quality level expected of the resulting item.
I only did minimal combat, killing rabbits to get pelts and meat, but it was fluid and responsive, ie press button-> something happens.  One of my biggest pet peeves in games is a clunkly/slow response UI so I'm pleased to report that Novus did not disappoint in this regard.
Overall -
The game is certainly playable now, though I'm not sure how many hours of content are available at this point.  It really looks to be something that I will easily get addicted to once I can make a girl character (since piloting boy characters always feels wierd to me), and once there's a bit more direction.  At the moment there is a lot of 'wander around, click stuff, build stuff' and I hope that this doesn't get lost along the way, as it is pretty relaxing to play.   This may just be the PvE sandbox I've been looking for, and fingers crossed it doesn't end up an open pvp mess like so many of the survival type games out there.  And even then, there's an offline mode in the works.
The devs have posted up their trello planning tool so planned features etc. can be monitored and seem quite keen on getting things done.  I have to say that compared to other early access games I've tried, many of which I last about 10 minutes in, this is a refreshing change!

Freedom Fall is a fun game.  The art is well done, the controls work well and consistently, and the level design is interesting if not particularly inspired.
Probably the most engaging part of the game is the way it conveys it's story, limited as it is.  None of the characters speak, instead the tower's designer communicates with you through the scrawled grafitti which litter the levels.  Many of these messages are rather ammusing, and putting together the bits of background they offer to work out what's going on was an engaging exercise.
For completionists, there are three medals to be earned in each level, gained by attaining par scores for loot collected, time spent, and deaths.  Failing to obtain these medals will not hinder you from moving forward though, so they serve as extras for those interested rather than barriers for those who are not.

Overall, it's certainly worth a try.

For me the best game of 2014.
Beyond Earth combines the elements of old school Alpha Centauri and Civilization V into one solid, beautifully made package.
The vanilla version (no doubt there will be loads of DLC and some expansions in the near future) is very streamlined and organized, while still managing to offer many different approaches towards achieving your ultimate goal during a scenario. For somebody, who haven't ever played any Civ game, it might seem confusing at first, but that will pass, trust me; for a veteran, you will hop in straight into a game, being instantly familiar with many features, yet still you do not feel it is just a Civ V rip-off. The wide spectrum of policies and quests allow you to tweak your civilization in more ways than ever before.
As great as the gameplay itself are the visuals. Civ V set the standards high, yet BE has them beaten. A variety of planetary landscape (earthlike or completely alien environment) is soon littered by your domes, biowells, generators etc., which all look futuristic and fit well with the visual theme. Your units and cities change looks based on your affinity, allowing you a little personal touch.
The soundtrack is breathtaking - the "violin theme" gives me chills, reminding me a lot of the First Contact theme every time I hear it.
There are sone cons, however...
Diplomacy - is exactly the same nonsensical crap as in Civ V. Being on friendly terms with another civ does not mean squat, they attack you randomly, because reasons. Only way how to prepare for backstabbing a-hole AI is to keep a decent standing army of highest technological level possible. Luckily there is no United Nations in the New World and lets pray it will keep that way.
AI could have been smarter I guess. On the higher difficulties, the AI shamelessly cheats, but that is not the problem - the problem is that when attacking, the computer behaves like a moron, just bluntly rushing one of your cities with 4+ mobile units and when he fails, the remainder of his armies wanders aimlessly around where you kill the units one by one. When defending, the AI neglects defensive structures, which is fatal. Unlike in Civ V, the cities do not get upgraded in strength/hp when reaching a new technological era (since there no eras in BE, it would be affinity levels), so it is vital to build up both city strength and hitpoints to withstand a siege or a rush attack.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary: Beyond Earth delivers the highest quality among turn-based games. One has to wonder if the coming new content won't spoil such a masterpiece, like Brave New World did for Civ V - the strength of the game is in its simplicity (ok, simplicity is a poor word considering you have zillions of technologies to research, 80 policies to take and a customized choice of an upgrade for each building), while providing you with tons of fun, complex content.
Lets hope that further additions to the game will expand the already rich, beautiful new start for the Mankind.

This game offers a large number of changes from mainline Civilization games. I am honestly a fan of a lot of them - they offer new and unique takes on systems that Civ V already turned on their head. Some quick ones are:
- Unit types unlock from researching a specific tech, but upgrade instantly based on Affinity progress - which has a lot of consequences for when to build units and when to go to war.
- Different tech paths encourage different ways to use the land around you, offering the player a wide variety of different build strategies for their improvements and ways to use resources.
- Strategic resources are used not just for units, but also for powerful buildings, giving the player a tradeoff choice between great army and great infrastructure.
- New Covert Ops is a fun alternative to Spying, even though it mostly devolves into a Science/Energy boost because the AI is rarely foolish enough to let you flip their cities.
- The tech web supports actually different branching paths of technological development, rather than just prioritizing Iron Working over Pottery for now.
But after playing through a few games, one thing has stuck out for me.
Civilization: Beyond Earth offers five paths to victory - Domination, Contact, and 3 Affinity-aligned paths to victory. Domination aside, the other four victories revolve around building a special wonder that occupies its own tile and then fulfilling some goal related to it completing its progress - essentially they are non-violent victory conditions.
Civilization V, on the other hand, offers four paths to victory: Domination, Diplomacy, Cultural, Space Flight. The Cultural victory evolved in Brave New World to be less solo-oriented and more versus-oriented. Therefore, there are three non-violent paths to victory, compared to Beyond Earth's four. So that seems like a win for Beyond Earth on the "non-violent" front, right?
Well, not quite - because in Beyond Earth the *only* way to deal with someone else potentially winning the game ... is to go to war with them and destroy their creation. You can't out-pay their allies in order to prevent a Diplomatic victory. You can't boost your culture to incredible height or collect lots of artifacts before they can to prevent their Tourism from overtaking your Culture. The tech web doesn't have enough layers that you can really get ahead in tech to start your wonder before they do. So if they build one of the four game-winning wonders, your only response is war (unless your clock is already ticking, in which case good for you - go up a difficulty level).
So I'm torn a bit on the end game scenarios. But overall this game is solidly enjoyable. It may not have the staying power that Civ V picked up in its expansions, but I must say that I hope to see Beyond Earth continue to get the after-launch care that the mainline Civ game got. In the mean time, keep playing one more turn.

Ok. Hardcore fans will be disssapointed that some stuff present in previous games are missing and that this game is more "casualized". They may be true, but this game has improved on some of the stuff in Blood Money and previous games. For example, two bodies can be dumped in bins and places to dump bodies can be now used to hide bodies in. Also a cover system, though not good, is introduced to the series.
Instinct can be used to highlight enemies, targets and objects of interest and for point shooting. Point shooting and blending in with a disguise drains the meter. Hardcore gamers and Hitman fans say Instinct makes the game too easy but that's not true. It replaces the map of previous games, which displayed a map of the area and all people, points of interest and VIPs. Instinct is similar but actually displays less information so the game is more challenging. Hardcore fans keep saying casuals will keep relying on it but I didn't use to advance through the game. I only used for fun and then reloaded to the last checkpoint.
The disguise system is probably what I disliked the most about the game. It seems like IO Interactive has gone backwards in the system. It is like Hitman 2, probably worse. If people in the same outfit 47 has sees him, they'll be suspicious of his disguise and the only way to blend in is to use Instinct. The developers just wanted to show off the new feature. The change of the disguise system is good but it is unrealistic how every cop in Chigaco would know every of their fellow policemen and how people can see through masks. Strangely, if 47 hides behind an object while wearing a disguise, someone in his outfit will not recognize him. It's also more suspicious to scratch a head or tip a hat when walking past someone in the same outfit than just pass by them. I thought developers were smart.
I loved the infiltration missions. They are a nice change to the series. Hardcore Hitman fans will be dissapointed though but there were infiltration missions in the first two games.
The dialogues are funny and made me feel like I was in the world that Absolution was portraying.
This game is a must buy. People keep saying that they didn't care about getting the best rating possible for every level because the game is so hard and they just shot threw the level. That's not true. I lack brain power but I didn't find it hard. My first play through was on Normal and then I moved to Hard. This game requires more thinking and planning than the first 4. Oh yes and for a few missions, improvisation.

From what I've heard, this game is fantastic and one of the best of the Assassin's Creed series. Unfortunately, my PC (which is a high-end gaming laptop at the time of writing) cannot run this game without horrible graphical tearing. When I get a new PC or they fix this issue I'll write a new review, but until then I cannot recommend the PC port.

While it does not follow the classic trend set by the previous installments, Hitman Absolution follows the story of Agent 47 in fast changing environments in order to fulfill a promise for a long-time friend.
The graphics are very well done painting the changes of each setting to fit it. Also the music is cued at precise moments to intensify the feel and the atmosphere of the whole thing.
Also when you're done with the main story there is a Contracts mode which revives the play mode of the previous Hitman games. This mode portrays various ways of killing different enemies. Also it's nice that, through this way of playing, players can have a multiplayer shootout by seeing who can complete a random contract with the highest points.
In conclusion: while purists may say that the game changed too much with this version, I suggest you play it and make an opinion of your own. It's fun and will take many many hours to actually achieve all the challenges.

If you have been waiting for Sid Meier's Alpha Centuari 2 then you will be greatly disappointed.  This game falls very short of the potential of what made that game unique and amazing.  The complete lack of water development and terraforming brings the lack luster of this game to an apex.  Does this stop me from playing, not exactly.  I do find myself wondering why do i keep playing it.  The trade system in the game is so completely unbalance it is depressing.  The end game is anticlimactic, and the quests quickly blur together into repetition.  I would have liked to have seen more of a cross between Alpha Centuari and Call to power represented here. That is not why i cannot bring myself to recommend this game.  I can not recommend it because I feel like this game was released because it was time for a new game to come out in the series people and franchise held with little to no regard.

Overall, I believe this game has a lot of potential but needs a few major tweaks.  The core content is solid, the tech web is an interesting change from older Sid Meier's games and the upgrade system is interesting as well since it makes you feel more involved in the progress of your colony.
The problems I have this game come in two forms, pacing and voice acting.  I will discuss voice acting first since it is the shorter one to explain.  There is not a lot of phrases and I personally got sick of hearing the exact same phrase constantly, a tiny bit of difference would have been wonderful.  Pacing though, is a much bigger issue that can make the game go from fun and engaging to boring in a matter of rounds.  Unless you are going for a domination victory where you are fighting constantly, you can hit points where you are doing nothing but waiting for something to build, or something to finish researching.  With the tech web instead of a tree, you can go right to the items you need and your cities production doesn't always grow at the same rate as the items you want them to build.  With the tree you were forced to go through a lot of 'junk' to get to the end game victory techs, this 'junk' gave you things to build and interact with throughout the entire game and added infrastructure to your cities to make them overall better and easier to build the end game stuff.  An example is when I did the transcendence victory.  I was in a well fortified spot so when I got all the stuff for the mind flower, I spent 50 turns basically just hitting next and fiddling with refreshing my trade routes waiting for the thing to build, and did the exact same thing waiting for transcendence.  I had 75 turns of knowing I won, just sitting there waiting, and waiting, and waiting for the stuff to finish.
Overall, I do suggest this game, because it is a good game, I just hope it gets patched or fixed in the first DLC pack to fix the major pacing issue.

I have played many story driven games. I’m quite fond of them. But very few have had me as invested in the ending as this one. The concept is divine and the execution is touching. One of Tacoma’s crowning achievements is that it made me deeply invested in featureless holograms. I attribute this to the voice acting, which I found to be superb! The voices and the writing go hand in hand. Every character struck me as a person I might come across in everyday life. The amination is lovely. I do not have a single complaint. There were occasions where I disliked the way a character acted or how the story progressed, but in every single instance the game worked it into the bigger narrative in ways I hadn’t expected.
Now, there have been some impatient and foolhardy people claiming that there is not enough information about each character to become invested in them. Well, there most certainly is! There is a dearth of interesting personal information that you can learn about each and every crew member by exploring their offices and rooms. If you are only able to build a picture of a person by what they say or what is said about them, then don’t bother playing this. These characters are intricately explorable through their subtleties like the books they have, the state of their spaces, the people they choose to interact with, the gifts they receive, the letters on their desks, etc. etc. etc. In short, it’s like real life. It feels real. If you are willing to read a letter or grasp implications then you’ll do just fine.
The plot will go fast if you are not willing to take the time to see each person’s part in each available scene. Attention to detail will make or break your playing experience.
Lastly, for God’s sake, stop comparing every last story based game to Gone Home. That’s like comparing every single FPS to Bioshock Infinite. It’s silly. Each game has its own budget, staff, limitations, intentions, and merits. Especially games such as this. And if you don’t enjoy “Walking Simulators” then don’t play them or leave nasty reviews about how you hated them. You wouldn’t order food you didn’t like at a restaurant then complain about not liking it, don’t do the same on Steam.

This game started out fun. But pretty quickly it becomes apparent that the game is pretty pointless to play without a controller, so points lost for that. The mechanics also start off being fun, but later tools are dodgy at best. The cloak mechanic is downright inconsistent and unreliable in it's behavior for anything more than basic attraction/repelling. Later level design just feels like the designer wanted to throw a bunch of really impossible stuff in just because it was the end of the game. The parts that are impossible just make the game downright boring. Sure, throw in the hard stuff; but learn to balance it. The trial-and-error/rinse-and-repeat method is terrible. These developers clearly have no idea about balancing gameplay with challenge, and the number of people frustrated with the end game shows it. In addition, there are too many places where I got stuck permanently (sometimes without even the ability to escape by death), which mostly occured because direction in the game was sorely lacking. If you get stuck, you either have to die, or replay from whatever arbitrary point you may have last auto-saved, which could be 5 minutes or 15 minutes back. All this points to a game that looks cool, but who's developers obviously lack skill and experience in good game design. If you're looking for a puzzle platformer that's satisfying to play through in all aspects, this isn't the one.
EDIT: I was reading some other reviews that described better what I meant. The mechanics are too sluggish for the sort of action required in the puzzles. The response time and tightness of movement just isn't there, and I'm playing with a controller, not even a keyboard. It makes the game way more frustrating than it needs to be.

I've been very excited to play the Stanley Parable for many years and I finally got to play it last weekend. It wasn't at all what I expected.
I remember when this game was first released it was receiving a lot of praise for it's breaking of the 4th wall and comedy. All that was true, it is indeed quite funny but the game ends up being being a novelty and, finishing the "main" ending in 30 minutes, a short one at that.
The novel idea is the multiple endings. See, this game touts almost 20 different endings yet after reaching most, if not all of them, I don't see why they are so well received. A few of these endings are incredibly funny, others literally force you to restart the game after playing off a joke. I found at least 5 of them simply poking around before finishing the game (main ending) in 30 minutes time. After multiple playthroughs, I decided to look up some of the endings I thought I had missed. Again, some were funny, others, not so much.
In a nutshell, The Stanley Parable is a walking simulator. You play as Stanley, an employee of a company who finds himself alone after exiting his closet-shaped office. You proceed to walk around, interact, and question the circumstances that you're in. I won't say much more than that; any more and I would be spoiling the entire game.
In my opinion, it's just way too short and does not have enough content to warrant a $15 purchase. The novelty is interesting but after the 3rd, 4th, 5th playthrough, are you really going to keep searching up the last 15? Probably not.

Freedom Fall is a nice little platformer. It has some issues though. For me the length of the game was a little disappointing. You beat the campaign in max. 2 hours. After that there are some additional levels to play, but overall the content is fairly limited. I would expect just a little more. Especially if you consider the difficulty, which is definitely too low. It was not enough of a challenge, in my opinion. Even, if you always choose the hard route (there are many parts of the levels where you can choose between an easy and a hard section), you won't have any trouble completing the game. One more thing: there is not enough variety in the platforming. Gunman Clive's campaign can be completed in half the time, but has so much more to offer (gravity flipping, rocket rides...).
On the pro side there is solid platforming (including items for double-jumping and gliding, and switching between them), nice story-telling (every few meters you can read surprisingly funny messages, the princess left there), and a nice twist to the typical platformer story cliche (you search for a princess, yes. But she is an evil, insane sadist). I really enjoyed the game, despite all the issues mentioned above.
Overall Freedom Fall gets a thumbs up, but it could have been much better. I wouldn't recommend it for full price. The current 35% discount is not bad, but maybe it's better to grab a bundle key of the game.

This game is awesome. I really don't really understand why some people hate it, a lot of the complaints are very nitpicky or ignorant. A lot of people call it a "reskin" or say that any modder could do this, despite that being impossible. Some of the best games of all time were made on previous game engines, such as Fallout 2 as well as Fallout 3 and New Vegas, most of the Street Fighter series, Super Mario Galaxy 2, and just look at what all has been made on the Source and Unreal engines.
Beyond Earth is very refreshing. I've played over 300 hours of Civ 5 and after a while, it became me running through the motions, and something to pass time with as I catch up on podcasts or audio books. This game is similar to Civ 5, but very different, and it feels naturally very alien. You have to learn a lot of new things to get by on this strange alien planet, and early on, the alien life forms will slaughter your guys. I wouldn't even say that there is much that guides could do to help, there are general tips that can help a lot early on, but a lot of it is just learning as you go.
Once you pick a spot to land on, the space is very limited, you don't just start with settlers and travel until you find the best spot. That does work since, if you started with settlers, they would fall prey to the aliens. An interesting part of how you grow is the less linear structure of learning technolgy, here there's a large web of tech trees and some techs have 1 of the 3 afinities that you will focus on as you grow. There's purity for the warlike player that wants to take over every settlement and make this world a new Earth. Harmony is to coexist with the planet and merge genetics with the aliens. Supremecy is more about using the alien world to create better technolgies, like robots and other advanced creations. There are also 5 victory types to pick from, and there is an easy to follow quest tracker that tells you each step.
For the most part, that's all you need to know about this game. It is very much like Civ 5, but they've added a lot of new features and created a whole new take on Civilization. Naturally, what flaws the game does have, will be fixed when they release an expansion pack. Civ 5 didn't start out perfect either, Brave New World wasn't made in a day.

Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth isn't a bad game, but it's in no way a great game either. Let's get on with some pros and cons.
Pros:
-Sci-fi world! Who doesn't like sci-fi?
-Quests are fun to do and has quest decisions to keep you involved with the quest and gives you rewards depending on what you choose.

-There are three affinities, and each one gives you unique benefits
-Trading routes are improved and work well
-Orbital units are nice and give you good benefits
-Spying is cool and fun to do
Cons:
-The other civs can get on your nerves. They will keep telling you about something that you did they didn't like that happened maybe 300 years ago
-The ADVSR can also get annoying, telling you about the same thing over and over again.
-Aliens will murder you now matter how much you insist on not killing them. (Could be because other civs are attaking them, but I haven't seen any other civs done that)
Overall this game isn't worth the full price. Wait for it to go on sale or until they add DLC. However, if you find yourself getting bored often and you don't already own civ 5 then this is the game for you. It is very addicting and will keep you saying "Just one more turn...".

Tacoma
Pick up any object an front of you, examine it, and describe it. Now, rotate that object and describe it again. Turn the object upside down, and add to your description. What if you could do this to a story? Tacoma can best be described as an experience in multidimensional storytelling.
If you have played Fullbright's previous game, Gone Home (and you should), then you already have a baseline for Tacoma. It continues the developer's narrative based style of game. The premise this time is that you have been hired by a corporation to travel to an abandoned space station to retrieve the company's AI core. In doing so, you learn what happened to the station's crew and how it came to be abandoned. This is conveyed through environmental detail, but most importantly, through recorded interactions of the crew. These recordings take the form of "ghosts" of scenes that played out over the course of the crew's time on the station, akin to echoes of the past. The main story evolves in a non-linear order, so you need to mentally track the dates of conversations. Time becomes another dimension of the story as you progress.
Speaking of time, this is a game that isn’t afraid to let the player be in the moment and not feel rushed or pushed forward. Sit and absorb the story. Spend the time. Savour the details or it is a lost experience. If you need fast stimulus, this isn't the game for you. It is a slow burn. Tacoma is a game of detail and intricacy that you have to spend the attention to get the value. When viewing the scene playbacks from different perspectives, it changes how you feel about the conversation. Walking into a conversation with a different pretext changes your understanding. The ability to rotate an item to rotate it and view it from all sides is transposed to the ability to view a scenario from all sides. It is almost an intrinsic aspect of this type of game that not only are the physical objects fully viewable, but so are the interactions of the NPCs. This was likely a core idea of the development team, and it has been realized in spectacular fashion.
From a technical standpoint, Tacoma perfectly uses its visuals, audio cues, and physics for a complete experience. Graphics are clean and fit the theme of the game. The rotation of the space station with the ambient lighting as it changes with the rotation is an example of  the small graphical touches which enhance your immersion. The background audio evokes the serenity that space engenders. On a technical note, the game is much better with headphones. Ambient noises  tend to be low in presence, and might not be heard without headphones. The soundtrack is decent, but not as good as Gone Home in my opinion. The in game physics are shown off by useable items such as a pool table, dartboard, basketball hoop. Being able to interact with these really anchors you in the experience. Lastly, I wonder if this game was made with VR in mind. Some of the aforementioned physics hubs (e.g. basketball hoops in zero gravity) feel very much like a tech demo. Tacoma would be an incredible experience in VR.
The voice acting deserves special mention. It is not typical videogame acting; no intensity, shouting, or directive dialogue. The acting is much more conversational in nature and harder to do with proper inflection to evoke the right sentiment. Fullbright clearly has a good contingent of voice actors that fit their style of game. Credit to both the actors and the developer to have a sense of emotional timing and tone, understanding of the human condition, and how people deal with things. This all comes across very well in Tacoma.
When playing a game, I am always cognizant of the range of emotions it manages to evoke. Tacoma had many moments that struck me. Firstly, I felt the singularity of space. You never come into contact with another live person throughout the game, yet you never feel alone. One of the most consistent feelings I had was a strong sense of voyeurism, almost to the point of being overly invasive.  You learn so much about the characters personalities and lives that when going through their lockers, living quarters, or personal communications, you feel a palatable sense of guilt. It almost feels like you should not be in this place. I can't recall another game that made me aware of this feeling, and that is a good thing.
The main story itself is good, but not the game's reason for being. The secondary stories of each character are much more interesting. Character development is key. Understanding who they are, their role, and relationships with each other is what keeps you playing. The first scene you encounter (the party) is a good opening for what lies ahead. Tacoma creates nuanced real people, in a believable scenario. No budding psychopaths or heroic champions. It feels grounded and familiar. This isn't an archetypal hero story. Or is it? The menace ramps up in the last 20 minutes, and it could be argued that the ending does not follow the emotional beats of the rest of the game. A big reveal that is not really developed throughout the game occurs. As we have come to intimately know these characters, it would have been nice to have some closure in that regard. At the end of the day, the ending felt somewhat contrived for me, but others may disagree and I could probably be convinced as to why it was necessary. Ultimately though, I feel it could have gone a different route, or at least offer an alternate ending.
In total, Tacoma is approximately a 5 hour experience. When you consider there are only 8 primary characters, and everything occurs within a relatively small contained environment, the phrase “deep but not wide”, is how I came to conceptualize this game. There is no real replay value here, but if played the right way, that is perfectly fine. In the end, Tacoma's innovation is how the story is told, not the story itself. It is a more dynamic experience than Gone Home, which could be seen as the prototype of this game. How will this genre evolve? I am on board for Fullbright's future games, and excited to see where they take the genre next.
PS. Not sure if the developers are fans of Sierra, but naming a character Roberta Williams is a great homage if they are.

I guess you could call this an Open World Puzzle Platformer. Unlike in most platformers where you complete one section after another in a linear fashion and you never go backwards, here you have one giant platform network which you have to explore. New areas are cut off by electric barriers which will kill you if you touch them (eg try to jump a gap and land on it) but death is irrelevant as you respawn nearby. You'll often find yourself going back the way you came to search for a route to new areas. You can check your general whereabouts with the Map button which shows you not the whole map but just a few local sections so you can get your bearings.
You play as a young boy who, at the start of the game, has to outrun a scary-looking man chasing him into a big tower. Early in the game you pick up a blue and red glove. These are used to punch blocks and barriers which gives them +/- magnetic polarity to attract them or release them to open passages, crush enemies etc. A bit later you acquire the 'blink' ability which teleports you a short distance, allowing you to get past electric barriers and jump gaps which would normally be too far. There is a lot of jump+blink necessary to traverse high+wide gaps. Later still there is a red/blue cloak to be acquired, I know this because there's a controller option for it, but I haven't reached that stage yet.
There are what you could describe as cutscenes occasionally. As you pass a theatrical stage the camera zooms in to view a medieval play performed by cardboard cutouts featuring kings, knights and princesses. They don't give any clues to the puzzles but they are very charming and entertaining. As I understand it, they depict the storyline of the game and how the boy is involved, but you don't find this out until the end (which I'm nowhere near so far).
Now and then you run into a boss. There's no shooting weapon so the first time I met one I was a bit baffled. I just ran and dodged and punched some boxes which launched up into his mouth and he eventually died. Strange (in a good way) to fight a boss without shooting.
Hidden throughout the game in hard-to-reach areas are 36 scrolls to be collected, each unlocking a Steam achievement. You can progress without collecting them, and to all intents and purposes they don't seem to have any use at all. However, having done a bit of research I discovered (before I started playing, yay!) that you need 19 of them to fight a boss towards the end of the game. There are many complaints about people not realising this and having to go all the way back to collect scrolls.
It's possible to play with keyboard but a controller is an absolute must. The character drifts a tiny fraction on landing at the end of a jump and this does cause some frustration at first, but after a while you get used to it and apart from that the controls are natural and responsive.
The artwork is superb, plenty of 2D eye candy and interesting scenery changes. Music is also pleasant and has character; good sound effects. All in all a very satisfying environment.
Puzzles are tricky enough for a good challenge but it's not hardcore. Controller skills come into it as well, but most of the challenge is in the maze aspect of the game, finding your way around and working out solutions to get through to new sections. For me the overall level of difficulty was just about perfect.
I played on both Linux (mostly) and Windows. It was consistently smooth, no glitches/stutter/lag at all, and the game seems very solid and stable in general. All screen resolutions are available - I played in fullscreen. Controls are fully configurable in-game, which is good because I did need to set up my Steam controller properly before I started. The game auto-saves, there are also a number of manual save slots and everything is uploaded to the Cloud, so no danger of lost progress.
It has the big 3: Achievements (36), Trading Cards (14) and Steam Cloud.
The puzzle platformer genre is crowded but this stands out as one of the best I've played. The sense of freedom and exploration, constantly discovering fresh puzzles, bosses and cutscenes, is wonderful. If you like platformers then I strongly urge you to buy this, I guarantee you won't be disappointed. Great value for the amount of content too.

There is never really any feeling of satisfaction or progress in Teslagrad, and the game is just flat out boring whenever it isn't frustrating. More critics need to realize that just because a game looks nice and is playable does not mean it is a good game. If people do not point these things out, then more games will continue to use them because developers will not see a problem with them. It is because of these design choices that I find myself developing distaste for puzzle platformers in general. I like the idea of them, but if they are going to keep making these mistakes then I do not see the point in spending my money on them.
If I wanted a game based on reflexes and quick thinking, I'd play an action game. At least then the game will be based around it. Teslagrad, however, tries to do two things but fails at both because the two things go together like ice cream and gravy. I ultimately found Teslagrad to be unsatisfying and just not very fun to play. There is no shortage of retro styled Metroidvania titles on Steam, so it is not as if Teslagrad doesn't have any competition. As such, I'd suggest passing on Teslagrad, as it turns out that opposites do not always attract.

Don't be fooled by my hours on record. I have about 30 hours invested into this game through the Nexon Launcher
Overall, this game is somewhat mediocre.
I had hyped this game for a while, because the idea of literally just jumping on a random dragon's back and riding it around for the hell of it seemed so badass. Needless to say, I was wrong. The combat, while somewhat impactful feels clunky, and unfinished. The game is obivously designed around tab-targeting, which by itself wouldnt be bad, but they also decided to integrate action-combat as well. Now don't get me wrong, there are plenty of games that have done this right, and have succeeded as a result. This game is not among them. Playing as an assassin felt so slow-paced and awkward to control. As a side-note, the "action combat" really isn't action combat at all. You're given a reticle that you would assume you're supposed to aim your attacks with, but no. Instead all you have to do is click on an enemy, and boom, you're locked on and can now sit back and enjoy pressing the 1-9 keys in specific orders to execute a combo.
To be fair though, what this game does get right, it tends to do fairly well. There's no transition between instanced, and multiplayer zones, enhancing your immersion, but this really isn't anything revolutionary. Instead, the game's two crowning acheivements are its looks, and its taming system (which, to be fair is its main selling point). Graphically there isn't much to talk about. The game looks pretty, and it's nice to look at. The taming system on the other hand has a lot to talk about. After initially using the skill to tame a mount, you have to undergo a series of super easy QTE's and then bam, you have a pet dragon, horse, wolf, spider,parrot-thing, pegasus, unicorn, etc to call your own. It may seem odd to list so many different animals, but that's simply to show how much variety there is in the many, many monsters that you can tame in this game. This is arguably the most interesting part of the game, as essentially any dragon, horse, wolf, spider, parrot-thing, pegasus, unicorn, etc that you see, you can tame. This creates a ton of variety in the different pets that you see players riding in the game (if you happen to run into another player, which I should warn you, is rather rare).
Overall, if you're looking for the next big f2p MMO, this isn't it, I promise you. Other MMOs that I would recommend investing hours into before this are Wildstar, and Tree of Savior, both of which I have reviewed.

If you liked Fullbright's Gone Home, you'll probably like Tacoma. Between the two, I think Tacoma is the better game with the better environment and story, but then I am a sci-fi geek. Regardless, Tacoma won't please everyone. If you can't enjoy short, linear games that focus on deep narratives, you won't enjoy this.
As in Gone Home, Fullbright have created a world where memories and objects tell the story. Explore the ship enough, and you'll fall in love with the crew, yes, but you'll also uncover Earth's history from the last several decades (Tacoma takes place in 2088). There's been genocide, the restructuring of borders, and a ton of late stage capitalism. Fans of The Expanse / James S.A. Corey will appreciate Tacoma especially.
Fullbright do some really interesting things with perspective and time. An AI has logged events—essentially its memories—for you to view throughout the ship. Each event is its own segment in time. You can follow a conversation a couple of crew members had during one of these segments, but you might miss out on what another crew member did somewhere else in the ship. To follow up with that character, you simply rewind the logged time segment and go to the space they were in, then replay the segment. This means Tacoma is technically in both first-person and omniscient perspectives. I'm fairly certain I've not seen anything like this in a story-rich game before. I would LOVE to see novels turned into VR games this way.
My only complaint about Tacoma is very similar to my one complaint about Gone Home: The ending could be better. While I wouldn't say Tacoma's ending drops off as badly as Gone Home's, it's still abrupt.
And, unlike an ending in a game such as Campo Santo's Firewatch, it can't claim to be especially literary.
I loved Tacoma, overall, and I'll try any and all future Fullbright games. Still, I would like to see them produce a bigger game with a more satisfying ending.

So I love and hate this game. I'll start out with what makes it great. The artwork kind of put me off at first, but it is actually really nice and unique. Kind of reminds me of braid. The "magnet" mechanics, didn't impress me at first, but the developers explored a lot of really cool uses and puzzles implementing them.
The problem with this game, however, is in the incosistancy of the gameplay. The actions feel very sluggish, which would be fine if this was a puzzle game. However, there are several bosses in this game that are just extremely frustrating when you have a delay on your jumping. In addition, the delay on the dashing feels more equiped for a puzzle game than an action platformer. The puzzles, despite being unique, never really go out of their way to stump you and feel more like action-y challenges, which of course would be fine if the mechanics were more tuned to an action game. The biggest flaw of this game is that it can't decide if it's an action game or a puzzle game. Of course, both of them can exist in the same game, but this game draws a very big line between the way the game plays and the way it makes you play it. In addition, throughout the game, there are enemies that will kill you if they touch you, sending you back to the beginning of the area. Towards the end of the game, you get a gun like device, but again, the response time on it is very sluggish, you can only aim in cardinal directions and you can't move while using it, resulting in many frustating deaths. I don't mind frustating games, I love super meat boy. The difference with this game, however, is that the controls aren't tight enough that I feel like the death was my fault, and as a result, I don't feel like I'm learning and getting better at the game.
On a side note, I saw a different review that said that the story in this game was a perfect example of "show, don't tell" in a story. I couldn't disagree more. With regards to a game, what that phrase means to me is that a game is able to describe a universe simply through the environment. Dark souls is a perfect example of this. Teslagrad, however, literally shows you backstory by way of "puppet show" when you reach certain rooms. You walk into a room that looks like a theater, and suddenly you are greated with dull puppet exposition on an even more boring story. Just because there are no words does not mean it isn't exposition, which in essence is the opposite of "show, don't tell".
So that's my rant. Despite all of that, the game is only 10 dollars, which is a great price for what you are getting. This game had a lot of potential and missed out on controls, but it is not a bad game at all. The bosses are extremely frustrating (read: not fun) and the enemies seem misplaced in this game, but it is definitely worth 10 dollars.
I'm marking my recommendation as a "No", but at the same time, I don't regret buying it at all.

I've been very excited to play the Stanley Parable for many years and I finally got to play it last weekend. It wasn't at all what I expected.
I remember when this game was first released it was receiving a lot of praise for it's breaking of the 4th wall and comedy. All that was true, it is indeed quite funny but the game ends up being being a novelty and, finishing the "main" ending in 30 minutes, a short one at that.
The novel idea is the multiple endings. See, this game touts almost 20 different endings yet after reaching most, if not all of them, I don't see why they are so well received. A few of these endings are incredibly funny, others literally force you to restart the game after playing off a joke. I found at least 5 of them simply poking around before finishing the game (main ending) in 30 minutes time. After multiple playthroughs, I decided to look up some of the endings I thought I had missed. Again, some were funny, others, not so much.
In a nutshell, The Stanley Parable is a walking simulator. You play as Stanley, an employee of a company who finds himself alone after exiting his closet-shaped office. You proceed to walk around, interact, and question the circumstances that you're in. I won't say much more than that; any more and I would be spoiling the entire game.
In my opinion, it's just way too short and does not have enough content to warrant a $15 purchase. The novelty is interesting but after the 3rd, 4th, 5th playthrough, are you really going to keep searching up the last 15? Probably not.

I've played well over 1500 turns at this point and still haven't had what I would call a "fun" game.  The UI is pretty miserable when compared to Civ 5.  The tech tree, for instance, doesn't really *pop* out anything except the affinities.  You get to search and hover over everything to figure out where the wonders are.
And on the topic of wonders...why don't many of them build anything at all?  They feel very uninspiring and not very wonderful at all.  I built 3 or 4 last game and not a single one of them had a building on the landscape.
The aliens are annoying.  You go from barbarians that can be turned off or at their worst can be defeated in a 100 turns or so to aliens that are never ending, respawn nests, and harass your units ceaselessly.  Or, you can build your tech tree to focus on being friendly and adapting to them.  Who cares though?  That isn't really very interesting, and again, the lack of anything physical from this (other than alien units) is very bland.
As for the AI, it is downright annoying.  Diplomacy is one thing.  Being spammed by the competition every single turn with the exact same boring audio and requests is awful.  It doesn't take very long for their voices (especially the Asian lady) to grind on your ears like nails on a chalkboard.
Speaking of annoying, the trading is just awful.  Every 20 - 30 turns you have to reassign your traders.  They should adjust this to only needing interaction if they are attacked, the city is attacked/under siege, or if something changes with your relations with the other faction.  If you have 10 - 20 trade convoys or vessels running, you can easily expect to spend 50% of your interactions in the game just managing them.
Oh, another UI problem....the victory types aren't explained.  You can hover over most things in the setup of the game and get some information, but the victory types just say Domination (ok, duh), Contact, Promised Land, Emancipation and Transcendence.  I had to look them up to figure out what some of them were.
The game **could** be fun, but it really is just a slightly different take on past Civ games with less of a physical presence in the world.  Most of the things you do augment what you've already built, not build anything new.  It is very common to have the territory and your units looking bland and similar at turn 1 and turn 200.
As it currently stands, I would not recommend this game.  Civilization 5 was so well done, has so many mods, and the expansions are actually most of what this game contains.  There is no reason to upgrade, and it is arguable that this is not an upgrade at all.

Just a warning to anyone looking to buy this game. TLDR - Horrible porting job.
There are no graphical settings. You are locked in to 720p and have no control over texture quality, antialiasing  or anything else. You can use GeDoSaTo to get around this, which will allow you to get the resolution up, but it has no effect on the pre-rendered cut scenes (of which there are plenty).
The game couldn't tell the difference between a 360 controller and a joystick, wouldn't let me choose, and refused to accept the latter's input until the former had been unplugged.
It's a good thing that the save points are so close together, because pressing escape will immediately  exit the game. No warnings. Straight to desktop. Why did they bind the ragequit button to one that is normally used to exit a menu?!?
Don't expect to alt-tab either. And attempt to minimise the game will make it crash. If you're unlucky enough to have something minimise the game (add new hardware wizard, I'm looking at you!) you're going to be re-loading your save from the most recent point.
If the one-man team behind 'From Dust' can do an awesome PC Port, I don't see why Square Enix can't. Not worth the money in it's current state.

I just finished my first game, and this game is great.  Its not as good as CIV: 5 yet; but its a great foundation and I have confidence in Firaxis producing some great DLC for it.
The leaders don't have as much personality as they did in CIV: 5 or Alpha Centauri; but the variety of units (hover tanks, hover battleships, robots, giant mechs, a genetically engineered Godzilla, the Rocktopus, etc.) and new strategies you can employ (teleporter and laser satellites, using spies to destroy or throw a coup d'etat in a city) make the game a lot of fun.  The tech web and the virtues system are both improved over CIV: 5 and the spying and covert ops are vastly improved and actually a lot of fun this time around.
I am dissapointed by the way in which cultural, tourism and influence victories have been scaled back and hope that they make a return in the first DLC as they happened to be my preferred form of victory in CIV: 5.  Also the lack of natural wonders is odd as their addition would make exploring the alien planet more interesting and I'd likewise like to see the trade of luxury resources reintroduced and maybe some options to interact with the stations (city states) other than just trading with them.  I'd also like to see DLC that adds a unique unit and building for each faction to make them more distinct as well as the addition of some ideology driven factions that have a bit more personality like the factions in Alpha Centauri (Communist Human Hive, Neo Spartans, Cult of Planet, etc.).
All in all its a great game and if you like CIV: V and you like Science Fiction as much as I do then its a must buy.  I pre-ordered it and I have no regrets.

Let me start by saying that I've been avidly awaiting this game's release on Steam for quite some time, so I might be a bit biased about it.
Now onto the review itself.
Freedom Fall is fun and charming, if a little frustrating at parts. The music is about as unobtrusive as you can get, while still adding to the mood, and fits the levels very well. The art (my initial draw into this game as I follow the art director on a popular art site) is VERY well done and the animations are smooth and natural. Marsh is adorable, our dear little Highness the Princess is beautifully handled, and everything just has this almost childlike charm to it.
The design choice of telling the story through graffiti on the wall is excellent in ways I cannot describe.
But there is a reason I said that its frustrating. While the gameplay is smooth and the default controls are solid (though personally I would have had the three glider types set to A, S, and D rather than having to change between them in a loop with C) I keep hitting X when I mean to hit C and C when I mean to hit V and there are times where you only have a split second time frame or have to jump from a specific pixel in order to have the slightest chance of successfully completing the jump. Compared to the fluid ease of the rest of the game, these specific parts quickly become frustrating and irritating. This is made even worse by the large hitbox on obstacles in later levels (to a brutal extent in the bonus level).
Early on, these parts are a nice challenge, but in the later stages it it quickly becomes apparent why this game doesn't use lives.
However, even with those issues, Freedom Fall is a nice, short game that can be completed in an hour if you know what you're doing, and three tops if you don't. Its a fun game well worth picking up and more than worth the money.
Do be warned of some bugs that myself and my friends have encountered.
I'm using a MacBook Pro OSX:
-I have encountered random temporary "hiccups" in loading (all animation will cease for about half a second). These did not affect my gameplay but they are a thing.
-On my second play through I got caught in a Lightning trap and was returned to a redstone as expected, however Marsh was stuck in the electrocuted animation loop. I did not attempt to replicate this bug, I simply restarted the level.
My PC using friends:
-For one of my friends, Freedom Fall will fail to open. Steam will claim it is open, and Freedom Fall will claim its open, but it cannot be located. I'm unsure how he fixed this, if he did, but restarting Steam did not help.
-Another friend had the game crash in the middle of the fight against Madam Sharkie Twinkletooth the 3rd. We do not know what caused it to crash, and she could not replicate it.
-Around the "You weren't supposed to get this far" graffiti, the same friend's screen bugged out again, slowing down and moving Marsh to the side of the screen and going completely unresponsive. She had to close the game and reopen it to fix it, and we're not sure what was done to cause this.

This is a very good and solid jRPG title that has been awfully ported to PC. It is a real shame that SE released a broken and unplayable game that
Yes, the community fixed the game with GeDoSaTo and you can play it with 16:9 resolution. Texture quality is still 720p, but lets be honest, we all played worst looking games then this one; and with this price tag it is not that bad of a deal regardless.
As for the other issues:
It is dropping below 60fps, but never below 30fps, and given the nature of this game, the frame rate doesn't really matter. This is not a first person shooter that requires high precision, this is a turn base combat game, for crying out loud, and as long as you are above 30fps you'll be fine.
As far as I can tell there is a working solution to this issue, I have never tested it, I am using a controller.
Wrong. There are, you just have to go to the in game settings menu and turn them on. The game does not switch automatically when the controller is detected.
Is the game worth it?
Yes, it is. But be advised:
First two chapters are boring and annoying. You are thrown into the middle of things, you have no idea who your character is, who the other characters are, you have no idea what is going on, and the game tries really hard not to explain you anything whatsoever and to confuse you even further. Also, majority of that time you will spend on controlling Snow and Vanille, because playing as Lightening is too mainstream.
During those two chapters you are constantly interrupted by cutscenes and battles. Battles are especially annoying because you have one fight every 5 seconds, the battle is one hit = one kill so it is usually over after (literally) 3 seconds and on top of that you are forced to watch unskipable intro and unskipable statistics screen every single time which adds another 5-10 seconds to each battle.
After 2-3 hours you are in the 3rd chapter gaining access to Crystarium (magic) and the fun begins. Battles are longer and more challenging, killing monsters is more rewarding and the game finally starts to explain the story. Unfortunately, the game insist on being painfully linear to the point where you cannot even choose your team and the party leader.
Aside of that, it is a solid title, grab it if you enjoy this genre, you'll not be disappointed.
Also, shame on SE for this laughable port. If the community managed to fix the game in two hours there is no excuse for releasing it in this miserable state.

The factions are well developed, each with their distinctive strengths and weaknesses. I have enjoyed this game for about two years, and I still come back whenever I can.
Unfortunately, things were not as good as it used to be. Descendants of the Dragons faction is constantly blamed for being too overpowered, an opinion I also share. The Avatars are way too strong. Some factions are downright weaker than the others - in this kind of game, it is very important to keep things "different," instead of either "superior" or "inferior." The
collaboration was somewhat brilliant, but Klingon faction is perhaps a bit too strong. The new campaign system is bland to say the least. The list goes on.
Still, I believe that
can be improved, as it was first introduced. I'm counting on it. Hence the upvote... for now.

I'm pretty much done with Fullbright, I think. I'm right in the demographic that this game should appeal to (as with Gone Home) - queer, female, yadda yadda. Sure, it's really cool to get more diversity in games. There should definitely be more of that in gaming.
But, call me greedy, I want gamePLAY as well. Yet another "eh" story, with yet more "eh" mechanics, with an almost on-rails gameplay that really just makes "collect the plot tokens" more obvious than usual. Even the reveal at the end was more like "FFS, can I not even decide here what my choice is?" even though it's the kind of choice I would have made, had I been given one. Even if you think of it more as a story that is being shown through the medium of a game, it's a pretty blah plot as well (even though I do like the setting and the BASIC plot).
When you compare with Dishonoured - Death of the Outsider, you pay about 50% more, but you also get 50% more gameplay time. On top of that, you get some awesome game mechanics, a decent plot, great graphics, diverse INTERESTING characters with some actually having a backstory, and so on and on.
And to make another comparison with Dishonored (the original), that's 13GB installed, while this is 10.2GB. How big are those audio files?
I feel like this is the gaming equivalent of mass market books and films featuring queer characters in the 1980s, and we'd put ourselves through putting down money on pretty average (and often, really poor) quality stuff because we were so desperate to see ourselves in the media. Surely we can do better now (and in fact we do - think of FemShep, etc etc).
I wouldn't mind so much if this game were cheaper - sure, it's good to have fluff to play. But the only thing "good" about it is the voice acting (not so much the scripts) and the basic premises (being a classic libtard).  However, I really don't think this game is worth the price.

First bad review for me since joining Steam and enjoying a plethora of content. Let me preface with the fact that I love 2-D side-scrolling puzzle-platformers - I grew up in the 80's with hard gameplay and wonky controls. Any game with a Metroidvania feel, I'm in! I thoroughly had a blast playing through Cave Story+, Valdis Story, Unepic, Chronicles of Teddy (and others outside of Steam like Axiom Verge, Strider, Shadow Complex, etc.).
For some reason, I thought this was going to be that same side-scrolling platformer with a Metroidvania twist - Wrong! It was trying to be Swapper or Abe's Odyssey or Limbo - Now, being compared to these games is not a bad thing at all. However, Teslagrad falls miles short of the caliber of the aforementioned. Just going to list my Pros and Cons below and a quick summary...
Pros:
- Art style - It is a beautiful looking game
- Boss battles were pretty nice - However, this has a con - see below
- When I finished and never had to play it again...
- That's all
Cons:
- Horrible controls...played with the Xbox One gamepad - the game allows you to bind movements to keys. Super laggy - I have a pretty high-powered gaming rig and monitor - no lag on even the twitchiest games. It really drove me to a point of frustration.
- No voice acting or script - just unspoken puppet shows and cinematics. Hey, my favorite game of all time, Super Metroid, had absolutely no written or spoken directional clues in the main game, however, it did it right - this game - blah.
- I said I enjoyed the bosses - yes, I did. I felt they were well-fleshed and inventive, and they cleverly used the mechanics of the game. I didn't get to experience what I found through YouTube to be the last boss. After defeating the giant eye, the penultimate boss (which was enjoyable), I was just kind of dropped in a pit. After some searching, I found a room directly opposite of where I headed first that alerted me that I needed to have a minimum number of a certain arbitrary item in order to pass the gate to the final boss. Now, at that point, I'd already had enough of the game (in only about 4 hours); no way was I going to grind back to search for them. And, the menu doesn't even show how many of the item you have in your inventory - This design forces you to go out into the Steam achievements and count them...ugh. The game doesn't even really have a menu-based inventory. The map sucks too.
In summary, even for $10, I wouldn't recommend buying this crap. Pay a couple bucks more (or a few), and enjoy all the games I suggested above. As I'm writing this, I'm thinking of Guacamelee, a game this game tried to kind of emulate in a way - get that game. Beautiful graphics, great story, compelling gameplay, and a fruitful end. Take care...
Addendum: Must be a glutton for punishment...either that or it's just my OCD. I went back and ground to get the extra couple ridiculous items to unlock the door to final boss. Boss was ok. Again, the lack of responsive controls was a bit of a detriment...especially when blinking (teleporting). Spoiler: Another con...and, this is just my personal gripe with the whole hipster fascination with cats. What is with indie dev hipsters and the inclusion of weirdo cat characters? This awkwardly placed cat in the endgame cut scene completely went against any content previously seen in game. Just cringy. Again, buy a better puzzler or Metroidvania...better yet, go back to the original and play Symphony of the Night or Super Metroid.

Missing them fills the Hyper bar which, when full, sends you to a black and white version of the game with Pong-like noises. Keep missing, and your game ends. Save yourself by filling the top bar, and you go back to the colour and the fun.
Not an easy game, but addictive... and it even has boss fights!
