I love the exploration-encouraging idea behind this game, but after playing it I can't in good conscience recommend it to anyone outside of hardcore, borderline masochistic platformer fans.
The basis of the game is you are the white square trying to reach a door in each room. Thing is, the room is blank when you start, and ledges only appear as you leave a trail of ink by moving along them or you release a burst of ink from double jumping or killing an enemy. This seems like a great idea for a trial-and-error platformer as you can repeatedly use your double jump to plan out jumps or see if there's a ledge you can't see at the moment.
Now, for the bad. The first red flag that should come up for anyone playing any game is a lack of an options menu. There is no in-game way to turn down the volume. Additionally, there are no graphics options, which may seem strange for a small indie title. Thing is,
. This is an absolute dealbreaker for a platforming game. On top of that I can't help but feel like this game is trying to be Super Meat Boy, with the unforgiving spikes in difficulty less than 10 levels in and the merciless demand for perfect, precision jumps. This wouldn't be as much of a problem if the ink burst from your character didn't make it hard to keep track of where you're going after the double jump, nor if the same happened every time you kill an enemy, but it does. To top this all off, the controls are ridiculously floaty, again a major dealbreaker for a platforming game. Can't tell you how many times I died simply because I jumped to a platform, only to skid across it and die for touching the side of the screen.
TL;DR
Pros:
- Simple, innovative platforming approach
- Relaxing soundtrack
Cons:
- No options menu
- Seemingly unoptimized even on modern hardware
- Controls feel floaty, especially when landing jumps
- Ink bursts make it hard to know where the **** you're going
- Touching the left or right side of the screen kills you, even if you're on a platform
This game would have been a lot better if they kept the Ink idea and made it more like Thomas Was Alone and less like Super Meat Boy.

Disappointing.
There are some good changes to the Civ formula here, but it isn't enough. There's just so much that feels unfinished or half baked. If you're looking for a successor to Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, this isn't it. In the end, it just makes me want to play Civ 5 again.
Good: The map feels much more alive. I like that the aliens can be tolerated or destroyed. Eventually those alien nests become valuable, though, as they conceal a strategic resource.
Mixed: I don't actually miss trading technologies, but what are favors and why do I want to gain them?
Mixed: The addition of the orbital layer is kinda neat, but it doesn't really add that much. It will get some attention in the first expansion, but this is not a review of future potential. It's a review of what I already paid $50 for.
Bad: The science fiction technologies available in the tech-web are sciencey sounding gobbeldy-gook. There isn't a solid sense of scientific or technological progression. Thus, the implicit narrative of progress is largely lost. This is a major bummer. It just feel like you're constantly choosing the next bonus.
Bad: The endings are largely unuitive, anti-climactic, and unsatisfying. The writing and lore don't bring a satisfying or coherent sense of narrative and once it's done there isn't so much as an animation to pat you on the back. Worse yet, the old series of ranking, replay, and analysis screens are absent. About all the fanfare you get is a ticket back to the title screen.
Bad: There's a general sense of unfinished clunkiness to a lot of the UI. It doesn't even bother to remind you what a city just finished building when prompting you to chose the next project.

INK is a platformer that reveals the platforms as you touch, die or jump near them. A good idea in concept, but executed terribly. Since this game's mechanics are so unbelievably similar to Super Meat Boy's, you might think this is a good game, but the game suffers from a large list of problems under the surface. Firstly the good parts; the platforming is solid. The ground control isn't too stiff or slippery and the mid-air control (especially thanks to the double jump) is fantastic. And thanks to the fast restarts, the game has very little downtime. The graphics are a mixed bag. The levels *can* end up being really colorful as you jump around it, but rectangle enemies on rectangle platforms on a black background get really old really quickly. Look at the official screenshots. See how most of them are taken in the middle of a jump, where the player spits out ink all around it? Unsurprising, since that's the only time there's a lot of color on the screen.
But the level design is just the worst. When you fail in a level in Super Meat Boy, you tell yourself, "okay, I know where I screwed up, so when I try this again, if I do this differently, I'll win this level". But this is not true for this game at all. The game seems to drop inputs especially at times you don't want it to and thanks to the 30FPS framerate, screen shakes that occur when you kill an enemy leave you disorientated. Your double jump ability, although it is supposed to recharge when you land on a platform or kill an enemy, recharges whenever it wants. The levels get excruciatingly long, especially for this level of difficulty with no checkpoints at all. And at around level 60, the game introduces enemies that launch projectiles (like missiles in Super Meat Boy) that follow you in an unbelievably short curve, leaving you wondering how you were supposed to escape.
Essentially, it's a platformer which is difficult, but not fair.

Having so far logged about a days worth of game play I feel I can write a decent enough review.
Having seen reviews saying Beyond Earth is a reskin of Civ V I can only repond with; and? Granted we have the same hexagon grid, the same combat, the same general premise of build and conquer. But that's not the point. What the point of Beyond Earth is is now instead of building a historic civilisation, you are now building the future. Yes, we can't chuckle at the historic ironies of Iroquois becoming a word superpower or India nuking you within an inch of your life because now we tread in uncharted territory and that is what I love about Beyond Earth. You are taking a group of people from Earth and building a civilisation that will not only stand the test of time but one that survives and survives well in an environment Humans aren't adapted to.
This game is different and subtly so. In Civ V it wouldn't matter where you are on the planet, with time and planning you could become powerful but the linear attribute of the Civ V tech tree meant that when you research something cutting edge your opponents are close behind. With Beyond Earth, where you and determines alot of what you do. The resources around you could determine what affinity path you go down or what strategy you have to employ either to work with what you have or get what you want.
Beyond Earth challenges you in ways Civ V never would. I now find myself having to think alot more in advance, not ony with technology but with unit placement as well. The additions of terrain features like canyons, miasma, craters, mixed in with mountains and the like can make for hellish playing fields. Do you force your way through dangerous terrain to get to your goals or do you go around? For instance, I want to take an alien nest nearby one of my cities. I tried to march through the miasma to get through but found more and more aliens as I went. My men were dying from repeated attacks and attrition so I pulled back, made a fortified position between the ocean and a canyon and sent combat rovers (cavalry) up and around the canyon range to come down and pincer the nest. What made me smile was another alien nest. I then had to change my strategy again.
Time and again I have been tested by the planets I land on and each time I have loved it. Beyond Earth is not a game where you stick to a tried and tested method of gameplay to win. It's a game where you have to be careful with your management and strategy, generally the wrong decision comes back and gives you a swift kick in the crown jewels. With happiness being replaced by health, a much harder resource to come by, this element of thinking ahead becomes much more apparent. You have to plan ahead what you need to research in order to get what you need for a heathy population but to steam roll straight to that tech you risk having less firepower or less production or less science. Again, Beyond Earth forces you to play a balancing act.
The civilisations of Beyond Earth, granted, do leave a lot to be desired. Generally, I find most civs to be friendly and amicable early to mid game. Maybe a bit needy once you get a few resources. I am also intrigued at what the great huge empire near me has done to make sure their cities with 10 or 11 population each aren't greatly unwell but then so am I when it comes to something similar in Civ V.
All in all, Beyond Earth is a good game that I highly recommend if you want that extra little aspect of strategy and challenge.

Will throw my 2cents out there, doesn't feel like another cashgrab. Anyone familiar with Life is Feudal should feel right at home. Swap the medieval theme for a sci-fi overtone and it's a similar experience.
For day 1 alpha, performance isn't wonderful but it's reasonable, hit a few random ctds though overall quite stable. Graphics look the part, could use a few more options for system scaling. Amazing soundtrack, both the music and fx work is topnotch. UI was readable and translated well, intuitive though further tweaks like multiple crafting slots would be great to cutdown on clicks required. Starting with little more then a knife and some blueprints, running into new tasks during gameplay tutorials popped up offering more information and further guidance.
Biggest issue for some will be running out of things to do. Anomalies appear which could be explored, offering rarer ingredients along with chests containing new blueprints. Fort building is implemented, no terraforming was available. Botany, Fishing, Harvesting and in-depth crafting is in. Only aggressive creatures I noticed were wolves, otherwise you'll be killing crabs, rabbits and deers. Something to keep in mind if wanting to play with friends is at the moment you cannot. Game is played in 'ghost' mode, effectively singleplayer that has all the server architecture in place. Also means a requirement to have an active internet connection. One EU server online, didn't notice any latency issues playing from Australia.
Looking for another survival rpg fix? Novus Inceptio is worth checking out or keeping shortlisted. Just understand it's early days and like most worth a damn (including ARK) they can often take a while to mature. Use a low-end system, expect to spend 10+hrs a day playing 'fresh content' or generally detest grinding? Might leave a little disappointed for now. Will tidyup this recommendation after more game time. Early copy was provided, never changes my thoughts. Cheers folks.

Final Fantasy XIII changes things up bigtime. Sure, your characters still attack and cast spells, but you don't have to pick them. Instead, for the most part, the battle takes place in a way that's more like a real time strategy game than a traditional RPG. You tell your character what role they play, and they go to it. You'd think the whole 'auto battle' option would make things easy, but you'd be wrong. Boss battles are tough of course, but even normal fights can get rough. You need to pay attention in most fights, and use some strategy. If you don't, you could easily die in even the simplest encounter. Fights happen fast, and speed is encouraged. You get better loot for fighting faster, so the game is constantly encouraging you to find the best combinations, and giving you a reason to do so. Final Fantasy XIII's battle system is by far the most inventive and most satisfying of any Final Fantasy. Honestly, I think the only way you can get an accurate gauge of whether this game is right for you or not is simply by playing it. Don't play for 3 hours and decide you don't like it, this is a game that gets exponentially better as time goes on, and it takes a full twelve hours to fully mature. if you're not sure about this game, give it a spin to make sure, but not until you have a whole free day.

I already spent few hours in this game as a part of alpha testing. The game is already fun as-is - with existing content and features. You will love the game if you like sandbox games - no mission, no quests, just opportunities to explore, scavenge, craft, build, survive - and build your own world. Beautiful graphics and catchy music will follow you on your expeditions. And challenging and slow crafting will make you think about every next step. Please be aware that the game is in a very early stage and so far it is singleplayer only - so the game did not demonstrate its full potential yet.
You definitely should try this game if you like survival sandbox games. You will like how difficult/complex/slow (choose by yourself) is to progress - which grants you many hours of fun in the game. On the other side - do not invest into the game if you expect some quick action, fast leveling or simple questing in style of "go there and bring/kill...". If you look for anything like that, wait until the MMO multiplayer is implemented. So stay tuned...

When I read the description for this game, I was super excited - it sounded like loads of fun. It's still ok - though I wish I had refunded, but I passed the limit. But it's an ok game, with a number of really annoying problems, let's mention the main ones.
1. Bugs -  the main one being if you either close down & open the game & or reload saves a few times causes pretty extensive lag so you have to close the game, sign out of windows & sign in again. It's not a horrible one, but annoying as hell. And it's also one that there's no way in hell they shouldn't have noticed in proper beta-testing. And I'm not running a bad machine, I have far above the capabilities of the recommended.
2. Really long & animated cutscenes before boss fights with no way of restarting the fight within the fight or after losing. Extremely annoying.
3. I'm not really sure what the game wants to be. An RPG? The battle is good I guess, but story development & characters is too flat. Most of the skills developments happens through a simulator type of thing. Would have been much better to run a regular RPG with the world-building they are doing. They say you can "choose the personalities" - not really. The amount of options you are given, at least as far as I got - pretty limited.
So, is it a decent game? Yes, it is. But it's making itself out to be a lot more. I'll say 5-6/10.

Get used to fighting with and against the same 3 factions again and again because the rest are not even viable anymore 80% of the time. The dev's warped idea of card rotations is give the same 4 factions over 10 new cards every expansion and give the other factions maybe 4 if you are lucky, or if you are really unlucky like sleeper players then just 1 new card that is kind of "meh" in comparison.
Instead of killing off the faction and the end of the rotation block like they should do, they instead kill off the older factions early by denying them any new cards save for maybe a pitiful amount which creates a power vaccum where 2-3 factions litterally have no reasonable counters to them.  As of this moment sleepers and exiles have a rediculously low amount of cards whereas warpath and genesis has almost triple the amount of cards than any other factions making them versitile for amost any situation, especially when the new cards they recieve every new expansion usually ends up outclassing the older cards. You're probably better off looking for a different card game.
And then there are the glitches. The game is full of glitches that have never been patched that pretty much break certain decks and make them harder to play. You can guess which factions experience the most glitches, it's pretty obvious from what I wrote above. That's not to say that the other factions don't have a large amount of glitches, but the amount of neglect the abandoned factions have let alone the game as a whole has is absurd. I have litteraly submitted  about a dozen obvious bugs for months and not a single one of them has ever been fixed to this day.

It starts off with a simple concept, then gradually adds layers of complexity for gameplay that is thought-provoking and challenging.  Many times, I found myself so angry at my stupid thumbs for making the same mistakes over and over until getting it right.  This game will frustrate gamers who fail to learn from their mistakes quickly.  Certain bosses (looking at you eyeball monster machine) cost me plenty of lives, and Teslagrad can be a bit unforgiving if you don't recognize patterns well.  Longer battles will turn into choreography before you succeed, but it's super gratifying when you do.
All in all, a fun game with nice hand-drawn graphics and visual storytelling.

The skeleton of the plot is, admittedly, pretty much pure sci-fi cliché, but the diversity of the crew, their interactions and their reactions to events (and life) flesh it out like just about no other game story I've seen.
It's not a huge game, but it felt the perfect length to me - I finished it in one very satisfying session.

There's a similar premise to Prey here, but it's a very different game. Just to clear up any preconceptions you might have.
That's not a bad difference though. Tacoma is a very very good game. There's not much "gameplay" - you don't shoot anything, or anything like that - but that gameplay is polished and smooth. Everything is easy to do, the UI or controls don't get in your way at all. There are a couple of very cool mechanics, as well, although I won't spoil them.
The real meat of Tacoma is the story. And boy, what a story. If you love SF like Blade Runner or The Expanse, or you're a fan of that wonderful genre of near-future SF literature, this is a game for you. Again, no spoilers, but don't try to speedrun this. Stick around for the story. It's not a long game anyway (that might be my only complaint) but that short time is well worth spending exploring and figuring every little bit out.

Teslagrad is a metroidvania style game in which you have to overcome hard puzzles and neat mechanics which reflect how magnets or electrons and protons work with each other.
You have the ability to use a gauntlet that you get at the beginning and the cloak later on to manipulate your or environments state. You can change your or a props colour into blue or red, which affects how you or the latter acts. If for example you toggle red cloak, you either get attracted to blue props or pushed away from red ones. Just like magnets. This has other, more complicated uses and plays a major role in solving puzzles and traveling around the tower.
You also get boots that you can blink with, which adds more depth to the game, since you can blink into cages, through fences and it's even used on bosses as part of a puzzle.
The puzzles themselves are pretty hard. They have that feeling, where you solve them for hours and when you finally find out how to do it, you think for yourself that the answer was in front of you all along. There aren't too many of them in the game, although, a single puzzle can take to around half an hour to complete.
The game puts you in the body of a child, so, naturally, you don't have the ability to fight the beings of the game. You also die in a single hit, which translates into a pretty hard experiance, to a level of something like Dark Souls.
It isn't a problem though, since the checkpoints in this game work very well, after death, most of the time teleporting you either to the start of the room or after some major point of a room, like a big, difficult puzzle.
With enemies, comes bosses. And bosses in this game are very imaginative and interesting. As I said, the protagonist doesn't have the ability to fight, so the bosses are "puzzles" in and of themselves.
There are no cutscenes and the story is not huge, although it is interestingly provided by giving the player a chance to visit rooms with a cardboard theater and watching a small performance. It is also somewhat vague, which means that most of what is seen can be interpreted differently and everyone can have a different take into the whole idea behind the game.
The game isn't long, packing only 5 hours of gameplay, which is not bad, because you wouldn't suffer from fatigue or boredom after completing the game, Also, the game being short also makes it worthwhile to speedrun.
The way the game looks has a touch of a clockwork artstyle. The game is atmospheric, well drawn.The music is nice, but nothing too impressive. That's also a good thing, because you won't get too distracted while going around doing puzzles.
Teslagrad is a hidden gem that everyone should experiance and I feel bad that it was out of my radar for so long. Although, as I follow the rule of 1 dollar=1 hour, I would just wait for it to go down to at least 5 euros, other than that, the game is totally worth getting.

This was the first Hitman game I've played, and I really enjoyed it. It reminded me of an R rated Splinter Cell Conviction. It generally wants to be a stealth game, but you can also have fun running and gunning if you get spotted or just want to get through a level quicker.  The stealth aspects are fun and generally not frustrating.  You can disguise as different people to get to certain places unnoticed, you can hide bodies, etc.  Most levels have several different very creative ways to get through them.  You could just shoot your mark, but maybe you'd like to poison their sushi?  The graphics are good, the voice acting is great, the plot is fairly straightforward - it might have been better or worse if I knew some history of the Hitman games, but as a newcomer, it worked.  It took me about 12 hrs to beat, but there is tons of replay value.  Fist, every level has mutliple ways to beat it, with little mini awards for each.  Then there are several difficulties which change the gameplay significantly - for example on easy you can go into "super spy no one can see me" mode unlimited.  Finally there are "contracts" which are mini levels created by other players... Think "HORSE" in basketball, but with assassinations.  Great game, def worth checking out when on sale.

Good storytelling requires technique and content; The Stanley Parable has plenty of the former, but none of the latter.
The biggest gimmick of the Stanley Parable is that the game is very self aware, with copious amounts of fourth wall breaking and self-referential narration. There's also a very liberal dose of "lol so random" content as evidenced by the name of the game's achievements. What sets SP apart (not in a good way) is that while other games I've played used these devices sparingly for getting a few chuckles here and there, SP takes the ideas way too far and makes the entire game simply about pointing out that it is self aware. What I got out of the game is that it's using literary and storytelling devices for pointing out the fact that it's using these devices.
As for cleverness, there really isn't that much. All computer games must respond based on the user's input. This one just does so in very peculiar ways (e.g. "are you doing that just for the achievement?), which falls into the "lol so random" territory once more. While I really like that type of humor, it's just not executed well at all, and simply having it does not automatically make the content amusing.
Finally, there's certainly an air of hype surrounding this game, which is somewhat funny; because while I couldn't really figure out what kind of parable this game is supposed to be, the parable it does remind me of is The Emperor's New Clothes.

INK has the potential to be a fun game but it has a bunch of design and technical problems that just drag it down.
The game is basically a Super Meatboy clone, down to some mechanics like homing missile launchers and keycages blocking progression, and I mean its the same cage graphic. The main draw of the game, the thing that makes it different, is that it takes Meatboy's blood splatters and it makes them the way you reveal the levels, because every level is completely invisible when you start playing it. And to be honest I don't understand what its trying to do with it, when you die the level stays colored, so it's just meant to make you die to stuff you cant see a couple of times before you have a regular meatboy level, hardly very impactful other than making you complete half the level before killing you and saying "Complete it again now". That's okay I guess, its still fun to color the level.
My main grip comes with the technical problems: The game's air controls. Now, if you're gonna copy meatboy (which this game pretty blatantly does) then you gotta understand that what made that game so good is that the controls are incredibly responsive. INK's controls are inconsistent, when youre on the ground you stick to it, theres no sliding, you stop on a dime, but when you jump in the air the controls turn incredibly floaty, you lose a lot of maneurability, and taht wouldnt be too hard to get used to, but every time you doublejump you get a small boost of speed that throws you off, and when you bounce off enemies the same thing happens, you you gotta predict these things way before you decide to jump to another platform or youre gonna get pushed off the edge by the boost. The unresponsibe controls make what should be a fun platformer incredibly frustrating.
Other than that, theres no options menu, so if you want to mute the rather boring music you might as well do it from the windows audio mixer.
I can't really recommend this game, it's 5 bucks but I got it off a humble bundle so if you happen to find a good offer like that give it a shot, its just a very frustrating and unpolished platforming experience, but at least it looks nice.

Freedom fall shares a lot in common with other platformers that are meant to be difficult to the point of driving you insane. However It is very toned down in difficulty compared to other games I have played which feels like it misses the point.
The main goal is to escape a tower by reaching the bottom. This means most of your movement is falling through the air, hence the title. As you progress through the tower you can buy new gadgets changing the way you play. For me the double jump gadget is immensely more useful and ended up being my main method of moving around. Although some of the sections can get difficult, for the most part I made it passed many traps without even blinking. There are multiple paths through most of the levels which are clearly marked as easy or hard. I took both types throughout the game and for the most part didn't find any path particularly more difficult than the others. There are also numerous checkpoints scattered through each level making the times when you do die much less frustrating. The last boss is actually in my opinion easier than the rest of the game which was a little disappointing.
The game does control very well and each gadget is easy to use. The variety of traps is also nice.It was rare that I felt a death wasn't my fault. Even the swimming mechanics manage to be as little of a burden as possible.
The art is very nice and each level has just enough variety to make it feel different than the last level. The antagonist also leaves messages painted all over the walls which tell the story and can sometimes be pretty funny. The music is excellent and makes the game feel a bit more intense with its electric guitar.
My one big gripe is not the difficulty but the length. The game has only around 10 levels and because it isn't incredibly difficult can be beaten in a couple hours; if that. It does have various challenges you can go for on each stage increasing the replayability a bit. Many of them however, I obtained without even trying. After my first play-through I already had around half of them.
In conclusion this game is a great introduction to unforgiving platformers but may not be enough to interest those who are looking for a real challenge. The presentation is very nice and the controls are very tight, I just wished there was a bit more to♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.

I want to like Beyond Earth. I really do.
As someone who continues to load and play SMAC on a regular basis, I've wanted a follow-up since 1999.
I recognized from the outset that Civ: BE was NOT going to be SMAC 2 but... it's barely even a Civ game.
Generally, follow up games in a series will either have *more* features or, failing that, the features that exist will have been streamlined to some degree.
This trend does not hold true for BE. The game plays identically to Civ V with the notable exception of a greatly stripped down city-state system, happiness system, cultural system and diplomatic system.
Affinity, while seeming to be a unique concept in theory, does not reflect your gameplay choices at all. Rather, you choose which affinity you want and "purchase" it with research. The way you actually play and interact with the planet has no impact on your affinity level, quite counter-intuitively.
As a result, Affinity is nothing more than a meaningless measurement of what tech level you are at.
About the best thing they added was an enhanced covert ops system but even *that* has some glaring issues in the form of rushed city takeover.
All in all, I'd wait for the inevitable DLC that will make BE into something more than the forgettable waste it is now.

My take on all of this.
Does this game equate Civ 5? No. It is not as good as Civ 5, but please bear in mind that Civ 5 also has 2 expansions that drastically improved the game. This game IS in fact good, miles better than Civ 5 on launch, but it does not have enough new content to make up for the stuff it removed. Forget about the funny military advisor, World Congress, Religion, interesting leaders, Era progression, and the statistics at the end of the game. Say hello to a highly improved espionage system, a nice affinity system, SATELITES (this is really interesting), and a barebones quest system. Frankly I don't think it makes up for everything, but it is a good start.
This game relies heavily on the Civ 5 formula so if you didnt like that, you wont like this. Health system is somewhat broken and highly punishing. Think of it as happiness. It is considerably harder to maintain it in the positives as there arte no luxury resources nor "WE LOVE THE KING DAY". It kind of makes it pointless to trade with AI if you already have what you need strategically and there are costly technologies to improve health. Do yourself a city and don't settle more than 3-4 cities early on in the game.
To sum things up, the game pretty much plays like a sci-fi Civ V witha few new twists. It is a good addition for the franchise, but it needs more charm and content (did I mention there are only EIGHT civilizations this time?). All in all, it is worth a buy, but I would recommend waiting for a price drop. Try the demo first.

Incredibly short but well worth the $1.99 / 6 paid for the bundle price I paid.
I would recommend the game under normal circumstances because it is somewhat well built with destructive buildings, etc.. but there are a lot of issues that leave something to be desired...
The negatives are:
- The ai is terrible on all levels from Story, Easy +, etc.. ( They look at you through walls and start shooting holes through solid concrete walls to target you ); they need a slight modification so when someone comes into their field-of-view they have a slight delay ( hesitation based on target recognition to determine friend-foe ) before firing, or not..
- The "toggle" Objectives button isn't a toggle despite trying different keys ( such as caps lock, tab, etc.. )
- In addition to the objectives "toggle" switch not working, when you hold a button down to keep the results up ( also so you can see where your character is ) it turns itself off when entering / exiting vehicles among other circumstances.
- The player character is easy to lose; the camera system isn't intuitive.
- The camera system is absolutely is disgusting. It moves more to the top-right than bottom-left making it hard to aim ( while enemies can shoot at you when you can't see them meaning you end up needing to use the compass to line up the shots ) and it's easy for the crosshair to get lost in the effects ( because the crosshair is one color which doesn't negate on like-colors ).
- Driving is sluggish and non-responsive - also armored vehicles seem to blow up when side paneling is shot.
- Buildings don't seem to collapse after destroying all supports.
- Vehicle lighting can't be changed.. ie what the ai leaves you with is what you get.
- You can't drive 99% of vehicles; the doors have to be open to drive them ( ie cop cars, armored, etc but civilian cars are off limits )
If these would be fixed, it'd be an entertaining game.
Some positives:
- Everything is essentially destructable.. Buildings, trees, poles, etc..
- Decent weapon balance for a flat-plane shooter ( ie assume all shots are body / center-mass shots ) with some targets taking more shots to take down based on armor and range.
- Vehicle damage looks nice from what small bit I could see; it looked like the pole indented the hood as it should but these may be pre-fabbed and unimpressive ( stuck it in pros to give benefit of the doubt for the limited time viewing the game )
It's worth a look if you get it on sale. I was able to find it on Indie for $1.99 in a bundle of 6 or so games.

Teslagrad is a beautiful puzzle platformer, with a very interesting story told solely by images (there's not a single spoken nor written word in the game.) The gameplay is solid, the art is wonderful, and the game itself can get challenging yet never impossible.
The start might be a little confusing, as it does not tell you anything. You start off just running from your home in the town Teslagrad towards the tower, because you're being chased for some reason. Once at the tower you will get your "weapon" and the game actually starts there. Using the power of electricity you will go through the tower to unravel the history of it and Teslagrad, solving electricity based puzzles to progress, finding upgrades to help you further on. Every so often you will come across a theater that will show you more of the story, explaining what is going on and why you're there.
The game is metroidvania style, where you sometimes have to backtrack once you get a new powerup, so you can get objects you couldn't get before. This only is needed a few times though, and most of the game is straightforward. There are hardly any enemies in the overworld, most of it is puzzlebased, but the few bosses you will encounter make up for the lack of enemies and are probably the biggest challenge of the game, besides some of the hidden scrolls you could find.
The achievements are linked to each hidden scroll you can collect, and the 36 scrolls complete the story in a tarot deck style. If you want the full story, you have to find all 36 scrolls, and that will also open up the true ending. Some of these can be very hard to find, or really tricky to obtain.
My main complaint is that the game is too short for me. I would have loved it to be twice as big. I 100% the game in less than 10 hours, so I don't feel like I got the worth out of the full price. But at any discount it becomes worth it to get it, and at 75% off (summer 2016 sale) it's a steal!

INK has the potential to be a fun game but it has a bunch of design and technical problems that just drag it down.
The game is basically a Super Meatboy clone, down to some mechanics like homing missile launchers and keycages blocking progression, and I mean its the same cage graphic. The main draw of the game, the thing that makes it different, is that it takes Meatboy's blood splatters and it makes them the way you reveal the levels, because every level is completely invisible when you start playing it. And to be honest I don't understand what its trying to do with it, when you die the level stays colored, so it's just meant to make you die to stuff you cant see a couple of times before you have a regular meatboy level, hardly very impactful other than making you complete half the level before killing you and saying "Complete it again now". That's okay I guess, its still fun to color the level.
My main grip comes with the technical problems: The game's air controls. Now, if you're gonna copy meatboy (which this game pretty blatantly does) then you gotta understand that what made that game so good is that the controls are incredibly responsive. INK's controls are inconsistent, when youre on the ground you stick to it, theres no sliding, you stop on a dime, but when you jump in the air the controls turn incredibly floaty, you lose a lot of maneurability, and taht wouldnt be too hard to get used to, but every time you doublejump you get a small boost of speed that throws you off, and when you bounce off enemies the same thing happens, you you gotta predict these things way before you decide to jump to another platform or youre gonna get pushed off the edge by the boost. The unresponsibe controls make what should be a fun platformer incredibly frustrating.
Other than that, theres no options menu, so if you want to mute the rather boring music you might as well do it from the windows audio mixer.
I can't really recommend this game, it's 5 bucks but I got it off a humble bundle so if you happen to find a good offer like that give it a shot, its just a very frustrating and unpolished platforming experience, but at least it looks nice.

I just finished the story, and wow. Tacoma is a great game. Just like in Gone Home, Fullbright's previous game, the enticing aspect of Tacoma is learning the story of the setting you're in at whatever pace that suits you.
You're a contractor who sets out to recover data from what is now an abandoned space station, but in between large, time-consuming data transfers, you're exploring the station; unlocking various scenes which play out before you with Augmented Reality implants. You are given many opportunities to get to know the previous inhabitants of the station, and taking the time to meander through the conversations, the data logs, the letters, baubles, and wordless scenes is was makes this game come to life. It is well worth the ~3 hours it takes to play the game and become fully immersed in a futuristic world.
The puzzles take a back seat to the story, and don't hinder the natural progression of it at all. They were easier than in Gone Home, and the lack of clutter in a sterile space station makes it easier to spot items that could potentially be used to solve puzzles, or to learn a new thing about the world.
The voice acting was amazing. Some parts nearly brought me to tears. Some parts were fun and light-hearted. All of it made me feel. And that's all I ask for in a story.

I picked this game up cause 1) I liked 'Firewatch' a ton and have discovered that I like walking/story-type games quite a bit, and 2) I got a 33%-off coupon on Steam.
I started and completed my first playthrough of the game one evening ago.
Things I liked:
- The story was great
- The scenery was wonderful, with a consistency of style and design that is refreshing in newer games
- The play controls were pretty great when using keyboard + mouse (once I got some issues sorted out, see below)
- Story is pretty engrossing
- Cast of characters is interesting
Things I didn't like:
- Control issues. I don't have a controller plugged in, but had to zero out controller X and Y sensitivity in the settings to keep my view where I wanted it instead of just spinning in place
- Lack of character development. I wanted MORE, but that ties into the next point
- Super-short game!
About the length of the game...I do not think the game was worth the original $19.99 asking price, but the 33% off doesn't make me feel too bad for finishing a $14 game in two and a half hours. My playthrough was pretty thorough---I read everything, learned everything, accessed everything, and unlocked everything---so someone that just wanted to finish the game could probably come in way under that time. I wish there was more to do with this game, but there's just not a lot here. I believe I've played demos for other games that lasted longer than this full game.

Honestly finishing my playthrough in Civ:BE has to be one of the most bland experiences i had in a civilization game. It was mostly just "city building" and getting to know the new techs etc, while searching through the ugly UI for infos.
Ah yes, and clicking tedious trading routes again and again, as well as always the same stupid diplomatic null messages of some very generic leaders, which were already annoying in CiV.
I had no war or any great interaction with other civs (except against those pesky aliens, which always pop up if you leave some empty space - which is unavoidable on the "borders"), the AI just kept begging me, mixed with the occasional dennounciation (hopping from friendly to guarded back and forth).
Empire building is limited due to the "health" factor (was happiness in CiV), which annoyingly begins to deteriorate already after your second or at least third city.
Much is similiar to CiV, but with a worse overview for the player or/and less variety.
For example you only have around five standard unit types, mixed in with up to three or so special types for your kind of specialization. The units also get small extras for your "affinity", blocking the other types at the same time.
The affinity specialisation also contributes a big part to which victory condition you can fulfill.
Sadly these conditions (as is much of the whole techtree) are hard to differentiate and just have a bad overview imo.
This is especially sad since the affinity, combined with the quest system and the possibility/requirement to focus your tech research are the main new gameplay elements imo. There also is a new orbit view in which you can use different satellites, but i honestly found them mostly useless.
So, in the end, you have a CiV 1.5 in space, with a terrible UI and interface, a few new elements, many old ones (sadly also the annoying ones).. and - for me at least - much tedious work, instead of fun gameplay.
Will keep watching this game (especially if the modders, once again, can rescue a game), but can´t see me playing it again in the near future.. which really is a shame for a civilisation game.
ps: yes, and the ai movement still sucks too...

Good storytelling requires technique and content; The Stanley Parable has plenty of the former, but none of the latter.
The biggest gimmick of the Stanley Parable is that the game is very self aware, with copious amounts of fourth wall breaking and self-referential narration. There's also a very liberal dose of "lol so random" content as evidenced by the name of the game's achievements. What sets SP apart (not in a good way) is that while other games I've played used these devices sparingly for getting a few chuckles here and there, SP takes the ideas way too far and makes the entire game simply about pointing out that it is self aware. What I got out of the game is that it's using literary and storytelling devices for pointing out the fact that it's using these devices.
As for cleverness, there really isn't that much. All computer games must respond based on the user's input. This one just does so in very peculiar ways (e.g. "are you doing that just for the achievement?), which falls into the "lol so random" territory once more. While I really like that type of humor, it's just not executed well at all, and simply having it does not automatically make the content amusing.
Finally, there's certainly an air of hype surrounding this game, which is somewhat funny; because while I couldn't really figure out what kind of parable this game is supposed to be, the parable it does remind me of is The Emperor's New Clothes.

Your weapon arsenal while on the ship consists of mortars, fire barrels, swivel guns, chain shots, broadside and chase cannons, heavy shots and a ram. You can attack any ship that isn't an ally. Once the ship is weakened you may board it or sink it and take its loot. Infinity Wars is an excellent card game. Those who like games like Magic and Hearthstone will likely enjoy this free game noting similarities in gameplay.
There are 8 factions cards can be a part of but you generally have 1-3 of these types in your deck so the game doesn't try to limit you to specific cards from only one faction. Each faction has a certain advantage and style to the way the cards are. Personally my favourites are the Sleepers of Avarrach (zombies), Warpath (powerful beasts), Exiles (unpredictable demons) and Cult of Verore (Spell focused).
Cards can have specific advantages like Charge, Flying, Reach, and special abilities which make the game interesting. Like most games of this manner, the goal is to reduce the opponent's health to zero by attacking their fortress directly, but you can also win by reducing the opponent's morale by killing many of his/her cards. This adds a variety of ways to play and no game is ever really the same.
There is a shorter to medium length campaign that is relatively interesting. They did only have it for 4 of the factions but added 2 more which leads me to assume they will make 2 more for the remaining factions. New players can get cards through the campaign and you can get more cards by
a) signing in daily
b) leveling up
c) buying them in the shop using in-game currency or real money
There are tons of cards to collect so don't worry about collecting them all and having nothing left to do.
After campaign there isn't too much to do besides online battles. However, there is a decent online community and finding a match for me has ranged from 20 seconds to 4 minutes. There is some options online however I have only done constructed battles. It is completely random I believe because I have ended up playing against people way better than me with very rare cards and also against people not that good. Expect anyone playing online to have completed campaign and to be somewhat skilled. The cool thing about online is that you can use any deck you want (as long as it is legal) so there is unlimited replayability.
For someone who isn't very good at the strategy and just enjoys collecting cards, making a deck, and trying to win with it, this game is very fun and although not always forgiving, not overly hard to get a win here and there to keep it fun.

Freedom Fall is a pretty looking game that seems to involve… falling for your freedom. And it doesn’t disappoint, the game is an exquisitely crafted, easy on the eyes, smooth platformer in which you escape from death row by navigating an ever perilous descent out of a deadly tower.
Really, this game is pretty. Perhaps because I have been playing some games that have been disregarding graphics lately but I really enjoyed the visuals in Freedom Fall. The towering heights, the deadly spikes and spinning blades, the cloudy backgrounds, and best of all the graffiti scrawled around the tower. You’re treated to some equally impressive visuals if you make it to the bottom and looking around at this fantastical world.
So the justice system in this strange world involves locking people up in insanely high towers and then giving them the option to wait in their cell and be executed or attempt to find freedom by navigating a fairly suicidal descent. It’s a brilliant premise and I really am almost gushing at how brilliantly the story is told in this game. Developers and game designers take some notes here! A way to tell a fairly deep and engrossing story without heavy handed cut scenes or dialogue boxes and never interrupting the flow of game-play.
The princess in the tower is not some damsel in distress that needs rescuing nor a helpful guide that you might think she is at first. No she is a monstrous, murderous, malevolent creature who has designed this mad death trap for her own amusement. Although you’ve thrown a wrench into her intricate mechanism by your uncanny ability to resurrect quickly after each of your painful deaths. I guess that’s why you got locked up to begin with, stealing (or being framed for stealing) the elixir of life, making you immortal.
You might be immortal but there’s plenty of ways to send you back to the nearest resurrection shrine throughout your descent. The variety of deadly traps is quite impressive with spikes, blades, scythes, flames, fireballs, water, electricity, killer mechanical shark, and a dragon all out to kill you. The levels keep coming at you with more and more challenges but it’s not so frantic and unforgiving that you want to quit. The best feature is the game quickly resurrecting you, not wasting time on monotonous death scenes or loading screens and instead throws you right back into the action to try again when you fail. And you will fail a lot. A LOT!
The only problem I really have with the game is it’s short length. Once you’ve gotten used to the various death traps and mastered the upgrades you’re fighting the final boss and then it’s over. Taking my time I beat the game in a little over an hour, then played again trying to go faster and beat it in under 50 minutes. Despite it’s short length and price tag though I was really satisfied by this game. It is highly concentrated goodness that delivers. Better to make a really good short game than a really long, drawn out, bad game.
I recommend if you pick this game up to go slow your first time, read all the notes from the princess, the story that is told is really worth it. Then after you beat the game once, try again going as fast as you can for some extra challenge. I got a nice thrill testing my blade avoiding parkour skills as I tried to beat the game a third time as fast as possible while trying to die as few times as possible. And with a built in leader board you can compare your skills with all of the internet for bragging rights. I can understand not wanting to pay the full price for a game that can be completed in under an hour but at its current 35% off sale it’s definitely worth it!
Final Score:
Graphics: 9/10
Game Play: 9/10
Music / Ambiance: 8/10
Story: 9/10
Value: 5/10
Overall: 8/10

The game itself is amazing. It's a bold deviation from the norm in the Final Fantasy series, and I commend them for that. Unfortunately, for someone who has played the original version on Playstation 3 for hours on end, I can't bring myself to reccommend this version to anyone. This is an insult to us Final Fantasy fans.
FINAL FANTASY XIII PC is whittled with bugs, crashes, and graphical glitches. Not to mention the annoying frame skipping despite them unlocking the framerate from 30 to 60 fps. It is also locked at a measly 720p, which for those of you with 1366x768 monitors shouldn't be that noticeable. However my monitor is at 1920x1080, and the image gets blown way up, making details look fuzzy. Now, normally, this wouldn't be much of an issue for me. I don't really care about resolution as long as the game is playable. But what's annoying is the constant pauses and frame skips that the game does, cutscene or not. I have an NVIDIA GTX Titan Black Edition + Intel Core i7 Extreme OC @4.8 GHz combo (In other words, FAR superior to the reccommended requirements) so I should not be getting frame skips on any game whatsoever, much less this one. There are zero (count them) ZERO graphical options to lower or raise the quality of any part of the game to increase or lessen the load on your PC. The movement in this version is a tad wonky as well, making your character jerk from animation to animation whenever you move. Some npc's will randomly disappear and the mouse controlled camera is... something left to be desired. Top that with the numerous crashes, for 60 GB and 15 bucks, this is not worth your time.
There aren't many positive points, but one that I would consider a plus is the Japanese voiceovers. I watch anime regularly, and listening to the cast speak in their native language is rather refreshing for me. Another plus is someone is already working on a patch for this game to get 1080p and hopefully fix some of the bugs and frameskips.
So I would wait until a patch comes out to address these issues before buying this game. The game itself is amazing, as I've said before. But this version... I'm sorely disappointed in Square-Enix. They're far better than this. Yet it seems they've gotten lazy lately.

So I have put roughly 3 hours so far into the game. I recommend this IF you don't mind that the game is locked on resolution as well as framerate. I personally don't care A LOT about it being locked at 720p. I have noticed many of the negative reviews here revolve around that particular issue. Granted also, you may have to tweak your graphic options slightly depending on what you use (nvidia/amd/intel etc). So will you have to mess around a bit to make the game run perfectly regardless if you're using a godly computer or a low-budget setup? Yes. If you're not willing to put a little extra effort into making the game run properly, then do NOT buy this unless an official patch gets released later to fix said problems. Make no mistake, this is a badly done port but by no means impossible to play and enjoy.
If you are happy being able to play the game smoothly regardless of definition, then this should work out fine for you. If you are very adamant about having your flawless hi-defintion and auto-optimized settings, then stay FAR away from this. This is also under the assumption that you meet the recommended settings to run this game. My own computer surpasses the recommended and sure enough, it runs fine (after I did some tweaking in my nvidia control panel). It is also worth mentioning that you may experience "stuttering" at a consistent interval. While I can't speak for everyone, this was fixed for me by simply plugging in a wired xbox 360 controller (which you don't actually have to use, you can just set it aside after plugging it in). If anyone is curious to the programming aspect behind this, in simplest terms, the game is "searching" for a compatible device nonstop hence the stutter you may experience. The controller is the "missing" device the game is looking for. Again, this just further supports how poorly done this is as a pc port.
Now in my 3 hours of gameplay, I haven't noticed any big problems either. I know some have mentioned something about missing audio, or random crashes, etc etc. Maybe I'm just lucky and haven't experienced any of that YET? Time will tell. IF I do experience any major problems like that, I will update this review. Otherwise, this is where I stand in my review. The game is perfectly playable which for me is always the deciding the factor.

Blockstorm is a blocky and cartoony FPS game with a wide variety of maps, gamemodes, guns and other awesome features. The game is great with fantastic workshop creations made everyday. This game comes with a map editor and a weapon customizer which allows you to create your own very personal beasty looking gun, or if you're feeling lazy to make a weapon. You can pick and download from the thousands of already created weapon skins in the workshop so you can show off in battles! There's also a character creation tool fitted within the game so you're able to upload your character to the workshop! This means you are aloud full customization. So if you want to be a Pope with a giant pink RPG then you can sure as hell do that! Also, almost EVERYTHING is destroyable.
So Blockstorm is a fun game you can't say it isn't. However the thing wrong with it is, it's very repetative. It's missing something that adds something interesting to the game. So far it's just spawn in, kill, die respawn that's it. There's no leveling, upgrading, unlocking at all which is quite sad. It would make the game more interesting and would give the player something to work towards. The only time when you are going to have fun and ignore that the game is lacking fun features is when you play with 3 or more friends. That's when things get highly enjoyable and worth playing.
In my opinion the price is perfect for what this game has to offer. It's not much. So if you and your buds have $5 in your bank/steam wallet and are looking for a fun game to hang out in. I will recommend this game. There's a huge amount of maps which you're able to download to have even more fun in.

- Difficult character model editing (might want to check some tutorial vids on youtube towards that.)

Tacoma captures all the thrill of the audiolog gameplay from BioShock and combines it with all the gameplay of Gmail!
OK, that's a bit harsh, but that's about what you get here. You'll be walking around a space station, watching some replays, reading some e-mail and walking some more. The game, from start to finish, is pretty short. My time says nearly 4 hours, but I may have left it paused for a bit - it didn't feel like it took nearly that long.
The premise - figuring out what happened to the 6 or so inabitants of this space station - is a bit of a mystery, although maybe that's pushing it a bit as the only real mystery concerns their final fate.
The graphics and environment is top-notch. If I had a VR headset, I'd probably give this game a shot in VR - it seems well-made for it.
The plot itself is a bit run-of-the-mill for space station "mysteries" - no new ground is tread here. It's a touch of 2001 with a touch of Alien but I don't want to give the impression there's any action or thriller aspects - there is not. Most of the interest comes from interpersonal relationships, but you never really get too deep into these peoples' lives. The most interesting story - that of the doctor who had a bit of a troubled experience - would make for an interesting tale on its own, but it's not touched upon here to the depth that I would have liked.
One interesting side note: the station features 6 people. Of those, 3 people are gay. The game is not remotely subtle about this. Combine that with the frequent notes, posters and e-mails about workers unionizing and a lot of social issues get ticked off on the checklist. It did feel a bit ham-fisted in this regard.
All told, a quick, light story set in a gorgeous environment. Recommended for walking simulator aficionados: 4 out of 5.

I played for a little over 3 hours, seeing most of the obvious content and being reasonably thorough in exploring the environment. This feels like the perfect length - any more and you'd had to spin the plots out much, much more. This makes it a similar proposition to "Gone Home", but it's different enough to be worth exploring as well.
It's a nice self-contained story in a self-contained environment. Well worth the playthrough.

Teslagrad can be referred as a soft 2D platformer of Dark Souls. Hard, but rewarding. It has most if not all basic qualities that define worth-playing game. Good art, interesting puzzle mechanic and decent soundtracks that match the situation.
The game is pretty challenging for platformer, and there's no difficulty setting, so one for all pain. Unless you're a seasoned veteran, you'll die alot since one hit from enemy or dangerous objects will kill your character. Thankfully the checkpoint is usually saved at the beginning of each room, so even when you die doing a puzzle again and again you don't need to backtrack alot. There's a problem with some incredibly hard to think puzzles that I had to resort to video walkthrough to find the solution, and of course the bosses' mechanics are quite challenging - you need to build the bosses' attack patterns in your memory and adapt to it. Overall, game mechanic can be frustrating, though, and annoying, but when you beat it you'll feel satisfaction.
This game mechanic and platformer genre in general require gamepad. It's not necessary, but you'll be thankful if you use one. Xinput is supported natively so you'll have no problem with most gamepads. For Dinput, as always, you can use x360ce. The controls can be awkward and take some training first, but if you can't keep up with default settings, there's an In-game function to remap key assignments.
Teslagrad as a product seems polished, it even has Linux + Mac builds. When I played the game I found no issue, no crash, no weird stutter or game breaking bug.
If you like Puzzle Platformer genre, go ahead and pick up Teslagrad.
Thoroughly enjoyed!

I am overall quite happy with this game. The game delivers exactly what it advertises: the chance to tame and ride into combat on a large variety of mythical creatures. The storyline is at least as good as any other generic RPG, and I quite enjoy the combat and gameplay mechanics.
Here are the biggest pros and cons as far as I'm concerned:
Pros:
Fairly immersive gameplay
Engaging story
Tame the mount that suits you
Dragons! :) (lots of them)
Good game mechanics
Some really great and helpful players
Cons:
The game still has some kinks to work out. One of the biggest is trying to attack or collect across the edge of a "chunk" of the world. It can tell you it's "Out of Range" when you're standing right on top of it, and you'll need to change your angle a bit to make it work.
The amount of gold buyers has really exploded the game economy - it can be a little tricky to keep up on the AH or in-game trading if you don't buy gold (which may or may not be against the ToS). Doesn't impact actual gameplay that much.
Like any other MMO, many of the players can be a bit elitist and snobbish at times. Don't hold that against the game though.
So overall I am happy to recommend this game. If you like MMOs, mounted combat, picking your mount from a wide variety of creatures, and an action-based combat system, this game is for you.

Freedom Fall is a down-scrolling indie platformer set in a very tall prison tower. You are a prisoner who is trying find your way down to the bottom of the tower through all the traps set up by a twisted princess. The goal is to get your freedom back by escaping the tower.
The writings on the walls in the tower are funny and drives the story forward as you get to know more about the princess. If you are any kind of fan of the platformer genré then you should definitively try to pick this game up. The game is for Windows and Mac which is always nice and the replay value of the game is pretty good since you can try to improve your scores and times for the levels. As far as I'm aware there are two different endings you can get decided by which way you go in the tower.
At the time of writing this review the achievements are glitched but I'm sure they will fix that soon[EDIT: They have indeed fixed it]. The menu screen is good and you can have a few different save files. I personally like the art style and level design in this game and these kind of games are right up my alley. The game has full controller support but I haven't had time to try it out with a controller yet and the keyboard controls work just fine.
Another part of this game that I enjoyed was that you can choose between harder platforming and easier platforming.
The harder platforming rewards you with more cogs than in the easier parts, cogs which are the in-game currency that you can use to buy equipment like a pair of dragon wings or a glider. As the game progresses it gets harder but even if you aren't very good at platformer games it shouldn't get too hard and it is not a game that frustrates you as for example Super Meat Boy.
As a conclusion I would like to say that I recommend this game with all my heart even though it is a bit short but as I stated above the game has good enough replay value for me to still really recommend it for anyone who is looking for a good time. The music is nice and fitting for the game and there are also trading cards which everyone always seem to like :)

INK is a fast-paced platformer that comes across more frustrating than fun.
It showcases a fun idea of revealing a level as you play through it, forcing you to be careful but also keep moving. It also feels a lot like Super Meat Boy, since after every death you're put right back into the action without any death-downtime.
It features fun level design and challenges but is brought down by it's slidey and imprecise controls, which instantly take you out of the precise and fast-paced environment of the overall game.

Each level can be completed in multiple ways, though it requires such precision and care, you can forget doing it on your first attempt. Or second. Or third, for that matter. It's like one of those old arcade games, where the slightest mistake, your fault or not, will cause it to become a bloodbath.
The beauty of the older games was that it was a sandbox. You could complete the level in the way you wanted. You could put on a disguise and become a GOD. Disguises now serve next to no purpose since anybody with a similar outfit will be able to recognise you.
The graphics are nice and some of the levels have that same old Hitman magic (the ones where people don't just shoot you on sight). However, the game is far too frustrating to play properly. If you want to reach the end of the game, expect to give up and shoot everybody in some of the missions, or to be at this game for months replaying every level hundreds of times before you learn and perfect the exact route that works.
If anybody doesn't know what to expect from a Hitman game, you have to kill certain people and you get a better score if you do it secretly or make it look like an accident. The levels are large and semi-open-ended, with lots of NPCs and pointless but fun details. If you want to know what all the fuss is about, try Blood Money, which is a really good game and has aged wonderfully. This game, on the other hand, was dated in its style before it was even released. Oh and there's no such thing as the colour black in this game, since it's always smeared with a filter. Sometimes it makes it look very cinematic, other times it's downright annoying. But that could be ignored if the gameplay itself wasn't so perfectly flawed.

Hitman: Absolution. 9/10.
This game was absolutely fantastic! Though, in honesty, I really didn't like it at first. When I bought it I was really expecting a classic Hitman game, despite all the reviews I'd seen saying it was nothing like it. I wanted to give it a try anyway, being a Hitman fan and all. At first, it was difficult to get used to because I did see that it was nothing like previous Hitman games. I found I was rarely using disguises and instead sneaking around a lot more while wearing my suit. Evidence to suggest that this game wants you to sneak is the cover system. Simply put, it's the best cover system I've used in a game. It was tailor made for the game, so if it was used in another game it might not be as great. The maps of the game are also quite different, and at first quite annoying. You'd have to make your way through a number of areas completing objectives (not assassinating people) before you got to your target to kill them. At first I thought this was annoying, as I felt like I was never actually a hitman... But then I started thinking of it as GETTING to your target to kill them. In previous games, you'd just appear in a map, kill the target, then leave, but in Absolution it's letting you play the part of getting into that area. Granted, maps were a lot larger in previous games, but this sort of linear way of getting to your targets almost worked with that frame of mind.
Overall, though, I didn't see this as a Hitman game as such, and that was mostly because of the sneaking, not much assassination and linear progression. Instead, this game told a story. And a great story at that! You'd have to be a Hitman fan to let it impact you the way it impacted me, and I loved it. Seeing past all the non-Hitman characteristics and focusing on telling the story made the game fantastic, and it was at the final moment of the game where I started to think that this is the best game I've played in a long time.

For 15 bucks it's an older AAA title with the option to play undubbed.  Generally speaking, that alone is probably worth the 15 dollars.  The port itself is fine, although limited compared to standard PC games.  As you see everywhere it is graphically locked but there are 3rd party plugins to work around this.  I haven't had any stutter or graphical issues with standard settings or with mods in place.
As for the game itself, it is a great RPG with a very deep battle system if you get far enough.  The full battle system, jobs, upgrades for weapons, etc unlocks throughout the game and many people who think you can finish the game with just auto-attack have not gotten that far into the game at all.  Battles are focused on more strategically picking jobs on the fly and having solid paradigms set up for the characters that are currently in the party.  Yes, you can let the game choose what spells work "best" against a particular target, but honestly that doesn't bother me much considering every other Final Fantasy 95% of battle is just pressing x to perform the basic attack.  Real time battles are done well relative to other attempts (FF12) and automated selection of the skills allows the player to focus more on selecting targets, picking jobs, interrupting enemy attacks, etc.
The story is pretty standard Final Fantasy fare.  Political corruption, larger than life god-like beings, fate of the world thrust unfortunately onto the main characters.  It can get convoluted at times if you don't pay attention, but the logs provide depth for anything you missed.  Characters are often paired with their foils and while most of them are charicature this is again pretty standard for JRPGs.  I actually very much appreciate the game forcing you to play with all of the characters and watch their stories develop.  Again, if you only play for 2 hours you'll likely feel frustrated that you don't get to "know" a main character because of all the jumping around, but as the game continues it makes sense to watch the stories weave together.
Overall, the game is solid.  It's debatable if it was worth it at 60 dollars when it was new (although I think it was,) but it is a no-brainer at 15.  It's not a traditional JRPG in both the battle systems and the more linear playthrough, although the more linear map style lends itself towards the story as well as helps push players along to unlock more of the battle system and upgrade system.  There is essentially no grinding in the game at all what so ever (minus end game.)  If you fight the fights available to you, most of the time characters will max out their stats/abilities for that story section.  All in all it's a bit of a hyrbid with a more standard JRPG story which is probably why it has been so polarizing of a game.  If you approach it with an open mind, it is a good experience.

Torchlight is an immensely entertaining hack-n-slash role-playing game with a surprising amount of variety, despite the seemingly limited class selection. Traverse the treacherous tunnels of the Ember mines, battle hordes of foes with your ever-vigilant animal companion, and progress beyond the main story through the innumerable randomly-generated alternate dungeons. And once you've bested the beasties of the cavernous underworld below the town, kick back and take a break by breaking out your fishing pole and having at a nearby pond.

I recommend this game. Why? It plays well, albeit slow for my taste and it adds new ideas and functionality that will throw open the doors of possibility for future expansions. While not perfect upon release, it is still a great game. Civ V was no better on release, so don't listen to most of the complainers.

Really well balanced play while still providing largely diverse playstyles and awesome mechanics to strategize with. Quick match speed with long-term (instead of bursty) combat. Much more about strategy and utilizing your kit to its fullest than about getting the jump on people. Much better than any moba I have played as the support and "tanks" feel useful with melee being properly rewarded. However matches are only 1v1, 2v2, or 3v3 (1v1 is custom, v ai is only 2v2) with focus on just killing the enemy team (no minions, towers or bases) so this game will not take up much of your time, it is very much a hobby game that you come back to every once in a while. Another thing that is kind of a bummer is some "battlerites" (passive modifications to your kit) will never be accessed in most game you play because you choose among a set of 3 ascribed to each round, which means if the game is one sided (which sadly most matches are) you don't get access to the  latter battle rites nor can you pick the order of these selections. Meaning if modification on round 4 is what improves your combat with that character the most you can't access that unless the game is close(r than usual).
I look forward to more modes or larger fights (or both) and I would love to see some pve stuff added in. All in all a great game to visit for that weekly urge.

This game is a true gem with a few edges.  The story is incredibly rich and based on old Chinese Novels about the Jianghu.  As a Chinese American, I can't read Chinese, but I can speak it fluently.  I've watched TV series and movies based on these novels and it's very refreshing to see a game with such a large background to it.  This game, from what it seems, this is a sequel to a really old chinese game, when you actually play as the "Nobody" mentioned in this game.  Except that one was purely free roam.
Despite some translation issues, it does not prevent anyone from playing.  In certain parts, such as poem comparisons, they would just give you the answer, so no need to worry.
So the gameplay:
Most of your training and decision making are done in the simulation mode, where you decide what your character is going to do, train, work, visit people, etc.  Combat is done in a turn based tactical grid style.  There are so many events in this game that it is impossible to complete them all, even if you decide to focus on events, rather than training.  If you don't save scum, then all your runs are going to be different.  Your choices matter, and can dictate how the story will end.  If you decide to not talk to anyone, then you're not going to have a pretty ending.
Warning:
It is super addicting and has that "One more turn" attraction.
I'd say, give it a try.

If you enjoy MMOs and I personally do, this game, with some fairly minor fixes, has the potential to rival World of Warcraft. My career, which is over, was in IT. If I was in my prime I would beg for a job with this company. They are so close to taking over with Riders of Icarus. I have seen lots of MMOs.
I play WoW almost to the point of addiction from its infancy. I was never great but I did OK. Eventually I grew tired of the egos that came to overwhelm chat and the mean spirited people who just came on to make an epic entertainment software turn into a worldwide joke. There were also many kind people that tried to help each other and help new people.
I played Riders of Icarus for a while and let it go then came back. My son became interested in it and a random person at a high level came to help him just out of the goodness of his heart. I found this odd and my son being 12 I asked about this "friend". Turns out he was a 13 year old kid who was just very nice. I say this because watching chat I have never seen one negative thing. I would easily recommend this game for families to play and I would as highly do so for parents and grandparents to spend time with the kids and other families as a safe and fun for all experience.
There are some bugs. None of them are difficult to work around and I'm sure given time these will all go away. I hope the company listens to their user base and responds as quick as they can. I sure that is the case and I am basing this novel of a review on that assumption. These developers are very gifted and are so close to taking a good amount of the people who have left WoW and have been jumping from MMO to MMO since. A fraction of these players would be win/win for everyone. The company would be very profitable and the players would be extremely happy. Each getting what they deserve. Families getting closer playing (if the atmosphere stays as friendly and helpful as it is) and the company having a huge cash base to further development and hire extremely gifted devs and artists.

I liked this game, I don't know if I really enjoy so-called "walking simulators" but this had enough detail in the characters and enviroments that I remained attached to the storyline. All in all, I liked it. a good, ableit somewhat brief experience. compact i guess.

Quite a neat game. I'm not a big fan of platformers, but Teslagrad had just the right amount of puzzle, challenge, and story. I picked up Teslagrad in a recent Humble Monthly Bundle and have enjoyed playing through it the last couple of days.
The puzzles and rooms themselves are fairly clever with beautiful artwork and pleasant music to match. The storytelling is stylish and subtle; in fact, there really is no parts of the story you're forced into following. Instead, the game offers interesting backdrop with artwork and puppet shows that are just enough to pique one's curiosity.
The platforming has some flaws. In particular the character doesn't feel as responsive as it should, and for some reason the controls aren't auto-mapped. I can see how some people could be frustrated with one-hit deaths, especially since the boss fights can be unforgiving and tedious until the mechanics are learned. Aside from those little tid-bits, I have no complaints whatsoever with the game.
If you're looking for a metroidvania puzzle-platformer with quality visuals, I definitely recommend Teslagrad.
