Howler 10 is a digital painting program that does a hundred things that aren't digital painting.    So it does everything.. but what is Howler 10 really good at?  Like what will Howler utterly clobber the competition when time of production is a factor?
1. nature landscapes -nature backgrounds

Three things that make Howler unexpected:
1. How it handles transparency
2. People often come from Adobe and the clones, but Howler is more of a dance between compositing and digital painting.  For example, compositing methods of magic pink, drop magenta, bluescreen, and greenscreen are used instead of opaque layers.  I personally wasn't very fond of Howler until I understood it was a dance.  hopL hopR hopL
3. RGB morality.  When the base layer is on, the RGB value shows regardless of whether transparency is on or off.  Turn the base layer off and you'll see the checkerboard transparency background.  In the older 9.6, you always had to check whether transparency was on or off.
This tutorial series will make other people think you know what you're doing.
PD Howler Playlists:
:
i5m, ATI 7820m 1GB GDDR5, 8GB ram DDR3, Win 7 Pro x64
Toshiba 11 2-in-1 Intel Baytrail/wIntel built-in graphics, 4GB ram, Win 8.1
Works.  Several functions like particle brushes are too slow on the Intel Baytrail.
Last notes:  PD Howler is not a software that lives on simplicity.  If you've played with ArtRage or OpenCanvas and you come to Howler, it'll feel overly complicated.  There must be half a dozen different ways to save* and at least 5 different types of brushes that come to mind.  Brushes can give you more options to adjust than you thought of wanting(I'm not talking brush styles, I mean types, like orbicles or particles).  That said, the depth can be enjoyable because the right tool or method is always there... somewhere.
update: I just checked, there's at least 7 ways to save when animation is taken into account, and 1 additional way to save with the batch converter.  You'll never be so confused with saves in your life.  Remember lyr saves swap and saving through the brush buffer saves transparency into pngs.

Okay, I have to admit that headline is a little misleading, but when two games share the same developer and has similar mechanics, then comparisons will be drawn. It is only natural. That being said, it is not completely like Gone Home, otherwise I would not recommend the game and direct you to buy Gone Home instead, Luckily, Fullbright Games are not one-trick ponies.
In most video games the player can only really see one side at the time because you as the protagonist is stuck in the present time. You cannot, say, go back in time and go to another place and listen to what other people have got to say about a situation. This is what makes this game radically different from other games. Under the guise of past AR recording you can reverse, fast forward, and pause characters' conversations. As there will often be several conversations going on at the same time you now have the power to rewind time and follow another conversation. This unique form of storytelling allows you to follow many sides of the narrative at the same time. As you might imagine this type of gameplay will be very hard to write without causing some sort of plot hole or paradox. But the Fullbright team had pulled it off extremely well. It also goes a long way to explain why you get such a short game: it is extremely resource intensive, as you are often telling two or three stories
Talking about AR, it features heavily as a gameplay mechanic. The game does a good job of exploring the full potential of AR You receive written messages through your headset, you have things translated for you in floating text above the object, and you see things as they were in the past through an overlay. It of course begs the question: what if those things become commonplace in real life? We know the benefits, but what are the detriments? Who own the data needed to create the AR envionment? And why does the crew's every move have to be monitored this way? Gameplay wise it is very helpful in giving information quickly, and allows for multiple languages to feature in the game while still allowing the the player to know what it says.
Several things, otherwise it won't be compared to Gone Home so often in the first place. The prop huning element is back in full force, this time with a lot more detail about the world and the context characters are making decisions in. What makes it different from the previous game however are the references to the outside world. Gone Home is very personal and insular, limited to the experiences of a family. Here you get hints of politics and economics of the outside world that affects possibly millions of people. Sure, you still get personal relationships motivating the actions and choices for the characters, but because they are mature adults they have much bigger elements to consider too. The props themselves are highly detailed and fun to explore.
The setting itself is much the same. Plotwise a large home and a spaceship is very different but gameplay wise you are still dealing with a limited envionment used by several individuals. A spaceship is still a home for them and much alike a normal house there are distinctive communal and personal areas. The only major difference is how you move around the spaceship. The main corridor is zero-G and that is fun to mess around in.
What definitely stayed the same was how well-written the characters were. Each character has different motivations that sometimes clash and each character has something to hide from the others. This affects how they behave around one another. Once again, Fullbright is the master of 'showing, not telling.' None of the personality traits are explicitedly said but they can be inferred. This is due in part of the masterful acting. You get to know the characters well, their habits, likes, dislikes, and their deepest, darkest secrets.
Okay, I'll still admit it is Gone Home IN SPACE but there are few new fresh takes on gameplay ideas that should keep it interesting for people. In fact, it feels like a promising EP for an awesome album. I sincerely hope other game developers in the future will use the new gameplay mechanics to tell compelling stories like this. If you enjoyed Gone Home you will almost definitely like this game too. Don't just float off, alright?

This game is terrible at being a Hitman game, and it is terrible at being a Splinter Cell game.
Hitman: Bloodmoney was like chess. You'd play it for an hour just thinking of the best way to play your only move, and everything had to be perfect. You had your level layout, your target, and many ways to approach this.
You have none of that in Absolution. Instead of infiltrating - you're hiding behind dumpsters and convenient blocks of random crap.
Everyone instantly thinks he doesn't know you. Even in a level of 1000 cops, everyone's suspicious of you, and you have to have your "instinct" to pull down your cop cap or hide your face a little (whichs is unsuspicious as hell) to prevent them from "finding out" that you're not a cop, for instance.
It would be a decent Splinter Cell game if you could hide in the shadows, since that's a very big part of action stealth. You also have none of that here.
If you've never played Hitman before - you might love this, so go ahead and buy it, but if you're a fan of the old chess-like Hitman games, then please, do not waste your money on this.

I just finished my first playthrough of Tacoma, after having bought it on a whim because of the 33 percent off coupon given to Gone Home owners. I loved every minute of my time on the station. The way in which the story was presented was on a level of quality comparable to other narrative gaming hits such as Firewatch and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. I loved the possibilities the science fiction world of the Tacoma opened up for the means of storytelling through character posture and personal logs. I have to say I am biased though; While every story told in the game could be done in another setting, space holds a special place in my heart. And I am a huge fan of any so called 'walking simulator'. If you are considering purchasing this game, I definitely recommend it.
PS: If anybody tells you $20 is too much for a narrative adventure, don't listen. Budgets are a concern for everyone, and you can always wait for a sale just like I did. But don't let a negative mindset devalue the hard work that was put into this game. It may not be the pinnacle of action or strategy, and it may not last more than 4 hours, (I took ~3.5 hours and still missed half the achievements) but it did take plenty of thought and dedication to create such a dense and diverse cast of characters, and to script out entire scenes like a stageplay where the fourth wall can be everywhere in the set. I could go on about the respect I have for the art that is this game. But don't listen to me, find out for yourself.

Welcome to the review of Omega Quintet, a hybrid between an idol simulation game and a role-playing game, developed by Galapagos RPG and published by Compile Heart.
Before I start, I want to make it clear that I had never play any Hyperdimension series before, and I heard many game mechanics are came from that series which I might not appreciate if I had never it before. Also, this review is based on my opinion and perspective of how I see the game, whether you want to try the game out or not isn't in my responsibilty. You might have a different opinion than mine. One more thing, this review will contain SPOILERS. Let's start.

Omega Quintet takes place in a world where humanity is on the verge of destruction, which caused by a phenomenon known as "Blare" ( "Beep" in JPN ver. ). The only people who can fight off this phenomenon are known as the "Verse Maiden", who used the song to fight.
While this can be pretty decent plot for newcomers, later on, the story become predictable and boring, but in what way? By boring, I mean it took you to get to chapter 7 where the story started to get interesting( they are a total of 10 chapters, will explain later on in gameplay section ). From what I have seen here, if you play
enough, you might get to an interesting part, but let me ask you a question, do you think the players will be patient enough continue? SOME may be patient, but I'm talking about general playerbase here. Playing game for a story is like reading a book, if it doesn't have a strong hook and a fascinating storyline, reader will get bored and stop reading, same thing as playing the game for storyline.

The gameplay is really good. This game's battle system is more complex than any JRPGs I ever play before. I advised you to experience for yourself since this review will be very long if I were to write every details. You can simply go to Youtube if you want to see the battle gameplay.
After you finish the battle, you can return to the hub, or mansion, or whatever i guess, this is where you can build armory, buy items, and where most of the story took place. In this mansion, A workshop, where you can build weapons and armors, repair outfits, disassemble parts to make new items. A collector box, a place where you can use coins to trade for new outfits, cosmetics and CGs. Training facility, where you can farm EXP, fighting enemies, and getting blueprints for new items to craft. In menu, you can set your Verse Maiden's outfit at will, you can also set your Verse Maiden to equip any weapon to desire, but you would rather have each Verse Maiden use their own weapon to make each other unique in one way. Skills can also be unlock by the using "Disc Analysis", this way you can unlock each Verse Maiden of how you want them to be. While each character have their own unique ability and EX skills, remember what I said earlier that every Verse Maiden can equip any weapon? Yeah, every Verse Maiden can also use the same Mic skills and E skills too, which pulled away their uniqueness. Also inside the mansion, is where you can raise your affection of each Verse Maiden, if you reached certain level of affection, you will get to see a fanservice of that character. See for yourself. Affection will also affect your endings too, will explain later on about the ending requirements. Quest can also be submit in this mansion, and sidequest can be receiveved in the town map outside the mansion. These quests can earned you a fair amount of EXP, items, blueprints, or even Verse Maiden's abilities. Outside the mansion is an overworld, you can choose to go "anywhere" as story progresses. Items , Archives and Blueprints can be found around the area. Also there is a PVS, or Promoting Video System, where you can edit your Verse Maiden concert at will. I won't explain this.
From here I'm going to complain the heck out of gameplay, if you don't want to read, you can skip it. Are you ready? Here we go. Gameplay as a whole is in a mixed. The battle system is very good......if they learned to shut their mouth, you see, everytime when a character take a turn, they speak, when they attack, they speak, when they use skills, they speak, how about this? let's make it worse by adding the broadcast voice too, so whenever you defeat an enemy or land a hit, they won't SHUT UP, good thing you lower their voice volume. Remember when I said sidequests are good? let me ask you something first, what is the main purpose of sidequests? To give a player something to do when they are bored of main storyline, and does this game have that? Yes, and NO. OF COURSE, you can skip all the sidequests if you don't want to do it, but there will be a point where you need to use Verse Maiden ability of level 2 which required you do a certain sidequest before you can proceed, and what happen if you don't do it? YOU CAN PROGRESS THE MAIN STORY, even worse, if you haven't done or finish any old sidequests before turn in main quest, those sidequests will locked out FOREVER, which means you have to start the game ALL OVER. You may probably know about this, but you think newcomers will know this? WHO KNOWS? AND WHY DOES THIS KIND OF SYSTEM EXISTS!? IT'S 2017!!!!! (Of course I know that this is a PS4 port and this game came out in 2015, but come on, this is unacceptable ) And yea about the endings, there are normal and True ending. Do you want to know the requirements of true ending? Do you want to know? Ohohohoho, you are going to be surprised.*Spoilers* The true ending requirements are :
You might think, doing all the quests isn't that bad, right? I can just finish all sidequests first before submit main quests, easy right? You underestimate this game. The sidequests are boring, most of the time they ask you to defeat monsters, bring the item and stuff. Some quests even need you to collect certain items for the quest to appear. Affection? you can increase it by looking at events in the mansion, while you can grind for it, it incredibly slow. Support rate? just keep 1-shot hoards of enemies and you'll doing just fine.

Soundtracks are very good, they are blend in to the environment. Also songs by Omega Quintet are pretty catchy. My favourite song is
. Graphics? don't ask me, I'm not that great at saying about it. If you want me to say what I thought, it's like playing a PS3 game.

It’s been… what? Four years since Gone Home? Yeah, four years since I got a message in the middle of the night saying something like “DUDE JUST PLAY THIS”. I followed the orders. Two hours later, I was tearing up, a big smile on my face, sure of the enormous potential videogames had for telling stories.
I’ve been following Tacoma’s development since it’s been announced. I’ve been curious about how Fullbright would amaze me this time. I wanted to feel the same I felt with Gone Home.
But I didn’t. I didn’t feel like I had just played a masterpiece.
Tacoma is a good game. Its writing is good, its visuals are good, its narrative concept and design are good. And it was worth my money and time. But it wasn’t… It wasn’t a Gone Home.
Is it because Gone Home is a magnum opus, never to be challenged? Nah.
Maybe that’s because it’s been four years. Four long years of frenetic growth in a volatile industry such as the games industry. Gone Home’s been part of a groundbreaking change in how stories are told in games. Now, mature storytelling in games is a giving. Good storytelling, more than common, is expected.
Tacoma being “just good” makes me happy. For it means this media has reached a dreamed level of maturity.
Can’t wait to see what Fullbright will bring us next.

A very mediocre jrpg with tons of frustrating elements.
Cons:
* Extremely low-quality story by jrpg standards. Hard to tell what is worse, the main concept or the execution (quality of dialogues, etc).
* Boring characters without any depth whatsoever. If you heard one line from a character, you know everything about the character.
* Over-simplified combat. You either spam one button (during trivial encounters) or one mega-combo-attack (during boss battles).
* Super-frustating exploration: imagine any Neptunia game with like 10 times larger locations, 2 times less enemies per square meter and slower movement speed, and you'll get this. Getting to where you want to be takes literal minutes of just running forward. I was told it gets better near the end because you'll unlock a speed upgrade or something, but it doesn't matter since you'll probably die from the boredom before then.
* Terrible grinding aspect if you care about the good ending.
Pros:
.. emm... I don't know. That 2d sprite animation system that they recycled from Neptunia still looks great. Also, the character development system... exists, I guess. You actually make choices that will affect your characters' stats a little bit. Nothing else strikes me as a strong side of this game.

Do you like instant gratification?
Do you like a game were you don't need to think?
Do you like to always win?
Do you like pay to win?
If you answered NO to all those questions then this game maybe for you!
First I would like to say I am a 100% free player.
This game is tough for new players. It takes time to gather cards to build the decks of your dreams. Expecting to get all that in a few weeks will not happen. If you are going to play free, it will take time to gather cards (6 Months to get good). You will get a lot of free cards if you play regularly. Sinking in 1h during evening a few days in a row and get rewards, play a few round and you’re good! You can also play all day, get in game currency at the end of every game and buy more cards with it. If you’re patient it build up fast.
This game requires careful planning. Preparing your decks, making every card count before you even see the opponent, is key. You need a plan!! BUT every deck has its strength but also its weaknesses. You can never find an unbeatable deck… hard ones to beat, yes, but there’s always something that can tear them apart... including luck. The question is “Dose your deck have the right cards to do that?” If it doesn’t, then work towards getting those cards. If you don’t like working towards your goals then you answered yes to the first question.
That game has amazing strategy. There are many variables to take account of. The type of deck that are in play (Knowing all that cards in the game, when they can be played and with what deck is important, it takes time to get familiar but that comes naturally). Luck of the draw. Placement of your unites in the right Zone. The order of unites (The one at the front will enter combat first, actuate order can determine damage, both health and morale). When to use the right cards. Guessing your opponents moves. Card turn order (some cards will be played before others). Even if you play vs the exact same deck, the game (even sometimes the game outcome) will be completely different because of all those factors. Lots to think about.
You will lose a lot. I view myself as an ok player. Probably lose 50% of the time. Some days I win 1 game out of 10 played, the next day win 9 out of 10 games using the exact same deck. Some days are just frustrating and others you just feel like a GOD!!
It’s not fun to lose… I know! That said you only lose (sometimes win) the match, but you ALWAYS get points for finishing a game. NOT if you quit…
If you lose a lot, look at other good player decks and copy what you like or work out you’re deck weakens. Speed? Defense? Attack? Cards combos? Neat card abilities? (I know, you need more cards… than go back to question 1)
I don’t view this game as pay to win. Pay to get ahead faster, yes, and I am all for it! The devs do need money to run the game and add content over time.
A player that buys cards gets certain cards, sometimes alternate card art but never gains access to cards that free players can’t have. As a free player you can have it all, as a paying players you can have it all faster. That’s it!
The only negative for new players is that they will face players that have a lot more cards to their arsenal. There are different game types available and premade decks available for players that are still building there card library. New players will fell a bit like the underdog till they build the card library and that can take time as a free player. That said, if you had it all from the start, there would be no incentive to play to try and get all the cards!
The game can be grinding but that’s the challenge I set my self! I play just to try and get all the cards and its fun PvP. As a free player, I am very close to that goal!!!
Hope to see you on the battle field!

After hearing from friends and seeing on various websites that this game was "awesome", "intelligent" and very-well written, I finally decided to give it a shot, and, I have to say, I've been really disappointed. Let me explain :
Obviously, this game is very original, wrapped in mystery from the very begining of the game to its end. The graphics are OK, but definitely not trumendous, and humour is everywhere, which is a very good point. You will laugh playing this game for sure.
But here I come to the nitty-gritty, and in my opinion the cons of this game are more numerous than its pros.
First of all, this game has a terrible lifetime, even if you decide not to follow the narrator's orders, you will have finished in less than a hour. For the price it costs, it's almost unacceptable.
When it comes to the gameplay, it is not either good or bad, it is just commonplace.
There would be a lot more to say about this game, but, even if I've been disapointed, I decide to recomend it, because I hope the developers will have enough ingenuity and courage to do better in their future game.
To be short : The Stanley Parable is a well-written game, ingenious, clever and funny, also mocking our society, but in the same time incredibly short and commonplace when it comes to gameplay, graphics, music and so on.
Not that bad at all, but the devs can do (way) better !
Note : The way of getting some achievements is incredible :p

First, my specs:
Windows 7 Home Premium (x64)
Intel i3-2120 processor @ 3.30 GHz
8 GBs of RAM
NVIDIA GeForce GTX550Ti
Now let's compare that to the recommended set-up provided by Square-Enix:
Windows Vista/7/8
Intel Core 2 Quad (2.66 GHz)/AMD Phenom II X4 (2.8 GHz) processor
1 GB RAM
NVIDIA Geforce GTX 460/ATI Radeon HD 5870
Despite the fact that I exceed the recommended requirements by a wide margin, this game still struggles to maintain a consistent framerate with or without the Durante fix. The audio also skips every now and then, mostly during visually intense sequences. Further tweaking would be for naught, as the tweaks I've made had little to no influence on the game's performance. I'm not the only one experiencing such issues either--plenty of people with much more powerful hardware are experiencing similar problems. As such, I can confidently attribute this game's erratic performance to poor optimization on the part of Square-Enix.
In it's current state, I cannot recommend the PC version of Final Fantasy XIII. While it's perfectly playable (controls are decent on either joypad or keyboard and mouse, despite their respective lack of rumble and sensitivity settings; it's also more fun than the naysayers will have you believe), it's full of audio/visual stuttering, takes up a massive amount of hard drive space, and is locked to 720p by default. If you can put up with the poor performance of this port, do yourself a favor and wait to pick it up when it inevitably goes on sale.
Hopefully Square-Enix learns from the poor reception of this port and decides to put more effort into their XIII-2 and Lightning Returns ports.

IW:ATCG is the next step in strategic CCG's. They build upon previous popular CCG's so if you are new to the scene, it may be difficult to catch on. Hell, I've been playing MTG for years and I had a bit of trouble. While the verbage on the card is not always clear, there is a wiki on the different types that can help you get a grasp of the concepts. This is where experience comes in handy.
There is also a twist on the "stack" that many MTG players are familiar with. While cards play out in order, any character cards placed in the way of the effects after the fact are affected. There is also the concept of "initiative," which begins randomly with either player and causes that players "stack" to resolve first. It's an interesting concept that creates a whole new dimension to gameplay and is used to develop strategies that would never be considered outside of this particular game. I enjoy the new rule and look forward to using it.
However, the game still seems new. There are many details that could be worked out for rules and what is considered a "character." This is the verbage I was speaking about above. Sure there are more examples, but most can be worked out while playing the tutorial campaigns and there are sufficient AI's to test your decks prior to delving into PvP.
IW:ATCG does have an arena style mode where you create a deck from random cards ala Hearthstone. I have yet to test those waters.
Overall I think it could develop into something fun, and is already interesting. I look forward to playing more and will update my review accordingly.

Civilization Beyond Earth is a grand remapping of a popular franchise; but this has dissapointed short sighted fans who expected something... more? I dare say, load up vanilla Civ V or Civ IV if that's your preferance; that's right, free from any DLC, Expansions, or Mod Packs and tell me if Civ BE doesn't out compete these games.
You have some mechanics that are simplified; units come in a few flavors that upgrade over time. While others are far more defined; such as the tech web that will have you scrathing your head to find a path that will work for you at the given time and for the future (no insta-build tech paths like we were accostumed too in Civ V). Trade routes seem to have replaced specialists in terms of power, and they do get a bit tiresome to reset every twenty turns (perhaps putting the "Previous" location at the top of the list? Espionage seems to be a fully different mechanic that will take more time to learn how to master; rarely can I keep an agent within a city long enough to pull off a level 5 act.
The game is visually stunning. If you zoom in you see strange little plants growing on the canyon's edge. The GUI is initially strange (things are moved around) but it feels right overall for the game. And the screen is far dimmer (washing away those white fluffly clouds of war) and the pallete is more neutral; this may frustrate some but it feels right for this game.
The sounds are also very well done; CNDR sound appropriately robotic while flaring up some goopy soudning Manticore. The voices of the AI leads you to wonder how their culture came to be; but also wishing for a few more phrases. I can only know what myth you think of Adam Smith so often, Sterling! This leads me to another enjoyment; the statements as you level an affinity or build a wonder have odd puzzlements; making you wonder if this is even from our timeline or some other world's. (All lists of five things have one lie, as one example; and Mythic Heros appear in completely new stories: Anansi, Casey Jones, etc.)
A lot of love and charm was put in this game. A game that loads quicker and smoother than Civ V. A game that is a new direction and not merely some total conversion mod. A game that should earn a fine place among other Civ games in due time. I already day dream of new leaders, better benefits from merging affinities, strange new religions, and a forming of great peoples to populate the new world. I look forward to what modders can come up with and hope to see some more content down the pipe soon: notably to better visualize trade deals and perhaps more phrases for the AI leaders; as they almost always say the same thing each trade (seriously, just two to four more should manage that a bit better), and maybe; just maybe have the stations land throughout the game and not all at once near the start. They almost always locate about where you were planning to settle, and disappear near mid/end of the game where they are most beneficial.

As a hardcore Civ fan I have to say I was more than a bit let down by this release.  I completely understand some issues are bound to be in the release version of the game.  What I am mystified about is the sheer number of obvious game play breaking bugs that were in the initial release.  And when I mean obvious I mean glaring in your face omissions.
I have to wonder what the internal testers were up to?  If core mechanics are barely functioning then maybe you should have just disappointed the community with a pushed back release instead of dumping a half finished game on us.
Sadly this game feels half finished.  The lack of even the most basic ending sequence was a major let down.  Want to see some stats on what you did? Too damn bad.  Expecting some neat cut scenes for world wonders?  Too damn bad.
The tech web was a let down as well.  In the end you have virtually cleared the whole thing anyway.  They only real choices you are making are within the leaves that concern the affinity system.  So the hype of "choose your own path" was complete hogwash.
Another let down were the actual units.  I get the affinity system changes the looks and abilities somewhat of the units.  It just seems very sterile.  Very few options for units.   I guess I was simply spoiled on older Civ games with a much wider selection of units.
In the end I can't say I am satisfied with my purchase.  I have hopes some patches will fix some of the ciritical problems.  So if your planning on buying I would wait a few months until the dust settles and pick this up on sale.

This game is considered a sequel of the much-loved Chinese Wu-xia game created in late 1990s based on Jin Yong novel characters.
In order to appreciate this game, you would likely have to be well-versed in Chinese culture, and knowledgeable about wu-xia themes and the various plotlines in the more famous wu-xia movies/novels in Chinese culture.
The english localization was very weird for myself as an Asian, until i found an option to play it in Chinese in the game properties in my Steam Library. Never looked back since. For the Chinese version, there is also a so-called "beta" which is only available in Chinese, but is actually 2 full-blown DLCs made available in the Chinese retail version, given to Steam owners for free!
In a nutshell, in this game, your choices do matter, and if you screw up (which you probably would, as ingame tips and tutorials are sparse), you would find yourself unable to win fights you should be winning in order to get the desired ending. But once you read up more (on the Chinese forums for this game), you would realise that this game have many hidden gems and events which you would have to trigger in certain time periods, in certain order, so that they can unlock certain skill sets. Do pick it up, but you would most likely only appreciate the full depth and fun of this game, if you can play the Chinese version i.e. read Chinese.

Since I keep reading bad reviews about this game, I'll just write down my two cents.
Those who downrated this game are either delusional old Alpha Centauri players, or Civ V players who didnt give a crap about learning and understanding what is added on BE compared to Civ V.
- First off, the price (50€) is absolutely fine when you consider that it contains all the features of Civ V vanilla, BNW and GNK (30€ each for an awful 90€ total).
- Second, its not just Civ V with a sci-fi paint, given some new additions that change the strategies, such as the tech web instead of a long tech tree, affinities empowering your units giving you different bonuses on choice and finally bonuses that favor a wide empire from every point of view.
- Third and last, aliens > barbarians. Barbarians on Civ V have always been nothing more than an early income of culture and gold, while aliens on BE are quite dangerous at the beginning of the game and can be a pain in the *** if not kept under control.
Then, of course, the game isnt flawless. The trade routes are incredibly tedious to keep up once you own several cities, theres plenty of minor graphical bugs that occur every now and then, and the AI is still quite dumb despite a few improvements over Civ V. Oh, and theres no Gandhi :(
Long story short though, this game deserves better than its being given so far.

It's been years since Diablo II left a dungeon-crawling hole in most of our lives. Torchlight fills that void nicely. While there are only a few classes to choose, the dungeon themes repeat, and you'll see the same monsters over and over, the game manages to have more than enough variety to keep you entertained and digging for hours, days... you'll be surprised how much time you've sunk into discovering the secrets of the ember-filled caverns below the town of Torchlight.
The only major drawback is a lack of multiplayer, which is outright criminal. Supposedly there's mods out there in the internet aether that allow friends to cavern-dive together, but it's not immediately obvious how to get that running.
Pros: Great dungeon crawler, keeps pulling you back in for "just one more level"
Cons: No multiplayer (without modding), things will get a bit repetitive during long sessions
Verdict: Well worth the money, even at full price.

The first few hours of playing Riders of Icarus it reminded me of games like Lineage and FF, with a few elements copied from WoW...then after a few days it becomes obvious this is just a cheap copy of Neverwinter (with worse graphics/gameplay, better and more open world), another bad game.
More specifically,
-'free'
-fast framerate/no lag, good ping
-separate NA and EU games and 3 separate servers each
-interesting taming concept (familiars are used as mounts, pets/combat helpers, consumables and more)
-ground/air mounted combat
-big world to explore
-guilds and alliances
-alt-tab and uninstall work
-pay to (not) win
-very bad graphics (cryengine is just a clickbait) that makes you wanna cry at some points
-bad gameplay and combat
-laggy/unresponsive combat skills especially in mounted combat (chaining broken)
-very primitive UI
-primitive and very basic crafting system with lots of trash, items expensive to craft, takes too long to farm materials
-skill tree is a joke since there isn't one: 3 talent groups of 6 (total 18) but you can have up to 8 talents at lvl 55 (max?)
-solo leveling not smooth, group nearly impossible to find
-many boring and repeated quests (even has 'repeatables' and 'dailies')
-very small and bad dungeons (so far seen 1 boss+mini bosses)
-no voice acting for the most part and dialogues very basic with primitive UI
-game full of botters and gold spammers
-very primitive party matchmaking system (where most entries are by gold spammers)
-no end game (only 5 dungeons with story/elite/heroic tiers with subtiers-heroic is for 5 players and 1 'raid' for 10 players)
-intrusive/annoying marketing for premium in-game(pop-ups that cannot be permanently disabled etc)
-most guild facilities like gbank, fort etc not present
-very few players in game (apart from bots and spamers) and most don't know how or don't care to use chat
-game engine so bad I had to run it at 30 FPS to avoid excessive coil noise from video card (and still no visual difference from 60/120 FPS)
-many bugs and graphics glitches
-Nexon Anti-Cheat system (what a joke) occasionally crashes and won't close/kill game/AC (even hanged my Win 10 once and had to do hardware reset, first time ever for Win 10)
This is the second Nexon game I'm reviewing and turns out even worse than the first, which speaks volumes about the studio...
The devs have copied entire areas and dungeons of Neverwinter (which itself is a copy of other games) and put them blatantly around just changing the names a bit...you know if you copy a bad game the result will be even worse and that's the case here. I remember reviewing NW in the past (not on Steam) giving it a 3 out of 10, well in that sense Riders of Icarus worths at most a 2 out of 10. I won't even try to compare it to good MMOs like WoW, GW2 and Eve...
The game simply needs a lot of polish before it becomes barely playable and half-descent. In this current state it is total garbage pay-to-win and should be avoided at all costs, don't waste your time and money here.

This is the english launch of a Korean game that has been running for several years overseas.  Content in Korea is properly leveled and balanced at level 60.  What we have is the first translated build of the starter continent and first add on zones up to level 35 by Nexon USA.
I really wanted to like this game.  I tried to recruit my friends and guild mates into this.  I leveled all 5 classes to the current max level of 35 and outfitted them in heroic armor and gear.  I maxed out the bestiary in the starter continent.  I have over 500 hours played outside Steam.  Like many, I patiently awaited the PVP update and like many others, have never been so let down in my life by a MMO or company.  The PVP update had serious problems.  Customers service has major problems with response times to tickets and is overloaded with complaints.  Overall, this game was a major, major disappointment.
The recent PVP update was plagued by bugs.  People had massive framerate issues.  People had problems even getting into the zone.  If more than about 35 people entered the zone frame rates dropped to unplayable levels.  The game engine just cannot take it.  Before you say "its your hardware" I run a GTX 980 with 8 GB of video RAM on a PC with 32 GB of RAM with a 4.1 GHz P7 HX6830 and SSD.  I have games I can run stable at 60fps at 4K.  My machine should be able to take it.  The game however and their engine just fails.
People were upset over PVP.  Mechanics were broken.  People camped the zone-in killing people that were lagged entering the PVP area.  It was a major issue with assassins and their damage as they could one-shot kill all caster classes.  People voiced their opinions.  After the huge uproar in the forums, the Devs immediately did their lethal knee-jerk reaction and nerfed damage in PVP trying to "equalize" things.  Only they ended up nerfing it across the entire board.  So people that used to do 50k damage when mounted using their dragons and crossbows now did 6k.  This basically crippled PVE heroic encounters for everyone and some PVE encounters and tames undoable.  The entire game became broken since the entire game is based upon the Korean game that is properly balanced at LEVEL 60.  They have since tried to fix it and undo their changes, but its becoming too little too late.  People are leaving the game in droves.  I was in a guild of 45 that has since dropped down to zero active.  Entire zones are dead now.  You barely see anyone in cities.  For a game only about 60 days into launch with 3 USA servers, people are already calling for server merges to "maintain the viability of the game".
So.. more about the game.  It is a theme park game.  You do a set series of quests and you WILL level to max.  Just do the quests.  It appears to be an open world but it is not.  Fly too high or exceed a barrier and you hit invisible walls.  The zones just look big but in actuality are very small.  Some areas are open flight, but many are capped or land mount only.  It is far from an "open" world or sandbox type game.  You cannot go where you want or openly explore.  You follow the themepark paths.  Dungeons follow a set one way route.  Definitely a themepark style.
The game is entirely about your mounts.  Ones you can tame yourself (up to elite) and "heroic" ones that you have to fight 20+ other people for to try and tame.  Heroics are way over done.  It takes 10-15 people to battle down over 30 minutes at times to try and get a Heroic mount down low enough in health to "tame" and when that happens it is a battle for whomever can click the tame button and get lined up fastest to try and tame the mount.  Even then you have to complete the mini-game successfully and face the RNG of the game to see if you tame or not.  Some heroics being 1/6 or 1/14 chance to tame.  Each chance consumes the "mark" you have to craft or buy which could cost you hundreds in gold per attempt.  Quite possibly the WORST system I have ever seen.  So you may waste an entire DAY trying to get a mount and fail or watch in disgust as someone who came in late to the battle just runs up and ninja's the mount from underneath everyone.  Or watch them fail and see the heroic mount reset to full health again.  Its pure frustration and broken.
Another painful mechanic is armor and weapons.  Most armor is Bind on Obtain or Bind on Loot.  So you accidentally loot armor for another class it is stuck in your inventory until you can go to town or destroy it.  Group with someone and they loot or roll on items they can't use and they win (out of greed) and you are SOL.  You cannot sell it to another person or even trade it on your same account.  Also all looted goods roll random stats when it drops from ALL possible stats for all classes.  So getting a "good" roll or appropriate stats becomes a lesson in pain and futility as casters will get items with melee stats and vise versa.  Store purchased items are also character specific and bound to a character.  Most crafted items are also character bound - so you must craft if you want crafted PVP/PVE armor and weapons.  Each character has a fixed inventory and "ellum" wallet so cash shop goods are character specific.  This leads to massive real world money cost inflation with multiple characters as even ellum you buy with real world money is character bound and is not shared across your account.  It becomes a major money grab by Nexon at higher levels with the gear upgrade potions and taming chance potions.
Another major issue is their new "auto-ban" detection system.  They put this in place to try and detect botters, hackers, gold sellers, gold buyers or other people that they deem bannable.  Only thing is their system bugs out.  If you do anything abnormal in game, its an automatic 4+ day ban.  People are getting auto-banned for shouting too often in regional chat.  People glitch out or fall off their mounts and are getting banned.  Anyone emailing or receiving gold in game email is being banned.  The witch hunt has gone INSANE.  Funny thing is, they are most likely banning all "whales" and major cash shop buyers with their bans as well.  Since most whales are also gold buyers, they are all getting permanent bans.  Funny that this may kill their entire game.
Overall, I wanted to like it.  Lack of content, bugs, apathy from customer service and bad management choices seem to have already killed it.  A shame.  So much potential.  So much frustration actually trying to play it.  But stick a fork in it, because I can't see them resurrecting this thing.  As a new game so close to the USA launch, I have never seen a game fail so quickly.

Teslagrad is one of the better puzzle platformer, metroidvania titles on the gaming market.
Instead of relying on cutscenes and dialogue via speech bubbles, Teslagrad establishes its engaging narrative through gameplay. There are cinematic moments where the player character has to stand still to let the camera focus, but the camera's focus can be cancelled by moving around. Movement is never locked, so the game never forces the player to sit through a cutscene.
Movement and puzzle mechanics are introduced at a good pace, and the all the puzzles encountered will rely on the player's understanding of the mechanics. For movement, I'd recommend a controller.
Granted, there are a few areas where I did get frustrated from constant deaths, but I was able to recognize the patterns eventually. Mostly, the frustration was overshadowed by how much fun I had while learning about the lore through puzzle-solving. The risk-reward system worked well since the 36 collectible scrolls were usually hidden behind some kind of skill barrier based on already established puzzle mechanics.
Finding everything the game had to offer was fulfilling, making Teslagrad a rewarding experience from start to finish.
The port is excellent(60FPS/4K) and the production values are very high,so if you're a fan of japanese RPGs this is highly raccomanded for you.

Steamified Revisits is a new concept on
where we will be running a feature for games published onto Steam in 2014 and prior that never made it onto the Steamified Countdown. The games that we feature within this program are those that are much beloved titles or are highly wishlisted or just never received the type of recognition by the gaming press or Steam players. If you have a game that is from 2014 or earlier that you would like to see featured on Steamified either post in the disqus comments section below or submit your suggestions on our Steam group forums. I cannot make any guarantees but I will promise to get into contact with the developers and to show them your interest in having their game(s) featured and if they agree then we will feature them for you.
The very first game in our Steamified Revisits series is Rain Games Teslagrad. It was released back in December of 2013 and has remained one of the most criminally underplayed games in the entirety of the Steam catalog. This is such a shame because the title fared reasonably well with the critics scoring 77/100 on Metacritic and 78/100 on Game Rankings. The highest number of people that have ever played the game simultaneously on Steam is 169. It’s a much better game than that and as a result is one of the driving forces behind the new Steamified Revisits feature of the website.
So what is Teslagrad? It’s a puzzle-platformer that also fits within the metroidvania genre. It tells the story of a young boy whose exploratory behavior gets him mixed up with a long-forgotten conspiracy involving the king of the land who rules with an iron fist. The knowledge that the boy possesses could change the course of history for his land. Of course, you will not know this at the beginning of the game. Rather what you are told is that men dressed in red and looking mighty official are after him and that the boy is attempting to escape on what appears to be a cold stormy night that no boy should be outside in. Throughout the course of the game the developers do a superb job in telling the story in a minimalistic manner as there are never any words provided of the written or of the spoken kind and you are given just enough that you’ll want to play on and discover more of the story until it plays itself through to its compelling completion.
As there are no words in the game greater importance is placed upon the art direction. Thankfully the visual presentation of the game is absolutely superb. The hand-drawn environments are among the best that I have seen. The lighting effects have been perfectly designed and serve only to contribute beneficially to the game without ever detracting from the experience – a critical balance that is so very difficult to get right. The audio too is among the game’s great strengths which may be difficult for some to consider given there is no voiceover work. The visual presentation is based upon a steampunk world.
Another critical component of any puzzle-platformer is the level design. Rain Games have you covered here.  The game has been designed almost flawlessly with the opening levels of the game serving as a tremendous tutorial to the game without being overtly difficult or easy. The puzzles fit nicely within the spectrum of the game and are well designed and possess a high level of execution.
Two of the criticisms that I’m willing to lay upon the game is that I wish that the devs had spent a little more time in determining the layout for the controller. Some of the important options lack a button. Yes, you’re able to customize the options but unless you’re someone who checks every option before getting started you will not notice this until you’re left wondering what on earth you need to do. The other critique that I have of the game is that the controls should have been made to be a little tighter. Occasionally you’ll have to redo a small section of the game because you’ve died through no real fault of your own.
However, in all, Teslagrad truly is a game that should have been experienced by far more people than have played it. It’s one that is bound to provide several hours of entertainment.

Infinity Wars is a pretty cool and quite unique entry in the recent digital CCG boom. It requires some really deep strategy decisions about when to attack or defend, and you have a lot of control over how you want to maneuver your troops around the battlefield. One of the interesting things about these strategy choices is that Infinity Wars has figured out how to solve one of the big drawbacks to digital CCGs: player interaction. In physical card games like Magic, player interaction is quick and easy; you perform an action and then I can quickly respond by saying, “okay, before that resolves, I do this.” When it comes to digital card games, those interactions can be hard to implement. What was easy and took two seconds in real life can be digitally dragged out through a series of prompts and pop-up boxes. Digital CCGs have dealt with this in different ways…Hex: Shards of Fate tries its best but is ultimately just awkward and clunky, while Hearthstone gets rid of this sort of player interaction altogether. Infinity Wars’ solution is simultaneous reveal, which is a *perfect* choice. This means that the game can have Magic-style tricks like surprising your opponent with a Giant Growth, or giving one of your characters Flying at the last second. You need to think hard about what your opponent might do, how he or she will move troops around, what buffs or removal cards he or she might have access to, etc.
The other big feature that Infinity Wars brings to digital CCGs is deck-building complexity. In Hearthstone or Shadowverse or most other digital CCGs, a given deck is always tied to a certain class and its card pool. If I want to make a Warlock deck, I only have access to Warlock and neutral cards. This is really restrictive, but it’s also very friendly to new players or to anyone who just wants to play casually. You don’t need to lose sleep over possible card interactions – there are only a few cards to choose from, and you get to know them pretty quickly. In Infinity Wars, however, deck-building is truly opened up. You create a deck by choosing three Commanders, and each Commander can be from a different faction. You can mix and match all sorts of cards and create really crazy and creative combos. This does mean, however, that the deck-building experience is kind of overwhelming and hard to master. There are so many options that you can't really take a casual approach. Many people will see this as a huge draw, but I can see some players feeling daunted. You have to be open to the fact that the process is going to be a little unintuitive and hard to crack at first. I think that if you're eager to get your hands dirty with some creative and messy deck-building ideas, you'll be in heaven with Infinity Wars.
The theme of the game is definitely compelling and neat…it has a strong sci-fi bent to it, which I tend to prefer over high fantasy. The factions include a Warhammer 40K-style military, a robot-building corporation, dark magic users, and tech-angels with Uzis. You'll be able to cast demons, mutant animals, giant robots, siege cannons, assassins, and psychics. In a way, the game’s theme kind of reminds me of a CCG from the 90s called Shadowfist (if you’ve never played this, check it out). Shadowfist also had factions of pulp heroes and sci-fi warriors battling for control of rifts and secret portals, and Infinity Wars shares its weird and kitschy sense of humor. Infinity Wars’ theme really shines through its animated cards: characters eternally fly through the battlefield, stomping enemies, and cities blow up over and over in cycles of never-ending destruction. It makes you feel like every card is rare and special. The art itself is a little hit and miss, though. Some cards are beautifully drawn and some are sub-DeviantArt stuff. Looking at the recent Rebellion set, Lilariah the angel and the Martyr of Death demon are awesome, but Lucca, Rebellion Leader...the foreshortening on that raised arm, yeesh.
While I’m absolutely recommending Infinity Wars to anyone interested in CCGs, I do have a few critiques that bring down the game’s overall quality. The whole package is actually a bit buggy and sluggish. The interface is just clunky and hard to navigate, and it froze up on me a few times. It was difficult to play Infinity Wars after playing Shadowverse...even though Shadowverse was originally a mobile game, the interface runs like butter at all times, and Infinity Wars feels amateurish in comparison. Secondly, the player base seems a little small, so it can take a while to find a game (when you do find a game, however, the netcode is pretty decent). Finally, Infinity Wars is quite stingy about packs. You get packs whenever you level up, which is great (I heard this ends after you hit a certain level, though...?), but otherwise it's quite a grind to earn in-game money. Not the biggest deal in the world, but if you want to get one of those nice pre-made decks, it's going to take you a good while.

Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag is honestly the highest point the whole franchise has reached since Debuing in 2007. While people will still say that 2 or Brotherhood are the best (they are still fantastic games though), Black Flag offers a sense of scope and exploration that just hasn't been matched before or since.
The Caribbean open world that the game offers is HUGE and not only that it's dense as is tradition in any ubisoft open world game so there is tons of stuff to do. Hell being able to sail to remote islands with your ship, the Jackdaw, makes all the crazy item hunting to 100% the game more entertaining than just running around like a rabbid parkour runner.
The customization in the game is some of the best I've seen in any game. The variety of upgrades you can offer to both yourself and your ship gives you a ton of options to live out the ultimate pirate power fantasy as well as having a crafting system in the game just like in the previous AC game. Except there is insentive in this game cause you WANT a lv 4 gun pouch or better armor so you look like an even bigger op badass.
The PC version is buggy as hell though. But not in the sense that the game crashes every other auto save BUT the graphical glitches are nothing short of a borderline Unity in terms of faces dissappearing, NPC movement clipping, and other texture ♥♥♥♥ery.
But that does not stop the game from being GORGEOUS when everything is actually working. The lighting and rain effects are still phenominal almost 3 years later and it isn't that demanding if you pc is a bit more modern so most people can enjoy this game a very high graphics settings.
And finally in regards to the story. Edward Kenway's story and overall development is the best in the series since Ezio in AC2 (untill they dragged is character through the dirt for 2 more games) with some expected but still interesting twists as well as having memorable characters such as blackbeard and kidd.
This game is super cheap on sale at this point (got it for 7.50 this summer) so I more than recommend AC4 to anyone who wants to play quite possibly the best pirate game ever made.

I'm a huge fan of stealth-action games, which is why I've rated Batman: AC and Deus Ex: HR so highly, but this game seems to be the exception. I don't mean to imply that the stealth in this game is of a lower quality than the two I've listed, in fact it's probably on par with them, but the real issue I have with this game is the way it approaches gameplay in general. In each level, you have a score at the top of your screen. Points are gained for completing specific challenges and lost for doing things wrong. While it's possible to ignore the score, Hitman focuses very heavily on score being integral to your experience with the game. The challenges are sometimes easy and sometimes difficult, but it's often impossible to complete multiple in a single run through a level. As a result, you'll find yourself replaying the level over and over again in an attempt to complete the challenges. And then, one time, you accidentally do something majorly wrong, like killing an enemy in plain sight ("I SWEAR THAT GUY DIDN'T SEE ME!!!") and you lose the majority of the points you've spent an hour-and-a-half cultivating. Well, it looks like you're just going to have to reset the level (replaying lets you keep points and challenges, resetting resets all your challenges and points to 0). As stated previously, you can ignore the challenges and score, but they're such a core part of the game that if you ignore them, the game becomes a generic "kill this guy and don't be seen".

I have been playing this card game off and on for over a year I think. It started out just looking for something a little different from other card games. Saw this was free to play and bam! I got hooked to it. The fact that it has a single player and many different types of ways to play with other people. There is a cool campaign mode where you can play as a faction from anywhere between 4 to 6 missions. Each mission getting more difficult, to make you find combos and learn some important mechanics to the game that will help you play against other people. This also rewards you with free decks of cards. After you beat all the campaign you end up with a pretty decent card pool to make decks that you want to experiment with and play against other people.
This game also has an group of advanced tutorials (aka Academy tab) where you learn some excellent strats to help you win future matches. I enjoyed this game so much i got a few family members to play it with me and they have really enjoyed it as well. It has a lot of different factions that each do something a little different or have completely different strats. The Community seems to be really awesome and helpful as well. It isn't toxic like a lot of other games I have played in the past.
The only negatives I think I have about the game have to do with connection issues I've had personally lately. But the Studio behind the game is helping me to fix it. So give it a real shot, play more than 2 or 3 games and you will be hooked too.

The newest game in the Civilization franchise. A well rounded, polished game, with tons of replay value.
The new affinity system makes sure the game is different everytime, as you can focus on just a certain affinity, or you can mix and match them.
The tech web is much better than the previous tech tree. There is just so many options to pick, and that makes it different, and fun. In Civ 5, for example, you could finish the tech tree, and your progression was the same every game. In Civ: BE, you cannot obtain every tech in the tech tree, and that makes for an interesting experience, where you have to pick your techs based on where you settled and what your current situation is.
Trade routes, once again, are OP, to the point where you need to rush the techs needed to construct trade routes.
War has become quite easy, or at least it seems like it so far. Once you have the upgrades for your troops, you will either crush everyone, or be met with an even army, and you'll fight until both armies are gone.
Overall, Civ: BE is the most polished Civ game so far, and I think once expansions come out, this game will be great and have the same depth that Brave New World had.

Civilization: Beyond Earth has been an enjoyable experience in my opinion. After clocking in over 300 plus hours on Civ 5 (Steam's play time is inaccurate), I can say Beyond Earth is just as addictive. Whether it was systematically exterminating the aliens in a Starship Trooper-like fashion, or emerging victorious in a three-front war, I certainly do not regret my purchase. I recommend this game to anyone who loves Science Fiction, and you will see a lot of inspiration as you play through the game. While the game is awesome, it is not without some flaws though. Here are some things I liked, and disliked since I've been playing.
What I liked:
1. You can choose various bonuses to your civilization before you start the game such as having the ability to see outlining continents, or start with a worker.

2. The alien worlds are awesome with diverse terrain, unique resources, and new threats to your civilization. (i.e. siege worms, miasma, alien nests)
3. Unlike barbarians from previous civ games, aliens will not always be hostile towards you, and you can even choose to domesticate them should you wish not to eradicate them.
4. The music in Beyond Earth is BEAUTIFUL! The music really fits the tone of the game as you ascend from a little colony, to a great empire.
5. There are three affinities you can choose from: Supremacy, Harmony, and Purity each with their own ideology, bonuses, and victory condition. As you conduct research and play the game, you will start to focus on a certain affinity depending on your play style, and as you level up a specific affinity, you will see visual changes to your cities as well as your units.
6. The victory conditions themselves are awesome. There is one where you build the "Emacipation Gate", and must send military units through to conquer Earth for its own good. Also, some victory conditions do not require a specific affinity to achieve such as the good old domination victory.
7. The new research technology web allows players more freedom to choose which technologies they want to prioritize. Some argue this system is too confusing, but if you are patient, and pay attention to what you are researching, the tech web can be rewarding.
8. The military units are badass, and get better as you level up an affinity. (My guys looked like Enclave soldiers from Fallout when I leveled them up through a specific affinity.)
9. The virtue tree acts like the policy tree from Civ V, but I think it is a little better in terms of rewarding the player as you progress through a virtue. You can choose, Might, Knowledge, Prosperity, and Industry each providing their own advantages.The game also rewards special bonuses if you sacrifice maxing out one virtue, and pick two (or more) instead.
10. Espionage has been overhauled since Civ 5, offering more options, and opening new covert operations as your spy levels up, and increases the intrigue in an enemy's city. Intrigue works as a double edged sword. It can benefit you if a city's intrigue level is low, allowing you to complete covert actions without the target player knowing, but as you perform more successful operations in that player's city, the higher the intrigue will get meaning operations will become more dangerous. Therefore, you must think strategically on how you use your agents, because if you use them right, you can attempt a coup in an enemy's city which is extremely satisfying.
What I Disliked:
1. Factions are boring and there is only eight of them. Despite each faction having their own cultural backround, bonus, and leader, that's it. There are no special units or buildings for each faction, and none of the leaders have any personality. They all act the same, and only change a little when they focus on an affinity.
2. Once again diplomacy is F**king stupid. For a game that has some real depth, you would think by now the developers would have found a way to make diplomacy rewarding, but it's the same damn thing as Civ V. Like Civ V, diplomacy is bare-bones, pointless, and frustrating at times. The only good thing they've added is the favor system where other civs will trade a favor for something of yours. You can then bank these favors, and use them to get other civs to do something for you.
3. Despite military units looking badass, there is not very many of them. Since no civ has their own unique military unit, everyone has the same units. However, choosing an affinity will grant unique units, but compared to other civ games, unit diversity is lacking.
Overall, Civilization: Beyond Earth has been a blast to me, and I can only image what the workshop will bring to this game as well as future expansions from the developers.

Even real farmers play Farming Simulator! Whilst it is still a little way from being a simulator in the true sense of the word (for example, gears are not fully simulated, tractors do not show real damage, crops grow too fast and its a bit too easy to make money), nevertheless, the positives far outweigh the negatives, and for every weakness, there are many realistic features. It's great fun if you have any interest in farming and you like the productive strategy type game rather than the fast paced shooters. I worked on a farm many years ago, and I played with Britains farm toys as a kid. This game, 40yr later, allows me to own and drive any type of tractor & implement, and farm any crop, & the physics and graphics are easily good enough to bring back the memories of driving the real thing. Giants also give good support, they updated FS2013 regularly, so I hope to see the same improvements and developments in this one;and they offer good (many free) addon mods form time to time.
It's also very moddable, so if there is an aspect that lets the game down, it is very likely that someone has added a mod to fix it, or else you can do it yourself. For example, it is not difficult to edit the start machinery and funds, or to change growth rate or values to make the game more difficult, or even to create your own map with a bit of learning.
Stand by to be labelled a farm nerd (similar to trainspotter), but that matters not to me. Excellent game, worth at least 8 out of 10 on release, and expecting that to rise with future patches.  :)

This is among the best games I've had the pleasure of playing, hands down.
It's a shame this game doesn't get the attention it deserves. There's a small, yet loyal following that genuinely wants this game to be the best it can be. Even though it's a voxel-based FPS, it far exceeds your run-of-the-mill CoD or BF in many aspects. It's the simplicity of Blockstorm that makes it beautiful.
What's great about this game is amount of customization available through the in-game editor. You can create your own knife skins, guns, mechas, player models, and can even forge your own maps with ease. Because of this, there's a ton of free community-created content via the Workshop. You don't have to sell your house, car, and your left testicle for a knife skin like you would in CS:GO. Just subscribe to an item in the Workshop, and you're good to go.
There is one main criticism I would give this game: The ping. If I had a lamborghini for everytime I shot someone in the face without them dying, I would be Tai Lopez. It's not uncommon to see pings above 150. It can be frustrating dying to someone you KNOW you should have killed. This is one of the reasons why this game may never be competitively viable. However, you'll learn to shrug it off and keep playing. It's still a blast to play!
For the price of a burger, you just can't beat it. Skip food for a day. Buy this game.

Although this is a negative review I hope the developers, if they are reading this, are not discouraged because I really want there to be more games from China in the west.
Tale of Wuxia is an interesting game that has its flaws. It's not often you see games come out of China. Similarly the game has many mechanics which are different from typical RPGs. I found myself enjoying the game overall. I would recommend this at the current low price and if you have interest in the setting. In terms of general public I would not.
Ultimately the theme and somewhat different (not necessarily better) game mechanics made it new enough to be fun for me.
There are many areas the game could improve on however.
1) Tutorial and explanation - Things are explained at a pace that is too slow in the game. By the time the combat tutorial shows up in January of the 2nd year you have already battled quite a few times. I learned a considerable more by reading the few game guides. Similarly by reading the game guides, you realize how many game events you would have missed if you followed the slow tutorial.
2) Localization vs Translation - There's a difference between localization and translation, which shows in the game. As a Chinese American I am familiar with the background so I was able to grasp the concepts easily. However I feel like for people who are new to Chinese culture they may feel lost by the game. Even with my knowledge I had no idea what the game meant when it used historic chinese names for hours. Localization is not an easy task.
3) UI - Chinese is more space succinct than English, which leads to various parts of the UI not being designed for the translated version of the game. Furthermore there are many game mechanics which are insufficiently explained in game or are strait up confusing. Other parts of the UI are also confusing. Ex. the Books tab of Character Bio, I don't undersand what to make of it. Also at the very beginning when you roll for stats only some of them have tooltips and for newcomers to the series it's hard to tell what is good or not. My first runthrough I died to chickens because I had no idea what I should have rolled for.
4) UI and Game Design - More clear explanation of stats. It is not clear what exactly each stat does, and there are honestly too many stats. I had to learn from reading a guide that 50 points would be required to gain another movement point. Many of the stats should be flattened or something instead of making a difference every X points. It would be more clear if you gained a movement every point, but gaining a point was 50x slower.
5) UI - I would like a way to skip text in game since I restarted quite a few times in just the first year. I don't know, maybe there is one that I'm not aware of, I've mashed my keyboard many times.
6) Game Balance - When I read the guides and they say that the mining game is the way to get stats up (given the mining game has horrible hitbox detection), that is not something which brings confidence to game balance. Similarly if you lose battles you don't get stat bonuses, which means you are not going to win the next battles. It leads to dead ends, why allow the player to continue playing if they are going to have to restart anyway?
7) Misc - Ability to skip credits please.
8) The game says you can build your character how you want without trees, but all the guides I see basically say 'focus one tree or else you won't win'. Part of this is the time constraint part of the game and the lack of grinding. Lack of grinding is good. However this does mean that experimenting with different internal styles (which I did as a new player because I had absolutely no idea what the advantages and disadvantages of each style were) means you end up with a bad character.
Even with these problems I enjoyed the game when I played it. I don't think I will be finishing the game however, as the Rune Factory series has many aspects on Tale of Wuxia (like fishing, mining, etc.) without the drawbacks in this game.

A solid game with excellent ideas, but some flawed execution, and very flawed localization.
Tales of Wuxia is a Eastern RPG based on Chinese wuxia stories, with plenty of references fo Jin Yong stories. Even if you're not familiar with the genre, this game has plenty to offer... if you have patience to wade through some bad translations.
The game has a randomized character creation screen, plenty of branching story arcs (for the main story and side character arcs), a turn-based strategy battle system with adequate depth, and a time management role-play system where players must manage character interactions and their own stats. What's clever is that the players' own stats can have a drastic influence on how certain plot points proceed. If there's a downside, it's that some of the mechanics are simply not explained well (though the basics are explained well enough, leaving room for player exploration).
Due to the sheer depth the game has to offer, not to mention the shoddy translations (more on that in a sec), players will practically *need* walkthroughs and guides to help them get the best out of the game, but thankfully there's plenty of guides available.
As for the localization, the translations are actually pretty solid early on, but once you hit the halfway point you'll start to notice more and more bad grammar. There's even some minor scenes later in the game that go completely untranslated. Hopefully, a patch will come out to fix these issues soon. The bad translations don't make the game unplayable, but it's pretty darn annoying.
If there's one other issue I have with the game, it's the visuals. Part of the game takes place using more "realistic" portraits, but the time-management segment of the game uses "chibi" portraits. The transition between the two can be pretty annoying, since there's not much reason for the switching. Also, the "chibi" portraits actually show different moods while the "realistic" portraits don't... personally, I actually find the "realistic" portraits kinda flat most of the time.
Overall, I had lots of fun with this, but would only recommend it to people with either the patience to figure out bad translations, or wait until a patch which can fix it comes out. If you're a fan of Wuxia stories, then I defintely recommend it either way.

Omega Quintet is the story of a man surrounded by pretty ladies who take to the field with their mics to sing the otherworldly critters into oblivion. Ghostlight brings us the PC port of the 2014 PS4 release, and contrary to the suspicions in the Discussions, the game does not appear to have been censored in any way...
Not that the original game had anything that Western audiences would consider worthy of censoring as a general rule. Some might disagree, but that's up to them. No direct nudity, just the rare CG of clothing falling apart. Per the norm, the game comes with the lowest tier of the DLC from the original already on board, and the rest of it won't run you an arm and a leg-- knock yourselves out.
Technologically, the port is solid. It ran smooth as silk on my machine, and shouldn't be an issue at the minimum specifications. I found all the buttons where they were on the PS4, and they've added all the elements I would expect of a PC port to the config menus.
The story is fairly typical of Idea Factory and Compile Heart's combined works, although the inclusion of the girls getting embarrased/angry/etc if the camera drops low enough to risk upskirt shots was a nice touch-- Almost as if Takt was the camera...
The only gripe I've ever had about this game is the choice of English voice actors, specifically Takt, voice ny Johnny Yong Bosch. Yes, he's in all the games, usually as an antagonist. This time, he's our protagonist, and the voice of Tohru Adachi as the "good guy" was one I found jarring. It gives Takt a touch of the unlikable in what was essentially a solidly-written character. That said, it's my opinion, so take that for what it's worth. A lot of Persona 4 fans will see major paraqllels between Takt and Adachi, not only in voice, but attitude. /rant.
That's my take, but I encourage you to form your own opinions on the matter. If you're inclined to get it, do, and do it before Ghostlight realizes that they're giving the entire farm away with the steep release discount. If you can't get it before the sale expires, the $30 asking price really isn't terrible, so go for it anyway.
If not, give it some thought. I enjoyed the game, and I think you all will too.
