So I'll preface this by saying that while I *do* recommend this game, it is a very niche sort of title so not everyone will enjoy it. Those that will enjoy it, will enjoy it a lot.
Here's what it is; if you've played any of the 'Total Extreme Wrestling' games, or its older free version called "Extreme Warfare Revenge', it is similar. In fact it uses the same in game world, promotions, and wrestlers. But rather then taking the role of a booker and handling all the behind the scenes stuff, you actually step into the role of a wrestler as you guide the wrestler through their career.
You have multiple modes for this, either a career mode where you can take control of any wrestler in the game, or the more difficult "Rookie To Legend" mode, where you create a wrestler from scratch and set out to make your name in the independent scene and get signed with larger and larger companies, as you carve out your legacy.
The career mode works like this; choose an available storyline, wrestle in four matches spanning the four weeks of a month, hope you succeed in said story, then repeat. As you win matches you get experience points you can spend on upgrading your stats, or save them up to buy special attributes to give yourself other bonuses. Winning the storylines gets you popularity which you can use to get signed into new companies.
KEEP IN MIND, that at the start, especially in the "Rookie" mode you will be severely outmatched by a lot of your opposition, similar to an old school wrestling game like "Here Comes The Pain". You'll have to persevere, cherishing the few victories you get and improving your stats correctly to succeed. At the time of this writing, I am seven months in with a record of 10 wins, 20 losses, with two storylines that didn't succeed or fail, several that I failed outright, and ZERO I managed to succeed in. This isn't an easy play for sure.
The character creation is awesome, as you can choose your size, and your style and depending on what you end up going with, you can only choose certain moves. No 280 pound guys doing shooting star presses here, at least not from what I've seen. You have a crazy amount of moves you can choose from, and you can work in almost any pro wrestling region, from Canada to the UK to Japan. It's not something you'll be dissapointed in.
BUT the big part of all this, is the actual gameplay. It is essentially a turn based wrestling game. Without getting too deep into percentages and dice rolls and all the calculations, you choose a move to attack your opponent with, hope it succeeds and then continue the attack. If they block it or counter it, they go on the offensive so then you need to counter or avoid their attack. However it takes into account things like being outside of the ring, being in the corner, your opponent being on the ground, etc. It's very, VERY, in depth and requires a lot of thinking on your part.
I will point out this is all text based, with no music or sound to go with it so make sure you have a great soundtrack to listen to as you play. You also have a couple of other modes based around the matches without any career stuff, such as an exhibition mode, a league mode for singles and tag teams, and a streak mode where you try to go undefeated for as long as possible. Cool but it's not where the meat of the package is. Lastly, one of the big *in game* achievements calls for you to go through career mode for 25 years, win 1000 matches, and a lot of other crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥so whether you get it on sale for $5 like I did, or pay the regular cost, you're gonna get a great 'dollars versus hours' ratio on this.
Honestly the best bet for you, reading this, is that if you aren't sure, do the following: buy the game, get yourself into a match or two and play around with it. If you like it, great. If not, get your refund within the two hours. It's not for everyone but if you can get into it, you'll find a slightly frustrating but very enjoyable wrestling experience.

Before getting Area-X, I had heard lots of good reviews on it so I was very happy when I finally got the chance to play it for myself. Without a doubt, it is one of the best visual novels to come out ever. Where do I start?
For those familiar with X-Note, Area-X is the second game in the series. It could be considered either a prequel or sequel, depending on how one looks at the storyline. Basically, you take on the role of Elcia, who is from the Future and has the capability of traveling to different time dimensions via the use of a time machine. Although others do have this ability, Elcia can use it more. I won't go into spoilers as to how since that should be reserved for the true path. ;)
Basically, Elcia travels to different time dimensions originally with the goal of negotiating for natural resources since in the Future, these are lacking. However, events take a turn for the worse...Without giving away spoilers, I won't reveal what they are. Buy the game if you wish to know what happens. XD
There are a total of five guys in the associated time dimensions that you can pursue although at the start, you're only given two of these guys. As you complete paths, you'll be given letters to assemble passwords so you can unlock more paths. Basically, you should play for both good and bad endings to get access to passwords to unlock more paths. Now some might say that this is a bit inconvenient although I can understand the developer's intent. If one were to get access to all of the paths early on, it would be spoiling the story and personally, I prefer to unlock paths as I go so I can learn more of the story. ^^
Aside from the story, the gameplay is pretty standard. There are puzzles to solve and some of them are challenging. In addition, the art is absolutely stunning. I think it's a great improvement from X-Note, and I loved that game. The music is fitting as well and I found myself crying a bit as I got near the end of the true path so yeah, I think this game is beautiful.
Overall, I'd totally recommend getting it and it's interesting to see how elements from X-Note are implemented in Area-X. I'm excited to find out that there will eventually be a sequel although we shouldn't expect it any time soon. Still, I can't wait and again, I recommend getting Area-X, especially if you're a fan of VNs. ^^

This might be the point where I tire of the Assassin's Creed formula. I didn't enjoy AC IV nearly as much as I did the previous games. The story was barebones and not as interesting compared to the other main entries in the franchise. And almost every mission seemed like it had a Tail Someone section, which is incredibly dull and tedious. Halfway through the game I decided to focus just on the main story mission. Everything else just seemed to get in the way.
The main addition to the franchise here is the sailing your ship part. However I must say it is not nearly as enjoyable as I though it would be. The combat is simplistic and almost no one can pose a serious threat to you, it just feels like you're going through the motions. It came to a point where I started actively avoiding fighting with any other ship. Which meant I couldn't get enough resources in order to upgrade my ship. So the game started pestering me with warnings before starting a mission that I should really upgrade my ship. But it didn't really matter if I had an underpowered ship. I did the missions just fine. I don't want to think about how tedious the missions would have been if I had a properly upgraded ship.
All in all that's the main gripe I had with this game, everything just seems so tedious. This might be franchise fatigue, but I think the deeper issue is that everything is so simplistic. This has always been a problem with the franchise, but in previous iterations I managed to get interested in the story enough so that I overlooked that part. And I think the missions were also structured better. Although by the end I did start to get invested with the main character, it's just a shame it took so long.
I'm still going to recommend this game. Newcomers to the series will appreciate the game, and franchise fans like myself will want to get some more story in the AC universe (even though there isn't that much of it).

What with the giant backlogs Steam sales and freebies entail, I tend to wait to buy games until they hit a certain price range.  As a result, I've been lagging on Assassin's Creed games pretty regularly, so I know I am a little late to the scene for this particular entry in the series (having played all of the main series, story DLC's, the first Nintendo DS title, and Liberation HD up until now as well, just as some background).  I'll be honest, Assassin's Creed 3 felt like the series had lost its way a little.  None of the characters felt likeable, and the lines between good guy/bad guy were blurry without the added benefit of making the plot seem any deeper for it.  The alt-history DLC was alright, if only a bit short and nonsensical, and Liberation HD had the unfortunate flavor of diet cola, feeling almost like the real thing, but never quite getting there.  So to say I had fallen out of favor with the series would probably be a bit of an understatement.  The magic of the Ezio arc had seemed to expire, which the series managed to pull off even though it was annualized.  All of these reasons combined with the fact that I wasn't interested in naval combat dominating a game (as I found the naval portions of AC3 to be a bit of a distraction, not something I wanted to revisit) made me really hesitant to try this game, but several of my amigos continued to press the issue so I finally got around to it in my backlog.
Wow, I was wrong, and I am so happy for it.  Gone are the emo, edgy character archetypes, replaced with likable heroes and compelling villains alike.  The bland rural colonial America has been replaced with a bright and vibrant tropical Carribean landscape, and the pirate motifs don't even end up feeling shoved down your throat.  Some naval combat is necessary but the mechanics are much more enjoyable this time around, and I really do feel a lot of this comes down to Edward's charisma versus Connor's ugh-ness.
The present-day portion of the game is weird, and first person, which makes me want to switch between a gamepad for third person portions and a mouse-keyboard combo for the rest.  It plays similarly to the Subject 16 DLC from Revelations, but without the spooky computer-ghost feel and any of the Mirror's Edge style mechanics (you're just a dude, in an office complex).  This had an opportunity to be boring, but always served to further the story both in the past and in the present, and even managed to weave in some closure from the ending of Assassin's Creed 3, so even if I tried I couldn't hate it.
The Deluxe Edition contains an additional 1-3 hour campaign where you play as Aveline, which feels like what I wish Liberation HD could have been.  It felt great to control her with her full range of abilities without the technical limitations of the Vita port.  While it seems the ship for a full-fledged Aveline game has sailed, the plot heavily alludes to more going on in her world that we may see someday.
Having bought the DLC with the base game, I am unable to post a separate review for Freedom Cry, but this expansion is also totally worth it, eclipsing the Aveline adventure in enjoyment and thrill levels.  You're looking at a 6-8 hour expansion set in a separate chunk of the ocean, with new mechanics based around the slave trade.  Many of the minor side-quest activities have been replaced with slave trade related goals.  Due to the shortened length of the game, your ship can only be upgraded so much, and now many of the upgrades revolve around how many slaves you free either from side activities or main quest lines, as well as how many slaves are recruited into the revolution you help to fuel.  Adewale, while a different sort of hero than Edward, still manages to improve on the past couple of AC heroes in many ways, and is immediately so much more enjoyable to spend time as versus Connor.  The writers continued with the steam they built up from the main campaign and managed to surround the protagonist with an array of good, bad, and somewhere in the middle characters that are all compelling and (usually) benefit the plot's richness from their introduction forward.  I hope to see more expansions like this as the series starts to get re-evaluated by Ubisoft and transitions away from being an annualized title into something more.
AC4 just has so much more energy, passion, and smiles all around, while still maintaining "hey, there's consequences for all of this crazy stuff you're participating in".  I'm back in for the series now, and am looking forward to playing the acclaimed Rogue next.

You can also play it by yourself, but I'm sure you have plenty of single player games already.

Area-X has a pretty complex storyline with a ton of endings that can be reached. Each major branch of the storyline is quite different from the others, so players aren't repeating so much of the same story as they play through multiple times. Area-X is definitely a game you will want to play through over and over, as more of the story is unlocked and more of the mystery is unravelled with each different completetion. Really, the game doesn't get started until you complete the first four basic endings, and then there is still a lot left to experience. The replay factor for this game is huge, and grinders who love to take a Visual Novel to its full extent will be fully satisfied by this game.
Elcia is a really strong female protaganist with a bit of a sadistic streak to her. Still, she is able to make connections with the other characters in the game, and some of the endings are super sweet. The game isn't about hooking up with the various characters or even finding true love. Some of the endings are more about making a special connection with a character, and the endings are really rewarding.
The writing for Area-X could be a little better, but as the writers have done a ton of work for this very long game, some players might be willing to accept some of the weaker parts of the story and move on.
Overall, if you can get past some cheesy writing at a few points and press the "I believe" button at a few story elements, this game can be a lot of fun. Hard core VN players who love to experience every scene and ending will be rewarded with Area-X, and those same players should find that they certainly got their money's worth out of this game.

The Technology "tree" has become a web instead, and it feels much more responsive than it did in previous games.
The new threats are a nice addition, as there are planetary gasses that could harm or heal your units depending on what you've been researching, there are native "boss"-type creatures that you could attack, and hopefully win against, and there is a new quest function that adds story, and depth to your decisions.
So, basically the way Quest decisions work, is you'll have a prompt show up, asking for you to make a decision, usually based on things that you've been researching. For example, it could say something like "Our scientists have invented a new plant that grows by itself and provides materials for faster production, however we could also use it to feed our civilization." You would have to pick whether you would want +2 production or if you would want +1 food, as an example. There are several of these and I never saw one quest decision that looked similar to any other, they all felt unique and the benefits actually helped me define my civilization far more than I anticipated.
are a part of the game, which are essentially just challenges that give you points towards and Affinity.
For example, you could have a quest that says something like "research x technology", or "build x building in this colony", or "kill this specific creature because it did x to me".
is a new feature, there are 3 of them, and they are:
: People who want to live exactly the same way they did on earth and change nothing about their life style, while adapting somewhat to the planet.
: People who wish to adapt to the alien planet/life forms. This basically means living peacefuly (or not), with aliens while researching how they live, so that your workers for example get healed from Miasma, for example, which is a deadly force on the planet.
People who essentially want to completely terraform the entire planet to be a secondary Earth, exactly like it in every way, and rule it.
This is only a fraction of the game that I could think up to write about, and if you've played previous Civilization games, this is a very good refresher and I strongly, STRONGLY recommend you take the time to learn the new features of this game if you can get your hands on it!

This game is amazing. Just buy it. Now. Its atmosphere, cryptic nature, level and world design and lore are truly amazing to explore blindly. Me and a friend were playing this game for about 12 hours straight we were so sucked into the world and exploring every crevice of each area.
The game takes inspiration from metroid and castlevania for its gameplay loop and from games like Dark Souls for its approach to storytelling, worldbuilding, atmosphere and lore. It just throws you in and intuitively teaches you the basics by making you experience them first hand. It's trully an amazing experience that you have to play.
Don't let this game's difficulty turn you off. While it is quite a difficult game to beat it's rewarding and completely fair (appart from that final arena challenge). The fights are fun, epic and rewarding with fitting music! The animation and visuals are stunning and enemies clearly telegraph their attacks, so if you pay attention you can theoretically go through this game without taking a single hit!
Please do yuorself a favour and go in this game knowing as little as possible! Exploring the breathtakingly beautiful dying world of Hallownest can be charming, beautiful, and scary depending on the area you're in. Each area is distinctly unique with its own theme, atmosphere, enemies and visual theme, and there are no cliches like "the lava leve" or "the snow leve". Every area is pretty original in my opinion and if you've seen a theme done before chances are you haven't seen it been done so well before. Just beware if you're an chievement hunter as there are a few missable achievements, so be warned! Also know that the main ending to the game isn't satisfying. After beating it look up how to get the "true ending" which is satisfying and interesting, otherwise you'd be missing out an entire platforming area, a really boss and a few pretty serious parts of the main character's personal story.
Other than the map system which is a little too convoluted (in my opinion you shoul only have to buy the map once from the chartographer and craft your own map for each area from scratch) the game is pretty flawlwss! I did have some performance issues with sudden lag spikes even when lovking the game at 60fps but it seems to be a issue just for me as I haven't heard of anyone else having these issues from people who have the same hardware - regardless, I'm using a Ryzen 5 1600 @ 3.7 with an RX 560 and 16gb DDR4 @2933 ( as you can see it's probably an isolated software issue )
overall score: 9+ appart from a few weird quirks it's pretty much a masterpiece.

Unless you have a crippling fear of cartoon bugs, buy this game.
Prior to playing this game, the only experience I had with games of this genre was with old grandpappy Symphony of the Night. And while that game is fantastic, Hollow Knight blows it out of the water. There really isn't much I can say bad about this game. From a gameplay perspective, the boss fights are great (especially some of the last ones you encounter), the controls are tight, combat is really fun, and deeply exploring the environment is very rewarding. Backtracking (when you have to do it) is rarely a chore thanks to the changing central environment and the ralways hidden around the map.
Now, one should note that this game is not easy, especially if you want to 100% it. There are some absolutely brutal platforming sections and boss fights to get some key secret items, but you don't have to do most of them to complete the game. There is also this one fight that doesn't really have a close save point, so trekking to it can be frustrating if you try to tackle it early in the game like I made the mistake of doing. If you like challenging games though, that's not a big deal. Just get good and you'll be fine.
I guess that the music and art style are worth noting, in that they are FANTASTIC. The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard in quite a long time. There are all these awesome little moments were everything just falls into place. For example, the music for the city area is grand, epic, and serene which perfectly fits the massive rainy cityscape. There is one boss that is really creepy ghost lady, and the music is so unnerving. It's just a pleasure to witness it all.
That's about it. I hope I convinced you this game is well worth the money.

I abolutely adore this game and everything about it. I hardly ever play platformers, and this was the first one I made it 100% of the way through; it's that good. I'm more of a first-person shooter or 3D adventure game type of person, so this genre was a little different than what I was really used to. I wouldn't have picked it up if my friend Pumpkin Head hadn't told me to, and I'm really glad he recommended it to me. Hollow Knight has easily become one of my favorite games of all time.
As an artist, I seriously appreciate the absoutley stunning style, effort, and craftsmanship of the backgrounds, animation, and character design. The art style is magnificent and inspiring, and has influenced my own art in a way. I have always loved the theme of darkness, pale face dark eyes, and mystery. This game includes all of the aesthetics I love into a wonderful looking platformer. The main character, the Knight, has such a simple yet cool design, and I get pretty picky with my characters in videogames. I typically will dismiss a game or show very quicky if I don't attach to or like any characters, but in Hollow Knight, I've fallen in love with the designs.
The mechanics in the game are so solid and feel so genuine. A mix of sound, animation, and mechanics really make it feel like you have absolute control of your character. Everytime you'd get a solid hit, you'd feel it, and every time you'd get hit, you'd feel that too. Every win or loss was by your hand, and it never felt like the game had cheated you or it was was anyone elses doing besides your own. The variety of ways you can play not only make the game feel more dynamic, but it also means that it caters to the different playstyles of the person with the controller. You have a choice to use certain charms, abilities, magic, and the nail itself. The variety of which you can play just makes it feel like the game never really ends.
Music is so important in videogames, and the Christopher Larkin has done a phenomenal job creating the soundtrack for Hollow Knight. The action and emotion behind his work fits flawlessly with the style of the game and the overall story. I listen to the soundtrack all the time, it inspires me and reminds me of all of the adventures I had in-game. The variety of styles in music correlate perfectly with the play areas in-game, and the mechanic of changing a few instruments in the song based on location was executed perfectly. It really feels like the music follows you throughout the Hallownest.
TDLR, I absolutely love the art style, the mechanics are solid and have variety, and the music brings the game together with the story flawlessly.
100/10 I definitely recommend anyone pick up this game and give it a try. It's not an easy game, and it doesn't hold your hand and tell you where to go. It's an adventure, but it's your adventure! The story is phenomenal, and it's worth more than the store price, at least to me. Beautiful game, best one I've played in a while.

At first I didn't like Hollow Knight. It was my first Metroidvania game I had ever played, so I didn't understand what I was supposed to do at some moments at the start. Now in gaming, you never have to learn for yourself. You never need to explore or take your own journey, and once I realized that in Hollow Knight you were meant to get lost, you were meant to die, I started loving it.
This game is difficult, you need to learn the attacks of the enemies. One of the best parts of Hollow Knight are the bosses. All of the bosses are different in their own way, their original, look amazing, fun to fight and most importantly, they are fair.
The artwork is stunning. Somehow each new are looks different than the last. You can understand the history of each area without being told anything. The areas are extremely detailed, and with the beautiful enemy sprites, its easy to get lost in this world.
Mainly, you explore the world and attack enemies. The controls are tight and you know that if you take damage, it is your fault. I can say that almost none of my deaths felt cheap, they were my fault so the only person I was angry at was myself. You have multiple attacks, and as the game goes on you gain more, variety is very important and is used well in this game.
There is not very much dialoge, so the story is told through the envirment, with only small lines of text here and there. After completing, I'm not terrible positive what the story is, but I do have a vague idea. Its always intruging and if you search hard enough, you can find it. This is a pro because I was always invested in what I was to do next, and because the characters are so charming and lovely, I had to mention it.
Lastly, the game is huge. It took me 38 hours to complete this game, but I haven't 100% it. With all of the extra exploring I did I'm sure it wouldn't have taken me as long, but since the world is so interesting its almost impossible not to get side tracked. I still am finding new areas and new mobs, and it still amazes me. It is very easy to get your moneys worth.
I stated in the pros that you get more attacks later on, and while this is true I found them to never be as useful as my original attack. I never had to use the new attacks, and maybe if I was forced to I would have used them more. Due to the design of the game I understand how forcing the players to use certain attack would be impossible because they may not have found them yet, but it seems like a waste to have these attacks if they are not used.
Since this game is a Metroidvania, there was a lot of wondering around not knowing where to go. Of course this is good and bad. It lets the player explore more and make their own adventures, but at the same time its frustrating when you have no idea where to go. To be honest, this isn't  huge deal and I only included it here because I didn't have any other issues with the game.
As you can tell from there not being a lot of cons, this game is amazing. It is fun from beginning to end with interesting characters and areas. I never would have thought that I would have enjoyed this game as much as I did and it makes me excited for Team Cherry's next game!

Civilization Beyond Earth is a Civ V reskin with some interesting changes, but feels half finished. I'm sure when it gets fleshed out with DLC it will be great but for now it feels bare bones and is marred by horrible design decisions that make it very hard to identify resources, units and the tech web is very hard to navigate.
After finishing a game of Beyond Earth I immediately went and played a game of Civ V and had a lot more fun. If you didn't like Civ V then you won't find anything different enough to like here. I get the feeling this was a proof of concept for the next proper Civ game, I hope for a more navigable tech web in the next one.
Some of the problems in this game stem from the fact that unlike true civ games, theres very little sense of progression. There is something very entertaining about leading a stone age tribe that hasn't even discovered the wheel right the way up to flying stealth bombers and dropping nukes. Knowing historical leaders, finding out your neighbours are montezuma, napoleon and alexander the great, you know what they are about, you know you will need to kill or be killed first. The new factions and leaders in BE are so bland and generic, I don't care about them, I don't know them. It fails to captivate me.
Positive changes are a much more in depth spying/intrigue system, quest system, trade system, and balanced health system as opposed to the happiness system that could cripple you in civ V. The lack however of a strategic map that was present in civ V is a strange and sorely missed feature.
This game is getting rave reviews, but once the hype dies down I honestly think it will be quickly left by the wayside. There just isn't enough meat on the bones here, Its one note, very stripped down and basic, it promised much and hasnt delivered. Too little changes from the basic civ formula and too little personality. Wait for the dlc if you haven't purchased already, I'm sure it will flesh out and become interesting but at the moment I'm fairly underwhelmed. It has however reminded me why I loved civ V so much in the first place, and thats never a bad thing.

Having finished the game before on PS3, I feel qualified to say that, for all intents and purposes, this is a pretty decent port of the game that all Final Fantasy fans should try. I'm not going to give my opinion of the game in detail but I will say that it is very underrated and, if nothing else, worth experiencing at this price for the visuals and audio alone. Square Enix is truly in a class of their own when it comes to audio/visual design and FFXIII is one of the best places to see it until XV is released. This new port of the game is optimized to run at 60 frames per second, maximum, though you might have a hard time hitting that consistently if your system isn't configured properly. By enabling Vsync through my GPU drivers for this game, forcing Anisotropic Filtering (which is unrelated but really helps the visuals), and setting my PC to Maximum Performance in the power settings I was able to get 60fps at almost all times during battle and field scenes, though cutscenes (especially the pre-rendered ones of course) tended to hover around 30fps, which is fine.
In general, if you were ever interested in this game and are very easily swayed by gorgeous, artistic visuals and sound, you will enjoy this game, especially at a discount like this. The Japanese dual audio option also helps if you find the English voices grating on your ears, which is subjective; I'm fine with them but options are always nice! It's true that, at the moment, the game is locked at 720p and you use the ESC key to quit the game, but those are not nearly as big of a deal as they're made out to be as long as your GPU or monitor properly scales the game to your screen size. The game uses a lot of post-processing effects so that the 720p visuals are barely noticeable on my 1080p screen except for occasional aliasing, and the game runs so smoothly with those small tweaks that I barely notice anything "wrong" with how the game looks anyway. In the end, if you've intended to give this game a try or even experience it again, there is no better time than now.

CPU: Intel i5 3570k OC'd from 3.8 to 4.2ghz
GPU: Nvidia GTX 770
Monitor: Asus 1080p 60hz

---------------------------Additional Findings----------------------------------
Updated:October 11th, 2014 @ 5:30 PM
Playtime:~5 hours
So I am about 5 hours into the game at the time of writing this update. Throughout my additional 4 hours of playtime I have noticed a couple of things. The lag is not going away further in game so get used to it. I have noticed the lag to be Somewhat Consistent throughout each of the levels so far (and SOME of the battles have no lag at all). More visually impressive environments and levels seem to have little affect on the performance, the game just always seems to lag and stutter consistently (most likely due to how the "texture and lighting" Load Subsystems are put together, but that is just a guess).  Dont worry it really is playable in my opinion, I am a Gamer who considers framerate to be one of the most important factors to consider when playing a game, and bad framerates have kept me from enjoying many different games. Dead Rising 3, Assassins Creed 3, and GTA 4 (one of my all-time favorite games) are all examples of games whose experiences were negatively affected by poor performance. 5 hours into the game and I can say one thing for sure, this game DEFINITELY has poor performance. In my opinion this is the biggest (and really the only) serious problem this port has. So far at least.
The Controls are tight (at least when using a gamepad) and the resolution really doesn't bother me. I downloaded Durante's fix to upscale the resolutions to 1080p bilinearly and I ended up scaling back down to 1280x720 with AA forced on. (in my opinion upscaling to 1080p made the game look great, but made the HUD extremely pixelated and ugly). The game honestly looks just as brilliant in 1280x720 as it does in 1080p (aside form the minor aliasing which can be fixed with Durante's update). The voiceover Audio quality is stellar, in both Japanese and English, and you can freely switch back and forth between japanese and english audio during your playthrough (no need to start a new game to change language settings, however language is changed out-of-game, so you will need to quit and restart if you want to hear the other voice-overs). The same could be said about the quality of the music. It's as amazing and beautiful as it ever was, and you already know that if your'e a fan of any FF game.
I still haven't experienced any of the crashing or Glitching that others have claimed to experience, however i am only 5 hours or so into the game. I am still thouroughly enjoying my laggy, stuttery, Adventure through FFXIII. But here's to hoping that Square Enix is working on a Patch to improve performance, i suppose we will have to wait and see (fingers crossed). If you can muscle through some lag and can entertain yourself during the LONG download then i still recommend picking it up for its $15.99 asking price. I am still taking notes on what I am experiencing and will continue to update these impressions as I progress.
------------------------FIRST MPRESSIONS--------------------------
Keep in mind that Everything that Follows is my personal opinion:
I personally feel that most of the Negative reviews on here are slightly exaggerated, I understand the dissapointment that the community is feeling,  but It really isnt all THAT bad. Yes It's true, this IS a terrible port, Square Enix should have done a MUCH better job. However If you're someone who loved FFXIII (like me) then it really shouldnt bother you too much. If you have always wanted to play FFXIII on your PC then this version is still worth the $15.99 asking price (in my opinion). keep in mind It DOES lag and stutter quite a bit but it's not TOO noticeable in battles. It mainly lags when you are running around the world and orientating the camera. The cutscenes look great (in my opinion) and dont stutter at all for the most part. Throughout the game you probably won't see TOO much aliasing except for when you are in-game, the cutscenes tend to look quite smooth comparitively. I have seen many people complain about the controls, but in my experience; if you use an Xbox One/Xbox 360 Controller and change the in-game button prompts to use "gamepad prompts" instead of "Keyboard prompts" in the Title screens' settings menu, then you really shouldn't have any noticeable trouble with the controls. Now onto the screen resolution problems. This game has NO resolution settings (the only option you get is to run the game in either windowed or fullscreen), however this doesn't matter too much if you happen to have a 16:9 display. I am playing on a 50" LCD TV at 1776x1000 and I don't see hardly any problems (aside from the aforementioned minor aliasing in-game). However if you are a person whose display is a 16:10 ratio, i can't say for sure that you won't have problems with the games resolution (I have heard that a modder has made a fix for the resolution problems). I haven't experienced ANY of the crashing or glitches that have been described and i found that using a microsoft gamepad fixes the "instantly quits when you hit escape" problem.
The real down-side to this port is the fact that nothing seems compressed, having to download 49.4 GBs of data for a game that came out on the XBOX 360 and PS3 is kind of ridiculous. ESPECIALLY when you realize that there are no higher resolution textures then there were in the original game (which WOULD make up for the size of the game if they WERE there, which they are NOT).  I believe most of the extra space is due to the fact that languages for the games audio and text are not region locked to what country you downloaded it in. What do i mean by this? Well, Everybody who downloads the game has to download Both Japanese and English audio files as well as different languages for all the text in the game: German, Italian, Spanish, and French ON TOP of having english and Japanese. Being able to decide on either Japanese or English audio is actually a really welcomed addition, however the amount of data that decision ended up adding to the game kind of ruined its practicality.
Now you might have read this review and concluded that this game is not worth buying, and in many ways that is probably true; however, if you have got some free time for a long download and plenty of space on your hard drive, Then I sincerely do recommend this game for the $15.99 asking price, It's still beautiful and it's still FFXIII on my PC. Which i never thought would happen. I am only an hour or so into the game and these are only my first impressions, i will continue to update this review If more problems appear down the road.

Tacoma is the long waited successor to the game Gone Home. From the people who brought Gone Home comes Tacoma which is on par with Gone Home except set in space and in the future. So if you have played Gone Home, then you will feel right at home with this one. Even if you haven't played Gone Home, this game doesn't require playing Gone Home to know what is going on. Though I do recommend checking out Gone Home if you don't know the hype for it. Now for the plot of Tacoma, the game is set in the year 2088 A.D. approximately 93 years after the year Gone Home took place in. You assume the role as a woman named Amy Ferrier, an employee of a space station operations company called Venturis, who is assigned to a mission by traveling to the abandon space station Tacoma, and learn what was the fate of the crew that operated the station. The movement and audio records of the crew are all monitored with the use of an augmented reality program where you "visually" see the crew members' actions and movements with the audio records that are found in certain sections of the space station. As you progress in each section of the station, you slowly learn more about the crew by finding their living quarters, documents, photos, text messages, and objects that help establish who each of the crew members are. This game was a great addition to Gone Home as it has a similar game structure except with better visuals and a more complex plot. There is more voice acting than what was offered in Gone Home, Sarah Grayson who voiced Sam from Gone Home returns as the voice of Amy for this game. While Gone Home was a period game, this one is a not too distant future setting. It's unknown what the world will be like in the year 2088, but I do like how the game explored subject matters that either improved or worsen by the year 2088. Show casing that as human beings evolve, society will always have its share of problems. If you like narative exploration games like Gone Home, then this game is a must for anyone who likes to sit back and explore a wonderious future that may yet to come.

A lot of people laughed at this game, and so did I. Then I tried it out of curiousity, and promptly lost a couple of days in it.
You need to play this game as you would minecraft. It's kind of a zen thing, you do repetitive tasks, but it's really compelling in a strange way, and it sucks up so much time and you know you should go to bed but you just want to go back and do _one_more_thing.
The graphics are decent for a game of this time. The mud effects on vehicles are nice, and the lighting is good. Skyboxes are very pretty. Vehicles are amazingly detailed, every time I buy a new one I spend a good couple of minutes just looking at all the work they put into the model. The environment textures are relatively low-res, which is a shame.
The driving physics are... adequate. They're not great, but you don't really notice when you're playing. It's not like OMSI or ETS2, where you are really into the driving aspect of the game. That isn't really the point here. I'd like to see some improvements, though.
The forestry physics are... surprisingly good. They're still quite buggy, but compared to other simulator titles, they're pretty damn good. It's perfectly functional and enjoyable, but not exceptional.
Sound design is good, the vehicle sounds are surprisingly nuanced, and you can hear the engine and transmission system working independently of each other. The environment sounds are just lovely, with animals, wind noises, planes passing overhead... It's quite immersive. For me, sound design like this is lacking in a lot of games. It's no OMSI, but it's better than ETS2, and this is a core part of the game's immersion in my opinion.
Overall I definitely recommend trying it, especially if you enjoy resource gathering games where you can just zone out and relax, like Minecraft or Terraria.

The plot of Tacoma develops step by step in a very innovative way.
As you start with no information about what has happened and why exactly you’re here, you dig for more information while you’re floating and walking around the space station, and the story and its intrigues begin to unfold. You immediately want to learn more about the (very diverse!) characters, who are the driving factor of the story, and you do get to know more about them in an interesting manner of getting chat glimpses, photos, visiting their personal quarters and listening to conversations, which you can rewind to look at them from different angles and follow different characters.
Lots of love for details and making the characters very close to the player in the way their stories are presented.
The Fullbright team really knows how to tell stories!
I really enjoyed this game in almost one sitting. Yes, it is rather short, but the atmosphere of the story and the thought-through execution of the characters' personal situations make it feel a lot longer while playing.

It breaks my heart to give this a thumbs down.
I am an independent professional wrestler, so the subject matter of this game is extremely interesting to me. I love the idea of playing a game as a struggling Indy wrestler trying to make it in a cutthroat and difficult business. Indy wrestling is driving 250 miles to get paid $20 to wrestle some has been who thinks he's too good for you and intentionally makes you look bad. Its about passion and love for the carefully constructed performance art that is professional wrestling.
This however offers nothing to simulate that experience. Instead, you have a completely luck based system that in my few hours of play seems heavily and consistently biased toward the CPU (the last match I played I did five strikes early in the match, calculation gave each around an 80% chance to hit, four missed). You face no name indy wrestlers that inexplicably have unbeleivable statistics and are seemingly impossible to beat because of the luck based gameplay determined by the statistics. There is no incorporation of match psyychology, or anything to make this a pro wrestling simulator in the least bit.
Worst of all, the performance art aspect of pro wrestling is completely lost in this game. Your success is measured exclusively by your win/loss record. Putting on a great match is absolutely meaningless unless you win, and the matches are simulated completely as competition rather than performance art.
I don't understand how GreyDog can simulate pro-wrestling so well in TEW and so poorly in this game. If you are looking for a great pro wrestling simulator go for TEW 2013. And if you want to experience the life of an aspiring wrestler, either play WWE 2K16 or train to wrestle yourself. It will be easier and less frustrating than this game.

I almost didn't write this review. I almost didn't have the patience to get to the end of Teslagrad. And that would have been a terrible shame, because it's a beautiful and intelligent game from start to finish. It just does one thing wrong that nearly killed the whole experience for me, a thing that you really need to be prepared for if you want to see the rest of what it offers.
Teslagrad is unsurprisingly set in the city of Teslagrad, a sprawling, steampunky place with one hell of a tower in the middle of it. You play a small boy of auspicious ancestry who flees capture one night to find himself in that very tower. This is where most of the game will take place, with you working to unlock the upper floors as you find new abilities to advance. The theme of the game is magnetism, so your powers will allow you to attract and repel objects to great effect. It's a neat, tricky gimmick with some clever puzzles, but it's a very directed experience with few branching paths and no sequence breaking.
It's not a long game, either, clocking in at around three to four hours from start to finish. There are secrets to find, however, in the form of 36 scrolls (also the game's only achievements). You'll have to do some searching and some challenging puzzling to find them, and you need 15 to get to the endgame anyway. There's an alternate ending if you find them all so there's a few more hours of magnetic wizardry if you want, but it's hardly necessary. The actual platforming handles well, aside from a bit of that floatiness that tends to plague indie platformers. It's nothing damning, and it does allow for some fun physics shenanigans in a few of the puzzles.
You'll also face off against a few bosses, and this is where the game nearly lost me. Like the rest of the game, the bosses are clever and beautiful and challenging, but one little detail transforms them from climactic battles to infuriating slogs. You see, you have no health in Teslagrad. One hit kills you, usually starting you back at the beginning of the room. Coupled with bosses that have challenging patterns that must be memorized, this is a recipe for intense frustration. You might have to repeat a pattern three or four times as it speeds up and gains new hazards, and one wrong move will see you starting from scratch. Some of the puzzles are equally lethal, the standout being an anti-gravity ascent through a field of electricity that took me dozens of tries.
There is a very real possibility that Teslagrad will make you rage, and it's such a tragedy because the game is otherwise brilliant. The art style is gorgeous and animated in incredible detail, the story is excellent (told through charming puppet interludes), and the setting is a real stand-out amidst a sea of steampunk dreck. I have to recommend Teslagrad for its many strengths, but there's no shame in checking out of this one when it gets too tough. Approach this one with as much patience as you can muster, or give it a pass if you're prone to fits of controller-flinging.

I've been playing for several years now, and I wanted to write an honest review, so here it is.
tl;dR: skip to the Conclusion at the bottom.
This game is an exceptionally good DTCG (Digital Trading Card Game), it kicks MtG and other cards games (Hstone) butt by far, which is saying a lot considering both those games are made by huge companies.
Overview
This is a Free game that manages to give a balanced and challenging experience while avoiding P2W (Pay to Win) altogether. It focus on strategy, anticipating your opponent's moves (thanks to simultaneos turns, see below), and its artistic aspect is excelent (all cards are fully animated).
Pros:
+ It's Free! You can play this game for free, or you can choose to spend some bucks in it to get more cards. Even if you don't want to spend real money, you can still get the same cards by playing and earning in-game free currency which will allow you to get boosters with more cards. You also get free cards almost daily.
+ Real TCG. There's a reason TCG are called that way, Infinity Wars Reborn lets you trade your spare cards to get the ones you need, be it for building a better deck or just to complete your collection (there's a collectible aspect with premium cards that have platinum or gold borders, and foil effects).
+ Simultaneos Turns: One of the strongest points of this game is simultaneos turns. Unlike MtG where you play, then your opponent plays, and so on, in Infinity Wars Reborn you both play and the turn resolves at the same time, so you need to try to anticipate if your opponent will attack, defend, use abilities, etc, which makes for some very interesting mind games, and actually requires skills, not just having 'good cards'.
+ Animated cards! Each and every card is animated. I dare you to find another free online card game that offers you the same (100% animated cards). Not only that, the artwork is just amazing, professional artists work on this game and the quality is superb.
+ Competitive, challenging and balanced gameplay. Infinity Wars Reborn has many factions you can play with, they are all balanced and they can all beat each other in many (I really mean it: many!) different ways. The amount of strategies and combinations is endless, and two people using the exact same deck can still use the cards in very different ways to win.
+ Good starting card collection. When you make an account and start playing, after you go through the tutorials, you can play the Campaign, and you'll be rewarded with pre-made decks of each faction (WIP) after you complete each campaign. Not only that, you get a free 5-cards booster each time you level up. As if that wasn't enough, you can complete daily quests to get in-game currency (which you can spend to get more cards), and you also get a free daily reward just for logging in (cards from different rarities, XP boosters, and even 5-card boosters). It's incredible the amount of cards this game gives you for free.
+ Store. When you play you win IP (Infinity Points), these is the free in-game currency which you can spend to get more cards. You can also spend real money if you want, either to get more cards or to dress up your battlefield and decks with beautiful artwork.
Cons:
- Some minor bugs that are still being worked on. Development is slow from time to time, but these guys aren't Wizards of the Coast or Blizzards, so it's to be expected.
- Lacks proper marketing, this game is ideal for streaming and chilling, but somehow it's not that known (yet).
- Addictive, you'll find yourself wanting to play moar and moar. You have been warned.
Conclusion (rating: 8/10):
If you like TCGs, if you have ever played MtG in real life and miss the feeling it gave you the first time you played it, then you need to try Infinity Wars Reborn. It's a rock-solid card game with beautiful artwork.

Infinity Wars is the type of digital TCG that blows you away on many fronts.  It has many innovative features and in a lot of ways it is the best digital TCG out there (though it has some shortcomings).  Why do I believe this?
-  All the cards have animated art!  Yep, you heard that right.  This gives the game an aesthetic value and beauty that is unmatched by most other digital tcg's.  Some of these cards have full animations!
-  The tactical depth of this game blows away all other TCG's.   You have a support zone, assault zone, defense zone, and command zone.  It's easy to get used to and allows for a lot of tactical depth.  If Hearthstone is checkers, this is chess.
-  The factions are cool, cards have a lot of flavor, there are custom battlegrounds, card backs, avatars, and card effects you can purchase.   But it is NOT pay to win.  You can unlock packs pretty easily without spending a dime; trust me, I didn't spend any money for a very long time.  But eventually I started to spend money on some of the preorders when new sets were released.
-  Yes, you can actually trade cards with other people so it is a true TCG.
-  The draft format is fun and doesn't cost a lot of points.  And yes, you can buy in using Infinity Points that you earn in the game so once again - you don't have to spend money.
-  There are ranking systems, prizes, etc.
Some of the Downfalls:
-  It needs more players so I'm hoping this new release draws in a new audience.
-  There were bugs from time to time in the past, though ever since a new company bought the game, I haven't run into any more bugs.  So this seems improved.
Conclusion:
This is an amazing game.  Play it, get a couple of your friends to play it, and help it blossom.  There is real potential here.

The cards are well balanced and attractive if simply animated, and acquisition is fair if a bit grindy. The excitement of opening a new pack as real as a physical TCG. The factions and commander system in which you combine them provide lots of variety from game to game and deck to deck, as well as each faction having plenty of its own character. The playerbase is far smaller than the quality deserves, but friendly and non-toxic as a whole, and especially for online pvp. The queue times are a begrudging criticism, but the pve campaign is frequently improved and expanded, and can still offer some challenge and progress towards acquiring cards.
I begrudgingly admit its not without faults. The queue times and matchmaking suffer from a lack of players, and there are bugs that sometimes persist over several patches. The core gameplay is so fresh and charming even to a veteran card flopper it's worth forgiveness for its flaws.

This was a learning experience, but not a pleasant one.
People have gone so far as to call this a reskin, Civ V in space with nothing substantial added and many key elements removed. They're closer to the truth than I would like to admit.
When the game was initially shown off, it looked like Civilization V running a beautiful, polished mod. When the first screens were posted, they showed off a game that was essentially the same as the game before it, down to the damage summation screen. This unspoken (but obvious) similarity continued to shine through with each new revelation.
So, really, the question is 'why am I so disappointed playing a game that is exactly what it looked like it was going to be?' The fault in this case may live as much with those of us who had this suspicion and bought anyway as with the developer who knew we'd do just that, but however you place the blame there were choices made in the development of this game that simply must be addressed.
Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth shows a clear and unmistakable LACK OF EFFORT. Not only are many systems simply cut-and-pasted over from Civilization V, but even much of the diplomatic and interfacial dialogue is word-for-word the same. Any of the additional personality you would hope for to compensate for a lack of leaders to play is not only missing, it's actually reduced from what Civ V offers. But really, that's not the part I feel is most damaging. No, that's a combination of THE PRICE and, still worse, THE INEVITABILITY OF PAID DLC that will address the obvious oversights made at launch. It feels almost as if this game was stripped of features and released in this state with the intent of giving fans something they would have to keep supporting through DLC to get the experience they thought they had already paid for.
I do not recommend this game in this state or at this price, I let my adoration for the former title and the company behind this cloud the evidence offered during the game's development. Patching alone is not going to be enough to fix this game's shallow presentation, and unless the developers commit to MEANINGFULLY improving the experience of this game through a free expansion, I doubt those of us who are currently unsatisfied will feel anything other than exploited by a company we trusted to give us more than they did.

I did not play much FF-like games. I guess the only ones were Agarest and Last Remnant. You can count parts of Evoland, too. I liked both Agarest (although at some point combat became too much of a pain even on auto-battle) and Last Remnant. I hoped this one to be close to Last Remnant. It was not.
Battle seems confused with itself: like, should I be auotmatic, or should I make user push buttons? Should I be real-time or turn-based? The idea of a time limit on your actions is a good one, since it can help keeping the pace and provide a real challenge, but when it's not something like a slo-mo, but rather than, practically, real-time it becoems a pain. You need too much concetration and too good a reaction time to be able to keep-up. And inability to do some actions, because the gauge has not filled in does not help. And the fact that you can't dodge anything (in real-time battle!) a big part of the battle becomes luck-based, rather than skill-based.
But screw the combat: maybe story and characters are ok? Well... I was not able to sympathise with any of them. They seem to be too cliched, too presumtious... Like they're a lacking an actual soul. I mean really good characters just grab you by the throat from beginning of a story. These ones wer enot able to do that for me in an hour. Hell, Talion from Shadow of Mordor or Altair from Assassin's Creed seemed to have more behind them then Lightining or Snow or whatever. If it was a low-budget anime for 10-13 episodes that could have been ok, but in a supposedly AAA project - not so much. And why the hell some characers keep their mouths open after they stopped talking?.. Can't they breath through nose like most other people do?
Graphically game is good. At least cinematics are. Even though they are 720p they look very detailed in fullHD monitor. And the game in general has some style, but... On PC you forget that when you get into actual gameplay and see lots of muddy textures. Dunno how it was on consoles, but it seemed like it looked better somehow. On PC... More like PS1 game, rather than PS3.
So, in the endd - meh. Gonna stick with FFXIV, I guess.

When Game Informer magazine came out in August 2015 - two years ago - it had a compelling cover for a game which had yet to be released.  I read the entire article, and realized I had to play this game.  There was just enough detail balanced with mystery, especially as it relates to the story and the game mechanics, that it drew me in. I wanted this game.
This isn't a first-person shooter (although, thankfully, it is first-person).  You won't be shooting bullets, or slicing and dicing with a sword.  If you've played the game Gone Home, and liked it, you'll like this game even more.  If you're not a fan of Gone Home, especially because of the "shortness" of the original game, Tacoma has a lot more story, depth, and a slightly more complicated game mechanic.
With Gone Home, I felt like I was playing a character that was coming home after being away for a while.  Role playing is fine, but it's been a long time since I was a teenaged girl returning home to my family's creepy mansion in the middle of nowhere.  Oh wait, no, I was never those things.  And I think that's what confuses some people about Gone Home.
Playing as the main character of Tacoma feels more realistic because you haven't ever seen the spaceship before. You aren't coming home. You've never been here before.  And neither has your character.  So, things are more congruent. It's more believable to the average player, as a person.  Tacoma has a more human element to it.
Then, there's the game mechanic.  You're on the ship, exploring, and trying to figure out what happened. I mean, you and your character are.  You've been contracted to retrieve data from the ship's artificial intelligence which, thankfully, isn't just a straight-shot rail from beginning to end.
There's zero gravity in The Hub, plus different areas (with gravity), containing one or more locations per area.  The ship is surprisingly small, but it ends up feeling larger.  One, because you are the only person there in the ship.
What happened to everyone?  You'll have to find out.
The nice thing is, this game will not leave you questioning anything in the end. You won't be shaking your tiny fists at a random author who killed off everyone you loved, one by one, until there's no one left.  There's closure, and that's sometimes enough for most people.
Does the game hand-feed you at points? Yes. But I think the game developers tried to make the interactions seem more human.
We start out knowing nothing, and only through exploration of the physical ship, and the ship's virtual-augmented-reality system, do we learn more and more about the ship, and its inhabitants.
Protip: If you want to get all the achievements, especially the last one I got ("ARdcore") make sure you go into every room, view every desktop, click every icon, expand every picture, click every "link", open every door, unlock every lock, and be methodical.  If you don't care about achievements, just play and have fun.
You experience the game through a combination of "the real world" and a holographic heads-up-display augmentation.  Both the interface and the story are immersive, so you'll feel like you're uncovering a mystery.  It feels like you're reading a good mystery book. One that's not going to leave you hanging.
As much as enjoy watching TV shows, or playing games, where answered questions simply uncover more questions, I also prefer a simpler story. I don't mind twists, but I want things to finish, or at least leave off in a sequel situation.
I've heard a few people complain about a bad cost-to-gameplay ratio.  This game doesn't really have any replay value. You'll play it through once for fun and, if you need to, perhaps a quick but thorough walkthrough to get achievements.  If you blast through the game, not reading everything, not clicking everywhere, you'll probably get a few hours' worth of entertainment.  I've seen a low estimate of two hours, but someone on YouTube did a full ARdcore run with waffling in just over an hour.  Me?  I have ten hours in, and feel like I'm done with the game. All achievements, and didn't miss anything.  If you divide the cost of the game by the average play time of 2-10 hours, I don't think you'll be disappointed.  If you really want a good deal, just add it to your Steam wishlist, and you'll be notified when it goes on-sale.  I paid the pre-order price, which was $2 off, so it ended up being $17.99.  Even at the low end of two hours (any faster and you're going too fast), you're basically paying $9 an hour.  That's close to minimum wage, so I'm cool with the cost.  I probably wouldn't pay more than $20, though.
Sadly, I don't think there will be a Tacoma sequel. The game wraps up too nicely.  It would be bad.  But I'm super excited to play whatever Fullbright and associates come up with next!

An excellent story from the creators of Gone Home. It attempts and succeeds in innovating on the "walking simulator" genre in a way that introduces novel game mechanics and cuts through a lot of the sameness that has come from other studios in the wake of Gone Home.
What the game does right is in how it uses its primary story telling device, a game mechanics which allows you to play and reverse briefs snips of the lives of the crew of the abandoned space station, Tacoma. How amazing this mechanic was did not set in until I had encountered it once or twice and managed to see the full potential of it. Without spoiling too much, it allows you to be a fly on the wall of incredibly intement moments all happening simultaneously. The story plays out in multiple places  at once and it manages to break away from a linear story, while still being contained to a straight path.
There were multiple times during the game where I found myself craving a full experience with combat and the story mechanic intermixed in. I think moving forward, story driven action games should take note on how to tell a narrative without the need for a simple cut scene. This game shows the potential for similar fly-on-the-wall mechanics.
The game does have some pit falls, one being the atmostphere itself was not quite as inviting as other walking simulators. Essepcially when compared to Gone Home, where you felt like you where snooping quietly through a house whose owners might return any minute, Tacoma feels a bit bland in comparison. A little bit of tension does build, but you never really feel in danger at point. A story unfolds before you, but you are never really sure what your stake in it is. I was certainly interested in what happened to the crew and that propelled me forward, but the atmosphere did little to establish my characters personal stake in the story.
There is one mechanic which I felt was under utilized, and that was your contacts with the outside world. Periodically you do receive Emails and messages from your company, but these are never straight forward and offer little more than reminder of your quest. I would read them expecting something to give me an insight into potential dangers or help create some personal stakes. But unfortunetly it never happens. You are a silent observer, and it feels like you have very little impact on the actual world for the most part.
I'll say again, the story itself is enough to make up for this. But I think it shows that setting is very important for these kind of games. Gone Home works because the personal stake is very easily understood. The kind of voyerism that it employs, going through people's cupboards and dressers, is something we are conditioned from birth to know is wrong. So it feels dangerous to do it even in a simulated enviornment. A game by a seperate company, Firewatch, has some similar beats to it. Walking through a forest park, finding people's personal belongings, conversing with a distant friend. The stakes are personal and more readily relatable. Tacoma doesn't manage to hit this stride, which is disapointing because it would have moved the game from really quite good to excellent.
Overall, I highly recommend the game. The story is fun and good sci-fi and the game mechanics are novel enough to elevate the story even further. The game may be a bit short for some, but for those who are fans of the Walking Simulator, it really sets the bar for inventing new ways to tell a story beyond the linear copy-cats which have flooded steam. It shows that there is a lot more to be expected and gained from this genre from truly creative designers.

This is a very good puzzle platformer.
While playing through I felt that the creators drew inspiration heavily from Metroid and Mega Man, a feeling which is actually confirmed in-game via some background objects and animations.
The artwork in this game is gorgeous. It's Rockman platforming with Metroid atmosphere. Lots of lonely and anxious jumping with some upgrade collection in a giant maze.
The plot is unveiled mostly through static and dynamic imagery. Text is almost non-existent.
There are not many enemies to defeat. The majority of fighting is done against a few difficult bosses. There is no health, ammo, or lives to worry about and you respawn in the last room you entered so the game is very forgiving of mistakes.
Controls are a bit slippery at times and could use some tightening up but it's never frustrating. The control scheme is a bit strange on keyboard. Switching between tools mid-action requires moderate dexterity at times.
Overall I enjoyed everything and can't complain about anything.

Teslagrad is somewhat oddly categorized on the steam market. I went in expecting a metroidvania and got a platforming puzzle solver game instead. Although I was surprised, the game exceeded all expectations for me.
The entire game has no dialogue and the story is gathered from grabbing these battery shaped objects throughout the tower you are climbing. You solve puzzles with the power of polarities and some teleport magics. The puzzles are fairly simple with a few difficult ones here and there but the true challenge is solving the puzzles to grab the batteries for more story. Enemies are fairly rare and you will most likely die to the environment rather than being attacked by anything.
Bosses however, are the games absolute strongeset point. Given that you die in one hit regardless of the situation certain bosses become very difficult as they require accurate jumps, reactions, and knowledge to overcome. You will die probably a minimum of three time per boss. The later ones will cause slightly more headaches as the patterns have surprises added in. The game is difficult by no means and repeated attempts will probably result in victory.
The music is pretty good with some influence from Russian culture. The art is also quite pleasing to look at. My one gripe about the game is that navigating up the tower you are climbing to collect batteries you have missed is a huge pain. At the end of the game, you are required to have at a minimum of 15 batteries so for those who wish to avoid backtracking up a long climb I would recommend you collect 15 before the end of the game. The game also seems to use an excessive amount of power for what is present in the game. I'm not sure if it is the Unity engine or bad coding practices but my processor was certainly doing some work running this despite being a fairly good processor.
I would recommend you buy the game and give it a run through if you enjoy puzzle games somewhat akin to portal levels of thinking and thrilling boss fights. I'm sure the game would be much longer than the three hours I spent on it if I actually made an active attempt to find all the batteries. Running through the game took me about 3 hours with some time spent backtracking for the 15 batteries.

It's difficult to put a finger on what genre Tale of Wuxia belongs to.
It's an unique blend of Visual novel, Rpg with both on "rails" and free roam/multiple choise moments, charecter training segment, dating simulator / friendship management aspects  and tactics type combat with mutiple endings based on choises and statistics with morality paths, crafting and bucket loads of martial arts techniques to find.
Sounds complicated ?
You'd be right.
You start as a novice who know's nothing about martial  arts but has big dreams of following the footsteps of his greatest hero nobody, who was a legendary kung fu master.
As a hero you spend your early years training with your master, designing how you build yourself by managing your daily tasks, participating in evens and running chores. As time passes you get to make choises that shape the story that at times can lead to unexpected things, while gradually getting more and more freedom to act inpentendly, without your masters guidance.  These choises start with few simple training choises a month and  eventually lead up to a free roaming around china.
Gameplay is split to mainly five main parts.
- Training where you get to choose how to practice, you can do chores, earn your living, practice internal and physical martial arts or choose to roam around looking for events.
Training :
- Visual novel like Choise and test situations during discussion events, where you get options to choose from that all have smaller or larger consequences ( in long and short run).  As example you can see rival clans fight you can pick a side or ignore them, choise can affect your reputation or friendships, even endings.
VN segments :
- Tactical fighting, either as scripted event or result of your choise, anyone who knows, final fantasy tactics, tactics ogre, agarest so on... know's what kind of game play I talk about, you move in squares alone or with few people fighting enemies.
Fight mode ( style select window open):

Group battle :
- Free roam segments  come in early game when your master sends you to do chores or you follow some of your friends with their adventures. This is when the game turns in to a  normal top down rpg  in a set location, usually a town, where you can do side quests.  The twist here is that you always have an objective with time limit, so you can't always do everything with one try. As an example : you arrive to the first city  at 9 am, but you will be leaving at 3 pm, it's up to you what you do in between.
Town roam :
- Then there is map roam segmet that kicks in at year 4, and then things get confusing when you can move about china visiting old and new locations with new things to do and missions to follow. you could say it's exploration ish segment of the game, here you can also fight animals and learn harsh truths like : Stating who you are to a bear tends to have little effect.
Map roam:

Bonus image : Menu's and one internal art ( each has cool drawing)
There are lot of interesting aspects on all these game play segments but going in detail would take ages,  so I just highlight few.  Your  skill and friendship parameters affect what kind of styles you can learn from people you meet, for example train enough with musical instruments you can use sound as weapon. You can also find books about martial arts you can learn, hunt antiques, treasure chests, animals, whack a mol.. I mean mine.. collect herbs, fish, make medicine, craft weapons.. .. so on.
In combat itself you can use every style you have learned switching them on fly, you can even change your internal styles to mix to situation and use "ultimate skills" you find from the 14 legendary books of Nobody The known yet unknown legendary hero.
There is metric crap ton of things to do in this game, but it has a massive flaw that can be  a turn down to some people :
It's fan translated from chinese as far as I know, so some segments are well written but others are just plain confusing and painful to read, but if you can get past that, this is a very rich game experience with lot of replay value, specially for waifu hunters and morality testers ^.^ ( I had maximum friendship with all the ladies of kung fu world but only 3 came to meet me during valentines, I clearly fail at waifumon T.T).
Another thing that can be a game setter for some is the complete lack of quest list, you need to write up what you have to get or where to go, most npc's do not repeat their instructions, leading to confusing situations if you do not pay attention.
I fully recommend this game, it has exeptional amount of things to do for the price tag once you get out your first few training years ( you start at age of 15 aging along the game), but it does suffer from translation issues and some segments are untranslated , although those are not related to any of the stories, just side npc's mostly and at times that can create lot of confusion ( specially li's grammatical poetry tests that while cultural and lovely tests of wit in chinase become save/load trial and error in english-ish-moonspeak). Some of the minigames are also quite repeative and dull, I personally dislike fishing quite a bit despite it having the best art overally. And as for reated play troughs 20+ hours in not finished one yet so..  yeah.
Just.. remember, it's dangerous to go alone, take paper and pen with you.
Also : Be humble, respect the difficulty choise,  or not, you'll regret it =)

*cough* Diablo *cough *TItan Quest *cough* Now that I have your attention, I don't really think I have to say anything else. The two games mentioned at the beginning of this mini review tell you exactly what you want to know. Yes, it's an action RPG (all the mouse clicking is probably going to hurt your fingers). And yes, there's random loot. I hear you think; does this game show us anything new then ? Well... yes. You now have a pet that's with you 24/7. Bought the game last week, played over 100 hours.
The game is rough around the edges, I really can't deny that. Before I bought it, I was scrolling through all the reviews, almost didnt pick it up based on some issues I read.
Were there any bugs?
Yeah, some. I wasn't really affected by them to the extent some others had, but they did pop up every once in a while, nothing major though.
User Friendly?
Not really. Honestly, you'll get the hang of the general systems in place, but the game doesn't hold your hand in the slightest. There are some very good wikis though, great work to those who made them, really helped. I played the first playthrough without one, but really needed them for subsequent playthroughs. If you want certain endings or romances, you're going to have to follow them. Also, the UI could use some work.
English Translation any good?
Firstly, I have to say I truly appreciate the work the translators did, since I believe it was all fan made. Without them, us English speaking players wouldn't actually be able to play. The translation can go from great, to quite poor. It is common to see misspelled words, grammatical errors, broken English sentences, it can be jarring at times, but I got over it fairly quickly. That might bother some people, so keep that in mind.
Difficulty
Played on veteran, was quite challenging, got to the end game and was completely destroyed. Recommend playing on normal, even then the end game gets dramatically difficult, prepare yourself. (really though, end game is on a whole other level. Rookie might be best for some, though you can always lower the battle difficulty by changing it in the save file.)
Performance?
Ran reasonably well. Gameplay was generally smooth, though framerate did drop in some of the larger cities. Hard to comment on since its situational, but didnt have many problems with it.
Now outside of that, the game is basically a hidden gem. I really don't like using that phrase, but thats what it is. Found it on a whim, and it became one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences Ive had in a while. Combat is fun and engaging, managing your character and training him from a nobody to a martial arts master is rewarding and fulfilling, many different combat styles to choose from, forming bonds with characters feels worth it, huge amount of events, 4 main endings with branching routes and a long list of various sub endings. Its the game I always wanted to play, but didnt know existed.
For the current asking price, the amount of content in game is surprising. Some of which I have still yet to see, and a new patch is on the horizon for the English version which adds even more content, though it seems to have been delayed for a little while now.
So, I say give it a chance. It's one of the few games where I genuinely feel my purchase was worth it and it may end up being the same for you.
