A pretty good, if somewhat short, 2D adventure-RPG-or-something-like-that heavily inspired by Bloodborne. You play as a contract killer tasked to eliminate a target hiding in a manor invaded by unspeakable entities.
+ Excellent atmosphere, made even better by the sanity mechanic. The more you die, do unholy stuff, or give in to madness, the weirder the manor and its inhabitants become. Rooms will get crowded by Cthulhu's friends, and a lot of very strange timey wimey occurences will happen (this is the part I liked the most).
+ Solid gameplay, similar to Dark Souls / Bloodborne (managing stamina, rolling, parrying, resetting areas, finding your corpse to reclaim your XP, etc). It takes a bit of time to get used to it and the standard gamepad control scheme can feel weird at first. There are a few hitbox problems (that's more or less a feature in this kind of gameplay anyway) but it works quite well once you get the hang of it.
+ Complete freedom of movement. You can explore the entire manor from the moment you set foot in it. Some doors are locked, but you can always take an alternate route if you don't have the key. You can take on the bosses in any order (which could be deadly, since there's a high chance the first boss you'll encounter will be Len, who's actually an endgame boss).
+ You can replay the game as some of the bosses after you defeat them once. Their gameplay is very different from the main character's sword & gun playstyle, some of them being pretty OP.
- Level design is a bit confusing. As I said before, you can stumble on an endgame boss five minutes after starting the game, and get lost without finding the people who can level you up (there are several, each governing one of your attributes). Transitions between rooms can sometimes be hard to find.
- Lack of equipment variety. You can upgrade your starting gear, but you won't find better weapons or armor. Since the game is not very long, it's not really a huge problem. The ability to play as the bosses bring back a bit of variety.
7/10 Since we're probably never getting Bloodborne on PC, get this instead. It's obviously not as substantial, but it's still good, and manages to have a few original tricks up its sleeve.

Shrouded in Sanity is a magnificent little gem of a game that I stumbled upon by accident, and I consider myself fortunate to have done so. It is a wonderful action/adventure/rpg with clear influences by Bloodborne, as well as the Souls series, utilizing the aforementioned game's sense of constant danger, terror, and nuanced lore in order to draw players in and keep them engaged throughout the, about, 4 hours that the first playthrough lasts.
In terms of story, the game starts with our unnamed protagonist being unearthed and resurrected from her grave by a mysterious person, absent any recollections of who she was before her death. The mystery man tasks her with exploring a large mansion, and its surrounding estate, in order to determine the origin of a forbidding fog that has veiled the land and, if possible, lift it. In exchange, this cryptic benefactor promises to reveal her identity, as soon as her mission is completed. The plot is wonderful, the lore being progressively revealed by strange characters the protagonist will come across in her quest, as well as nuanced by examining various objects and points of interest throughout the environment, classic Souls style. There are strong Lovecraftian elements incorporated in it as well, which was a huge plus for me since I am a great fan of his work.
Gameplay-wise, the game is a straightforward action/adventure/rpg, as mentioned in the introduction. You explore the mansion, fighting and slaughtering any enemies you find obstructing your path in order to survive as well as salvage their lifeforce, which can be used to strengthen your character's various stats, be it health, damage, stamina or number of "potions" you can carry, among others. If you have ever played Dark Souls, the game's mechanics will strike a familiar cord immediately, as will its interface. Their mentality is also the same; explore huge, imposing settings, battle imposible boss fights, piece together the lore of the game and, finally, die. Alot. Just be prepared for that last part because, at least during your first playthrough, chances are your character will meet an untimely end more times than you can count. But each death will bring knowledge, information on the behavior of certain enemies as well as specific places that you need to pay special attention to, making you more formidable with each ressurection. So, persevere, and you will emerge triumphant.
Regarding music, the game mostly consists of ambient sounds and soft, background tunes to keep you company without distracting you, which I liked. The sound effects are also great, further adding to the experience.
About graphics, Shrouded in Sanity uses a detailed, pixel-based art style which I loved. The artist has worked meticulously in order to convey the oppresive and mysterious atmosphere of the setting, having constructed a darkly ornate mansion and lonely, surrounding garden that will suck you in immediately, as well as a few other environments which I will not reveal, to avoid spoiling the surprise.
In conclusion, I totaly recommend this game, especialy if you are a fan of games like Dark Souls and Bloodborne. It is quite difficult, yes, but never unfair, and will reward you handsomely if you persevere. The story is deep and meaningful, the gameplay easy to learn and not so tough to master, and the setting both terrifying and alluring, just like the eldrich horrors you will face while exploring it. I am really looking forward to the sequel.

This is a solid online TCG for any TCG fan.  If you like MTG but are looking for something similar but different enough to feel fresh, this is the game for you.
PROS:
*There is a great variety of factions, each with their own unique theme and play style.
*The animated card art is spectacular.
*Battlefields and avatars can be bought with either real-life money or in-game currency for personalization.
*The game mechanics themselves are innovative.  I especially like the Commander concept.
*Mixing and matching factions and commanders really brings a lot of depth to deckbuilding.
*Speaking of deckbuilding, the deck building UI is easy to understand and user-friendly.
CONS:
*Match-making for PvP is... spotty.  There is an option to match with other new players, but you'll be waiting a while because...
*The community right now is made up of a lot of veteran players who have a metric ton of cards and run over newer players, making the barrier of entry for competitive play rather high.  You'll be losing a LOT trying to build up a base of cards without spending real-life money.  This game definitely isn't Pay To Win, because you can win with free cards, but you really have to be skilled or devote a lot of time into the game to do it.
*Speaking of building up a card base, you're only really guaranteed enough cards to build a deck with four factions playing through the single-player campaign.  If you want a deck with the other four, you'll have to put in that time and/or money.
Overall the positives greatly outweigh the negatives and I would recommend this game to anyone, but especially TCG fans of any kind.  This game could really use more people in the community, and with the new expansion out and the meta potentially changing with it, now is as good a time as any to get in on the action.

Dear Final Fantasy Fanatics,
Stop down-voting this review in defense of the franchise. I love the franchise as much as you do, but this game sucks and you know it. You wouldn't down vote this review if Squeenix named it outside of the FF franchise like they did with Last Remnant. Grow a pair and remove the downvote, will you?
====================================================
"Novelty at the expense of enjoyability"
BOTTOM LINE: Enjoy the story for what its worth by playing this game on Easy; otherwise, the entire gameplay experience is boring, time consuming, and grossly linear. Prioritize other games over this one, and only buy this title when it's on special.
TERRIBLE CAST OF CHARACTERS, not the least of which is the unwelcome return of FFX's Tidus under the name 'Hope'. The only character whom I remotely have a sense of respect and admiration for would be Sazh; the rest are emotionally underdeveloped or flat out immature, atrociously generically archetypical, and have hard-to-take seriously character backgrounds. Take Lightning, the main protagonist and heroine of this game: prior to becoming Keanu Reeves' "Neo" from The Matrix, her position and experience was roughly equivalent to being part of the neighborhood watch or school safety patrol. Technically she attained the rank of 'Sargeant", but even within the world of FFXIII that still suggests fat cops and donuts over being super human.
BORING STORYLINE; they really stretched out a relatively straight-forward story... they should have made this into a movie instead of a game like they did with the movie "Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within" (2001)
MONOTONOUS LOCATIONS; LOW VARIETY/HEAVILY RECYCLED MONSTERS: The vast majority of the time you're walking in a straight line, and the scenery and monsters never fail to be more of the same. This game has the least variety of monsters of any RPG in existence, including the first generation 8-bit games.
TERRIBLE BATTLE SYSTEM; Usually different isn't better or worse, but in this case it very much is worse from prior titles. You have substantially less control with nothing to make up for it. It's Active Time Battle system is hard to keep up with and is much slower than ATBs in previous revisions, or the synchronized system used by FFX. It is irritating as hell how unrealistic the character and enemy behavior is while idle. It is also irritating how unrealistically disproportionate enemy stats are in relation to their appearance (especially the larger machines). Some battles take forever to complete (5-15 minutes) minutes), and you're barely rewarded for the effor.  Oh, and let's be honest: you can win every battle by button-smashing auto-battle, including boss battles. In other RPGs, I'm making decisions, but in this game, I find I can just press confirm repeatedly and win every battle. I've literally stopped looking at the screen during battles; I now find myself reading a book while button smashing my way through any battle, including bosses, even on Normal (as opposed to Easy) difficulty.
USELESS EQUIPMENT, TERRIBLE UPGRADE SYSTEM: Equipment contributes so little in this game. You could probably stick with the initial equipment, never upgraded, and not miss out on much versus the supposedly best equipment out there. The upgrade system is terrible, in which there is no indication of what components can best be used in what combinations for upgrading; you'd have to either take notes or look up a guide online ('cheating'). By contrast, other games such as Elder Scrolls (Morrowind/Oblivion/Skyrim) record how components (ingredients) interact with other components so you can make better decisions in the future. It's basically a worse version of what Last Remnant had. As for the level up system... it is a primitive version of FFX's sphere grid: less versatile, and harder to use because you don't have all-or-nothing unlocks of nodes; it's always a guessing game if you have enough CP to advance a node.
MISPLACED SOUNDTRACK; would you play polka at a funeral? What about reggae at a Biker's Bar? The soundtrack to this game is great on a standalone basis, but completely misplaced. I don't want to hear JPop in the forest (or at all), and I don't want to hear Jazz in the wastelands! Honestly, the music is better suited to a dancing game; whenever I enter a battle, I feel like I'm about to showcase myself in a dance-off rather than engaging in combat with a foe.

Beyond Earth is an entry to the franchise that is at best a spiritual succesor to Alpha Centauri (AC) in theme and scope with Civilization V's (Civ5) mechanics in addition to some great ideas with the tech tree, affinity, virtue and quest systems. At worse, however, it will dissapoint those who have played Civ5 and/or AC to death as it doesn't revolutionize Civ5 and lacks the depth and personality of AC.
It needs rigorous patching, specially for multiplayer, and some balancing with the wonders and trade system. However, Beyond Earth has some interesting ideas and compelling mechanics. Recommended for those who are either new to the franchise or haven't squeezed much from Civ5 or AC. Expect some robust replayability with the affinities and modding scene, as well as any balancing/content patching and DLC.
EDIT: It seems that the DLC Rising Tide improves the game mechanics but sadly seemes like the game has been forgotten now with Civ 6 taking the lead.

Short Version:
To state the obvious first of all, this game is very charming.  The graphics and music are cute and very pretty, so pretty that a good chunk of my time in-game has been spent taking screencaps of the lovely environments and the adorable player character.
The pretty backgrounds and objects aren't strictly for show - with no dialog whatsoever, the story is told through the environment.  You can piece it together by looking at optional puppet shows that play in the background of various rooms, scattered propaganda posters, signposts, graffiti, murals, wreckage, statues, hidden rooms, and even the achievements.  Some people might find it a little disappointingly vague, but I think it adds to the mystery of the setting and enhances the "lonely" atmosphere (I mean, you ARE mostly alone in a huge tower).
The controls are simple - your standard movement, jump, and pause/map/achievement-checking buttons with 4 special ability buttons.  I would recommend using a gamepad if you have one (I don't), as a lot of the puzzles require a great deal of precision that's difficult to achieve with a keyboard.  The game auto-saves whenever you enter a new room, which is great because you'll probably die a lot.  Thankfully dying in this game isn't met with a lot of fanfare and you're quickly dropped back where you entered the current room.
Each puzzle is quite different.  They vary wildly in difficulty and fun-ness, although there do seem to be a few that are universally reviled (the notorious "Scroll #30") and some that are universally loved (hamster wheel room!).  While the game definitely doesn't focus on combat, there are 5 boss battles.  I found myself dreading the boss encounters, which sort of added to the narrative: you are playing as a mostly-defenseless little kid, so it makes sense for these huge machines to curbstomp you.  That said, the bosses are unforgiving and will make you hate your life.
Overall, I really enjoy this game and will probably replay it quite a bit if only to take in the gorgeous atmosphere again.  I have 2 tips for anyone about to start the game:  1, use a gamepad, and 2, get all of the achievements before you go to the final boss.  The final boss is a huge pain and the "normal" ending isn't really worth it IMO.  Finishing with all of the achievements gives a better ending and lets you restart the game with all of your special abilities from the very beginning.

* MAY CONTAIN VAGUE STORY SPOILERS*
I have played a fair number of 'first person snoopers' and enjoyed Gone Home immensely, so I had been anticipating Tacoma for some time. To be honest, the trailers released during development had left me a little cold, mainly due to the derivative setting and aesthetic, but I was hopeful that the game would put a fresh spin on the abandoned spacecraft trope.
Unfortunately, Tacoma is a quite underwhelming experience, particularly given how involving and thought-provoking I had found Gone Home to be.
To deal with the positives first, Tacoma's spaces are well laid out and full of lots of little items that add believability, if not character, to the environment. The conversation-scrubbing mechanic complements the exploration of this game-type pretty well. Following different strands of conversation as people traverse through spaces is reasonably fun. Also, the game's writing and performances are decent if unmemorable.
And this I guess, is at the heart of my criticism of Tacoma: the events that you are investigating, although they are life and death situations, feel very low stakes and undramatic. There is almost no conflict between any crew members, and given that they have been trapped in close proximity with each other for a year and that they find themselves in a very stressful predicament, you would expect nerves to fray and people to start turning on each other. Or for one of them to have a hidden agenda. SOMETHING to inject a sense of tension. To use some of Tacoma's inspiration points as examples, this game was crying out for a Carter Burke, or a HAL, or a Trey. As it stands, all six crew members in the game have problems, which we learn about through their emails and conversations, but no satisfying character flaws. I feel like Fullbright was determined to care equally about each character's portrayal and ended up with a half-dozen individuals who are all different shades of nice. As a result, the narrative has no real ups or downs and ends in a surprisingly abrupt manner.
So, if the story and characters are disappointing, is this least a game world that is enjoyable in which to snoop around? Not really. Part of the reason that the house in Gone Home was so enjoyable to explore was that having such a familiar real-world setting to inspect in detail in a videogame was actually kind of unique. Conversely, the abandoned space station is such a familiar trope in games that it's hard to get excited about slogging through that kind of sterile, cold environment again. Especially as this particular space station compounds generic architectural design with bland choices in terms of its lighting (dim, neutral) and color choices (beige, pastels). The crew members' individual cabins manage to add a little more personality to things, but picking up objects and opening drawers in Tacoma feels a lot less satisfying than it did in Gone Home.
So, ultimately I was left pretty cold and underwhelmed by Tacoma. And it's really disappointing to write that, particularly after waiting four years for it. I can't recommend buying it, particularly not at full price.

This game isn't for everybody. This is a slow, walking simulator that has you follow and listen back to the conversation of 6 people on board a space station. If you are looking for something highly interactive with gameplay mechanics you won't find it here. But if you are into science fiction, and walking sims in general Tacoma might be for you. Tacoma does a beautiful thing where it takes the genre, and shows a new interesting mechanic to tell a story and that is in the form of a rewind and fast forward function. Hard to describe written down, but if you have the time, check my review link above where I show you how Fullbright have implimented such a neat little mechanic into their neat little game.

Teslagrad is an interesting puzzle-platformer based on electromagnetism. The game's story is entirely show, don't tell, which is pretty uncommon and it allows for some player intepration whilst still being straightforward enough to follow. Exploration, finding play rooms and scrolls expands upon the story, which ties the story into the gameplay nicely and makes doing such exploration rewarding.
visuals and the
good soundtrack really set the mood, harmoniously matching the tone of the story.
I highly recommend the use of a controller as the keyboard controls are not superb, thankfully everything is rebindable, but even then a controller is much easier to use. As for the gameplay itself, the bulk of it is puzzles, some hard and some easy, most of which focusing on the use of magnetism to progress. The layout of the map is reminiscent of metroid games, and thanks to how they split the areas up, it is easy to backtrack and find missing scrolls. The hardest part of the game for most is probably the 5 bosses, the final boss is considerably challenging, however all the bosses have patterns and it shouldn't be so hard once you figure them out. The bosses do feel dissonant from the rest of the game, some meld well like the 2nd boss, which is the most puzzle like in my opinion, whilst other bosses are more luck/skill based like the 1st and 3rd bosses.
Overall I'd say the game is roughly 5-6 hours long, more for those who want 100% completion. I'd definitely recommend picking this up if you're a fan of puzzle-platformers, just be warned that the bosses are harder than expected.

Bear with me, as this is the first review I've written that wasn't in the pursuit of a community badge (I think). Generally I've tried to avoid the Steam review system, as despite the best efforts of a great many reviewers the big blue and red hands at the top of each label each review as calling the game GOOD or BAD. There is little room for subtlety in such a system, and while many reviews list both good and bad qualities of a game and insist that certain tastes and demographics should definitely avoid / immediately buy the game, the specter of the big, colored hand trumps the text of a review.
But Teslagrad, though.
This is a game which I have absolutely no trouble in plastering a big, blue hand on. Were this just a series of puzzle rooms with no connecting narrative, I still would have had a blast playing it. Maybe it wouldn't have possessed me to sing its praises in a review, but I would have finished it. As it stands, Teslagrad is one of the great meldings of narrative and gameplay to exist in the modern age of gaming. Teslagrad's is a story (nearly) without words, a story told through the environment and the somewhat optional collectibles. The few and far between mechanical puppet shows which play out are the closest the game comes to an exposition dump, and they are short enough to not impede enjoyment and completely skippable besides. The story is not that complex, but it is different enough from the usual fantasy offerings that it was a reasonable part of my motivation to finish.
Visually, Teslagrad is pretty damn tops. The character designs are simple, cartoonish and pleasing, while the environments and bosses have what I feel to be the perfect degree of detail and fidelity to fit in with the tone of the game. Had this come out in a time before every other indie game of note was a stylistically striking platformer I might gush more about the graphics, but our cup runneth high enough that I wasn't as impressed as I might have been.
The mechanics and feel of Teslagrad compliment the game perfectly. While gameplay concerning blue and red magnetic polarities is no longer a particularly novel concept, the execution of the puzzles and the way that they tie in to the story and world make up for this game coming too late for the idea to be novel. The puzzles never become too hard, and while it's possible that you will be tripped up at several points it will most likely be due to platforming difficulty rather than the inability to wrap your mind around a puzzle.
While there are faults in Teslagrad, none are so glaring as to ruin or even mar the experience. The game is slightly short, though this could be said to be to its advantage, as it never overstays its welcome or stretches itself too thin. One or too puzzles almost necessitated deaths to learn how they worked, and while trial and error is not an inherently bad method of teaching the player there was at least one occasion where I felt cheated into a death that the game could have been designed for me to avoid. Finally, without spoiling anything, the final boss could have been handled better. Their attack pattern and design didn't quite meld with prior revelations about the character and the end result is just a boss that feels designed as a generically powerful figure than the unique character he was subtly built up to be.
If forced to attach a number to the game, I would give it an 8/10. For context it is one of my new favorite games, but the parts that fail to shine as brightly hold it back from a higher score. Having said that, absolutely play this. If you enjoy puzzles and and platformers, or even just wish that more games had narratives that were married tightly to the gameplay, this is for you.

Made it as far as the first boss before deciding to just not play anymore because it was clear that this game was not going to be fun because it wants to copy the Souls games, which also aren't fun or well designed, and thus have gameplay that entirely revolves around trial and error.
So here is a review of the first boss.
She has three attacks.
One where she instantly swipes the player with her scythe, the attack is immediate, there is no animation for her preparing to swing; she just instantly hits the player.
One where she jumps up and smashes the ground for a small area-of-effect strike.
One where she summons an orb which lingers around the room and explodes.
The boss fights in two ways. One is by constantly spamming the jump attack, constantly. Literally seventy percent of the time you cannot hit her because she is flying towards you in the air. When she smashes down, if you try to attack her since that is the only real opening; she immediately recovers and will use one of her two other attacks. So you can't hit her while she is jumping, but when she smashes down there is a fifty percent chance when you try to hit her that she will instantly swing back at you and hit you. The other fifty percent chance is she will go to summon an orb, in which case you can actually hurt her while she does it although if she spawns the orb onto you that also will hit you instantly.
That is half of her attack pattern, is being constantly invincible while the only time she is vulnerable there is a fifty percent chance she will trade hits with you unavoidably and a fifty percent chance she won't but there is then another dice roll that she spawns the orb onto you which thus also hits you for unavoidable damage.
The other half of her attack pattern is her constantly running towards the player, and is faster then them, and when she gets in range she will use her immediate swing attack. You cannot avoid the attack without dodging or blocking, you need to do that before she catches up to you otherwise her attack will always land; which means you must spend stamina to save yourself from a mandatory hit. Problem is the player regenerates stamina extremely slowly, so while the boss is using this attack pattern you constantly have her bearing down on you always in offense mode while always having to lose stamina blocking or dodging her instant attack while she constantly pressures you.
So basically, if the boss is using her jump attack pattern; you randomly are forced to receive mandatory damage in order to hurt the boss. While the boss uses her run attack pattern, you have almost no time to actually function or attack back at her or even recover your stamina because she is always running at you always ready to instantly hit you the moment she gets in range which she will because she is faster then you.
How do you beat this boss, you beat it in the same way you beat the Souls games and most other pseudo difficult games; by trial and error mixed with random chance until finally you win because you kept playing until you memorized everything and eventually the random number generator let you succeed. That's it, that's these games.
There are other poor elements to the game that could be mentioned like how to gain currency from each corpse the player has to stop and perform a harvesting animation, but no, this is the only thing a potential player needs to know. The very first boss is incredibly unfair, poorly designed and fighting them is exclusively subject to random chance combined with memorizing their pattern down to every single frame; which their animations have very little of by the way.
That is the gameplay you will get, trial and error. And it's too bad, because the game world looked decently intriguing to learn more about. But honestly it's not remotely worth it because the gameplay is just going to be completely unenjoyable time wasting drivel. It's not going to be fun, it's not about fun, it's about generating an artificial sense of challenge which preys off the human desire to succeed and progress by making them face a trial which has a mandatory time requirement attached to it. Because you can't beat the challenge by being dextrous or thoughtful about how you play, you can only beat it by playing it until you memorize every poor, shoddy element of the fight. Then after that you then have to wait until random chance lets you win as well.
It's a great way to pad out the game since players are forced to spend far more time trying to complete everything since it is mandatory to have to dwell on every single part in order to actually complete it, as opposed to games where you can win by just thinking things through and having moderate intelligence.
Go play something fun instead.

This game inspirations are obvious. It has combat revolving around stamina management, dodges, learning enemies patterns and precise attacks. It has monsters that can and will (almost) insta kill you, but also allows you to roll away and heal with limited number of medpacks. It has death related resource that is dropped after death, monsters respawn after using save point and from the beginning you have access to almost every room and area except for few specific parts, like bosses lairs.
So yeah, it is like Dark Souls - or, to be more specific, Bloodborne, with its mad enemies, blood, insanity and cosmic horror themes, and XIX century Victorian era aestethics - but with waaaaay lower budget and one man's dev team. But it's very sincere soulsborne clone, that nails it's sad, oppresive atmosphere perfecly, has quite big world to explore and memorize (shortcuts, secrets and interesting lore included), and offers nice bonuses like NG+ (if you want to discover all endings) or fight chalenges. There is also some Ethernal Darkness and Resident Evil inside the mix, but the Souls part is the strongest.
Because it's low budget one man's team project some of the graphics are a bit too simple (except for backgrounds, those are quite lovely in horrific kind of way), animations lack frames, combat is clunky and too simplistic (only one sword, only one gun, only one light roll style. On the other hand you can stun and stab enemies and also counter their attacks, which is always nice), there is no equipment management and stats one is very basic, enemies lack variety (by that I mean I saw the same enemies in too many places), assets reusing is painfully obvious and there is some small, but irritating design choices / bugs (enemies can attack you seconds before you change rooms, you can't pick up items that dropped at the door et cetera). But as far as cheap soulsclones goes this one is solid and worth picking up.

I thoroughly recommend this game to any TCG fan or even any type of strategist for that matter.

Last shoot out, I was a notorious bandit, whenever you walked into any city you hoped and prayed you never ran into me.
Some asked me, what's it take to be a bandit - let alone a notorious one like me. Shooting to kill all folks you happened upon just cause.
Well it takes nerve. Lots of it. Anyone can hit the Mouse 1 button. Anyone can aim from far away and shoot, but it takes a special man to take fire and still maintain your nerve.
Why? Because that's when it counts.
Example, in elektro, at the power plant. On the roof, been laying there for at least an hour. Waiting for a bambi to run the field, maybe another bandit to shoot. You see I make them boys famous, at least I did. When suddenly a lowly coward got the better of me. Was on the hill. Shots fired. I could hear the snap of the bullets hitting inches from my head. Did I flinch? No. Did I cower and run? No. I let off a few rounds, spook the wannabe bandit. Then reload. I feel a pain in my right, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hit me. Flesh wound. But it will  hurt me if it keeps bleeding. So I heal up. See all bandits come prepared. Bandages, blood bags, the whole works. Maybe not an arsenil. But you carry enough to keep you alive.
So I yell to the man, "You hit me! You drew first blood! I hope you are proud of yourself, boy!" another few shots, all miss. The kid is scared, I can nearly smell it.
"Keep shooting! I am just bandaging up!" I yell out.
BANG BANG BANG! All miss.
"You missed me!" I yell into the mic.
Bang bang bang! then silence. Guy has to be reloading. I get a good reading on the shots. The snaps after the bangs. He is on the hill alright. I make a run for the ladder, I head down, I keep the buildings between me and him. That hill is high but it has many trees. Trees that cover him AND hide me from him. So I snake my way around. I go silent. I don't need to run away from this fight. See when you hunt people, you get a pretty good feel of who is scared and cowardly and who isn't. I been killed by better shots, I been killed by lesser shots. This guy was just trying his hand at banditing.
Long story short, it took me nearly 30 minutes to run around the hill, track him, see he left, track him more from his shots, then find him, hauled up on another hill over looking a road. I sneak his way. Gun in hand. Slow like. Quiet as death himself.
Feet away I play a remote mine at his feet, then walk away. I laugh once I am at a good distance. "YOU MISSED ME!" then I laugh and laugh. He heard me. He gets up all quick like and boom. I remote detonate the bomb. He is dead. I am alive.
See, keeping your nerve and finding creative ways to kill a man, is part of being a bandit.

TL;DR - if you liked playing Civ 5 + DLC, you'll like playing this. Call it Civ 6. Barely worth the $50 though. Think it's more worth 30 or 40. If you haven't played Civ 5, don't bother with playing Civ 5, just buy this instead - it's clear they're going to put most of their effort into this going forward.
--
Civilization: Beyond Earth is basically Civ 5 with a much more efficient engine underneath. Forget the 2 minute loading times, compared to the Civ 5 engine, this thing blazes through loading. In general it seems to be much more responsive than the Civ 5 engine, although you can see some lag in the animations occasionally. Nothing that interferes with gameplay, but to some game studios (like Blizzard) animation lags like this would be a no-no.
For the $50 price tag, what else do you get? Well, they've replaced the old tech tree with a tech web. However, IMHO it's more of a gimmick than an actual new mechanic. Sure you can cherry pick more stuff than you could before, but if you do so, you'll find that, say, your cities' health starts dropping precipitously. So instead of the tech tree being an explicit thing, it's now an implicit thing, that YOU now have to keep track of. Yay. What fun. Along with the tech tree, once you build buildings, they will often give you a choice about how to customize the building further through a new quest chain. Some of those choices are interesting, choosing one will affect how other competing civilizations interact with you.
They've added about 3-4 more strategic resources, and this mechanic called misma, which is a tile attribute that damages you if you stay in it. You can spec for misma manipulation and neutralization, so it is what I'd call a moderately interesting game mechanic.
Barbarians are now native alien life, barbarian strongholds are now alien nests. However, if you wish, you can actually convert the barbarians to your side and then they help defend your cities. Another moderately interesting mechanic they added in. Some of the barbarians now pack quite a punch - you have to pick and choose which barbarians you attack, and be prepared to build more military units than you used to.
They've added on an orbital layer to the map, you can launch satellites of various sorts, to attack and defend. Ruins have been expanded on, and your explorer actually has something more to do than just uncovering tiles now. They've added in crashed satellites, that only your explorers can recover, so keep one around nearby to send out. Basically ruins now spawn periodically and can mostly only be mined by your explorers.
Compared to Civ 5 + DLC, the number of starting civs is quite small, just a handful. I suspect they'll probably add a bunch later on via some DLC, but if you were paralyzed at the number of options for starting in Civ 5, you'll be relieved at the relatively small number of choices. If you liked all those choices, you might be disappointed.
In summary, much more efficient engine, additional interesting game mechanics, different enough from Civ 5 to be its own game, but it's questionable that it's worth $50. If you really liked playing Civ 5, you're going to buy this, if you're not a big Civ 5 fan, I'd wait for it to go on sale.

I went in to this game expecting a carbon copy of the Impossible Game, but a bit more tacky looking. It did seem this way at first, being perfectly linear and having many of the same spots as the IG. However, later in the game it came into its own with new unique paths and vastly varied challenges (likely inspired more by Geometry), and colourful visuals. I do have some individual criticisms, both good and bad:
- As someone who prefers to use the keyboard, it would be nice if space could instantly respawn the block on death
- Holding space/mouse should allow continuous jumping in my opinion, just to help the flow of the game. It feels clunky and janky otherwise.
+ The game is just as frustrating and addicting as I would hope, with you having to learn each section after repeated plays to overcome it.
- Relative to the above point, this means that the music resets every time you die, so you pretty much only hear the same part over and over again. It would be nice to hear more...maybe with a no-checkpoint mode?
+/- The music is nice and metronomical, but not all too immersive or motivating.
- The trail on the block seems tacky, in that it is always full whenever you land. It might appear better if the trails started smaller and got larger the longer you spend on a single straight without jumping.
- on the subject of the trail, it is already present in mid-air on respawns, and if you collide with and object in mid-air and fall, which doesn't look too immersive.
- The block doesn't change its angle on inclines/declines, so it appears to be a horizontal block sliding diagonally.
+/- The different foreground colours and changing obstacle and platform styles are nice, but it would be cool if the background changed with them.
+ Rolling obstacles and spikes jumping and falling is a really nice touch, and sets a nice challenge and feeling of pace
Here are some specific gameplay issues that I just wanted to air:
- There is a checkpoint around the mid 50,000 score point which drops you annoyingly close to an edge, so (at least when using the keyboard) it is pretty hard to instantly not fall to your death.
- At around the 70,000 score point, there is a decline with 2 rolling balls. Most of the time both balls will fall into the pit at the edge, but sometimes the second one rolls straight across and literally makes the game...impossible :P
Ultimately, the game is refreshing for only being £2 and actually feels like how Sonic the Hedgehog should play in some circumstances. The biggest issue is that the generic sequences at the start of the game are still very difficult, and people may lose interest before getting to the more fulfilling and vibrant parts of the game later on.

Not as good as Civilization 5 with 2 expansion packs.
This game is mechanically very similar to Civ5.
It has a lot of ideas that seem good, but don't actually work particularly well.
The tech web, for example, seems good, but necessitated lowering the power of wonders. This is because each player is unlikely to be at the same tech point and competing for them. The web also doesn't feel great, it's difficult to parse, making it easy to overlook certain techs. (it's very confusing in your first couple games)
The victory systems are interesting , but the AI players go for them very directly and all at once. This makes it difficult to prevent militarily, basically you need to have started building yours before any of the AI players.  Aditionally the game doesn't tell you what the winning condition was. If you like to have a longer game you need to turn some of these conditions off.
The aesthetic of the game I personally don't like, though I didn't realize this until I started playing. The terrain, improvements  and units really blend together on the screen(less so on some maps). This makes it somewhat hard to distinguish important facts and unpleasant to look at. (forests are oddly hard to see) In Civ5 everything stood out well and you could always tell what a piece of terrain was by looking at it, rather than needing to mouse over tiles constantly. The menus and UI are serviceable, but minimalistic, again not something I care for.
The game lacks the personality of the previous Civ games and Alpha Centauri. The whole experience feel pretty bland, you have no investment in the leaders you see in the diplomacy screen.
It is also disappointing that each faction doesn't  have a unique unit, though each of the three affinities has one.
There are no great people.
The virtue system, replacing social policies, isn't as compelling. Most of the options are simply stat changes. Though you get more of them and there are interesting synergy bonuses for combining a number of unlocked virtues in parts of the trees.
The covert-ops system however is nice, lots of operations that can be performed.
The orbital layer is a positive, allowing you to launch a variety of satellites that help you in various ways.
The aliens are a bit more interesting than the barbarians in Civ 5.
There are assorted artifacts an explorer can perform expeditions on, similar to archeology in Civ5, but with more results.

There is a dynamic quest system that allows you further customize you civ, mostly  giving you a choice of extra stats for buildings. It also gives you rewards of affinity points, science, energy(gold) etc.
The customization of the faction at the beginning of a game is also nice, allowing you to pick a number of traits that your ship lands with. This also might contribute to the blandness of those factions however.
Overall I'd say the game feels like a very extensive mod of Civilization 5 that certainly should not have cost 50 dollars.

I've been playing Civ since Civ I came out in '91. I was a huge fan of SMAC and played that game to death in the late 90s... it's still probably #1 on my favorites of all time. I remember well the release of Civ V and how everyone flipped out over the issues with the game. I'm currently 36 hours into C:BE having played two games to completion.
So it's tough to rate C:BE. Is it a perfect game? Of course not. Is it what I was hoping for? Not yet... but I can see where it will be. And that's the problem here, we have gotten ourselves in a situation where games are released half-finished with much of the content set aside for DLC. You can see a lot of gaps left where DLC will plug in later. But that is pretty common with almost every game out there, so should I not recommend this one because of it?
Here's why I do recommend it. First off, and most importantly, it's really fun. Even with the shortcomings compared to Civ V, there's a lot to do and it's interesting. The game is considerably different than Civ V, and unique among the Civ franchise, and these changes are a little tricky to figure out at first.
Next off, it runs virtually bug-free. No hang-ups, no crashes, it's smooth as butter on my four year-old mid-level PC. Everything works the way you would expect it. There are a couple of minor bugs in the quests and (as usual) some users can't even start the game but I think for the most part they did a great job on releasing a bug-free product.
Finally, even with the obvious opportunities for DLC, this game is engrossing and interesting. The sci-fi setting is really fun. The tech web, while confusing at first, is a lot more interesting to pursue that traditional linear tech trees (admittedly, this is an Endless Space innovation) and I can see how no two games will really play alike because of it.
If you were to ask me today, in October 2014, whether you should buy Civ V or C:BE I would say go with Civ V. It's a four year-old game with two expansion packs. However if you already own Civ V and want something new, definitely buy C:BE. I like it better than any of the 4x titles that have come out in the last few years. But as I said up front, I'm kind of a fanboy so take it for what it's worth.

I have very mixed feelings about this game.  As a long time fan of the Civ franchise, I want to enjoy it and there are a fair few parts of the game I really like.   I also love the rework to the trade system, allowing trade routes to be based off a max number per city instead of a max number over your entire civilization.  The outpost into city idea is a nice addition to the game as well, making it far more risky to simply plant new cities without the proper protection.
On the other hand though, there are quite a few things this game is lacking compared to past Civ games.  For one, there are no real air units.  Sure there are planes but there is only one type of plane that can be upgraded through the affinity tree system.  Because of this, you dont have bombers or jets or helicopters.  You simply have one type of air unit that spans your entire civilization.  They have also removed unit types almost completely, essentially making it so the only types of unit are ranged and melee.  Gone are the days of mounted units or armor units.  Gone are the days of special units to then counter those units or SAMs or anything of the like.  They've removed one time use units as well (missiles) which disappoints me greatly.
All naval units are now ranged (One boat, one carrier) which is another step back I feel.  Further more, the 'veterency' system (replaces the leveling system for units) only has one option.  You can either upgrade their attack or you can heal them instantly.  No more tile tailored soliders or units that move twice as fast.  Many of those buffs have are now placed in the affinity upgrade paths but again, these upgrades will span every unit of that type in the civilization that really lessens the combat of the game, I feel.
They have removed great people, replacing most of the benefits associated with them with the new quest system.  The quest system in itself is a great addition but I truly do miss the great people of games past.  Through the quest system, you can rank up your affinity level, give certain buildings extra stats or even make your trade ships safe from aliens.  It is a nice system that allows for some direction within your over-arching plan but it really doesn't make too huge of an impact on your game aside from the building specific ones and tile improvement quests.
Miasma is cool and the whole removal/adding of it based on your affinity can lead to some fun play but this game is a shadow of civ 5, even when that game was a fresh release.
If you like strategy games and you dont have Civ 5, buy that game and it's expansion packs.  If you want a dumbed down sci-fi version of Civ 5, by all means, purchase this game.  Hopefully through updates and expacs (hopefully less expacs and more updates) they will re-add much of what makes the civ games so much fun.
TL;DR
PROS:
-Units all upgrade at once
-Health (replaces happiness) has some cool functions
-The virtue tree synergy and the tree itself
-Bad♥♥♥♥♥looking units through the affinity trees (Supremecy and Harmony.  Not so much Purity)
-The miasma mechanic
-Cool aliens replacing barbarians
-Quests
-Diplomactic AI seems stronger than in other games
-Favor system (Diplomacy)
-Spying system is stronger than ever
CONS:
-No real upgrade for units through leveling them
-Very limited amount of units
-Only one air unit (Can upgrade down other paths but you still only get one that spans your playthrough)
-No SAM or Anti Air guns
-Only ranged naval units
-No submarines
-No anti-armor/anti-tank units
-No Great People
-Very few wonders compared to other games
-Dumbed down win conditions (The affinity based ones are basically the same, merely requiring different techs to complete each respective one.  Flavor text varies, requirements to win do not.)
I want to reccomend this game because I love the Civ franchise.  I've been enthralled with it since Civ 3 but each game, they make it simpler and simpler.  If you are a hardcore fan of the series, pick this game up and give it a spin.  If not, not that I would every advise someone to torrent the game, but torrent it.

I have to echo other reviewers in saying that this is less a game and more of a story. It's a great experience, and I loved it, but I would have liked a longer game for the money. That said, I'd still buy it again.
I really liked the plot, but I'm not sure the execution lived up to the premise.  On the other hand, the visuals, music, and atmosphere were stunning. (Acoustic track that plays in that one bunk scene is out of this world, pun intended.) And the characters were believable: they felt like real people, with strengths and weaknesses, and they made choices that real people would conceivably make. I would have liked to see the crew fleshed out even more, but it certainly makes for a tighter game as is.
My major complaint is that I could have done with a bit more of an ending. I do think this one is effective, but given the high stakes, the wrap-up feels rather quick. Overall, it's great work, there's definitely room for a sequel (which I doubt will ever happen, but I'm just saying, there's that huge poster in Nat's office...), and I'm excited to see what the folks at Fullbright will come up with next.

INK is a surprisingly good platformer!
Despite having some fairly difficult levels, it's not comparable to, say, Super Meat Boy. In some ways, this is a good thing! If you're looking to scratch some of SMB's itch without dedicating dozens of hours to mastering a game, this is a good option!
It took me less than 2 hours to finish all 75 levels, and around 3.5 hours to beat it again, this time collecting every coin (20), which was both harder and more time consuming, as you had to both play riskier to grab the coin, and spend more time exploring the levels, looking for it.
You probably know that the main mechanic is that you have to "paint" the levels to see the platforms. Even this is evocative of Super Meat Boy, in which I sometimes wasted time painting levels... with blood.
This seems an obvious mechanic in hindsight, but it's surprising how well it works!
In INK, you can double jump and wall jump. Touching a wall replenishes your double jump. The levels have you go through platforming, and sometimes having to jump on enemies (killing all of them) or collecting keys to unlock the end level's door. The levels should take much longer than a few seconds (most of the time).
When you die, you explode in colors splashes, coloring nearby walls. When you double jump, a similar explosion happens. Touching tiles will also color them.
This is basically the game (with a few more obstacles later on).
The color mechanic gives depth to the game in several ways. The most common is just how you'll generally play for the first time, sacrificing yourself to gain information. That's cool, but not
interesting.
It gets more interesting when you throw in speedrunning and flawless runs!
Flawless runs (no-death runs), although I can only imagine them being infuriating, should be very cool, because you'll also to play very carefully, trying to reveal the platforms without sacrifice.
Speedrunning is similar, because a sacrifice costs time. It may help you on the long run, however, if you choose the best places to die.
It also helps that the game is pretty short for speedrunning, or even multiplayer races should be fun (although I don't think there is built-in multiplayer).
I don't have much to say about level design. There are 3 patterned bosses, but they're not too difficult.
Level do get harder, introducing new hazard every few levels.
The first set of 25 levels has only holes and basic enemies; the second introduces spikes; the third introduce heat seeking missiles (that are a huge pain!). There are also collapsing platforms and keys, but what I mentioned above seemed the defining obstacles, in my experience.
Some of the levels follow a similar template, but get progressively harder, by introducing some spikes, or cannons.
The controls felt pretty good to much. It's a faster game than SMB, but not as tight, in places. What threw me off somewhat, was wall-jumping, because you jump off with quite a lot of speed. Other than that, I felt that the controls were really good. After getting used to them, some platforming feats were very satisfying!
One complaint that I have, regarding the no-death achievements, is that they're not very well supported by the game's interface. They have you beat each "world" (25 levels) without dying. If you die, though, you'll have to manually quit to the menu, and select the first level again. It's annoying because levels are placed linearly, so you'll have to go through 1-2-3-4-5-6...75 every time you have to switch for a distant level. Maybe a simple system to restart at 1-26-51 would have been better for these achievements.
I meant, in this game especially, I feel that the achievement reveal a different aspect of the mechanics, instead of being "just another challenge", since the paint mechanic does provide interesting choices or paths. As such, better support would be welcome.
It's a fairly minor complaint, though. I had a lot of fun in the game, and I may play some more, going for speedrunning, or flawless runs.
Recommended!

Alright. First of all, this game is Super Meat Boy. Keep that in mind.
Now that we have that out of the way, let me express how disappointed I am in INK. It has a lot of potential, but despite solid graphics and a moving soundtrack it is a mediocre platformer.
When I say it is Super Meat Boy, I mean that it has directly lifted a ton of its mechanics. Sawblade launchers, homing missiles and key-block barriers all feature heavily in INK. This would be forgivable, but...
It is not nearly polished enough to compete with Super Meat Boy. The game is 30FPS-locked, movement is slidy and imprecise, enemy hitboxes are unusual (small for rectangles, absurdly high for the "circle" missiles)...
In conclusion, INK does not feel anywhere near as fluid as its name would suggest. Give it a miss.

When you double jump while running off a ledge, if you jump a little late, the game uses your double jump. Mechanically this makes sense, since you ran off the platform, but in practice it's just really annoying.
A ton of the negative reviews for this game mention the character feeling very slippery. Yes, the character slips a little bit. However, of the ~60 levels I played, the slight slip only became a limiting factor in one level. I didn't get the feeling of sliding all over the place as other people have mentioned.
So as you can see in the trailer, the level is revealed through splattering ink on the level. Don't worry, when you die, the ink remains. While creative, it has some outstanding problems.
I don't know why this is the case. I expected the level's bottom to kill me (duh!), and I was sort of suprised to see the sides murder your little white cube, but why oh why does the TOP of the level kill me? Mind you, there's virtually no leniency. You touch the top, you are now little paint blobs. Congratualtions.
"

For the first twenty or so levels, the revealing-thru-ink part of the game is really cool. You get this sense of exploration, and you start to learn to splatter ink at the start so you can see what's going on

They have a lot of personality and are very deep, there is a lot of backstory to explore here and I explored every piece you could in the game. My issue was that they didn't explore that enough. With Gone Home, the focus was on two people and in 2 hours they were able to develop those characters well. In this game, we have 6 or so characters in this game but it wasn't much longer in terms of time of play. I left this game wanting more, lots more. I wanted to know more about their history and their moments here.
This was a great game, no doubt about it, but I think they had way more room to expand upon this world and give me more information and allow more time for the story to develop. Teslagrad is a combination platformer/puzzle game.  Apparently the plan was to take the two more consistently terrible genres in video games and combine them like some horrific Frankenstein nightmare and hope that the resulting concoction is somehow playable.  Oh, and let's throw in boss battles because boss battles obviously belong in a puzzle game.
So yeah, Teslagrad is a mess.  The platforming is sticky and not particularly satisfying.  The puzzle parts of the game fail in all the predictable ways - trial and error solutions, timing as a component, and the One True Solution.  The primary mechanic is a sort of opposites attract  mechanism (supposedly to mimic magnetism), and it somehow feels incredibly limiting and totally arbitrary at the same time...nothing you learn earlier applies later.
Then there's the art.  For some reason people like it, but I think it's awful.  The main character has a sort of blank expression the whole time.  The game doesn't even pretend that the levels belong anywhere except a puzzle game.  finally, in many places, the art actually makes it hard to tell what's going on.  In a puzzle game, clear information is key, and Teslagrad goes out of its way to not be clear.
In summary, this game fails at everything it tries to do.

This game is great if you enjoy Wuxia. If you have no understanding of Wuxia or Chinese culture then a huge amount of the story might go over your head. It draws heavily from Jinyong Wuxia stories and the game itself is translated very poorly at certain parts. In fact some parts aren't even translated.
As for the gameplay, the battle system is similar to many other turn-based strategy games. It's like Disgaea. It's not very deep but it's hard at certain points. The main difficulty comes from character development. If you don't know what you're doing, you can actually completely ♥♥♥♥ up and make a gimped character that has no chance of clearing the final stage and therefore can't win the game. It's a fairly obtuse system that is hard to figure out without a guide, and the♥♥♥♥♥♥translation doesn't really help things.
But the bulk of your time won't be spent battling, it'll be in a 'simulation' mode that reminds me of the downtime in Persona games. It's essentially a dating sim where you choose to spend time with different characters in order to build a relationship. There are huge portions of the game that are entirely missable if you don't choose to spend time with a particular character at a particular place within a set time frame. In fact, I'd say that if you want to see more than 50% of the game on a single playthrough you MUST follow a guide. There are a couple on steam so that's not a big deal to me. Although people who enjoy figuring♥♥♥♥♥♥out on their own will struggle with it.
So to sum it up, if you enjoy Wuxia, I'd say this game is a must-buy. I haven't enjoyed playing a game this much in years. If you have no idea what Wuxia is, probably give it a pass unless you really like the idea of a Persona style game where instead of dungeon-crawling you have turn-based strategy battles ala FF: Tactics or Fire Emblem.

Where can I even begin, and I oh my God it's a great game. So Honest Review Time!
Tale Of Wuxia, is exactly as it title says...it's a Wuxia, and it has Bo Staffs...a pervert launching himself with a pelvic thrust...a thief girl (who is waifu) a medicine  girl (waifu) hunter girl (waifu...) poision girl (eh...waifu-ish.) Are you seeing a pattern here, no? READ!
Anyway, let me just say this, if you're looking for a cheap game ($17) that is actually well developed, fun, and has a lot of asian themes to it. Then, you're looking in the right place. This game is set in China (After The Three Kingdoms.) The game has you as a nobody, and let me just say YES you're a nobody at the beginning. You will have even trouble fighting a F***ing chicken at the beginning on grandmaster (by spoiler there is a ending to the defeat from the chicken.)
Anyway, moving on.
The Gameplay is great, every style has it's advantages and disadvantages, and it's up to YOU to figure it out. However, it's not all that easy. Since literally the beginning of the game can change how you play, or stylize your character early on. It challenges in the way of either going purely brute, relying on you're internal styles to give you a tank-like combat style or you can focus on other basics to increase your base stats up to being a glass cannon.
Try to fnd balance.
Anyway, fists, sword, and um...heavier swords are your three starting styles you can try to learn. (Fists allow a higher combo chance, Sword allows an early extra boost in health regen, and heavy swords are a damage adder.) A gew things can be done to increase the early roster, from doing chores to get the leg (fast, high combo chance attacks) and the finger (ranged attacks that actually do good damage.)  The Bo staff is a little tricky, but well worth the investment if you read the guides.
Difficulty
(Okay the first part of this rather simple, welcome to you basic dating-rouge-like screen (education mode) where you can increase stats, and every victory like that in the later game give you small stat boosts (THAT ARE IMPORTANT) for then and later on in the game.)
The latter half of the game, towards the end of it actually is where even on noob things get dicey. You see it's best to see what style fits you soon, because once your put in the effort you'll have very little time to change your choices, and add into the other aspects.
Also, you're victories are very important, because IF your lose at this stage in the game it's game over, and it adds the stakes to the level of gameplay. In fact, there are chances to befirend certain characters through out the game, and befriending them can add them to your party.
(For THE LOVE OF HOLY BUDDHA) do not go at it alone, it's  like the trivia/tips say, it's a quick way to the worst ending. Get the medicine girl, she is literally your white mage in this, and she is your lifeline in the hariest battles. Try to maximize your relationships early on, for (at the moment) you can have the advantage of having a large party if you chose to do so.
This game isn't really causual as it's tagged to be either, since most of the time you're gonna be trying to figure out new paths.
The Endings are all well fleshed out, and some are funny self pointing jokes.
Anyway as you noticed, I been calling every girl Waifu material in this game...it's because for the first time EVER, I found a game where each love interest isn't a cookie cutter. There is an actual personality to them, from the poison girl's dejectful attitude, to Jen Wens princess/wild girl persona. Quite literally, investing time into the romance of this game is rewarding in of itself in story.
Sometimes they yield increases in base stats (mostly energy and health)
The music is the game is great, but it can get nerve wrecking sometimes after repeated loops.

Jackie Chan's Drunken Master/Rock Lee's Loopy fist is a style in game.

quite literally, there are easter eggs, and they are very good to both Anime Fans, and Wuxia Fans alike.
final verdict.

Ill be honest although I liked Black Flag I found many a time when I just gave up on the games many flaws. Lets jump straight into the immesurable pile of corpses in the haystack, Usbisoft have yet to fix many graphical and gameplay bugs three years after its releace; The movement system is as simple as ever, who knew that holding SHIFT and W could make you go on a three mile parkour run?; I dont give for graphics (neither does my computer) so I set all the settings to low after finding my way through the Abstergo menu system - which is frankly confusing - and obtained a briliant FPS of around 25 (after switching graphics cards I had around 35), lo behold, two hours into the game (ten minutes of which are running through  a forest holding SHIFT and W) the screen froze but the minimap and visual markers continued moving, after some digging (google) it turns out that the game requires you to turn volumetric fog on for it not to freeze, so yeah; graphical errors may be my falt but still at one point Ed's hood gliched and dissapeared leaving me looking like Sam Worthington with a pirate fetish; lastly but not least in the corpse pile is me feeling that Ubisoft could have done a lot better with Black Flag if was a stand-alone game not involving all this Assassin and Templar rubbish, without it I would have actually connected emotionaly with the charicter, but no every time you feel yourself getting piraty it chucks you out of the game into a ten minute walking simulator constantly pressing E and talking to people with creepier faces than Captain Thatch himself. Despite this i found the sailing responsive and smooth with an actual hardness factor in both the fighing styles (not just pressing E to kill everyone) and the movement system (drifting ect), the weapon switching was a little unexplaned but you get the hang of it. My only problems were that the storms were a little short and randomised and that you could pick up an entire crew of shipwreck survivors in five minutes. All (most) considered this is one of Ubisofts best games (minus the Assassin storyline), but im not reccomending it unless you can get it for under £5.

tl;dr: Go buy the game...like yesterday!
This game is amazing. Just buy it. Now. Its atmosphere, cryptic nature, level and world design and lore are truly amazing to explore blindly. Me and a friend were playing this game for about 12 hours straight we were so sucked into the world and exploring every crevice of each area.
The game takes inspiration from metroid and castlevania for its gameplay loop and from games like Dark Souls for its approach to storytelling, worldbuilding, atmosphere and lore. It just throws you in and intuitively teaches you the basics by making you experience them first hand. It's trully an amazing experience that you have to play.
Don't let this game's difficulty turn you off. While it is quite a difficult game to beat it's rewarding and completely fair (appart from that final arena challenge). The fights are fun, epic and rewarding with fitting music! The animation and visuals are stunning and enemies clearly telegraph their attacks, so if you pay attention you can theoretically go through this game without taking a single hit!
Please do yuorself a favour and go in this game knowing as little as possible! Exploring the breathtakingly beautiful dying world of Hallownest can be charming, beautiful, and scary depending on the area you're in. Each area is distinctly unique with its own theme, atmosphere, enemies and visual theme, and there are no cliches like "the lava leve" or "the snow leve". Every area is pretty original in my opinion and if you've seen a theme done before chances are you haven't seen it been done so well before. Just beware if you're an chievement hunter as there are a few missable achievements, so be warned! Also know that the main ending to the game isn't satisfying. After beating it look up how to get the "true ending" which is satisfying and interesting, otherwise you'd be missing out an entire platforming area, a really boss and a few pretty serious parts of the main character's personal story.
Other than the map system which is a little too convoluted (in my opinion you shoul only have to buy the map once from the chartographer and craft your own map for each area from scratch) the game is pretty flawlwss! I did have some performance issues with sudden lag spikes even when lovking the game at 60fps but it seems to be a issue just for me as I haven't heard of anyone else having these issues from people who have the same hardware - regardless, I'm using a Ryzen 5 1600 @ 3.7 with an RX 560 and 16gb DDR4 @2933 ( as you can see it's probably an isolated software issue )
overall score: 9+ appart from a few weird quirks it's pretty much a masterpiece.

Prior to playing this game, the only experience I had with games of this genre was with old grandpappy Symphony of the Night. And while that game is fantastic, Hollow Knight blows it out of the water. There really isn't much I can say bad about this game. From a gameplay perspective, the boss fights are great (especially some of the last ones you encounter), the controls are tight, combat is really fun, and deeply exploring the environment is very rewarding. Backtracking (when you have to do it) is rarely a chore thanks to the changing central environment and the ralways hidden around the map.
Now, one should note that this game is not easy, especially if you want to 100% it. There are some absolutely brutal platforming sections and boss fights to get some key secret items, but you don't have to do most of them to complete the game. There is also this one fight that doesn't really have a close save point, so trekking to it can be frustrating if you try to tackle it early in the game like I made the mistake of doing. If you like challenging games though, that's not a big deal. Just get good and you'll be fine.
I guess that the music and art style are worth noting, in that they are FANTASTIC. The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard in quite a long time. There are all these awesome little moments were everything just falls into place. For example, the music for the city area is grand, epic, and serene which perfectly fits the massive rainy cityscape. There is one boss that is really creepy ghost lady, and the music is so unnerving. It's just a pleasure to witness it all.
That's about it. I hope I convinced you this game is well worth the money.

I abolutely adore this game and everything about it. I hardly ever play platformers, and this was the first one I made it 100% of the way through; it's that good. I'm more of a first-person shooter or 3D adventure game type of person, so this genre was a little different than what I was really used to. I wouldn't have picked it up if my friend Pumpkin Head hadn't told me to, and I'm really glad he recommended it to me. Hollow Knight has easily become one of my favorite games of all time.
As an artist, I seriously appreciate the absoutley stunning style, effort, and craftsmanship of the backgrounds, animation, and character design. The art style is magnificent and inspiring, and has influenced my own art in a way. I have always loved the theme of darkness, pale face dark eyes, and mystery. This game includes all of the aesthetics I love into a wonderful looking platformer. The main character, the Knight, has such a simple yet cool design, and I get pretty picky with my characters in videogames. I typically will dismiss a game or show very quicky if I don't attach to or like any characters, but in Hollow Knight, I've fallen in love with the designs.
The mechanics in the game are so solid and feel so genuine. A mix of sound, animation, and mechanics really make it feel like you have absolute control of your character. Everytime you'd get a solid hit, you'd feel it, and every time you'd get hit, you'd feel that too. Every win or loss was by your hand, and it never felt like the game had cheated you or it was was anyone elses doing besides your own. The variety of ways you can play not only make the game feel more dynamic, but it also means that it caters to the different playstyles of the person with the controller. You have a choice to use certain charms, abilities, magic, and the nail itself. The variety of which you can play just makes it feel like the game never really ends.
Music is so important in videogames, and the Christopher Larkin has done a phenomenal job creating the soundtrack for Hollow Knight. The action and emotion behind his work fits flawlessly with the style of the game and the overall story. I listen to the soundtrack all the time, it inspires me and reminds me of all of the adventures I had in-game. The variety of styles in music correlate perfectly with the play areas in-game, and the mechanic of changing a few instruments in the song based on location was executed perfectly. It really feels like the music follows you throughout the Hallownest.
TDLR, I absolutely love the art style, the mechanics are solid and have variety, and the music brings the game together with the story flawlessly.
100/10 I definitely recommend anyone pick up this game and give it a try. It's not an easy game, and it doesn't hold your hand and tell you where to go. It's an adventure, but it's your adventure! The story is phenomenal, and it's worth more than the store price, at least to me. Beautiful game, best one I've played in a while.

At first I didn't like Hollow Knight. It was my first Metroidvania game I had ever played, so I didn't understand what I was supposed to do at some moments at the start. Now in gaming, you never have to learn for yourself. You never need to explore or take your own journey, and once I realized that in Hollow Knight you were meant to get lost, you were meant to die, I started loving it.
This game is difficult, you need to learn the attacks of the enemies. One of the best parts of Hollow Knight are the bosses. All of the bosses are different in their own way, their original, look amazing, fun to fight and most importantly, they are fair.
The artwork is stunning. Somehow each new are looks different than the last. You can understand the history of each area without being told anything. The areas are extremely detailed, and with the beautiful enemy sprites, its easy to get lost in this world.
Mainly, you explore the world and attack enemies. The controls are tight and you know that if you take damage, it is your fault. I can say that almost none of my deaths felt cheap, they were my fault so the only person I was angry at was myself. You have multiple attacks, and as the game goes on you gain more, variety is very important and is used well in this game.
There is not very much dialoge, so the story is told through the envirment, with only small lines of text here and there. After completing, I'm not terrible positive what the story is, but I do have a vague idea. Its always intruging and if you search hard enough, you can find it. This is a pro because I was always invested in what I was to do next, and because the characters are so charming and lovely, I had to mention it.
Lastly, the game is huge. It took me 38 hours to complete this game, but I haven't 100% it. With all of the extra exploring I did I'm sure it wouldn't have taken me as long, but since the world is so interesting its almost impossible not to get side tracked. I still am finding new areas and new mobs, and it still amazes me. It is very easy to get your moneys worth.
I stated in the pros that you get more attacks later on, and while this is true I found them to never be as useful as my original attack. I never had to use the new attacks, and maybe if I was forced to I would have used them more. Due to the design of the game I understand how forcing the players to use certain attack would be impossible because they may not have found them yet, but it seems like a waste to have these attacks if they are not used.
Since this game is a Metroidvania, there was a lot of wondering around not knowing where to go. Of course this is good and bad. It lets the player explore more and make their own adventures, but at the same time its frustrating when you have no idea where to go. To be honest, this isn't  huge deal and I only included it here because I didn't have any other issues with the game.
As you can tell from there not being a lot of cons, this game is amazing. It is fun from beginning to end with interesting characters and areas. I never would have thought that I would have enjoyed this game as much as I did and it makes me excited for Team Cherry's next game!

Shrouded In Sanity is a faster paced look at the Soulslike genre - offering slick combat with enemies more than capable of murdering you in a few quick combo's and being wholly unapologetic about it. Lovingly animated in pixel, the game's set in a delightfully macabre victorian manor, where the serving staff is more than happy to attend to your need for suffering with a wide variety of implements repurposed for greeting guests.
Whilst enemies can be relentless in their efforts to murder players, players have a number of defensive options such as :: Invincibility frames (Hello dodge rolls, executions, and parts of the heal animation), Parrying, Blocking, casually running away from the enemy as fast as your stamina bar lasts. Offensive options are more limited in the form of a light attack, a heavy attack, a dashing attack, and a pistol (the latter of which does not have scaling damage, but which can be used to safely stagger an enemy so they can be riposted).
Upgrading is minimalistic, as there is no upgradeable gear, and only a select few stats exist to raise- but they are enough to provide some degree of player choice and a sense of empowerment.
The game's soundtrack and especially those of the boss fights -shine-. Whilst the enemies can be a considerable obstacle to an inattentive player, it's bosses are outright devastating, especially when an unwary player comes face to face with their mechanics for the first time.
That the game is -still- in the process of receiving updates to address issues players may have, alongside minute content updates is fairly amazing giving how cheap the game is. Money well spent.

When I get a new game, I am usually excited about playing it. I think about it when I'm not playing. On my days off, the first thing I want to do after I get up is go downstairs andstart playing. CivBE.. not at all.
Yes, BE is just a repackaged 5 with a fresh coat of paint (Think StarCraft 2). Unlike StarCraft 2, however, this new paint doesn't feel better. There's only a handful of leaders, and they all play the exactly same. The AI leaders are more "A" without any "I". Very limited units. Too many buildings. The map looks like a hex map even without the hexes showing. Orbital units are more fluff than substantial. The tech web is a mess. Etc, etc, etc... Oh, and  each city gets 3 trade units (Caravans), which have a tendancy to pop up each turn for you to select a trade route from a long list of choices. My last play I had 6 cities, and an average of 3-4 trade units per turn had to be assigned. I haven't looked into if I can alter this in options, but think of the tedium with a huge empire if not.
I hate to just be negative, but as I sit here trying to find some positive additions, I am having trouble thinking of any. A few minutes later, and I am still trying to think of something positive. And I give up. I honestly just cannot point to anything that is an improvement or new and fun, which is unfortunate.
I will likely give CivBE a few more goes, to get some use out of my $50, but I have a strong feeling I will just be back on Civ5 after that. I wonder if we will have to shell out money for new expansions to make the game a bit more enjoyable.
