Civ V in general was great -- really great -- in most ways with a few exceptions. This is on the same Civ 5 engine, with the same (never fixed) bugs, a reskin (nice), a redressing of the tech tree (nice), conversion of concepts from Earth to Sci/Fi (OK) and a serious lack of depth. It doesn't matter what you build it all ends the same. Very little work went into this game balancing. You just never develop the sence of personal investment in your society like you felt in nearly every Civ 5 replay.
The maps look pretty good. The art is OK but not impressive, the music is extremely below par considering Civ 5 -- next time find a decent writer (ie Bear Mcreary?). This is no conglomoration of ambience to draw you in like Civ 5 which grabbed you almost immediately. This plays like a poorly written sci fi novel... take a couple of big concepts, throw in technobabble (such as the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ quotes you see when finishing a technology), publish and sell, sell, sell.
Diplomacy is still aweful and at least in Civ 5 it was so aweful that its funny, since the characters had history to add to the mix. There is no real sense of attachment going on in this game... no buld up other than ...in the future..., sure the lack of a common frame of reference (ie. all of human history) makes it a more difficult to relate but there are ways around that... The wonders are not very exciting, there is little lore, you can't see what the hell you are producing from the main map screen. There is no real replacement for religion/writers/artists etc like in Civ 5 (which would be OK, unless you are simply reskinning the engine which in that case you would want to re-emulate the better qualities of said engine). After having played Beyond Earth, I cannot really come to any positive conclusion.
The whole idea about Beyond Earth is great and I like the change of scenery. The thing is, in civ 5 we could set ourself in the leader we played and the structures we build. We know our leaders history or what they did in their life span, with a very good introduction when you start the game, you get a good idea of who you're playing and the voiceover is amazing, its like getting a story told and you build upon it in your own way. Its the same with the buildings in the game, especially wonders. With some very good quotes and an image of the wonder itself, you get this feeling of accomplishment, because of the way the game itself presents it to you.
In my opinion, when you want to make a Civ game in a sci-fi univers, you have to make a very big effort to personalize the game and give it charm in its own way to keep players interrested. Because none of us know anything about what we're building, what we're reseaching, who we are and what story the leaders have to tell. The wonders have to be extremely well written around it and they need to give this feeling of accomplishment to really make it feel different now that we're in space. Since we're tailoring our own future, customization has to be the center of upgrades and improvements. The feeling of making choices that are difficult, but have powerful benefits in their own ways is what we want as a player, we want to tailor our own leader into the future and give them our own personality.
Beyond Earth lacks in many aspects, all those written above are examples from what i've experienced this far within the game. Since it doesn't have any of those i wrote. What strikes me the most is the massive lack of personality and general feel of the game. there isn't any charm to it, you don't get attached to the leaders you play or the building you construct. For the most part you don't really know where you are to be honest or what you're doing.
When you start up the game there isn't any introduction what so ever, you jump straight in and have no clue towards who you're playing or what his or her name is even. This lack of story that drives you towards making the future for his or her people, is just flat out terrible and really disappointing when you compare it to other games in the genre. When you speak with other leaders in the game you don't get this personalized image the leader is standing in like in civ 5 that really gives you this idea of who you're talking with and who they are as a charactor. They just pop up on the screen and thats it.
And when you're done with a game most of the time you don't even know if you won or lost, especially if you lose, you just get a pop up to exit the game, without any kind of statistics or formulars about your jouney. And to be honest, i didn't get this feeling of "YES I won on very hard", but more like a "umm okay, did I lose?" or "okay I won, what now?".
Wonders are just lacking in every way, a few of them are interesting that gives different benefits that isn't just flat out production or food. It gives them this unique bonus, that when you choose a playstyle you might go for it to achieve different goals within your game. But when you build them you get this blueprint image of it, which is okay if they could imrpove upon it to make it more interesting. But I would rather have (example) a coloured image of humans in suits building it or looking at it in all its glory, it just has a bigger impact on the player and Civ 5 is a good example towards this. And at first its hard to even see if the building is a wonder or not. very disappointed.
This might be just me, but for some reason every leaders cities looks totally the same on the map, if there wasn't any colour to the game, you wouldn't know who from who. I know that space technology is mostly the same for everyone right as of now, but giving them that little thing that makes them different, like in Civ 5 when you compare leaders to earhother on the map, you mostly knew who from who and visually you would know when you played China or Atilla.
The AI is totally the same as in Civ 5. I haven't noticed any improvements in it, they still don't act towards what is best for their empire and the favour system doesn't really work as well as I thought it would be. The AI just ask you constantly about gold or resources so you get a favour for it, but when you want to use the favour you get close to nothing out of it, in my experience that is. So I just ignore it really.
The only good things are:
- The agent system that gives you more of a choice towards what you want to do in different cities, but it could still be better in a costimizable aspect and a better leveling systems to the agents themself so they feel more important.
- The tech tree in some degree, some people hate it, some people don't. for me personally it has grown upon me and I've started to like it more.
- I like that you have a choice in the start towards what different kind of benefits you want to start out with, this is really a big plus from me. and it gives a very good start towards which kind of playthrough you want to go through with.
- The aliens are more interesting and they give you the feeling of being annoyed by them which is good and you have to make a choice towards if you want to eliminate them or live among them. This could still be better, more variations in the aliens, make nests more interesting by making them harder to capture or doing so that the longer the nests stays in the game, the bigger and harder it becomes to have them around.
Conclusion:
Beyond Earth could have been so much more. The presentation of the game and its leaders, wonders, building etc. is just lacking in every way and I'm very disappointed. There isn't any personality to the game, there isn't any charm to any aspect really. visually the game is totally the same to civ 5 in the matter of textures and unit polish and personally I would have liked an improvement here. Trading with other leaders are great, but while being so its just stupid and annoying without an automatic funtion so you don't have to choose where they go all the time. If you have 10 cities with all the trade convoys you can get, good luck keeping your sanity stable, its very frustrating.
I dont know what else to say really, would I recommend the game as of now? No not really, and It saddens me to do so. I expected more from Firaxis and I'm disappointed. If you're a new player and wants to experience a true Civilization game, I would recommend Civilization 5 with its expansions and wait with this one for a much lower price or/and an expansion to improve the game in close to every way.
After some improvements it may be a true follow up to Civilization 5 and its expansions. But right now, it's simply not.

About two weeks ago I was lamenting how few space games actually allow for zero-g movement, usually they are set in locations that while technically in space, have some sort of artificial gravity. Then along comes Tacoma and what do you know, it's got some sweet zero-g movement. Nice!
Tacoma is a (quote unquote) walking-simulator story game by Fullbright, the studio behind the somewhat polarizing Gone Home (in my library but have not played yet - shame on me). I dislike the term walking-simulator, not because it's wrong - lets face it you walk around a lot in most first person games, but because it's not really what you spend most of your time doing. Tacoma is a "pick things up look at them and-put them back simulator".
I don't mean that in a bad way either, the level of detail that goes into every object and the environments of Tacoma is ridiculous. Each item you can pick up is made to look and seem as real (in the game world) as possible. And it's not for nothing, these items make up the world, give you details and flesh out the time and place you are in. They add gravitas, humor and more. Yes you can blow through Tacoma without picking up a single object, but why? Stop look and smell (well pick up and closely inspect) the flowers.
That's not to say that's all there is to Tacoma, the core of Tacoma is the story it tells and in order to not accidentally spoil anything I will be brief. You take on the role of Amy Ferrier, who has been tasked with investigating the events of what happened on the Tacoma space station and retrieve the on board AI named ODIN. Exploration and interaction will reveal the events of the last few weeks/days/hours leading up to the current situation. Throughout the game you become familiar with the small crew of diverse and real-feeling people that make up Tacoma's staff.
The primary game mechanic is to watch pre-recorded sequences of conversations via an enhanced reality interface. You will see and hear the crew walk around the locations of the ship in these sequences and be able to scrub back and forth through these recordings as people come and go. Sometimes you will follow a person or conversations out of the room, only to have to scrub back and watch from a different angle to see another part. It's quite brilliant and the format is something that really only works in video games. I honestly hope it's something that gets used again in other games.
There were a few things that bothered me such as not being able to see your feet/legs except in particular pre-set circumstances and how some of the interactions limit you for story reasons, nothing game breaking. Really I just wanted more - more recordings, more interactions, more story background (more zero-g!). I was compelled by what they gave me and much like last weeks review of Signal From Tölva, we only get the tip of the iceberg, and I want to sink my ship on the whole thing.
Interacting with these recordings and peaking into the lives of the crew has a slightly voyeuristic feel to it that at first I wasn't sure about. Not in an uncomfortable way, just more along the lines of wondering, is this really necessary? But your character is really just a neutral observer and it's far more about what you put into it, your interest level as the player. You can complete Tacoma by doing almost nothing but standing around and waiting, but the design and detail of the station invites you to investigate. "Come take a look" Tacoma says, "I have such wonderful things to show you" (just kidding on that last one - this isn't Event Horizon).
Tacoma isn't long and it isn't complicated but it is a fascinating piece of interactive fiction featuring a well designed mechanic that's put to great use. Take your time when going through the space station Tacoma, it's not a race and it will reward you. Play it with someone, like movie night - only with more freedom.

Narrative games like Tacoma, and it's award-winning predecessor Gone Home, are really condensed forms of entertainment. It's closer to film than to other games. It's not a roleplaying game, you don't make decisions; it's an on-the-rails experience with a beautiful backdrop, great voice acting, and a compelling story. You only hear from your character Amy at the very beginning and end of the game, but the six crew of Lunar Transit Station Tacoma will keep you entertained and enraptured.
You can run through the whole game in two hours, or with closer to four hours you can explore the many nooks and crannies of Tacoma, finding its puzzles, easter eggs, and unlockable secrets. $20 may seem steep for that short run, but given how packed with content those few hours are I found it a good deal.

Teslagrad is a puzzle game that appealed to me, even as someone that my friend calls an irrelevant fool. Why? I'm not really sure. Maybe it was the action element that crept in, or the fiendishly clever puzzles. But suffice to say that it's a blend of action, puzzle, platformer and who-knows-what-else that really has no business working as well as it does.
Its art and music are phenomenal and work together to create a fantastic environment with a rich story hidden in the works of the ancient magitech tower of Teslagrad. The silent protagonist makes his way through with a stoic expression and an expanding arsenal of puzzle-solving gadgetry, accompanied by only the ghosts of the past and the music of Bear & Cat Studios.
Teslagrad is by far one of the greatest games I have ever played, and I can't find very many if any flaws with it. It was a delight to play through the first time, and just as fun on repeat performances. Even as a man who doesn't often go for puzzlers, it was truly a great adventure.
Even though it was a good game and I enjoyed it...I beat the whole thing in two hours. I would not reccomend buying this game. The price is not worth the little you get to play it.

Hmm. Where to begin. A lot of people have already talked about how the silent storyteling in this game is great--and it is. There's absolutely no dialogue whatsoever. The music is, well, there are a few songs in the game that are good...but there's a lot of quiet sounds/none whatsoever, so for the most part it's just you and your polarized gear.
As for the gameplay itself, I enjoyed it. The puzzles are interesting with the polarity mechanic, for sure. Enjoyable, overall. The boss battles are a little bit...unforgiving. You die in a single hit (from anything), meaning you have to restart the boss if you get hit by anything at all. Personally, I thought this was a good thing. However, I've also played all three of the Metroid Prime games, so I'm used to tougher bosses. (Speaking of Metroid, Samus' helmet and a pair of Chozo statues make a cameo)
Overall, I'd recommend it if you like Metroidvanias. The game took maybe 7 hours of investment from me, so it's a shorter game if you know how to handle it. Use your moves, fire the Tesla beam upwards (because you can, the one thing the game never tells you that you also absolutely need), and don't die. You know what you've gotta do.
So get Teslagrad, and fulfill your destiny as an electrical wizard.
If you've enjoyed narrative games in the past, you'll love this one. Put some effort into immersing yourself and the game will do the rest.

So some guy's wife tasked me with finding a tiger's sexual organ to feed him with. Met a girl who constantly questions why she was born so beautiful.  Talked with a little girl whose name was Doggy.
And this all happened in the first area.
In this game, you start as a typical nobody in the Jianghu world (Ancient China filled with fantasy martial arts) who strives to be a master kungfu fighter as he adventures throughout the land.
Most of your time will be spent in a seclusive valley, together with your master and fellow disciples training in martial arts, practicing skills such as hunting, fishing, mining (aka Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Simulator), going outside, and whatnot in a turn-based text and graphics game. One thing to pay attention to is your mood during this phase, as happier moods reward more experience for activities.
The second part of this game is real time strolling through the various locations in the game world, doing quests and exploring. The biggest setback here is there is a time limit, not only for exploring the town/city but for certain quests as well. With the massive amount of things to do in the game (almost approaching MMORPG level), it is annoying to find your freedom arbitrarily limited. Furthermore, there's no map or detailed quest tracker, making managing your time even harder.
I've also seen critical reviews about bad or non-existent translation, so far I've only seen a few of those, and they don't detract from the experience that much, IMO. If anything, this game has some of the funniest dialogues in video games.
There is a HUGE number of set-encounters in the game, whether it be for flavoring/immersiveness or just pure combat. There are many secrets, hidden paths, and choices for players to explore, in true classic RPG spirit. The combat is turn-based but fast, requiring you to pay attention and plan out moves on higher difficulties. You can learn many different martial arts, unlike traditional class-bound RPGs.
For fans of Wuxia fiction like me, this game is a must buy in a market saturated with your typical dragons, guns, dungeons, mana potions. It's also cool to see some of the characters resemble those in Jin Yong's novels. For newcomers to Wuxia, prepare to enter an exotic world, filled with exotic people, and kill/defeat them in hand-to-hand combat :)

Before I go much into detail, I just wanna say this:
Live2DViewer is still a pretty nice tool and very easy to handle for those who simply want a cute animated second screen or something like that, still while I was testing it, I stumbled over a lot of things that I didn't particularly like.
Pro:
- Very responsive UI
It's clean and easy to find and adjust things, this is actually very well done.
- Many different customization options
Pictures, Videos, Filters, Effects, Widgets, there's plenty to pick from.
Con:
- The Engine.
On my search for the actual model files, I discovered that this tool is actually using Unity Engine. Now I'm not trying to "hate" on it because it's using Unity. It's just that the usage of a full blown Game Engine for something as simple as a desktop tool that, in some or even most cases will constantly be running in the background is absolutely overkill and unneccessary. Which also brings me to my next con.
- Memory Usage
I had it running on one screen in FullHD, displaying a video with 60FPS and had the model it comes with pretty small somewhere in the corner. It used a whopping 300MB of RAM for just that.
As a comparion: Wallpaper Engine, running 3 different videos (all 1920x1080@60) on 2 fullHD displays and one 2k display didn't even use 70MB of my memory.
I know in our day and age with people having 16GB of Ram by default it doesn't look much, but it's just unneccessary waste of space.
And it's pretty much what you get for using a fully blown game engine - that was not build to modify your desktop - instead of natively written code for this specific purpose.
- Editor not included
As I read the description I stumbled over this little bit "[...] and lpk files(a format from Live2DViewerEX)", so I though, hey, it's this programs file format, so surely there should be a way to create them, right? Eh... nope, turns out another program is needed for that. Either clarify this or add the Editor, please.
- Little variety in content in the Workshop
There's the mainstream anime characters, a couple videos to test out things and that's pretty much it. I get that the tool is in early access, but I figure if it would be made more clear how to actually create content for it or include the editor in the actual program, there would be more people trying their hands on it.
Conclusion:
While being very simple to use, it's still far inferior to what I see as the main competitor (namely wallpaper engine), both in performance and in content. For a tool that will be running in the background of whatever you're doing on PC, be it just browsing or playing games it is absolutely crucial to be very adaptable in it's usage of system resources and so far I could not observe this with this tool.
This is the main reason why I'm currently not recommending to get Live2DViewer in it's current state.

Where I came from: While I have played all of the games, I had only played Hitman Blood Money exstensively before playing this. All in all I liked the game. I feel it departed somewhat from the Hitman style, but at the end of the day I still had a lot of fun with it.
Technical:
The game looks very good, the visuals, the details and effects are very good. The controls are also good, and one can trust that Mr 47 will do what you're telling him to do. You'll quiclky learn to use the HUD to your aide too.
Gameplay:
This game differs from the previous ones in that 47 isn't coming in to a big level with a target and with lots of room to navigate. Where in Blood Money, you'd start a level, find your targers, eliminate them in some clever way, and exit the level, in this game each level is divided into multiple stages in a sort of one way street. So you won't be going back to where you started, you'll come in at one point in the level, do your stuff, exit at the other end. The game is more set around story telling, and the levels progresses with the story, you won't return to any safehouse. Another thing about the story is that you're more or less hunting for the same bad guys all along the story line, and everyone you kill between the start and then is basically just henchmen. But you're also hunted. In most levels, guards are out to get you from the get-go, which means sneaky sneaky from the very start of most levels. I would say that the game has taken a few to many hints from Splinter Cell in that regard. Not every mission has an assasination in it either, some are just plain sneaking, infiltrate this, escape from that.
My last negative point about the game is the lack of the mini map. Instead you have a radar and "instinct" which allows you to see enemies, interesting stuff to interact with, see where the enemy might go, and lastly, help you sneak past people who would otherwise see through your disguise. You don't have a load-out screen either (which ties in with the story, so that is good in a sense). What this means is that you can't get to know the layout of the areas before starting the mission, you can't study the routes of the guards to the same extent as previously, and you can't plan beforehand how you would like to take out your target. Everything except fiber-wire and silver ballers is very much procure on-site. It's pretty much the same for planning too, you won't know the layout of the level before you have explored it yourself, and you won't know the routes of the guards before you have done your own surveillance. I guess it's more realistic, and it isn't all bad, in fact, it can be very fun and challenging, but it has taken away from the precise playstyle of previous Hitmans.
Game modes.
This is where they have been really ingenious with the game. Previously, you got a ranking. Now you get scored by everything. You did a silent kill, you'll get a certain score, but you did a creative kill involving an overhead light rig or you tricked someone to kill your target for you, you'll get an even better score. Each level is riddled with challenges and stuff to do which can't all be completed in one playthrogh. So after you have completed the game and you don't take the game so seriously any more, you might be tempted to go back and explore all the ways to kill your target, play through a level without using anything more than your suit, or even try to get all disguises in a level. There's also secret challenges and some quite absurd ones. This adds tonnes of fun replayability to the game. For each challenge you complete, you'll be able to get a better score. And then, you can compare your score with your friends and see who's the better hitman. There's also Contracts. Player created challenges. A player will chose the level and up to three targes. The player will chose what weapons that are to be used, which disguise and other criteria for the contract. This is also timed, and gives the game even more great play time
I would score the game very highly, its flaws are pretty much outweighed by its genious. I would recommend this game. I know that after I played it, all I wanted to do was play more of the same, I didn't really want to go back to regular action games, I only wanted to figure out how to assasinate videogame characters in clever ways without being noticed and without using any guns.

Hitman: Absolution has been developed by a Danish video game developing company, and their games are published by Square Enix. Hitman: Absolution is a stealth based action game!
Hitman: Absolution is a stealth based action game in which you play as an modern life assassin under the code name Agent 47. All Hitman  series are connected, so the story keeps on building up after each Hitman game. In this particular game, your objective is to keep one girl safe.
During that job you will face various different enemies. You, though, don't need to kill almost anyone! Your main mission is to kill just one person, and if you can manage to pass the mission by killing only your main target. Or, pass the mission without killing anyone, if your mission is not to kill anyone. So yea, as you may already guess, this game requires you to have A LOT of patience! And concentration!
This game is, in my opinion, quite hard so the developers made it slightly easier than the rest of the series. In this game you have a thing called "Agent 47's sense" which you can use as often as you'd like. What it does is allow you to predict where certain people will move so you could avoid them or kill them as you wish. It also highlights all of the usable items that are close to you and that you can use for what ever you need them. And it also highlights doors that you can open and secret passages that you can use to move from one to the other one unseen (such as vents).
During your mission you will encounter many different weapons and collectables. You can also unlock every single clothing that you see in game. All you need is kill the person and exchange clothing. Or go into a locker room (if there is any!) and change it there. As much as I have been playing the game, I haven't seen why would you need the clothing for. Civilization: BE Is a rather interesting game. It has a lot to live up to, but it has a lot going for it aswell. It runs on the same engine as Civilization V, and a lot of parts carry over from that, no unit stacking, hex grid, etc. It would be fair to say at least half, if not more of the game was a sci fi reskin of civilization V. But its too easy to just say that and walk away. There are a lot of things kept over from the previous game, but a number of things have also been fleshed out better. Trade routes are now capped per city, not per country, which makes more sense. Trade routes now have much better rewards and choices between internal and external routes. City states have been downgraded to stations which give early game boosts, but are usually gone late game, and don't take up more then a single tile. There are now quests which give both short term and long term boosts, as well as ways to customize how buildings in your empire will benefit you (e.g. A building might offer a choice of +2 production for the city, or +1 energy). Affinities have replaced ideologies, and have an entirely new way about getting them, separate from Virtues (social policies), which upgrade units, what buildings your empire can create, and AI players appearance will even change based on their affinities, which was a nice touch. The tech web allows for players to become more advanced in entirely different ways, offering many branching paths in a radial format. And then the planets themselves. Not as many default world types as Civilization V and its expansions, but still a number of the more popular ones, and 3 distinct environments for those worlds to have allow for a lot more replayability then the same old earth types that Civ V had. Along with other distinct starting qualities to the new Civilizations, it is a fun game that has significant potential, especially since Civilization V was decent, and its expansion packs made it that much better, It'll be fun to see how far any Expansion packs take Beyond earth. And one final note, with Steam workshop capability like its predecessor, it has a great flexibility in terms of additional content, at least in singleplayer form. I have not tried mods and multiplayer, but since it's on the same engine, its doubtful they will work past having to physically mod both players games manually.

I'm kinda suprised seeing such odd reviews. I understand most of the feelings people have with this game, as I've played civ5 extensively and civ B.E. as well. But that doesn't take away that it isn't a good game, cause it is! It does lack a bit of personality compared to civ 5, but it makes up in alot of other circumstances.
The main pro point of this game is the renewed research system, in my opinion is this a huge step-up compared to civ5. It finally gives me the freedom to research the stuff I want exclusively and mixes up my playstyle from time to time. It gives me the freedom to try and develop new tactics and ways to win. The old civ5 system was too direct and didn't allow for alot of flexibility.
The main con for this game is that it isn't as broad as civ5 "yet". The civilizations are a bit lack luster, but it makes up for variaty in choices in the game menu (wether you want to start with a clinic in the beginning or 1 extra population as example). Beside that the civilization don't give a whole lot of unique abilities like in civ5.
This variaty in choices in the menu does give freedom again though, you are able to mix things up and try to develop your own gamestyle.
Beside this, the game plays beautifully, I have a lot of fun playing it and does got a civilization vibe to it. It's a good thing it's sorta a "retextured" civ5, cause I loved civ5, and I would hate it if they completely revamped the whole concept behind civ.
The game could use a bit more variaty, but they could as well release more DLC's for it!
For now, is it worth your money? I would say yes, as it really does play solidly. You always got the urge to press the next turn button and the freedom in this game is beyond civ5. It really does give you the freedom to mix things up and try different kind of things. I, atleast, had a lot of fun so far playing it and experimenting with new things. I even had to relearn alot of things even though I played alot of civ5, this only shows there's alot of new things in the game :)
Give it a try, don't throw the game off because it's not the civ(6) you had hoped for. It does deliver in alot of other ways!

This is a puzzle/platforming game where you utilize magnets to kill/outrun your enemies and jump where no man has jumped before. There are two basic colors of interactable objects, red and blue, which are attracted to the opposite color and push away the same color.
The graphics are simple but beautiful and effective, especially when you reach the top of the tower. Simple is the word for this game, but it is executed so well.

I feel like I should preface this review by saying that I have been waiting for this game for years. I was a huge fan of Gone Home, and have been checking for updates and following Tacoma since 2014. Maybe my issues with the game are simply because I built up too much hype that the game couldn't deliver.
First things first: this game is short. If you read quickly (or don't read at all) and don't stray from the (very linear) path, you could easily finish this puppy in an hour or so. I finished my initial playthrough in 2 hours, and that's including the longer-than-I'd-like-to-admit amount of time I spent trying to sink all of the pool balls in the lounge. It's also as I mentioned, extremely linear. There are a few levels that have branching hallways, but they always lead to the same place and more often than not, they have little to no value to add to justify the exploration. It makes exploring feel like a waste of time.
There is also a lot of Odin's story line that I wish was different.
The ending feels rushed and abrupt, and overall, it feels very shallow. If you're expecting the feels train that I know I personally was after Gone Home, you'll be disappointed.
Aside from all of that, I'll admit that I had fun. The two hours that my initial playthrough took went by quickly becasue I was intrigued by the story, even if I wish they had done more with it. The voice acting and writing are well done, and there are quite a few visuals in the game that I loved. Overall, I'll reluctanty recommend the game for what it is: an enjoyable few hours of sci-fi mystery.... just make sure that the game is on sale when you get it.

As someone who wasn't a huge fan of the older Hitman games Silent Assassin and Blood Money, I really like the improvements in gameplay that Absolution made. Surely, hardcore fans of the older titles may be disappointed with the somewhat more linear structure of this game, but I thought that the superb stealth, shooting, and movement mechanics were exactly what this series needed, and Hitman Absolution delivers big time in the fun factor department. Gorgeous environments that are incredibly lit, fantastic sound mixing, and moody ambience really make Hitman Absolution a title to remember. It's a generous game with a lengthy campaign and a separate Contracts mode if you want to dig deeper into what the community is doing within the game. Rounding things out is a surprisingly cool story with some very memorable characters, including a blood-curdling, redneck villan that you'll never forget. Hitman has always been a hard game to classify, as it has practically become a genre unto itself. But while this title may polarize fans of the older titles, there has never been a better Hitman game for the newcomer to jump into and discover the one-of-a-kind experience that the Hitman franchise offers.

While I appreciate the occasional good walking simulator, I do so with the full knowledge that other than its presented narrative, there will be little else to carry the game onward. Tacoma, in that regards, is one of the weaker experiments in the genre.
The story barely lifts off of its feet before you establish that it will be going nowhere, and rather than ending it with an O. Henry twist, the resolution falls flatter than the page that Fullbright wrote their concept brief on.
An interactive narrative based in a space station, with a HAL-inspired--though not in morality--AI should translate to a win. Not in this game, not in the least.
Sure, play it. There are one or two moments that will attempt to achieve something, but the overall experience is an utter letdown. There are far superior games out there.

So this game is really  fun...for me; and anyone else that really ejoys wuxia novels, manhua, etc. Frankly, the game makes you feel like your living a wuxia novel. You decisions in the game actually matter and leave a lasting impact on the game from then on out. The mini games for collecting resources are kinda silly but are quite fun. The combat is a fairly straight forward hexagonal turn-based strategy with a few tweaks added in. But even so, there is enough depth to keep each new combat fresh and interesting. However, before purchasing this game, be aware that progression is rather slow and can at times feal a bit grindy. This is because you actually train your characters aspects one by one with minimal stamina for any actions each day. You can go through the days fairly quickly but often times events or conversations will add to this time spent cultivating. However, it is possible that through adventuring (taking a stroll) that you can stumble upon a great chance for sudden increses in stats or new arts.
Long story short, Its a wuxia novel in game form where you control the story. If you like that sort of thing then this is the game for you. If not, you can still enjoy it but i doubt you'll last through a full life...unless you die really early on which is very possible.

I can assure you that much time will pass until you see another example of a little marvel like this. What we have here is a combination of one person's dedication, craftmanship and enviable fantasy that bloomed while exploiting given limitations. And that is a recipe for a work of art. The game is short, the story is simple and the mechanics are too much "souls-like", but those will not feel as negatives, because playing this game you will notice little details that will make you admire it deeply. How the form of a souls-game is implemented in this exquisite pixel art game, what stunning new ideas the developer had, and what unique atmosphere he created with his mixture of inspirations are some general examples. It has some flaws (when enemy dies near the exit, its remains are uncollectible, and the game feels ultra hard on the beginnig and ultra easy when you progress), but the contract, the way of collecting the "souls" (and what are those), the clock of (in)sanity, the disruption of monsters that resembles a mixture of The Thing and Hellraiser, all the secret recesses of the manor you do not have to visit, but will be eager to explore, and some surprising achievements will stay with you for a long time. Even if you will never come back to this game, every time you will see it while scrolling through your library, you will think "oh, this was a great game".

I've beaten Persona 5, Breath of the Wild, Horizon Zero Dawn, and multiple others in this fantastic year for great video games, but Hollow Knight has risen above them all for me.
Every aspect of this game fires on full cylindars, The world is huge, it feels like when it can't possibly get bigger, it does.
The gameplay is streamlined greatness, the difficulty is just right, with pleny of challenges for those looking for something harder in every core aspect of this game (Combat, boss rematches and many other hidden bosses, Platforming, a brutal challenge available in the late game remeniscant of Super Meat Boy, and Exploration, which lies in trying for 100%, there are some devilishly well hidden secrets areas and items,).
The mostly ambient music is also fantastic, but often understated. There are a few times when the music picks up, and when it does its salivating.
The visuals are the most striking and noticable part, this game is drop dead gorgeous, the Tim Burton to Cuphead's Walt Disney (And also Hand Drawn too!), I don't often stop to smell the roses in some games, but I did here. Quite a few times.
The games story structure and characters are very similar to the often compared Dark Souls (Along with many other aspects of the game, Hollow Knight does feel like a mix of Metroid, Darksouls, and a hint of Castlevania), and there is a lot of marit too that, characters come and go with small exchanges, ending in different ways depending on if you managed to see them every time. Hollow Knights lore is fairly deep, with a pristine attention to detail and continuity, but its not obtuse to as confuse the average player, piecing together the main story, and the background of the title character was magical on my first playthrough.
Does the game have flaws? It does, some areas feel undercooked, lacking boss fights/npc's/items where it feels there should (Hive and Deepnest are the largest offenders, but this can change with the later expansions, as it looks like the Halloween Update will be expanding on Deepnest in specific.), the combat gets a bit lopsided with the final weapon upgrade, and charm balance is bit wonky. These are nitpicks though, this game comes very close to being mastercraft.
For $15 this is some of the best value for dollar you will ever get out of a non randomized game, I got slightly over 28 hours out of my 100% file, and its only getting better with more free content expansions on the way! I fully reccomend this game if I havent made that clear already, don't wait for a sale, its worth your time and your money!

It's kind of a shame that I am not recommending Beyond Earth because it is a legimately enjoyable game. The problem is that it is almost the same game as Civ V, with less civilizations to play as, less victory conditions (there is little difference between the three affinity victories which could bring the number down to 2), and less overrall content. While some parts of the game have been changed, they have not really evolved to the point of them being considered any different. Social Polices are now Virtues (although the fact the trees go deeper now is a welcome change). Barbarians are Aliens (and they will attack you, no matter what, but you can simply just fortify and hold them off for someone else to take them out). The tech web was a great idea, although in the end everyone ends up with similiar functioning units. Other than that everything is just a different name. Happiness = Health, Gold = Energy. Stations serve no purpose other than an excuse to build trade routes, as you can't become allied with them, you can only trade or take over Stations. Personally I think the worst offence of the entire game is if regardless of whether you win or lose, the game simply ends. No screen telling you who won by what means or by how many points, just simply Quit, or one more turn (unless if you lose, in which case that option is locked).
In short it is in no way a spiritual successor to Alpha Centauri and it really should have been marketed and release as an expansion (standalone or otherwise) to Civ V. Buy on sale and/or wait for expansions.

I've seen a lot of negative reviews and don't agree with them. So here is a few points.
Is the game good?
Yes it is. It is definitely one of the best 4X games out there.
Is it as good as CIV 5 with all its DLC?
No it just doesn't have the content that the full CIV 5 experience does.
Is it as good as Vanilla CIV 5?
Yes, but only if you like a Sci Fi experience.
People here are comparing a game that came out a few days ago, to the full CIV 5 and all of its DLC. I played Vanilla CIV 5 a few times before buying all of the DLC. And compared to the total experience, Vanilla CIV 5 is complete trash. By the same idea, Beyond Earth just doesn't have the content of a CIV game with all of its DLC. Beyond Earth is a fun and different take on the CIV series. But it isn't for everyone. A big problem is that people are thinking it's the same as other CIV games. It's not. It is heavily Science driven (it's a Sci Fi game). And it doesn't have all of your favorite charachters of history. But it is still fun.
The affinity system allows for your Civilization to develop in a non-linear way. This means that picking what you're going to research next is a huge factor in your strategy. Do I want to research Terraforming to get Terrascapes, or would I rather unlock a new affinity-based military unit? Additionally each affinity plays quite differently.
The base 8 Civs are not terribly different from each other. However, you also get to pick your colonists, cargo and ship to further customize them. Do you get more culture and health in each city? Or would you rather have more production? Would you like a free worker at the beggining? Or a soldier instead? These all affect how your CIV is going to begin and play.
My big complaint however is the Health system. Health is the replacement for Happiness and it is somewhat wonky to manage. In CIV 5 you would found a new city near a luxury resource you didn't have and that would offset the unhappiness from founding the new city. Then later you could buil buildings in order to increase it further. Beyond Earth has no luxuries. Founding a new colony (especially early game) basically means taking a large hit to Health. Then you slowly have to build your health back up with new buildings. This also makes keeping cities taken during war very difficult. It takes much longer for cities to become useful again (on the bright side there are no Courthouses). I feel like you'll end up burning down more than half of the cities you take.
If....if we could just have more players tho.

I went in to Beyond Earth with a lot of Civ baggage in my trunk, having started with the series back with the very first Civilization and having loved every game in the series and thoroughly enjoying the tried and true mechanics. However I was excited to see the new changes in Beyond Earth, a fresh take on the series from the masters of 4X.
The research tree (or research web) and development of your colonies is non-linear, with no tech being outright better than the other even later in the tree, just different and with different priorities depending on your chosen strategy.
Units also do not become obsolete as the upgrades through your affinity keep them up to par with those unlocked later in the game, again it's not about better or worse, but different.
The big problem with the research web is not in it's function but in how it relays information to you. They obviously tried to go hard for a futuristic aesthetic, but this means that everything is reduced to a simple white icon. It's extremely hard to see if you're unlocking a unit, an ability, a building or a wonder making decisions take a lot longer as you'll have to mouse over every single item.
This problem persists in the Civopedia where clicking on a unit does not give you the description and image of the unit, rather you have the description and a giant icon.
In the world the readability is not much better. The miasma which damages your units can sometimes be extremely hard to see, and the difference between tundra, plains, desert and grasslands is miniscule. I don't know what the reason behind this is but it makes it very straining. People with impaired color vision will not have a fun time with that.
The game keeps the old resources of Production, Food, Gold and Happiness even if it renamed Gold to Energy and Happiness to Health, though your rivals will comment on your colonies low health with the same flavor blurb used in Civ 5 to denote low happiness. It feels a bit lazy sometimes.
Is this a bad game? No. Is it a good game? No. But it feels uninspired. Something is missing and it's hard to put your finger on what it is. It's a bit like looking forward to an exciting day trip and hearing it's been postponed until tomorrow. It's not outright terrible but certainly not what you hoped for.
The best part of the game is before the game starts, where you customize your faction. This is a very interesting concept that I hope will be adapted for future games in the series or expanded on in this game.

Things that need to be fixed in this game:
Specialists!!!! OMG!!!! they are useless in this game. Unlike in Civ 5 in its current state, specialists literally are not worth using in this game. Unlike Civ 5 where they provided points toward great people and provided some good food or hammers, they dont provide anything worth while in BE. They are literally useless. Like perhaps 2 science for the science tree, 2 hammers for the industry tree, or 2 food for the food tree. Making specialists worth while, heck even have some of them provide extra resources like more floatstone or xenomass or something.
Lack of resource variety and ocean variety! A huge thing would be hunting animals, fishing for aquatic life, even terraforming tiles to be earth like and growing earth foods for purity. Unit balance, to easy you find affinity units super powerful and one shotting most lower level units. I also would think we would have more unit variety. Like Civ 5 where you have missile cruisers, submarines, helicopters, battleships, destroyers, bombers, fighters, mech units, paratroopers, marines, tanks...etc, they should add more to this game with more options and strategys.

The Story in Teslagrad can be interpreted differently from player to player. I won't be spoiling the story, so I'll rather talk a little about how the story is presented. Teslagrad does not use dialogue or text, but rather shows the story instead of telling it. There are rooms with distant stages, and you are presented by a scene from a play. Again, no dialogue, it's just motions and actions. This is the main way of storytelling. There are also a number of somewhat hidden scrolls, that add to the story. Again, these scrolls feature no text, just pictures. This way of storytelling can be confusing at times, but nonetheless, is a nice touch and something different.
The game play is quite enjoyable. The controls are solid, and easy to get used to. Teslagrad focuses mainly around puzzle solving. The puzzles it revolves around, are similar to magnets or charges; opposites attract, like (charges) repel. You have various tools to help aid you through areas, such as the Magnet Glove. With this, you can change some objects to the desired colour; blue or red. Blue on blue repels, red on red repels, red on blue attracts, etc. The puzzles don't drag on, and don't feel like a chore to complete. The game also features boss fights, five in total. They are very difficult, due to the fact that if any hazardous thing touches you, you die. This goes for anything in the game, not just bosses. They aren't impossibly hard, however they can be rage inducing at times. Once defeating them, it's very rewarding. This can be seen as a pro or con.
Right off the bat, you'll notice the animations are smooth and slick. The textures are sharp, and the overall art style is beautiful. The music is simply excellent, and creates such different atmospheres for each area of the map. Not much left to say.
Teslagrad is a well made puzzle platformer. With clever puzzles, and rage inducing bosses, this game won't lose your attention. If you're interested, definitely try this out. Well worth it.

INK is a fun and enjoyable experience and the overall level design and aesthetic is great, but the entire game is jarringly short. There are only seventy or so super short levels and three bosses, and I beat it all in just 68 minutes. The thing that might draw me back is that there are invisible collectibles in some of the levels, but like all the terrain in the game, the collectible is only visble if ink gets splashed on it. The idea of randomly splashing around levels that might not even contain a collectible sounds kind of tedious.
It has a lot of the trappings of games that are made in GameMaker, such as having no options menu or support for controllers other than an Xbox controller. Also, mysteriously, the entire game seems to be locked at 30 fps! I can't imagine that this game would have performance problems running on most machines at 60 fps, so it feels like developer started building the game with GameMaker's default tick rate which is 30 fps, which is kind of bizarre. I hope that in the future, the developer would consider rewriting the physics to support higher framerates.
(This is a very minor complaint, but the UI elements don't switch out based on wheter you are using a keyboard or controller. For example, button prompts appear as T/(A) which is kind of ugly. This is of course super minor, but it's these kinds of details that remind you that it was made in GameMaker and the developer probably neglected to include a system that detects which device you are playing with.)
I received this game in the GameMaker Humble Bundle, so the price was not an issue to me. The core design of the game is great, and the sound and visuals are top notch, and considering it was bundled with so many other games I feel like I got my money's worth. I'm a fan of platformers like these and the time I spent with it scratched that itch. If the developer ever considers reworking the game's code to unlock the framerate and adding more content, I think it would be worth the price. Right now, I'd say if you are really interested, like this type of game and won't be bothered by playing a precision platformer at 30 fps, I'd say go for it. Even though it's just five bucks, I personally was hoping for a smooth 60 fps experience like Super Meat Boy, and definitely some more content. The main reason I chose to not recommend this game was that it felt like the minimum viable product, but I am hopeful about where this developer might take the idea.

Fullbright’s focus on character-first story and gameplay should have figuratively lifted off into earth’s orbit with vast potential in Tacoma’s space-centric story, but the result is a failed launch that face plants into earth. From the moment you step into the claustrophobic station, and propel yourself through a hollow and empty hallway, whilst anti-gravity garbage lists by, you prepare yourself for a rollercoaster of unraveling what happened. Sadly, you find out “not much”. Tacoma preps you with the knowledge all the crew members have been evacuated, and therefore safe. Looking back on Gone Home, this was not the case, as that game pulled you through unsure twists and turns inside the seemingly benign house. Thus it had a story that came together through the nonlinear interweaving of characters’ journals, artifacts, memories of the past, and paired with the main character and her sister, who were narrators  capable of painting an honest word picture that showed a family at a time of crisis. Yet in Tacoma, this honesty is absent. After passing through the first area, I felt uneasy knowing pretty much all I would need to know about these characters’ situation. There are no story points that challenge these expectations, which is tragic because these are characters I don’t think Fullbright had the intention of writing.
Despite the effort to connect with the characters through AR sequences, I found I was left with a handful of relatively hollow verbs to a sentence that desperately needed more adjectives. Looking through their trash, under their beds, in their drawers, the most we find are discarded papers echoing internal yet futile hopes to impress and succeed. Despite this, it seems none of them have conviction to really stand up for themselves. When catastrophe strikes, we are left with atonal dialogue. It doesn’t help that Tacoma swings wildly from what this story could be about. Oden, the AI equivalent to a nicer “HAL” from 2001 a Space Odyssey, is barely developed. You play as a contract AI extractor, who finds some necessary reason to watch AR recordings. But I presume this data could have been recalled from the AI’s central database.
You will never find a stressed conversation in Tacoma, and whatever sympathetic plight the characters may have, is sheltered in moments of Oden taking over the situation, calming the crewmembers down. These are a group of bright individuals, beaten into submission by circumstances and are unfairly primed by Oden’s AI. Let’s not forget Ms Purple, one of the leaders, who speaks down to her crew members telling them to “just deal with it”. If there were to be an award for “least sympathy towards a character” in Tacoma, she would win it for me.
Gone Home was a tremendous experience in seeing subtext be a valuable key to storytelling. Such subtext in Tacoma was thinly veiled, pieces come together much too quickly and easily. You might find a key to a locked door, to which you hope to find something revelatory, but there is nothing of the sort.
As much as I wish to give Fullbright the full opportunity to get a pass on this one, since they’re still making honest and personal games, I cannot recommend this on any basis of good storytelling or character development. This could and should have been so much more, and it leaves me wondering why not.

A completely linear, outright railroaded narrative with limited depth, little environment to explore, flimsy worldbuilding, mediocre acting and writing, and essentially zero actual gameplay or even decision-making.
GAMEPLAY:
There are no puzzles aside from the "narrative puzzles" of piecing together the story from a handful of voiced/animated setpieces and half-corrupted chatlogs, save for two or three "find the 4-digit keycode" challenges that each gate a small, ultimately inconsequential piece of narrative from the player. There isn't even anything in the way of a branching path - you are told where to go, when to go there, and are provided with unfettered access to every piece of story (again, save for the passcodes). You are free to pause, rewind, and fast-forward every acted bit of story, and access data logs at-will. Even as a walking sim or a 3D VN, the game falls short of its own genre limitations. You walk down the path and press Mouse1 to read the only thing the game will let you read.
STORY:
And what you do read is filled with inconsistencies, showing us a world with all its thought put into its aesthetics. Once you start putting together the two-and-two of the environment and the narrative, it quickly begins to deconstruct itself. I don't want to spoil anything -- not that I think there is much to spoil in the first place -- but rest assured that there are many, many silly tropes this sci-fi story stitches together without stopping to make sure they're making any sense together. It almost makes sense, then, that the meatiest part of the story is the political intrigue that occurs entirely off-station and over a much longer timeframe. But it's painted in strokes so broad and far apart that nothing really comes together. There's too much space between the decisions and the mechanics of the game's greater universe, such that anything interesting about it will only exist in fanfiction or future Fullbright games.
PRESENTATION:
When the story is operating in-the-moment, unveiling the events in intentional disorder through animated and voice-acted setpieces, it's not asking you to think, but to feel. And in this capacity it's... functional. The voice acting is consistent, but suffers from a general lack of emotion. The lines are all delivered with run-of-the-mill affectivity - inflect here, put emphasis on that word, stick a sob in the middle of this phrase - but the performances fall far short of eliciting any kind of visceral reaction. The oxygen runs out, the hardware explodes, the two lovers may never see each other again, but it's all just words on a page, spoken into a microphone, replayed at the location of a virtual biped. It's impossible for the characters to make you care about them, because they don't care about themselvesin the first place.
AUDIOVISUAL:
The look and feel of the world is actually quite nice, if sparse on depth and detail. The station invokes shades of works like Bioshock and 2001: A Space Odyssey, without ever feeling like it's ripping them off. Bright LEDs striking down the walls of a dark hallway, or a humid room with real plant life all the way up here, juxtaposed against the smooth curves and platonic geometric shapes of the station's spartan architecture and cold grey tones. The music, too, applies itself in colourful bursts, breaking the generally bleak and ambient soundscape with solo acoustic guitar in a bedroom, or a tight cut from some electro-rock group playing against a pair of technicians in a bedroom. These are the all-too-few moments where Tacoma feels real - staccato flashes of weight and depth and meaning, in a space station otherwise filled with weightless stories and colourless people and empty space.
TECHNICAL:
There is nothing to really speak of in a technical sense, aside from the game's curiously-awful performance on my machine (R9 290, i7-3770k at 4.5GHz, 16GB DDR3). Though essentially free of glitches and bugs, Tacoma routinely drops well below 60fps when there is nothing but a short hallway on-screen. There is no excuse for this kind of performance in this kind of game but, being what it is, it never truly suffers for it. The options menu only provides a handful of settings to play with, but it's enough for what Tacoma does. Nobody will bemoan the lack of multiple antialiasing types or raw mouse input, and if they do, they're being extremely silly.
TAKEAWAY:
Tacoma ultimately falls short of nearly every game it shares a soul with. It's less interactive, less explorative, less emotional, less believable, and/or less variable than anything else you might play if you're looking for Not-Tacoma. Take your pick. And at a mere 2 hours of content, it is certainly not worth the price it asks you to pay. You can get twice the game for half the price almost anywhere you'd care to look.
Walking away from Tacoma makes more sense than Tacoma ever will.

First of all the levels are much more liniar compared to the other Hitman games, combining that with the fact that your cover can be blown if you come too close to a person that is wearing the same uniform as you, witch mostly results in killing everyone to pass a certain part of the level because for example only police man may acces a certain area and every person in that area will discover you if you try to pass them. I mean you're a hitman, someone wants someone dead and you're hired to do the dirty work, no need for a fancy story there.

Before I start off this review, I wanna give people an idea what this program is. Live2D Wallpaper is a program that allows you to apply live wallpapers to your desktop, very similar to Wallpaper Engine. The main difference with this program is that you have the ability to personalize the wallpaper by adding Live 2D Mascots (identical to the facerig models) that react to your mouse, a background picture/video, effects, filters, widgets, music, etc. You can essentially customize to your heart's content.
As a person who's been using Wallpaper Engine for quite some time, I was quite pleasantly surprised with this program and I've found myself playing around with the program, trying out a variety of combinations. While I don't see this replacing Wallpaper Engine any time soon, I do see it as a great alternative.
One thing to keep in mind is that this program is in its early access stage, so you can expect the program to be a bit barebones. At the moment, there aren't many widgets/filters/effects to mess around with, and the workshop is currently full of anime girl models (this may be a downside for some, or a selling point for others).
As far as cons go, my only real complaint is that Live2D Wallpaper requires steam to be open in order to run, and it can take quite a bit. I'm hoping this can maybe be changed in the near future, but it's not a deal breaker for me.
For $3.99, you can't go wrong with Live2D wallpaper. I look forward to seeing this program expand and include a variety of new features down the road.
It appears that this program is certainly making progress. The workshop is still lacking variety, but now we have the option to use 360 videos for backgrounds, which is quite nice. While this hasn't caused any performance issues on my end, I do worry about lower end PCs.
While I'm at it, I feel I should address some of the noteworthy changes that have been made. This program has gone through a few name changes, with the new current name being Live2DViewerEX (quite the mouthful), and its base price has increased to $4.99. I'm still unsure as to why these two changes happened, but these changes are too minuscule to affect my review. The program is still reasonably affordable, and it has only gotten better with the recent updates.

"Shrouded in Sanity" is the beat-em-up of Soulslike games mired in eldrich horrors.
While the artwork is simplistic in its design, the aescetic comes across as both functional & readable. Some of you may be put off by that alone, however such a design choice makes sence for development time as animation can be one of the largest parts of development for 2D characters. No awards on a technical level.
Exploring the mansion was the larger portion of the game, navigating until one comes across the several bosses needed in order to progress. You have limited healing & limited ammo; all of which is replenished at one of the two 'bonfires.' Depending on how power hungry you are the environment becomes more threatening. The difficulty will similarly increase with dying or just being good at the game (...the how would be telling.)
Bosses were varied in difficulty, some predictable with obvious patterns of punishment,with others offering sudden variety to the conflict as the fight went on. Battles will feel 'bullet spongey' if light attacks are your go-to for offence. The game wonderfully connects lesser enemies to upcoming bosses, never leaving you unprepared for the blind first-attempt.
In summary "Shrouded in Sanity" is a short yet enjoyable challenge with incentive for multiple playthroughs.

Absolutely amazing. Frankly, I would hardly call this game Assassin's Creed. It's just so different from other entries in the franchise, and it's just so much better. I love this series, even despite bad entries like AC3 or Unity, and this game is exactly the reason why. This game proves that Ubisoft actually isn't a bunch of idiots. This game ditched the overly preachy Assassins v Templar shtick that all the other games had, sure both of these are still present, but they are pushed so far to the background that they hardly matter. This game is really about PIRATES. You don't see Assassins or Templars or historical figures on either side taking the stage for this game, you see the famous Caribbean pirates of the 18th century. Edward Kenway, who is the first main character of an Assassin's creed game to not even be an Assassin in any way, takes the spotlight, befriending such characters as Blackbeard, Stede Bonnet, Bart Roberts, all famous pirates of the Caribbean. You won't be confined to a single large city or multiple small cities like previous titles, instead you'll be able to set sail across the Caribbean, attacking other ships and exploring small islands. The story, as usual, isn't much to look at, but the gameplay and characters are FANTASTIC. To anyone who felt burned by other entries into the franchise, I implore you to try Black Flag.

I had a lot of trouble with the game in the beginning, because it would always crash within 10 or so minutes of me booting up the game. However, once I got past the beginning and a bit into the game it became a lot more stable, and I have yet to experience a crash like I was having in the beginning.
Tale of Wuxia is a great RPG featuring deep strategical combat, a compelling story, and a great albeit at times very repetitive soundtrack.
The combat has a turn-based, hex-grid strategy system. Based on your various stats you may move a certain amount of hexes. If you strike from in-front of your enemy, they have a much higher chance of countering you. As such your character positioning is very important. Some characters have special effects, such as one of the characters you start with, whose ability is to defend characters he is within one hex of when they get attacked. The combat can get a bit complicated--even though I am only playing on the easiest difficulty, I am having quite some trouble with some of the battles.
Another part of the game you're going to be seeing a lot is perhaps the part of the game I like the least. After the first part of the game, you join a martial arts sect and spend a lot of your time training there. Over time you get access to various activities you may participate in. These include doing chores, training your basics, your internals, your skills, producing wares, and going for a stroll. All of these require stamina, and the only way to recover stamina, is to rest, which after a certain amount of times will progress the story.
A couple of hours into the game, I feel incredibly underpowered, with my main character only surviving one or two blows by an enemy, whereas my supporting characters are a lot more powerful. I know I am supposed to be weaker than them, however I can't help but feel like I did something wrong in training my character.
Aside from those issues, I am truly in love with the game. I am not a huge rpg-fan, nor am I  a huge-wuxia fan, yet the game in-spite of some lack of polish is great. Try it out, and if you don't like it, or if it keeps crashing for you; refund it.

Shrouded in Sanity is an interesting little game with major influences from Bloodborne, as well as several other games. It feels rather similar to The Last Door, if you have played that game, except that it a side on brawler as opposed to a point and click.
Firstly, there is an unfortnately common bug with the engine which causes the game to be unable to start. There is a fix in the forum.
The game contains 5 bosses in the main storyline, and also has an optional boss. All these bosses feel interesting and unique from one another, which is an area where other "Souls-Like" games often fail. The game world is extremely small, however. It focusses entirely on a 4 storey manor and the gardens surrounding it. The game took me just under 4 hours to beat in a single sitting, and everything feels really close together. This isn't helped by the fact that you spawn in in the middle of the map, so nothing feels particularly far away. Regardless, the lack of a map and the constant perspective changes make it difficult to navigate and I would often end up back going around in circes without even realising I had doubled back on myself. The game is in desperate need of a map.
When I first started the game up, I thought that it was far too difficult. Even standard enemies can combo you to be close to dead but, as with any good game with difficulty this high, it seems to get easier as you go on as you master the mechanics of the game. Whereas the first boss I fought utterly destroyed me multiple times, by the end I had defeated two of the bosses first try. This is a game where it's gratifying to "git gud".
One of the game's big unique mechanics is how sanity works. Basic enemies have a slight chance to instead spawn as more powerful  counterparts. The lower your sanity, the greater this chance. By the end of the game, it wasn't uncommon to walk into a room filled with powerful enemies where I had expected just a few easy kills. Sanity is decreased by using upgrade materials and by dying (I think - this is never openly explained). I found this mechanic interesting and it kept me on my toes.
The soundtrack is not bad, but neither is it really something to go out of your way for. The same can be said for the story - it does its job but doesn't exactly enthrall me.
The other major complaint I have about the game, besides its length, is the fact that you cannot customise the gear you are using. It would have been nice to be able to use something besides the katana and pistol - which I almost never used anyway. Riposteing doesn't do enough damage for it to be worth putting yourself at risk for. It doesn't even knock enemies to the ground, so they can attack you as soon as the risposte animation is finished, often without you having the chance to get out of the way first.
Still, Shrouded in Sanity is a neat little game that is well worth your time, if you don't mind the lack of polish in some areas.

As of 2016, it has been 10 years since the release of Hitman Blood money, the game defined the Hitman style of play and is regarded as one of the best stealth games of all time, to which I agree.
6 years later we now have Hitman Absolution developed by IO interactive and published by Square Enix, is it better than Blood money? or does it fall flat? Let's start with the plot.
Hitman Absolution kicks off right after the Hitman book: Hitman Damnation by author Raymond Benson, which took place after Blood money. Agent 47 (The main character of the Hitman Franchise) is told by the new head of the ICA: Benjamen Travis, to assasinate 47's former handler Diana Burnwood. When 47 shoots Diana, she tells 47 to save a girl by the name of Victoria as her last dying wish. I thought the plot was pretty well done
Let's get this out of the way first, the game is absolutely gorgeous with highly detailed locations, great lighting, sharp textures, great character models and animations. However, there is a bit too much bloom, especially 47's bald head.
The gameplay mostly consists of you having to get from one end of a level to the other while trying not to get spotted by enemies. Some missions have you killing a certain target within an area and these sections are by far the best parts of the game. You have a variety of ways to kill your target which goes from using electricity, blow up, grind, burn alive, blow up, stab, and yeah you get the idea. If you're not the sneaky type and want to shoot your way through the game's serveral chapers, that is also an option, the gunplay is perhaps one of the most tight I've played in a third person shooter. In each level there is a item you can find called evidence, which can be used to boost your score, and this takes me to the new feature for the Hitman franchise: the points system.
In almost every level, you will be scored on how you completed a level, such as losing points if you had to kill an NPC and didn't hide the body, killed the target in a creative way, lose points when spotted, etc. When you got enough points, you can learn assassin techniques which can be used to make 47 more efficient, such as reducing the time it takes to reload your gun, run faster, more health, and you get the picture. A returning feature is the much loved disguise system since the first Hitman game, although it works a bit different here.
If you find a disguise in a level, you can then wear it and move among the enemy, however it does not shield you fully from the enemy. If an enemy or civilian sees you while wearing their clothing, they will take longer to realize that you don't belong here and will investigate, however the other people in different clothing will not find you suspicious. This new system definitely works in my opinion, and if it was like blood money, the game would be almost impossible to fail.
A new mode to the series is contracts mode, you pick one of the many levels in the game, look around and then mark 3 targets, kill them how you want, and put it online to see who can do the same hit more efficiently. This mode is probably the closest you'll get to Blood Money gameplay and is definitely a mode that shouldn't be avoided. When you complete a contract in contracts mode you earn money which can be used to buy upgrades for your guns, buy disguises, and more guns.
The sound design of the game is top notch, the music is well done even without Jesper Kyd, and the voice acting is superb, especially David Bateson who voices 47 who does an exceptional job.
The A.I. in this game is also pretty good, they will actively search for you if you are hiding and know when to take cover during fire fights. Although there were still parts where they did act strange, such as ignoring dead bodies and shooting in the wrong direction.
In the end, Hitman Absolution is an excellent edition to the Hitman franchise and shouldn't be overlooked just because it's not that much like Blood money. I even think Absolution is just as good as Blood money.

What this game draws it's inspiration is clear: Resident Evil 1, Dark souls and Devil May Cry. If i didn't know better, i could be fooled to believe that Dante has somehow found his way into the RE1 mansion, Zombies have learned mechanics from Dark souls universe and are now having a diverse attacking style instead of lumbering towards Dan.. ehem, our hero.
The sanity meter was another thing that was an interesting part of the game, the more you level up (or die!), the more insane your character becomes. Since you are resurrected from the dead, that messes up a bit with your head, or if you're using black magic to increase your skills, that isn't especially safe either. The more insane you are, the more vicious monsters you see roaming the halls trying to attack you. But are they there? Or just in your head?
The story itself is told through exploring various objects found all around the mansion, and then piecing them together in your head. The whole "world" is fully explorable minus some few rooms where you have to do some extra work to get into, but they're not required to beat the game.
That has its up and downs. You can run through this game really quick if you know what you're doing, but then again, you can wander around aimlessly if you don't know what you're doing :D This game is strong on exploration.
Combat is based on timing your attacks and dodging. Enemies hit hard, so you won't survive if you don't learn the mechanics. There's decent amount of different enemies, with different attack patterns, so not just a re-skinned versions of familiar enemies, and the insanity brings even more monstrosities.
There's also a good amount of optional stuff to do: An optional boss, a whole underground area where you don't need to go if you just want to finish the game, 4 endings AND you can play the game as the bosses. Having their own attacks and stats, so they're also way more than just a skin.
