There are those who describe this game as a "souls-like" and then there are those who think the term is stupid, so they just say it's like Bloodborne. Either way, now you know what the genre and gameplay is like.
The game starts off fairly difficult. Several mechanics have a delay, because they activate according to when you release the button, not when you press it. When you realize this, the game becomes much less frustrating.
I did enjoy how the game was laid out. I drew out a map of the mansion, and it actually makes sense. Some rooms have nothing, some rooms contain easter eggs, some rooms are only there to screw with you. The enemy variety isn't large. It's easy to ignore as the game progresses, as you'll find that the more difficult enemies each have their own gimmick on how to defeat them. In other words, the enemies are fairly bland at the beginning, and creative toward the end. The short time it takes to beat this game is welcoming of the small enemy variety.
I still have some secrets to find, and some secrets require a higher madness to uncover. The madness mechanic is confusing, to say the least. When you die or level up, your madness increases. As many times as I've died or leveled up, it seems to be stuck at the point just barely before I max it out, locking me out of some of the game's supposedly secret areas. To this, I mean that there are areas which claim to require a high level of madness to enter, and you are locked out of them until you reach that point.
As for sound design, the creator could have at least modified some of the clips they used. There are a few sound bites in this game that were ripped straight off of pre-existing unlicensed recordings. One example is the Cassini recordings of Saturn's aurorae, recorded in 2003. No sound editing, just straight ripped audio.
Graphics and animation are spot on for how the game presents itself. The sprites are polished, though the hitboxes could use some work in regard to their behavior near doorways.
I'd say it's worth playing, and the price is worth it for the few hours it'll take you to complete the game. While it's possible to win in less than ten minutes, if you want to experience everything it has to offer, you'll have to sink hours into the game.
I recommend it for people who enjoy lovecraftian themes and Bloodborne.
The game isn't recommended for people who hate adapting to new control schemes.

I would not recommend this in its current state. The game feels good at first and seems new and inspiring. Thats until you start playing and you begin to realise that Civ 5 was way better than this and of course Civ 3 and Civ 4 had more as well. Health equallying happiness is the biggest pain in the butt throughout the game and with no luxury resources like Civ 5 to help you keep it up, it practically eats your empire apart. having only 8 factions and so little unit variablility is very disappointing. The trade becomes a huge pain unlike Civ 5 where you are limited in trade this one almost pushes you to have every city running multiple trade routes to keep them going.
The diplomancy has not changed much and I find myself not reacting to the other factions for anything. Thats not saying much since Civ 5 diplomancy was lack luster as well.
All in all you can translate everything going on in the game to Civ 5 minus the wonder of the wonders and that they focused to much on the "new Barbarians." actually I think they did not focus enough there is no variety from the bug life forms. Like if I want a cold world, why cant I have huge wild mammals with alternate style of play or Dinosaur like creatures on a tropical hot world or more aquatic life forms on a aquatic world, or why not be able to build underwater cities and such.
All in all, the game is like Civ 5 from the beginning and it wont get better till someone pushes a Mod that improves everything they fell short in or they make an expansion to take more of our money to improve a game that failed from all the hype. Save your money and get Civ 4 or 5 and play that until this game gets improved dramatically because those games will give you more.
Granted I am still going to play this game more since I already laid down the cash and try to find some enjoyment though I may go back to play Civ 5 since at least that game is more polished.
Update:
So I wanted to update my review a bit, the above part is still valid.
Things that need to be fixed in this game:
Specialists!!!! OMG!!!! they are useless in this game. Unlike in Civ 5 in its current state, specialists literally are not worth using in this game. Unlike Civ 5 where they provided points toward great people and provided some good food or hammers, they dont provide anything worth while in BE. They are literally useless. Tiles provide way more than any specialist would provide. I think the biggest fix would be in the virtue tree to make them provide extra stuff based on which tree you went down. Like perhaps 2 science for the science tree, 2 hammers for the industry tree, or 2 food for the food tree. Making specialists worth while, heck even have some of them provide extra resources like more floatstone or xenomass or something.
Lack of resource variety and ocean variety! A huge thing would be hunting animals, fishing for aquatic life, even terraforming tiles to be earth like and growing earth foods for purity. Would love to see some things provide health points as well instead of relying on virtues, biowells, and buildings.
Orbitals are annoying, the idea was good but instead they should have made them to not fall from the sky after a certain time but instead made them simple and as you advance in tech you can add upgrades to them to do more. slowly becoming like spacestations.
Unit balance, to easy you find affinity units super powerful and one shotting most lower level units. I also would think we would have more unit variety. Like Civ 5 where you have missile cruisers, submarines, helicopters, battleships, destroyers, bombers, fighters, mech units, paratroopers, marines, tanks...etc, they should add more to this game with more options and strategys.
For example: How about gunships like helicopters that advance to more sophisticated units or just add submarines and special forces. They also need to speed up water transports for units, takes forever to cross oceans moving two tiles at a time... civ 5 had it to where you where traveling faster across the oceans as you advanced eras. This game they crawl at 2 tiles at a time, even after you get hover tech and some units can transverse the sea they still are slow.
Some people say oh they got satellites, thats the new units. Those things sit in one spot, few actually fire weapons, and its very easy to destroy them. Also where are the NUKES?? Hell I would think we would still have nuclear weapons.
Stations are a complete failure, they are not worth trading to dont provide any unique quests or special resources and many times they spawn right where you are looking to grow to. The computer will attack and destroy them randomly even if your trading with them. They are nothing compared to city states from Civ 5. What they should do is start them out like they do now at tier one. Then each completed trade route with them they grab a tile around them like an outpost does. Then they are tier two after becoming like a new city providing both more of their points and also providing any resources in their influence. Then repeat the process for tier 3 (only now they would be two tiles out) and then they provide a unique trade bonus based on the type of station like a unique unit, health points, or that city thats trading with the station can build a unique building, as well as more trade points, any resources in their area, a special quest that unlocks a unique wonder or a hidden tech in the web.
There is much more I could add but  figured that covers most of the major things that need to change.

A pretty shoddy roguelike with very little to recommend it. There are plenty of good games in the genre out there, so there is no reason to waste time and money on this one.
As best as I have been able to determine (see more about the many impediments to actually trying to play the game below), this is a very generic and simplistic "roguelike"/action rpg-style game with some feeble attempts at humor thrown in. The game being in Early Access, you can argue about the game not being finished etc etc, but honestly, there does not appear to be much for the developer to build on in what is being sold here. Sure, he could, theoretically, toss everything out, start over, and perhaps produce a worthwhile game, but there would be little reason to try to salvage anything of the current game. So, on the off chance that this will happen, I'm sure there will be opportunities to buy that game, without having to subject yourself to this abomination.
As for the technical shape of the game, as mentioned above, I know it's early access, but it is essentially unplayable due to bugs, crashes and plain shoddy programming. I mean, come on - when I changed the resolution, the game itself rescaled it's ugly blocky "retro graphics" to match, but it did not do anything at all about the GUI. Nothing. No, I'm not talking about the failure to re-scaling it so you can actually read the text and similar things, which is bloody annoying, too.
No, I'm talking about not even moving the elements to fit the new resolution, meaning that the placement of the UI elements that were supposed to be on the right and bottom edges of the screen uses absolute positions, with the result that those elements now appear, i.e., in the middle of the screen.
In closing, this is a great example of the current sad state of the Steam store, Early Access and the Greenlight system. I hope that people will have enough sense, not to waste their money on "games" like this, and certainly not the $10/€10 the developer seem to think it is worth....

This is of course subject to change once it's balanced, but right now I do not recommend the game. This is coming from someone who happily has played 400+ hours of Civ V too.
It feels like a poorly balanced Civ V mod. There are some novel things in there - the affinity trees for instance are pretty neat. The questing (done better in Endless Legend) is also ok as is the esponiage. But there are too many annoyances - health severely limiting growth, overly aggressive native life forms, oribtal layer not being very well developed, bad AI - combined with balance problems and a real lack of personality make this one a pass. Frankly, I've found myself clicking "next turn" over and over again because the game punishes you from exploring, the health problems prevents you from conquering and there's nothing else to do. What's the most maddening thing is that Civ V encountered - and then patched OUT - many of these same issues. There's no excuse for them to happen in Beyond Earth.
The real killer is the lack of personalities. Yeah, I know that this game isn't a remake of SMAC but it's supposed to be inspired by it. Well, the thing that SMAC did that was so innovative was to give each faction a very distinct - almost unique - personality. The wonder movies, diplomacy and even the tech tree descriptions were all written around those personalities. Instead of copying this strength, the factions here are all faceless until far too late into the game (and by then it's too late). It's an absolute deal killer.
Even after patches it's still a collection of half-baked ideas that simply don't work together. There are far, far better 4x games on the market. Skip this one.

Teslagrad is one of the games I've enjoyed the most, recently!
It's not perfect, and some of the issues will certainly put some people off, but I found it great.
It's a metroid-vania in structure, but a puzzle-platformer in its mechanics. Being a metroid-vania, it already hits a soft spot for me! You have a fairly big map with different areas to explore, gaining several abilities as you progress that let you reach previously undiscovered places.
The puzzles mainly revolve around magnetism, as you could guess from the game. It bares some similarities with the game "Magnetic By Nature", but, while that game has more ... imaginative puzzles, Teslagrad is more polished, and it stands out with its awesome artstyle and unorthodox story-telling.
I haven't found most puzzles to be too difficult, nor the physics to be too unpredictable. Sure, there were a few times that the game was a bit frustrating for
rather than
a puzzle. But the difficulty was just right, for the most part.
The artstyle has got to be one of my favourites aspects. Reminds me quite a lot of older, hand-drawn cartoons, and it works surprisingly well with a few modern touches in the lighting effects.
The music was also really good! Unfortunately, it was a bit sparse, and the sound designed lacked in several occasions. Boss fights especially... while trying to carry a bit more impact by stopping the music right after the fights were over, the game felt a bit empty, while leaving the impact behind. Not something that is easy to explain... PID was great in this regard! Using the music's intensity to carry a given vibe.
When I mentioned "unorthodox storytelling", I meant the way that the game presents its backstory. There are 36 scrolls hidden in the game, which are usually harder to spot or get to. Most of them, you can see, being alerted to it if you want to get it. Some were completely hidden, sometimes by abilities which you did not have, at the time...
More on that next, though!
These scrolls are just little cards (almost postcards) with very simple, but representative drawings of this country's history. It shows how things evolved from medieval times to the more developped world, and then crumbling world. I found it really cool, and it certainly gives players the chance of exploring the world by searching for scrolls... twofold.
The only problem, as I said, is the gated scrolls. As a result, you'll have to go back right after/before the final boss, and go through the
game again (-- with all of your abilities and the map explored, though! Still, you'll have to solve many of the puzzles again, even knowing the solution). In more combat-oriented games, it's a great technique! It lets the player feel overpowered by going back to old, previously difficult places.
In a puzzle game, traversal is rather annoying.
Regardless, most of them are well in your grasp, less than 10 (if that many) requiring backtracking.
Not much more to say about it. The game is beautiful, and the puzzles are pretty well designed. Certainly worth a shot if you're into the animation, puzzle-platformers or  metoid-vanias in general!

NOTE: If you haven't figured it out by now, this is NOT a typical game. Call it a "walking simulator" if you feel the abstract need to categorize it, but it's a guided story with no typical gameplay or puzzle elements. Go into it with that understanding and you won't be disappointed.
Now that that's out of the way, this is one of the best stories I've played in a game in a long time. Imagining "Gone Home" catapulted to the end of the 21st century may help to describe it, however the ability to use the in-game AR to actually see the conversations taking place adds life to the story where sometimes I felt that Gone Home was lacking. Replaying each recording to follow each crewmember and see/hear what they're doing really made me feel like I was a ghostly observer watching the drama play out. The excellent voice acting coupled with the realistic animations made these characters real in my head, living out a situation that none of them asked for. Sure, you can speed through this game in a couple of hours, but by doing so you'll miss all the little pieces that make up each character and flesh them out into real people. The graphics are great too, nothing super fancy but enough to make the station seem real; I could only imagine how much more immersive this game would be in VR.
Again though, the story is what makes or breaks a game like this and I'm happy to say it delivered more than I expected and went in a direction that happily surprised me. The ending took me completely by surprise and I was smiling through the end credits. In the end, I think the best way to describe this game would be as an interactive movie with your character as a participant. By that description, it's a five-star game.
Plus there's a cat. Cats are awesome.

What a gem of an RPG this game has been. It single-handely puts most modern-day RPGs to shame. Turn-based, multiple endings, multiple paths, choices and consequences, fantastic combat, wonderful music, many secrets, reasonably good story, memorable characters, you name it.
The whole theme of the game runs loosely on Jin Yong's Wuxia novels. Most of the martial skills you learn are either of Jin Yong's established skills in his novels or game dev invented or other irrelevant powerful moves known to martial arts history like the Wu Ying Jiao or Ru Lai Shen Zhang. A good refreshment over the usual Western fantasy RPGs.
While you get to visit villages, towns and cities throughout the game, a good part of the game is spent in "learning/training" mode. In this mode, you get various choices, in the form of an artistic 2D UI, on how to build and train your character. You're given a set stamina number, which you spend either training yourself up in various skills, doing chores, gathering goods / crafting, training in the arts, or strolling around to interact with other Wulin heroes and hopefully learn a thing or two from them.
When you visit towns and cities, you're presented with the usual town hubs in RPGs except of course this is in the Eastern Wuxia theme. You get to buy stuff from shops, do sidequests, collect items and help people. And this is where we come across the biggest flaw the game has to offer. Visiting certain cities and towns have time limits, and the time limits are pretty limiting. Forget about taking your own sweet time to explore the city. Just rush through the major sidequests that benefit your character most. The learning/training mode is also pretty much limited by a 4 year limit, although it's a hefty  limit to build your character, would easily last for tens of hours or more and is equivalent to numerous turns. Many events will happen in the 4 years, some minor, some major. You will, however, get to free-roam around the game world in the end of year 4.
Skills and secrets are plentiful in the game. There are several martial skills for each category of weapons: sword, broadsword, staff, fist, finger, kicking, throwing weapons, music instruments, fan or brush. That's in addition to the collection of Internal Arts skills you can collect. Each skill comes with 2-3 moves and their unique bonuses. The skills are have their own animation, movesets, buffs/debuffs, and dmg stats. Needless to say the skill list is staggering, makes for multiple playthroughs to experiment, and is interesting and varied. The more powerful Jin Yong skills are in the game. Who wouldn't get excited with the mention of being able to obtain skills like "18 Dragon Subduing Palm".
Skills come from various mentors, events or chests. In a way, some of them are secrets and the most powerful of them are quite difficult to obtain and very very easy to miss. Their power relate to your other artistic skills like calligraphy, music, or chess or to your personal combat stats. Once you miss the chance to get the skill from a person or events, it's gone for good. There's no way you can obtain the skill short of restarting the whole game or reloading an older save. That game design decision might be good for some bad for the rest.
The game has a tonne of mini-games. There are mini-games for every gathering / crafting skill in the game. While they can appear to be fun at first, they quickly become a chore. Mining requires you to popamole, literally. Fishing requires you to play tug of war with a fish that you can't possibly lose, unless you don't ever release the line. Smithing requires you to play the game "2048". Painting requires you to put a set of jigsaws in a limited time. Collecting Herbs has you playing a memory game etc etc. Sadly, some of the most powerful weapons and internal art skills require you to go through some torturous amounts of mini-game play and some of them are hard, which probably requires many reloads to get through. Unlocking chests is also a mini-game, it feels daunting at the start but it's easy once you get the trick to it.
What makes the game truly shine other than the awesome number of skills in the game is the multiple paths you are able to walk in the game. The game has multiple endings, there are good endings, bad/evil endings, and even the grey endings. What endings you get depend on the path and choices you make throughout the 4 years of building your character and going through events. There's even an ending for losing to a chicken at the start of the game.
The liberty and freedom of building your character is amazing. You're free to specialise on a martial art or mix and match to your liking. Although the latter will most likely fail badly on higher difficulties.
Music is simply fantastic and adds to the game a lot. The standard Wuxia flair with a mix of Chinese, Hong Kong drama themed music. Combat is crisp, responsive and always interesting. Character art potraits are full of character and are eye-popping to look at. Story is decent enough and there are multiple paths to walk which will definitely affect your story. This game is already a great classic, imo. If they removed the town/city time limit and put less emphasis on the mini-games, optimise it a little, it'll become even better.

You are sent to Tacoma space station to investigate the crew that lived and worked on the station, and what happened to them when faced with disaster. You learn about each character on the station, and even a bit about how their lives were back on Earth. I found it was a good balance of detail, plenty to help me get to know each character, but not so much as to become tedious.
The bulk of the gameplay is watching and listening to the crew member’s past interactions with each other as it’s presented using the station’s 3D surveillance system, and see how the characters develop and how the story plays out. Different crew members interactions run parallel to one another. It’s pretty neat to see the story from different perspectives, and make use of the rewind and fast-forward to make sure you don’t miss out on any details.
The rest of the gameplay entails moving around the station, reading documents and other correspondences, and interacting with just about any object you’d like to. There are some clues you will need to find to unlock specific door codes, but there’s not much in the way of difficulty.
Tacoma is all about its characters and the overall story. I find the price tag a little hefty for how short it is, but the game is a quality product. If you enjoy walking simulators, especially ones that provide good, and immersive story experiences, then you’ll likely enjoy Tacoma.

As of 2016, it has been 10 years since the release of Hitman Blood money, the game defined the Hitman style of play and is regarded as one of the best stealth games of all time, to which I agree.
6 years later we now have Hitman Absolution developed by IO interactive and published by Square Enix, is it better than Blood money? or does it fall flat? Let's start with the plot.
Hitman Absolution kicks off right after the Hitman book: Hitman Damnation by author Raymond Benson, which took place after Blood money. Agent 47 (The main character of the Hitman Franchise) is told by the new head of the ICA: Benjamen Travis, to assasinate 47's former handler Diana Burnwood. When 47 shoots Diana, she tells 47 to save a girl by the name of Victoria as her last dying wish. I thought the plot was pretty well done
Let's get this out of the way first, the game is absolutely gorgeous with highly detailed locations, great lighting, sharp textures, great character models and animations. However, there is a bit too much bloom, especially 47's bald head.
The gameplay mostly consists of you having to get from one end of a level to the other while trying not to get spotted by enemies. Some missions have you killing a certain target within an area and these sections are by far the best parts of the game. You have a variety of ways to kill your target which goes from using electricity, blow up, grind, burn alive, blow up, stab, and yeah you get the idea. If you're not the sneaky type and want to shoot your way through the game's serveral chapers, that is also an option, the gunplay is perhaps one of the most tight I've played in a third person shooter. In each level there is a item you can find called evidence, which can be used to boost your score, and this takes me to the new feature for the Hitman franchise: the points system.
In almost every level, you will be scored on how you completed a level, such as losing points if you had to kill an NPC and didn't hide the body, killed the target in a creative way, lose points when spotted, etc. When you got enough points, you can learn assassin techniques which can be used to make 47 more efficient, such as reducing the time it takes to reload your gun, run faster, more health, and you get the picture. A returning feature is the much loved disguise system since the first Hitman game, although it works a bit different here.
If you find a disguise in a level, you can then wear it and move among the enemy, however it does not shield you fully from the enemy. If an enemy or civilian sees you while wearing their clothing, they will take longer to realize that you don't belong here and will investigate, however the other people in different clothing will not find you suspicious. This new system definitely works in my opinion, and if it was like blood money, the game would be almost impossible to fail.
A new mode to the series is contracts mode, you pick one of the many levels in the game, look around and then mark 3 targets, kill them how you want, and put it online to see who can do the same hit more efficiently. This mode is probably the closest you'll get to Blood Money gameplay and is definitely a mode that shouldn't be avoided. When you complete a contract in contracts mode you earn money which can be used to buy upgrades for your guns, buy disguises, and more guns.
The sound design of the game is top notch, the music is well done even without Jesper Kyd, and the voice acting is superb, especially David Bateson who voices 47 who does an exceptional job.
The A.I. in this game is also pretty good, they will actively search for you if you are hiding and know when to take cover during fire fights. Although there were still parts where they did act strange, such as ignoring dead bodies and shooting in the wrong direction.
In the end, Hitman Absolution is an excellent edition to the Hitman franchise and shouldn't be overlooked just because it's not that much like Blood money. I even think Absolution is just as good as Blood money.

Torchlight might as well be Diablo 2.5. It basically takes the structure of Diablo II and copies it exactly, while adding a few things, upgrading the graphics, and putting it underground. It's a good action RPG, as Diablo II was. From what I've seen, it's light on story, but pretty fun.
I couldn't bring myself to finish Torchlight. That's probably because the game's single player only, and I only finished Diablo II because it was a lot more fun with friends. I think the lack of story probably contributed too, since I didn't have a motivating factor to push me through it.
If you really liked Diablo II, just buy it now. If not, you won't like this either. If you're on the fence, then I'd wait until Torchlight goes on sale. As far as $20 games go, it's not a bad choice, but I'd rather point you to Neverwinter Nights 2. NWN2 has slower, more complex gameplay but a far superior story. Or, if you can spend more, check out the Dragon Age games, which I find superior in both ways.

So, FFXIII. One of the (if not THE) most hated Final Fantasy in existence, has such infamy that I expected very little of the game when I got it here on PC....
....and it's not THAT bad.
Well, I can see why you'd hate it if you came in from all the other FF's. The world map got, for the most part, reduced to corridor walking, no towns to speak of, the story is incomprehensible if you don't read a primer sitting somewhere in the menu, the game takes a long time before it gives you full control (the famous "it gets good in 20 hours) and battles are quite simplified, to the point that most of them are basically automated.
...but all of these turned out not to be that much of a turn-off to me. In battles, the stagger system helps turn things around, with quite a few enemies gaining weaknesses that didn't have before (ie: status ailments are finally useful in a FF game)
Graphically, the game looks very good! I'd say unusually good for a 7th gen game, and until recently, only with mods could you see it in full 1080p, but latest patch thankfully adds resolution & GFX options. Unfortunately, framerate is still a hot mess, with SE promising 60fps, but the game actually having a hard reaching that, even with good hardware (4670k+R9 280). Expect battles to run @ 30fps for the most part.
So, to sum my opinion: Good game, "heh" Final fantasy game, terrible framerates. Recommend buying it on sale if you have some interest in the game/series.
PS: note that the Asian version is regionally restricted AT RUN-TIME! Meaning you can't run the game outside of Asia if you bought it from there. Unless you really want JP subtitles, you should try to get someone to gift you the western version, as it includes both ENG & JP voices.

Hitman : Absolution can be hit and miss.  There are some changes to previous Hitman titles which put me off the game quite early into my first playthrough.  These changes include being unable to select the weapons you want at the beginning of a mission and more of a focus on a story from one chapter to the next over a separation of each level as individual missions.  These are faults in opinion as I sometimes found myself completing missions the same way using the same style of weapon.  The story is also not very exciting or interesting.  Hitman excels though as you progress to more complex settings, you find a wide variety of choices once you are free from the initial few introductory levels.  When repeating levels, you begin to discover more ways to progress, more weapons, more choices.  These become clearer the further you progress into the game.  There are various difficulty modes that allow you to increase or test your skills.  The trials offer some major replayability as well as a fantastic online mode that allows you to create your own missions and play other created missions.  The game itself looks good and I never experienced a drop in frame rate at any time.  The voice acting is excellent and despite a poor story, it was enjoyable to listen to the various characters.  Highly recommended for stealth game fans and even for fans of old Hitman games, as long as you can accept some disappointing changes.

I've beaten Persona 5, Breath of the Wild, Horizon Zero Dawn, and multiple others in this fantastic year for great video games, but Hollow Knight has risen above them all for me.
Every aspect of this game fires on full cylindars, The world is huge, it feels like when it can't possibly get bigger, it does.
The gameplay is streamlined greatness, the difficulty is just right, with pleny of challenges for those looking for something harder in every core aspect of this game (Combat, boss rematches and many other hidden bosses, Platforming, a brutal challenge available in the late game remeniscant of Super Meat Boy, and Exploration, which lies in trying for 100%, there are some devilishly well hidden secrets areas and items,).
The mostly ambient music is also fantastic, but often understated. There are a few times when the music picks up, and when it does its salivating.
The visuals are the most striking and noticable part, this game is drop dead gorgeous, the Tim Burton to Cuphead's Walt Disney (And also Hand Drawn too!), I don't often stop to smell the roses in some games, but I did here. Quite a few times.
The games story structure and characters are very similar to the often compared Dark Souls (Along with many other aspects of the game, Hollow Knight does feel like a mix of Metroid, Darksouls, and a hint of Castlevania), and there is a lot of marit too that, characters come and go with small exchanges, ending in different ways depending on if you managed to see them every time. Hollow Knights lore is fairly deep, with a pristine attention to detail and continuity, but its not obtuse to as confuse the average player, piecing together the main story, and the background of the title character was magical on my first playthrough.
Does the game have flaws? It does, some areas feel undercooked, lacking boss fights/npc's/items where it feels there should (Hive and Deepnest are the largest offenders, but this can change with the later expansions, as it looks like the Halloween Update will be expanding on Deepnest in specific.), the combat gets a bit lopsided with the final weapon upgrade, and charm balance is bit wonky. These are nitpicks though, this game comes very close to being mastercraft.
For $15 this is some of the best value for dollar you will ever get out of a non randomized game, I got slightly over 28 hours out of my 100% file, and its only getting better with more free content expansions on the way! I fully reccomend this game if I havent made that clear already, don't wait for a sale, its worth your time and your money!

As of late AC series is not experiencing its best days, and its understandable, recent games have neitehr been good, nor innovative. Rehashed, some say, a yearly brand with nothing to show for.
AC4 was non of those things. Black Flag is beautiful game, set in pristine locations and told with story that both inspires and makes you dream and wish, that for a second you could be a part for it, if just for a little while.
The characters and cast are abosulutely amazing and the memorable scenes and storylines will keep in wanting for more long after you've finished the game.
Building upon the open world, hunting, stalking. exploring and wandering that was AC3, Black Flag perfects it in a way to fit a true pirate game, and without doubt one of the best pirate themed games ever created. Edward is a wanderful character and only loses to Ezio because the time with him was rather short. Had it been a trilogy, the wits and charms of Edward would've, without doubt, won him the greatest AC character title.
The ship battles are exceptional, and even the buggy boarding can not cast a shadow on the well crafted system and the thrill you get when hunting for your next prize.
If you have not played it yet - do it, you're guaranteed to enjoy every second of it!

The gameplay isn't remotely balanced. That's a bit key if you're making a Souls-like, isn't it?
Shrouded in Sanity is a decent game, particularly coming from a single developer, but it has a wealth of problems that keep me from recommending it. In addition to the gameplay just not feeling complete, the level design ranges from quaint to hideous to blindingly repetitive, and the writing chops on display are -- no pun intended -- soulless.
One-on-one combat is alright; decently fast-paced. If multiple enemies enter the fray, combat tends to turn into button mashing and a race to either escape or separate enemies. Speaking of escaping, you can bypass all non-boss combat by running away. Could be cool, but it's clearly not intended. Fighting enemies will consist of quick sword swipes, heavy sword swipes (pointless -- they don't do much more damage and put you at risk of attack), and either dodging or blocking attacks, coupled with the chance to parry enemies using a gun or timed-attacks a la Buttborne / Dark Souls.
More likely you'll choose to either roll or block exclusively rather than combining tools during your enemies' frenetic onslaughts, making whichever you don't use a pointless addition to the gameplay. The gun is also useless except for one or two specific bosses, who, due to poor design choices, open their arms wide to welcome a stunning bullet over and over and over and over without break. (Think Gothic 3's awful stunlocking boars, or, more accurately, getting to be that stunlocking boar.) Enemies who themselves sport guns aren't programmed correctly, and instead of offering any attempt at challenge, run up to your avatar and fire in the wrong direction until you kill them. (This includes a boss!)
The game's full of poor or incomplete design choices like that. Admirable for a single dev with an eye for Souls' formula, sure, but still glaring -- annoying -- faults.
The art style itself ranges from beautiful to hideously drab. Mostly this impacts the level design. Room by room, most of the game's Victorian setting look too similar, making some halls and rooms almost indistinguishable from one another. Moving between rooms isn't consistent, either -- you'll enter a south-facing doorway (i.e., 'down'), and the next screen that loads will reposition the world so you're entering from the E, W, or even S. Your view repositions itself a lot, which is...just a bizarre decision. Some rooms and some objects are an ugly mash of pixels that require poorly-written text to explain that Yes, you're looking a a dead body and Yes, it had lots and lots of stab wounds and a gunshot wound.
On the topic of the writing: My god.
The storytelling potential in games is often key to me, even over gameplay, and the developer shows no interest in constructing an interesting world with this game. You play a hunter with a contract: Raised from the dead with enforced nebulousness, you're to banish the fog oppressing the gameworld by defeating four knights and disposing -- blah blah blah -- of a corrupted king. The narrative and the in-game text are mostly meaningless word-vomit stolen from Buttborne or Lovecraft, with no care or even real interest underlying them. You can almost feel the train of thought behind some of the misspelled text: "Didn't Lovecraft write about something called Nyarlathaloops and it had some Egyptian Illuminati thingy on it? That'd be cool here. Breasts are cool, too, so this room should get a lot of text explaining that these books contain my porn collection. Hmm, 'The book is just lots of obscene sexual acts....' Yeah, that sounds cool, and the ellipsis sells it. This room will explain to the player that it has 'impossible geometry' because that sounds cool, too, and Lovecraft is cool."
Most of the in-game text serves no purpose, nor does it add to the game's lore: It's all about telling, not showing. Interacting with objects simply describes that you're looking at blood; that this one body among hundreds has a bullet wound in it; that this chalkboard equation looks 'inefficient' -- whatever the heck that's supposed to mean to the player or player character; that this room simply is "...impossible geometry," despite the "geometry" in question being your run-of-the-mill Tetris blocks. It's just...braindead and boring. And rife with spelling errors and run-on sentences and broken English and characters MUAH-HAH-HAAAAHHHHHHH-ing at the player while twirling their insane mustaches. Yeugh.
Shrouded in Sanity scratches the Souls itch once you've exhausted From Software's modern catalogue, sure, but only for 3-4 hours, and not nearly to the degree of some other 2016 titles. I'd still recommend this for the curious and those just desperate for the genre, but players are better off trying Momodora IV (an easy GOTY contender), DarkMaus, and Salt & Sanctuary first.

This game good, but not great. I enjoyed it, and I recommend it as a nice stealth action entertainment, but there were things I did not like. Facial animations were awful, for instance. The story felt a bit... forced. It felt like it was written by someone indifferent. The automatic game saving system does not let you save where you want, but I never managed it to save at all - I just had to select the next mission from the menu, instead of getting ahead by clicking "Continue". In a nutshell the game is a set of missions where usually you need to kill someone, avoid being noticed, and manage to escape. Sometimes the timing is essential, so you need to think your strategy through. Sometimes it is a matter of luck. If you just take the shortest route, the game feels very short and uneventful, which is unfair considering the amount of work invested in designing the levels. I believe it is meant to be played over and over again, finding alternative, better ways to achieve the goal, getting achievements for non-trivial executions and competing with other players. For me it does not reach the level of Deus Ex: Human Revolution, but it's still a well done game that definitely deserves to be given a chance.

I'm really enjoying the latest iteration of the civilization series. The setting brings a huge breath of fresh air for me, I'm so excited to see the Civ system brought beyond earth. The tech web is probably my favourite addition as it adds a whole new dimension (literally) to research and helps you gear where you want your faction to go. Deviating from known history is exciting to me, although they could have done a better job with the flavour text and descriptions of research. They could have also had the economy symbols (energy, food, culture) beside the research name to tell you what kind of units or buildings are unlocked. I did get a little tired of mousing over every improvement in the research list to find out which research would bring my health up etc.
The unit/affinity system is quite cool. Loving the upgrades and the visual look (at least of harmony and supremacy, next playthrough is going to be purity). I do however wish there was at least one more air and naval unit, there are definitely enough ground units however. Perhaps a bomber and a large scale battleship or what have you.
The wonders are okay, mechanically the advantages are there and there is some flavour text, but again thematically they could have hired a small time sci-fi writer to fill in the descriptions a bit more. What the hell did the Crawler actually do? The abstract small text is a little disappointing.
I'm fine with the faction leaders, sure there could be more fluff dialog but it was never a strongpoint of the civ series.
The aliens are okay, I don't think they are quite as much the selling point as firaxis intended them to be. They are basically just barbarians that a) spawn more and b) can actually kick your♥♥♥♥♥until you develop some research. They don't really respond intelligently, it would be nice if this was bumped up in the future so that these aliens evolve as you push them around and beat them up.
The orbital layer is really cool, you can actually spawn resources through special orbitals. It's awesome! Terraforming at its finest. There are other orbital units that boost your economy on tiles or can be used offensively, think of starbases in galciv (boosted production in a radius).
The AI is ok, typical Civ AI so not much to say here.
Overall, I really enjoy the game. Would I pay 50 bucks for it again? That's a really big maybe, but it's definitely in the ballpark of 30-50 bucks. I am crossing my fingers that Firaxis is going to have an expansion pack for beyond Earth that will help address a few small interface issues (trade and research).

Hollow Knight is a fantastic game in every sense of the word. It's an outragious bargain at a £11 (or $15) and it's worth oh so much more than that. It's a ridiculously huge 2D Metroidvania that's centered around platforming and action gameplay and it does a very good job putting it's own unique feeling over the plethora of Metroidvanias out there.
You play as this cute little bug-man who murders or friends his way through many other bug-people out there. Hollow Knight is set in this underground, medieval style bug kingdom. It's dark and desolate landscape contrasts very well with the cute art style meaning the Tim Burton esc tone never feels like it's trying to overbear you with a depressing feeling. All of the NPC characters you meet are usually very cartoonish and lighthearted and they'll reappear at different parts around the map so it's not like the game will force any dialogue into you if you're purely in it for the gameplay. These NPCS will also help you try to understand the games story, a story which is only really drawn from your own interpretation from the world building.
The art in this game is simply amazing. The hand drawn art style, mixed with the subtle and effective partical effects make the game very aesthetically pleasing to the eye and the light is subtle enough to never distract the player from the game. It's extremely satisfying to go around and hit different breakable objects and make the shine of your blade reflect of spikes, it makes the game seem alive when you're able to interact with the different things in the world.
The overall gameplay of Hollow Knight is pretty basic, which can be a good or bad thing depending on how you enjoy your games. You begin the game with you only being able to use your Nail to attack and bounce off enemies. As you explore the world and gain new abilities such as the dash, the combat becomes a lot more fluid and it allows for you to mix up how you go around attacking enemies and clearing out areas. The game manages to be extremely tight this way as every enemy is designed around you using your nail in way to defeat them as it's your only offensive attack aside from spells and charms.
Spells which use up your soul meter can be quite useful throughout the game, but I always found myself using them more for the healing ability, which uses up your meter in exchange for more health.
This style of gameplay could get repetitive to some however, since you'll be using the same fighting style for quite a majority of the game, with only the enemy quirks changing.
Taking hits and missing attacks never feel like it's the game being unfair or over powered, it always feels like I'm messing up on my own. In fact, I almost feel like I'm improving each time, as I'll usually find a part of the game I find much harder than the next after defeating a boss.
Hollow Knight also has very stellar sound design, the sounds of creaking and slicing never overbear the player with constant destruction noises and I think it works very well within the game. I loved how different areas had different sound effects for what was hit, giving an air of newness whenever I entered a different area.
The orchestrated soundtrack is phenominal, I'd recommend listenening to it on Spotify or buying it on Steam if you can, it's very immersive and some of the songs blew me away when I first heard them, such as Soul Sanctum or Hornet. It perfectly sets the mood for Hallownest and represents each of the bosses and areas well.
The map for Hollow Knight is gigantic and leaves a lot for exploration. I actually found out about whole areas that I missed within my playthrough and it was a pleasant surpise everytime I found a secret area or boss I missed. There are millions of things in Hollow Knight that you can miss or ignore throughout 20 hour playthroughs and this encourages replayability of the game. I think if a game for such a low price can feature so much content, content that many missed and didn't even know existed it must be a true gem in every sense of the word.
Hollow Knight was such a pleasant surpise to me. I never expected that a low price Unity game would give so much content and replayability. Hollow Knight is a 10/10 and defnitely my favourite game of 2017 so far, I'd recommend it to anybody who enjoys 2D action games that feature a lot of exploration and don't mind backtracking to the freakin boss if you keep dying.

Okay i'm almost at 60 hours into the game, and apparently 100% runs are supposed to take around 41 hours. But i'm just so caught up in everything about this game, I haven't even completed my first run of it.
First of all this game is so damn beautiful. The different areas are so distingushed and I could keep gushing on about how amazing the animations are too, but that would mean I wouldn't have enough time to talk about the story.
It's your decision if you just want to dive right in and play, heading straight towards the final boss , without even touching main areas-let alone different parts of lore. But trust me - if you do this, you are missing out on A LOT. And I mean a lot. Areas, charms, lore (and a lot of it too), etc. Even if you aren't into story games, there's still charms to collect, and places to explore. But, if you are interested in the massive, but yet, very subtly hidden story behind the Kingdom of Hallownest,
.
The actual gameplay. Oh my god, it is the one of the most fluid and (eventually) fast paced Metriodvania's i've ever played. The combat is so satisfying - mixed with the gorgeous sound design, when you kill an enemy, it transfers to the player in such a satisfying way. The bosses are some of the best I have ever had the pleasure of fighting, and there are SO SO SO many different enemy types. Each area of the game is so refreshing, and especially if you're aiming at 100%, you will NOT get bored of traversing the different areas, with the plethera of different enemies scattered around.
One thing I need to mention as well, is the absolute SOUL CRUSHING DIFFICULTY. This game is hard, something I did not expect, because I didn't read the tags, and bought this game on impulse. I am so glad I did that. The difficulty, in my opinion, is very welcome. Yes, at times, a boss can be so frustratingly hard that you want to drive your nail down your throat, but if you push on, then I guarantee you'll overcome it. Bosses (or even normal enemies) can be made easier by customising your own charm build.
Charms are a huge part of the game - there are up to 36 (or something around that) to collect, and each will enhance your different skills, or simply give aid. Creating your own charm build is defintley a highlight of this game. Let's say you kept on getting killed by a certain boss. To help, you could try different charms builds and combinations to take down the boss with ease. Or, you know, you could just go in with no charms whatsoever and completley wreck the boss like a badass.
I have one more thing to say and that's the GOD TIER music score. Chistopher Larkin, you are a genius. I actually find it hard to explain how good the music is, and how it sets such a great tone for each area.My favourite tracks probably come from the newly released Grimme Troupe DLC. But, all of them are so damn good, I can't really pick a favourite.
With, well now, 1 more content pack left to come out, and already TONS of content available for such a low low price for this good a game (seriously, Team Cherry, you should probably conisder raising the price), this game is a must- buy. One of the best; if not the best, Metriodvania's ever created. I was sure Zelda:BOTW would be the most fun I would have this year, but Hollow Knight has smashed that out of the water. Sadly it won't be a contender for GOTY, but in my books, it defintley is the most fun i've had this year, and probably the best damn game i've ever played.
So, with that, I give Hollow Knight a solid score of 10/10. Even though i'm never forgiving Team Cherry for the Soul Sanctum. Or Primal Aspids, oh my lord.

While Units, Buildings and basic gameplay are basically the same as in its bigger brother Civ 5, Beyound Earth is NOT quite like it, which is properly the reason it so suddenly got so much hate.
To put it simply: The Metagame is different.
It's faster paced and, in a way, flatter - but the individual decisions matter more.
Comparing two standard campaings in Beyound Earth and Civ 5, the Beyound Earth game will end quicker, you'll be able to make lasting differences quicker. Beyound Earth plays more fluent. You don't have to wait the first 10 till 20 rounds walking about your warrior until you actually can make a sensible difference in your city. You have less unit types, no more having three different types of melee units around. You get all the interesting toys quickly - no more waiting till industry age to fly about with planes and aircraft carriers. The quest system is robust and gives quick ways to customize your civilisation. The intrigue system is robust and fun. Trade's not hassle unlike in big civ, although the time a trade route lasts is a tad to short.
I enjoyed my fair share of time with Civ 5, and to be effective in that game, you need to spent a lot of time with a lot of fiddly bits with minor, but stacking impact. In comparison to that Beyound Earth offers less choices and fiddly knobs, but each makes far more of a difference. It's far less hassle to pick up and put down a Beyound Earth campaign than a Civ 5 one.
If that's good thing or not, now that depends on your taste in games.
For me personally, Beyound Earth will definitivly be my go-to Civ game, unless I really, really want to fiddle, then Civ 5 (or Civ 4, or Civ 3) has it beat.
On a last note: I love, love the music and sound designs in this game. It's one of the best Fireaxis made, up there with x-com's sounds.  And I love the style of the sleek looking UI and most importantly, I love the feel the alien worlds. The mood the game sets works very well for me, although that depends on your taste again. Prepare for blue and purple. A LOT of blue and purple.

Long version, for people who want a little more insight:
The puzzles are well thought-out, original, and not recycled. Other than the post-game clean up, I don't recall ever seeing the same exact puzzle or room layout twice.
This game is beautiful. Although it's a somewhat cartoonish art style, it really worked for this title, especially when things took a turn for the dark.
Teslagrad manages to tell a really great (and sad) story without ever saying a word. Seriously. It's all done through the gameplay, creepy cardboard puppet shows, and music. It's refresing, attention grabbing, and just pretty freakin cool.
Not too hard, not too easy. The boss fights are by far the hardest parts of the game, but they feel really great when you finally figure out the patterns and emerge victorious
A common problem with indie titles is that the game either drags on too long or ends to abrubtly. Teslagrad does neither, and could probably be finished in under 4 sessions. The game can take longer if you choose to collect everything (which I recomend, the "scroll" puzzles are awesome), but it still feels pretty good.
The controls are really good for about 90% of the game. Going through rooms, solving puzzles, flying through the air, and all sorts of other things are great and feel good. The problem comes when you get to boss rooms.
The boss fights are all pretty original, which was a nice surpise. The controls (mentioned above) can make them quite frustrating at times. It's hard to really explain, but the bosses can be a bit hectic and hectic + the control desgin don't merge super well.

Think of Dungeon Defenders as a four-player tower defense game combined with a third-person action title. You pick an avatar from one of four iconic classes: the Apprentice (aka Mage); the Squire (aka the Warrior); the Huntress (aka the Elven Ranger); the Monk (aka...well, the Monk). Each class has unique special abilities that they combine with specific defensive structures. The Monk, for instance, is a fighter class that can summon sphere-shaped auras that can do things like slow enemies or do damage over time. The Squire, on the other hand, summons more direct defenses, putting up walls and other direct damage defenses to stop enemies and give other classes a chance to put the hurt on.
The goal, of course, is to survive all the waves of enemies. Each wave grows in number as you go on, and get increasingly difficult with each player that joins the fight (players can join mid-fight in between waves). Between each horde of enemies players get a chance to rebuild, upgrade and tighten up their defenses. The ultimate priority is defending the Eternia Crystal; if it falls, the level is over. Early in the campaign the levels have very simple layouts with only a single crystal and relatively few choke points, but things get much more strategic in the second half, where you're given multiple crystals to protect and a much greater variety of enemies to fight. A formula that you'd expect to become utterly repetitious manages to stay fun throughout because each level forces you to adapt to its unique layout and the various types of enemies you encounter. Crisis control is also important; when barriers start to fall, only a cohesive and communicative team will recover and hold the line.
Each class has a role on the battlefield, but they're definitely not all created equal. Play a few games online, and you'll see why the Squire is the most popular class. Not only can he wreak havoc with his melee attacks, but his defensive structures can deal damage as well as stop enemies in their tracks. The other classes catch up to his prowess in the higher levels, but the Squire rockets ahead of other players early on since experience is regrettably not shared. The Squire just doesn't seem to have any major weaknesses – something I don't think I could say for any other class – and can be a little frustrating to group with when they're killing everything before you have a chance.
With a good party, even a pick-up group made up of random strangers, I quickly found myself utterly addicted to Dungeon Defenders. Every level boils down the same objective, but as I said before, strategic adaptation keeps things interesting. What also keeps me hooked is the constant stream of loot and experience. Leveling up your hero and collecting that oh-so-precious booty keeps the proverbial carrot on a stick constantly dangling before you. I'm a sucker for that carrot, too, and it makes even defeat a bit easier. You see, losing a battle sucks in Dungeon Defenders, but you get to keep the spoils you find regardless. If you die you just equip the new hotness you've acquired, allocate points into stats if you leveled up, and go at it again.
While acquiring loot hooks me, after it's in the bag, I'm left with mixed feelings. The look of your weapon changes – and man do they look awesome sometimes – but that's it. No matter what helmet you put on, or breast plate you don, your character looks the same. It may not sound like that big of a deal to everyone, but for RPG nerds like me, visually distinctive gear a big part of the appeal; I love loot grinding, but I want others to see how badass I am just by looking at me.
On the upside, though, I love how you can level up weapons, giving you a reason to hang onto gear, and something to tweak in between the times when your character levels up. Killing monsters yields Mana, which you use to buy towers during each stage. After each level there's usually Mana left over, so you can use this – as well as any Mana you get for selling unneeded items – to put into your equipment. Each piece of equipment can usually be upgraded several times, allowing you to tweak its stats to better suit your playstyle. My Monk, for example, is all about Auras rather than direct attacks, so I constantly spend my excess Mana on equipment levels that allow me to better my role as a support class. Leveling up weapons is a nice way to keep me occupied when I'm not acquiring loot or getting experience, always giving me something to do to feel like I'm progressing.
I can talk all day about how engaging a round of Dungeon Defenders is, but I can't emphasize enough how important it is to find people to play with. Whether it's four-player local or online play – or any mix thereof – you need to play with others. Playing alone is, well, lonely, and results in frustrating and boring gameplay. Mix together a few classes, and the competition of players who can do better and each level becomes a frantic frag fest.

Game synopsis says:
You are the liaison astronaut on Vega 237 spacecraft. Somehow, all crew members are dead and you are alone trying to figure out wtf happened. Goal seems to be establishing the "signal's nature", whatever that means...
It is a pseudo walking simulator with some basic FPS shooting.
You wander around, exploring. Well, more like go where the dev wants you to go. You try to figure out why you're alone in an unknown planet. Then... as you explore, you find dead astronauts and some have notes. You try to survive against the enemies that world throws at you: squid-like jellyfish aliens, some tiny UFO that shoots electricity, black jumping goo, astronauts shadows and the "last boss", a floating black shadow astronaut.
Eventually, you do find a "hover bike" that increases the pace much more.
Sadly it doesn't last long! The controls are quite wonky too.
The landscape truly gives you "50 shades of grey" pun intended ;) , as that is the main color you see everywhere... beside some dark grey, white and black. Some green leaves from trees...
The music goes very well with the ambiance and I'd be interested to get the game soundtrack as a DLC (free would be very appreciated).
The "last boss" is very B I T C H Y.
Once you do "beat" the game, there seems to be a survival "horde" mode, where you try to survive against those squid-like jellyfish aliens but the thing is, you aren't armed but can only use fist. And with the slow
running speed, that mode is totally pointless. You don't even know what to do.

Overall, an 'okay" kind of a game. Great ambiance and music without a doubt but the controls aren't intuitive. The checkpoint system is too spaced between eachs. Increasing their frequency would help "skip long portions of walking back to where you died".
WORST is the movement. You cannot run longer than 3 seconds. Takes 10 seconds to cooldown too so makes it pointless. You cannot jump higher than a sidewalk border. Clearly, these needs to be addressed for another game because that truly kills the gameplay. I've skipped the jumping "puzzles" since I kept falling down from lack of running speed.
That is the kind of game that have some good and bad elements. I'd hate to not recommend for an indie developer but again, I just can't get myself to recommend this game to anyone. I'll leave it at "YES" because there is some good to experience and I do hope ROCKETSHIP improves upon this project and makes a better game later on.

A 2D side-scrolling puzzle-platformer, this game is lovingly hand-illustrated, but very minimalistic in some ways. You are… a boy, who is running away from… some bad guys. You are the last heir of Teslagrad, a bunch of… people in pointy hats who seem to harness… electricity? But not just any electricity – two colors of electricity!
A game focused on navigating a 2D environment and finding secrets in the form of hard-to-reach scrolls, over the course of the game you gain the ability to punch to change the colors of blocks, surround yourself in a field which causes you to be repelled from or attracted towards blocks of the same/opposite colors, a flash-step horizontal teleport which can take you through most things, including some designated walls, and eventually a staff which can kill enemies and change block colors at range.
The entire game is set in a pretty tight little environment, a tower which has a central pillar you can use magnetism to travel up and down via a colored field beam. As the game progresses, you go through a number of themed areas and fight a series of bosses. Death is generally fairly cheap, starting over at the last checkpoint, which is in every room, and often after most significant obstacles within a room as well – though there is the occaisional exception.
On the whole, the game is centered around a variety of platforming puzzles which rely on your special talents. Some of these are reasonably creative, but after you gain the first three items, you go through several consecutive areas without unlocking anything new. While these areas are decent enough, in the end some of the puzzles do start to feel a little samey.
Fortunately, the game is fairly short – 100% completion took me 5 hours according to Steam’s internal clock – and the game does present some real challenge without being daunting. That being said, it is very simplistic and minimalistic, and while the graphics are attractive enough, there’s nothing in this game which really goes above and beyond – just a bunch of platformer puzzles which are decent enough, but never really cross the line into exceptional.
I didn’t feel like I wasted my time with this game, but at the same time it is hard for me to recommend anyone else spend their time on it; while it is decent enough, its lack of actually excelling in any way means that there are other, much more memorable experiences you can have. The story is very bare-bones and there is pretty much no real investment in it, so all there is is the puzzles – and while they’re okay, it just does not excite.
Pros:
* Decent puzzles.
* Decent challenge level.
* Decent bosses.
Cons:
* Minimalistic story which creates no emotional connection to the action in the player.
* Minimalistic design starts to hurt a bit towards the end as the puzzles start to feel a bit samey.
* Does not excel in any real way.

Tacoma is further proof that while the team behind Gone Home and Minerva's Den can design an environment like nobody's business, they're still struggling to find a really great story to tell in that environment. Minerva's Den is lavishly produced and beautifullly designed but honestly in terms of the actual plot, it was more than a little generic, with one neat twist. Gone Home is probably their strongest work, with an array of colourful characters revealed through notes and objects found in it's meticulously constructed environment. It lacked a really strong connecting narrative to tie it together, but it's characters felt fleshed out enough that it was fun picking through their histories.
Tacoma, though? There's barely anything there. And I don't mean "hurr durr there's no gameplay", I like these kinds of games just fine, I mean that, in a narrative sense, Tacoma is incredibly slight.
There are characters, and they're ok, but we don't have the time to flesh them out properly beyond the surface level. We know certain things about them, but those things never really play into anything else or mesh with the personalities of the other characters. Learning about these traits in a game like this should ideally be something of a eureka moment, suddely this thing is explained! This thing makes sense! There's nothing like that in Tacoma. Exploring the characters of Tacoma through it's environment has the narrative satisfaction of reading a wikipeida plot summary. No moment better exemplifies this than in the first (of three) areas, you can find a key to one of the locked gym lockers. Excitedly, I took the key to the locker I found earlier, wondering what I could learn about this character from the locker. What did I find? Nothing. Literally nothing. There was nothing in there that reflected her personality, revealed something new about her, or cast the things I did know about her in a new light. It was just a locker, with locker-y things in there. That locker represents Tacoma better than anything else in the game.
There's a plot, but it's generic, predictable, and almost totally devoid of conflict. Because of the way the narrative is presented (we see different chunks of the story play out over the course of a couple days), there isn't a sense of building tension, or urgency. What we're seeing is a mediocre episode of Star Trek with half the episode just kind of...missing.
The best thing about Tacoma is probably it's worldbuilding, which manages to paint a picture of a depressing future world that I don't want to entirely explain. It's not terribly subtle, and it's not terribly unique, but it does a good job painting a picture with a few words and that's all well and good.
Ultimately, while I appreciate Fullbright's work and this type of game, I can't recommend Tacoma. It's not a terrible game, I enjoyed the couple hours I spent with it, but even for a game this length, Tacoma is disappointingly shallow and uninteresting. In the years since Gone Home came out, it's  been well and truly dethroned by classics like The Stanley Parable, the Beginner's Guide, and Firewatch, and Tacoma can't offer any challenge to these three games. In fact, it doesn't really offer much of anything, except perhaps a cure for insomnia.
That's maybe a little harsh. But in a year which saw the release of Prey, a wonderful game that contains about ten or twelve Tacomas within the halls of it's labyrinthine space station, there really is no excuse for a game that does so little to engage the player. On sale, Tacoma is worth a look for fans of rifling through desks and reading people's emails. Just don't expect anything more than a reminder that the team at Fullbright are really good at this whole environment design lark.

Tacoma is an exploration game with minimal gameplay in the same vein as Gone Home, and made by the same developer. It is lore-rich with believable and relatable characters dealing with a crisis that is rather normal for its setting.  You’re not fighting necromorphs or travelling through time. Instead, you’re on a recently evacuated space station trying to retrieve an AI. You’re able to see recordings of the crew moving about the station using a neat augmented reality system that allows you to eavesdrop on conversations as well as rifle through their stuff.
With only about 2.5 hours running time, 20 dollars can seem a bit steep. If you’re a fan of Gone Home, this may seem like a no-brainer. If you’re not, but you’re still interested – pick this up when it inevitably goes on sale.
At its full price, Tacoma is hard to recommend. It's competent - but just too short. It’s a solid and interesting game. Grab it on sale.

Ah, a game well tailored to my tastes. Tacoma is the latest space disaster tale from Fullbright, the company behind Gone Home. Those looking for an experience with more interaction than the team's last game should look elsewhere. Tacoma is very much in the same vein as its predecessor. The game follows Amy Ferrier, a contractor sent to an abandoned space station in order to collect its central AI. Along the way Amy encounters fragments of recorded AR recordings and begins to piece together what happened on the station. These AR segments are what make up the core of the game and its most compelling feature. Most areas of the station have a central event that the other characters experience and it is up to the player to follow them as they go about their business, occasionally intersecting with the others and slowly fleshing out the situation. Its a novel mechanic but unfortunately the rest of the story-telling isn't always as strong. Much of the world-building is done with loads of emails, texts, and letters spread throughout the space station. Its these moments when the game hits a bit of a lull, even with its relatively short run time. Overall, its highs outshine its lows and Tacoma is still worth seeing. Shrouded In Sanity is basically what you get when you cross the aesthetic of resident evil and castlevania with the gameplay of final fight and bloodborne, it is very much lovecraftian, very difficult, and quite possibly one of the most addictive, if indie titles i've ever played.
I recommend this because it's got that "raw" feeling that the very first souls game, demon's, gave off, like the developer had captured lightning in a bottle and didn't quite know where to take it, it's got some obscure mechanics, and just when you think you know a level, you find out that your pace through the game alters how enemy waves are distributed, go into an area too fast and the game will spawn a time-bending puppet witch at you who crushes you with compressed air, go in too slow and two tentacle maids will summon tentacles to keep you away from certain spaces while you engage them. enemy design in this game is fantastic, you've got an enemy who releases gas and is invulnerable to attack unless you hit him with your flashlight, and even then you've got to get in close and swipe at him with your sword, which will have him summoning one last gas puff to hit you with if you don't watch your spacing.
there's an enemy who warps the level, turning everything upside down and inverting the control scheme, an enemy who can be killed with one well timed shot, but otherwise is so difficult that you'll have a hard time even damaging him. the normal maids are the basic enemy of the game, yet one hit from them and you're doomed. etc, etc. enemy design in this game is sublime, and the atmosphere is genuinely creepy and was clearly crafted with care and attention, in fact, the environmental art style looks pretty much JUST like the environmental art style for final fantasy seven, the character sprites are indie as hell, but even then they fit into the game world perfectly and only add to the overall aesthetic.
if you want to find yourself trapped for hours in a punishing resident-evil style bloodborne clone, this is definitely the game for you.

Pros:
-Strong stories based on the most famous Wuxia novels authored by one of the most well-known writer, Jin Yon.
-Massive contents involving Chinese history, novelty, literature, art, and culture.
-War Chess style battle interface allowing strategic positioning of your characters.
-Several various ancient Chinese martial art techniques to learn & play with, coupled with attractive effects.
-Single-player Wuxia style games with great story-telling is a dying breed. This one is a classic to behold & embrace.
-Multiple story lines and endings giving it more replayability.
Cons:
-Frustrating random glitches.
-Cut scenes can't be skipped.
-Can't save during battles.
-Some Terrains & objects getting your character stuck while exploring towns & big map.
-Random freezes during various battles, some end battles can't be un-frozen by switching between desktop and the game.
-No rewards given for playing higher difficulties and completing the game.
-Gauntlets for Fist fighting styles are bugged and have zero effects on the stats.
-Weapons have very minimal impacts on your damage/defence.
-Forging the strongest weapons are extremely difficult but since they don't make much difference it's un-rewarding.
-Some of the most powerful techniques are actually weak in this game, making it unsatisfactory to train.
-The battle UI limits to one style, with the more powerful styles of each technique on long CD, greatly reduced the freedom during battles. Even though you can hot-swap techniques this makes it pointless to do so due to the long CD.
-All final battles are very unbalanced. Boss-class enemies deal massive damage.
-Unbalanced enemy buffs especially evasion + combo can go on forever until you die.
-Each story line and ending requires a certain events to be triggered and those events are way too random. In most cases you will be stuck with the exact same story line on every replay unless you get lucky or spend hours save/load all day. And there are no hints to direct you.
Conclusion:
All in all, still a fun game. If you like single-player games with strong stories that involve the Chinese Wuxia background, you will love this game. This is a dying breed that's being destroyed by the online gaming trend. The fact that Herou and the devs are still willing to create a game like this is really appreciative and players should still support them nevertheless. Their efforts should be respected and appreciated. Despite the bugs/glitches, I still give it 8/10. It's a great game in its own right.

If I was making the list "games from 2016  that didn't get the attention they deserved" then this would be somewhere in the top three.  How is it that so few people know about this game?  I think the dev needs to hone some new advertising techniques, because I honestly can't imagine anyone in the target audience not loving this amazing little gem.
Let's get something completely clear right now:  this game is hard, and it doesn't care if it makes you cry.  You're more than likely going to die, repeatedly, just trying to complete the tutorial.  This will be a theme throughout the entirety of this experience.  However, much like the games that inspired it (Demon's Soul, Dark Souls, and Blood Borne) it *is* fair, provided you're able to master the controls for the combat mechanics.
To address the other issue some people might have with this game:  yes, this is basically a 2D, side-scrolling, pixel art version of Blood Borne.  However, it dives into that persona so deeply, and bathes in the atmosphere so thoroughly, that I found myself not caring how closely it got to mimicking its inspirational source material.
The dev got the spirit of the game just right, with the brutal difficulty being framed by the gorgeous, yet decaying, Victorian age backdrops.  The variety and detail put into the settings and backgrounds makes for a wonderful treat for horror fans, and that's exactly what this is:  a Gothic horror action-RPG.  The main antagonist's motivations are horrifying, as are the end results of those motivations, as are the actions taken to stop said antagonist, and so on.  It's a giant chain of madness that gets continually more F***ed up, until the notion of a zombie swinging around a sword-cane to chop up a room full of murder-maids actually sounds fairly mundane compared to the rest of the stuff that's going on.
I also want to mention the backstory of the setting.  It's in an alternate universe where certain historical events went very differently than our own world.  This is a subtle story element that is never directly touched upon, but only hinted at as you find various documents and books scattered around the estate.  It's a little thing and doesn't effect game play, but it's still a nice touch, giving the in-game world a tiny extra boost of immersion.
In summation, I recommend it.  Apparently this is the dev's first game (yes, this game was a one man production, minus the musical score).  He's currently working on another right now, and after the performance of this one, I'm going to be anticipating great things from this guy.
