If for you a games worth is determined mostly by its length or difficulty, you may be disappointed by Tacoma's short 3-4 hour length and near-total lack of difficulty. If however you value a game based on the amount of passion, competence and hard work that went into making it, based on the quality of the time you spend playing it, or the hours you spend thinking about it afterwards, then you are likely to enjoy Tacoma.
If you enjoyed Gone Home, you are certain to love Tacoma. Here you'll find the same fine attention to detail, complete with intricately crafted cluttered places which feel natural and lived in, which is all the more awe-inspiring as the game is set in space. (Spaaace!) Here you'll also find many well painted and likable characters, depicted with outstanding voice acting and animated with care.
The augmented reality in the game is a marvelous storytelling device, allowing you to explore a story with many layers of detail and content. We observe what the characters share with each other, and, more crucially, what they choose to hide. Much like a good novel, Tacoma leaves much to the players imagination. The games AR playback represents the approximate position and posture of characters in the room, but eerily leaves out the expressions on their faces and the objects they carry. Thus it leaves the players mind to fill in the rest of the ghostly scenes which play out.
In short, Tacoma is a masterfully crafted game, full of wonder and intrigue. I liked it a lot, and if you've read this far into my review I think you're likely to like it as much as I did.

A combination of RTS and RPG genres. You assemble an army, complete quests, fight enemies to make the world a safer place and save it from annihilation. You have a wide variety of available troops from human, orc, elf and goblin races including close range fighters, long range troops, mages and even heavy artillery. Also possible to add demons to your army. As you fight enemies, you and your troops gain experience. Your troops get stronger with each level of experience and when a unit reaches level 3, you can upgrade them to a better unit, but demons can't be upgraded and have only one level. Upgrades can be done in any available town of the right race (human troops get updated in human towns etc.). Not all kind of towns will be available though, since you will travel to far away lands.
You aid your troops with spells, healing and empowering them, summoning Magical spirits to aid them. You also have a wide variety of damaging spells you can use on your enemies. Spells require mana to be cast, with no mana you can cast only the spells you put in quick access (F5-F9, F10 summons Magical spirit and can't be changed). After casting a spell from quick access, it takes a while to regenerate. When you gain experience, you can use it to learn new spells, learn new skills or upgrade your max mana, mana regeneration or maximum army size and more. When you reach a new level, a new set of spells gets available. There are three schools of magic available - Nature, Chaos (fire) and Energy. You can study them all or you can choose what spells you wan't, but spells have dependencies, that is, to learn a higher spell, you must first learn the necessary lower spells.  The dependencies are indicated with vertical lines that connect spells.
The towns also can level up, to do so, they need resources - wood, stone, food and gold. The town has peasants who work in mines, sawmills and windmills and delivers the resources to town. With every new town level, new set of troops gets available.
The game itself proved to be fun and interesting. Just as I thought that it has became boring, it spiced things up, thus keeping me entertained. There are also some hidden surprises, like a chance to add a demon to your army. The game is old and it's noticeable via the graphics, but it runs smooth and it doesn't hurt the game play. I can't tell about the other languages, but at some parts English dialogs were terrible.
Overall I would recommend this game if you like RPG or RTS games, this game certainly delivers what it's supposed to.

This is a game entirely focused on exploration and narrative. You explore an abandoned space station to retrieve the AI hardware that is left on the station.
While doing so you get to know the crew that lived there and what happened to them. This is done by examining notes/letters/computers and other objects.
Also you get recorded "memories" in which you can observe the crew (which are represented by holograms). You can rewind/fast-foward these recordings to repeat a certain scene or follow different crew members and see what their were up to.
While it is nice to observe the body language of the different characters, what I found really enjoyable was that it enabled simultaneous story telling. For example: After you listened to a father speaking to his son another crew member walks in. The father asked her something regarding his health and she seems distracted and a bit annoyed when answering. Now you can rewind the memory and follow her and find out that the father interrupted her in a important conversation with the ship AI, explaning her annoyance. To be able to see the mindset of the different crewmember before/after conversations or their private thoughts when they split from the group is a lot more engaging than mere audiologs and a great addition to games with enviromental story telling.
The plot featured some sci-fi elements and touches upon AI and the corporate world in regards to automation.
It is however a niche game and definitely not for everyone. If you want heavy gameplay and get bored with reading through logs or hearing conversations, then I would not recommend it. Also, while there is a good overall plot which is a bit more adventurous, a lot of the fun for me comes from the fact that the station and the characters feel very real and have "mundane" lives. So if you care more about people who save the world or superheroes etc. and find relatable and "normal" characters not interesting this game may not be for you.
Also the game will not hold your hand in regard to the story. It is very nice paced and the different plot elements are discussed/mentioned often. However you need to put some effort into the game and be more thorough in exploring than your average first-person-shooter game. If you do not listen to the memory recordings or read through notes/computers etc. and like to just rush through the game, the ending will feel abrupt and not satisfying.
It is also relatively short ( I needed 7 hours to complete it, but I am a very thorough player, I would guess the average would be around 3-4 hours. Quality wise these 3-4 hours are among the best you can find, but I am a very big fan of walking sims and I know many people would object to my evaluation.
The voice acting is really good on all characters and graphically it is just great. The space station feels  realistic and actually lived in and the attention to detail is insane. You can read detailed cautions and warning on the back of medicine bottles, observe the rotating rings of the space stations through the windows or just enjoy the view of the universe as the sunlight slowly moves across the room over a cup-ring stained table on which a guitar with one string snapped is leaned against.
This game greatest strengths are a relatable and fleshed out cast of characters and a very detailed space station to explore. If you have played and enjoyed games like Firewatch, Gone Home or What Remains of Edith Finch, or loved finding out about the people in Bioshock through audiologs and exploration and would not see the gunplay as a requirement for your enjoyment of the latter, I would highly recommend it.
If you are a fan of the genre I would say the full price is worth it, if you are not or if the shortness is a dealbreaker for you I would suggest to simply wishlist it and buy it on sale.

Helium is a (very) hardcore sci-fi FPS and exploration game. You are on a planet which has had it's colours sucked out for an unknown reason, and you will uncover some information through transmissions on corpses. Soon you will encounter horrid enemies who want you dead, and later on even use a hover-bike. Helium is well paced and tense.
- Helium has a very unique visual style and this was what got me initially interested. The colour palette is very minimal and the visuals are numbingly bleak. The unique visual style works fairly well and the rare few colours create good contrast and are quite impactful. The texture quality is fairly low though, and there's only "low" or "medium" graphic quality settings. Objects pop-in is quite bad, you'll just be walking along and bushes will spring up in front of you. People with powerful comouters should be given the option to increase the quality. Overall though, I personally liked the visual aspect of Helium, it really delivers a unique experience.
- The audio in Helium is pretty good and there's not much to criticise it for. It delivers solid feedback and the sound quality is fine. The music is nice and fits in well with the aesthetics of the game. The audio aspect would have been better if the transmissions had voice-acting, but overall the audio is pretty good.
- Helium is a slow paced exploration games with moderately frequent combat. The constant fear of enemy encounters is very tense considering they're such a high threat. The combat against them however, is very lacklustre and lacks proper feedback. The AI is under par as they will get themselves stuck in objects frequently - **This have been fixed now**. When out of combat, you'll mostly be walking and exploring. The sprint option barely even works unfortunately, so you'll be stuck at slow strides for mostly. There's no puzzles or anything, just buttons to activate, so the gameplay is quite shallow at times. Some gameplay elements are very confusing and lead to trial and error. This is not very good gameplay design, there should be more implicit clues rather than complete lack thereof. One example of this is an enemy encounter section, where there is a forcefield wall blocking progress and enemies that spawn in front. After killing the enemies, the forcefield was still on and I thought the game was broken. I didn't realise that you had to attack the metal pole emitting the force field to destroy it. For the first forcefield gate, there should be at least some explanation of what you're suppose to do with it. On a positive note, the hoverbike is amazing and was the big redeeming factor for this game. It was a nice change of pace and was so much fun to control and ride. Overall, Helium offers quite lacklustre gameplay and no rewards or incentives throughout that might make you keep playing, save for the hoverbike.
- The story was very intriguing and instantly engaging. However it is not very well developed and barely any actual story ever unfolds. The english isn't the best, but it's still perfectly readable. I think if more explanations were given throughout the course of the game, Helium would be
more enjoyable, as there would be motivation to continue and learn more. Overall, Helium starts a good story which hooks you, but doesn't really get anywhere.
Helium was made in Unity and runs pretty well most of the time. However, in times where there's 5+ enemies the game slows down heavily. To counter this, there shouldn't be any more than 4 enemies spawned at one time. **Performance is much better now after recent updates**. A mentioned prior, the massive pop-in from objects is deterring and immersion breaking. There should be an option to increase LoD/pop-in. I encountered a few bugs in Helium, which resulted in death. One of these was dying from walking down a small step, while I was at full health - **Fixed now**. Another was getting impaled from the stone elevator pillars and dying - **Also Fixed**. What Helium needed was beta testers. I would happily beta test any game from the developer in the future to help ensure a more bug-free and well polished game. Overall, Helium's optimisation needs more work but still performs mostly well. After recent updates, the optimisation is fine now.

The game has a unique look and the puzzles were challenging without being unfair.  I had some issues with controls, but I'm not sure if they were the game itself or my controller. Civ: Beyond Earth is a 4X game, we all know that. We also know that Civ is a franchise and we all expected something grand out of it. This review will try to bring some perspective to the amount of reviews released so far, and cover some of the issues that both sides have stated.
First and formost is AI/Difficulty.
The AI in all Civ games is shot. That's it in a nutshell. I haven't seen one review yet that praises AI. Why? AI makes stupid decisions for choices that occur in the game. But we are forgetting that AI is simply an advanced RNG in the Civ franchise. One thing we also all forget is that as humans we adapt strategies as we encounter things. We learn from our mistakes and so on so forth. The AI that the franchise uses is generic and probably operates on a yes no principle with what has occured. This makes it predictable over many or long playthroughs. We learn this pattern and adapt. The AI can't. And this ties in with difficulty. When we play its hardest difficulty (Apollo/Diety or equivilant) in Civ, we want something to challenge us. Yes they provide bonuses to the AI, but the AI is essentially running of a script. So as stated in the first line, AI is Shot and needs to be revamped.
Units
I read somewhere following this, that there were too few units. I Agree. There are very few units in this game. However you can't compaire this to other Civ Games. Civ 5 for example (with all DLC) lasts from Prehistoric through to Space Age(ish). That is a lot of HISTORY! We know that we used swords for thousands of years and to this day, we still use blades. It is a reliable trusty weapon that has stuck as part of us. Beyond Earth is in the future, and we just slot our history behind it. This means we wont be recieving a hundred different units. We have infanty, Tanks, planes, ships. We as humans rely on and keep what is efficient. We don't know what the future will hold, and we can only assume so much before we start going into Psi Powers and such. So The units we get are only a handful, and yes much the same between the factions. But they didn't go fanciful and we may yet see more if/when they release expansions.
Factions/Civilizations
It's hard to get some real ties when doing a 4X strategy game dealing in Sci-fi. The main way you do is through campaigns. Civ does not offer this luxury. They give us a back story, and how we got there, but its a generic historical overview. Its was easy with previous titles as we all know about the Byzantine Empire, Romans, Iraquois, Spain, Germany, etc. We are taught about that as children. Beyond Earth does not have this luxury. Yet is can be considered a blessing and a curse. A curse because we don't know how they react in reality. They seem to all have a generic history, but we don't know the gritty details that can dictate our play. But not knowing can also be a blessing, as it gives players a way to Imagine and stretch their brains. We can make history up for them,  and not worry about how they're supposed to act and how others percieve them.
Science/Research/Tech Web
This is truly one of the best features of this game in my opinion. Gone are the days of linear progression. It's becomming too stock standard and dull. With the web we can dictate what is most important and prioritize to what we want, from almost purely military to becoming masters of Economy. It's possible. I do recall reading a review that stated in a nutshell that hated to to rely on purely science to win. Every strategy game relies on science to a degree. Unless your Zerg. But to get better units you need Science. Or research (Science). You want a Mutalisk? Resarch it. Civ is the same. Before you can do stuff, you need to research it, and its the same with any game. It lengthens the play, so you can get more game then the two minute brawl that would occur if they gave it to you from the beginning.
Diplomacy/Resources
Diplomacy is dictated by the AI. People say that this is crap. Others that it is good. I find that it is a balance. I am thankful that gone are the days like in Civ 5 were you were in the modern Era and kept getting offered Iron for that nice uranium deposit you had. Resources at least are useful in this game throughout. Faction resouces are required for your faction specific units, Strategic for your satilites and such, and basic seem to be useless, until you find that a few Virtues later can change them from inconsiquential to improving your health or energy rating. Everything has a use. You just need to find the right combinations and make best of what you have.
I could go on with more but it comes down to this. Don't compaire to previous games or others. Its a spiral down from there. Look at what they gave you. All Civ games are much the same. This is beyond Earth, a sci fi view of the future. It doesnt have real history to dictate what has happened.
Go in and play with no expectations, and if you find you have found something that you enjoy, good for you.

Firstly, there has been a lot of hate/reviews recently that downvote Dungeon Defenders (DD) because of the kerfuffle between Trendy and Wildcard.
Now on to the important thing, Dungeon Defenders is a relatively old game (considering the amount of new content released to steam every few months), However, that does not stop it from being, at least as far as im concerned, the greatest game of its genre.
Now the graphics of DD are what I would describe as slightly "cartooney" and while that might not be some peoples first choice I believe its perfect for the game.
The gameplay itself is quite nicely balanced accross all the difficulties (easy-insane) until you hit nightmare (the difference between medium and insane is the same as insane and nightmare) and the levelling system is pretty evenly scaled. Beating the game is quite possible both solo and playing online, it just requires a little bit of time. The gear system is one of my faviourite things about DD, that and having your own person tavern to show off the amazing loot you find.
To play the game on all difficulties and succeed you definitly need the dlcs (at least the character ones) nightmare difficulty and tinkerers lab for some easy farming, but if you pick up on sale you get get it all for pretty cheap, and its worth the investment if you like the game as much as I have.
Community wise the players are usually pretty fair, if you need any help or advice
usually has people on that will gladly help you out or provide advice. Occasionally people will kick you without reason when joining a public game, or you will find the odd person with "hacked" gear. But as far as I'm aware these are just people who dont know how private games work and people who don't have the skill to beat the game without cheating. Also thanks to the hard work of the Community Development Team we've had 2 new patches this past year both with excellent maps and rewards as well as cheating players on the decline.
When first getting into the game you may not find too many servers up, this is generally because of 1 or 2 reasons. Reason 1 theres no one on at that moment/your level is too low to see their games, Reason 2 the people that are on are playing private games not public games. This may be an older game yet somedays I'll open up the custom game browser and find a full page of games to join (and you can always host one yourself!).
With over 700 hours in DD I think I have the experience first hand to safely recomend Dungeon Defenders to anyone interested!

The "anti-cheat" system that runs on startup disables the game and keeps it from running. Why? Apparently, all program-altering functions cause the failsafe, including anti-virus programs, graphics card softwares, and any other standard auto-run programs one might regularly have on any common gaming computer. This "anti-cheat" system has to be one of the stupidest things I've ever encountered. The solutions suggested online are to disable ALL extra processes not imperative for running Windows, or to completely reinstall Windows, or get rid of your anti-virus, etc. and so on. I'm sorry, but I'm not willing to do all that just to play some "free" game, not even knowing if I'll enjoy it or not. If you enjoy detailed worldbuilding and characters, this is for you!  It's far on the "interactive novel" end of gameplay -- there is one ending, and no way to not get there -- but the characters carry you along at a satisfyingly fast clip.   It's set in 2088 and the near-future world is eerily plausible.  The designers have a backstory for *everything*.  Pick up the empty snack cup, there is a brand name (usually in at least two languages) and ingredients; look through all the crew members' bookshelves and little doodles on their sticky notes, check out their band posters.  Pretend you're the station cat and methodically remove everything from the administrator's desk and then throw it on the floor.  You can just play it straight through to get to the end as fast as possible, but that would be almost missing the point.  The joy of Tacoma is getting all the tiny little details that add to the backstory of how these people ended up in this place and this situation.
If you like getting all the Steam achievements, I'd recommend looking them up ahead of time, because many are amusing but not obvious and the nature of the game means that you won't necessarily want to play it through again for the fifth time just to get that last badge.

I've just played through the campaign and I'm obliged to write a meaningful review now.
First I'll tell a little about the game.
The best way to describe this is a Total War-Warcraft-Heroes of Might and Magic mix, where you can't control towns, but only buy troops from them and carry out quests. Something very similar is perhaps Praetorians.
Every troop (units are broken into troops, you can't control soldiers individually) gains its own experience and can be upgraded in a town when it reaches every 3 levels.
Monster dens are scattered around every map (the campaign is broken into maps) specificially for grinding experience, money and items, which can be equipped on units.
The most powerful units are perhaps battle mages - you can control them individually, they have multiple useful spells to  cast and they fire destructive area-damaging spells like they're semi-automatic artillery or something. Though it takes long to grind XP to upgrade them to the maximum level.
The player's main character is presented as a spirit flying in the air in front of the camera. He can't participate in the battle directly. He gains XP along with the player's army and just hurls spells.
Here are controls for the camera:
WASD or arrow keys or move the cursor to the edge of the screen - to move the camera.
Hold ctrl+WASD or arrow keys - rotate the view. This actually gives the impression of first-person view.
You can pause with Space, and you can't move the camera while paused, but you can still rotate.
Right-clicking on a troop instantly brings the camera to it, even when paused.
I noticed that the mana does not play any role. It's never spent when I cast spells. Nothing ever happens when mana becomes 0. I'm allowed to cast spells which cost more mana than I have at max. So leveling the mana skill is a waste of XP.
Units sometimes get stuck on cornerns of the terrain. It doesn't happen too often, it can be fixed by manually moving the unit to the other side. But it is damn annoying.
Music suddenly interrupts all the time and only resumes playing when a battle starts. There's a volume slider in game options, but no checkbox to switch music on/off so that you could restart it.
You will not be able to play this game on normal speed, because in that case it is too boring. The speed can be regulated with (+) and (-) keys on the number pad of the keyboard. I couldn't find this option anywhere in the game settings or explained anywhere, so I'm writing it.
Not a single crash has occured. Brilliant.
Now, the actual review.
First off, the tutorial doesn't cover 90% of gameplay, you have to figure it out on your own. Difficulty of that depends on how many RTS games you've played.
The kind of mage you choose before the start of the campaign only affects the starting skills and spells you get. And the avatar icon, yes. Everything else is the same.
The campaign is extremely, punishingly difficult at the beginning and becomes too easy starting somewhere from the middle of it. Saving often is adviced, because suddenly you might lose a battle mage, which is too valuable. Using multiple save files is adviced, because sometimes you can get unexpectedly cornered by overwhelming enemy troops, who were just passing by and you happened to make company with them.
The quests are completely uninspired: go there, talk to that person (you can't even choose replies in dialogue), bring that item over there, escort a slow♥♥♥♥♥wagon from point A to point B. And completely nothing happens while you escort a thing or go from A to B. Nothing. At all. And the wagon is sloooooow.... Seriously, most part of the game is walking around the map. You can tell your army to move somewhere and go away from the keyboard for 3-4 minutes. On maximum game speed.
The voice acting is really good, although that wolf howl is a pain for the ears, and some voices (goblin's) are not so great.
The cutscenes are something like in Warcraft 3, except really poorly done (I mean it, year 2003 is in no way an excuse for this) - you can tell it even by how the camera is flying around. Very often it's showing a single place and flying around it for 40 seconds, and nothing happens. Absolutely nothing happens. The characters are just standing, playing their completely out-of-place idle animations, and the camera is rolling around and ugh... No words can explain this.
The graphics don't seem to be designed to look good, even for 2003, except for a few models and unit and special effects animations. The faces of the elves are especially ugly, but maybe they're supposed to be? The map models are incredibly plain - just textured ground (thanks God, not plain ground - it contains hills, bumps and stuff). Occasional trees and rocks and buildings, but in limited quantities. It does manage to set the mood, though.
The plot.. Um. I can't say I'm disappointed, because somehow it seems fitting for a fantasy-themed game, but let me explain. It is all fairy-tale cliche mostly. The missions are brutally straight-forward: we need to do something in order to achieve something, in the process we learn new information and get new tasks to do.  The plot does get confusing in the middle and in the end, when seemingly random names of mages of the Guild of Mages are mentioned. Near the end it hardly makes sense even.
The only things that can be interesting about it is how new information about what's going on is revealed to the player (although it may appear kind of stupid..and random). The most exciting things are perhaps intermission cutscenes, they are really well done. They contain drawn black-and-white images, with amazing voice-over (sadly, without subtitles, but you probably won't need them). It looks beautiful.
The core combat mechanics, combined with RPG elements, spell-casting and rock-scissors-paper tactics, give an exciting mix. The game is not boring during battles and you may really want to slow the game speed down (unless you're grinding on monster mobs) and get to microing your ranged units away from melee attackers. The battles are the main part of the game, and it turned out although not perfectly, but still incredibly satisfying.
I recommend this game only to those who enjoy RTS, grinding and leveling, and who have enough patience to bear the plot, old graphics, generally slow pace and bugs.

I enjoyed Tacoma, and I'd like to recommend it, with one major caveat.
Tacoma is an enjoyable, medium-hardness sci-fi drama. The standard "walking simulator" is mixed up by the addition of replayable "AR Data Recordings", which showcase the lives of the crew. The voice acting is well-done, and the characters are likeable, if not complex. It's a solid game, with a solid plot.
BUT:
It's short. Incredibly short. I completed the entire story in about 3 hours (the extra time was spent away from the computer), and if you want to get things done quickly, and aren't curious about investigating everything fully, you could probably finish it in 1-2 hours.
Is it a good story? Yes.
Is it a good game? Maybe.
Is it worth $20? No.
When it goes on sale, however, it is most definitely a solid purchase.

Shrouded in Sanity is essentially an attempt at a 2D Bloodborne, and it becomes obvious as you play it. Combat consists of a combination of light/heavy attacks, guarding, parrying and riposting, and dodging. Defeating foes grants you Vitae, the life-force of enemies which you use as the in-game currency. However, despite its obvious ties to Bloodborne, the atmosphere and visuals remind me more of Castlevania, as the mansion holds a majestic, yet mysterious Gothic feel to it, aided by the outfits and general designs of characters and enemies.
Unfortunately, though, Shrouded in Sanity suffers from the lack of polish one may expect from early access. Combat is clunky. The gun mechanic works much the same was as in bloodborne. However, many enemies require you to be within a certain range before they'll start their attack animation: a range which places your gun through them and thus causing you to miss the parry. In addition, the controls just feel strange. I'm sure a large part of it is just getting used to a new control scheme, much like the Souls games were when I first started them. However, I question placing sprint as B and roll as X, as this makes it rather difficult to transition from sprint to roll without accidentally hitting one of the other two face buttons. I also believe that having the gun require holding LB and pressing RB to be rather unusual; if the only thing one can do with a gun is a normal shot, why bother having a multi-button input at all? Why not simply have LB be a shoot command?
Other issues include stamina regen, which is sluggish to say the least. For instance, if you use a heavy attack against a common enemy, you will never get yourr stamina nearly back to full, or at least not without some kiting. In addition, enemies seem to be damage sponges. By this I don't necessarily mean that they have too much HP. Rather, the enemies never stagger, even for a moment, unless they are parried. This even gets to the point that an enemy will throw out an attack or two between you landing the fatal blow and them actually dying. As a whole, these issues just make combat painful and unsatisfying.
One other tiny complaint goes toward the in-game economy. In the short time I have played, I've come across one merchant who sells bullets. However, bullets are apparently ridiculously expensive for how easily consumed they are. A single bullet costs over 1000 Vitae, whereas each enemy at that stage gives little more than 100. This means that you have to grind 10 enemies for a single bullet. Admittedly, this doesn't sound like much of a task, but there are surprisingly few enemies scattered about, which means buying bullets is just not economically feasible.
That said, all of my complaints so far are just about polish and balance. That is, these are issues that are easily fixed and simply need time. As such, I have no problem recommending this game, and I admit that I am excited to see where this goes.

Not sure where to start with this review, but I will say this: this game messes with your mind!
In terms of mechanics, this game is incredibly simple. It is a walking simulator set in a bland office building. But, in a game like this, mechanics and visuals really don't matter. For this little game, all you need to worry about is the satirical narrator and your choices.
The Stanley Parable is an extremely peculiar but hilarious game. The humor is witty and sarcastic, and on occasion, can be rather dark. Also, forget the fourth wall in this one; it is practically nonexistent. Of course, we have the narrator to thank for that. He is extremely reactive to the player's behavior and will comment on the strangest things. (Get the Door 430 achievement; that's one of the best pieces of commentary in the game!)
However, he also has some moments where he will either rail on the player in a fierce rant, or seriously guilt trip him/her in a somewhat dejected manner. These rapid changes in his dialogue can be a little disarming but give the narrator more depth as a character (if that is how you see him), thus having the potential to affect the way you play the game.
Despite its fantastic humor, the game's primary focus is on its philosophical topics. Most of the time, those topics dance around in the background and are alluded to by the narrator. Where the really shine is in the "endings". Each one, no matter how quirky or funny, has some sort of message to convey. Some, as would be expected in this type of game, focus on the nature of choices, and whether or not they matter. Others may touch on subjects such as the meaning of life or one's perception of reality. These "endings" can be incredibly thought-provoking and deep; one in particular left me staring at my computer for about 15 minutes in contemplative shock. And, when I describe it as a shock, it's not hyperbole.
Of course, what you get out of said endings is completely up to you. How will you interpret the endings and what the narrator has to say about them?
So, to sum it all up, The Stanley Parable is an extremely clever and philosophical game that is sure to keep the player's attention all the way through(?). It is one of those special games that can give you both memorable laughs and the occasional existential crisis! Enjoy!

Final Fantasy 13 is the most recent installment in the series to be released for PC.
While a controversial game, for many reasons such as it's inability to disguise a mainly linear game and 20-hour long tutorial it also holds ground with a deep combat system that's easy to learn, lifetime to master.
The games follows 6 humans turned into l'Cie, servants of fal'Cie(gods of sorts) to do their bidding and destroy Cocoon. The story picks up immediately into a conflict and throws you straight into action, albeit you mash your mouse button for a while before things get interesting.
Provided you beat the gruelling tutorial-hallway, you are rewarded with an extensive world to explore freely with numerous sidequests and great scenery to accompany it.
PROS
[] Great Soundtrack
[] Massive end-game
[] Fantastic storyline
[] Very deep combat system
CONS
[] Linear for a fair amount of time
[] A few main characters are pains in the butt
[] Squeenix limited it to 720p for some reason
All in all, I'd say if you are willing to try a game that has a bit of a slow start, you are rewarded with a great storyline, a deep combat system and a fantastic story!

Pros:
+ A game that does not hold your hand and tells you where to go.  It expects you to explore and fail
+ I'm just at the surface of all the features of the game (after 20 hours)
+ For wuxia lovers, a definite try (especially since it's in English)
+ Many amusing/annoying minigames to simulate mining, smithing, herb gathering etc (the treasure chest puzzle with 4 colours and 20 moves?  insane)
+ The only game so far I know where every NPC has a name or a unique title, and between them they never say the same things.  Sometimes, talking to an NPC will trigger a quest or even a small minigame (usually a riddle)
+ The translation is quite acceptable (if you are a reader of wuxia light novels translated to english, it feels similar).  Humourous at times, poetic at others.
Cons:
+ I hate the music, or it's just me.  If they took the soundtrack from Prince of Qin it would be so much better.  (FHXY : PLEASE TAKE NOTE!!!!!)
+ You really need to know a lot about wuxia (internal arts, battle style, meridian systems, chinese poetry etc) to make heads or tails of it.  I can guess it will be very difficult for people who has little knowledge or appreciation of wuxia.
+ Potential to really screw up your character build if you have no idea what you are doing.  Too many stats (though it will be explained to you slowly over the course of 10 to 20 hours of gameplay)
+ Translation bugs (a few npc did not have complete translation.  So unless you can read chinese, either get someone who can to help you, or just spray and pray).  As mentioned by some other reviewers, some description for people/items are not complete as it got cut off. (if some items can have its font minimized to fit into the description box, why not others.  Don't be lazy, developers)
Advice for players
+ Google is your friend (barely)
+ The meridian system translation will be found in your character sheet - books - medicine.  Then take a picture of each meridian point (cheat...lol).  you will ace every medicine task (crucial to access pellet making ie potion making.  Pellets and potions are very expensive at game start, and few and far.  Some pellets/potions provide permanent boosts to your attribute, so swig em.)
+ Many of the poetry and sayings mentioned are directly translated from Mandarin (that's why it sounds so exotic/ridiculous depending on your POV)....pay attention when they are bolded or different colour (usually an indication a minigame or riddle will come up)
+ you will start really really weak, compared to other games where you start able to hack and kill normal mobs.  IF you cannot win, try to keep your (personal) character from dying.  Use the experts that the game usually include for you to weaken or kill the enemies.  In due course, you will grow.  The game letting you use other experts with other weapons and internal styles is to give you a picture of what your character can potentially learn and become (yes, there is a son goku style kamehameha move somewhere in there)
+ don't bother to master all the production /crafting skills - personally i went with mining/smithing/medicine/music.  You won't have time to max them at the start (im not sure about end game...barely there)
+ the more internal skills you obtain and upgrade (even if you don't equip them) the higher your hp and energy will go
+ a lot of the food/tea/wine/consumable stuff provides permanent boosts to hp and energy.  if you have the cash, buy em and eat.  No point to store em.
+ Sometimes the game will proceed when you haven't finish a particular quest.  Deal with it, it's mostly gone.
+ I had 2 crashes.  Once when fiddling with the graphics setting, another when during gameplay.  I cannot comment on the persistent crashes other people are facing, and have no idea.  Try to play on lowest graphical setting
+ talk to everyone and everything.  You never know.  Explore each and every map.  It's not that big.  Buildings can be entered, you will notice a faint golden glow at the entrance, or the doors will open up.
+ safe the game before opening any treasure chest (until you can recognize which one does not require a puzzle to be solved, and which one does) treasure chest keys are not easily obtainable
+ some minigames (for crafting/production)  will frustrate you to the max.  Take it easy.

These reviews don't give this game justice.
First off this is not Alpha Centauri, it never was suppose to be. If you have that expectation you will be disappointed. If you have not played and loved Civilization V in the past, there is a strong chance you will may not like this game. This is a turn based strategy game, which means that this is not for everyone.
Features/Gameplay compared to Civ V:
This game uses the same engine as Civilization V however, there are major differences in gameplay. First and most important: the aliens are not like barbarians in Civ V. Sometimes you leave them alone and they will leave you alone, they have these unofficial terroritories and if you don't go into those areas they usually will not come to you unless somebody has been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥them off by killing them. Two important aliens are the siege worms (land) and the kraken (sea). It is a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to kill these things in the beginning to mid game unless you are near a city firing ranged.
Trade routes are available from the start, and who you trade with impacts diplomacy with the AI players. Stations will leave if nobody trades with them.
There are tiles that are infected with Miasma, a poison. Depending on the type of Affinity you choose, you either destroy the Miasma (it hurts you) or spread it (it heals you). Each player chooses their own Affinity so there are inherent conflicts of interest.
Technology is no longer linear, it is now a web. Which means you can go in any direction at any time. As you gain new technologies you gain Affinity points. When you get more points your units globally upgrade instantly.  You can also complete quest and do a few other things to get Affinity points. In order to win certain victories, you have to have a ton of Affinity points. You will NOT get all the technologies in a single game. Mid to end game units are unique to Affinity.
Spies are more important, in my last game I had a coup and took a player's CAPITAL from them, peacefully. (We did not  go to war). You can detonate a dirty bomb in peoples cities ,attract siege worms, steal tech, steal science, steal money etc with spies.
I almost forget the orbital system. You can use these satalites to give you every advantage (economic, military, add/remove  Miasma, counter-intelligence etc)
The victory system is not so sudden. You can tell the progress each player has made toward winning. You will know early on how far ahead/behind you are and if a full scale invasion may be necessary to prevent the leader from beating you. It is easy to stop a player in the final stages from winning if you have the military to do so.
My impression:
This game takes the Civilization series in the right direction. The gameplay changes made are beyond the scope of a mod or expansion pack, this is a NEW game that goes beyond new skins and units. I love the game, it is well made, and definitely worthy of being a "civilization" game.

Civ:BE is a highly-modified Civ5 with many innovative elements.
---------------------------------------------------
1.Gameplay
Most Civ5 features are changed:
Tech tree is in a web form;
Espionage includes more options;
Aliens have responsive aggressiveness;
Wonders are less determinant with great persons removed.
New features are funny and complex as well:
Diverse quests;
Amphibious hovering units;
Orbital units fulfill various functions;
Xeno-gas can be defensive or supportive terrain features;
Explorer can achieve various bonuses through expedition;
Affinities differ in terms of resources, quests, upgrades, units and buildings.
---------------------------------------------------
2.Visual
BE is visually appealing with concise UI, gorgeous artwork and decent sci-fi style.
Bright colors, dynamic lights and vivid terrain features combine to build scenic and exotic worlds.
However, some UI elements seem over-simplified. Wonders appear as mere blueprints in popup window. All tech, unit and building icons are logo-like.
---------------------------------------------------
3.Music
Music is as grand as in Civ5. Some tracks resemble the Blade Runner theme with an industrial, cyberpunk and apocalyptic atmosphere.
---------------------------------------------------
4.Other
Most conceptual designs are relatively original. Narratives and fictional references are affluent and profound.
However, the leaders lack personality and speak few sentences. Achievements are boring and unfulfilling. The AI is still dumb.

I have to say "very good game" at first. It was a really fun metroidvania game even tho I'm not exactly a big fan of the genre. On the flipside, stealth is mostly avoiding people using cover while using disguises to make people notice you just that little bit less. This would be fine, except the points system only actually rewards one playstyle, even though the levels simply, at times, don't feel designed with harder difficulties in mind. More on that later.
The graphics, while beautiful, do sometimes end up a bit distracting. Namely because bald heads don't shine like that. Seriously, that♥♥♥♥♥♥stands out as much as the out of character actions in the story.
Most obviously there is a MASSIVE contrast in the game between levels. You'll end up with some wonderfully crafted arenas dedicated to creatively murdering a target or targets... Before or after having to get to the arena through linear levels with boring stealth that have almost no resemblance to what you'd picture the Hitman series having. In the end, you have a very schizophrenic sense of pace and gameplay as a result of mixing Hitman level designers with Kane and Lynch level designers. This is even further compounded by the fact that, while Jesper Kyd didn't compose the score for the game, they mixed previous game's tracks in with the new score, only serving to emphasize how at odds with itself the game is.
The challenges, while doing a wonderful job of forcing you to know the levels (good and bad) by heart, singlehandedly break the scoring system, and while I do encourage the scoring system since it's a rarity in games these days, it needs a very serious overhaul in this game due to a number of serious loopholes and glitches.
All in all, you're left with a very flawed gem, not unlike the Hitman franchise, but not of the same sort by and far, a very, very mixed bag no matter who you are to be sure.

I wouldn't recommend Civilization Beyond Earth at this point. It is extremely basic and barebones of a Civilization game, like playing a demo of something that was supposed to be grander. It doesn't feel like an alien world experience at all, the random roaming aliens are very generic, and every tile in the world (excluding miasma which is a hard to see and annoying unit damaging element that the AI is unable to pathfind around) is direct copy of Civilization 5 tiles. There is barely anything new to see in Beyond Earth, even though it's supposed to be an hostile alien world it ends up being less hostile and less alien than our very own Earth.
The civilizations of Beyond Earth are also plain, there are only a few small statistic changes between them. They have exactly the same units, same city graphics, and obviously they are all human too, just different races / genders) so they definitely don't feel alien, just generic.
Many of the things are just reskinned to look new, but underlying mechanics are the same. All alien resources are just normal resources in Civilization with sci-fier names, all alien tiles are literally the same functionally but just have a different visuals to them. Sadly even the visuals of the alien terrains are a bit bad, there are barely any variation (like visual difference between desert and plains, or tundra and grasslands) and everything is similar shades and covers. Mushrooms are alien, right? Lets put mushrooms everywhere. Purple is alien too? Yup, lets shade everything with it. Obviously every terrain type has their own textures, but the contrast between visuals of area is very very low.
Happiness has been removed and replaced with health (it works the same, except your citizens don't get super healthy when they get ecstatic :D). Gold has been replaced with energy and at least I haven't seen much difference there. Policies have been replaced as Virtues and the Virtue system is more interesting (with bigger talent trees) but barely different from Policies of Civilization 5.
Pure complaints aside, there are good things in the game too. It is nice to see a non-linear tech tree, even though they could have gone a bit wilder with it, instead they were afraid of really mixing things and ended up with half-linear tech tree that is more realistic but less fun as game mechanic. The satellite overlay is a nice concept, but they only work as temporary boosts. There is a simple unit tech upgrading system and it seems really nice.
Perhaps at a later date in DLCs they'll fix and add things to spice it up. Currently it is not worth buying at a full price and you'll end up with very bad value for your money if you pay a full price now and add expensive DLC later.

Other games dip their toe a bit in environmental storytelling -- Prey, Bioshock -- but they don't fully embrace that sort of experience, and don't quite fully reward players for exploring every nook and uncovering every detail about the characters who inhabit the world.
In Prey, for example, at first I was a detective, paying close attention to the various dead characters, where they were located and what their lives seemed to be like. But in Prey, this sort of detective work quickly grows overwhelming; there are too many characters, and the space is too big to keep it all in your head at once. I quickly moved to just the main story and the labeled side-quests.
A game like Prey is trying to do a number of things at the same time -- it's trying to tell a story about what happened, while also providing a great combat experience and thrilling RPG-like experience. These goals compete with eachother, and make the various aspects of the game suffer.
Tacoma, on the other hand, is a distilled, focused experience. It is trying to tell you a story. Unlike other games I've played, you are absolutely rewarded for uncovering every nook and cranny of the game. The more you explore, the more you'll uncover about these fascinating characters and imaginative world they inhabit. Your time won't be wasted. Not even if you flip over every single box in the game.
I highly recommend it.
Total play time for me was about 3 hours 40 minutes; I did a lot of exploring and note-taking, which in my opinion would be the recommended approach for the game.

Metroidvania games are basically absent from the triple-A game space. While Konami and Nintendo used to produce some high-quality adventures, we're now relegated to the indie sphere to find any kind of action/adventure game in the vein of those classic series'.
Teslagrad may not be the most diverse of it's kin, but it certainly earns a recommendation for it's quality and simplicity. You play as a boy who has dominion over electricity. This allows him to change the polarity of certain blocks, blink through thin walls, magnetize to specific blocks and shoot electric beams.
This all unfolds through a castle that subtlely reveals the story behind your character. You jump through obstacles, avoid enemies and death traps and collect capsules to clear up some of the backstory. This isn't too far removed from something like Symphony of the Night, often feeling like a spiritual successor at times.
The art style is very expressive and feels extremely fluid. It lends a sense of smoothness to the gameplay that always empowers you. Even when repeatedly dying, you never feel like the deaths were your fault.
That is, until you hit the boss battles. For everything the game gets right about standard platforming, someone forgot how to make bosses interesting. Taking a page from Super Meat Boy, these bosses employ a one and done style of battle. One hit and you restart the whole ordeal, regardless of length.
It gets super bad towards the end where you are required to hit the bosses a total of 9 times. Going through the motions of a 5 minute boss battle to fail at the end is almost enough to make me hurl a controller through a window. If it weren't for the wonderfully built castle, I'd have given up after the second boss.
Getting through those roadblocks does feel rather satisfying and buckling down to overcome a fierce adversary is always a treat. I just wish more could have been done to alleviate some of the repetitive nature of those encounters. At least the platforming is always throwing new tricks your way.
Interestingly enough, the achievements seem to matter in this game. There is one linked to each scroll you can find in the game. Finding all of these will give you the "true" ending. It's refreshing to play a game where, even without knowing what the achievements are, you end up collecting them all out of sheer fun factor.
At the end of it all, I really recommend this to people who are dying for another Metroidvania game. There are a few newer ones that may have more developed mechanics, but simplicity is always appreciated, in my opinion. I like having as few barriers in my way as possible when playing something.

Tacoma is a very subjective game. I loved Gone Home and rate it as one of my favorite games ever, as I do with many immersive sims like Bioshock, Dishonored and Prey. Both Gone Home and Tacoma builds on the true pleasure of these games - interaction, discovery and leaving a lot of information for the player to find.
While the combat puzzles of games like Bioshock is not here what so ever, it gives the developers more time to focus in on a few key things, such as telling numerous stories and creating probably the most detailed game objects ever. Notebooks, ramen containers, pens, mugs, pool balls.. Everything is exquisitely detailed. If you for some weird reason like me love picking stuff up and just checking it out, you'll love this game, as the attention to detail is a bit ridiculous.
Gone Home, as well as Tacoma, follow the formula of snooping around and discovering recordings of previous events. Where Gone Home offered you more opportunities to connect the dots and fill blanks, Tacoma is a bit more linear and obvious in it's storytelling of at least the main story.
It is very good then that the story Tacoma tells is such a wonderful tale of speculative science fiction. I found it quite down to earth and way too realistic (in a good, yet frightening, sense) in it's depiction of societal struggles and technological challenges yet to come. The individual stories of the characters you encounter also make them believeable and fleshed out.
Highly recommended for anyone looking for a good story and like to discover every little detail. Length might be an issue, but I spent about six  hours going through absolutely everything I could find, and I found the game perfectly paced and just long enough to make an impact.

While it isn't a bad game in and of itself, the game is brought down by pretending to be an entry in the Hitman franchise.
If this were a game about an assassin from an agency doing awesome things, I wouldn't mind in the least.
The gunplay feels satisfying enough to be preferrable to actual stealth for a number of people, which is a nice change from Kane and Lynch, the developer's last game. On the flipside, stealth is mostly avoiding people using cover while using disguises to make people notice you just that little bit less. This would be fine, except the points system only actually rewards one playstyle, even though the levels simply, at times, don't feel designed with harder difficulties in mind. More on that later.
The graphics, while beautiful, do sometimes end up a bit distracting. Namely because bald heads don't shine like that. Seriously, that♥♥♥♥♥♥stands out as much as the out of character actions in the story.
Most obviously there is a MASSIVE contrast in the game between levels. You'll end up with some wonderfully crafted arenas dedicated to creatively murdering a target or targets... Before or after having to get to the arena through linear levels with boring stealth that have almost no resemblance to what you'd picture the Hitman series having. In the end, you have a very schizophrenic sense of pace and gameplay as a result of mixing Hitman level designers with Kane and Lynch level designers. This is even further compounded by the fact that, while Jesper Kyd didn't compose the score for the game, they mixed previous game's tracks in with the new score, only serving to emphasize how at odds with itself the game is.
The challenges, while doing a wonderful job of forcing you to know the levels (good and bad) by heart, singlehandedly break the scoring system, and while I do encourage the scoring system since it's a rarity in games these days, it needs a very serious overhaul in this game due to a number of serious loopholes and glitches.
All in all, you're left with a very flawed gem, not unlike the Hitman franchise, but not of the same sort by and far, a very, very mixed bag no matter who you are to be sure.

I have never played the original Hitman games, so remember that everything I'm about to say is from the point of view of a newcomer to the franchise.
Where to start?  I suppose the first impression any game has is it's visuals, so let's start there!
The visuals in Hitman: Absolution are simply astounding.  This game has one of the highest levels of detail I've seen out of any game.  Its visuals are simply unparalleled within my library of games, and it has been well optimized.  Crowds of people, numbering in the hundreds, can be seen on-screen at time with extreme levels of detail on each individual while fireworks explode in the sky and you silently move through like a shark, just waiting for your moment to strike, and all of this with a smooth 57-60 FPS.  I must admit that the bloom effects are a bit overdone, but I believe this adds a bit of dramatic character to the game.
As for the story, it's very cliched, but in the best of ways.  If there were a sweet spot between movie logic and videogame fun, Absolution would be it.  The story plays out like some kind of stereotypical action movie, giving the game a certain charm.  You will often find that movie logic prevails over real world logic, but it's for the better if you ask me.  Some of the themes in this game are dark.  Very dark.  I can say with certainty that this is NOT a game for children, and that's coming from a guy who played GTA III when he was 10.  Just about every terrible part of humanity is shown in some way in Absolution, but, sadly, it really doesn't delve much into any of it.  Rather, it just uses it all as a backdrop and gives you a reason to not feel bad for the people you kill.  Still, it's not something I'd let my little brother play.
The gameplay itself is hard to describe as it's very much dependent on the player.  You can walk in the shadows and be a ghost, eliminating your target without anyone knowing you were there to begin with.  Or you could go in guns ablazing and kill everyone.  It pays to simply walk around the level and get a feel for your surroundings and strategize.  The stealth mechanics are hit-and-miss.  The cover system and hiding system are very fluid and Agent 47 moves like a cat at times.  The disguise system, on the other hand, could do with a major overhaul.  How the hell can someone who's part of a 300-man private security detail tell that I'm not one of them?  Can he really remember the face of every single one of his co-workers?
And all this without mentioning Contracts mode.  Not to be confused with the older game Hitman: Contracts, Contracts MODE in Absolution allows you to walk around the singleplayer levels and pick out up to three targets.  They can be the main target in the singleplayer, or just that poor Chinese takeout guy in the corner.  The game will save whatever weapons and disguises you use to kill them, whether or not you hid their body, and your escape route, and it will create a contract based around your technique for you to share with your friends or the world.  The trick, however, is that you must be able to pull it off yourself.  There is no editing menu to just select a target, a weapon, and a disguise.  No, no, no.  You must walk the walk first, and successfully escape while doing so.
While I have not had the chance to really delve into Contracts mode, it seems like it could be good fun both playing the contracts and creating them.  This is the closest thing you will get to multiplayer in Hitman: Absolution, but I believe this is just one of those games that's better to play singleplayer.
So, to wrap things up, this is an amazing game!  Yes, it has its drawbacks and negatives, but its strongpoints far outweight them.  Many fans of the series have decried this installment and said that it ruined Hitman while others claim it's the best installment to date.  I can't really comment on that, but I will say that it's an excellent game all on its own.  I would most definitely agree with the general 8/10 rating this game has received.  It's not perfect, but damn is it good!

I have to confess my mouse was hovering over the no button for a while there, But I'm going to give this one a qualified 'thumbs up'.
I sometimes think it must be very difficult to be a game developer. You make a game called Civilization: Beyond Earth, and people complain that it plays like Civ. Well, if it didn't, people would probably be complaining about that, too.
Personally I also started the first game thinking the map was a bit Earth-like.  But actually there are different map pallettes; if you prefer a Mars-coloured landscape or a purple one, just restart until you get the pallette you like.
People also complain that the aliens are a bit passive. Actually they reflect the attitude of the human player. If you start playing for harmony, and leave the wildlife alone (a pretty common option, it seems) they'll do the same. Try exterminating them from the outset, and it's a different story.
I've also seen complaints about not being able to complete quests/ complete victories. Players need to look around the interface a bit to check whether any new buttons/ options have become available when the active item is clicked. These complaints really arise just as a matter of inexperience and unfamiliarity.
Explorers are too weak: yes, they are weak, but you only need Purity 1 to make them immune to monster attack. This is not a game where you start from the outset hammering every choice in your own tree and ignoring the others. Try acquring useful basic abilities in all spheres before making a bid for victory in your chosen specialisation.
Further, BE is Civ-like, but it is not Civ. There's no need to complete every tech, just the ones that you need to win (once you've acquired the basic skills needed to prosper).  This makes the game quite a bit shorter (at least the ones I've played) for the human player. Victory by around turn 330 is quite possible even at harder difficulties.
Beefs: balance, mostly.
(1) the health mechanic seems to make acquiring several prosperity virtues more or less unavoidable. You will also need to build many Biowells mid-game, to avoid the poor health penalties, which are quite severe if you are aiming for a decent score.
(2) The key to winning at the moment seems to be trade, trade, trade. An ordinary convoy by around turn 150 can easily be yielding 9 energy, 9 science, the equivalent of quite a few developed tiles/buildings. Since routes have a time-limit this can make the game pretty micromanagey later on. (you can also make trade vehicles immune to alien attack by choosing to 'reverse the polarity', when offered the option). Note: INTERNAL trade (between your own cities) also provides massive production/ food bonuses), particularly when building victory wonders)
(3) The other key to success seems to be having a LOT of workers (2-3 per base) as soon as you can afford them. 300 turns is not long to fully improve all the tiles you need, and the good improvements (maglev, terrascape) take many turns so you need plenty of them. Since worker AI seems to be pretty basic you have to operate them manually, which is also micromanagey given the numbers needed.
(4) There's a HUGE penalty (- health) for manufactories/improving petroleum resources. Since the latter are needed for most of the interesting satellites, let the AI build on those tiles and trade something else in exchange - they seem to be quite willing to do this.
(5) The satellite portion of the game is fun, but generally underwhelming in game play terms; the game is not long enough to become strategic in that way (or they need to be beefed-up)
(6) Wonders take too long to build, given the AI's ability to cheat. You can win without, anyway.
All in all, not the game as I would have designed it, and capable of improvement, but no doubt these issues will be worked on. Apart from the gameplay issues, personally, I'd like to see:
(a) some human impact on the environment (as in Alpha Centauri - greening, changes in sea level etc.) Because it's cool.
(b) maglev over sea and canyons, please!
(c) some work on the relative sizes of units - some, like the Battlesuit, seem way out of proportion..
(d) some evolution of the alien units, which just become one-shot kills after 150 turns or so. At the moment, they seem a bit sad, once the colonisers have decent weaponry. A few Demon Boils would not come amiss!
Buy it and try it, without too many preconceptions. It's a solid, if not inspired, game for the money.

A new era in eSports with a company who /really/ listens.
Battlerite is all the things we love about arena games: Fast-paced action, rapid decision making, and huge requirements for precise execution. Now, take all that, and put it into the top-down RTS/MOBA format we've all grown to adore over the last few years through staples like League of Legends, Starcraft, and more.
Imagine if League of Legends was all about team-fights, and was played in a number of short rounds, more akin to competitive Counter Strike. That's Battlerite.
Take this wonderful game as a basis and then tack on Stunlock Studios (SLS). SLS is the first gaming company in recent memory that I feel legitimately takes their players' opinions into consideration. We're talking about a company who's already launched opinion polls on their subreddit and IMMEDIATELY adjusted their priorities to release the asked-for content in the next patch. Has Riot Games, Blizzard, or anyone else done something even remotely like that?
Battlerite is an amazing game, with an amazing future and infinite potential. Getting in now, during the Early Access, lets you go hand-in-hand with Stunlock Studios helping to build this game collaboratively through it's infancy.
Come for the game, and then stay because the company behind the game will always do their best to make the game what you want it to be.

Played this back in 2014 and recently gave it another shot. One of the better card games out there at the moment, in my opinion.  A lot of work went into the cards visuals, which are very nicely done. Not an easy game to get into, but if you give it a chance, it can be very rewarding and fun.
Seems like marketing and PR is/was nonexistant, which is a real shame beacause I think this game deserves a bigger playerbase. The small playerbase doesn't do the matchmaking much good, either. And that's sad, because this just drives the new players it so badly needs away.
I wouldn't say it's very pay to win, but there's that feel here and there (a good number of older cards being not near as good as more recent ones, for instance). Once you reach level 20 and don't get the level-up rewards anymore, it can get a bit grindy to earn the in-game currency to spend on boosters, but that shouldn't be news to anyone. All in all It all felt relatively fair to me. Draft tokens, however, are on the expensive side.
Solid 8/10 for the game itself. Hopefully the playerbase will grow into the healthy numbers, otherwise this game might go out with a fizzle.

Civilization Beyond Earth is a great hame in it's own right, but saddley its in the crossfire of people expecting something similar to Alpha Centauri, and people who want a Civ 6, with that being said, keep in mind that most of the reviews for BE where and will be written based on how closely the game conformed to the preconsived lexicon of what BE should have been, instead of how it actually is.
Graphics; The graphics aren't bad, bt they aren't the best, nothing to write home about, but they are better then Civ BE. You won't destroy your computer playing the game if you've bought one in the past 4 or so years.
Sound; where as civ V had an inspirational soundtrack this one is diffrent.
Techweb. The web looks really simple, and its not aligned in any fashion. its not randomized, but you will research the same basic techs, and depending on the resources you have acess to, you'll research diffrent things to use the resources, and to increase the affinity associate with said resources
Age progression; As you expand you gain more acess to more resources, and you will want to expand, in order to gain acess to things like Xeno mass, which you need to make cool things like Kaiju like monsters, but there are mechanics in place to make it possible to be a cultural or technolgical powerhouse with only a handful of cities.....
Your units get stronger as you increase you affinities, affinities are increased via quests, and researching tech. It is quite difficult to research everything being that by the time you get around turn 220, people start going an endgame mode where if you don't try to stop them, you'll lose.
War; Cities still need to be taken meele units, like marines or tanks, and you will usally go to war over the rare affinity resources that are uber valubale and useful. A sumpremecist might have expanded into a region with a lot of xenomass, and they don;t want to trade. You want it. You can usally get away a snach in grab on a city that take 30 years if the colony happens to be disconnect from the mainland.
Ai; I guess making an AI thats really good is hard, since most games including this one end up giving the AI cheats. You won't have trouble if you know what your doing.
Diplo; Compared to the Civ 5 ai, the Ai in BE is less warlike, but if you don't trade, or attack their trade partners, there will be little in the way from stopping the Ai from trying to eat you.
Endgame; The endgame is coupled with either someone building an affinity alinged wonder, or the AI making lose alliances, or eventally going to war with people with diffrent affinities then theirs. Eitherway their will be conflict, and it can get pretty cool lategame with gaint monsters fighting people in powerarmor.
Trade; Trade seems great, it can become the powerhouse behinds your Nation most of the time, and it allows other nations to raid trade routes to cripple cities as opposed to occcupying have a country
Factions; Where as in Civ V you played as the Egyptains in the Frozen tundra hunting elphants, i.e. playing with historical figures along a linear technological lines, in beyond earth you don't really play as a faction, but you chose a fictional background that give you a small buff, slightly smaller then in Civ5, but they have a more lasting empact on your choses throught the game as aposed to thematic buffs that may or may not help. In contrast your faction was predetermined in Civ 5, with your goverment being really the only thing that evolved, and in BE your faction evloves based entirely on your surrondings and research and cultural developments. There are no goverment choices.
My rating;8.5 We all know its going to get improved with future expansions, and there really is not use whinning about it. If you don't like it(based on reviews and the demo), wait a year or two for it to go on sale, likely with the expansions,
I don't recommen this to science fiction illiterate fans, or history buffs. If you loved Civ 5 for it's charm, wait a while.

I'm here to finally write my review on this game, as I have started to play it again after a substantial amount of time away. To be quite blunt, the game plays fairly well, and progress is fairly linear throughout the main maps of the game, however, that is where the hand-holding stops. Upon finally defeating your big, friendly, final boss and the basic challenges, those who bought the DLC are in for a pleasant treat of hours upon hours of grinding. Don't get me wrong, this is actually a good thing; you are forced to take your old strategies and constantly improve them to conquer nightmare mode, and you will reap the reward for this effort, but this, while to me being a fun grind, may be to others, simply dull. This is where I talk about the community of Dungeon Defenders; there are still many high level players who are friendly enough to help out newer players to get started, be it early game, or nightmare mode, they are there. That being said, this community is still very friendly, and most of them will be there to help you out if you ask for it. All in all, I'll rate this game positive, with my long, dull review. There have been many changes since the community took over development that I dislike, and balance issues are nowhere near being addressed in an orderly fashion, but the feel this game brought me from day one still remains, and that is what truly matters to me.

What a fantastic playthrough. About 2 and a half hours and I'm ready to do it again. Its refreshing to play a title that hooks you in the begining and follows through with a satisfying end. Arriving on the space station tacoma, you quickly forget you are completely alone while you are welcomed by the ships a.i. Odin. Except for some questionable transmissions from HQ, you are left with the augmented reality recordings of each crew member and their actions throughout daily life leading up to obselence day. Who were these people, how did they live day to day, and what happened in the end? And how can anyone ever trust a.i?  All questions that kept me going with out stop. Eventually you feel a part of the crew, like you were there the whole time, and in a way you were.
The game lets you be in control of the story with play, pause, fast, forward and rewind complements of AR playback. So its up to you to decide where you stand and who you listen to. In a way, you're the director of this story. As you break down conversations and pause to investigate personal logs a larger picture exposes itself. Attempting to make some sort of sense out of everything, the game is paced to keep your attention but not drag. Tensions rise and you are driven to find the anwsers.
My first playthrough was one sitting, and well worth the money considering movie ticket prices these days. This is better than a movie, its a story you experience.You are in control, so the cinematic quality is left in your hand, as with any game. But the art direction, engaging conversations, and underlying story make it easy to achieve.

Now that I have reached about 70% total synchronization, I feel that I'm ready to review this.
Now let's start with what "Black Flag" does right and not-so-right:
-Naval combat is very simple, yet very fun
-Melee combat is also simple and pretty much unchanged from previous AC installations. Is that good that's for you to decide.
-Plundering ships is fun at start, but when you have to do it for the Nth time it can get a bit boring
-Ship upgrading doesn't require tons of tedious grinding as the more upgraded your ship gets the more powerful ships you can tackle, and acquire more resources!
-The four legendary ship fights (each at the respective corner of the map) are fun and different from each other, and provide a reason to upgrade your ship, as they are very powerful and require a well suited ship
-Lack of ways to customize your ship, the only thing you can change are sails, the steering wheel, and a decorative figurehead at the front of the ship!
-Now, I liked Edward as a main character and how he grows in wisdom during the progress of the game, starting as a drunken pirate, and ending as a full fledged assassin and a
, yet I can feel that they wanted to create another Ezio. They have tried to recreate the charm of the beloved Italian heartbreaker, yet not understanding that Ezio had three games to build his character but Edward only has one.
-The plot was pretty good, I liked it, maybe it's not the strongest plot in AC history, but it's still enjoyable. Takes about 35 or more hrs to complete depending if you're going for 100% sync
-The game has waaaaaaay too many trailing and eavesdropping missions, so much that it actually gets tedious on the final parts of the game
-The outfits I feel are very similar and I found myself using only a few of them
-Getting 100% synchronization, Is absolutely boring and useful only if you're a completionist. There is just too many chests and animus fragments, that give absolutelly minuscule rewards that there's just no motivation for me to find them!
-Kenway's fleet is pretty much useless, and I rarely checked it and sent out ships to missions.
-Freerunning is fluid and fast as in every AC game, yet there's also the same problems: Edward jumping where you don't want him to jump, and not climbing a ledge/tree gap that is 100% climbable. But despite those problems the freerunning compared to AC 1 is very refined, and is continually being refind with every new AC title
-The game looks good and runs well too, haven't run into crashes or serious FPS drops.
-Uplay gave me absolutelly no problems and works fine, kind of a useless program tho.
-No useful ways where to put your money, yes, you can buy decors and renovate your stupid house, but I pretty much had forgotten about the place, and It is pretty useless.
-As in every AC game you can meet a lot of historical personalities such as Cpt. Blackbeard or Hornigold
-They still have a modern day subplot that kinda continues the Desmond's story ( but not really), I personally don't care about the present day, they could have just dropped the whole modern day stuff
-At anytime you can leave the animus and explore Abstergo building and hack stuff to get info about all kinds of stuff, so that's kinda neat, I guess, but as I said I don't care about the present.
-I have never liked the whole precursor race thing, couldn't they just made them to be simple aliens or something, would be more believable, but that's just me.
-Doesn't really feel like an AC game tho, because for the most part of the game you're just a pirate who stole an assassin's robes and doesn't really give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about Templar/Assassin war, you just want to get that cash
Now, I have always liked AC, yes, it's an annual (well not anymore however) franchise, but I love the freerunning and seeing different time periods and places. Some people say it's getting too boring but I still love the games. And in TL;DR I can say that ACIV:Black Flag Is a great game that feels like a game with AC mechanics set in AC world but really isn't an AC game, but will still be enjoyable If you're an AC fan or a newcomer to the series! Plus if you can get it on sale like I did (5 or 7 euros) your getting your money's worth!
