This is a fantastic game, and I hope to see more from the developer. It is an almost literal breath of fresh air into a genre that is becoming a bit too cliché-ridden, "arcade-y" and sometimes childish (NB: I'm an old school CRPG fan, and I'm not saying that PoE, DOS2, Tyranny or Witcher 3 are bad games at all, though we have fallen far since the golden age of Fallout 1/2, PS:T and Baldur's Gate).
Pros:
- You are not the chosen one of the gods. At best, you are a reatively competent guy who happens to be in the right place, at the right time.
- People you meet will most of the time will try to trick you, steal from you or kill you. Or, at the very least, they will mistrust you, and not ask you to rescue kittens the first time they see you.
- You are not the ultimate badass (yes, you can be a good fighter - but this means you will suck at a lot of other skills)
- You can't see everything in one playthrough. If you are not a combat specialist, better not take too many chances in fights. If you are not a "social skills" specialist, many quests will be impossible. Some places require highly specific builds to access (which is only fair, if nobody has been able to get there in years!)
- Regardless of your level, you can't survive a couple of direct axe blows to your head: you will die (as you should)
- Game feels mature, without resorting to sex or unnecessary graphic violence
- Several factions to join, all of whom are morally dubious
- World is unfair, violent and inhospitable
- Interesting and original setting. Avoids a lot of overused fantasy tropes.
- Believable NPCs
- Good writing
Cons:
- Game feels a bit rough around the edges (in general). Could use some more contents (more NPCs, more dialogue options, more side quests) and polish to flesh out setting. Setting feels a bit "arid" and not completely lifelike as it is.
- Main storyline is too short, and not outstanding
- Arbitrary skill combinations (e.g.: on my first playthrough, I built a character with high Lore. Little did I know that this skill is almost useless if you don't also specialize in Crafting, which is *really* not obvious)
- Sometimes an action has illogical consequences
- Some builds get to see a lot more content than others (ok, I mentioned "Unfairness" as a Pro - however, this is a point where developers could have exercised some excusable poetic liberty)
- A few bugs
Bottom line: buy it now. Tihs game is excellent in its own right. Maybe just as importantly, the developer is obviously trying to do something new (in an old-school sort of way) here, and deserves our wholehearted support.
P.S.: If you disagree with this review, go play NFL 2016 on your Playstation and get out of here

I have to admit that I reversed course on my opinion of this game.  Originally I had recommended it, but that was as a Civ junkie still in the first flush of playing a new Civ game.  Now that the dust has settled and I can take a more objective look, I have to give it a thumbs down.  The factor that changed my mind is simply that I'm not playing it any more.  If this game were of the same caliber as previous Civ releases, I'd still be playing it, but I got tired of it weeks ago.  Ironically, though, other than this first paragraph, I don't have to change a single word of the rest of my review to fit my new conclusion.  That in itself should tell you something.
Make no mistake, this is "Civ In Space" and not a reincarnation of Alpha Centauri.  It's obvious that the old Civ V game engine is under the hood, and the gameplay is very similar.  In fact it's almost more of a "total conversion" of Civ V than a whole new game.  Other than the superficial window dressing (alien landscapes and units and a UI overhaul), there are only a few significant gameplay additions -- as well as some glaring subtractions.
On the positive side, the most significant change is the new tech web, a huge improvement whose significance I don't think will be truly appreciated for some time.  In previous Civ games -- as well as in most every other 4X game ever made -- the tech progression is more or less linear.  There are often different "lines" of research, but they're usually highly interconnected, and by the time you get to the "modern" era the chances are that you'll have researched *all* the "primitive" techs already, or at least be able to acquire them in a few turns of hasty catch-up research.
Not so in Beyond Earth.  Research progresses outward from a central hub, with each new node in the web consisting of a "branch" that must first be researched, as well as 1 or 2 optional "leaves" off that branch that you don't have to research to be able to progress to the next level.  The leaves you do choose to research will depend on your chosen affinity (see below) and how you want to tailor your gameplay.  Ultimately, by the time the game ends you'll probably have only about half the techs under your belt.  The effect is that for perhaps the first time in a 4X game,  you truly have the ability to customize your faction's technologies in a way that makes a significant difference to gameplay.  I suspect that tweaking the tech web will be the major focus of the modding community, and that a web format will become the de facto standard for technology research in future 4X games of all stripes.
Another major change is the addition of a "quest" engine, which not only adds a narrative to your game, it mandates the necessity of making choices that affect gameplay, albeit in a minor way.  When you resolve a quest -- which involves anything from constructing a certain building to killing a certain native alien unit -- you are given a reward, and often also asked to choose between one of two bonuses.  Individually they're small -- typically a +1 modifier to the effect provided by some building -- but if you choose the same type of bonus consistently, they can add up,
The last major change is the addition of "affinities".  Depending on the techs you research and the choices you make in quest resolutions, you gain points toward one of three affinities.  Higher levels in an affinity provide unit upgrades and significant gameplay bonuses, such as immunity to the "miasma" terrain scattered around the map.  You'll generally want to focus on a single affinity (+3 in two affinities is not as good as +6 in just one), so the net effect of this mechanic is to encourage a certain style of gameplay that further customizes your faction.
On the negative side, there are some game mechanics from Civ V that are glaringly absent in Beyond Earth.  First and foremost is the dramatic nerfing of natural resources.  Luxury resources are completely gone.  The happiness system from Civ V has been replaced with a functionally equivalent health system, but the luxury resources that provided happiness in Civ V haven't been replaced with resources that provide health in BE.  Strategic resources are still present, but you don't really need them: it's nowhere near as debilitating to be without titanium or "firaxite" in BE as it was to be without coal or oil in Civ V.  The net effect is that (a) international trade and therefore diplomacy is pretty much *entirely* absent; and (b) there's little incentive to find and settle (and fight over!) strategic map locations because everyplace is pretty much the same.  IMO this is a crippling loss of gameplay that needs to be fixed at some point.
Another negative change is the nerfing of the culture system, although I have to admit this may just be perceptual on my part.  There is no culture-oriented victory in BE, and although culture points are still used to purchase upgrades as they were in Civ V, somehow they don't seem as important.  In the games I've played so far, I didn't see much difference between those in which I focused primarily on maximizing culture, and those in which I completely neglected it.  I intend to look into this one more carefully, so for now take this assessment with a grain of salt.
Wonders have also been nerfed -- or again, at least it seems that way.  They're still present, but the perks they provide don't seem anywhere near as substantial as those in previous Civ games.  More to the point they just aren't as interesting.  Maybe it's the fact that they're made-up techno-babble rather than something rooted in the context of actual human history, but the wonders just seem really underwhelming.  In Civ V, you'd often base your whole early-game strategy around being the one to build, say, The Oracle or The Great Library, but I don't see myself caring enough about any of the wonders in BE to bother doing that.  The last game I played I won easily without building or capturing a single wonder (other than the victory wonder).
Less significant but still mysterious in their absence because it seems like they would have been really easy to have are natural wonders.  That has GOT to be something they're saving for a DLC!
A more abstract but still very important issue is that the pacing seems off.  There's no question, at least, that games are much shorter.  Maybe that was the intention, but at the point where you'd be just getting into the meat of the midgame in Civ V, you're already building the victory wonder in BE.  It's like there's no midgame at all, which for me was always the most fun part.
All in all, I welcome the change of setting, but there are some things that clearly need fixing, and since they're gameplay issues rather than technical problems I doubt they'll be addressed in a patch.  The cynical part of me can't help but suspect that the omissions were intentional and that Firaxis is already busy on the DLC to re-add the missing features... for another $29.99 plux tax.

This is a good old-school RPG game. However, it has one big flaw - the flamboyant things you can read in the description on  store page, are a blatant lie. Let me explain:
1)Here, in AoD you ARE a Chosen One, solitary hero on a quest to save the world.  As usual. All is scripted, and very predictable overall. Choices doesn't feel or matter much, cause everything is scripted. And, I must admit - scripted very poorly. You have no freedom of movement, and sometimes game force you onto choice - in normal old RPG's, you are expected to deal with most situations according to your character skills. If you lack a certain skill - you should be able to find a companion/slave/mercenary who posesses such traits. In AoD - nope, you have to be the Jack-of-all-trades. The Skyrim type of SuperHero.
2) You will have to fight anyway. And you have to exp sneaking for a noble. And lore for brute mercenary. Do quests you don't want to do, make side decisions you don't want to make/et. Forget the RPG (Role-Playing) part. Here, for each chapter, you have limited moves, a serie of quests that trigger each other, and a very limited number of skillpoints to collect. You can't know when you will get them - this quests does, and this similar one - not. So the only choice is to do all the quests and try to RNG a correct quest order since the outcomes seem completely and unrelated/unrealistic.
3)Combat system here is simple as a wooden deck and EXTREMELY RNG-related. Tactics? Nah. Clever character building? Nah. Save-Load. This is the only how it works. If  this game had a party system, it could have been even fun, with mechanics like shields blocking arrows/flanking wih spearmen/etc. But it is not. You are Rambo, the Chosen One. You need to kill everyone you met for skillpoints. Not because you want it or something...you just need this skillpoints
Overall: AoD tries to create a dark fantasy world but it can't. It has a good prospect but it fails in details. Starter stories of all the 8 various personalities of MC done well, but everything after is a damn chore.
5/10 at best. Get on sale if you ran out of classic RPG to try....

So I have played multiple games so far on quick standard and epic in the 25 hours of game play i already have. To the idiots out there who call it a repackaged civ 5, you are wrong. One of the best old school RPGs I ever played - if not THE best.  If you liked the original Fallout, you will like this.
Great setting and story, multiple ways of solving quests, a LOT of non-combat ways to play (and finish) the game, meaningful and interesting ways to use tipically underused skills and stats (such as intellingence and charisma for a fighter, or skills like impersonate).
Keep in mind that the game is a bit short, but can be replayed many times to see different quests and visit different areas  (no character can do everything in a single run).
Combat is very hard for non-pure fighters, but if you have mediocre combat stats, you can use consumables and smart tactics to compensate . Most fights can be avoided or made easier with the intelligent use of some non-combat skill or some items. (and pure "non combat" runs can be made and are actually quite easy).
The game is very old style and a bit text heavy, so if that's not your cup of tea you should at least try the demo first.
I recommend it.

I played Alpha Centauri back in the day and was ecstatic about this remake.  This game is Civ with a more interesting tech system, faction creation and unit customization.  Through the tech web and faction creator the player can experience virtually limitless different ways to experience the game, my personal favorite at this point ends with primary affinity Harmony secondary Supremacy, making my race very Bio-techy.
The first run-through I felt almost bombarded by choices.  I was deciding not only the mechanics i wanted to take advantage of but the ethics behind those decisions, the gravity of which I love to analyze even in real life (genetics, cybernetics, ecology... etc).  The mechanics effect your factions functionality and the ethics of the choices effect the way CPU players react/respond to you, and if you like to role play the way you respond to the world.
Highly recommend this game to anyone interested in a complex futuristic strategy game.
PS: Really hoping that they bring back progenitor races from AC's expansion in a dlc :D

Growing up I became quite familiar with Troma movies. Our trips to the video store would often end with one of us bringing home "Class of Nuke 'Em High" or "The Toxic Avenger", or another oddball Troma film. The AAA movies were usually picked over (this was before a dozen copies of the same movie existed at one place) and nobody wanted the piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥Troma movies that were always lurking in the horror section. They were cheap, easy-to-find, and they horrified clean-cut tight♥♥♥♥♥ultra-orthodox families. In other words: these movies were made for degenerates like me.
The best way to describe a Troma movie is by imagining a steaming turd left to sautee in a vat of brown toilet water in a public restroom and occasionally puked on for a month. After that they take it out with a pair of pincers and dip it in fondue, then sprinkle it with confetti and truffle oil. It's Trash folks. But it's gold-encrusted trash made by sick-minded filmmakers for trash-loving fans; and when you grow up with that kind of art you learn to appreciate it like a fine French wine.
Lloyd Kaufman and Michael Herz really tapped into something original when they started making these movies. I mean how do you categorize a film that has a handicapped kid getting slaughtered for points or a buxom beauty getting her butt burned by a mutated monster? A buffet of violence complimented by rock 'n roll music and sexual humor? This is the wonderful world of Tromaville and it is clearly a genre of its own.
The video game is your basic RTS without the advanced tactics stuff. Honestly I could only stomach a short play. But its full of violence, foul language, pictures of naked women, and classic Troma songs (which can also be found as MP3s in the root folder). So what am I complaining about?

Fun Action FPS/Hack & Slash game with a fitting battle soundtrack, meaty combat and some humorous one-liners.. among other things.
Pros:
+ Melee combat and variety in guns.
+ All weapons have their uses except the flamethrower (early on).
+ Upgrade system and balance in getting those upgrades (partly)
+ Game frequently saves and lets you continue from any point of earlier chapters in your playthrough.
+ The combat is fun and you can kill enemies with various environmental objects too.
+ The game has good graphics and a lot of beautiful/unique environments.
+ Cool story, even if some of the world and encounters are a bit over-the-top.
+ About 10 hours of single player content (if not rushing or going for secrets, but taking a good look at each room).
+ Difficulty is just right overall
+ Enjoyable to watch if letting a friend play or if taking turns
Cons:
- Later on boss enemies feel like bullet sponges. Killing a miniboss on insane+ difficulty requires a lot of ammo or sword hits and boss fights make you run around gathering ammo more than actually hitting their weakspots  unless you are using the crossbow and buying bolts as necessary. The crossbow is much better compared to other weapons when it comes to fighting bosses, because the charged shot accurately deals high damage on the armor and exposed weakspots, whereas weapons like the SMG need about 100 hits just to expose a weakspot. Unless you use the crossbow, those fights are going to be long and possibly expensive.
- Shotgun's firestorm ability doesn't seem to be as effective as it says against certain enemies (at least the shielded ones).
- Upgrades cost too much money and getting upgrade-related achievements (full upgrades) requires a second playthrough.
- Achievements require up to 3 separate (normal or hard, insane, heroic), long playthroughs and you don't know what specific secrets you are missing if you are going for the mr. jones achievement but miss one or two secrets in your first playthrough(s).
- Some enemies block or dodge gun shots a bit too often..
- Unless you search and loot every room, you are going to be a bit too low on cash and ammo because you also need to upgrade your weapons.
- The game can rarely bug and you can die from simply dashing down a ramp or some stairs.
Even with the cons I listed, I would definitely recommend trying it out if you want something refreshing.

I very much liked this game. I'm not very into walking simulators, nor have I played very many, but I do usually play games specifically for the story. If you like narrative sort of interactive story/walking simulator games, or if you like a good story, I would highly recommend this game. If not, this game is definitely not so remarkable or outstanding that it will overcome a dislike of the genre. Also be aware that even as much as I enjoyed the game, I feel like $20 is a LOT of money for the length of time it takes to complete the game and the amount of content in it.
The voice acting is great, the environments are pretty, and the story is good (even if not necessarily the most original or surprising story ever). It's an enjoyable game to walk through--not lots of empty time just moving around, you're almost always doing something/uncovering new details. I also enjoyed the pacing. It felt like good story telling: the action ramping up at the right pace to keep you interested, and by the end you are genuinely eager to find out how it all plays out.
It is VERY short, however. I finished in 5 hours after snooping in every single possible corner and reading every single possible note and also just wandering aimlessly for a bit enjoying the environment. Most people will probably finish it in closer to 2 hours or less. It feels rewarding to uncover all the info the game offers you, but there just really isn't enough content to justify the $20 price. If you are already very interested in playing this game, by all means, buy it immediately, support the developers, and enjoy! If you are a little on the fence, I would definitely recommend waiting for a sale.

Now that I have reached about 70% total synchronization, I feel that I'm ready to review this.
Now let's start with what "Black Flag" does right and not-so-right:
-Naval combat is very simple, yet very fun
-Melee combat is also simple and pretty much unchanged from previous AC installations. Is that good that's for you to decide.
-Plundering ships is fun at start, but when you have to do it for the Nth time it can get a bit boring
-Ship upgrading doesn't require tons of tedious grinding as the more upgraded your ship gets the more powerful ships you can tackle, and acquire more resources!
-The four legendary ship fights (each at the respective corner of the map) are fun and different from each other, and provide a reason to upgrade your ship, as they are very powerful and require a well suited ship
-Lack of ways to customize your ship, the only thing you can change are sails, the steering wheel, and a decorative figurehead at the front of the ship!
-Now, I liked Edward as a main character and how he grows in wisdom during the progress of the game, starting as a drunken pirate, and ending as a full fledged assassin and a
, yet I can feel that they wanted to create another Ezio. They have tried to recreate the charm of the beloved Italian heartbreaker, yet not understanding that Ezio had three games to build his character but Edward only has one.
-The plot was pretty good, I liked it, maybe it's not the strongest plot in AC history, but it's still enjoyable. Takes about 35 or more hrs to complete depending if you're going for 100% sync
-The game has waaaaaaay too many trailing and eavesdropping missions, so much that it actually gets tedious on the final parts of the game
-The outfits I feel are very similar and I found myself using only a few of them
-Getting 100% synchronization, Is absolutely boring and useful only if you're a completionist. There is just too many chests and animus fragments, that give absolutelly minuscule rewards that there's just no motivation for me to find them!
-Kenway's fleet is pretty much useless, and I rarely checked it and sent out ships to missions.
-Freerunning is fluid and fast as in every AC game, yet there's also the same problems: Edward jumping where you don't want him to jump, and not climbing a ledge/tree gap that is 100% climbable. But despite those problems the freerunning compared to AC 1 is very refined, and is continually being refind with every new AC title
-The game looks good and runs well too, haven't run into crashes or serious FPS drops.
-Uplay gave me absolutelly no problems and works fine, kind of a useless program tho.
-No useful ways where to put your money, yes, you can buy decors and renovate your stupid house, but I pretty much had forgotten about the place, and It is pretty useless.
-As in every AC game you can meet a lot of historical personalities such as Cpt. Blackbeard or Hornigold
-They still have a modern day subplot that kinda continues the Desmond's story ( but not really), I personally don't care about the present day, they could have just dropped the whole modern day stuff
-At anytime you can leave the animus and explore Abstergo building and hack stuff to get info about all kinds of stuff, so that's kinda neat, I guess, but as I said I don't care about the present.
-I have never liked the whole precursor race thing, couldn't they just made them to be simple aliens or something, would be more believable, but that's just me.
-Doesn't really feel like an AC game tho, because for the most part of the game you're just a pirate who stole an assassin's robes and doesn't really give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about Templar/Assassin war, you just want to get that cash
Now, I have always liked AC, yes, it's an annual (well not anymore however) franchise, but I love the freerunning and seeing different time periods and places. Some people say it's getting too boring but I still love the games. And in TL;DR I can say that ACIV:Black Flag Is a great game that feels like a game with AC mechanics set in AC world but really isn't an AC game, but will still be enjoyable If you're an AC fan or a newcomer to the series! Plus if you can get it on sale like I did (5 or 7 euros) your getting your money's worth!

A thoroughly enjoyable experience! But only if you are willing to invest effort in it.
You play as Amy Ferrier – a contractor hired to investigate what happened onboard the titular space station Tacoma. Your task is simple: board the Tacoma and download system data from different critical systems around the station – but what starts out as a simple job becomes much more when you start learning more and more about the crew members onboard.
Tacoma has top-quality world building and it establishes its cast of characters pitch-perfect. The world of Tacoma feels real and lived-in – and thus comes across as a believable vision of the future. The crew members feel like actual living human beings with desires, hopes and fears.
The story itself is also very engaging as you want to find out what happened to the crew – but there is a caveat. Some reviewers have said that story is too short and/or the characters are not introduced enough that you don’t care what happens to them. I completely disagree – but with that being said, you do need to explore as much as possible around the station in order to get the full experience. You need to keep an eye out for possible door codes and keys that will open up side rooms for you to explore off the main plot path, as well as read notes/emails/chats from different workstations and communication interfaces. This may sound dull – but trust me it is not as you really want to learn as much as possible about each crew member and the world they inhabit. However, if you don’t like reading and/or listening to conversations of up to 2-3 minute length then Tacoma is probably not for you.
This need to explore side areas is where Tacoma is most different from Gone Home, where you could get a lot out of that game’s story by simple traversing through the main story points. Otherwise, Tacoma feels gameplay-wise a lot like Gone Home, you traverse, pick up/inspect objects, read notes and listen to dialogue. And as with Gone Home there is no hand-holding in terms of keeping track of “what happened” on board – the game treats you like an adult and leaves it entirely up to yourself to keep track of characters and plot-points as if you were actually there. Therefore I recommend playing through the between four to five hour story in as few sittings as possible.
If you are willing to invest that extra effort by keeping an eye out for side areas, then you will be rewarded with an excellent story that pays off very satisfyingly. Tacoma cements Fullbright’s status as some of the very best storytellers in the game industry with an engaging story and characters that you will be laughing with, weeping with and rooting for. Highly recommended.

From the team behind Gone Home, Fullbright has really raised the bar for immersive storytelling with Tacoma. Part of me actually wishes I didn’t play this game and instead held off to experience it in VR (I don’t believe this has been announced but it would be a perfect fit). While I mostly enjoyed Gone Home, the space station setting and science fiction elements drew me in much more.
If you only enjoy fast paced action or FPS games, then this isn’t for you most likely. This is more of an experience than a “game” per say, but personally, I am glad Fullbright embraces that – this experience was more about being an observer than a participant for me.
The world setting and environment felt so “lived-in” and real in a way few games have been able to make me feel. The voice acting was superb, seriously some of the best voice acting in any game I’ve ever played. Realistic characters with realistic lines, filled with plenty of awkward/funny moments and charming interpersonal or even
relationships.
Normally, I prefer to play games with a Twitch stream or a podcast in the background but this game drew me into the world so much I just had to turn those things off. I became fully immersed in the Tacoma setting and the fantastic world Fullbright created. It’s cheesy, but I felt the loneliness of space and the helplessness of being human in extreme conditions like space. I also experienced how weird it would be to live 24/7 with the people you work with and the awkward situations this could present over the course of a year isolated together. It was an unforgettable experience for me. I won’t go any further into my experiences because of spoilers but put simply, just play it!
My advice to someone picking up this game would be to take your time and explore as much of the space station as you can. Act as if you really are investigating what happened to a crew in the near future and your experience will be much better for it. Be patient, read things, pick up toothpaste, examine the ingredients on a bottle of medicine, and please, try playing basketball with a robot vacuum in zero gravity. The attention to detail and the inventive minds of the developer are shown from those small details all the way up through the overarching plot of the game. I can’t recommend this game enough for someone who appreciates great story telling and science fiction.

This is one of the best games ever made.
Yes, the combat RNG can be a brutal, fickle mistress, and there are numerous unexpected *hard* skill/statchecks where failure means instant death or quest failure [usually death]. But once you embrace those things instead of being bitter about them, you're in for one of the most rewarding gaming experiences of your life.
Sure, your merchant can't successfully fight his way into a heavily guarded military compound, your semi-literate sword-for-hire won't be able to broker an alliance between two rival factions, and your clumsy learned scholar won't be able to infiltrate a tower by rappelling up the side.  etc. But do you really want them to to be able to?
Your inability to do a specific thing with a specific build actually leads to a huge amount of replayability with
different outcomes each time, to a huge variety of unique handcrafted quests, instead of just repeating the same quest lines over and over with different builds, always getting to pretty much a carbon-copy ending no matter what choices you make with any character.
If you think who you are and the choices you make should have an effect on the world you play in and the way NPCs react to you, this is the game for you. If you'd rather be able to climb to the top rank of every organization of the game in a single playthrough regardless of your character, there are other games for you.
Even after my 12th complete playthrough, [which doesn't include the dozens after dozens of false starts with abandoned characters, and hundreds of loads to points 10-15 minutes back to try a different route], I was still discovering completely new areas I had never set foot in, and interacting with NPCs I never knew existed before then. The replayability factor for the game is off the charts.
The graphics are decidedly subpar compared to modern AAA games, but all the information you need to be able to experience the rich, incredibly detailed world fully are adequately conveyed either through what's happening on the screen or one of the numerous text prompts.
If you feel like being challenged both in general and to think outside the box, while experiencing a rich, vibrant & unique handcrafted world with deep and fascinating lore, where every playthrough is markedly different, and the world feels
like it's trying really hard to hold in there, this is the game for you.
Vince & Co. have created a masterpiece, and they should be receiving way more accolades than they have.

Disclaimers: made little progress into the game, and the review is based on the Chinese version; more importantly, this is really intended to counteract negative reviews possibly driven by sabotaging intent.  However, I have played an older title by the same creator, and that experience should afford me some credibility.
Before all else, let it be known that, in this game, traditions remain strong; you won't find much room for whim or cosmetic individualism here. no dye for special snowflakes, no 5 functionally identical items, and no option to make ahem...socially progressive choices.  The protagonist is male, and all romantic interests are categorically female with virtually no noise for changes.
At its core, this game is a narrative, one that focuses on idealized customs of a different time, a different place.  The state had no top-secret technologies or weapons of mass destruction; the people stand a chance when taking justice into their own hands, and this vigilantism culture resembles the worlds of Marvel and DC better than anything else.
In the end, gated by translation and cultural barriers that may warrant trigger warning for some, this game isn't for everyone.  If, however, you find the aforementioned essence of the game interesting and remain impartial and understanding of a worldview different from you own, then I would recommend this experience.

In it's current state, it is a poor port. I have a GTX 970 and this 4 year old game stutters and drops well below 60 fps constantly. The game also doesn't have any graphics options.
The game itself is fine. Having completed it on the Xbox, it is a good game with some huge flaws. The game has great combat, some good characters and an interesting world. No other JRPG combat comes close to how fun this combat is. It uses  an active time battle system where actions can only be perfomed when a meter is filled. The main goal isn't to select the right attack (by looking at things like weaknesses), the game does that automatically. Your goal is to look at the current situation in the battle and set the state of your party to work with that situation. For example, if one of your part members is low, you need to switch to a state which allows a party member to heal. Switching between these states is fast and the most important part of the battle. This is why the game is set to autobattle by default and is what you should stick with.
The problem with the game is the linearity. You are constanly walking down a path fighting enemies. There are no branches or side activities. There is no option to go back to older areas which would be a problem if there was anything else to do.
The game also insults the players intelligence by having the game introduce gameplay concepts incredibly slowly. Where the game could spend 15-20 minutes explaining and allowing the player to try something, it spends 1-2 hours doing so. This leads to the game not unlocking the full potential of the great combat system for several hours (around 15 if I recall). This slow tutorial combined with the lack of side activities means that after the novelty of the new mechanic or idea is gone, you still have to slog through a good hour of gameplay before you get to anything interesting
The characters are good but are let down by some poor voice acting. It's not just the voice but some of the delivery and animations make some scenes in the game incredible cheesy. The slow pacing of the game also hurts characters because the time between story sections is so long that characters don't seem to grow or change until much later.
Without the graphical issues, I would give this a 3/5. It's definitely worth trying and it's a game I love despite the flaws but it's not a good purchase until the problems are fixed.

For the re-release, Nintendo made very smart decisions about what to update and what to leave alone.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Message to Reskin and Civ 4 Fanboys
Those complaining of it being a reskin need to shut their yaps and crank up the difficulty settings. If you play this like Civ 5 you will get your cities ripped apart by aliens or have some insane terrorist detonate a dirty bomb in your capital. This is not Civilization 5.
Now for those who still cling onto the overly byzantine and needlessly complex systems that Civilization 4 had, I want you to consider something. Remember Civilization 4 vanilla? Yeah, I do and it was rather basic and came across as an engine improvement and not much more, but after many excellent expansions it turned into an engrossing game that would suck you in with its complexity. This was the same case for Civilization 5 and will likely be the case for Civilization Beyond Earth. Go take your mindless unit stacks elsewhere and complain to someone who cares.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Onto the review!
Civilization: Beyond Earth is a fantastic entry into the Civilization series. The gameplay is if someone took the Civ 5 engine and grabbed the leaders from Alpha Centauri, after they have been dosed by a ton of Prozac, and lobbed them all together in some kind of miracle scifi blender. Beyond Earth has iterated and refined further the core gameplay elements of Civ 5 and has further expanded on the already solid and easily approachable presentation that was established in its predecessor. This refinement and progress has come at a bit of a cost as some features and art elements seem a bit lacking at times. The overall performance and gameplay is slick, engrossing, and oozed an aura of "I have options." The freedom of nonlinear decisions that effect your technology and philosophy is where Beyond Earth really shines. You are humanity's future, you are the scion that has inherited the responsibility to move our species forward, and you are our last best hope.
If you are a Civilization fan, scifi lover, or turn based strategy addict you owe it to yourself to get this game. Newcomers to the franchise might want to wait for a few expansions to fill in some of the scant spots.
90/100
The Good
- UI Changes
- Demographics have been removed in favour of a more robust diplomacy menu (IE more information)
- Animated leaders show up in multiplayer mode
- Much snappier, minimalistic and cleaner overall presentation
- Less cluttered messages (IE less denounce spam)
- Buttons and menu size seem to be themed around player use and necessity
- Performance
- Performance on my machine has seen a huge improvement over Civ 5
- Saving and loading times have been dramatically reduced
- higher frames per second
- Few bugs and seems to feel like a well-tested game (IM LOOKING AT YOU CREATIVE ASSEMBLY)
- Multiplayer worked flawlessly (IM LOOKING AT YOU CREATIVE ASSEMBLY)
- Visuals
- Leaders clothing reflects their ideologies and the decisions they have made for their people (IE cybernetic implants)
- Cities and units change gradually over time to reflect changes in ideology as well
- Distinct alien worlds are a welcome change from the terrestrial conditions of previous Civilization games
- Beautifull "concept art" style presentation of sponsor selection (I want more of this and wallpaper versions)
- Gameplay
- Culture system with the synergies rehaul is a welcome addition that allows for more creative strategies and prevents the feeling of wasting policy points simply to max out a tree
- Game feels snappier and seems to have a faster pace to it. (IE cities fall easier and city spam happens far faster)
- Tile upgrades, there's a lot of them...
- AI seems to be far sneakier and seem to clash or cooperate with you far more as your ideologies and choices diverge or converge
- Units now benefit from formations and flanking which makes excellent use of the hexgrid
- Quest system is excellent and really gets your imagination going of how your people are progressing and making decisions for the future
- Music
- Absolutely fantastic (Everything from Forbidden Planet vibes to Prometheus and Interstellar)
The Bad
- Art
- This game lacks a lot of the great art or videos that previous Civilization's possessed (What is with these bland blueprints?)
- The plain text boxes need something visual for us to look at rather than a wall of text (I wanted to see the cyborgs from the solid-state citizen quest)
- You completely missed the opportunity to incorporate the ability to see ones own leader evolve and change as they get transformed by their affinity
- Give us more distinct planets (IE primordial with volcanoes, different coloured oceans, unstable weather systems, harsh worlds, meteors falling from the heavens occasionally)
-Where is the background for the leaders? ( I want to see Mecha Daoming 3000 screaming at me in front of her techno-utopian city)
- Still no animated climates, weather or rain
- Animated buildings ( I loved watching that rocket launch from my city in Civ 5, and I want to see my Contact Beacon shoot a green laser into space)
- Narrative
- The leaders are entirely fictional and lack personality compared to the historical figures of other civilization games. Give us more quotes and make the leaders have more personality or find a way to give them more depth
- Need more voice acting work and not the same generic woman reading the quotes of Hutama
- Make quests seem more epic and meaningful (Get a few english interns to write up some juicy scifi pieces for the quests)
- I have beaten the game over 3 times now and still have no clue what the great mistake was
- Present some of the information and descriptions in the civlopedia on the unit description screen ( I loved reading about the CNDR and its development and history) (IE Battle Robot made in the year bla bla for basic defence and excels at bla bla)
- Gameplay
- Unit diversity is rather lacking (Its a bit much to ask for but give us sponsor based custom affinity units)
- Needs more leaders desperately
- The wonders currently seem very mediocre and don't seem to carry the weight they did in earlier civ games ( I have found nearly no reason to game wonders and steal them from others)

(This review will mainly be based on the technical side of the game and is made by a normal mortal with common understanding of computers and graphics; AKA the average buyer)
---------------
Score: 9.5/10
---------------
Okay, first of all, you all need to understand something. I know very well that some reviewers say how the graphics only are at 720p, but it's
. After reading several reviews on here waiting for the install to finish, I was scared that it would look messy and laggy on my laptop (read: laptop!), but it far from did. I might not understand much about computers, especially when it comes to graphics, but I do know this: I was breathtaken. Square Enix has done a great job yet again. There's being constructive, and then there's being whiny (Though I suppose that some people only play a game for the graphics, so if you're that person, this game might upset you, apparently). No one ever promised you anything over 720p. You havent been conned, your money hasn't been stolen. It's the same great story, the same great graphics. If it can run this beautifully on my Asus S550C, then I'm sure you'll be just fine - graphics wise, at least.
---------------
Score: 7/10
---------------
If you read the previous section you know that I'm playing this game on an Asus S-series laptop. I suppose this has its challenges prior to a PC (seeing as a PC is bigger and therefore more capable of running big games like FFXIII), however, it hasn't crashed on me yet. The only big issue is the fact that my game froze near the 2nd save station in the beginning when I tried saving, and since I haven't tried again just yet, it could be a one-time error only (I played in Windowed Mode, too, if it helps anything). On the other hand, if it is a recurring issue, I could end up losing a lot of play data from being unable to save, but I'm not going to cry wolf just yet. In fact, this game is running smoother than Skyrim is for me, so I'd say they've done a pretty good job. Some lag, yes, but that's on me. With hardly 10GB left on each drive and the game running alongside a good 150 processes, I wouldn't expect otherwise; the fact that the game is even able to run so smoothly is impressive.
---------------
Score: 10/10
---------------
Everybody knows the classical FF combat system. Although this isn't the exact combat system as the one in FFX (as an example), it's still a lot like it. If you're too slow at striking, your enemies will strike you instead - and you can even strike at the same time. No turn-based combat like that, other than an ATB (attack bar) working the same way as stamina would do with a melee-weapon in any other (J)RPG. Generally easy to control with a keyboard (Unless you've got a controller, which is recommended in the system info). Personally I like the combat style they used for the Kingdom Hearts games, but seeing as this is a game of the Final Fantasy series, it would almost be a shame if it didn't have the CS it has. Either way, it's alright for me.
---------------
---------------
I've always liked the FF-series, and this game is no exception. Even if the PC version disappoints some, my eyes still lit up like a Christmas tree when I heard it was coming to Steam. I still haven't played it alot (i.e: Look at recorded play time - like you should on any other Steam review), but I know I will. This is one of the only games on Steam that I've bothered reviewing properly, only because I think it's a shame how much it's being downvoted due to its graphics. I'm not saying it was wrong of people to do, as some people genuinely play a game mostly for great graphics, but if you're a fan and usually like the story and the classical turn-based combat (which it isn't quite, but it is), then don't hesitate buying this. However, if you're in doubt, I do recommend buying it when it's on sale to at least tell for yourself if you enjoy it or not. If you don't, you haven't spent as much money as you could've, if you do, then it's a win-win situation. But if graphics is the least of your concerns and you know that your computer can handle running it, then what are you waiting for? ;)
Graphics score: 9.5/10 - Not bad at all, runs fine on a laptop, graphics are really beautiful even though some think it's a downside with "only" 720p (Most likely because they know it's that low prior to the fact that it looks just fine).
Gameplay (technical): 7/10 - A few general issues here and there, nothing too buggy but still up for fixing.
Gameplay (battle): 10/10 - Final Fantasy style as you know it, with a twist of a more "autonomous" enemy attack system.
I hope you found this review useful. And remember, try to not judge so hard just because it's a game of the FF-series.

One of the best RPGs I ever played.
The main characteristic is its realism, and it permeates everything from the story to the combat.  Too few games put an emphasis on realism sadly and it shows.  Yes, we play a game, but I think that  the story and your actions should respect logic and make sense in the game world. Too often we need a healthy dose of suspension of disbelief to be able to enjoy a game. Not so here, as the post-apocalyptic world of the game is so harsh and unforgiving that some players may abandon the game in frustration.
The combat is indeed challenging. However, if you invest some time you can learn how to use crofting and alchemy to even the odds, that are always stacked against you. One of the few games where consumables are useful and needed.
The story is truly remarkable and the way you fight for every piece of ancient lore in order to piece the past together is very rewarding, especially if you succeed. (You can easily finish the game without learning all its lore)
Another great aspect of the game is it's replayability. You can join different factions and the main quest changes accordingly showing you different facets of the same events. Even through the same faction you will have diverging paths based on your choices.
A lot of things can still be said about Age of Decadence, but all reviews must end 😊.

What a fun game!  I have not played any of the other titles in the Hitman series but really considering that now if they are anywhere near as good as this game.
Game has a really good story and lengthy single player campaign.  There were a lot of good cutscenes between missions and the voice acting was well done.  I have a sneaking admiration for Agent 47 after playing the game.
What I really like is the dynamic gameplay.  The player can approach any of the mission target(s) any way they wish.  You can be as direct or discreet in taking out the target(s) but also have to be mindful to plan a way out once the target(s) are eliminated.  The dynamic nature of the gameplay forces the player to adapt to the situations as they happen.  In fact there are many challenges that are tied to these different approaches that will affect the final mission score.  Clean and discreet methods are generally more rewarded with a higher mission score but there are many ways to simply succeed at mission completion and that choice is entirely up to the player.
The contracts mode extends the life of this game once the single player content has been exhausted.  The player can design contracts for other players to play and compete for highest ranking on the online leader boards.  Players can also enter into contract challenges to determine who can complete the contract in the fastest and most efficient way.  The player also gains in-game currency when completing these player-made contracts and can spend this on weapon upgrades to make future jobs easier.  This form of online content was a very smart addition and fits the theme of the game nicely.
I really do like the scoring system that the game uses for both the single player campaign on the contracts mode.  This system keeps enticing me to try the missions and contracts again in a different and more efficient way to achieve the highest score.  This along with the dynamic nature of the gameplay will keep this game fresh for me for quite some time.

A new era in eSports with a company who /really/ listens.
Battlerite is all the things we love about arena games: Fast-paced action, rapid decision making, and huge requirements for precise execution. Now, take all that, and put it into the top-down RTS/MOBA format we've all grown to adore over the last few years through staples like League of Legends, Starcraft, and more.
Imagine if League of Legends was all about team-fights, and was played in a number of short rounds, more akin to competitive Counter Strike. That's Battlerite.
Take this wonderful game as a basis and then tack on Stunlock Studios (SLS). SLS is the first gaming company in recent memory that I feel legitimately takes their players' opinions into consideration. We're talking about a company who's already launched opinion polls on their subreddit and IMMEDIATELY adjusted their priorities to release the asked-for content in the next patch. Has Riot Games, Blizzard, or anyone else done something even remotely like that?
Battlerite is an amazing game, with an amazing future and infinite potential. Getting in now, during the Early Access, lets you go hand-in-hand with Stunlock Studios helping to build this game collaboratively through it's infancy.
Come for the game, and then stay because the company behind the game will always do their best to make the game what you want it to be.

***THERE WILL BE FAPPING***
THIS GAME IS SO BAD, IT'S GOOD.
Ok, there, I've said it.
But OF COURSE, it's bad. It's from Troma.
"WHO THE HELL IS TROMA?" you might ask yourself.
TROMA Entertainment.
The purveryors of crazy, zany, sick, twisted, hardcore, grindhouse, action/scifi/horror/romance cult movies in the universe of B-movies. That's who. They even had a Saturday morning cartoon show at one point. Their fame stems mostly from the movie: "The Toxic Avenger", a fugly, but "lovable good guy superhero mutant", and an assort of other movies, with other characters that have developed large cult followings. They've been around for about 40 years now.
SO now these guys have a PC game. ACTUALLY, about 15 years ago; said they didn't release it then, figuring the game would get totally banned.
*Update: "DrSpikee" shared this was originally a 1999 Polish game called "Rezerwowe Psy"*.
Thanks dude! :D
It appears Troma was able to use it to make their own game. (seems minus the original sex/nudity!)
THE GAME:
Starts with a disclaimer; and Lloyd from Troma pointing out you don't need it: you already bought the effing game! LOL, NICE! :D
Then, a "Troma" intro, a collection of clips from their many old movies: gross, gory, hardcore grindhouse, with boobs in one scene (more on boobs later). There's the menu, pretty straightforward. Start a New Game.
The game is an isometric, tactical, turn-based, squad-based shooter.
You start out with 3 dudes: The Toxic Avenger (Toxie), Sgt.Kabukiman, and The Stranger.
Your goal: to wipe out the Surf Nazis (see the movie "Surf Nazis Must Die").
The game is very similar in handling to the original Fallout game, but with complete emphasis on COMBAT only. Even the inventory menu looks inspired, so fans of Fallout 1/2, will find some familiarity. When you bag someone, they die, leave a bloody mess, and their loot in a nice pile for you to pick-up through the inventory screen.
Everything costs action points. Action points to walk, action points to shoot, action points to reload, to move things in your inventory even.
The game is divided into "missions". The level areas aren't big, this is not an RPG, this is a pretty straightforward clean and sweep game: GO AND KILL ALL OF THE BAD GUYS.
From this point, that is all you do. There isn't anything to interact with, but you can blow away all the different pedestrians with names with the likes of:  "Hooker", "Freak", "Fat Guy", "Crazy With A Shotgun", etc. Some will randomly draw weapons and shoot you. Shooting a "overworked office worker" might yield you some loot, like booze, drugs, money, a mobile phone, a porn mag, or whatever. Most of the loot appears to be just "novelty" items. The only things of value are any weapons/ammo they have. Like Fallout 1/2, you can waste ANYONE,  but there is no "karma" penalty in this game.
You can also target individual parts: legs, torso, or head. Just right cilck on the target to get a small menu with attack options. Works well.
However, it doesn't seem to really do anything. For example, you can't blow off legs or heads.
Haven't seen any animations other than the character falling to the ground, and then a pool of blood appearing. I noticed when I shot someone with alot of strength still, in the head, they died immediately.Other times, I aimed for the head, and they were just lightly wounded.
I suspect this is probably something they never had time (or budget) to finish or properly implement.
To complete the missions, you only have to snuff out the BAD GUYS (with various weapons).
Once that is done, there is a "Thumbs Up" button that appears.
Click it, and you are done.
Between missions, you are treated to the narrator telling the story.
LOL. Man this is so bad. Sometimes, you will see a random, non-sequiter video clip. One, shows the creators of South Park in a fake commercial about hermaphrodites. Another, of Lemmy from Motorhead doing a weird PSA type thing. Another is a metal music video. Another is a montage of super-gory moments from Troma movies.
(**NOTE, you will miss these if you "left-click". I tried "right-clicking" and then they played. However, the game glitched-out when the next level started.)
Graphics:
Not bad for a game 15 years old. There isn't anything to interact with, there isn't a load of detail in the hand-painted backgrounds/levels, but the areas are diverse and seem to look better as you progress. The animations were good.
Sound:
The sound FX are alright, a couple times, they didn't play, but was rare and only in an instant.
A couple of sounds, seem to be right out of Fallout, like when reloading or messing with the menu. Hmmm. When you kill someone, they let out a really long, over-the-top blood-curdling scream. The characters/NPCs will make funny comments or noises at times. Like, Toxie might run out of action points while trying to go somewhere you told him to, and will stop and say something like:"Yeah, I'll get to it as soon as I finish taking my toxic waste dump!"
Music: Varies, from PORNO music, to alot of  SKA and METAL, with R or X rated lyrics. It's like they couldn't afford GWAR and got some other bands who weren't as extreme. The narrator might pop-in once in a while to give a game hint. Whatever.
PROS:
-Straight-forward, old-school Turn-based Squad Action
-Good bloody, dark humor
-Interface design is simple and efficient at the same time
-Novelty of playing classic cult characters from the TROMA movies and fighting other characters from the movies
-If you like games like POSTAL, you'll feel right at home
-Great music
-the game proudly doesn't take itself seriously
-Tons of bonus features, including old CD-ROM style Macromedia player interface (will be in your Steam folder), where you get a bunch of "behind-the-scenes" stuff. A lot of blood, boobs, and booty. There is a whole section of the "Tromettes", hot, naked/scantly-dressed chicks in sexy or PORN-Y poses.
CONS:
-Seems like you never get enough action points to do things
-Some lite-RPG elements would have been nice
-Inventory system is glitchy as heck!!!! I recommend when clicking an inventory/ground object, to click REAL FAST (tap) and do this in the upper-left corner of the object. Glitchy inventory system can cause you to easily pick-up/put-down an object costing you valuable Action points
-How managing your inventory is never explained well. For example, took awhile to figure out character's "backpacks" can hold seemingly infinite amount of items!!
-For a "Troma" game, it greatly lacks the gore; it feels dare I say: unfinished? Fallout, Arcanum, Postal, and just many others games even from that time, were bloodier, gorier. So this was a disappointment.
-Sometimes, you'll spend TOO MUCH time hunting for that ONE LAST ENEMY on the map
-Game mouse-scroll is way too fast and there is no way to use the keys or to slow it down
-Wished the world was more detailed and fleshed out
-Rough around some edges
MAYBE:
-Permadeath! If one of your first 3 guys gets wasted, they're OUT.
You advance into the next missions with whoever survived. OR, if you can reload from your last saved (you can save whenever)
Some people will like this, some will not. So far with my game, I got a hot chick added in one mission.
-Doesn't seem to be anyway to restore health during a mission, so might be too challenging for some.
-Sick, Troma style humor isn't for everyone (gosh, maybe anyone, LOL)
OVERALL:
Remember, it's not an RPG or even some big epic game.
AND DON'T TAKE IT SERIOUSLY!
You go out and kill the bad guys (and whoever else). That's it.
It would be interesting if they make a new game where they implement more things to do, more gore, more interaction, etc.
Some will FAP to the (mostly partial) nudity in the game (or tons in the bonus features), others might FAP to the silly, ridiculous violence.
If you're a TROMA fan, you'll probably FAP to all of it.

Tacoma drops you straight into an interesting and believable near-future setting that is intriguing to explore, to the point where I was looking for scraps of lore anywhere and everywhere I could find it. Each item you pick up, each pamphlet you read, and everything you see slowly adds together to create an immersive world that doesn't always make sense. What is Loyalty? Why do the apples have blue bottoms? As you progress through the station, you will learn a bit more about everything--but as there is very minimal exposition, you will have to connect the dots yourself. I never did figure out why the apples had blue bottoms, but this, along with several other small details, help bring the story to life without being overbearing.
If you play this game, take the time to examine everything you can pick up; you will find yourself surprised at how much you can learn about a society based on the packaging on consumer items, or from mundane things like a crossword puzzle!
I can see many people being upset about the short length of Tacoma, as many were with Gone Home, but I think there is a place for shorter games like this that are focused on quality, to-the-point gameplay, rather than stuffing in a bunch of filler to reach a certain average playtime.
If you liked Gone Home even a little bit, get this game right now. If you didn't like Gone Home, there are features about Tacoma that put it at a level above--the story is more developed, and the setting is more interesting (though it lacks the charming nostalgia of Gone Home), so I still recommend giving it a try.

Fullbright has really expanded on the whole "piecing a story together" concept seen in Gone Home. I wouldn't evaluate Tacoma as necessarily better, but as a larger and longer experience. Unlike Gone Home, where I often found myself searching for ways to progress the story, Tacoma gives you enough guidance to allow you to figure everything out yourself, while still not making it too obvious. The overall aesthetic and the relationships between characters made it all the more believable.
The game has its flaws though: some of the dialogue during general crew interactions I thought was not quite believable, and graphics occasionally staggered, though overall this did not disrupt the experience. I also had some personal reservations about how the plot comes together. Nevertheless, I thoroughly enjoyed playing Tacoma, which provides the same sort of voyeur experience from Gone Home and the immersive theater works of Punchdrunk, and in turn makes them bigger. I really look forward to Fullbright's next project.

Tacoma is far more engrossing than the typical walking sim. That's because Tacoma, like Gone Home before it, is essentially an immersive sim in the tradition of the Deus Ex and Shock games (no surprise, given that the folks at Fullbright cut their teeth on the Bioshock series).
No, you won't be sniping augs or bashing splicers with a wrench in Tacoma. You won't be spending hours crawling through vents or hacking turrets.
However, you *will* be scouring every nook and cranny of an incredibly well-realized near-future environment in order to reconstruct the lives of the crew of Lunar Transfer Station Tacoma. You'll be rummaging through their drawers and nosing through their augmented reality desktops to uncover keys and codes that will get you deeper into the station and help you to piece together the events that brought you to Tacoma.
If, like me, you're the sort of person who simply likes exploring video game spaces, then you'll almost certainly enjoy your time onboard Tacoma. This has to be one of the most thoughtfully constructed and painstakingly detailed game environments I've ever come across. And pretty much everything is interactive (you can even play a game of pool and shoot some zero-gee hoops).
One small example: the station's botanist likes to sketch plants. He has a tin of drawing pencils (with a hinged lid that swings open as you spin it around). You'll find those pencils scattered around his office, but they're not just copies: there's an HB pencil, a 2H, a 4H, and so on. That level of detail is everywhere in Tacoma.
It also helps that the people who left those artifacts behind are all unique, interesting characters. You'll get to know them through a novel system that lets you scrub forward and backward through their conversations as you tail their augmented reality ghosts around the station.
After 4.5 hours of exploration, I cared about the fate of the Tacoma crew. And I was satisfied with the resolution of the story, which thoughtfully subverted my expectations about abandoned space stations and artificial intelligences. All-in-all, well worth the trip to orbit.

I was a little leary about buying this, with all the people talking about game breaking bugs, inconsistent translation, and numerous crashes, so I'm writing this because it's the sort of review that might have put my mind at ease.
While the translation is not completely consistent, it is ultimately understandable and honestly pretty well done for such a huge game.  90% of the dialogue in this game is not only understandable but decently written and engaging.  The other 10% is either cut off by text boxes (I have encountered only 2 or 3 instances of this), hilariously bad google translate, or localisation that doesn't quite match the rest of the game (characters using British colloquialisms, a villain saying "peace out", etc.).  None of it is particularly damning or immersion killing, and a lot of it gave me a chuckle.  So far I've been able to find answers to the untranslated quizes (such as the acupuncture point) either online or in the forum here.  I should add that I have no experience or knowledge of the chinese language.
I have also not encountered any major bugs or issues.  That doesn't mean you won't, I may just be lucky in this regard.  For me, the keyboard and game are responsive with a controller plugged into my desktop and I haven't seen a single crash so far.  In fact, it runs remarkably smooth for me.
Now I'm going to talk about why you should buy this game.  There are very few kung fu RPGs out there, which is a shame.  Jade Empire was decent but it suffered from Bioware's heavyhanded writing and the port was kind of a buggy mess, and I'm not familiar with any others like it.  This game is far more open and ambitious than Jade Empire, and frankly better programmed (at least than the PC port).
Beyond that, it has an ambition that you don't see in RPG's anymore.  While not strictly open world, there is an openness to this game in that it allows you to make your character into whatever you want, to make friends with whoever you want, and make choices that impact your character and the world he lives in.  While there are some questionable design choices and I wish there was more information given in the UI, I absolutely appreciate the scope of this project and I think it was largely succesful.
My favorite part of the game, beyond watching my character improve from getting stomped by thugs into a respectable fighter, is how pretty and immersive it is.  The graphics are admitedly a little dated, but honestly I find that charming in an age where everything is either hyperrealistic or retro, and the hand drawn scenes are very nicely done.  The music, however, is where this game really draws you in.
This is a good game.

TL,DR:   This is a great game!
Yes it is. The negative reviews are from people who played the PS3/XBOX version of the game and now expected an upgraded, 4k @ 120 Hz PC-Gamer-Masterrace edition. Which this - admittedly - is not. It's a port (and not the best one), and you can feel it throughout. Most people rated the portation and not the game itself. Fair enough.
If you are a pc-masterrace-gamer and willing to miss out on a really good game, just because it doesnt run at fullHD, then this game is not for you.
If you played this game on PS3 or XBox before, then this also is probably not for you, because the PC port brings nothing new (yet.... modders working on it right now).
If you havent played this game before though, then you should most definitely buy it! (Especially for such a low price) It is a great game itself (and still a good game when compared to other final fantasy titles), so don't  miss out on that one because of bad reviews.
BattleSystem, Variety of Characters and Music are top notch (as expected from all final fantasy titles). The story is compelling and told from different perspectives at once, that get tied together later ("Lost"-Style) and will keep you excited throughout. The game is linear for the most parts, but that is not a bad thing, because it works in the favour of fast progression of the story telling. Graphics (and cutscenes) are VERY good for a game of that age. English dub is very well done AND you get the original japanese dub version for free as a bonus (which is very rare these days). Subtitles can be tuned via steam and are probably in your mother tongue.
There are some problems with this port, this is true, mainly 2 things: Game stutters if you don't have a controller (because it searches for a controller every few seconds and drops the frame rate while doing though), but this can be fixed by plugging in and out (any - even my flightstick/rudder pedals worked) usb controller after starting the game (you don't have to play on it, you can still use mouse/keyboard).
Second, ironically, the better your graphics-card the lower your framerate, because if your card is not challenged, it will run in power saving mode. This can be fixed in the driver though, by overwriting AA settings.
So: this is a very great game (with an "OK"ish port) and if you are ok with not playing it in ultraHD, tuning a few things before you start, then you should definitely get it. There's no other reason not to.

This will hands down be the best RPG experience I have had since playing 1997 Fallout.
When I bought Wasteland 2, I was hoping for a similar experience, where you can go full speech (or mostly speech). So the first thing I did in AoE, was make a suave talker. To my surprise, I beat the game without (directly) killing anyone.
The combat is very satisfying. It's punishingly difficult, but has many different loadouts ranging from swords, daggers, spears, ect.
The game itself is short, but it has an insane amount of different ways of completing it, making it worthwhile to go through with different characters. While playing some characters, like the Assassin, Thief, Or Merc, you'll go through similar plot points, but the encounters are entirely unique, similar to an interwoven story in a sense.
The audio is very well done, particularly the music. The Roman drums and chanting marches is some of the best music I have heard in a game. Most tracks feel appropriate with their respective towns. I feel like some points felt a litte muted. For instance, when turning on a generator in a mine, it didn't really make much of an impact audio-wise. I'm really just nitpicking, but having ambient audio can really make an environment a lot more immersive.
Graphically, the game is not very pretty, but it's been in development since about 2004 if I'm not mistaken, and for an indie game, it is till very impressive.
I enjoyed this game so much I even bought a copy for someone else. I REALLY loved the setting of Roman Era, and hope that a sequel gets made. After having such a good time in AoD, I'll definitely look forward to any future titles!

Speaking of bosses, there's so many of them! Some you have to beat to progress, and some that are completely optional, they are definitely not easy and I'm glad that they're not. All boss fights are unique, original, and so bloody epic that after you beat them you'll be filled with a lot of ecstacy and wanting to see what else this game will throw at you.

This is a hard game to review. On one hand, Age of Decadence (AoD) has a lot of what I would consider hallmarks of a great RPG: unique and interesting setting, reactivity influenced by player choice, in-depth character and combat systems, many varied and challenging quests, and a strong cast of characters. On the other hand, AoD is a game made on an obvious budget with all the shortcomings of an RPG designed by an idealist.
AoD is what I consider a work of love and pride, but that is not necessarily a great thing. It is necessarily a thing that will either make you love or hate this game. Vince, the guy behind AoD, wanted to make something that was his own, something that wasn't dumbed down for the rabid consumer masses, so he did just that by making his own video game company. Are you catching on yet? There are no quest pointers, no ancient evil to slay—I admit though, that last one is factually false—and there is definitely no mercy. AoD is punishing, intentionally so, and it has one of the steepest learning curves I've seen in an RPG.
If you're willing to look past that, or you're a glutton for punishment, you may find the experience very rewarding. AoD's combat system, while intimidating at the onset, had me hooked for hours on end. Every critical hit, every successful encounter where I left a dozen men dead, I relished it. Every failure, every reloaded save game, motivated me to succeed. And I did succeed. Once I got past the learning curve, once I was in control of everything around me, I climbed the nearest ziggurat and shouted my name to the masses below. I conquered destiny. I felt like a god.
Actually, nothing like that happened, but I did have a lot of fun. I think AoD's strongest point is that once you play through the game once or twice you can set your own goals, and achieving those goals can be very satisfying. And to be fair, the game does have a lot of opportunity for roleplay. A sultry merchant girl who also dabbles in the deadly arts of alchemy? How about a bald mercenary berserker who always keeps his word? Maybe an antisocial assassin who just likes to kill? All of that and more is possible.
It is also worth mentioning that there is no mandatory combat at all in the game—you can avoid fighting if you wish to, and many quests have alternative means of resolution. It's something you don't really see in a genre dominated by hack'n'slash. Don't take this to mean that combat is rare or doesn't happen very often. On the contrary, if you play a soldier, expect to fight. If you start a barfight, expect to fight. If you like fighting, expect to fight.
AoD is not a perfect game. The graphics are very basic, I'd place them somewhere around 2005 or earlier, and there isn't much in the way of character customization. The latter is a staple of character creation these days, and it may come as a surprise to see only six or seven hairstyles that you can choose from. On the plus side, the portrait artist for the game is phenomenal.
The reactivity, while very nice for the majority of the game, is not as well-featured in the third chapter. Many choices are given, but most of them are consequences of the events that will take place regardless of your actions; moreover, certain characters you expect to run into again are simply discarded, never to be seen again. Unfortunate, not unexpected.
The story and dialog writing are average to good, never particularly outstanding. There are two examples of some decent writing that stood out to me, but this is all a minor point. A sweeping, fantastic plot isn't what AoD is about, and much of the game deals with conflicting ideologies in a time of strife. In that regard, the characters are all varied and interesting. I do have a related complaint, however: After a couple of playthroughs the main character begins to sound the same. Most of the lines and reactions are the same regardless of who you play or how you play them, and the primary difference is who you serve and what quests you undertake.
It is easier to succeed in AoD if you do the sidequests, gain the Skill Points, and invest them at the right time to earn even more Skill Points. It is like an avalanche, you build momentum until you are unstoppable. The problem lies in that if you skip the bonus content, you are quite likely to fail important skill checks later, locking you out of other content. If you build for a combat-oriented or a conversation-oriented character, the game is also fairly easy. If you create some hybrid of the two, you are often setting yourself up for failure. Newcomers to the game do not understand this and for good reason. It's not really something you know before you actually fail a couple of times. Vince, the aforementioned developer, is active on the forums. He's actually pretty cool about answering questions. So if you're stuck, help is just a post away.
I still can't believe I sunk so many hours in to AoD, but it was over a period of weeks. If you're like me and can easily get absorbed into something for a long period of time, maybe you should stay away and spend your time more productively. Otherwise, welcome to the Greco-Roman RPG of your dreams. May your AP never diminish and RNG forever walk by your side. There is a free demo available on the store page that contains about a third of the game, so try that first. Recommended.

The game itself is pretty good. 7.5/10.  I'm giving it a qualified recommendation based on 22 hours of play, one complete game (a loss that came as a total surprise - more on that later) and one short game to learn the mechanics and the below observations:
I am more than a little underwhelmed by the end game screen.  If a grand ending is important to you, you might be well-advised to look elsewhere.
Things seemed to be going OK.  No warning that another player was about to meet one of the rather obscure victory conditions (which is perhaps realistic and therefore forgivable, but a bit disappointing) but there were no stats, no peek under the cover after-the-fact and no explanation of any kind what just happened.  It just sort of ended and said something like, "We thought we knew how to win.  We were wrong." It's not the worst ending I've ever seen on a game, just the worst I've ever seen on a Sid Meier game.  This really has the feel of something that was left for last and then got short-circuited when corporate accounting forced the dev team to meet a release date.  Are any of those people gamers?
Tech tree takes some real pouring over to make the right choices.  Use the filters to find the techs you need to focus on.  I suspect my loss had a lot to do with going down interesting but time-consuming rabbit holes that didn't lead to a logical ultimate victory condition for my chosen faction to pursue and our particular strengths.  I think I'll learn a lot about this in future games, now that I've been punked for 22 hours of my life.  I just hope the frustration of the crappy endings and the fact I can't sort out what it was that led to my demise doesn't wear me out before I learn to play the game well.
