People are not recommending the title because of some issues:
- Lack of graphical options
- Game locked on 720p
- Big♥♥♥♥♥download (~50GB)
This review is to rate the game itself, to give people clues about if they will enjoy the game or not. About the three issues listed above, there are the solutions:
- Use GeDoSaTo
- Use GeDoSaTo
- Sorry, the game is really big, no solution for this one
If you want to know how good is the game, continue reading, if you just care about the problems, they're over, you can ignore the rest.
First of all, the game is GORGEOUS! It is surrealistic like most titles of the series, the story is a little complicated, but well written. Most characters will captivate you, even the ones who lack a little depth(I'm looking at you, Snow). The plot twists are not monumental, but they will hold your interest. Everything looks done with attention to details. If you like to think about the characters and the events, you will like this game.
The game is VERY (I mean, like REALLY) linear. There is no open world to explore (exceptions in some chapters) and there is not much to do besides the main quest. I did not find this too bad, the main quest is good enough to make the game worth it.
The combat system brings something new to the series and, personally, I enjoyed that. It sometimes gives more action than Final Fantasy XII system. You cannot control your teamates actions, only the party leader's. The AI is relatively good (there is no much left for the AI to do, since you will select their role) and there is the paradigm shift mechanic, which allow you to change the roles of your team to adapt to different situations in battle. Those roles change a lot of things, from the damage you deal and receive to the actions/skills available and battle support. The stagger bar on enemies and characters brings a new aproach to damage dealing, sometimes is prefreable to do less damage in order to prepare a more efficient offensive.
The music and dialogs are nicely implemented, you can feel that the characters have life. The music ambientation and placing is perfect and will atract you even more to the game. The only thing I can blame in this section is the dialogs text. Although they're mostly interesting and full of emotion, some lines don't feel "natural", like "no one would say this"(I'm looking to you again, Snow!).
Overall, I enjoyed the game a lot, I played it on Xbox and now I want to play it again on PC. I hope the sequels come to PC as well.

Don't buy this game, unless you enjoy
- saving and loading most of the time. every step can be your last one (and most likely will)
- creating and managing many saves because a chain of events you just triggered can ruin hours of progress
- sadistic difficulty. every situation is hardly manageable, fights are almost impossible to win
- extremely limited resources. hard to get even the most basic things together to keep you alive
Now that might sound "challenging", but really, it's just very frustrating and not rewarding at all. Usually overcoming even the worst odds should leave one with a feeling of satisfaction. Like you actually accomplished something. That's not the case here. Because it doesn't get any better or easier, rendering even the smallest steps meaningless.
And the "replay value" of the game is that it doesn't give you nearly enough skills and abilities to do most quests. It's not even about paths or story decisions. You just can't do the quests that are straight in front of you unless you create more characters. Almost one for every quest.
The biggest asset seemed to be the freedom of choices in decisions. In truth even through there are different options to react to situations, almost all of them are locked behind near ridiculous requirements, leaving you only one choice - when you're lucky.
And before too long, after struggling for countless hours and keep running into dead ends, you will be forced to give up on the character in whole and start a new one or take the choices the game gives you instead of the ones you'd pick. Freedom of choice... joke of the day.

This is a hard one to review as it definitely has that additive vibe that the civilization games have but, it has so many glaring issues that are causing a lot of frustration.
The UI I don't particularly have any issues against though I have encountered times when it has been a frustration to work around like for example, selecting specific units in a city can be quite tedious. The only other UI annoyance I have is with the Advanced Options setup as I was expecting that to be on the intial setup screen rather on the screen where you select your sponsor (and in the upper right corner by itself) so I missed that for 1-2 games.
The visual design is fantastic as to be expected though, it does not go to any innovative extremes per say in terms of anomalies / extreme weather / day and night cycle (even makes a reference in-game to a planet having a longer one!) random unique events and so forth which is something I wished CIV games would try to experiment with for a long time since CIV IV and CIV V.
I also wish they would bring back the cinematics the previous CIV games had, they added personality and a sense of accomplishment when you completed a wonder or had a specific victory (which is something sorely lacking thanks to the sci-fi setting)
Instead, for the most part, there are just expanded counterparts for CIV V as in aliens for barbarians, pods for ruins etc. and just feels like a missed opportunity.
The audio is something I barely noticed in-game, it is there but it feels so subtle...not really sure what else to add on the audio as I have not had a chance to sit down and listen to the entire soundtrack itself but, in-game for the most part, it is still way too subtle for me.
Again, there is disconnect as there is no familiarity for me and the fact it is hard to beat CIV IV (Baba Yetu, Classical Pieces and Leonard Nimoy)
As expected, makes a ton of bizarre and weird choices that are beyond frustrating and a few examples of what has happened to me:
These are most likely oversights to having checks for these particular situations but, makes you wonder how these slipped though.
FPS and visually speaking it has been completely fine for me however, I did have launch issues trying to get the game not to crash to desktop on DX11 and Mantle to which I got DX11 working but, Mantle continues to crash for some unknown reason.
There is also a slew of issues with refresh rates and resolutions at the moment to which I have had the 1080p fullscreen issue and the HDTV issue of ending up in 24p thanks to the cinematics, I have resolved the HDTV issue (skip cinematics option) but, the 1080p fullscreen issue persists.
Some issues that have been irking me the most:
In all fairness, it definitely is a fun and additive experience as expected for a CIV game but, at the same time, expectations were running high coming from the polished experience of CIV V BNW and the legacy of SMAC that the hypetrain entered the stratosphere.
Instead, you have more of a barebones framework of sorts that just indicates that perhaps best to wait for patches / mods / content DLC / expansion packs. I can only speculate but I think a choice was made to follow the same route of how CIV V was released and developed with patches and expansions as opposed to the delay and polish paradigm other developers occasionally do.
I trust and respect Firaxis as developer so I am sure they will do their best to fix all of outstanding issues and they are asking for a variety of feedback on steam discussion page so I implore you to check that out and make anything known on those threads!
There is a demo (Yeah, A Demo!...such an oddity these days) if you wish to try it out and come to a conclusion whether to invest or not.
I am going to give Firaxis the benefit of the doubt here to make it into a great experience with more content as they always deliver in the end.

Although several years old, and followed by one sequel (Dungeon Defenders 2) and one re-imagining (Dungeon Defeners Eternity), the original Dungeon Defenders is still a ton of fun.  While it can be played solo, the real fun of this game is playing co-op with at least one other person, and coordinating your defenses. A very tongue in cheek art style, as well as pop culture references everywhere: on some maps, the reward for completion is a Monk staff that looks like Darth Mauls' double-light sabre, while on another, you get a chainsword right out of Warhammer 40K.
On sale the entire collection, including DLCs, will run you about $10, which when you see how many hours you'll sink into it, is a huge value.

I cannot recommend this game for one reason. It crashes/freezes all the time, and I didn't even race online yet. If you search the forums it seems online is even worse, with constant freezes and stutters everytime someone joins a server, making online racing close to impossible.
The base content is free, but be careful. It's very easy to be lured to buy additional and pricey content. I made this mistake myself and bough European track pack plus Suzuka, plus Bathurst. It was on sale and I paid 17 EUR for it, which wouldn't be so bad if the game didn't crash all the time.
My advice if you decide to download the free content is to test it for a good time, then test some more. DON'T PURCHASE ANY CONTENT until you're absolutely sure that the game doesn't crash. Test all the free tracks and cars, do some races.
Then be aware that if the game doesn't crash it may once you load some additional tracks that you just bought and are eager to race on. I've just learned this the hard way. Suzuka crashes for me after 3 to 5 laps during a race. I didn't have time to play other tracks yet as I'm trying to solve the issue. Devs on the forum didn't respond yet to my inquiry. I spent more time running integrity checks and trying to make R3E work than actually playing.
If not for the above problems the sim is quite good. Very nice graphic, very good sound, decent FFB, nice tracks. Problem is, R3E is not a new game and Sector3Studios should be able to make their game a little bit more stable by now. IMO they are more interested in creating/selling new content than making the game actually work. It's a shame.
In comparison to my favorite sim, Automobilista, R3E doesn't even come close to the way Reiza takes care of their userbase. Reiza team (the maker of AMS) is very active on the forum, and if the problem arises they are almost immediately on it (beside their sim just works).
I'm torn to give R3E thumbs down, but I have to with the way things are at this point. It doesn't matter how good the game is if it crashes way more often than it should. It's very frustrating.
I still recommend to download and try it, but with the caveat of testing and re-testing everyting before paying a dime for any additional content. If you see a sale don't run to buy stuff because you completed a few laps and liked it (don't copy my mistakes).
If the game worked I'd actually buy more stuff from Sector3Studios, but as is, I regret buying what I own from them.
Pros:
-fun (when it works)
-decent FFB
-good sound
-nice tracks
-good graphics
-decent physics
-free content is actually very nice
Cons:
-game crashes more than it works
-AI is not aware of you. It drove into me from behind on several occasions like I wasn't there.
-paid content is advertised all the time (while the game loads, while the tracks load, etc)
-paid content is expensive compared to other sims. At least make it work and I'd still buy it
If this sim worked I would put it on a podium, 3rd place, behing Automobilista and rFactor 2. I've tried AC some time ago, and compared to that R3E is better. If only it wasn't so buggy...
Get AMS first if you don't have it yet. It's a much better sim (with better FFB, physics, better AI, sim just works, and devs are awesome to deal with). Sometimes we start a new game with some preconcieved ideas.  A lot of things can prejudice us such as the cost of a game, how old it is or maybe even the type of game.  I must confess, that I wasn't expecting much at all with this one but wow, from about ten minutes in I was kind of blown away and got right into it.  Why?  Well, the katana action is really well done.  Lopping off arms and legs has never been easier and what's more, you do hit what you chop at so I felt this to be deeply satisfying.  Similarly, the gun-play is good and it mixes getting up close and shooting at a distance really well so that you can cause more carnage and upgrade your character much faster.
The protagonist might be a d**k but he's likeable with a good sense of humour.   Come on, he even has his own Batcave.  I also like the tone of the game - serious and bloody but it still has fun with its characters and story.  At the very beginning you can even see Godzilla in the background.  Having said that, the backstory about your companion is also quite well done and I genuinely wanted to know what had happened in his past.
Now, I must admit that I don't really like old school shooters.  Don't get me wrong, I've played them since Wolfenstein back in the day but I really do feel that games have left the old "open the door with the yellow key" formula behind for a good reason.  I don't like backtracking and getting lost and then fighting throughout the same level over and over again, it's just tedious to me.  Shadow Warrior does this but I was willing to forgive it.
Graphically, I really liked the style of this game.  They weren't anything particularly special BUT I did like the Asian theme and many times I would stop to think hmmm, nice garden.  Also it played particularly fast so it felt well optimized, even when there were a lot of demons on screen in the later levels.
I played this game on medium difficulty and found it to be okay.  The boss fights weren't too hard so if you want a hardcore challenge, definitlely crank the difficulty up.  When I completed it, I got the chance to go through again with my weapons (many of which needed to be upgraded a lot more).  I was actually really tempted to go again but alas, my Steam backlog of games is getting out of hand so I had to move on before the next sale.
So yeah, I really would recommend this game to anyone who likes a good looking, well designed shooting game.  I played Doom just after this and although I also enjoyed that one, I prefered this one much more - 10/10 from me.

I adore the walking simulator genre, and this was one of the best walking games I've played. The characters feel very real and lived in, as does the ship. Like Gone Home, there are plenty of small personal details to discover if you're willing to snoop (and if you're playing this sort of game, I assume you're more than willing). All of the objects - from photos to notes to coins to books - have been placed extremely deliberately to add to story and character.
The main mechanic of the game is playing through partially corrupted augmented reality holograms of the crew, and uncovering their emails/notes/texts. You can follow one conversation, rewind, and go follow a different conversation - like a slightly more controllable version of "Sleep No More". There isn't much in the way of puzzles - a few passcodes that you can enter in the right place to unlock specific areas, a few physical keys hidden in drawers, that sort of thing.
The game also includes excellent representation - POC, women in tech, queer couples, and combinations thereof, while crafting them all into unique and full characters (except possibly the player character, who is left mostly unexplored).
It is short - I played just over 4 hours and I'm very much a "stop-and-look-and-contemplate-everything" kind of player, but I've played longer games that had far less to them. I think if you enjoy this sort of game to start with, it's well worth your time and your money.

Disclaimer: My "time played" is not representative of the actual amount of time I spent playing this game (I left the game idling while doing other stuff).  My actual "time played" is just over 2 hours - this game is very short.
First off, Tacoma is a Sci-Fi adventure game with a small cast of characters set inside a seemingly-abandoned spacestation with a primary emphasis on narrative and character-building. The player controls Amy, a contractor employed by the corporation which owns the Tacoma spacestation, whose job is to retrieve the Tacoma's Artificial Intelligence and assess the series of events which preceded her arrival.
For fans of the developer's previous game, Gone Home, much of the skeleton of Tacoma should seems familiar: the majority of the game is spent passively observing the story via pre-recorded vignettes and interspersed bits of environmental storytelling.  Unlike Gone Home, however, Tacoma features what can be considered actual gameplay: as the player explores the various  environments they will be presented with short scenes recorded by the ship's AI, ODIN, which they can play, rewind, and fast forward in order to observe the scene from the perspectives of the various crewmates.  It's an interesting idea, and is the primary hook of the gameplay.  The voice performances of all the characters is top-notch.
With that said, as someone who quite enjoyed Gone Home, I cannot recommend Tacoma.
Everything about this game feels rushed: from the narrative, to the character development, to the world-building, not a single piece of this game feels fully-realized.  This shouldn't be surprising to those who have followed the development of this game; Tacoma was supposed to be an entirely different game before Fullbright revamped it to its current form, and as a result it reeks of the sense that "we need to get this game out there before we run out of money." And that really sucks, because across all of these categories there is a solid foundation but a disappointing payoff: the narrative hook is strong (albeit hackneyed) but ends just as soon as its presented, the characters feel fleshed-out but have no arc, and the world is interesting but it lacks detail.  Tacoma relies far too much on ellipsis, on the player piecing together a cohesive experience through the various and insubstantial bits and pieces the game deems important enough to reveal and speculating on the ones it doesn't.
The primary problem with this game is simply that there's not enough of it.  Gone Home was successful despite its short length because it's scope was so narrow - it's basically just a short story about a single member of a family set in a world that we're all familiar with.  Tacoma fails because it's scope is much broader - trying to cram so much character-building and world-building in such a short narrative leaves a lot of holes and an unsatisfactory conclusions. I almost gave this game a thumbs-down at several points while playing. I had gone into the game expecting “Braid with magnets” and Metroidvania-style exploration. Instead, I got a Super Meat Boy clone with long, frustrating, unforgiving platforming segments and annoying trial-and-error bosses. The magnets are mainly used as a means to traverse death gauntlets, often with twitch-action polarity shifting. One wrong move and you’ll either die, or fall down a long way and be forced to climb back up. The magnet puzzles themselves are pretty bland and uninspired physics puzzles, and ultimately pointless. The level design is about as linear as a Super Mario Bros. level, and all four of the important powerups are placed directly in your path. Backtracking is only required for 100% completion (or if you happened to not find at least 15 of the 36 collectables to unlock the door to the final boss). Overall, it failed to meet just about all of the expectations I had for it.
What redeems this game is the atmosphere, art style, and storytelling. There are no words or dialogue at all; this game tells quite a fascinating and unexpected story through the environments, characters, and pictures alone. The hand-drawn art and backgrounds are all beautiful to look at, and there’s no shortage of good music, both of the catchy and atmospheric variety. Perhaps it's style over substance, but for me it really worked.
Once I attained 100% completion and reached the best ending, I looked back upon the game and realized I was glad to have played it. It was a real emotional journey. There’s nothing at all awful about the game, it’s just average in a lot of ways. The difficulty isn’t actually all that hard, it’s just frustratingly out-of-place, and skill eventually did take over and help make the experience more enjoyable. And despite the lackluster puzzle design, there were some instances of great ideas in there; the secret scrolls were highly satisfying to find and collect. With minimal hints and hundreds of mistakes, I got 100% completion in less than 10 hours.
So, after much deliberation, this gets a thumbs-up from me. If you can get it on sale for half price, and if you can put up with the stupid platforming sections and the death gauntlets, you might also find there’s a lot to enjoy here.

I've been waiting two years for this game, anticipation building, and it was so, so worth it.
Tacoma is clearly a Fullbright game, as thematically thoughtful and tightly written as Gone Home, if without some of the timely punch their first title had. Which is not to say that Tacoma is any less engaging or even groundbreaking in terms of its chosen cast -- actually, it's definitely more so. It only feels less exciting because Fullbright already laid down this path with Gone Home, so the shock factor of seeing characters who aren't simultaneously straight, white, or male is lessened. Instead, it feels expected in the best sort of way.
There's loads more to explore in Tacoma than Gone Home. Gone Home had the unfortunate weakness of being completely (and even accidentally) spoilable. Players preemptively exposed to the major twist or even barebones plot were left without much else to explore and discover, and largely unaffected by the atmospherics. Tacoma solves this problem by incorporating multiple intertwining story threads and letting the player explore them in depth at their own pace. Although there is a Fullbright Twist in the third act, it isn't the driving force or even most memorable portion of the story. What stays with you are the quieter moments, like the notes characters leave on the inside of their gym lockers.
The mechanics, too, are completely different. Where Gone Home was fundamentally similar to Escape The Room games -- click everything, open every box, read all the papers -- with a side of Bioshock-esque diary recordings supported by brilliant and thorough set design, Tacoma is something new. Almost like an interactive movie, Tacoma invites players to walk around and seek out the details in character-populated and fully voiced cut scenes. It is quite literally like walking through a town full of NPCs, going about their lives without noticing you. An exercise in voyeuristic viewership with a bit of clicking-around thrown in. If you unironically love activating story events and reading the optional in-game lore materials as much as I do, then Tacoma is the game for you.
Tacoma rewards a detail-oriented play style. Despite flagging most key plot developments as Important and intentionally making them easy to find, the majority of the world building and character exploration is contained in branching side rooms and small interactive objects that players in a hurry (like the disgruntled Polygon reviewer) might miss. Considering that the depth of futurism is actually key to understanding the ending and completely missable if the player refuses to deviate from the bare-bones storyline, playing Tacoma in a hurry is a huge mistake. All in all, searching through every corner of the game took me about five hours, which I consider time well spent.
The graphics and art design are, once again, beautiful, and even better than Gone Home. The game did immediately start me out on the lowest graphic setting -- don't be fooled, this isn't an indy game with glitchy pixelated corners. The high settings for the graphics are completely gorgeous.
Expect to fall in love with the cast (yes, even the AI) and cry at the end. 10/10.

If you play the free demo you'll know whether or not you like this game, so this review is pointless and futile, which is entirely appropriate as the game itself revolves around pointlessness and futility.
You know how some games have hidden "easter eggs" that you can find by doing unexpected things? Well this is what you do throughout the game. You have to constantly restart from the beginning (Stanley's office), take different routes around the building, push different buttons and interact with different items. By doing this you eventually reach various different "endings" to the game. When you think you've found them all you can check one of the Steam Guides to see if you've missed any. There are one or two that you're extremely unlikely to find on your own. There are also several hidden secrets that you may or may not discover on your travels.
Good games have nice graphics, good gameplay, cool music... but how many would you describe as having great narration? That's what this game is all about: listening to a very English narrator, dripping with sarcasm and deadpan wit, giving a running commentary on Stanley's (your) actions - or lack of. Like listening to Howard Stern, you'll keep playing just to find out what he's going to say next. Who knew that standing in a broom closet doing nothing could be so entertaining? The theme/philosophy of the humour is to gently poke fun at the way gamers chase objectives, thinking they have choices, but really it's all futile. Have a look at the ridiculous achievements and you'll see what I mean.
The graphics details are set to low resolution by default within an obscure advanced options menu. I only discovered this after I'd more or less completed the game. Dammit. They're pretty good anyway but I would have liked to play the whole game in high def. Come to think of it, maybe this was part of the game...
Sometimes the game restarts before you've had time to read all the interesting stuff on the whiteboard or whatnot.
This game is too short, there's barely 3 hours of unique gameplay. The nature of the game means you'll replay parts of it multiple times, but like a good joke it inevitably wears thin.
The Broom Closet and the '430' achievement. Hilarious! There is a beautiful acoustic guitar song hidden deep.
Like a fine wine, this is a game to be sipped and savoured because as exquisite as it is, there's not enough of it. Buy it on sale and you'll get good value for your money.

The combat in this game claims to be "brutally challenging," but "unfair" would be a far more accurate descriptor.  With combat skills of 4/10 in both offense and defense (a fairly significant investment at the point where you've just reached the first major city), wielding what seemed to be the best weapons and armor available at this early point in the game, fighting 3 no-name thugs, I did so little damage I could barely scratch them and my to-hit chance topped out at 40%, yet they were able to punch through my cavalry shield and tricked out praetorian armor like it was nothing and connected with almost every swing, including called shots.  Positioning would have little impact on this fight, and all the tricky combat maneuvers that could have helped also reduce your to-hit chance, plummeting my meager odds of striking even lower.
While some people may find this fun, and the game does warn that optional fights are harder than required ones, this just seems ridiculous, unfair, and non-thematic to me.  A warrior-diplomat wearing the best equipment his liege can provide, with significant investment in combat skills (enough to be nearly half way to being considered a grand master of his fighting style) should not be getting punked out by 3 random thugs in an alley 5 minutes after he steps into the big city.  Even on one on I'm not sure I'd stand a chance.
EDIT: I should note that I reloaded and went back to this same encounter and tried to use my social skills to talk through the situation, which are similarly solid (4/10 Streetwise).  Apparently that's too low as well.  It feels like because I didn't pick one aspect of my character and crank it into the stratosphere as soon as I could, I'm completely unable to engage with this encounter.

A metroidvania game with a darkly cute art style, Hollow Knight is a both a blast to play and a joy to experience.  It's like if Metroid Fusion and Dark Souls had a baby and the baby was adorable.
The gameplay is perfection.  The controls are tight and while I didn't run into too many roadblocks on my adventure, there are optional things you can do that provide a tough challenge.  And there's a LOT of optional stuff in this game, which is a nice breath of fresh air for the genre.  You can just blaze through to the end if you want - but if you enjoy completionism, there's a lot of stuff to collect and fight.
The game has a Dark Souls style story where you're not quite sure what's going on for a portion of the game, and it's only later on that things start to make sense and tie together.  It's a fun, deep lore-filled world that Cherry has constructed.  That having been said, there is a significant problem with this game and it's that oftentimes you lack direction and get stuck.  You can sometimes get hints from NPCs about what to do/where to go, but there are times when you're just flat out stuck revisiting old places hoping you'll stumble your way into the next area and it can be kind of frustrating.  The requirement to get the game's True Ending (yeah, there's multiple ones) is also Cave Story levels of obtuse.
Game is still great though.  Buy it even if it isn't on sale, this team deserves your money.

The final score I give this game is a 6.5/10, with the following breakdown:
11/10 for game content - I really love how *branched* this game is; you can achieve multiple endings by travelling many different paths.
-1/10 for combat - This will be explained below...
1.5/1 for feedback...
I took an average of the first two and added the third.
The Content
I really loved how surprising this game was.
At first I thought it was going to be a Roman game where you level up your character and you lead your house to victory or be a diplomat of some sort. I never thought any sci-fi would be involved.
The most surprising thing for me was the slow introduction of sci-fi, its development, and also the addition of religion. I really felt it was awesome that "real" "gods" were in this game. Other games out there either make it a very poor development/interaction or they keep godhood to a distance.
All of this was a very welcome surprise. I'm not religious, so yes, I killed all "gods". :)
The Combat
Now this is something that frustrated me immensely.
I feel that this is a system that is heavily rigged against you. It seems that the developers have purposely written code/scripts to put your character down in combat.
Here's an example that occurred with me time and time again.
I am a Praetor in a fight versus three (3) thugs. Since the game says that combat is more realistic and not expected to always survive, I would somewhat expect to die in a 1v3 situation and not make it out alive.
So, without any buffs/debuffs (poison/whetstone/AP/etc) for either myself or the enemies, I start the fight.
First thing that is always occurring that is clearly rigged against you is that the enemies either start first, or if you do, the enemies then have two (2) consecutive turns. Always.
Second, once I realized that the combat was rigged, I decided to test chance/randomness. So I went into similar situations (1v3, 1v4, etc) with the exact same tactics/moves every single time.
Something like this always, always, always happens (in the following example I'll use the 1v3 thugs encounter):
As a rather trained in combat Praetor, I manage to defeat two (2) of the thugs and bring the third to about 5-9HPs. Then he kills me and I die.
OK, no problem. It's *somewhat* expected, 1v3 is tough anytime. So I try the fight again... and again... and the outcome is *always* the same: I kill two (2) of them and bring the third down to 5-9HPs.
No critical strikes occur, nothing. Just simple basic attacks (fast/regular).
Then I try the fight again. I get a critical strike!!! I manage to kill one (1) of the thugs without losing any HPs of my own!!!
This time it definitely looks like I can win this fight completely since now I'm going 1v2 at full health, and since when I'm in 1v3 I take down almost all three (3), victory must be within grasp!
I feel I can definitely win it this time.
So I get my crit strike and the first thug falls down. I feel great. Then I have 1 AP left, so I press spacebar to let the other two (2) thugs go.
Then they each get a crit strike on me and I die. Uhh. OK? So because I got a crit strike, they have to get one too?
OK, maybe it's just a very weird coincidence. I try again.
4-5 attempts later of nothing happening and me just killing almost all three (3) of them, I get the crit again!!! But... so do they. I die. Again. And I only managed to kill one (1) of them.
It's like getting a crit is punishable by death.
I get this in almost any fight I get into.
And for this reason I believe the combat to be heavily rigged against the player. There is no randomness/chance to it.
It took me one (1) entire day to defeat the Mining Outpost guards. 1v4, and they were heavily weakened by poison.
In the end, I cheated only once during the entire campaign regarding fights: the Centurion arena fight in Ganezzar. I replenished my health twice (so therefore I defeated them by using about 100HP for my character). I think I probably could have not cheated if I would have used AP buffs and bombs, but I was too disappointed with the combat by that time.
(And Agathoth but only out of curiousity, I didn't go with that ending)
Feedback
The devs seem to be responding to all your questions, which is great, so that's definitely extra points.
So, finally, even though the combat is so poor, I think everything else makes this game worth playing.
Thank you.

So, my impression after 12 hours: Can I get about $45 back?
First, let's talk about the tech tree. I'll compare it to Endless Space's "web" tree fyi. From the first turn, the "web" in BE is fugly beyond compare. There are so many techs and one tech rarely leads to another tech in any way that makes sense. Endless Space (ES) has a nice, orderly web to it. Military tech goes up, science/industry right, growth/happiness left, colonization down. I don't even have to look at anything to know where everything is. If I want a military option, I go up. BE though, there are so many links that have nothing to do with one another. My first game had me research something that required a special resource, where was the tech for that resource? I still don't fk'n know, buried within a million other options. The Web is a horribly ugly thing.
Second; AI. The AI is atrocious. Enemy factoin explorers can't figure out how to move, so they move between the same 2 tiles till I destroy it. Autoexplore is garbage, I hit that on my explorer and it sits there till I take control of it. Civ5 had AI personalities like Montezuma or Ghandi, but BE I feel like I'm playing against the same 7 people, all of whom are completely irremarkable. To top off the irremarkable factions though, the AI is completely passive. I've tried to anger it multiple times to no effect.
Third; Aliens. These things should make early game a pain. They do not. They will 1 shot an explorer, but they'll ignore my colony or the military that is murduring them into extinction. Seige worms? They are target practice. They don't "seige" anything, they sit there till I've taken the required 20 turns to kill them. Yawn.
Fourth; decisions. Here is something I thought BE was going to do well. My first game had me make choices, does my ___ give me extra production or food? Cool....next game I get the same exact choices to make and they all end up feeling boring. I would love to see some randomization, maybe a chance that something fk's up and my thorium reactor does something bad. but no, the same boring decisions each game. I never feel that the choices I've made actually make a difference. Some choices have you allow an invasive species to continue invading the planet or stop it, you choose and your affinity level goes up, but beyond that, nothing.
Fifth; UI. So, one gripe I've had with most 4x strategy games is the UI, especially the Civ games. What's worse is that Endless Space has an amazing UI. However, BE's UI is worse than I could imagine. Sometimes the "exit" button is on the bottom of the screen, sometimes It's on the top.... CONFIRM CONFIRM CONFIRM CONFIRM and, you guessed it, CONFIRM AGAIN!!!!! When I make friends, I get the same message from all my other friends talking about how we are friends with their friends....I don't like the "Let's get our names tatooed on eachothers butts and be BFFF(yes, an extra forever)" AI, much less the fact that I have to reconfirm it a million times. ES is amazing because everything I do can be done with the left mouse button or the rmb quickly, completely, and, most importantly, comfortably. This UI though, has me hunting everything down. It's fugly beyond compare.
Sixth; A glorified mod. That's all I can see this game as. It's Civ 5 on another planet but without civiliaztions that feel different from eachother. I didn't expect the game to be something so completely different so as to not be a civ game anymore, but I also didn't expect it to play it SOOOOOOO safe. Every design decision I see feels like the accountants decided to design the safest game they could. BE doesn't really do anything remarkable.
It's a decent game, but it's a glorified mod worth about $15-20 and not $60. And, worst of all, it's an ugly glorified overpriced mod that does nothing remarkably. I have no doubt in my mind that I will forget about BE as soon as the next competing game comes out. It's a good game, it's just a completely averge good game.
Final score: Gonna forget it within 1 year/10.

I'll begin this with a caveat: though I own the rest of the Hitman games on Steam, I have yet to play any of them. So if this game shatters some favorite paradigms of the series, I'm oblivious to that and it may increase my opinion of Absolution over that of a long-time Hitman fan.
That said, this game is fun. It's not groundbreaking, it doesn't introduce any innovative new mechanics, but it's fun to play.
I'll get the boring stuff out of the way first. The story is what I like to call "meh". It tries to be dramatic and build Agent 47's character, I think, but it just completely failed to capture my interest. I don't fault the game for that since that isn't why I wanted to play it in the first place, but it does mean that cutscenese trying to develop the mediocre story sometimes get in the way of me trying to enjoy the better-than-mediocre gameplay.
Graphics are adequate. Nothing earthshattering, but that's fine with me. It looks as good as I would expect a game of this generation to look, and (on my AMD card at least) there are no artifacts or other glitches that prevent me from seeing things I need to see.
As for the gameplay, it's just a fun stealth assasination game. The levels are fairly linear, but you are usually free to carry out the missions any way you want. You can barge in and shoot everything, you can sneak around and snap people's necks, and most levels have (fairly obvious) traps you can set to take out your target from a distance. For example, if a guy keeps wandering past a gas pump and tossing his lit cigarette, you can use the pump to make a puddle of gasoline on the ground in between his smoke breaks. This makes the game feel a little too scripted as your marks repeat the same routine ad infinitum, but it's mostly made up for by the fun of taking them out in interesting ways. My one gripe here is that the scoring system is entirely based on stealth and killing ONLY your target. There's certainly nothing stopping you from killing everything you encounter, and you will still pass the mission and progress the story, but you will get fewer (and maybe even negative) points. It doesn't really mean anything, it just rubs me the wrong way for the game to tell me I did the mission wrong when I did it the way that was fun to me. Some missions are fun to play full stealth, but some are *definitely* more fun if you go in like a wrecking ball.
I played the game with an XBOX 360 controller so I can't comment on keyboard and mouse controls, but with the controller at least it's fairly responsive. My biggest issue was that 47 sometimes doesn't seem to know whether I'm telling him to press his back against cover or jump right out in front of a guard, exposing his position. Another problem is that, since there is no targetting reticle, you sometimes have trouble targetting the right thing when pressing the action button. Do you want to stash this body in a dumpster, or endlessly trade your weapon with his? Sometimes 47 has no clue, and will happily crouch there by the dumpster swapping weapons until a guard comes around the corner and discovers him kneeling near the body of a colleague.
Overall Absolution is a fun game, but as is the case with most things on Steam, you might as well wait for a sale. At $10 it's absolutely worth it for the amount of fun I had, but I can't say I'd recommend it for full price.

It's not exactly groundbreaking, but it's got the potential to be. It can be a bit confusing at first, but after a game or two of it you start to get the hang of it. The Tech Web makes things interesting, even if the placement of some of the techs is a little frustrating (putting techs required for some victory conditions far away from the other techs relevant to those same victory conditions). I found the Quest system to be quite enjoyable, although the timing of them is pretty uneven (sometimes you don't get a quest for dozens of turns, sometimes you get a whole bunch on successive turns). There's also a bit of luck involved, as getting certain quests can make a much bigger difference than others. The spy system is wonderful. Much better than that found in Civ V. Overall, this feels like it's a solid foundation for something much bigger and better. If they consistently add DLC as well as add new features (in the same way that G&K and BNW added new features to Civ V), this will be an all-time great. On its own right now though, it's just decent. Still enjoyable, but not as much as it could be.

If you are a diehard Hitman fan, back away now. You will not like this game. Hitman Absolution takes a completely different approach to stealth as opposed to its beautiful, satisfying predecessors. Absolution is marketed toward sneaky-sneaky, hiding behind walls audiences as opposed to hide-in-plain-sight, poker face master audiences. Once again, if you liked the previous Hitman games, you will not like this one.
Now that we've gotten that out of the way, let's get to the game. Hitman Absolution takes place after the ending of Hitman Blood Money. You play as Agent 47, a perfect genetic clone of the perfect assassin. Diana Burnwood, the woman who has been giving you contracts since 2000, is your next target.
As implied before, Absolution is what most would consider a "traditional" stealth game with a little bit of Hitman injected into it. Like the previous Hitman games, you can disguise as guards and other personnel. However, the disguise system is so broken, enemies will see through you like glass, making disguises practically useless. Therefore flushing the reason Hitman was so popular down the drain. In addition, there is now a point system. Every time you kill or knock out anyone but the target, you lose points. If you are spotted, you lose points. Every time you do something that is not perfect, you lose points. It's quite a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ system, pardon my
French.
However, the game makes up for it by making the other mechanics shine. Guns are still finnicky, forcing you to use more creative means. Bodies can still be dumped in containers, which have a maximum capacity of 2. When you are inevitably spotted, you can fake surrender, which will turn the tables on the poor guard. When you attack a hostile from behind unarmed, you can either mash a key to choke them out, or press a key to snap their neck and kill them.
All in all, don't think of Absolution as a Hitman game. You're not going to get a Hitman game. Think of it as Splinter Cell with disguises starring a bald guy. Hitman Absolution is a good game, don't listen to the haters.

I'm so sad to write this review.  I'm a hard-core Civilization fan.  I've played Civ since the franchise was first launched.  I've literally logged hundreds of hours playing Civ 5 and all its DLC in Steam.  I also feel as though Alpha Centauri is still one of the best computer games ever made.  I've been looking forward to Civilization Beyond Earth for months.
This game is such a terrible disappointment.  And I'm going to be as constructive as I can be in my criticsm.
I hardly know where to begin.
First of all, Wonders of the World are completely nerfed and uninspiring. There are no video sequences upon completing one.   There's no sense that youv'e actually accomplished something by building a Wonder.  Even more galling, from what I've seen (and I've already played the game over 12 hours just this weekend), Wonders don't even matter much.  Most Wonders seem to give palty bonuses that are on par with a single city building.  Literally.  I mean, c'mon!  If building the sci fi equivalent of the Pyramids is no different than building the sci fi equivalent of a Granary, what's the point?
The Civolpedia is awful.  The help screens are appallingly unhelpful.  They don't link to one another.  It's not easy to understand what's going on in this game, and the "help system" makes it worse.  The prose of the "backstory" is dense and confusing, without any dramatic hooks to tie in a narrative, and make it interesting.  Even as a veteran Civ player, I was floundering trying to figure this game out, and the help system was about as useful as calling Comcast on a Saturday afternoon.  After about half an hour *just trying to figure out the Civolepedia* I started to drink.
The Affinity system makes no sense.  Why "force" me to adopt certain affinities just because I research technology in a certain order?  Why not give me the choice to engineer my society through meaningful decisions, in terms of Affinities?  Even more perplexing, how can I be a "humans first" "Gaia loving" "I am the Borg" society, ALL AT ONCE?  Affinities should be mutually exclusive.
This game is boring.  I played for over 200 turns and no one attacked me, other than some random aliens.  No one offered me any interesting challenges.   I'll admit, I tend to be a peaceful builder type, but to play in a world where no one goes to war, and where I don't feel the need to attack other factions or pump up my military to prevent being conquered... what's the point of that?
The health system (a.k.a. "happniess") is broken.  Until you unlock certain late game techs, or build many, many special terrain upgrades, it's basically impossible to have more than 3 or 4 cities.  Yes, you read that right.  Forget infinite city sprawl, this game punishes you for trying to found or conquer more than about 3 cities for the first 150+ turns.  Absoultely abominable.  Dumb.
Firaxis, I'm one of your biggest fans, but I feel like I should get my money back on this one.  If a developer were willing to e-mail me, I could offer about 20 helpful suggestions on how to fix this game, but until then, no one else should bother buying it.

The best Card Game I ever play.
This game utilize the advantage of being 'digital' to maximum.
You can have cards which have complex effect and almost impossible to play and track physically. (Sleeper Faction is a good example).
Another thing I like is that in Rift run (or Draft or Arena in other card game where you pick random card and fight each other for reward.), you can buy the 'whole' deck you build into your collection after the run end. The price is also fair and the price reduce dramatically for each victory. (to the point of it being free if you are good enough)
The simultaneously turn system is also very well implemented. It makes the players to 'read' the opponents as a human player. Compare to other turn-based card game which player just make "Maximize value" play, the simultaneously turn system encourage players to make deeper and more complex tactics to out mind the opponent and thrown him off balance.
This game also deal with zoo deck quite well. Because all card can block (taunt in HeartS) and many powerful abilities which can punish a careless mass zoo,
Also, the morale system help to deal with turtle player who just camp. (it's 2nd HP which go down everytime your minions die, like a manpower in Heart of Iron).
Also, except from the pack opening, this game have almost 0 RNG (except from Exile, which is not mandatory except you really want to activate the gamble ability). Which is a plus for me compare to HeartStone or other card game.

Tacoma is a first person exploration game. You play a contractor sent to a small orbital station that handles cargo deliveries to and from the moon. The crew was evacuated and you are tasked with retrieving information from the station's computers. While the data is transferring you spend your time investigating what happened in the last 72 hours. You watch recordings played in 3D augmented reality, read electronic messages picked from the crew's personal communicators, and scour the station for physical evidence like letters, reports etc. You discover the story of six very ordinary people placed in an extraordinary situation, how they choose to respond, and how they each cope with the consequences.
The station is small but believable, filled with sensible locations and items. I love that half of the game shows you life on the station before the "event". You get to watch routine work and leisure on the station and get familiar with the characters. Several of the scenes are just crew members chilling to their favourite music, which gives a nice change of pace, like similar scenes in Life is Strange.
Everything about this game is well made. It's visually gorgeous. Many rooms have external windows through which you can see the exterior of the station and space beyond it. The station is spinning so the sun comes in to and out of view, illuminating the room when it's present - the effect is striking. Animations are great. Voice acting is superb and dialogue sounds natural and believable. Music is scarce but used for great effect, and is always diegetic. The game is short but every moment is well thought out and executed.
Overall this is a fantastic game and I enjoyed every minute with it. I loved exploring the station, getting to know the characters, seeing them interact with each other and with their own social circles, and watching the story unfold. If this sounds interesting to you I'd highly recommend this game.

Tales of Wuxia is an interesting and unique game that has been translated from China. It's an update of a previous game and the first I'm aware of to make it into English.
What is it? One part is top down RPG, running around, talking to people, doing quests, buying stuff, whatever. Combat is handled in unique turn based RPG style where the accumulated effort of the sim portion determines your characters internal style, martial arts styles and stats.
The sim segments involve you making meaningful and vital decisions in growing your character, do you explore the town and encounter new and strange allies/enemies and possibly even learn new martial arts? Or do you try to master Music, which will learn you powerful techniques in combat?
There's a ton of different skills and minigames involved in raising your tea sipping alchohol drinking kungfu master, many of them interesting, a few sure to be a little frustrating.
Most interestingly, the game is actually pretty in depth with teaching the player a lot of fascinating stuff.
The bad is clear, the game has some technical hiccups which, if you're not comfortable browsing the forum to solve, can prevent you from playing. In my experience, once I figured out how to get the keyboard to work in game I encounter no technical issues as of my near thirty hours in game.
The second is the translation, it begins pretty strong and carries through on the main story comprehnesibly but some paths of various events are translated bizarrely and inconsistantly. If you can appreciate a bad dub, this is more charming than problematic but some segments are simply not translated at all. I'd put the translation at about 99.9% complete, but that .1% does pop up and will irritate some less forgiving.
Ultimately, I love this game. It's full of content, I'm not even done my first playthrough but already I'm looking forward to playing through as a villain, a womanizer, and so on. My first character has dozens of martial arts I haven't even begun to use, not to mention internal styles and so on.
This game really makes you feel like you're raising a badass martial-artist, and presents a full and fascinating Wuxia fantasy world for you to get lost in. I recommend it to anyone who loves unique games, sim-raising games, strategy RPG's, and cool translation gems.
The Good
Unique and well done melding of RPG elements, turn based strategic combat, and sim-raising gameplay
A fascinating world filled with interesting characters to interact with
A ton of replayability!
Meaningful and in-depth choices to grow your character
The best tea sipping alchohol drinking kung fu raising sim ever (small market but still!)
There's a kung fu style you get from learning how to play chess, from music, from even calligraphy!
The Bad
Only 99.9% translated so far it seems.
Some odd jank with keyboard stuff that you'll need to fiddle with initially.
Preset character

While initially exciting and new, you only have to scratch below the surface to find a largely lifeless and unenjoyable Civilisation experience. The supposed spiritual sequel to the much beloved Alpha Centauri, Beyond Earth is in a word, disappointing.
There is next to no variation between the civilisations, with much of the starting bonuses cherry picked at the start of the game. (This is a good system, had it been implemented for a player made, custom civ it would have added alot.) The lack of predefined civilisations renders your choice of civ irrelevant after about 20 turns, as you have no faction specific buildings or particular playstyle to take advantage of. Replacing this is the affinity system, which allows you to pick from Harmony, Supremacy or Purity with the three approaches having different strengths and weaknesses. While in theory this seems to be a viable alternative to the previous system. In practice it leaves alot to be desired with specific resources, (Did you start with no floatstone around? Don't bother with Purity then) more likely to dictate your choices than anything else.
The diplomacy system is a literal copy paste of the civ 5 diplomacy, to me that is genuinely unacceptable.
Most of these problems are the sort of thing that will get ironed out in a month or more with various patches (And lets be honest the hardworking modders who will fix the most glaring issues) but to me the biggest problem with the game is basically unfixable.
The writing and flavour for the game flat. Flat, flat, flat. Flat, boring and uninspired. The quotes and dialogue that Civ games are famous for are not to be found. Because the characters being quoted are fictional geniuses not real ones. These fake quotes and micro fiction are obviously designed to ape the approach that was taken in Alpha Centauri (oh it looms like some kind of space monolith). In Alpha Centauri the fiction was so intricately researched and lovingly crafted, blending real life quotes and philosophy with, speculative idealogical factions who all had an opinion about how the world should be.  In Beyond Earth they make an effort to emulate this, but it falls far, far short.
Overall, very disappointing game. As I said, patches and mods will add alot to it, but right now its not worth anything like the money you are paying. I wouldn't even say to wait for the sale because new Civ games very seldom receive any kind of heavy discounting.

I played Torchlight for nearly 100 hours - very addictive hack-n-slash dungeon crawler. If you like Diablo, you should like this. The guy who did music for Diablo made the music for Torchlight - and it shows - amazing atmospheric music. They also really came up with solutions to many of the problems of action RPGs.
For instance, the problem of having to slog back to town to sell your junk and get some gold. They give you a pet that fights alongside you (and can shape shift) that has an inventory - you can send it off to town to sell your items and come back with gold. So you get to enjoy the dungeon more - I stacked a bunch of enchants that made my pet leave and come back instantly, so I never had to go to town unless I wanted to buy something.
They also let you buy a respec potion if you have the gold.
It is also very mod-able. There are mods making your pet into a giant ferret or adding a new special dungeon or quest giver or a treasure vault.
Highly recommended.

Where to start? Well, the game is amazing. I'm only a little way into it but I can tell it is going to be ridiculously massive. Every skill seems to unlock something else - new characters turn up or I get a new ability or martial art or can make better stuff or whatever. Okay, yeah, that's how most games with a skill system work, but given that my character ended up drinking cheap wine till he gained the power of Drunken Kung Fu from a magical hobo I think it's safe to say that the skills you get are really unexpected and seriously fun. I wouldn't be surprised if you managed to master flower arranging and ended up being able to decapitate a man by pelting him with a handful of rose petals. The sheer amount of stuff available might be a bit intimidating to some people, but a good tip is just to grind hunting because then at the end of the day you can (I never thought I'd ever type this) go home and eat a big bag of tiger♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥for massive stat boosts.
The graphics are pretty nice - the 'control your guy and run around doing Kung Fu' sections aren't super ultra realistic high-def but it's still all nicely detailed and looks good. That and the music combines perfectly to really set up the atmosphere.
The combat sections aren't too bad either. It all plays out fairly well, there are (as far as I've seen anyway) no giant drawn out combats or sections where you can tell the dev's were making something else and didn't have time to really perfect this combat or that fight. I will say that early on some people might think otherwise (There are some brutally hard fights) but early on in the game don't forget you are playing an ordinary guy just starting out in the Kung Fu superhero business.
Now, onto the flaws. There have been a few people complaining about a bug where not being in fullscreen makes the keyboard stop responding, but I've never seen that or had the game crash so I can't comment. The translation is the only thing close to a complaint I have, and given how the game was actually translated I suppose I can't be too harsh. The developers basically open sourced it and got the fans of the series to help them out, so yeah, there are going to be sections where it is perfectly translated into The Queen's English and sections where urteh baonfo legging, though thankfully there's more of the former than the latter. Thanks to the size difference between English and Chinese text though, there are quite a few sections where the text overflows from a page and you can't read it all and where font sizes change from section to section so everything can fit in. If they keep working on the translation then yeah, this'll go from being really good to genuinely epic.
Do I recommend this game? Oh hell yes I do. Was I kidding about the Tiger♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ no. That is an actual thing.

Short Verison:
It's Civ 5 in space
Long Version:
From a core concepts point of view, its essentially Civ 5 with some feature polish. The biggest diffence though, is in the story, culture, and framing of the game.  I had always appreciated the smoothness of the core concepts in Civ 5, the ones that would allow me to play hours on end comfortable. The story was lacking, though. I as an individual do not find history appealing, and there is only but so much creativity you can put into "Earth 0AD ~ 2000AD". Beyond Earth fixes that though, with it's space colonization story. I feel like BE was the Civilization creative team letting loose. The story the game conveys is very believable, the atmosphere the game crafts is very immersive, and just generally everything that isn't a core game mechanic (i.e. build city... eventually be managing a civilization) is more appealing.
My only issue is that the game sessions dont last very long (in the sense that over the course of a single match I dont feel like enough -happens-), and there isn't the debth of content that Civ 5 had... but these are probably issues that will be solved with DLC (which I will totally be buying all of!)

Hollow knight is an indie, 2D-action platformer that is made in the style of Metroidvania by Team Cherry. This game allows the player to explore a vast setting with memorable characters, beautiful art styles, challenging bosses, secrets and unlockables to keep anyone entertained for hours. Whether you prefer to take it slow and explore the ridiculously massive Hollownest, grind it out on a huge variety of monsters, tackle difficult platforming,  take time to learn about the deep lore or try your hand at challenging tough bosses, there is something for everyone. 
 
Hollowknight, at first glance, comes off as highly simplistic, but the charm of the game is how much it can accomplish with such a minimalist approach. The game starts the player off without knowing anything. All that the player is given is a seemingly "hollow" character and the basic abilities to move, jump and attack. However as the game goes on, new mechanics are constantly introduced to keep the game interesting while keeping it manageable as not to overwhelm some players. It introduces game mechanics such as "nail jumping" which requires the player to attack downwards on an enemy or spikes to get a bit more airtime, and augments the character with new abilities such as dashing and double jumping. The game is set up in a way that encourages the player to go at their own pace as there is no penalty for taking it slow. Truly the most charming aspect of Hollowknight is the complexity found within the simplicity. The entire game is animated using a minimalist hand-drawn art style that gives almost everything a charming, casual vibe but also encompasses the intimidating might of the bosses and the creepy aura of the deep nest and the abyss maps. This is Hollowknights way of saying that games do not need amazing hyper realistic graphics to be absolutely stunning and acts as a statement to all the Triple-A games that oversaturate the market and the graphics make half the game. 
 
Each section of the Hollownest is themed in a completely different way ranging from caverns filled with crystals to lush green gardens, from eerie abandoned tramways to a kingdom of "tears". All the enemies are also themed as such and each one features a unique attack pattern that ranges from just charging blindly at the player to sophisticated swordplay, meaning the player has to learn how to combat with each one in their own unique way, which keeps combat exciting throughout the entire game. Hollowknight presents combat in a way that seems simple by itself yet when coupled with the vast ways to defeat the array of enemies and bosses, the simple controls that even a monkey can learn suddenly become challenging yet, not impossible as all it requires is to learn the enemy and a little bit of timing to overcome obstacles. The emphasis on timing means that its not just excessive button mashing like in some other games and when the player dies or messes up it feels like the players own fault instead of the game's. Due to the simple combat system, the chance of encountering a bug or glitch unintentionally is almost non-existent so the player feels responsible for their own misplays. 
 
The sheer amount of content that the player gets for a measly $18 (NZD) can rival that of a $50 game, with endless areas to explore, upgrades to unlock, side quests to complete and items to collect, of which many are stumbled upon by pure chance. The game has been out for more than half a year but players are still finding Easter eggs and secrets hidden deep within the game. Not to mention the lore scattered throughout the game as dialogue from NPCs, scripts from monoliths and clues in the landscape for the player to unravel the deepest secrets of the Hollownest kingdom's creation and downfall. Hollowknight works off the idea that the best way to tell a story is to not "tell" it at all. The exploration approach on the game allows each and every player to complete the game in an almost completely different order to others, beating different bosses first, finding different upgrades at different times or even uncovering entire areas in differing orders. The game encourages the player to constantly go back when a new upgrade is unlocked such as double jump in order to reach new areas that were previously unreachable. That means that every area in the game is important and none are made obsolete after fulfilling a single purpose. 
 
Hollow knight draws inspiration from many timeless classics such as having a similar theme to Darksouls and a platforming experience similar to super meat boy to give veteran gamers a familiar feel while still making everything its own original creation. The contrast within the simplicity and depth of the game makes it playable to anyone but still offers top quality entertainment. It takes very basic aspects of video games and applies them so well that it is unlike any other game on the market. Being such a simple game in many aspects yet, providing such depth and being so well crafted just show cases the effort and dedication put in by Team Cherry that is lacking so much in todays "high budget, cash grab, drool over the graphics" video game market. It is easy to tell that this game was crafted as an art as opposed to a way for corporations to make big bucks and sets an example for how games should be made. 
 
These reasons and many more are why Hollowknight has found its way into the hearts of many and has won many awards such as #8 best pc game 2017, game informer gold and the editors choice award despite being an indie game. I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to almost anyone who is willing to try.

This is currently my favorite metroidvania game, surpassing Super Metroid and CSotN.
The massive map is simply a joy to explore aesthetically and mechanically.  The controls are precise, fluid and polished.
Backtracking doesn't become a chore because you can travel quickly through the interlinking pathways, and there are also teleport mechanics that can speed things up when necessary.  There is a lot to collect including 36 charms that can be equiped to limited slots that grant new abililities and attributes that can result in interesting combinatons.  Boss challenge is sufficent without over-doing it, with much harder optional versions of many bosses.
A couple minor complaints.  The death mechanic can go unexplained and can throw you for a bit of a loop the first time you die if you're an intermediate/high-skilled platform gamer.  That is to say, you can play for 4-5 hours collecting lots of currency, only to die for the first time, lose all your currency and the game auto-saves  upon death.
You have no access to previous saves. Once you figure out you can get your currency back by carefully returning to where you died and defeating your whimpy shadow, the initial shock wears off.  You only get one chance tough, if you die before reclaiming your stuff it is gone for good. If you die on a boss it is easy to kill the shadow without activating the boss fight. You are then free to die on the boss again, reclaim your stuff, rinse and repeat.
There is a bank a couple zones into the game that can safeguard your deposited  money.  I never used it because it was a little out of the way, maybe it should have been closer to the starting town. It was always quicker just to return to the shadow than trekking to the bank and back.
Unfortunately, being a diligent explorer can have diminishing results in the sense that it becomes trivially easy to afford every shop item in the game, at least in the first play-through. The only consumable shop item to stock up on is rotten  eggs...which make it easier to fight your shadow and get your currency back.  By the time I found that shop I already had more currency and eggs than I would ever need.   There are speedrun challenges where currency demand is probably a lot tighter. The game also auto-saves upon item purchase, so it is hypothetically possible to buy the wrong thing and need to go grinding for a bit.

The PC Port: Final Fantasy XIII is locked at 720p, a hotfix has been released by Durante. There are no graphical options whatsoever, only the launcher, where you can set the language (Japanese or English), and whether you want a 720p window, or 720p exclusive fullscreen.
Gameplay: I'm new to the Final Fantasy franchise, so I can't say if this game is worse than its predecessors. So far, the game is very linear.
Graphics: The graphics are nice, exactly what you see on the store page's screenshots. There are pre-rendered scenes, which of course look better, but isn't day-night difference. Animation quality is good.
The huge size: The pre-rendered scenes are re-rendered in Japanese and English, meaning their lip-syncing are updated for the language.
Verdict: For a 13 EUR port, this game is enjoyable. Yes, it could've had unlocked framerate and resolution, or a more detailed options menu, but if you just want to play a game that has an average storyline, great battle system and soundtrack, this game is for you. If you can't put up with the limitations, then you shouldn't buy it.

If you have been playing computer games for a long while and have never heard of farming, let me now educate you on it and my personal pet peeve and vendetta with it. Farming is an action in role-playing games that are composed of loot and is needed in the progressing of the game in order to improve damage and defense output against enemies and large bosses. Farming is a systematic process and cycle that habitually reoccurs whereby players grind to get a variety of weapons, armor, pets and accessories with different tiers, rarities and qualities. So, farming by itself seems like a rather harmless endeavor that was originally meant for the progression of games in which a random number generator selects random stats, some good, some missing in key areas and some with all important stats that use specific algorithms towards item production which is then consumed by users for their own personal gain within the game and can even be sold on trading forums.

Hackers have been present in Dungeon Defenders since the first three months of its PC release in late 2011 right before the Christmas holiday. Item checkers were called upon to volunteer their time given special privileges and spreadsheets in order to validate the authenticity of all stats on weapons, pets, duped event items without a trace, and duped weapons, pets and armor that lie outside of the minimum and maximum values they are given to work with that are spawnable in the actual game. The random number generated catastrophe led others at the time in 2013 towards a new downloadable content map called Lab Assault that soon came out. Trendy's only motivation for releasing this map was to generate more numbers in the community since many people were leaving their game and numbers of people playing in the community finally reached an all-time low before summer 2013. In order to avoid this, they instituted what is now one of the largest farming endeavor maps into more modern gaming. Lab assault is a tedious and laborious map that last anywhere from three to four minutes per run meant to provide users with a very quick shortcut towards obtaining the highest armor in the game. Armor ranges in the following order of rarity: godly, mythical, transcendent, ultimate, ultimate plus and ultimate plus-plus.
In order to use transcendent items, one must be level 78, ultimate; level 90; and ultimate plus and beyond; the max level 100. The goal is to get armor pieces of the same kind in order to form a full set composed of four pieces. Then, once you get a full set, you get a set bonus which increases your overall stats as well as any resistances you have taken time to upgrade.

•A rewarding game environment in which other users collaborate and can farm items together while having fun smacking ogres, goblins, trolls and tough bosses together over and over towards mastery of different defense placements and setups
•A nice dedicated community of people driven by their love and passion to see the game's survival
•A tactful game that never gets boring, stale; there is always so much to do
•Great trading community, armor types; rarities, characters and downloadable content worth every dollar you spend on it
•Classes need to constantly be switched at the forge in game in order to place defenses, which usually one player on a good team does while the rest defend
•Terribly addictive and when I mean terrible addictive, I mean to the point of ad nauseam due to the farming nature of the community divided half and half into the casual and then the hardcore dedicated regular players that farm every day and week
•Hackers always present though there have been future steps in the sequel, Dungeon Defenders II to fully prevent hackers because they remodeled their servers to be client-side instead of server-side
•Endless replayability
•Each round can last up from forty-five minutes up to an hour per run on the top difficulty
Overall,
is a family-friendly game for all the kids, teens and adults out there looking for something fun and endless to play in the role-playing and tower defense cross-platform genre. However, due to its constant persistence on the farming side of the community, it has inevitably led to its downfall and any chance of surviving. The community development team currently has been doing update after update to improve upon the game's features, maps, rewards and mechanics. However, this also means that those that are addicted to the game like I was can never leave it or it will be much harder to.  I have presented my views towards this over time towards the community and also questioned it in light of all the paradigms that have overtime posed a great emotional, cognitive, psychological and illicit response in the community. At first, my thoughts both towards Trendy Entertainment behind their support I found on Facebook upon Dungeon Defenders II when it was in early access stating that people needed to take off work to farm all day long after the new update they had made, I decided not to support a company like this whose hidden intention is to keep a dying user base at times constantly hooked and coming back.
This is the reason why downloadable content in the early planning stages were released so rapidly to maintain that ambition and degree of pleasure over selfish greed, ambition and callous actions that promote a negative overall attitude in the community instead of humility and helping others before yourself. This alone led to people sometimes maintaining bragging rights and at the end of the time farming for virtual wealth while maintaining their own insecurities that some, though not all may have in  real-life.

The animated art for the cards are badass and really convey the feeling of whatever character/faction they are, the game is fairly balanced (although the sleepers faction has gotten ♥♥♥♥ed over quite a bit in the past, much to my dismay).There are a lot of diffrent cards with diffrent effects that allow for plenty of theory crafting. And if you do not like creating your own deck ideas and combos, every week there is a rotating array of free decks for new players who don't have real decks or for people looking for inspiration for their own decks.
Also, even if you do face mostly the main stream decks (well, as main stream as they can get with such a low player base i geuss), you do also face quite a bit of unique decks, or at least less main stream decks. The game has never really been as broken as MTG has been at some points where there is like only a few decks that work and all the rest are just trash.
The game also has a fairly unique deck building system where comanders take a big, big part as they directly alter what cards you can even have in your deck. Its also quite fast pace. Certain decks like a red charge deck will either have won or will start losing by around turn 6.
Also, turns are done at the same time as your opponent. This means that everything you do has to be proactive instead of reactive. If you want to counter a spell, then you have to predict that your opponent is going to use that spell this turn, and use it this turn, before they actually cast it. This does lead to a format where control decks are not quite as oppresive since you can't just auto-counter everything another player does, you have to predict their actions and not just blindy counter, as well as create a mind game. I can't tell you how many times i have been sitting on that last turn. Both players are just a hit from death, and i have to predict exactly what they are going to do.
Because of how combat works, you dont directly decide who battles who, rather every creatures does battle with the next one in line untill there are no more attackers or there are no more creatures to attack and they deal dmg to the enemy player.
All in all, this is a great card trading game, that is actually free isntead of freemium may i add. This game is a lot like league of legends in this aspect. U can get every single card in the game. no matter how strong just by playing the game. Get it now.
