There are two reasons to name drop Nikola Tesla.  1) You want to get some sweet nerd cred.  2) As a shorthand for electricity-based science magic.  Since this game features monsters that run around in the dark and kill you called "grues" I think we can safely assume this game has all the nerd cred it needs and we're looking at the latter use of Tesla's name.  Now don't take that as some snarling criticism of Teslagrad.  Despite having nothing else to do with Tesla, dropping his name in the title does set you up for abusing wondrous electricity and magnetism based powers amidst an oppressive Eastern European backdrop.  It certainly delivers on that count.
I'm going to assume you've already watched the trailer and been wowed by how good looking this game is with its smooth, forceful, hand-drawn animations.  It's certainly a beautiful game, but don't let that vibrant animation fool you.  This is a grim game about grim Eastern European seeming people doing grim Eastern European things with lightning!  And as somebody with a grim Eastern European family, I knows from grim Eastern European things (not with lightning though, that's new).  Teslagrad tells a basic story, but it does it elegantly without a single word of spoken dialogue or cumbersome written exposition.  Once again, this game is a stone-faced immigrant staring you down, and made all the more unsettling by inhabiting a world that looks like it was drawn by Walt Disney.
You've seen the trailer, though (or you need to just go do that already), and are already sold on the aesthetic of this game.  So let's talk gameplay.  Teslagrad is a bit of a Metroid game and a bit of a puzzle game and a bit of a precision (i.e. frustration) platformer.  You'll notice I said Metroid and not metroidvania.  The Castlevania games have always been a bit more combat oriented and Teslagrad features almost no combat.  There's a tiny bit toward the end and you kill some bosses in round-about ways, but for the most part Teslagrad is all about exploration and evading hazards.  And, remember, this is a grim Eastern European game with ligthning so everything including the floors want you dead.  And don't think they will go light on you because you are playing an adorable child!  There is no food for adorable children, only being lightninged into ashes!
When I said frustration platformer up there, I do mean that.  Teslagrad is absolutely unforgiving with the timing you require to navigate its many hazards, and not just for optional secrets.  Combine this with some imprecise mechanics (especially when magnetizing yourself to float), and I will bet many boiled cabbages you will not be able to beat this game without sighing, growling, or outright screaming "BS!"  So before you pick up Teslagrad, best make sure you're strong like bull and smart like tractor, or at least possess adult reflexes and patience.  That said, the game is pretty liberal with checkpoints.  Stick an incinerator on the end of your most barf-inducing carnival ride and you'll have an idea of the speed with which your ashes will be scattered.  But then you just pop right back up at the start of the room or right after the last ridiculous challenge you overcame.
Overall, Teslagrad is a great looking game with a large environment to explore and a wide variety of puzzles that make use of simple, elegant mechanics.  It would be nice to see an easy mode where the timing on some of the challenges is relaxed, but hey, in mother Teslagrad you must work hard at pixel forge for many achievement.
In other words, it's difficult, but satisfying.  Go play it if exploration-precision-puzzle-platformer sounds good to you.

For a long portion of last year every time I’d catch a glimpse of Zack Bell’s Ink I had to take a moment to pause and check that I wasn’t in fact looking at a more frantic DAGDROM. Perhaps it’s due to stumbling upon them both at nearly the same time (Ink may very well have nudged DAGDROM off the front page of itch.io only a week or two after I first played it), each sporting their own squiggly paint-flinging aesthetic, but on the surface I couldn’t help but find the two games near indistinguishable from one another. Which probably says more to my tendency toward snap judgements than it does to either game in question, as beyond a similar fascination with the messy possibility of flinging paint all over a level Ink and DAGDROM couldn’t be more dissimilar.
In far more ways that matter Ink actually shares a greater kinship with the brutal platforming classic, Super Meat Boy. You could almost speculate that Ink’s explosive paint mechanic was inspired directly by Super Meat Boy’s similar blood splatter effect, but where that served as little more than a macabre monument to your failures Ink turns it into a brilliant platforming meta game, dropping you into levels which are near entirely invisible and requiring you blast paint everywhere to reveal your way through. It’s a bit like the painting mechanics of the charming and underappreciated de Blob, albeit with fewer analogies to totalitarian governments and more jello squares finding their way through the darkness.
Ink’s concept really is dead simple in principle, but there is something wonderfully delightful about a game that is entirely about making as big of a mess of a given level as you can by means of so many gooey psychedelic colors. Ink’s look is minimal in the sense that it’s made up of little more than the most rudimentary of geometric shapes, but there is a liveliness to it all that is infectiously energetic. The way the little square protagonist jiggles with every move feels like far more than a flat stand-in for an actual character, overflowing with a joyful abundance of energy that is all but demanding you keep moving, always keep moving. Ink is often so understated that it verges upon ambivalence, but the little touches found in the way characters move or the way paint arcs just so give the game an enthusiastic personality, and look impeccable to boot.
What’s most special about Ink though is how it uses its visual flair in tandem with its level design, intertwining the two to form a mechanical and graphical synergy. Paint is used to reveal hidden platforms, but it also serves as a helping hand when you begin to fail repeatedly, each death causing you to explode in a shower of paint revealing more of the level and making navigating it that much easier. It’s a small touch but it’s one of the most clever answers to the problem of static platformer difficulty I’ve seen without eating away at the challenge enough to cause it to feel cheap. Ink is ruthless in its attempts to keep you from completing a level, but it always balances its difficulty by giving you enough room to breathe, to find your way through levels and suss out how best to approach them before murdering your square with wild abandon. I still found myself exhausted and out of breath upon finally making it through to the end, but it’s a testament to Ink’s design that it never felt like as if that end was beyond my ability, no matter how many dozens of times I might die to the same bloody turret. Or spiked wall. Or bottomless pit of my existential despair.
It probably helped that I was able to complete Ink in just over a very speedy hour, but this brevity didn’t come at the price of substance. Ink might be short (by many people’s judgement, at least), but it feels very full, lasting just long enough to exhaust its clever hook without diluting it with filler. It’s all remarkably well considered, with even the levels that are near mirror images of one another feeling essential and just as creative as their original counterpart.
Though it might have taken me too long to recognize Ink as its own game, it was a distinction worth making as Zack Bell’s mess obsessed creation is among the most enjoyable platformers I’ve played in quite some time. It’s as charming as it is infuriating, but it never dangles the carrot too far out of reach that you lose sight of it completely. Though it is likely hard to lose sight of a metaphorical carrot covered in as many different colors of florescent paint as this one surely is.

Sparkle's primary draw is its immersion. Graphically it is a simple but gorgeous aquatic landscape, accompanied by a lush ambient electronica track, which changes as the levels change. It offers some incentive to finish the level quickly as the tracks, as ambient music is apt to do, can become somewhat repetitive and tedious. Movement and speed controls via mouse/keyboard are basic and intuitive, though game controller support would have been appreciated. Gameplay itself is very much a rinse and repeat, but the boss levels are fun, and species customization is fun. Not a true RPG style via a menu, but there are unique strengths and weaknesses based on your chosen diet. And there is so much potential from a multi-player standpoint. To my knowledge the only multi-player option is race-based, but imagine a co-op vs computer opponents or the time-tested deathmatch. If Forever Entertainment chose to, they could pump in a few more updates and expand the look and feel of biomes, additional music tracks, and co-op options which could really add to the shelf life of a game like this.
Overall, I was very pleased. Fun game to chill out to (dark room, headphones, you get the picture), minimal learning curve, immersive environment, and a solid value at $5 (I got mine from Steam)

This is a complete remake of the decade-old legendary Chinese kung fu RPG.
Despite the English translated version doesn't carry the full spirit of the game in original language, this game would definitely provide western player a great opportunity experiencing the Chinese Wuxia culture.
Unlike some disappointing AAA games where the ending involves with space magic and different cut scene color, your decision in this game does matter and will heavily affect the story line and ending.  Almost all event decisions affect the ending in some way.  The story branch out into about four different main storyline in late game.
It is rare to see RPG nowadays where I really took my time to consider what I should answer, or decide what I should do when there is an NPC event --- "which side should I help?" "how about just take this item by force?" "it would be the best if I do nothing and stay out of this?".  Decisions do MATTER in this game.
Replay value is high.  I finished my first playthrough at around 35 hours.  So just three playthough will yield more than 100 hours, and every playthough would be very different than the those before --- all of this... just cost 15 dollars!
Not to mention free DLCs with new contents and storylines (in form of mandatory updates).
I recommend this game with the current price tag ($15.29).  If this game ever gets big sale (~$10 ish), you definitely need to give it a try if you are a RPG lover.

For the RPG lover, this game offers it all.
Choice: Your choices matter. From detailed character creation to hundreds of conversations, everything has consequences.
Lore: A fascinating, believable world. Unravel its secrets, or don't, depending on your character and playstyle.
Immersion: Characters you meet stay true to their own natures and priorities rather than being props. Quests are meaningful and progress the game, avoiding fluff and filler.
Replayability: To understand the story and setting completely, expect to replay this quite a few times. This is not a chore as once you've gone down a specific path (for example, playing an assassin instead of a soldier), much of the content is fresh.
Challenge: This game can be difficult, and you will die often from poor choices and poor tactics. Combat lethality is both realistic and rewarding.

This is a very different type of RPG, and I love what it represents.
Character creation is deep and satisfying; lots of fun skills to invest in, but a real viability of non-combat, thiefy and social builds opens up repalyability quite a bit.
Combat is very dangerous, and if you don't specialize in it, avoid it at all costs (and be rewarded for doing so!). One of the biggest pitfalls that can happen is when a game gives you multiple routes to an objective, but one is more desireable than other others in xp or loot. I feel like there's an equal balance here in terms of cool opportunities for different builds to shine.
The writing is compelling without being overly verbose or esoteric. It's writing in the vein of the Witcher series:  stories about people and tangible events rather than tomes and tomes of in-game backstory and nonsensical names that you're supposed to memorize. The Qozl invaded the Aarth in the year GH16.2dt and you're a Gnoth Warrior looking to reclaim. . . yeah. None of that.
Even the map is well thought-out. Instantly warp to any major location in town or hoof it from one place to another to find secrets and events. I hate being dropped into a gargantuan town and then having to spend massive amounts of time memorizing where everything is and rattling the handles of door after door un non-interactable interactable-looking spaces just to find the few that offer something cool.
A methodical, thoughtful game, a compelling role to play (no matter which role you pick), fun mechanics, and a compelling world make this a memorable RPG for me.

Both positive and negative points for this game.
Pros:
-Huge variety of creatures to tame, which you can ride or have run around as pets with you- most creatures are tameable, and it does tell you which ones are and are not.
-The avaliable mounts look pretty awesome.
-When you get all familiars in an area you can claim rewards.
-Daily rewards that are actually helpful!
-Don't start off as a nobody; you're a well-known warrior.
-Classes are a fun challenge to learn and look cool.
-Amazing graphics.
-Mounted combat and normal combat are both features; generally you can choose which you want to do, although aerial mounted combat is a little more tricky.
-Dungeon armour is avaliable at the auction house (albeit for exorbitant prices) thanks to other players, meaning if you don't have time or can't be bothered to grind the dungeon for ages then you can buy the armour.
Cons:
-Can only create 3 characters
-Repeated disconnects from servers
-Teleportation costs (not too expensive, certainly, but if you go broke and can't afford it it can be a mild inconvenience, just means travelling on mountback for a while until you have enough money)
-Takes ages to gather resources for certain familiars, even then not a guaranteed chance of taming. (Same as most MMOs in that sense, but it can get a little infuriating when you spend several hours getting resources to craft an item and fail the taming.)
-When lag hits it hits bad and at the worst of times
-Not everything in the trailers has been implemented in the game yet, although hopefully it will be eventually.
-The leveling seems to get a bit wonky at some points, although that might just be my own inexperience not knowing about it. It doesn't make the main story impossible, just means it takes longer to get to the same level as the entities around you.
-You CANNOT do a solo route, the game forces you to interact with other players to get good armour in dungeons. (edit; you can, as a person in the comments has thankfully added on quite kindly, if you're willing to have non-heroic gear for a while.)
The graphics are excellent, cutscenes are good and overall a good game considering it's free. Very fun.

The Stanley Parable is an interesting game.
It questions the narrative set-up for the player by the narrator, and human player agency.
In it; you play as Stanley, Stanley is a pencil pusher, he does what he's told, he sits in his office room, pressing the right button on his computer at the right-time.
This is where it gets interesting; suddenly, no one at Stanley's work is around anymore, the entire building is empty. Which introduces the narrative structure set-up by the narrator (whom has a fantastic voice mind you) as he tries to battle with you the player (indirectly) about what you should do.
You can do as you're told, or you can veer off the path, see where things lead.
Ultimately; this game is fun, the biggest issue for the game however, is the fact that to get to certain choices that branch off into two or more choices; you're gonna have to go through the same prompts with the same jokes with sometimes mild variations.
Not only that, but you have to spend a lot of time on some things to achieve your aims (such as the box room)
It's a fun game; by all means, I just would recommend it during a sale however at this point.

I have played many story rich RPG games and this was certainly the most impressive.
Apart from the immense detail and a really original writing, I think what impressed me the most was how this game was designed in a way that makes you replay with another character to see the whole story. The reason you need several playthroughs is the experience points that you can gain in a single game is limited. This means you can not be an expert in every skill, you can't even master quarter of the skills that are present in the game. So your character gets to be good in only a few things and several quests and information are locked behind skill checks. When you have finished the game, talking the every npc that you can find and checking every area for quests, you will not see the half of quests that are in the game. The ending and the whole playthrough you get will be drastically different depending on the skills of your characters and your decisions. I hate replaying a game even if I liked it, but this game is my only exception because you feel as if you are playing another game with new quests, new areas, new decisions and new endings. There are several guilds(that you can join only one) in the game with several quests that feel quite different. There are also over 10 endings.
If you like oldschool RPGs, if you want your choices and actions to matter, this game will be one of your favorite RPGs, if somehow not your favorite.

What you will expect from this Final Fantasy (tl,dr; if you interested please read all, I played with the X360 version):
Pros:
- Exciting new combat system
- Lovable characters with background story
- Epic music
- Amazing and captivating story, but...
Cons:
- ...Linear and complicated (only at early)
- Minimal open world
- Short especially for a FF game
- Not the best RPG
Playtime: Story: 45+ hours (ofc with cutscenes), Full Achievements: 130-150 hours(or more based on farming-luck)
Terms you may need to know first:
Fal’cie – False gods, machines responsible for the creation and maintenance of the land where humans dwell, and indirectly govern their lives. They can turn the people into l’cie.
L’cie - humans "branded" by divine entities (mostly fal’cies) and given great physical and magical power, as well as a Focus to fulfill. If they manage to complete their Focus they will become crystal or you will become a cie’th. People are afraid of l’cies.
Cie’th – those who fail to complete their Focus in time. They are mindless monsters who attack everybody.
Cocoon – A planet which floats in the sky above the land of Gran Pulse (it’s like the Moon), the events starts here.
Gran Pulse – A planet like the Earth, and Cocoon floats in its atmosphere. It is a world of natural evolution where animals and plants can grow to tremendous sizes
the human civilization of Gran Pulse had nearly been wiped out by the War of Transgression.
The War of Transgression – It was a war fought between Cocoon and Gran Pulse between six and seven hundred years.
Purge – It is a form of social cleansing conducted by the Sanctum, the fal'Cie-run government of Cocoon, to get rid of those believed to have been "touched" by Gran Pulse.
Story/Characters:
If you new in Final Fantasy games I can recommend this one, it plays on a planet called Cocoon, where you can control 6 characters, our heroine is Lightning who was a soldier (Guardian Corps) she is on the Purge train to save her sister Serah who is caught by a fal’cie and marked as a l’cie. Serah’s boyfriend Snow travels to the Hanging Edge to fight PSICOM and the Purge in the hopes of saving her. Meanwhile Sazh the old timer pilot boards with Lightning to save his son Dajh. On the same train Vanille (who is already a l’cie), Hope and his mother are part of the group of exiles onboard the Purge train. And Fang who will appear later in the story she searches for Vanille and aims to complete her Focus. Their ways cross them to Serah who fulfill her task as a l’cie and turns into crystal while the other party members marked as l’cie. With the fatal fate on their shoulders our heroes take up the struggle against the curse, rescue Serah and Cocoon’s people from the suffering of the fal’cies… “The Battle Within Begins...”
For me this game 10/10, if I need to compare to the other FF games then 8.5/10.
If you liked this masterpiece I can recommend the XIII-2 and Lightning Returns too.
Thanks for reading!

Oh, and he was probably over 50 years old; how many video games let you play as a guy that old? Just putting that out there.
Now let's look at Nu Wang, Lo Wang's modern-day politically correct younger alternate universe self (or something like that). He's younger, as mentioned; he's needlessly handsome compared to the original; wait, so... old or ugly people are out, but let's get rid of racism at least! One out of three, eh, Flying Wild Hog? Just a thought there. Moving on: Nu Wang says his lines kind of like he's phoning them in. I'm guessing he read the script, which
have its moments -especially with manzai-esque two-person comedy exchanges between Nu Wang and his demon sidekick- but otherwise tends to disappoint, especially in its treatment of existing material, i.e. jokes and lines ripped from the chest of the original and then mangled like so many demon hearts. Or ripper hearts if we're being oldschool.
The writer at FWH was quoted as calling his work on this game "a much more clever sense of humor and wit", which is kind of stretching the truth an awful lot. Fans of the original may recall the fortune cookies, which provided a nice health boost (now a pitiful, non-max-exceeding one) and a cute little line along the lines of actual cookie fortunes: "Baseball wrong. Man with four balls cannot walk." and the like. Well, in Nu Shadow Warrior, many if not most of these make a reappearance, only they've been edited to be... less funny. Even if we assume that it is racist to use and be amused by an engrish-style speech pattern such as actual asian nation residents would likely use unless they have extensive experience speaking english with native speakers -just as we would struggle with their languages, probably in an equally amusing way, and give them a good laugh- ...well, if we've assumed that, the writing still isn't very funny.
You know when someone's telling a joke and they draw it out longer than needed, like it was written in a hurry by someone who didn't really have a knack for comedy, and it ends up being more of a statement of fact or opinion than an actual joke? That's Nu Shadow Warrior's writing in a nutshell; drawn out, inelegant, unfunny. The combat taunts and victory boasts are much the same: "Looks like today wasn't your lucky day... too bad for you!" ...Yes, it is. Those enemies were unlucky that they met you and died, and it is too bad for them. What part of this statement is funny, original or otherwise worth a voice actor's time? Maybe the writer expected the same energy that John Gault put into the original Lo Wang's lines, which might actually have saved that last one. Classic Lo Wang certainly had a more amusing laugh, which made it less grating to hear him laugh at his own jokes -when Nu Wang does it, it feels like he's just affirming the fact that no-one else will. There are places where they're all sarcastic, like, "Oh, yeah, that was a bad joke, wasn't it!" ...Well, that could work if it wasn't the norm, but sadly, it kind of is here...
Phew! All that said, there are things to like, even love about Nu Shadow Warrior. Some of the weapons are pretty fun. There's a revolver that's a joy to use, except for the fact that it constantly runs out of ammo because you can barely carry any for it and the drops contain just over a single speedloader full. A number of the guns are drawn from or inspired by the original game, such as the quad-barrel shotgun or dual SMGs... except you have to buy upgrades to turn them into their true forms. Two separate upgrades for an auto-firing quad barrel shotgun! That's 6,500 cash if I remember right, and the average box or cabinet contains maybe 10-30 cash. Sound fun? Yeah, you get the gist. And even after that, it turns out the awesome auto-fire has been swapped for one big, comparatively weaksauce all-barrel blast, which just doesn't feel as powerful or satisfying. And who puts the shotgun at slot 5 in an FPS? That's nitpicking, but there it is; they broke the natural (or at least classic) order of guns.
Then there's the katana. It is everything you could ever wish for a katana to be, unless perhaps you want it to be a pony or something, in which case, just get a pony instead. It has neat moves, it has utility, it has potential, it has upgrades, and if you're bold enough you can more or less fight most enemies using nothing else. I enjoyed that a lot, and it does the team credit to see a melee weapon treated so lovingly in an FPS. It's almost worth recommending the game just for this.
The story is adequate. You could call it moving, in places, but I hesitate to use that term as I don't like assigning that kind of credit to a story which mostly just dumps a bunch of tragedy on you, piecemeal-style, until you have the whole sad picture. You're barely even interacting with the events of the story; Nu Wang himself is really just running around hacking and blasting things and occasionally people to pieces for various bad reasons. Because he was ordered to, because they're shooting at him, because they're invading his dimension... and then he sort of goes right off the deep end and
in favor of... er... plothole, anyone? Nu Wang burns his bridges quite spectacularly at one point, and the best motivation I can come up with for
is that he either expects his allies to betray him because he suspects they believe he will betray them -paranoia cycle, anyone?- or that his ego couldn't handle being mocked briefly by two women. So we're not sexist any more, eh, FWH? 'Course not, just that
.
The development team doesn't seem to have been very large, which probably explains why a lot of the environments feel very samey; everywhere you go, the same boxes, cabinets and so forth. It's not that there's no variety; between levels and sometimes within a level, there'll be dramatic changes of scenery, even if the levels themselves tend to be fairly linear, though the paths get a little pretzel-shapes in places. Sometimes you'll end up revisiting the same place (not counting if you get lost or can't figure out where to go), which feels a bit annoying, but overall they did a very good job for a team their size, I suspect.
The combat and enemies are both pretty good. It feels less like Shadow Warrior and more like Serious Sam, to be honest, but that's not really a bad thing; different, but not bad. The dodging system is pretty simple, though sprinting requires you to dodge forward first, which can be awkward; especially as you don't seem to be able to jump while sprinting or dodging, so when you're at a ledge facing a tricky jump, you'd better hope the old "get a running start" reflexes don't kick in, or it's a quick messy date with the pavement. Also Nu Wang can't swim.
A pretty good game all in all, but the flavor line writing, and Nu Wang's delivery of them, just bring it down for me.

Okay so, Blockstorm Review!
Basically this is a multiplayer only, based on minecraft, first person shooter, indie game!
With a bunch of game modes, and alot of skins, lets check this game out.
GAMEPLAY:
Simple gameplay, First Person Shooter, if youve played one you know how it is, but you can also place blocks and destroy blocks of others and the map`s generated blocks as well, this allows you to play tactically, and can also help you to get to place you couldnt before. Secondly, the class setup, basically you have a lot of choices to choose, you can choose a primary and secondary weapon, and equipment, the better weapons you choose (m240, RPG, MAC 10) the heavier that class will be and the heavier = you run slowly, now if you just choose a shotgun, grenade, pistol, youll run really fast and thats what the class system`s consequence really is, there are no levels required to unlock anything in this game. Now, I do have a few problems with this game, first of all there is too much grenade spam and without a grenade indicator it becomes very hard to be aware of grenades, which is really frustrating. Another thing, is the knifing, knifing is just like COD, and it is not clear when you have hit the enemy with a knife or when you have not, and is way too overpowered, shotguns as well, are overpowered. There are alot of game modes: CTF, DM, TDM are the basic, Castle battle (where you destroy the enemy`s loot), Hunt (where you hunt for stuff hidden in these canisters and whoever reaches the target first wins), and Assault which is like Block N Load.
Okay, so I feel like making a different section for the rest.
Skins and Creation of skins:
Okay so basically this game has a steam workshop where you can go subscribe and get free skins usable in this game, forexample I used the M4A1 Hyperbeast from CS:GO, in this game and the M4A4 Assiimov which was also from CS:GO, these skins I got from the workshop that other people made, theres 17,000 + skins in this game, so for those skins only are worth the whole game. There is also the AWP hyperbeast, which I used, I even got the butterfly knife in this game, from CS:GO. So yeah, lots of skins, but there isnt just custom equipment but there are skins for your soldier as well, the default skins, and the ones you can download for free, I became Gordron Freeman, also you can also have custom skins for your Mecha warrior, you can make your Mech warrior like Big Daddy. Whats even more cool, is that you can also make your custom skins in game, yes it allows you to do that, but im not so good at that so yea.
THE VERDICT:
This game had me just on skins, but its not a bad multiplayer game, and ontop of all this, if you are in the weekly top 10 for one of the game modes, the developers will give you other free games, so what are you waiting for!?

Hollow knight is an indie, 2D-action platformer that is made in the style of Metroidvania by Team Cherry. This game allows the player to explore a vast setting with memorable characters, beautiful art styles, challenging bosses, secrets and unlockables to keep anyone entertained for hours. Whether you prefer to take it slow and explore the ridiculously massive Hollownest, grind it out on a huge variety of monsters, tackle difficult platforming,  take time to learn about the deep lore or try your hand at challenging tough bosses, there is something for everyone. 
 
Hollowknight, at first glance, comes off as highly simplistic, but the charm of the game is how much it can accomplish with such a minimalist approach. The game starts the player off without knowing anything. All that the player is given is a seemingly "hollow" character and the basic abilities to move, jump and attack. However as the game goes on, new mechanics are constantly introduced to keep the game interesting while keeping it manageable as not to overwhelm some players. It introduces game mechanics such as "nail jumping" which requires the player to attack downwards on an enemy or spikes to get a bit more airtime, and augments the character with new abilities such as dashing and double jumping. The game is set up in a way that encourages the player to go at their own pace as there is no penalty for taking it slow. Truly the most charming aspect of Hollowknight is the complexity found within the simplicity. The entire game is animated using a minimalist hand-drawn art style that gives almost everything a charming, casual vibe but also encompasses the intimidating might of the bosses and the creepy aura of the deep nest and the abyss maps. This is Hollowknights way of saying that games do not need amazing hyper realistic graphics to be absolutely stunning and acts as a statement to all the Triple-A games that oversaturate the market and the graphics make half the game. 
 
Each section of the Hollownest is themed in a completely different way ranging from caverns filled with crystals to lush green gardens, from eerie abandoned tramways to a kingdom of "tears". All the enemies are also themed as such and each one features a unique attack pattern that ranges from just charging blindly at the player to sophisticated swordplay, meaning the player has to learn how to combat with each one in their own unique way, which keeps combat exciting throughout the entire game. Hollowknight presents combat in a way that seems simple by itself yet when coupled with the vast ways to defeat the array of enemies and bosses, the simple controls that even a monkey can learn suddenly become challenging yet, not impossible as all it requires is to learn the enemy and a little bit of timing to overcome obstacles. The emphasis on timing means that its not just excessive button mashing like in some other games and when the player dies or messes up it feels like the players own fault instead of the game's. Due to the simple combat system, the chance of encountering a bug or glitch unintentionally is almost non-existent so the player feels responsible for their own misplays. 
 
The sheer amount of content that the player gets for a measly $18 (NZD) can rival that of a $50 game, with endless areas to explore, upgrades to unlock, side quests to complete and items to collect, of which many are stumbled upon by pure chance. The game has been out for more than half a year but players are still finding Easter eggs and secrets hidden deep within the game. Not to mention the lore scattered throughout the game as dialogue from NPCs, scripts from monoliths and clues in the landscape for the player to unravel the deepest secrets of the Hollownest kingdom's creation and downfall. Hollowknight works off the idea that the best way to tell a story is to not "tell" it at all. The exploration approach on the game allows each and every player to complete the game in an almost completely different order to others, beating different bosses first, finding different upgrades at different times or even uncovering entire areas in differing orders. The game encourages the player to constantly go back when a new upgrade is unlocked such as double jump in order to reach new areas that were previously unreachable. That means that every area in the game is important and none are made obsolete after fulfilling a single purpose. 
 
Hollow knight draws inspiration from many timeless classics such as having a similar theme to Darksouls and a platforming experience similar to super meat boy to give veteran gamers a familiar feel while still making everything its own original creation. The contrast within the simplicity and depth of the game makes it playable to anyone but still offers top quality entertainment. It takes very basic aspects of video games and applies them so well that it is unlike any other game on the market. Being such a simple game in many aspects yet, providing such depth and being so well crafted just show cases the effort and dedication put in by Team Cherry that is lacking so much in todays "high budget, cash grab, drool over the graphics" video game market. It is easy to tell that this game was crafted as an art as opposed to a way for corporations to make big bucks and sets an example for how games should be made. 
 
These reasons and many more are why Hollowknight has found its way into the hearts of many and has won many awards such as #8 best pc game 2017, game informer gold and the editors choice award despite being an indie game. I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to almost anyone who is willing to try.

This is currently my favorite metroidvania game, surpassing Super Metroid and CSotN.
The massive map is simply a joy to explore aesthetically and mechanically.  The controls are precise, fluid and polished.
Backtracking doesn't become a chore because you can travel quickly through the interlinking pathways, and there are also teleport mechanics that can speed things up when necessary.  There is a lot to collect including 36 charms that can be equiped to limited slots that grant new abililities and attributes that can result in interesting combinatons.  Boss challenge is sufficent without over-doing it, with much harder optional versions of many bosses.
A couple minor complaints.  The death mechanic can go unexplained and can throw you for a bit of a loop the first time you die if you're an intermediate/high-skilled platform gamer.  That is to say, you can play for 4-5 hours collecting lots of currency, only to die for the first time, lose all your currency and the game auto-saves  upon death.
You have no access to previous saves. Once you figure out you can get your currency back by carefully returning to where you died and defeating your whimpy shadow, the initial shock wears off.  You only get one chance tough, if you die before reclaiming your stuff it is gone for good. If you die on a boss it is easy to kill the shadow without activating the boss fight. You are then free to die on the boss again, reclaim your stuff, rinse and repeat.
There is a bank a couple zones into the game that can safeguard your deposited  money.  I never used it because it was a little out of the way, maybe it should have been closer to the starting town. It was always quicker just to return to the shadow than trekking to the bank and back.
Unfortunately, being a diligent explorer can have diminishing results in the sense that it becomes trivially easy to afford every shop item in the game, at least in the first play-through. The only consumable shop item to stock up on is rotten  eggs...which make it easier to fight your shadow and get your currency back.  By the time I found that shop I already had more currency and eggs than I would ever need.   There are speedrun challenges where currency demand is probably a lot tighter. The game also auto-saves upon item purchase, so it is hypothetically possible to buy the wrong thing and need to go grinding for a bit.

If you liked Diablo back in the day and don't feel like waiting for Diablo III, then this is the "tide-me-over" title. Sparkle 2: Evo is a top-down game based on the flash game known as
.
In flOw, you play as a serpentine creature whose sole purpose is to eat other creatures.
As you descend, the enemies gain more hitpoints and become harder to kill.
At the bottom is a powerful creature that is fast and dangerous that you have to defeat.
Once you beat the final boss, the game resets and then control a jellyfish-like creature.
You then have to repeat the process with your previous creature now serving as the final boss.
Once you beat the final boss again, the game resets with the original serpentine creature.
The game got so popular that a port was developed and released for all PlayStation platforms.
Now that you know what flOw is, let's get to the summary of Sparkle 2 Evo.
This game is literally a stylized PC version of flOw.
You play as the aforementioned serpentine creature known as a Sparkle.
Along with the traditional mechanics found in flOw, you also get to choose between three different variants based on what you consume throughout each zone.
Each variant has a special ability that changes the gameplay and difficulty.
You'll know which one the Sparkle will become based on the colored trail it leaves as it swims.
The transformation happens automatically upon filling up your Experience Bar.
If you eat anything that glows red, you will become a Carnivore.
The Carnivore is fast and maneuverable, but can be hard to control sometimes.
Its special ability is Lunge, which shoots the Sparkle forward extremely fast.
If you eat anything that glows green, you will become a Herbivore.
The Herbivore is bulky and tough but is slow and cannot turn that well.
Its special ability is Inhale, which automatically collects any food within range of its mouth.
If you eat anything that glows blue, you will become an Omnivore.
The Omnivore is a jack-of-all-trades since it has the strengths and weaknesses of both sides.
Its special ability is Screech, which makes all animals run away from you for a short time.
You would think that since it's based on such a popular game with such a simple design and mechanics, there shouldn't be any problems with this game right? (ha ha ha, WRONG!)
For one thing, the Sparkle variants all move and turn at the same speed.
That means it doesn't matter which type you are since only the special abilities are different.
In addition, it only takes one hit from ANY predator to force you back up one level.
The second problem is that the camera is in a fixed position that spins around the Sparkle.
Imagine trying to walk while constantly looking at your feet and bobbing your head in a circle.
In other words, your field of view is hindered by the camera's motion since you won't be able to see what's in front of you until the camera spins around to reveal what's in front of you.
There are other problems as well, but I have to keep my reviews within a tolerable length.
Aside from the problems, this is a very amazing game.
The levels are surreal, the music is lovely, and the graphics look fantastic.
However, I'll be honest, the ending was a bit disappointing considering flOw had a final boss.
Regardless, it still achieved the same goal as flOw did, which is immersive relaxation.
Abosultely a fun game and worth the price!

Liking it a lot. While at its heart it's basically Civ 5, the significant deviations it's made as a system and in game design are all encouraging signs to me.
For those who are curious, don't get this game (yet) if:
- You're expecting a spiritual successor to Alpha Centauri. It's not. Not even close.
- You are driven more by the fluff than the strategic aspect of the genre. It's quite lacking in that too.
- You like the individuality of factions. It's not nearly as pronounced here even compared to Civ 5 - no unique buildings or units.
- You didn't like Civ 5. Because it's really similar.
If you're looking for a new 4X to try out anyway, though, perhaps Endless Legend might be something to try. Just beware that the combat/unit variety in it is kinda bland, but it seems to have the fluff down a lot more.
That aside, I see it as an encouraging iteration on Civ 5, which I did enjoy. Here are some notes.
+ Quests. Are such an awesome improvement. Gives you purpose when you're just sandboxing away at your kingdom before your victory condition. Helps newer players have some direction on what they should be doing in the way that the reactionary adviser never will. The first real sign I saw of making the game more newbie-friendly without it being tacked on like a tutorial
+ Health over Happiness. Speaking of newbie-friendly, this much-less-punishing shift makes people's first games much smoother. In Civ 5, even getting to -1 Happiness dunked you into -75% food growth, which was very punishing for when you tried to expand. Furthermore, getting past -10 Happiness made your combat units worse, made you unable to expand and hurt your production. Primary causes of unhappiness? Expanding and capturing enemy cities. It was a negative feedback loop that punished you in spades for going too far once (the Diplomacy AI doesn't help here). Far less punishing in Beyond Earth - unhealthiness dunks Culture/Science, and your hammers/expansions only suffer once you get to -20. This makes it much easier to go about expanding or conquering, and doesn't set you on a slippery slope to failure once you mess up once.
+ Military development being independent of particular technologies or virtues in the way of the affinity system. 'Being militarily-focused' is no longer a thing that makes you a special snowflake now that the aliens are much stronger and threatening than barbarians were in Civ 5, and I think it improves the game quite a bit, especially for players who don't see the need to go out and conquer from the get go.
+ Aliens are more interesting than the barbarians. This is aided by some of the early affinity benefits which change how they interact with your Explorers and expose the concept that they have an aggression level.
+ Orbital layer - the ability to project 'soft power' from your cities - is a nice addition, though right now it seems more like icing than anything substantial that's crucial to winning the game. But I haven't played the Slavs yet, so I can't call it very early. Rocktopus is a hilarious unit concept placed next to orbital death satellites.
= Tile improvements are a lot more varied now and so it's a lot more fun if you micro your workers. Sadly, sometimes you have to, because worker automation is a lot less good when the number of choices are higher and the algorithm is still pretty naive. Watch out for your automated workers turning everything into Terrascapes after you get Terraforming (they have maintenance equal to -six- buildings -per tile-), because they totally will.
= Tech tree is much more streamlined and feels better to explore around, kind of like FFX Sphere Grid. However, the interface for it is supremely cluttered and you can get easily bewildered figuring out what to do. Some of the techs are also unfortunately placed, resulting in drastic imbalances like how Generators are so much better than Farms as improvements (and subsequently, how playing a broad civ optimally is much easier than playing a tall civ)
= Trade routes are a very potent mechanic now, which is pretty cool in a lot of ways, but managing them is an absolute pain if you aren't playing tall.
= Spies are incredibly satisfying, very powerful (especially if you're the ARC) and incredibly non-interactive. They provide free power to the players in a way that you'll be significantly behind if you don't get on them early. Because they betray zero sum (everything you steal is conjured, not stolen - so you can get Techs the other player doesn't even have or units the other player can't even make) and have very little risk for the reward they're pretty overpowered right now.
- The starting game choice is cool in that you get to customize little things, but stop mattering after the start. This, sadly, includes the faction choice itself, which is much less impactful and has a lot less fluff. No unique units, no unique buildings, and the faction benefits are really modest and target high-level strategies. On one hand, this takes away a lot of the railroading implicit in the previous Civ games, on the other hand it makes it much harder to get invested into a particular faction (or, indeed, make more factions that are actually interesting).
- City-states are pretty bland right now. They give two quests, which is probably comparable to Civ 5, but is much more underwhelming compared to all the other quests that now exist for this game.
- Wonders are still interesting, though they no longer have global effects as often (and some quests for your normal city buildings sometime also confer global effects, making wonders even less special). Really wish they had cinematics though. But that's mostly a wish back from Alpha Centauri. It certainly seems that Beyond Earth had a lot less production value put into the little fluff things given how minimalistic the city interface is and how all the buildings lack pictures beyond icons. Which brings me to more below...
- Victory conditions are really bland right now. I guess it's better to not have a cultural victory condition than to have a lackluster one like Civ 5 base's, but right now victory mostly either involves being really good at production/hammers/gears, or being really good at punching people's face in. Nothing for the economy and culture buffs yet. Might have to wait for expansions for that.
-- And the most tragic of all, actually winning is also really bland right now. No cinematic for winning. No giant scoreboard of irrelevant ranks and numbers that you can read to derive amusement (Civ 5 base still had these I think, though it didn't have time breakdowns/graphs at first). Just an audiobyte and going back to the menu (or playing more, that's of course always there).
Definitely a promising game at launch, I'm looking forward to seeing the iterations.

Well, it is, as advertised - an RPG in which one's choices heavily impact the way things play out, with turn-based tactical combat, lots of text etc. I finished the game
Amazing, right? Yes, except that it was a royal pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to reach the end, because the damn skill checks are tighter than a virgin's ♥♥♥♥♥. Having messed up a playthrough (because I missed a few side quests, thus missed out on skill points), I started the same thing over again, making sure I nailed every single encounter and every quest I could actually complete with my loremaster. Most of the time, I chose what skill to level by starting a convo, trying to see if I can get it to play out as I wanted to, then reloading and applying a skill point where it was needed and trying again. This is how you beat the game, because you need the damn skill points from everything. If you don't want to have multiple playthroughs of the same and actually get it right eventually, save-scumming is how it's done.
I was also very surprised with how short the game is. With its unmemorable exposition, it almost feels like it only starts when you're actually halfway into it and then it just abruptly ends, once you've leveled up the needed skills and

All in all, disappointing, but still good enough to warrant a playthrough. Get it on a discount and give it a chance.

It's got a lot of good points ... with some work on card dynamics and PVP balancing I'd change my recommendation and overlook the poor splash screens and menus. The semi-scripted AI games and tutorials were VERY enjoyable, having been balanced in designed to provide a reasonable experience. However, PVP play is a different story.
As it is, PVP strategy is mechanically dictated. To win, you must build a deck that exploites -unlimited- (no limit on how many you have) cards enhanced by force multipliers and extermination cards. There are minor variations amongst factions, but they don't alter the basic formula. Once you've got the deck, you just repeat the pattern of play they enable. If the decks are evenly matched winning or losing is mostly a matter of who screws up the formula. Robots will probably enjoy it, I don't.
I'd suggest limiting  the -Unlimited- class of cards (drastically). Force multiplier cards should be limited to one per turn and should affect only a single targeted card. No more every allied card in play gets +3. And no more every enemy card in play dies. These simple changes might add some subtlty to game play and reward strategic thinking rather than encouraging systemized, predictable, turns.
I found the PVP matching system inadequate ... Clicking the -Only match me with other new players- button is a bad joke. I was consistantly matched with advanced players using sophisticated decks.
All in All I think you can find Better CCG games to spend time with.

A great game with obvious flaws.
The game is a huge departure from Civ V or Civilizations in general. Instead of a leader from History you play the face of future conglomerate of countries. This makes the leaders lose a bit of their charm, but it fits better with the overall theme of the game.
The barbarians of this game are varying aliens. You can gain affinities that will allow you to live in harmony with them or completely obliterate them. There's nothing like becoming one with nature and cranking out your own units of aliens to destroy your enemies.
There are a few changes that I'd like to mention.
1) Happiness is replaced with health. While having low health is bad, you can live with it until you have rating of -10, then things start to get worse. This is a more forgiving system than in Civ V.
2) Favors can be traded for when making deals with other players. If a rival doesn't have anything of value, they can trade you an IOU in the form of a favor. Gain enough favors and you can force them to do your bidding. ie, force them into a war they otherwise wouldn't be a part of.
3) Affinities. Affinities are your alignment and will direct the entire evolution of your civilization. Will you be harmonious or will you strife for supremacy? As you level up in an affinity you will unlock certain benefits and your troops will evolve down one of three paths. It adds variety to a sparse list of units.
4) The quest system is a great addition that not only teaches you the game and points you in the direction that you need to go, but also makes you feel like the decisions you make are important to your own civilization's survival.
Cons
1) Unit variety seems at first pretty small with each faction getting one unique unit and each base unit type having one of three directions they can "evolve" into.
2) While the factions are a unique twist, there is a bit of charm lost when playing against "faceless" competitors. There will never be anything as cool as nuking someone as Ghandi.
Pros
1) Absolutely gorgeous game. This is more than just a reskin of Civ V.
2) Streamlined interface. Fitting with the theme of this game the interface is very streamlined and is very intuitive.
3) This game makes me really feel like I'm in complete control of the future of my civilization. The choices you have to make in quests, the way you shape your future all weighs heavy. It's a much darker tone than other Civ games, there is an overwhelming sense of urgency in that the future rests on your shoulders and that at times you almost feel hopeless that your civilization will fall.
Final Thoughts
Overall this is a big departure from Civ V. Purists may not like all the changes, but as a season Civ player I welcome them. If you're new to the franchise it's a good place to start. While others would recommend Civ V as a starting point, I say aim for the stars and give this one a try.
If you're still on the fence, there's even a demo!

Having being very familiar with the PS3 version of FINAL FANTASY XIII, I feel pretty confident to write this review for the Steam version, thus why my playtime may not seem that high.(And judging by some of your comments, I am aware that there are some graphical issues currently surrounding the port)
FINAL FANTASY XIII is not a bad game. Honestly, it’s not. Not as bad as everyone says anyway.
As far as story goes, it’s pretty much the same old Final Fantasy formula. A group of unsuspecting heroes must travel to the farthest reaches of the world in order to destroy an ancient evil which hangs the very fate of the world in the balance. However, FINAL FANTASY XIII (referred to as FF XIII from now on) has probably one of the most convoluted narratives I have ever come across, which needed three games in order to straighten out (and even then they didn’t do all that great a job.) FF XIII is an epic adventure, and is successful in managing to make its self interesting and is sure to hook your attention for the 40-50 hours you will be spending there. However, the game does take a while to get off. Things start to get interesting around hours 10-20, where the pacing begins to move the game more steadily. The story is told from the perspectives of our new playable heroes; Lighting, Snow, Hope, Sazh, Fang and Vanille. These characters have been subject to a lot of criticism, which is understandable because most of them are extremely unlikable and far too whacky for their own good. They fit well in to the story however, and that’s probably the only thing that makes them bearable.
The gameplay is probably one of the better aspects of the game, as the new Paradigm System is a huge improvement on previous Final Fantasy battle systems. It allows complete customisation of the battle field and characters, as the new level-up system allows you to level up certain aspects of your characters.
As far as a Final Fantasy game goes, this really does break the chain and dares to be different. As the first FF game to grace the 7th console generation, it tried to be something new and I think it succeeded in doing so. It is a very enjoyable game, despite its many flaws – and is easily the best game in the FINAL FANTASY XIII trilogy. It’s whacky, it’s new and it’s different. But sadly, I think it can only be enjoyed fully by a fan of the series. If you are looking to join the Final Fantasy universe, do not start with this one. Try out FINAL FANTASY VII, and see how you feel from there.
All in all, FINAL FANTASY XIII does not deserve the criticism it gets. It’s not the best Final Fantasy, nor is it the worst.
If you decide to give this game a bash, then you DON’T need to play FINAL FANTASY XIII-2 and Lighting Returns to get the full story. They essentially tarnish the narrative in FF XIII, so only get in to the trilogy if you are ready for a commitment.
+ Great battle system, one of the best that the series has to offer
+ Story is told in an interesting way. Characters interact well with each other and the narrative
+ Level up system
- Convoluted narrative. Made worse by unnecessary sequels
- Poor pacing. Game takes  a while to kick off
- Bad port
- Over powered bosses. What else did you expect? It’s Final Fantasy

Note: This is a 2016 "After having played Shadow Warrior 2" review, specifically for people who, like myself, are now curious about the first one.
Sometime last year, I tried the demo for Shadow Warrior 2013, and wasn't terribly impressed. However,  I picked up Shadow Warrior 2 just a couple of days before release on impulse (price was low), and ended up thoroughly enjoying it (currently on my third playthrough there). So, my interest in the prequel (for story reasons) piqued, I did some digging around online, and found some folks (specifically the "professional" review sites) bemoaning part 2's general inferiority next to this one. Convinced I missed something, I went ahead and grabbed it.
Having now finished the campaign, my thoughts are:
1) This game has a MUCH better story and atmosphere. A surprising highlight, given Shadow Warrior's legacy in general. The environments can be gorgeous as well, with some areas bringing a similar sense of wonder that I felt exploring Na'Pali back in Unreal 1.
2) The level design is...not the greatest. The lack of a map- coupled with some levels devolving into pixel hunts for a key in the middle of a bloom-infested map- made some stages a downright chore. Visually they all look fantastic, but they can be dull to play in.
3) Mechanics are different. If you're coming from Shadow Warrior 2, this will seem downright slow in comparrision. Melee is also comparitively clunky. HOWEVER: Guns seem a  bit more useful in this one, and while the sword fighting isnt as much fun or as smooth as in part 2, it has a much more 'grounded' feel. As in, Shadow Warrior 2 turns you into an anime' style god of war, where as over here it plays a bit more methodically. It's fun for what it is, but it WILL take some getting used to.
4) Enemy types are where this game gets a definate nod. Each foe is distinct, with some being especially menacing no matter how many times you fight them. You are forced to prioritize your targets, as some of them can be downright game changers. Enemy numbers per battle are also pretty high.
Overall, mechanically I felt like the sequel was more fun, but this one is definately worth a grab for its story and visuals. The tone is surprisingly serious for most of the way, not nearly as tongue in cheek as I was expecting (and certianly not as much as Classic or part 2), and feels suitably epic.

Overall, I thought this was a good game. However, it does have some flaws.
Most of the time I find it enjoyable, but after a while you start to notice a trend.
1. Start level
2. Jump in place while trying to figure out what everything is
3. Die becuase of something you couldn't see yet
4. Play Level
Usually you'll die once per level to something currently invisible. Sometimes things will happen that you could only learn through dying. For example, the platform you're on crushes you into the celing after killing an enemy. It won't move unless you kill the enemy, and you (probably) won't react fast enough to avoid it.
Another problem I have is with the sides of the screen. If you leave anywhere of the screen, you die. This isn't a problem until levels where you need to bounce on an enemy near the edge of the screen while a missle is coming at you. Trying to dodge combined with your momentum make it easy to slide of the screen, starting the level over again.
The last problem I have is with the bosses. The first boss is a pushover, the second one is easy after you figure out what to do, and the third one is much harder. The bosses themselves are decently fun, but none of them use the games core mechanic. In none of the fights does inking the walls matter. You'll already be jumping to avoid their attacks, causing ink to spray everywhere. Plus the bosses themselves ink the ground, so threre's no need to think about what's around you.
All in all I did enjoy the game despite it's flaws, just some things to consider.

Black Flag was the first game purchased from the AC Series by me. Although I watched a lot of You Tube Videos to learn strategy use of the controls and gameplay for the mouse and keyboard  player, it was worth it. This game kept me spellbound. It is full of action and adventure, justice and revenge, educational and historical references, love and romance, happiness and extremely sad at times and much more. I found myself drawn into the story so much so that I never relized how much time I spent playing. I only wish the writers would have prolonged the story's ending, although it still ended well. I highly recommend this game especially for beginners.

Intro/plot
I wouldn't call it a marvel, but this game was an interesting experiment. It's so damn old and obscure finding anything on it is difficult. The plot is cheesy but fresh. Rather than focusing on fighting the antagonists directly (the aliens) earth finds evidence that they will be returning in one year to fire a cannon Looney Toons martian style to destroy our planet. You play as the leader of one of the two massive corporate arms dealers specializing in robots, Red Star (who focus on conventional firearms like missiles and machine guns) and Terraflux (who use experimental and odd parts). These two are competeing to see who can produce the better weapons to defend earth and more over who gets that delicious government contract to do so.
Gameplay
The gameplay is like a mix between puzzle and some old antiquated kind of RTS. Each unit is a combination of two parts, the Chassis (which controls movement) and the Weapon (which determines how the unit fights). There is no resource gathering, rather you have a set amount of resource to build robo troops and when they are destroyed you get a FULL refund on them. You only have one building, the base where you build all your robots, if the base suffers a certain amount of damage it explodes destroying all nearby enemies (except under special circumstances). It's anything but easy though, as I've often had difficulty getting past the second level. On top of this you have a certain amount of total funding inbetween missions your corporation has to spend on researching booster mods for your robots and secret technologies. The amount of funding you get is determined by your preformance in the mission (robots lost, time spent, base health, etc.). Controls are garbage, and this isn't a problem with compatibility they always sucked but that just comes down to the games age. It's still playable but I wouldn't cite this as an old paragon of late 90's games. However, If you can get around the lack of control groups and quick select you will find a very challenging game that will keep you frustrated/busy for hours. Many of the missions do not have a simple "kill the enemy" objective, and if they do it will be behind a unique circumstance. The two factions have completely different play styles and each has unique campaign missions.
Graphics
I've heard this was actually one of the first 3d games. As in TRUE 3d, you can move the camera all over the place. Infact in some versions of the game while paused the camera would automatically sweep the battlefield which was irritating because whatever wonky angle it happened to be at when you unpaused stayed, thankfully this was removed. I can't remember all the camera controls off hand, I think home might be the reset key though. The textures were very good for it's time, if you get nostalgic over those old doom graphics there might be something for you here. On a final note this game is VERY dark at times, which plays into it's creepy atmosphere.
Music
Speaking of creepy, say hello to audio nightmare fuel. I'm not even sure I'd say this game has a soundtrack, yeah there's some techno in there, but for the most part the music consists of these disturbing noises: a metal door slamming shut in the distance, some alien skittering sound, and alot of deep space noises and humming in an otherwise erie silence. Really sets a serious mood. It's in stark contrast to the ludicrous plot like how Red Alert's plot was so juxtaposed to Hell March. Too bad the steam version doesn't have it because, as far as I can tell, 'moving the audio files was too difficult,' but oh well, at least I'm no longer scared after playing this game for more than 5 minutes. You can get the audio back (I'm told) if you put in a disk copy of the game that has the music on it but honestly this is fraudulant buisness.
Compatibility
Yeah, it sucks, the game breaks if you alt tab, but at least it runs on Windows 10, so that's something. I wish there were more people that knew about this and who would work on it but I haven't even been able to find a fan forum on it. It doesn't help that the game is originally German.
In Conclusion
Buy something else if you want a good old RTS that will easy you into good game play. This game feels sad and lonely right now, there are several other old games like Transport Tycoon deluxe, Seven Kingdoms: Ancient Adversaries, and Red alert which have been refounded as Freeware projects by fans but this game remains untouched. So barring further updates, buy this game if you want a masochistic real time puzzle game that is marking down every error in every level you beat.
One last thing
Steam seems to have a bug with this game where it thinks the launcher is the game itself so what happens is, the launcher opens, you use it to open the game and then the launcher closes so steam doesn't realize your playing. It's a minor thing but that's why most people only have "0.1 hours played".

Tacoma, like its spiritual predecessor Gone Home, is a game all about exploration and environmental storytelling. I'm the type of person who spends hours upon hours in games like Deus Ex or Dishonored snooping around people's apartments, reading notes and emails, talking to everyone and finding out more about the world. Tacoma is basically an entire game of just that, and I absolutely loved it.
When I first heard about the augmented-reality playback concept, it seemed a bit contrived, and while I still feel that, I think it's interesting enough as a concept to overlook. The old method of having audiologs scattered throughout the world (which is also a contrivance of its own) works, but the AR stuff adds an interesting new dimension to it, making it feel more like immersive theater.
As for the story itself, I really enjoyed it. The characters were unique and interesting (and the voice acting was universally fantastic), and the plot and especially world building were fascinating. It's more of a "soft dystopia" that feels like a fairly realistic projection of where society might be in 60 years.
If you enjoyed Gone Home, or other story-driven games like Firewatch, What Remains of Edith Finch, or Night In The Woods there's a good chance you'll enjoy this. I'd been looking forward to this for years, and at least for me personally, it absolutely lived up to the hype.

Tacoma Critique: A failure of map design.
An often understated aspect of Gone Home’s success is the design of the Greenbriar house. Not the critically lauded moment to moment rooms of the house arranged with props creating a sense of realism to the household while still holding thematic relevance to the story Fullbright hoped to tell, but the actual pacing and design of the building itself. Calling back to games like the original Resident Evils, the Greenbriar residence especially worked through the ways which your exploration of the house was limited by locked doors; requiring you to look for clues in every room, pacing out the mystery through exploration. Part of the thrill of this was the ways some clues would recontextualize earlier rooms and create moments of backtracking as you realized there was a set of secret passages hidden right behind the parents’ bedroom.
Rather than simply exploring every room one at a time until you felt like you understood the story, Fullbright smartly led the players down a carefully planned pathway, using lighting cues and locked doors to effectively pace the mystery. Although the route most players follow from beginning to end all follow a similar path the game never feels like players are being funneled down a narrow corridor to the end. Similar to how the Spencer Mansion in Resident Evil technically has one specific correct route through it, the locked doors and interconnected pathways through the building lead to an incredibly effective and memorable play-space. Even years later I can recall the layout of both buildings from memory alone.
Tacoma, Fullbright’s first release since Gone Home, maintains the moment to moment attention to detail of Gone Home that creates a lived in setting while still maintaining relevance to the plot and its themes, but unfortunately fails in the map’s pacing of these details. Instead of the tight but interconnected rooms and doors of the Greenbriar residence, the Tacoma space station feels simply like linear set of rooms placed one after another. You visit one part of the station, then leave and go to the next, as though you are just checking off boxes of what you need to see. Further emphasizing this feeling of box-checking is the narrative through-line of data collection. From a diegetic perspective your character literally is just checking off tasks. Though I like the way the data collection’s loading bar is used to incentivize players to explore; on the whole the mechanic weighs down what exploration is possible, making it feel like you have to visit each section one at a time.
Tacoma most shines through the playback mechanic. Following individual characters as they move from room to room and interact with others achieves that spider-web like pacing that Gone Home achieved. Going back and forth through time as the group members split up and travel in interconnected paths holds a similar joy to the key finding and hidden pathways of the Greenbriars. It is unfortunate then that these moments are separated into specific moments and areas, making the holistic pacing of the game feel shallow and segmented.
An often compared game to Gone Home is Sam Barlow’s “Her Story.” I won’t go too detailed in the mechanics of Her Story as Mark Brown already has an excellent dissection of them; but part of the game’s success is that technically every clue in that game is available from the start, with the only limiting factor being the player’s ignorance of what to look for. Similarly a common misguided critique of Gone Home is the possibility to reach the ‘end’ of the game in 20 seconds; but like Her Story, only players who have played the game in full will recognize the secrets hiding in plain sight.
In both Her Story and Gone Home, the endings* (her story technically doesn’t have one) don’t act as a grand reveal but instead provide thematic closure; as attentive players likely will already have solved the mysteries for themselves by the time they reach the attic in Gone Home or choose to end Her Story.
In Tacoma the ending serves literally as a tiny room explaining everything. Unlike Gone Home where events were built up throughout the story and players realize clues that were hidden in plain sight the entire time, Tacoma ends with what is essentially a room that might as well be labeled “evidence” explaining in detail what the antagonists did and why and how the ship’s crew escaped all on a set off computer monitors.
In Her Story, if a player stumbled upon the confession early on, it would still leave significant mysteries of motive to uncover. In Gone Home if a player accidentally found the attic key at the start the ending would provide a description of what happened but without an explanation of why things ended that way. However in Tacoma because each section of the ship is cordoned off until each previous one is completed, it means the ending is allowed to serve as a clear and total ending. Rather than the ambiguity of Gone Home and Her Story that incentivize players to explore for their own motivation, if a player skipped to the end of Tacoma, the final room explains away every major detail of what happened to the crew, and robs the game of the simple closure that the other game’s endings provide.
Though likely built separate due to limitations of the Unity engine; Tacoma needed a single interconnected playerspace to explore. Imagine if instead of small sets of interconnected rooms, the entire ship carried the crews’ recordings, and characters would travel past locked doors that the character would be unsure of how to pass until later, instead opting to follow a different character until stumbling upon a key. Not only would this have given the player a greater sense of self-motivation to uncover the ship’s secrets, but would alleviate the need for a single spoiler filled ending room, and create a much more memorable environment, as players would need to create a mental map of what rooms were locked and what shortcuts lead where. As it stands, Tacoma is an interesting but forgettable addition to the walking-simulator genre and a game for Fulbright and other developers to learn from.

FIrst off, I'm a long time Civ fan, and turn-based strategy may be my favourite genre. I was NOT as big of a fan of Alpha Centauri as many of the other games, but I was really excited nontheless.
First thing you'll notice when you download this game is the size - only 2-something gigabytes. That will be nice for those without a solid internet connection.
Unfortunately, that size hints at one of the biggest problems I have with this game.  There seems to be a general lack of quality artwork. Dating back to Civ 2 (my first, which I played when I was 9) I loved the animations, music, and artwork associated with technologies, wonders, and ultimately, victory. (Probably a bigger deal as a kid) Games back then made up for the inability to create kickass graphics with awesome animations, graphics, and audio as rewards along the way. Age of Empires 1 was the same way.
Nowadays, the work goes into nice 3d gameplay, but the artwork, lore, and music just aren't there. The older Civ games put tons of time into writing beautiful descriptions and background for each technology and game concept. In BE, it's mostly short blurbs. Technology has no real artwork.
Wonders are even worse, only having some vague blueprint thing and short clip of text. I have no idea what I built most of the time, and the bonuses are spotty and generally uninspiring.
Victories are similarly lacking in artwork. The glorious travel to Alpha Centauri featured in all the other Civ installments is replaced by a quote and kind of crappy artwork. This is especially sad since the authors had so much potential to work with. Some compelling storylines with clear conclusions would have also been nice.
Overall, I enjoyed it, but I'm not about to go play another game right now. I would recommend that you all buy it when it comes around for $10 this summer, then give it a play-through.
