What everyone else has said is true, both the good and the bad.  Wait for a sale, the fix-it patch, or the DLC that makes it unique, but if you must have it now, go ahead.
I found my first play through to be ho-hum, which is not at all what you want your first look at a new Civ to be like.  But with 500 hours in Civ 5, nothing surprised--at first.
20 hours in a got an appreciation of the complex tech web and began to ferret out useful options.  Unlike every other Civ game, here you can get a little of this and a little of that, providing much more of an RPG experience than ever before.
Unlike every Civ before it, you can play right to the end and not be bored silly, even if you won the game 100 turns back.
Pursuing an affinity and upgrading your units is actually fun and so, so much better than the old tech tree with its endless proliferation of miniscule unit upgrades.
End game terraforming and city building keeps you interested as you continue to build your empire.
And yes, you can continue to build your empire.  Unlike Civ 5 where 3 to 5 cities was really optimal, you can build on happily here.  Unlike the city unrest/happiness of previous versions, health can be successfully managed so that you can still explore and expand well into the end game, something that makes the last 150 turns so much less boring than in the past.  To me, this is a big plus.
The resources available are interesting and give interesting perks as you learn new techs.  There's nothing static here.  Resources are used to build your units and some city buildings.  Placement of cities is still key to victory.
No play through is ever going to be exactly like the previous one or even close.
Trade is fun, useful and varied.
So, what's not to like?  Plenty, unfortunately.
As others have pointed out, some of the design is just lazy.  Here are my top peeves:
1.  No alert as to what you just built.  What, you forgot how to keep notes?
2.  Diplomacy broken (the AI went to war with me at turn 50 and refused to make peace the rest of the game or even discuss it.)   Requests are absurd in terms of resources and energy.
3.  Bad color choices.  Aliens and 3 of Civs have a slightly different shade of green.   It is almost impossible to tell them apart.  With the entire color palette to work from, this is inexcusable.   Overall, I found the game to be dreary to look at, even built up there was nothing eye catching about my cities, no uniqueness or visual interest.
4.  No customization of your Civ.  You can't rename your Civ or your leader.  Leaders are meaningless here.
5.  Civs are meaningless.  Yes, I'm sure the devs put a lot of time into figuring out what they should be called, but they have absolutely no emotional resonance.  Who cares?  You choose your civ for the perks, and once you realize what the best one is, you're pretty much done with the civ thing.
6.  City names, the same lack of meaning or resonance.  The good part is you can rename your cities.
7.  There's nothing wonderful about wonders.  Yes, they have building projects called wonders, but it is unclear if they really have a tremendous impact on outcome.  There is no must-have wonder for a particular victory and no clear indication which are great one-only wonders and which are civ wonders that can be build once by every civ.
8.  I was underwhelmed by the orbital frufru.   So much so I didn't ever bother with it after my first game.  It's impossible to tell what benefit you're deriving from an orbital.  And I found ignoring them had no impact on the outcome.  The use and placement of them is poorly explained in the Civpedia.
9.  And speaking of the Civpedia, what a waste of a space.  The most utterly generic blather imaginable.  If you don't know how to play, this pile of uninformation is not going to help you.
10.  Silly made-up quotes.  Sorry, but again, who cares?  I turned off the voices and ignored the quotes first thing.  No great voice acting and no beautiful reminders of actual great people.
No wonder movies (boo, again) just a grey scale screen when you've build one.  Another dreary visual.  And yet another dreary visual when  you achieve victory.  These are missed chances.  We deserve an exciting mini-movie when we succeed, but get nothing.  Pfft.

This is probably one of my favorite games on Steam, and probably one of my favorite RPGs ever for the mere fact that you can go through it without engaging in much if any combat at all.  It really brings the "roleplay" back to roleplaying instead of just being a stat-crunching action-adventure game like so many "RPGs" claim to be.  That said, I'm not confident many if any Steam players will appreciate this, so understand this game caters to a very selective niche.  It's very obvious that many of the negative reviews for this game are by players who don't like the game type and don't really care for the game's quality itself.
The game also has an incredible plot web with tons of details, intricacies, and nuances that amount not only to vastly different endings, but also intermediate conclusions.  This is because of the abundance of factions you can collaborate with and conspire against, the abundance of ways to do so, and the several classes you can play which give you different styles of collaborating or conspiring.  At this point, I've played the game for over 30 hours as the praetor class, and I have to say it's amazing how you can diplomatically maneuver between the three houses jockeying for status among the empire as well as the Imperial Guards and Ordu (who are like Hunnic or Mongolian nomads).
Furthermore, there's immense story behind it with lots of twists and turns if you're into it.  I don't want to spoil the plot, but just understand that while the game comes off at first as an alternate world for the end of the Roman Empire, it eventually reveals itself to be a post-apocalyptic world lost centuries or millennia into the future.  The "gods" aren't really divine either.  They just appear to be from the limited understanding of the world's inhabitants who have gradually forgotten their fading history and now treat it like ancient lore.  To clarify:
Lastly, there is a wiki for the game with lots of information on it, so if you get stuck with certain stats at certain points, you can look them up instead of getting frustrated with wondering what it takes to get past a certain point. I know a lot of people feel like this ruins the experience, but to be honest, there's so much this game has to offer that it's a really valuable resource to get the most out of your time.  Even then, every quest detail isn't described there, so there are still things to explore.
Ultimately, if you want an authentic roleplaying experience, this is the game for you.  If you're looking for something more sensational though, steer away.

I have 676 hours logged in Civ 5. It was my first experience with the Civilization franchise and I loved the game from the beginning, though as expansions were released I came to realize just how lacking the game had been when first launched. Despite this, I would still have rated vanilla Civ 5 as a pretty good game. Naturally, when I heard about Beyond Earth I was very excited.
I expected it to be very similar to Civ 5 but more polished and with innovative new systems that would enhance the user experience. I expected to get a Civ 5 game that was worth being its own game. I have been VERY disappointed. The jump from Brave New World to Beyond Earth seems to be the same as from Vanilla Civ 5 to Gods and Kings. This is a stand-alone expansion, not a full game. I can see the potential for it to be great, but it feels unfinished. I've played for only a few hours and I don't really feel any urge to play any more.
In my first play through, I noticed the following negatives:
-Some buildings don't actually work. I built a Progenitor Garden (+20% health in that city) and it did nothing. I spent a lot of energy to build it immediately and the building didn't provide any boost to health. I haven't built all of the building and wasn't really paying attention to most of the buildings that I did build, but I can't help but wonder how many other buildings didn't actually have any effect at all and were just wasting energy.
-Units weren't cleared from the Unit Upgrade window. As I upgraded more and more units, they simply overlapped each other graphically in the window. This is not a game ending issue, but I would have expected small stuff like this to be smoothed out before release. It adds to the rushed and unfinished feel of the game.
-Baffling AI. I actually had an AI offer to renew a trade with me and when I accepted it, they refused and demanded that I offer them more to continue the trade. THEY WERE THE ONES THAT OFFERED TO RENEW THE PREVIOUS TRADE IN THE FIRST PLACE!!!! There are too many examples of bad AI in this game, but this example really epitomizes the players experience in dealing with the AI in most aspects of the game.
- Related to the previous point, general diplomacy sucks. The AI holds onto old grudes FOREVER. For example, if you tell them to not build cities near you, that has a negative effect on your relationship for the rest of the game. I know that this occured in Civ 5 too, but I really expected some better diplomacy and international relations in this game. It's been 300 years... get over it already!
-Each colony feels the same. Each sponsor gives a unique bonus, but this is not enough to change the feel of the game. Playing as any of the sponsors feels exactly the same with no appreciable difference in cultures. Each of the sponsors is obviously supposed to represent some faction that controls some large portion of Earth, but aside from the accent of the leader, there is no difference in the look or feel of the resulting colonies these sponsors produce.
-Affinities. First, I like the concept of the affinities: that each group would have a different approach to the alien world on which they landed. That said, I would have preferred to have a system in which I could choose affinity abilities like with ideologies in Brave New World except using these new affinity specific resources instead of culture.
There were some things that I did like:
-Quests. The quest system adds a new level of customizability to the game. After constructing a building, a quest decision is presented to allow the player to choose one of two effects to add to that building. For example, you might be able to add +1 culture or +1 production to all of a certain building for the rest of the game.
-Improved espionage. I like the changes to the espionage system, though this aspect of the game also suffers from feeling a bit unfinished.
-Tech Web. Rather than a linear progression through a tech tree in which you will inevitably end up with all of the technology eventually, the tech web requires more strategic planning as to which direction your colony will take.
These are really fairly minor changes for a full game. It seems as if the developers decided that because Civ 5 already exists and was a big success, that they could get away with minor improvements, change the art, and pass it off as a full game. If this was a brand new franchise, Beyond Earth might have worked as a fresh concept. Civilization fans expect more than a passable game though.
I will probably buy the inevitable expansions and/or DLC, but only when they are on sale; the improvements that are sure to come should have been included in this release and I refuse to pay top dollar for upcoming additions.
I am actually very upset that I spent $50 on this game; if I could get my money back, I would. I will keep this in mind if you somehow manage to make another new Civilization game, Firaxis. Lesson learned... don't preorder because the game won't be finished.

The author of Age of Decadance has written so much about what he's trying to do with this game that it almost defeats the purpose of a review, so I'll add on  to what he's said.
First, he succeeded in making a game with meaningful choices, with distinct routes with a lot of route locked content, but short enough to be replayable. You can be a thug, a merchant, a thief, a nerd, or various classes in between. The stat and skill system are very straightforward, just pick a couple skills you aim to use to solve your problems and go. Every point matters; every advancement gives serious tangible results. Not some lame +5% chance to whatever nonsense. A few points in crit strike turns you into a crit monster, and nearly every other skill has similar rewards. The flip side of this is also true: Every point is necessary. If you expect to use a skill to get through the game, you can't just splash a little of it like you can in most other RPGs. You need to keep investing through the game. The checks and fights only get harder. But the game itself isn't hard at all so long as you remember this fact: You will win easily if and only if you take the stat screen far more seriously than classics like Fallout 1 and 2 ever demanded.
The game is packed with situations where you simply have to walk away if you don't have the skills required. The fighter can't do much in the ruins of the ancients, and the nerd really needs to just pay his lunch money or offer to do the bad guys homework to try to navigate various skill checks.
You're not The EPIC COURIER WITH THE MCGUFFIN TO CONTROL THE ENTIRE WASTELAND HERO, you're a dude. There is no random combat, no grinding, the first three on one fight will kill you unless you spec hard for combat and have scrounged up some good stuff before hand. This game means business.
The plot is similarly muted. It's all grimy and full of scheming ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s looking for reasons to murder you and quite often doing so with no reason, but it doesn't stray into the grimderp nonsense of modern TV. This does bleed over to the quests, which offer a great many options to welch or walk away or just be a total jerk because it would be too hard for too little reward to play the quest through. In fact, while it is not entirely unrewarded, being a hero is not exactly what you're here to do and very often it has you leaving quests empty-handed when there would be no penalty to just murder and come away ahead (One quest literally had two different people with different motivations and rewards ask me to betray the quest giver in two completely different ways. If you want to be a backstabbing jerk, this is your game!). Many people lie to you and try to cheat you, and as a result it is tough to grasp all the plot with one play. You are meant to replay this game. But you absolutely must clear away the completionist habits from other RPGs; here, there are a lot of encounters you will have to forego. And similarly, you should not expect to be handing the reins of power to whatever faction you side with. You'll have a big impact on the political makeup but you aren't going to be able to genocide every enemy faction and hand the reins over to the bootlegger family like you did in Fallout 2.
The writing is generally quite strong. A dying world with tales of mysterious gods and demons that could all be wive's tales. Grifters, cheats, bitter mercenaries, but also clever, driven leaders. Each town has a couple of NPCs that really overshare their lives to strangers but serve the purpose of providing the lore of the region in a pretty clever manner, and by the end of the game, you will have seen nearly a dozen different philosophical takes on this dying world; really human ones, too. Not the usual austitic quoting of philosophy like Caesar in New Vegas. Just a downside: The cities are full of NPCs and merchants in stalls that are just props, and the only way to tell if someone has something to say is to mouse-over them, so it becomes a scavenger hunt to find stuff worth interacting with.
However, despite the strong writing, I do find the overall plot to have one really big issue to it: The protagonist is a cypher completely without attachment to the story, and the writing plays that up pretty strongly. You are given no real plot hook to put any real stakes in the story. You are only really motivated by a treasure map that literally every single character you meet save for one or two says that nothing good could EVER come from chasing this down (Not to spoil it but the one thing Age of Decadence doesn't do is waste your time or mislead you... well, narratively. You'll get lied to a lot by in game characters. But SOMETHING interesting is gonna be at the end of that rainbow.). The only other motivation comes from guild quests, which run parallel, and often perpendicular, to the factions various moves and are the closest things you tend to have to a "main quest" that unlock the next town. When you do these, as I said earlier, you have so many opportunities to betray people you met thirty minutes ago for people you met ten minutes ago, the resulting feeling is you essentially have to invent in your head your character's motivation for anything if you wish to get into the feel of the roleplay half of this game, while carefully massaging it so your character wants to do all these side quests first or else you will end up short on loot and skills. The writing has some cool characters and really fun scenarios, but it can't shake a sense of total detachment and inconsequentiality to the whole affair. Maybe this is what PnP RPGers are used to doing in their heads... Either way, it is not a huge deal, but I think this is one of those little touches that keep a good game from reaching greatness.
The combat system is alright, offering a few aimed attacks, some simple crafting (Very simple, you can just break down armor to metal and turn X metal into Y armor without worrying about any nonsense. As you get better, you can make it into Y+1 armor of butt-kickery.), some alchemy... but beyond that it's pretty straightforward. If you make use of the combat, you will be able to kill a ridiculous amount of people, so long as you carefully navigate the early game and murder the right people in the right order to gear up. The problem is eventually you start getting into late game combat encounters of dozens of men. No matter what your AP is you're really just doing two attacks a turn. If you want to swap attacks to efficiently use an uneven amount of AP, you have to open an unwieldy right click menu on your weapon and then click back up on your target. Do this twice and then try not to fall asleep as you watch 11 other losers take pot shots at you. No matter how many doodads you craft, it doesn't make the late game combat go any faster. You only ever control one party member and you don't generally have much to think about in relation to how long it takes for the battles to play out.
So basically go one of the routes other than combat. The combat system is quite solid, it just drags the more you practice it.

Final Fantasy XIII has been a hot button issue for many fans of the series, and of RPGs in general.  It cuts a few of the archetypal role-playing elements, while adding little to make up for it.  It's linear, you're gonna be dealing with pre-made parties, tutorials, and little customization for about %70 of the main game.  Regardless of all that, I really enjoyed Final Fantasy XIII.  The combat is simple, yet fun and rewarding.  The game looks great, and the music and SFX are top notch, and even though the story and cast are a bit mediocre, it's still very much worth a play.
Now, the big elephant in the room...
Being locked at 720p isn't what most of us were hoping for, even if they did allow for 60fps.  I understand a lot of gamers are gonna be disappointed by this, but for me, Square Enix has delivered a product worth a buy from me.  The price is low, I have not experienced any bugs or glitches, and this could possibly open up a future of more Final Fantasy games on PC.
Overall, good game, but not what a lot of people wanted out of a main Final Fantasy title, and a mediocre PC port at a low price point.

Let's see if I can put my thoughts together on this...
When I first heard about Dungeon Defenders I was incredibly excited. I've loved Tower Defense games for a while and always been a fan of Co-Op games. So when I heard there was a Co-Op Tower Defense RPG coming out I couldn't wait! Once my friends and I got our hands on it we had a blast. Sure it had some problems... Squires were OP, Survival was too easy, ranged enemies would attack behind the spawn shield... but it was really fun! Eventually the first part of their
came out, that's when things went downhill.
Trendy decided to add a new difficulty level in their expansion, since players thought the game was too easy. On "Nightmare" difficulty Player/Tower stats were altered to make the game more
. A new item tier "Mythical" was added for Nightmare, presumably to incentivize playing it. Which sounds good until you find out Mythical items had massively inflated stats, trivialising past content. Though to be fair, getting said gear incredibly difficult. Drop rates on Mythical were very low on all but the hardest maps. Seeing how those maps were balanced around you having Mythical gear, pretty much the only way to get the gear was to join someone who was hardcore and farmed early maps for it or was also carried.
Did I forget to mention they added new enemies for Nightmare? The Spider was the first one they added. Having a new set of (invisible) spawn locations, chosen to backdoor common defense locations, they would web towers drastically reducing fire rate and increasing the damage they would take.
spiders would prioritize players, webbing them and reducing movement speed, attack rate as well as preventing the use of abilities. Djinn were the second ones added, flying enemies that have the ability to "instantly" destroy defenses with a cast time based on what tier the defense was. Also possesing the ability to buff enemy units, turning them gold and making them significantly stronger. Sharken were the third, having the ability to charge through defenses pushing them out of the way. Probably the least obnoxious of the new enemies. Lastly the Goblin Copter, flying enemies that would spawn from Wyvern spawn locations. They would spawn carrying an Ogre and proceed to fly somewhere on the map and drop them off. If you made the mistake of not killing it before then, it would proceed to fire player seeking missiles, anti-tower flares and rockets at players/defenses. They also made Ogres much more common on Nightmare, in case all the previous wasn't enough.
Trendy, confident in their new found balance, proceeded to add new maps with this in mind. Basically having the difficulty options be varying differences of Nightmare difficulty, new enemies included. Most of the maps they added were well designed (some not so much). Unfortunately to play these maps you have to own them (shocker). To be fair, Trendy had this odd business model of having (most) maps be free the first two weeks after their release. Now a days you have to buy them and there are A LOT of them.
They also added some new classes, Barbarian for pure melee DPS, Series EV able to wield two ranged weapons and use an
wall and a buff beam, Summoner for pure builders with
towers and Jester for pure ranged DPS and minor trolling. Though the first classes they added were gender swapped versions of the vanilla heroes, with slightly different abilities. All of these you had to pay for as well, though I'd say they're all worth it (excluding the gender swaps).
Overall, Trendy hit gold with this game and did a pretty good job at keeping it alive. Personally I don't like what Nightmare did to the game but I think they had a lot of good ideas. Dungeon Defenders is definitely a game worth playing, if you haven't for some reason. Just make sure you get some friends to play it with and don't expect to play all the maps unless you're REALLY into it. DLC strongly recommended.
Also Trendy seems to have granted a community team the ability to officially update the game, so maybe we'll see some cool stuff out of that.

Portal, Portal 2, The Talos Principle
You are a little boy in a dystopian land who has to run away from home. On your way you get haunted by some sort of soldiers until you get into some sort of castle or something where you soon find a mysterious golden glove that allows you to change the polarity of certain metal boxes etc. which you encounter on your way, so they react magnetically to each other. This allows you to solve various puzzles to continue on your way. Shortly after you get to a tower containing a blue something which looks like an excursion funnel of Portal 2 but only moves you while you're of the same polarity as that thing. One way of achieving that (and at the moment the only one) is by touching a special flower on the ground of the tower. Then you're moved upwards by that funnel thing, allowing you to get to one of the entrances which are located at both sides (in terms of 2D graphics) of the tower's wall. Now you begin solving various puzzles to get higher in the tower and eventually reach it's top, while encountering various bosses and finding various other "helper items" (like the glove) on your way. And when you get higher, you also come across some theatres telling you about the history of the land.
As mentioned above you have to solve various puzzles, mainly using magnetics but also buttons, funnels like the one from the tower and small robots which can reach smaller places, press buttons and have other side-effects - all in all it's a bit like Portal without Portals and the 3D. The puzzles are all well-balanced in terms of difficulty - you have to think a bit about them, but you don't end up being frustrated and looking in the internet for the solution. The bosses are a bit harder, but basically it's just about figuring out how they work, and then you just have to try a few times until you get good enough to beat them, making them challenging whithout being frustrating.
The basic controls are A and D for moving left and right as well as Space for jumping. The various actions of the "helper items" are triggered by the arrow keys and can be directed to the character's top or bottom using W or S. You can also view a map (showing only rooms which have already been visited) by hitting Tab. All in all the controls are comfortable to use, and if you're dissatisfied with them you can also change them. The only thing that annoyed me is that the game did not really introduce the map as a feature, I just discovered it accidentally when I found a secret and the game displayed a little information together with "Tab" as the key to view the secret (they can be viewed by hitting the right arrow key while in map view).
As others wrote before, the game has quite beautiful, handdrawn graphics with fluid animations. And really, there isn't much more to say about this.
The sound effects resemble the mechanics of the game well, but there is nothing special however. The music however is very beautiful and has a sad touch. During the boss fights I find the music to get a bit mechanical, and in other games this would probably be a deficiency for me, but in this game it actually works, mostly since most of the bosses are mechanical as well.

Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag is quite... different when compared to the rest of the franchise. While most games have the protagonists being trained as an Assassin at a very young age or at least have prior knowledge of the conflict between Templars and Assassins (With the exception of Ezio, Arno and possibly Shay.) Edward Kenway, the protagonist of the game, was unaware of the conflict until when the prologue of the game occurs. In fact,
ACIV does not feel like an AC game but it feels more like a pirate game (If one ignores the lore between the whole Templar-Assassin war) and I think that it is a good thing at least once in a while. Gameplay on foot is just as fun as ACIII. Watching how Kenway fights and kills anyone in his way looks brutal and feels satisfying, yet stealth can be difficult especially early on in the game where most of the good gear is still unavailable. The same way can be felt about the ship gameplay. Every weapon that can be used requires a bit of strategy and timing in order for it to be truely devastating to enemy ships and forts. The open world is massive when both the land and sea portions are combined, yet one must progress through the story in order to access every area. The voice acting is what I think one of the best that the series has ever had. The story is also great. Overall, I will rate this a 9/10. This is a must buy for those kind of people who love pirate games, games with sea ship-based combat, or for those who love a good story.

Story: The storyline is fantastic. You are a pirate named Edward James Kenway. You and your crew are after an ancient place called The Observatory. There are problems within the time it takes to find out its location. These problems are important to the story so I'm not going to spoil them.
Graphics: The graphics are actually pretty good. I usually hit around 30-50 fps. In menus I hit 60fps. I think the developers took more time than they did in the other games.
Combat: I feel that the combat is smooth most of the time. Sometimes 3 enemies will try to hit you and obviously you cant counter attack them all so the developers could have done something about that. Everytime I try to attack an "agile guard", right before I break their defenses a regular guard will always attack me so I have to counter them,kill them and then try to break the agile guard's defense again which can be repetitve.
Freerun: The freerunning is often good but sometimes Kenway will: for example, climb a tree instead of run and jump over a fence. This can obviously be very annoying at times because you sometimes have to get to the Jackdaw's wheel in about like 30 seconds and Kenway climbs random things.
Controls: The controls are responsive and easy to remember.(at least for me) I personally think everything is easier on the PC so this may be biased.
Overall: This game was great on console and on pc. The story is great,graphics are fantastic,combat is mostly great, freerunning can sometimes be annoying, and the controls are good. I would recommend this to other people if you are looking for a pirate adventures in the West-Indies sea. :)   (I got this game for sale only for $7.49)

First thing first: How can I review this game when I have (at the moment of writing) 0 hours in it? As I didn't know there's a demo available, I admit I've pirated it to check if it's worth paying for.  And, as I've found out, it definitely is. Now, I haven't finished the game yet, so take the value of the "review" with a grain of salt.
What makes this game different? I'll tell you a story of my first character.
I've played an assassin, doing what assassins do until the final mission of the first town. There was a battle, and I ended up as the last assassin alive. What's so special about that, you'll ask? Well...
If this was a Bethesda RPG, my boss would just lie down until the battle end when he was killed, then get up as nothing happened, as important NPCs tends to do, and the story would proceed. Or maybe not, but in that case, he would be scripted to die no matter what I do. But if he lives or dies would be out of my hands
If this was a Bioware RPG, I would get a big, dramatic cutscene of my boss being killed before the final fight starts. I would fight the battle, and then perhaps find out he's still alive but wounded, and, after some dialog, would be presented with *nice guy choice* of trying to help him (but he would die anyway), *neutral choice* of ending his suffering at his own request, and *evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ choice* of leaving him to bleed out slowly and painfully. The end result wouldn't matter, he would still be dead.
If this was pretty much any other RPG from the last 15 or so years, I would get black screen with "You let the important NPC die, load last save?" button, because the story just wouldn't work with the NPC dead.
What happened is that the boss (and other friendly NPC) died because I wasn't that great fighter, I held back because I was low on HP, and I didn't feel like "wasting" consumable items. I felt their deaths were my fault and the result of my choices, not some prescripted event. I could've save them, I could've loaded previous save to try again, hell, I could've loaded even older save and either betray my fellow assassins, or (try to? I wouldn't be surprised if they just killed me if I chose that option) walked away before the battle. I didn't. I made choices, and I faced consequences, and the game acknowledged that. The game would acknowledge if he was still standing at the end of the battle, and (while I haven't tested it, I've played with it for a while before I've bought it) I suspect it would also aknowledge if any other members lived. Or if the last companion lived and the boss died.
That feeling that my actions *really* matter, that it's not just "select the color of the explosion in the final cutscene" (and yes, I'm still bitter about that), that is something I haven't felt in an RPG in a long, long time. That's what make this game awesome.
Developer's time and money invested in making the world seem alive and react to my deeds, not in the latest graphics, not in hiring VAs so the NPCs can talk about arrows in knees or how horrible mudcrabs are, or whatever. That's what make this game great. Is it perfect?
Of course not, there's a lot of room for improvement. It requires a different mindset from other modern RPGs. But as far as I'm concerned? Definitely worth my money.

Absolutely loved this game! Felt like a more than worthy successor to Gone Home, without retreading too much of the same ground.
The premise (trapped on a space station) isn't anything new, but it's all in the execution - over the course of the 2.5 hours I spent playing, I felt like I really got to know the crew, their motivations and relationships, and I was rooting for them all to pull through. This was in no small part thanks to the voice acting, which was stellar throughout.
While this is definitely not a action-heavy game, the systems used to interact with the ship were really fun - piecing together conversations taking place at the same time over multiple rooms was really fun, and there were some really good 'aha' moments where things started to make sense.
The attention to detail is as you'd expect from Fullbright (read: fantastic) - lovely art style (with clever stylistic choices made to avoid expensive character model rendering), and the environmental storytelling is spot on.
The only small complaints I have are the length (I think the story was exactly as long as it needed to be - I just wish I could have spent some more time with the characters!) and the lack of development for the player character (without spoiling anything, by the end of the game I was wishing we could have had some more insight into who they were and how they got there).
While I still think Gone Home takes the title of my favourite narrative-focused game (mainly due to the more personal/relatable story), Tacoma is still one of the best games I've played this year, and I think it's going to stick with me for a while. Definitely recommend it!

With Tacoma, Fullbright does not attempt to reinvent the wheel. It goes without saying that if you loved Gone Home like I did, Tacoma is an instant recommendation. However, the game is far more than "Gone Home in Space", like one would assume.
At its core, Tacoma is far more interested in reinventing the idea of audio logs, an overused narrative device in games, from the ground up. Instead of collecting tapes or notes like in most games, you relive the experiences of the crew members via AR (Augmented Reality) data. This means that you see the actions happen, you can interact with them and the crew members might walk off and do something else entirely, which allows for multiple stories in the same AR recording. This is a far more compelling implementation of how to deliver past key events in the narrative to the player then other ways.
That is not to say this is the *only* interesting element that Tacoma brings to the table. No, Tacoma also goes out of its way to address the extreme lack of diversity in the wider gaming culture. The characters in Tacoma are not your standard white, cisgender, straight men/women and this effort should be celebrated. Each character is handled with care as well, and none of them come off as tokenization efforts. Tacoma also presents its characters without seeming desperate for you to notice that they are ‘different’ than most characters in video games, and is confident about letting them speak for themselves. An example of this is the completely realistic and super cute relationship between Natali and Bert, which does not seem artificial in the least.
The main narrative is also unconventional. Tacoma is a game that is very worried about our society’s current obsession with technocratic accelerationism, and portrays a very plausible world where Amazon and Google run their own universities and corporations provide their own (often non-transferable) currencies to their workers. Yet, Tacoma avoids plunging into dystopian navel-gazing and shows that even in such a horrible world, there is still joy, wonder and love to be found. It also dosen’t overstay its three hour playtime and I felt like I had a complete experience at the end, though I would not have turned down an opportunity to spend more time on Lunar Transfer Station Tacoma.
As for technical details and performance, Tacoma ran mostly fine at 1920x1200 on my GTX 1070, but some spots caused the game to hitch up. Exiting the game and relaunching cleared it up, however.
In conclusion, Tacoma is strongly recommended for fans of exploration games and those who like a good story. One can only hope that its experimentation with audio logs trickles down to other games.

Just beat a marathon game (Contact Victory), been playing 30+ hours and here are my conclusions:
-The game is a modern, professionally made Alpha Centauri mod of Civilization V. (Is it literally the same engine? Honest question.
-It is (currently) inferior to Alpha Centauri (sorry to compare to other games, for the reason, see below) because you can't do all of the crazy terraforming stuff in AC like changing elevation and having oceanic empires (you can't build cities on water). I imagine in 6 months they'll release a mod for $30 that will be like a professionally made Alien Crossfire expansion mod and then maybe it will become solid. Remember making a giant elevated pyramid of terrain and then placing solar mirrors on it, creating a gigantic energy pyramid? Well, you can't do that in this because elevation doesn't even exist. Am I wrong? Does elevation exist in Civilization IV+ or this game? I don't think it does. Alpha Centauri did (15 years ago!)
-The construction of wonders, and the stuff that happens when you meet a victory condition, are lame. This trend has continued ever since Civilization III. (See below)
-Whatever happened to those cool movies of wonders getting constructed? It's just scrolling concept art and expository dialogue again. A wonder seems like a minor event.
-Whatever happened to score titles (i.e. "The Great", "The Fool", "The Merciful)?
-Whatever happened to score giving you a pimped out palace/throneroom/space office and assembling it over time?
-Whatever happened to significant movies or epilogues that illustrate the different endings, other than a small image and some expository writing? What a brief, boring ending to mark the victory of a glorious empire: I thought as I beat my first game.
-Biggest of all, remember that thing as early as Civ I where they show a world map from Year 1 and show the different civilizations on a world map as blobs of territory absorb each other as time goes on, with notes at certain years (city conquered, wonder built, empire eliminated)? None of that. No cool history of the game, which may have taken 50 hours of your life, hours that I assume you were supposed to spend making a meaningful connection to the game?
-You know how most games give you a breakdown at the end about your score and how it was calculated? This one doesn't--but you do get a meaningless number on a blank top score chart!
The gameplay is great and the soundtrack is excellent and I think mods will bring it to good place. But whatever happened to the GRAND ENDING? That is the greatest weakness of this game. Otherwise, it is as Gamespot says: "Is Civilization on an alien world a real advancement for the series, or just window dressing?"
Remember the ending of Master of Orion II? The epic one where you beat the Antarans? Of course you do. Epic endings are important in strategy games.
Overall, the game is solid--If you don't mind having a long, epic history which ends in nothing more than a pat on the back and a meaningless score with no explanation.

10 hours in and civilization is as addictive as ever. The critical difference from every other game in the franchise is that Beyond Earth allows a degree of creative freedom historical civs could not dream of. With the ability to customize every start before diving into the truly unknown, every game WILL be different. Careful study of Civ 5 meant much of the game could be experienced in a single game. I expect to have to play Beyond Earth at least a dozen times through to really get every difference.
Two major differences do stand out. First, the game takes a major shift away from buildings towards tiel improvements being the real heart of the game. The importance of the land around your cities gives culture a very different feel. There is no culture victory that I can find, but building effective cities means maxing out the territory ASAP, therefore culture is still huge.
Really a much newer game than most people seem to realize, Civ: Beyond Earth is a welcome challenge for veterans and wonderfully engaging for new players. I give it a 9/10.

Your pace depends on the tempo of the song. The tracks are dynamic and audiosurf recreates the changes in tempo using its visuals flawlessly. There are various scoing modes which range from chilled to challenging.
Although the game visually recreates the tempo flawlessly, it often struggles with the thumps and notes of the song. It is very hit or miss depending on the song you chose to play. Rhythm games have custom tracks for this reason; there is a lot of fine tuning behind the scenes to recreate that "thump" feeling. The sound of the notes is also a bit iffy and sometimes feels out of sync and sometimes destroys the beat of music.
The Steam Workshop is integrated well. You can add mods without restarting game which can change two things: visuals and scoring mod.
You can use your music tracks. YouTube is also integrated if you don't have the song on your disk.
I highly recommend Thumper if you're looking for a focused rhythm game.

its hard to find a game more deserving of a perfect 10/10 score than hollow knight. it has so much good quality content that even if the price was tripled id still call it good value for money. the game just keeps going long after you think youve seen everything with new areas and bosses. i am not a fan of these type of 2d games but hollow knight has the best 2d combat and platforming ive played. unless you absolutely hate backtracking this game is worth experiencing
-
there are 2 different ways to judge a game in my opinion. one is a review, if something is worth your time and money. second is a critique, ignoring price and other outside context and just focusing on how successful the game is doing what it does. this weird distinction is important because while i would give hollow knight a perfect review score, its not a perfect game and some of the criticisms i have may sound absurd to someone who is more concerned about value for money
so now that we get to nitpick a 15 euro game indie game, one of the biggest strengths of the game is also the reason for its most obvious flaws. the game world is massive and you can go almost anywhere you want with just a few upgrades. its great but its also a problem for two reasons. i mentioned that this game has the best 2d combat and platforming ive played and while thats true, on your first playthrough before you know where everything is it takes a ridiculous amount of time to reach that level of enjoyment. its not padded with filler content, the game is still fairly enjoyable before you reach your full potential, but its the most obvious case of poor pacing i remember ever seeing in a game
the second problem is the openess of that world, when you can go almost anywhere the developers had to make sure you can also complete those areas with very few upgrades. youll struggle at first but as you gain more upgrades the game cant keep up with your progression and becomes easier as a result. even areas you visit for the first time a dozen hours later may be ridiculously easy because of this. there are only 4 areas in the entire game that take full or somewhat full advantage of all the moves you have available, 2 of those areas you might even miss because theyre secrets in order to get the true ending. the third, while very fun, is just an arena that keeps spawning enemies. only the 4th area is actually required to complete the game and that comes at the very end. these 4 areas are some of the best content the game has to offer and its a shame more areas werent locked off until later
the bosses suffer from the same problems. this game has tons of bosses most of them interesting, but in order to minimize taking damage that wasnt the players fault they cannot have very complex attacks and/or are very slow. nothing points to the potential this game has as the dream bosses, rematches against specific bosses that are essentially hard mode, as accessing those fights requires a mid-game item that most players wont realize can be used this way until later. the dream bosses are an excellent challenge that take into consideration some of the more powerful abilities you might have while not requiring for you to have all of them in order to not get hit. obtaining more abilities will make these fights slightly easier, but it wont make them pointlessly easy as can be the case with some regular bosses depending on your exploration
finally i think its worth mentioning just how much everything save for the actual combat seems to be inspired by dark souls. you even lose all your currency if you die and have to get it back but since theres no leveling in the game and only a very limited number of things to buy, death is only punishing early game and becomes meaningless later. the atmosphere and the world might remind you of dark souls but none so much as the supposed final boss, the hollow knight, who might as well be called 2d soul of cinder

This is the closest to a non-recommendation I can get while still saying the game's worth buying.

I want to be super clear. This game is unforgiving. Everything,
is instant death. This isn't too terrible in most sections, except for the larger rooms where death will set you back to the entrance and it takes a while to get back to the part that's thwarting you.
Where it really starts to hurt is in the boss battles. Yeah, I'm not sure why there are boss battles in what is almost completely non-violent game (a few exceptions, but they're mostly avoidable)
The boss battles are brutal. No checkpoints. Die? You're back to the entrance to the room. Hit? At all? Dead. You're back to the entrance to the room. Any mistake? Any misjudgement? Die. Over and over and over again. Also, I don't know if I'm bad, or the controls just aren't as tight as they should have been, but I found myself dying repeatedly to stuff that I think I should have survived. (I can't be more specific without some spoilers.)
I think that last boss killed me 100+ times before I finally beat him. (Then I had to do it again to get the right ending. Should have picked up all the scrolls the first time D: )
I can honestly say I'll never play this again. But I don't exactly regret it either.
That said, if there's ever a sequel, I'll have to think long and hard about playing it.

The major problems I had has all been fixed. There were two.
-Immediate crash at the first startup. I had to disable DEP, reset the machine, It works since then.
-There was a non-disturbing, but noticeable lag in the game, always. The solution is weird, but this is the only one - you need a controller. The game desperately tries to find a controller in every second, which causes the lag. I have a Dualshock 3 connected, and calibrated as an XBOX360 controller (XInput). It works with the game, and there is no lag anymore.
Still, the game needs ingame graphics options, and to support at least 1080p resolution, to meet the VERY minimum of todays PC gaming requirements.
I don't think S.E. will do anything about this. The only hope can be Durante, and his awesome work. I tried his early pre-alpha GeDoSaTo fix, it is great already, and it will be more awesome later.
Last words: try to think about this another way. This game wasn't meant for PC, unfortunately.

I rate this game a 9/10. It is a almost perfect game. There are few flaws
Story: The storyline is fantastic. You are a pirate named Edward James Kenway. You and your crew are after an ancient place called The Observatory. There are problems within the time it takes to find out its location. These problems are important to the story so I'm not going to spoil them.
Graphics: The graphics are actually pretty good. I usually hit around 30-50 fps. In menus I hit 60fps. I think the developers took more time than they did in the other games.
Combat: I feel that the combat is smooth most of the time. Sometimes 3 enemies will try to hit you and obviously you cant counter attack them all so the developers could have done something about that. Everytime I try to attack an "agile guard", right before I break their defenses a regular guard will always attack me so I have to counter them,kill them and then try to break the agile guard's defense again which can be repetitve.
Freerun: The freerunning is often good but sometimes Kenway will: for example, climb a tree instead of run and jump over a fence. This can obviously be very annoying at times because you sometimes have to get to the Jackdaw's wheel in about like 30 seconds and Kenway climbs random things.
Controls: The controls are responsive and easy to remember.(at least for me) I personally think everything is easier on the PC so this may be biased.
Overall: This game was great on console and on pc. The story is great,graphics are fantastic,combat is mostly great, freerunning can sometimes be annoying, and the controls are good. I would recommend this to other people if you are looking for a pirate adventures in the West-Indies sea. :)   (I got this game for sale only for $7.49)

The largest issues the game stem from its low player base and the nightmare that Lightmare Studios is.  Below is my negative review because, while the game is free, you should know what you're getting into and what its history looks like.
~~~
Changed to a "not recommended" because of the recent shop changes.  Long story short, you basically have to purchase lightmare points with real money to buy cards like you used to.
~~~
They've made changes from the original card packs to these new "penta-packs."  You can purchase faction packs, which made me really excited, until I realized you have to use lightmare points, 300 of them for 5 cards.  300lp =~ $3 dollars if you start with 0lp.
$3 dollars for a 5-virtual-card pack guaranteeing no more than ONE rare.
If you want to buy cards using in-game currency, you only have two options, where you used to have 8ish, one pack from each new set of cards released.  Now, you can pick from the original card set, or the entire bunch of cards available.  The IW2013 Penta-pack and the Collection Penta-pack.  These each cost 3000 infinity points, where you used to be able to buy a pack of 3(?) for a little over 1000.  We can no longer buy packs of 15 for a little over 5000, they removed that feature entirely.
When they made these changes, it became practically impossible for me to card hunt like I used to.  I would buy card-set packs containing the cards I was looking for, 15 cards for 5000 like I said before.
These are the changes they made to the shop, and were the last straw for an otherwise avid player of the game.  I cannot and will not recommend the game because this has crossed the line and become pay-to-win.
Infinity Wars has a history of making the game harder and harder to enjoy for those who are not willing to purchase from the shop with real money, which should never be the case for any sort of game, free or not.

At first I was really into INK. I got it as a part of a bundle and was curious. 5 minutes in I was thinking about the neat visual style and ambient music and how death is actually helpful in a way as it covers new hidden platforms. In fact, even running around covering platforms with ink was fun and I felt a bit of a Splatoon-ish satisfaction for covering as many surfaces as I could. You sort of swapped between scouting out platforms in a level and moving towards the level’s exit. Dying meant little other than a bit more ink near that platform you’ve been struggling on, making it a bit more visible. Finally, I thought, a nice stress-less, enjoyable platformer.
Oops. It was Super Meat Boy in disguise. I mean, I should’ve guessed. Slippery, momentum-based platforming where moving creates a color to show where you have been and where you have died. I don’t know what I was excepting.  I guess I was really just hoping for something a bit more relaxing after finishing some homework, buying the bundle containing and then giving it a play before bed.
There was one level that got me frustrated that was pretty early on. I had to do with having to jump from one side of the more longitudinal map to the other killing enemies to unlock the exit. I won’t get into too much detail but there were two enemies place on the far left/right, very close to the edge. When you touch the edge, you die. When you bounce off an enemy, you keep your momentum. So I tried and tried to make a huge jump up to the next platform and then jump on the enemy while also moving a little to the left to avoid hitting the edge but not too far to avoid falling or having the enemy run into me. And it gets weirder because the next level was a breeze. For some reason the game just really wanted me to experience this learning curve and really drive how a kind of minor scenario that could’ve been show through a much less frustrating experience. Heck, in the next handful of levels you don’t even really get close to the walls of the level.
This game, based off the little I’ve played, does this a lot. It has a just rude level that interrupts the occasional string of neutral or fun stages. Plus it’s hard to ‘hate’ at times as the visuals and music are very, can I say…relaxing? Interesting? Whatever it is, they kept me playing.
Meat Boy is a hard game. And I’m the sort of person who isn’t a fan of difficult games despite their more rewarding pay off for beating a level. Completing a level begins to feel more like a chore than a challenge especially when it comes to a scenario where you see yourself die every 15 seconds only to give another shot at preforming perfectly in the same seemingly endless level where you spend 10 minutes dying on the same part only to move forward a little bit but still have to go through and die to the previous part a few more times. That’s kind of what Meat Boy is for me.
It’s only really when you’ve died plenty of times and the bit of ink that is flung up from your death stops helping you that thinks get frustrating. The ‘exploration phase’ is over and now it’s back to the grind stone to perfect your jumps in order to get past the level.
I probably won’t finish it. I know it’s gonna become even more difficult and, well, if I want more stress I can just do Honor’s Bio homework.
Like Meat Boy and colors? It’s a pretty cheap game, give a buy. It certainly got me thinking even if that wasn’t its intension. Oops.
I’ll be honest though: I kinda just feel like someone played a ton of Meat Boy and found themselves trying to paint all the surfaces of each level for fun. XD
[Wait. Did I just play a game for 20 minutes and then basically right an essay on it that compares it to Super Meat Boy while also analyzing what really seems to be the root of why I didn’t like that game too much either? Dam. Rambling 101]

From start to finish, the game took me an overall 5 hours to complete (an additional hour to complete all achievements). Overall, the storyline of the game was fantastic, there are many mini-storylines within the overarching story for you to read about and learn more of the backstories on each of  the six crew members.

There were definitely some "red herrings" here and there that kept the overall ending to the story a mystery right up until the very end. I also enjoyed the larger, sociological pieces that were undertones within the narrative of the story. Whie "Sci-Fi", some of the subject matter (Universties being run by corporations, loyalty in lieu of currency, etc.) really made me think and added a richness to the story.
I would highly recommend this game to those who are interested in a facinating story and also the deeper contexts that apply to our modern society.

It's a good game, but I still hated it.
An indie RPG with terrific writing, original worldbuilding, and some extremely frustrating design decisions. The writing and worldbuilding are good enough to still get me through two extremely aggravating playthroughs, both with social characters.
The game has two parts: an intricate combat system and a social system where you try to talk your way through quests. I haven't paid much attention to combat yet, as it would have been a death sentence for my two social characters. Combat in this game is extremely unforgiving, and if you don't have a combat-focused character, you will die without even denting your enemies' armor. So, I'll only talk about the social part of the game here.
It takes place in a fallen empire. Once spanning much of the world, after a great war it has been reduced to three crumbling cities in a blasted wasteland filled with ruins. Social order has broken down - when not fighting raiders, the remnants of the Imperial Guard happily extort those they're supposed to protect, and the other characters you meet aren't any better. If you want to get ahead in the game, you'll have to let go of your idealism and any delusions of saving or improving the world - really, the community calls them 'combat-focused' and 'social-focused' characters, but 'thug' and 'schemer' would be better descriptions!
So what's wrong with it? There were some things which drove me up the wall when playing it:
First of all, it's really easy to accidentally screw yourself over with something that seems reasonable at the time. This is because dialogue options need a certain skill level to succeed (no random die rolls!). You do this by gaining skill points, which are mainly earned through quests, which usually require a high skill level to complete! Make a few mistakes, and you can easily run out of skill points later, unable to finish any quests. In my first playthrough, I messed up a quest for the Commercium by taking a completely reasonable, safe-seeming choice. This led to me being kicked out of their guild, permanently. Which ended up costing me so many opportunities, as well as precious skill points, that I was unable to finish the game due to an early-game decision! This was six hours later! The only way to prevent this is by knowing what's coming, either from knowledge of earlier games or by trial and error. This is not fun and, more seriously, discourages experimentation.
Secondly, despite the creators' warnings to avoid combat, this is unfortunately not always possible. If your social character says the wrong thing to the wrong character, you end up in a fight. Some conversations always lead to fights - which for a social character, means they always lead to death. Quicksave is your friend here, but it's not very enjoyable to  have to reload five times to look for the only dialogue option that lets you live! This problem happens even with apparently reasonable and safe choices.
Finally, there are the little annoyances. Why can't I hire help when my skills are too low - if I don't make a lore check, it would make sense to hire a loremaster instead of having my character just sit there, moping. Why do I have to mouse-over every last person to see if I can talk to them - would immersion really be so damaged by just putting a yellow dot or something over their head? And why can't I flee when a fight or conversation threatens to turn deadly?
These things are not so bad by themselves, but increase the aggravation from the big problems.
But the world... The world is fantastic. The fallen empire is fascinating, and despite the frustration, I couldn't stop pressing on, hoping to find more knowledge, information and locations. The atmosphere is great - Teron looks and feels like a ruined town barely scraping by. It has monumental, Roman architecture crudely but effectively fixed with wooden beams. Maadoran, with its crumbling temples and dry fountains, looks like a filthy hive that was once glorious. Ganezzar looks exactly like you'd expect a theocratic dump to look. Combined with the far more advanced construction and machinery in the many ruins, it is carefully crafted to evoke a once-great world in ruins. And you get to find out how and why it fell! Even the many unexpected deaths work out when they're not driving you up the wall, helping to bring a world to life where death can strike anywhere. And every detail fits - the squalor in the houses, even the description of the gold coins 'bearing images of emperors of various antiquity' serve to underline what this world has been, and what it has become. The hours of discovery made up for the hours of frustration, and I still haven't discovered everything yet.
In conclusion, this game is as frustrating and unfair as roleplaying with a smug killer DM, and I am looking forward to my third playthrough. Once your anger subsides, you'll be happy you've played it.

Very different to many contemporary RPGs, hard but rewards tactical skill in combat and exploration very nicely.
This is a game designed for multiple playthroughs, Its an RPG where you don't roleplay a warrior/theif/mage/rogue who can do every quest and become king of every faction.
Instead it presents a thouroughly interesting and believable world and your character will be one that fits with this. This design choice is not for everyone but makes you actually think about what you are doing and the consequences of your actions. This made it a very engaging experience for me.
The setting and story is the stand out of this game though, its best described as alterna-roman/historical/post-apocalyptic/cthulu-lite where all these parts come together seamlessly.
I did personally think the combat is a little too hard on non combat focussed characters. SInce this game is really at its best when you play a sneaky charismatic type this is a little jarring. I personally stopped worrying about this and cheated myself some basic combat skills to make it less frustrating.
Overall, its excellent.

A couple of things I have a problem with but for now lets get to why I love the game.
I decided to try this game after having seen the previews for it. I'm familiar with Nexon because of Mabinogi but after having played Mabi for 7-8 yrs, I grew tired of the weeaboo crowd it had gathered. It's sad but Mabinogi is completely ruined for me because of that.
When I joined, it was closed beta and the impression it left on me was not too good. After it hit open beta however, I tried it again and ended up loving it. I'm picky, the combat system in this game isn't hyper real-time action combat like that of Vindictus or even mostly real time like mabi. It's sort of a melding between traditional and real time combat. The action of the cool skills you get is pretty nice tho and the scenery is like an endless dreamscape that captivates your eyes.
You can tame just about every monster you find in the game. Those games where you have to BUY pets or mounts? Forget that, you just go into the wild and grab one of your own. I quickly got used to the taming system and battle system. After that it was just having an open mind for me to truly enjoy the game. Sure I can't be multiple classes at once and I have to watch out for my specific weaknesses as a squishy assassin but it's worth it. The fact you can customize your character to at least a moderately detailed point is sufficient enough for me. I'm sure more options will come out in the future.
I don't usually enjoy a game where you have to do quests in order to progress through the game but I decided why the hell not and just followed the flow. This is rare because this is almost immediately a deal breaker for ANY game I've played. The PVP is optional so that's good. I like full consent to a fight.
You can also earn the premium currency "Elluns" IN GAME by getting achievements or completing specific repeatable quests. Also daily quests are a thing too and they also give Elluns.
Time for the bad
Gold farming bots that spam the chat, there are hackers abusing the system right now and I have sent Nexon some videos showing them what's going on. As to whether or not they're going to fix that right away, I've no idea.
Steam Launcher is really buggy. Mine crashed 4 times in a row and I was trying to enter my character each time. :/

If you are a perfectionist with a taste for slick graphics and a bevvy of opportunities for improvization, this is your heaven. Even if you aren't normally the type to hunger for that 1000 gamerscore or shiny platinum trophy, you will find yourself jumping down the many varied rabbit hole levels again and again, rooting out every unique disguise, weapon and killing method while hungrily watching that mission score climb higher and higher.
As stated before, the game looks fantastic, but not only that, it's consistently fantastic looking. From cutscenes to quicktime events to every last inch of the scenery, it plays like a scene out of a movie with added elements that quicken your pulse just enough to push you over the edge, things like sound and color dampening and camera focus. It's all expertly mixed.
On top of it all, the storyline is compelling and deep. The actors play their parts superbly and the portrayal of events has a very raw, quick feel to it.
This isn't a game, it's an experience that has to be seen to be believed.
One note though:
Do NOT purchase the dlc if you intend to go single player only, I learned the hard way that those fancy suits and super-guns are only usable in multiplayer.

I felt completely disgusted when I realised how fantastic this game is for how much your paying. For 15 euro this game is an absolute steal. The movement and combat mechanics feel smooth. They're simple and minimalistic but theres still great depth to them. The combat, while tough in
most occassions, is perfectly balanced (you can't cheese bosses because healing yourself takes a short time). And charms can offer you great variety in playstyle.
The story and storytelling is what I liked the most about this game. It is very subtle and there are a very minimal amount of cutscenes. In Hollow Knight you really have to puzzle out the story yourself, and if you are like me, you will have plently of fun doing so. Not to mention that the story and lore are very interesting on its own.

I have a love/hate relationship with this game.  Mostly as in I love this game, and this game hates me.
So what's there to love?  Let's start with the music.  I'm a sucker for a good soundtrack, and oh man this game has a great soundtrack.  It's so great to get to a new area (or boss) and just pause and listen to the music.  (Side note: If you want to listen for yourself, look up the Dirtmouth theme.  It's basically the first place you get to, so no spoilers there.)  I seriously can't get over how much I love this game's soundtrack.
Next is the overall art.  I'm sure you've seen plenty of reviews talking about this, but this game is so pretty.  Every area has its unique ambience and it's great to see just what that is when you first get there.  As well, every area has (mostly) different enemies, whose appearances match with the area you're in.
Then there's the story.  There's not much to go on at first, but as you play more and more things just build up more and more and get better and better.  There's a lot of lore to be discovered in this game, so much so that it's hard to find it all in one playthrough.
Now why do I say this game hates me?  This game is hard.  If you're going through this game without ever having seen any walkthrough of this before, be ready to die a lot.  There are plenty of challenges to be had, especially when going for 100%.  (What you will probably have as the last 1% is brutal.)  And then once you complete the game for the first time, you unlock permadeath mode for even more of a challenge.
Otherwise, I've had my fair share of delay problems, which are partially due to my setup.  This has included things such as holding the heal button and not healing, holding down+attack and attacking forward instead of down, and getting hit while still in a black screen transition after landing on spikes.
Overall, this game is fantastic.  I highly recommend buying this game, even at full price.  Just be ready for what lies ahead.

Shadow Warrior is one of those games I bought, spent a few minutes with, and then forgot I even had. And boy was that disappointing on my part. But I'm glad I came back to it, because the 2013 reboot of Shadow Warrior is a wonderfully refreshing FPS game.
The story is convoluted to the point where I didn't much care after a while. But I suspect if you're into the whole Japanese-gods-and-demons stuff you'll like it. This much is certain even to my untrained eye: the art style is fantastic, and the game's presentation values are stellar. Seriously, it's a visually and aurally beautiful game three years later. It holds up wonderfully well.
But more important than any of that is the way it plays, and it delivers in spades. The key bindings are a little quirky for my taste (press X to zoom? Really?!) but the flow of combat and options available are stellar. I loved switching in and out of well implemented melee combat and gunplay. I think a few of the weapons could stand a little tweaking (like faster rocket travel for example), but it's all very compelling.
And kudos to Shadow Warrior for putting together a genuinely interesting arsenal of guns. Sure, there's the usual pistol, shotgun, and rocket launcher, but I thought the crossbow and flamethrower were as unusual as they were well implemented. And really more interesting were all the alternate modes. I particularly liked the dual sub-machine guns and used them to get me out of a lot of sticky situations.
But where the game really shines to me is the melee combat system. I confess I never quite worked out the right combination of moves to up my score and secure maximum karma points, but I never got tired of using all the different katana abilities. About halfway through the game combat with the sword became so much more interesting to me than the gunplay that I used it almost exclusively until some of the later levels, when the guns really helped at times.
And damned if I wasn't STILL finding ways to use even the basics by game's end. I took the rapid-fire upgrade for the pistol as my very last unlock before the last boss, for example, and that turned out to be my go-to firing mode to handle him. In how many games can you say you're still using the basic pistol by the end? What a great job Shadow Warrior does at making all the weapons worthwhile and fun throughout.
I could probably harp on a few negatives. LIke some of the levels (particularly toward the end) feel like they go on and on and on to the point where at least twice I was begging for every door I opened to be the end of it. These aren't quickie levels at all; some of them took me up to 90 minutes to work through. So plan to sit down and invest in a serious play session. I know for a lot of folks that's nothing, but when you're my age with my responsibilities at home, finding even half an hour can be a challenge sometimes.
I also got a little tired of the endless looking for money by the end. Many of the weapon upgrades are priced so highly that I don't think there's any way for you to come up with the requisite funds in a single play through, not even if you buy the upgrade early on to find more cash.
But then on the plus side, I already started a new game in the "Ex" mode, keeping all my old weapons, upgrades, and such. I'm looking forward to playing through it again on hard mode and seeing how many different ways I can find to kill demons. In short, stop reading and buy the game already; it's a delight.

there are 2 different ways to judge a game in my opinion. one is a review, if something is worth your time and money. second is a critique, ignoring price and other outside context and just focusing on how successful the game is doing what it does. this weird distinction is important because while i would give hollow knight a perfect review score, its not a perfect game and some of the criticisms i have may sound absurd to someone who is more concerned about value for money
so now that we get to nitpick a 15 euro game indie game, one of the biggest strengths of the game is also the reason for its most obvious flaws. the game world is massive and you can go almost anywhere you want with just a few upgrades. its great but its also a problem for two reasons. i mentioned that this game has the best 2d combat and platforming ive played and while thats true, on your first playthrough before you know where everything is it takes a ridiculous amount of time to reach that level of enjoyment. its not padded with filler content, the game is still fairly enjoyable before you reach your full potential, but its the most obvious case of poor pacing i remember ever seeing in a game
the second problem is the openess of that world, when you can go almost anywhere the developers had to make sure you can also complete those areas with very few upgrades. youll struggle at first but as you gain more upgrades the game cant keep up with your progression and becomes easier as a result. even areas you visit for the first time a dozen hours later may be ridiculously easy because of this. there are only 4 areas in the entire game that take full or somewhat full advantage of all the moves you have available, 2 of those areas you might even miss because theyre secrets in order to get the true ending. the third, while very fun, is just an arena that keeps spawning enemies. only the 4th area is actually required to complete the game and that comes at the very end. these 4 areas are some of the best content the game has to offer and its a shame more areas werent locked off until later
the bosses suffer from the same problems. this game has tons of bosses most of them interesting, but in order to minimize taking damage that wasnt the players fault they cannot have very complex attacks and/or are very slow. nothing points to the potential this game has as the dream bosses, rematches against specific bosses that are essentially hard mode, as accessing those fights requires a mid-game item that most players wont realize can be used this way until later. the dream bosses are an excellent challenge that take into consideration some of the more powerful abilities you might have while not requiring for you to have all of them in order to not get hit. obtaining more abilities will make these fights slightly easier, but it wont make them pointlessly easy as can be the case with some regular bosses depending on your exploration
finally i think its worth mentioning just how much everything save for the actual combat seems to be inspired by dark souls. you even lose all your currency if you die and have to get it back but since theres no leveling in the game and only a very limited number of things to buy, death is only punishing early game and becomes meaningless later. the atmosphere and the world might remind you of dark souls but none so much as the supposed final boss, the hollow knight, who might as well be called 2d soul of cinder

Audiosurf new and improved.
Audiosurf is pretty much the mother of all bring-your-own-music rhythmn games, as far as music-based games go this was the first one I can remember that let you use your own music to really customise your game.
This kind of genre game is usually for laid back casual games that you throw on when you're between games, want something chill or just want to jam out. For that purpose it's great. The original game had a lot of the same features but Audiosurf 2 has polished it up and added in a few essential things that has made it even better.
To start, pretty much everything in this game is customisable. There are various different game modes to suit your play style, game skins to suit your visual style and the ability for you to browse through your computer and pick out what music you want to play to. If you want something calm and psychedelic to cruise to, you can. If you want something fast, upbeat and thrilling, you can do that too. With the re-boot from Audiosurf to Audiosurf 2 though, you can now browse several categories given to you to find music online as well. As a lot of people use cloud storage these days or internet apps such as YouTube and Sound Cloud, I was pleasantly surprised to see this has been implemented into the game. You can easily find popular music without having it downloaded onto your computer, see what music your friends are into and even input a YouTube URL yourself to find something more specific.
Whilst still on the subject on customisablily though, Steam Workshop support has also been added, so if you get bored of the content within the game, you can always take to the workshop in search for something new.
All in all really, this new version pretty much replaces the first one. It's been a while since I played the first one, but i can't think of anything that it had that Audiosurf 2 doesn't. If you don't yet have either, I would suggest just buying 2.
I really enjoy these kinds of games and thought I would just try it out for a short while before doing some studying. These kind of games never fail to excite me and put a smile on my face. If you're a fan of the genre, be sure to give it a go.
TL;DR : It's basically the first one but better, with Steam workshop and the ability to find music via YouTube. It's a fun casual game that I definitely recommend.
