Just finished my first play through of Teslagrad and I've got to say it was at times challenging and frustrating, but overall
rewarding. ^_^
Teslagrad is mostly a puzzle platformer, with the metroid-esque power ups you acquire used mostly to allow you access to new areas and give you even more tools to progress through challenging levels. Throughout the game there was very little combat and more of a focus on story, setting, solving puzzles and avoiding hazards. And now, to the break down!
Much like the opening scenes to Pixar's "Up,"  the story is painted for you through the use of images and music only - there is no dialogue! Instead, Teslagrad's expressive art style, the 'cut scene' sequences, collectible scrolls and notes scrawled on walls tell the story of how a once great society of inventors met their unfortunate end at the hands of a selfish and bitter king. A+
The platforming mechanics and puzzles involve a lot of magnetism based effects and it all felt very precise. Your abilty to super jump, levitate and fly all seemed very consistent for the most part (unlike some physics engines!) and collision detection was particularly detailed and precise. There were only a couple of times when things were moving too fast that I wasn't sure if there was some muddled reactions happening... but otherwise each detail, from the corners of ledges to the speed of levitation, all felt incredibly smooth.
While some of them took me a while to grasp, or were physically demanding to complete, the puzzles (mostly) felt challenging and fun. There weren't too many times I found myself completely bewildered or frustrated... so Teslagrad's developers win more brownie points for making their puzzles fairly intuitive.
Since the physics of the game were so on point it gave you a great sense of flow throughout the game and heightens the sense of freedom over the environment... Particularly as you gain your power ups. You REALLY notice the difference toward the end of the game.
Honestly, not too much to say here. I either loved or hated everything in this game, so thinking of 'meh' complaints was tough.  If I had to say anything, I'd mention:

So, arguably the most difficult part of the game for me, involved flying upward on a magnetic 'updraft' as fast as possible through a series of electrical beams in order to get to the top before a quest item became unavailable. It was extremely difficult.  But that seems like a personal complaint rather than a design flaw.
Maybe twice in the whole game, it felt like the game was being deliberately abusive when it came to their forced camera angles. Typically the camera is focused on whatever you can see in front of you. However, for what I assume are cinematic reasons, your POV would shift in to focus on something plot-worthy. 99% of the time this was fine because you were somewhere safe, you expected it and you could walk away from this auto-focused location without issue. But once in a while, your focus would shift in such a way that you couldn't see a guard running at you (you only face gaurds twice in the game, btw) and you'd be insta-gibbed. Very sneaky! Very spiteful!
So, two points of contention. Two things that the game should have done, but failed miserably.
I don't mind collecting trinkets (in this case scrolls) as a bonus, or for achievement or what not. But for god's sake don't force me to do it! There comes a point in the game where you can no longer progress until you have collected so many of these freakin' scrolls that are hidden throughout the game levels. There's still one more boss to defeat, more story to uncover.... but you have to pass through the gate with so many of these damn scrolls in your bag before it lets you through. Of course, this could have been avoided if....
If I'm forced to play hide and seek through the ENTIRE GAME MAP... at least throw me a freakin' bone as to where these things can be found! For a game that communicates its story, SO FREAKIN WELL, you'd think this would be a non-issue. Clearly someone missed the memo.
In fairness, I collected approximately 90% of these things because their locations were obvious... it was just a matter of having the right tools and figuring out the platforming puzzle. But the other 10% were blatantly hidden offscreen in secret zones, or through passages that blended in with the scenery. After about an hour I decided to look online for the remaining locations. All in all, not the end of the world... but it would have been nice to have some sort of indicator on the map, or a tone, or light or something that would mark a location as important to guide me back to it. Those other 90% were somewhat fun to collect since I had to explore.... but those last 10% were infuriating! >_<
All in all, a fantastic game with a fantastic story line! Just be prepared to look for help (unless you like playing through the game for an extra dozen hours banging your character against each surface, in each level, inch by inch).

**I'm not a professional critic and this is an attempt at creating a review. Please bear with me**
Teslagrad is an amazing platformer where one uses numerous objects with their own special abilities to make it through various puzzles. Before buying the game, I played the demo. The demo, though, doesn't really show one enough of Teslagrad and its elements going in. Thus, besides how much I've enjoyed it, I've decided to write a review.
Just to give a quick overview of a non-gameplay related aspect, this game is one played in silence; in which there aren't voices. This, though, leads to an amplification of the game's story. Either way, adding voices would do little more than take away the adventure and prevent one from noticing the very fitting and melodic music.
Teslagrad is a real mix of three aspects: intuitive and trial-and-error puzzles, coordinated and reflexive platformer action, and exploration.
Puzzles: Teslagrad's main view isn't solely focused on puzzles. I'd learned this after buying the full game. One could argue that every room is a puzzle, and that's true. Teslagrad, though, is a linear game and most of these can be discoved with quick intuition. If you're a puzzle fanatic and are looking for a game with a Professor Layton type of challenge, this isn't for you. These puzzles can also be melded with quick reaction, and the bosses are puzzles in themselves; trying to figure out how to defeat them and the best way. You will also die over and over again to find answers.
Platformer action: This is especially seen from the implementation of bosses, many of which took numerous tries to defeat. Many of the puzzles and bosses require quick intuition (such as evaluating jump height and distance), coordination with numerous fingers, reflexive actions, such as to dodge attacks, and memorization (mainly of boss moves and how to defeat them). To look objectively, the boss fights are repetative, though: you dodge all of the attacks, you preform a certain action/counterattack, the boss becomes faster and/or has harder to dodge attacks, and repeat two more times.
The adventure: This is by far my favorite part. The story is very heartwarming in certain parts and leaves the guessing about the backgroung story. There are thirty-six scrolls scattered in hidden locations throughout the game, each telling part of the story. The story sequence, though, cannot be obtainable in temporal order unless you restart the game after beating it, leaving one continuously wondering about the plot. The ways that these scrolls are hidden also requires active thinking and guessing as to where they might be. It also requires planning combinations of certain moves to get to their locations.
All in all, I lreally enjoy Teslagrad, my first-ever attempt at making a review is getting too long, and I think it doesn't suit all audiences based on their "gaming-values". 9/10

There are certainly some issues with this port, no doubt.  Chief among these is that if you do not connect a game pad the game will stutter every second or two for a moment.  Luckily Dark Souls prepared me for bad ports and I had my own gamepad ready, but of course, that might not be the case for you.  Hopefully they get this fixed soon.
Secondly there is no video options, at all, in the game.  While I've found this to be a trivial problem, the game looks beautiful on my rig, others have complained about "streched" graphics.
The gameplay really leaves something to be desired as well.  Level design is poor, at least in the early game.  Pretty much you just walk forward for a short while until either a fight or cut scene appears, (I'm told this changes later on, but after playing 10+ hours on the Xbox, I eventually gave up on this).  The fights, so far, are practically automatic.  A few button clicks every once in awhile and the computer takes care of the rest.
The worst though is the sound of clopping shoes as you make your way through the game, who the hell signed off on that...
So with all this why do I recommend the game?  Well because if you can get it to work, it is a beautiful game, no doubt.  Also, while not the best Final Fantasy game in the series, if you are a fan of the series I think you will like this game.  It isn't everything we expect from a Final Fantasy game, but it continues the series's tradition of crafting a beautiful world and telling a wonderful tale.

Dungeon defenders has been quite an experience and was one of the first games I really got into. It can be described as a blend of hack and slash loot collection with tower defense, such as the gift from heaven that was Bloons Tower Defense. In terms of how this blend plays out it allows the player to help out the towers during the attck waves meaning a much more immersive experience than other tower defense games. In tradition with games such as diablo there is also a heavy emphasis on randomized loot that can always be improved. This however can lead to some frustrating encounters as loot may drop with better stats, but have a level requirement of 60, at the start of the game. Gameplay plays out very smoothly with the transitions between the building and defending phases, allowing for a breather between the heavy onslaughts, letting you upgrade and repair your defenses as seen fit. The traditional defend the crystal game mode may start to get stale after doing many a mission but thats brings us to my favorite part of the game, the challenges. The challenges of the dungeon defenders are unque mission that put a twist on the workings of the game by changing how fundemental  parts of levels play out. This includes a crystal that teleports around the map, a level in which golbins rain from the sky, one where no towers are allowed, and dozens of others thanks to the large amount of free and paid for content that Dungeon Defenders has recieved post launch. Overall the game is a solid blend of two enjoyable genres that is pleasant romp through many varied environments. I highly reccomend playing with friends as it increases the enjoyment of the game exponentially.

I recently picked up this game in a Humble Bundle. My intention wasn't to even play this game but saw a couple videos of game play and actually got really excited to play it. I am now on level 24 at the time of writing this review and I have a few things to say.
I know the whole, you haven't even got to a good level, you are mad because you are just bad, you need to play a game before making a review. I don't care as I am taking the view of someone who is new to the game and here a couple flaws i have found.
I'll start with some positives, the game looks ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. Its like the pixel gods have blessed the creators. The idea behind it I really like the sound and look of. The game is colourful and this is something that can be hard to find as the colours are used in the right way.
I can see how this game would be really fun - and I was enjoying myself at the start of the game - but then I ran into a couple problems.
Right from the start, handling yourself in the air is hard. It is a massive struggle to change directions whilst in the air. I feel like sometimes you move really quickly and sometimes you don't. When jumping up a wall, sometimes you shoot off the top of it at a really quick speed, this then leads to dying most of the time because I can't turn around to get back to the platform I was on. Killing enemies is also quite hard as when you land on them you slide straight off. This becomes extremely frustrating at times. In regards to in air movement, its like going over to a friends house who has the same mouse sensitivity but they have mouse acceleration on and you just can't control it.
I had very high hopes for this game but I was fairly disappointed. The game needs to have adjusted in air movements so that it is a bit easier. I will make a new review if I begin to 'master' the game because I feel that with this game, you are either good or bad and there is no in between. I don't recommend this game as it is very hard to get started and the in air controls need to be fixed. Other than that, the game is pretty good. And yes i have the badge lv 5 and foil badge, I personally think that the badges and backgrounds look pretty good.

The booster pack system is being refined soon to be more like Hearthstone: cheaper packs with less cards containing at least one rare. Additionally, you will be able to buy packs containing only a single faction (color). I think these two changes will make it a lot easier to build your own decks faster.
I'd advise starting with the campaign missions and trying out the weekly free decks against bots or other new players.
(Oh, and the animated card art is amazing. A common in Infinity Wars looks as good or better than a golden legendary in Hearthstone.)

So, arma 2 was like a really realistic army sim game made back in 2009 or something. It can run on some lower end PCs like mine, though you wont get all the pretty graphics. And you know what it doesn't matter. Because it isn't about the graphics, it's about the gameplay. And it has pretty great gameplay. Though I won't lie it is chunky when coming to movement. I'd recommend third person almost exclusively, though some vehicles are better to drive in first such as the bicycle, and it's fun to sit in first person in the back of a car.
Actually getting into the gameplay, the guns all have bullet drop I think it's called, since you know it's trying to simulate actual warfare and stuff. It's a little rough round the edges, but works good enough, a bit like fallout 4 almost, in that it's good but still needs a little work. They all also take about half a second to hit depending on the distance.
For dayz, I found that the clunkiness of arma 2 and oa doesn't entirely work with it. I mean it's a good mod, just a bit buggy. But I can talk about dayz in a review for that game xD
In terms of wasteland on oa, I find it great. My biggest concern about it is the base building, and how easily a base can be stolen. It adds to the realism kinda, your base being taken over. But all it takes is a chopper to hit you from afar and it can kill everyone. I do like it, but at the same time I don't because you and your teammates have worked hard making it. Though it's fun to have a sniping war with enemies around the base. And a really cool thing is that you can store a weapon in your backpack. And when you die or leave it stays there. The community for arma in general, from what I've seen, is probably the best gaming community out there. Everyone ive spoken to is helpful, and has played the game for a few years, they tell me what♥♥♥♥♥♥does and how to use it, one guy also spent about two hours making a base for about 6 of us and told us what all the defences do, and we all got a small group going.

The card game itself is pretty excellent from a design perspective, which itself is quite a feat when it comes to electronic card games. Most of them are just tacked on after a terrible exploitative business model. It's better than games such as Magic the Gathering or Pokemon as it leaves open much more strategy and bluffing. However, like all e-card games, it has a terribly exploitative business model where the idea is to frustrate the player as hard as possible into buying packs. This comes in the following forms:
-You earn packs as you "level up" and complete campaigns. However, all these cards are locked from trading. This means they're useless unless they go in a workable deck for you personally. "Binds on equip"-style crap has bee cancerous since it was invented and needs to stop.
-The conversion rate (in AUS dollars) for pack prices puts them at the same per-pack price and sometimes slightly higher than popular TCGs when purchased by the box. Anyone familiar with TCGs will know what I mean here. For everyone else, just know that in-game currency and real life money to spend on packs is heavily skewed out of your favor. Even with a fast deck, it takes 50 games to earn one pack of 15 cards.
-The absolute monotonous grind. How would I know, given that I only have 4 hours on record? I watched my girlfriend play this game for 40 straight hours and her collection is still small, and of that maybe a tiny fraction is tradable. As tradable cards are only gotten through packs you buy expensively with real money or grind forever in-game.
-The new patch is going to make it even MORE grindy by lowering the initial pack cost a small percentage then dropping it from 15 cards to 5. Each card was previously worth 350 ingame currency on average but will now cost 600 currency on average. Screw that garbage.
In short, it's just a time sink like every other e-card game. I hope a competent company buys out the IP and fixes most of its business model problems. That, or I hope they make this an actual physical card game which can be done easily with a few tweaks.

Shadow Warrior is one of those games I bought, spent a few minutes with, and then forgot I even had. And boy was that disappointing on my part. But I'm glad I came back to it, because the 2013 reboot of Shadow Warrior is a wonderfully refreshing FPS game.
The story is convoluted to the point where I didn't much care after a while. But I suspect if you're into the whole Japanese-gods-and-demons stuff you'll like it. This much is certain even to my untrained eye: the art style is fantastic, and the game's presentation values are stellar. Seriously, it's a visually and aurally beautiful game three years later. It holds up wonderfully well.
But more important than any of that is the way it plays, and it delivers in spades. The key bindings are a little quirky for my taste (press X to zoom? Really?!) but the flow of combat and options available are stellar. I loved switching in and out of well implemented melee combat and gunplay. I think a few of the weapons could stand a little tweaking (like faster rocket travel for example), but it's all very compelling.
And kudos to Shadow Warrior for putting together a genuinely interesting arsenal of guns. Sure, there's the usual pistol, shotgun, and rocket launcher, but I thought the crossbow and flamethrower were as unusual as they were well implemented. And really more interesting were all the alternate modes. I particularly liked the dual sub-machine guns and used them to get me out of a lot of sticky situations.
But where the game really shines to me is the melee combat system. I confess I never quite worked out the right combination of moves to up my score and secure maximum karma points, but I never got tired of using all the different katana abilities. About halfway through the game combat with the sword became so much more interesting to me than the gunplay that I used it almost exclusively until some of the later levels, when the guns really helped at times.
And damned if I wasn't STILL finding ways to use even the basics by game's end. I took the rapid-fire upgrade for the pistol as my very last unlock before the last boss, for example, and that turned out to be my go-to firing mode to handle him. In how many games can you say you're still using the basic pistol by the end? What a great job Shadow Warrior does at making all the weapons worthwhile and fun throughout.
I could probably harp on a few negatives. LIke some of the levels (particularly toward the end) feel like they go on and on and on to the point where at least twice I was begging for every door I opened to be the end of it. These aren't quickie levels at all; some of them took me up to 90 minutes to work through. So plan to sit down and invest in a serious play session. I know for a lot of folks that's nothing, but when you're my age with my responsibilities at home, finding even half an hour can be a challenge sometimes.
I also got a little tired of the endless looking for money by the end. Many of the weapon upgrades are priced so highly that I don't think there's any way for you to come up with the requisite funds in a single play through, not even if you buy the upgrade early on to find more cash.
But then on the plus side, I already started a new game in the "Ex" mode, keeping all my old weapons, upgrades, and such. I'm looking forward to playing through it again on hard mode and seeing how many different ways I can find to kill demons. In short, stop reading and buy the game already; it's a delight.

I was looking forward to Tacoma, so it’s with some puzzled disappointment that I have to report it was really quite underwhelming. Fans of the genre will find nothing original here, and in a year’s time there will be little reason for anyone to remember this game. This isn’t to say it’s bad, as such, indeed the dialogue is well-written and well-acted, but walking simulators have progressed, and apparently Fullbright haven't.
Something that really brings out this problem is the setting. You arrive, after a regrettably brief docking / intro sequence, and are tasked with travelling to a small number of areas aboard a space station in gated, linear order (though you can revisit past places at your leisure). There has been some kind of problem aboard the station, onaboutwhich you are to collect data. On your way you see recorded conversations, read notes, and unlock doors. It should be apparent to most readers that this general premise is extremely well-worn, and sadly there are no new ideas in the story that unfolds before you.
While Event[0] didn’t work as smoothly overall, it went down a more original / creative path... and they got there first. To my mind, it would be an injustice if Tacoma enjoyed more popularity than Event[0] primarily because of its creators’ association with past titles.
Tacoma is worth playing, but barely at half-price when there are so many more ambitious walking simulators out there. This game is more for sci-fi obsessives who need that link to get into walking simulators, or walking simulator obsessives who just want a story and don’t care too much how different or original what they’re playing is.

I love Arma 2: Operation Arrowhead (OA). Its such a improvement from Arma 2. The weapons and battle interface work much better, the graphics are significantly improved and most important to me the towns are much more in-depth. In Arma 2, the large majority of 'cities' were mere towns with no real buildings to enter. Moving is a lot smoother and just a simple rotation of your head or gun has been made smoother. This is not to say that Arma 2 is a bad game, rather that OA is such an improvement. Now the vast majority of buildings are enterable and have rooms, 2nd floors and small walls to surround the outside of a house, making close quarters combat a reality. Its vastly superior to Arma 2, but I believe plays best when bought with Arma 2.
OA also has one other characteristic that makes it appealing- its a cheap alternative to Arma 3. For those of us concerned with single player, the missions and campaign are interesting and fun to play. AI is somewhat intelligent on the team level, but on the individual side it lacks the skill of a human. AI will often move in the open and skyline hills (moving on the top of a hill where it is most visible). This makes them easy to spot and kill. AI infantry is like a poorly skilled human when moving and a decent shot. However, the AI in OA can make tremendous efforts to sieze a city, and in the field of tank combat the AI is as good as any moderatly skilled player.
One last thing that makes OA so appealing is the map. In Arma 2 large forests block your fields of fire and I cant recall any combat taking place at any range greater than 400 meters. In Arma 2 some combat (between tanks mostly) can take place up to 900 meters away (Very cool!). IED's add a lot to the atmostphere of the middle East and UAV's make combat a lot more interesting. The Armory is a lot more interesting with small challenges such as assasination, survival, hunting, defend position, kill house and assualt challenges (and many more).
All in all, Arma 2 OA is a worthwhile game and cant be beat when its on sale. For those of you looking for the Arma experience but are short on cash or unshure of the investment, OA is a very viable option.

I'm not sure exactly what I expected Teslagrad to be.
Having known next to nothing save its name going in, I still had some vague, unshakable idea about what exactly I was in for, and I wasn't too enthusiastic about it. But then I was introduced to the first magnetic mechanic and all I could think was "wow, this is really cool."
That's something I kept thinking again and again as I got higher in the tower that houses the game's levels, with each new area bringing with it a new twist on mechanics I, for whatever reason, had mapped out in my head before even pressing start, It continually and cleverly subverted the concepts I've come to associate with games of its ilk, smartly introducing new mechanics that build upon those that come before, while simultaneously developing a rich medieval steampunk world for me to get lost in.
There's not a single line of dialogue in Teslagrad, be it written or spoken or even just a tutorial, and yet it manages to create this abundantly interesting narrative of a kingdom obsessed yet terrified of technology, and the power it brings with it. Paintings, reenactment cutscenes, and pieces of the environment are used to tell this story subtly, in a way that hides most of its simplicity and had me wanting to find out more about it up until the very end.
Similar methods are used for each gameplay hook, most of which involve manipulating magnetic polarities. Tools are trickled out to you and then liberally experimented with before giving you another to try and work with, which creates an invisible learning curve as you apply what you already know to the new obstacles placed before you. Teslagrad is always conscious of making sure you understand it, and giving you time to figure things out without punishing you for mistakes or taking too long.
That is, except for the boss fights. Though they're likely the coolest moments in the game, these few encounters are rife with tedious and agonizing trial and error death loops, with one hit kills and the complete lack of checkpoints causing them to go on far longer and be much more annoying than they otherwise would be. It's not even that many of the bosses are that hard to defeat once you understand their patterns, but they're so pattern based and often consisting of numerous different parts that you're left with no choice but to die over and over until you've memorized their every move and can play them back exactly. There are a handful of moments like this in various puzzles throughout, which stand out all the more starkly because of how well the rest of the game avoids falling into the same traps.
The inconsistent difficulty was rather a lot more frustrating than I'm making it out to be, but that should also say something about the quality of the game outside of those moments, which I was enjoying so much as to push through the times I was ready to snap my controller in half and curse my reflexes to hell. It's a gorgeous, clearly guided journey in a genre that's become more and more uninspired and cluttered, positioned awkwardly among its less impressive peers that will likely cause it to be passed over in the deluge. And that would be a horrible thing indeed.

English:
A true successor to the series, although I must admit I am somewhat disappointed. It is still as addictive, but it is also still more of a leasure game rather than a simulator. They did manage to combine both Farming Simulator and Woodcutter Simulator into 1 game...but I'm not so sure how I feel about that...
The player takes on the role of a farmer, with substantial equipment and monetary resources already available as you start. As you try to make money you will find that it is pretty hard to go bankrupt, and before you know it you have the fields and equipment that justify the huge farm complex that you start off with. Then you notice that your equipment is getting dirty, which is a great addition to the game, even though it is only a visual effect and does not affect the way equipment is handling.
I have stated in previous versions how the game could really become a proper Farming Simulator, and I have read similar comments in the forums and from other players since, but apparently the developers haven't picked up on that; There is no crop disease, so whatever you put into the ground, it will come out healthy and ready to harvest, always. There is no soil quality, it is always in mint condition and the only purpose for manure and sprayers is to double / triple the yield. On top of that, you start off with a rediculous large farm complex that isnt justified by the 1 - 3 fields you also start off with.
The community has made some interesting mods that solve some of these problems, but I'd rather see them in the vanilla game.
For those that are familiar with the previous versions, here are some nuisances you'll encounter:
First off, remember the PDA? That little device in the bottom-left corner of the screen that showed you a map, demand, livestock info and all that? Ya, you now have to press I which will open an screen and pause the game. This is not much of a problem per se, but do you also remember the phones, where you can get information about just about anything, like a manual? When you interact with that you get a similar screen, but the game continues on the background. Which means that if you don't have the equipment to do something while your crops are growing, you will either have to go on a long strawl or read every page at the payphone; No more checking demand, livestock, etc while you watch your favourite handyman take the wheel of your combine...
All in all a good game, but in my opinion it still does not live up to its name, and the developers seem to have other things on their minds than adding more interesting game mechanics.
Dispite all of this ranting I cannot help but give this a thumbs up, because it is true to its legacy, addictive as hell, and it looks great without ruining the game (hint to Egosoft).

Nederlands:
Een waardige opvolger van de serie, hoewel ik to moet geven dat ik enigszins teleurgesteld ben. Het is nog steeds verslavend, maar ook meer een nutteloos tijdsverdrijf dan een echte simulator. Ze hebben het voor elkaar gekregen om Farming Simulator samen te voegen met hun Woodcutter Simulator...maar ik weet niet hoe ik daar over denk op dit moment...
De speler stapt in de rol van een boer, met veel werktuigen en financiele bronnen beschikbaar al vanaf dat je begint. Terwijl je probeert wat geld te verdienen kom je er snel achter dat het moeilijk is om failliet te gaan, en voor je het weet heb je de velden en de werktuigen die passen bij het formaat van je erf en de gebouwen die er al sinds het begin staan. Dan valt het je op dat je werktuigen vies worden, een goeie toevoeging aan het spel, hoewel dit slechts esthetisch is en geen enkele werking heeft op de werktuigen.
Ik heb in recencies van vorige versies al aangegeven hoe het spel een echte Farming Simulator kan worden, en ik heb sindsdien soortgelijke opmerkingen in forums en recensies van andere spelers gezien, maar blijkbaar hebben de ontwikkelaars daar niets mee gedaan; Je planten kunnen niet ziek worden, dus wat je ook in de grond stopt, het komt er altijd kerngezond uit. Er is geen grondkwaliteit, het is altijd in perfecte staat en het enige doel van de mest en sproeiers is het verdubbelen / verdrievoudigen van je oogst. Daar komt nog bij dat je met een belachelijk grote boerderij begint die niet overeen komt met de 1-3 velden waarme je begint.
Er zijn een aantal interessante mods gemaakt door de spelers die veel van deze problemen oplossen, maar ik zou het spel liever aangepast zien worden zodat het niet nodig zou zijn.
Voor hen die bekend zijn met de vorige versies, hier zijn wat irritaties die je tegen zult komen:
Ten eerste, ken je de PDA nog? Dat kleine apparaatje links ondering je scherm waarop je de kaart, prijzen, je veestapel enzo kon vinden? Ja, die is dus weg. Nu moet je op I drukken om een venster te zien waar datzelfde beschikbaar is, alleen wordt het spel gepauzeerd. Dit is niet per se een probleem, maar herinner je je de telefoons nog waar je informatie over alles kon vinden als een soort handleiding? Als je daar nu gebruik van maakt krijg je een soortgelijk scherm, maar het spel blijft op de achtergrond doorgaan. Dit betekent dat als je geen werktuigen hebt om jezelf mee te vermaken terwijl je velden aan het bloeien zijn je je of dood verveelt terwijl je wacht, een lange wandeling moet gaan maken of elke pagina in de telefoon moet gaan lezen; Niet meer kijken wat de huidige prijzen zijn of het voedsel niveau van je veestapel controleren terwijl je je favoriete knecht achter het stuur van je combine laat.
Al met al een goed spel, maar naar mijn mening is het nog steeds de naam niet waardig, en de ontwikkelaars hebben iets anders aan hun hoofd dat interessante spel mechaniek.
Ondanks al dit geklaag kan ik het niet helpen dit product aan te raden, omdat het in de lijn van de serie valt, verslavend als wat is en er grafisch geweldig uitziet zonder dat dat ten koste gaat van het spel (hint naar Egosoft).

As much as I hate to say it, I can't recommend this game in it's current state.  It just doesn't feel finished, or maybe if feels like content was gutted from it so that expansions can be released.

Pros:
1. Much improved espionage over Civ 5.
2. Virtues add a new dynamic to your interaction with other leaders, and how you approach technology.
3. Satellites also add a new dynamic to how you approach expansion.
4. Quests make things a bit more interesting,
Cons:
1. Boring leaders.  They are all emotionless cardboard cutouts.
2. Tech tree is stupidly convoluted, and looks like it was designed and laid out in game the day before it was released.
There's nearly no flow to it at all if you are trying to persue a particular virtue.
3. Wonders in the game are nearly useless, and seem to make little impact.
4.Tedious trade route managment from BnW is still in the game.
All in all, it's an ok game, but this is my last Civ game that I buy at launch, I'll wait untill the second expansion is out like I did for Civ 5 next time, and I'd suggest anyone who hasn't purchased Beyond Earth yet to wait as well.

There are a lot of aspects about Teslagrad that are great and I really want to like this game more, but there are a few issues keeping me from enjoying it to the fullest extent.
I really feel for the creators because I didn't hear anything about this game until I saw it in the store one day. The whole thing is beautiful, proudly displaying handdrawn visuals and fluid animations. The world you explore is mysterious and begs to be explored and its puzzles solved. The story is told completely through visuals with no dialogue whatsoever which was what got me interested in what Teslagrad was in the first place. The music is suitably ambient and fits the mood well.
The puzzles involve the concept of polarity and opposite attractions. They're fun and satisfying to complete, but...most of them are pretty complex and if you fail anywhere along the way, it's back to the beginning. There's no penalty for dying, but the pain of having to go through the same thing over and over again just to get to the one part that you screwed up on is enough. Boss battles have a similar curse and caused me a lot of frustration. Teslagrad is under appreciated for its beauty, but that beauty comes at a price: your time and patience.

You can't treat Beyond Earth exactly like you did Civilization V, but the apple hasn't fallen far from the tree. If you liked the rest of the Civ series, you'll like Beyond Earth; if you didn't, you won't. It's a cop-out, but nothing I can say here is going to change it.
With that out of the way, there are some fairly clear positive and negative points to be made of the game. The headline feature, the Affinities system, is superbly implemented: even though there are, at its most basic level, three choices, it still feels like you're taking your faction and making it your own, something that CiV's impersonal soldiers never really conveyed.
On the negative side, the shiny new tech web presents, if anything, too much choice. All too often, I find myself paralysed by indecision, something that is happening less as I play more, but still a serious problem the first few times you play. Diplomacy feels very lightweight after Brave New World, and the diplomacy overview is less informative than I'd become accustomed to. And the much-vaunted orbital layer feels underused, with your skies virtually empty for much of the game.
The variety of units in the game swings both ways. There are enough land units to keep things interesting, but only two naval units (a gunboat and an aircraft carrier) and just one aircraft. On water-heavy maps, things get a bit samey, feeling like you're just filling time until the next big land battle. It feels like Firaxis have deliberately left gaps to fill in with an expansion or two further down the line.
And, of course, no matter what it does, Beyond Earth is always going to be living in Alpha Centauri's shadow. The comparisons were inevitable, and Alpha Centauri casts a long, long shadow indeed. Truth told, Beyond Earth doesn't live up to that legacy, but that's because it doesn't try. Beyond Earth is its own thing, just as they've been telling us from day one.
But forget all that. You should get Beyond Earth anyway, because it's just different enough to be really interesting.

It is evident, after spending 18.7 hours with the game, that Civ Beyond Earth was shoved out the door way too early. Don't really understand why, when Civ fanbase is the most patient fanbase I know.
The most egregious example, is the lack of support of HDTV's, or the now infamous "120 Hz resolution problems", a problem that doesn't and didn't exist for ANY other Firaxis product.
My review in just one sentence : The game had a lot of potential and it is evident that developpers had ambitious goals with the title, but when playing the final product, one can't help but feel as if large parts of the game  got hacked out or never finished.
I'll elaborate on that :
For example, there are a lot of technologies and it is fun to explore them, but some technologies only offer one building and an affinity boost and nothing else. It feels  as if a part of the team did their job and the other didn't.
Also, speaking of technologies, the "Tech web" or technology tree is non-intuitive and is nearly impossible to spot out wonders (unless you look closely at the cost of the building).
As other reviewers have pointed out, there is a severe lack of polish (again, this adds to the feeling that BE was rushed) with very few voice over work, lackluster wonders, boring Diplomacy interface and lackluster victory screens.
Also, it seems that some mechanics were rushed (the favor and intrigue mechanic) and didn't reach their full or intended potential. The "favor" mechanic for example, is basically a new currency when trading with an AI. It should help you force trades that would otherwise be impossible or very expensive, but in the end, a favor point basically amounts to about 50 energy. That's it.
I hope future patches or expansion packs will help Beyond Earth reach its full potential, but everyone that has pre-ordered the game, like me, are left dissapointed and most of all frustrated that this game wasn't given more attention/money.
DON'T BUY, wait for a better game and get the (inevitable) GOTY/definitive edition or whatever... and NEVER preorder.

Sparkle 2 Evo. The second part of the "Sparkle-trilogy"; a series of so called "Evolution simulations". I own all three included "games" and I want to review them all.
I have already recommended the first, no, the "Zeroth" (don´t know whether this word exists) part, because of it´s epic looks. Previous point is basically the mark of all three games; epic visuals but, well, questionable gameplay. Evo comes up to those too, but with some changes which disturbed me in some ways. So now I am heading to describe the game a little.
There are just three aims in Sparkle 2 Evo:
Eat, grow, evolve. That´s it. So for this nothing changes. And here comes the publishers´ "clue": Competetive mode. Yes, that´s as hillarious as it sounds. You are "fighting" against an AI in matches lasting WAY too long. The one eats more stuff "wins" and if that´s you, you´ll unlock the next stage, which is basically the same as the previous, just with new colors and soundtracks. Wait, there´s annother way to obtain your progress, next to competetive mode: You can also eat EVERY SINGLE PIECE OF NUTRIENS on the ENTIRE map. Because of the "innovative" controls, that are as precise as my aiming in CS:GO, (trust me, you don´t even want to see me using the AWP) that can easily take you 20 minutes of your precious lifetime. Okay, just joking, but not lying.
Annother negativ fact are the "enemies"... They CONTAIN the nutrients you need to win the level, but there´s always just one way to get them. And if you fail by half a visual milimeter, you´ll be pushed into annother layer of the "Abyss" (that´s what the game-world is called) over and over again... Unfortunately your AI oponnent has better luck with that.
The only two things GOOD about this game are the visuals, as usual, and the fact you get the soundtrack for free. It´s not a extraordinary good one but at least a nice deal to compensate the EULA, which only says "No EULA, just have fun"...

They didn´t do a bad job (in relation to the other two games) but they also didn´t really make it better. What's there to be said more about the beloved classic The Stanley Parable? NOTHING! What can I possibly add to the tower of praise this game has received since its release? NOTHING!
I read, and I watch film, to a sickening extent. Seldom do I encounter a narrative that delivers a reaction such as this. This is a story that a videogame can only tell, no other medium can do it. The story is the game-play, for once, a narrative within a videogame is the soul mechanic the player’s left to toy with. This game is like a bug in a box that you poke, in order to derive entertainment from its reactions. I guarantee you'll laugh or you'll be shocked. If you aren't, well then I believe I have done a miss-service to the game by saying that you’ll encounter either of the two emotions, thus is the human minds nature to try to suppress a feeling it's told it will feel. This game will make you feel something, make you think about something, and for once in your life you should at least feel something. This game is a statement, no matter how vulgar thoughts that word may incite, it holds truth. I believe too many times have I slit a throat, and shot someone’s brains along the ground behind them and felt nothing but "Okay now I can get to point 'X'," within a game world of course. This game showed me that I could have any emotion churned up from something other than death and violence and inane humour, because I know I will react to them, and thus I don't. As I said before, you won’t feel those feelings because you're told you will feel them, and that explains the attitude towards all excessive consumption of media. I devour as much 'media' as I can, to the point where I've become a junkie, and only that which stands out can give me a kick, give my nervous system a shimmy. This game told me to stop expecting so much and to expect a lot more, but at the same to time realise that there's only these experiences can do.
Get the game.
Then go play something else.

Torchlight is an excellent old-school-style hack-n-slash action-RPG that is very reminiscent of Diablo and Diablo 2. Developer Runic Games was co-founded by Max Schaefer, Erich Schaefer, Peter Hu (veterans of Blizzard North and Flagship) and Travis Baldree (lead developer of Fate and Mythos), and in my opinion they have improved and expanded upun the classic Diablo gameplay style. Anyone who loved those games will feel right at home here.. it sports (among other things) randomized dungeon layouts and enemy spawns, unique bosses and mini-bosses, weapon and armor loot drops that are color-coded by rarity, and music composed by sound designer Matt Uelmen that further cements the Diablo feel. All told, yes, this game is very much like the classic Diablo games.. but if you played and loved those titles, how can that possibly be a bad thing?

Do I use this skill point to be better at Persuasion, Streetwise, or Impersonate? I can't get past the guards by bluffing and I can't win in the fight against them.
I need to buy something to charge this respirator I spent 500 gold on for a quest. If I sell everything I find, it'll only raise maybe 50 gold since my Trade skill is so low. I'm sorry to not recommend this game, but I'm definitely interested to see what this studio comes out with next. Maybe I'll play a demo version if it's available.

tl;dr - Good concept executed poorly
Pros:
+ Unique concept with main gimmick fleshed out well
+ No tutorials (not necessary)
+ Good progression of design
Cons:
- Sloppy controls
- Too much replaying necessary to complete a level
- Difficulty is all over the place
The basis of the game is it's a puzzle platformer with a strong action portion. You must get to the end of the level, and more requirements are necessary to get there as the levels progress from defeating enemies and unlocking areas. More mechanics are gradually introduced, often shocking you at first but nearly immediately becoming easy to understand so no tutorials are necessary. The mechanic of revealing the platforms around you is done as well as I'd like it to be done, and as the main gimmick I feel it was a strong point, however....
After the first boss the difficulty increases dramatically. This however is a nice change from the fairly easy preceeding levels. After the second boss, the difficulty changes for the worse, making most levels just a matter of memorizing the exact second to jump, trying to ignore the constant screen shaking from enemies and ink splattering, and trying your hardest to do everything frame perfect. Combined with the inertia and sloppy controls, it makes it more frustrating than fun. Combined with heat seeking missles that are faster than you, it becomes a real chore. The final boss was a good design, however how to damage it seemed inconsistent - what would hurt it one time kills you another with no discernable reason as to why. There is some replay value as there's a hidden item in (seemingly) each level, however I would not be inclined to play through again to collect them.

I've been looking for a FTP MMO to scratch the WoW itch for a number of years. Having a subscription meant that I felt like I HAD to play WoW to get that money's worth, which was a big part of the addiction for me. I convinced myself (hitting rock-bottom may have had something to do with it) that cancelling my sub and waiting for WoW to go FTP was the only course of action. That was many years ago. In that time, I have played GW2, Tera, Wildstar, the Perfect World, ESO, LOTR Online, Star Trek Online, SWTOR, Aion, the list goes on. If it's an MMO, I've played it, in the hopes of filling that void that WoW left. Nothing even clame close to comparing.
Then I came across Riders of Icarus. I started a Guardian class, and I fell in love. I got the feels, the dreams of the game while I slept, waking only to think about strats and what I would accomplish in game that day. I joined a guild and met people that actually helped, and were happy to give up their time to grind dungeons with me. I began to scour wikipedia to learn as much as I could about this game, and became a wealth of knowledge to my guildmates. Finding ways to counter botters in-game, memorizing locations of rare spawns, bosses and item drops. I found ways to farm gold and crafting mats. I found ways to profit on the AH. Days went by, 3 days after the game's release, I'd amassed 36 hours of game time. I was hooked. I'd found my WoW replacement; hell, in ways it was beginning to outshine WoW. But best of all? It's free to play.
Yes, it's a Nexon game. Just don't make purchases with real currency in-game, and you won't have any issues. (It's FTP anyway, serves pay to winners right).
Yes, botters are a problem, but you can create your own channel, and specify what displays in that channel. As for bots camping spawns, the system works on first hit. The bot timers for this are good, but not perfect. Just get the first hit in through spamming your auto-attack. Changing channels also works for this most times.
Yes, the quests are mostly kill x, gather x, escort x, but at no point did I become bored, at no point did the grind become tedious.
As I've progressed through the game, I've been repeatedly impressed by the difficulty of it. I've marvelled at the beauty of the scenery around me. I've experienced little to no lag (a miracle for an Aust player) I've grown attached to Elite pets and mounts that I've sought out and tamed, I've been saddened at saying goodbye to pets and mounts that had outlived their usefulness or been made redundant by better, stronger, faster mounts, with higher HP and Energy pools.
But my journey has only just begun.
I'm moving interstate for work IRL, and the week between moving out of the house that I currently occupy and the house that I'm moving to before I can access stable internet again will be difficult to endure. But I will be back. I will return to this amazing world, and I will grow stronger. I haven't even come close to discovering all that this game has to offer, and I can only imagine the lands and content that await me when I return.
Visuals: 9.5/10
Gameplay: 8.5/10
Story: 9/10
Overall: 9/10 - It's Free to Play, what are you waiting for? Download it and see for yourself.

I played through this game 2-3 times (offline, did not register as "hours on record") and it has an interesting enough story, but it is absolutely broken from a gameplay-design standpoint.   You MUST cheat to actually progress the story, so it is a complete waste of time.  The creators clearly miscalculated what it should take to move things along when they initially wrote the game and are too disinterested to go back through and fix it.
You MUST cheat no matter how your character is specced.  If you do not cheat then you will search high and low for a door through which your type of character can progress the story and find that there simply is not one.  You will start over fresh and try a different type of charater only to encounter a different brick wall through.  I have seen the responses to critical posts that try to defend the game by stating "it's supposed to be hard and high-stakes and you have to specialize to finish the game.  You just aren't used to it because modern games let you max out all skills and 100% the game with a single character."  This is a smokescreen. This is misdirection to persuade potential buyers to ignore the criticism and buy it anyway.
Functionally-speaking, the game is divided into separate chapters or acts like Diablo 2 and presented to you as locations or towns that you travel to and perform quests when you arrive.  The problem is that you can not actually complete the quests that you are assigned.  If you specialize your class, stats, and skills to be someone that does not engage in combat, you will not be able to progress the story because you'll be forced to walk down a particular path where you will always get attacked and there is no opportunity to talk or bribe your way out of it.  If you specialize in a combat character you will find that you will be unable to progress past a step on a quest where you must recruit this guy or persuade that guy.  When you try a balanced character you will be unable to progress past either of those steps.
However, you can unlock the next town long before you actually finish the quests for the chapter that you're stuck on.  Just go on to the next town and do some stuff to get your specs, stats, and gear boosted then backtrack and finish the quests so you can progress the story, right?  WRONG. As soon as you leave it auto-completes nearly every quest you had at that town.  When you go back and talk to the NPC's they're talking at you referencing things that you did and you have no idea what they're talking about. They are referencing the later steps of the quests that you were unable to complete beacuse you got stuck!  It doesn't make any sense.  You're praised for deciding things a certain way when you were never even presented with that decision.
Imagine playing Diablo 2 and you reach the end of the second to last act and just have to beat the boss that guards the path to hell.  The door to the boss room is locked and you have three options to get in the room, all of which is impossible if you are specced in any of the ways that would have allowed you to get to this point in the game.  You decide to just go to the last act and complete some minor side quests in hell to spec up.  You return to the 2nd to last act so that you can defeat the boss that blocks the path to the last act.  When you arrive at the 2nd to last act everyone is complimenting how you defeated the boss behind the door that you were never able to get through.
It's even worse that only certain cities on the map will trigger this automatic quest-finish thing and there is little indication ahead of time which locations are safe and which ones will break all your quests. Since this problem denies you the quest rewards that you need to level up your character, this only breaks the game more and more because you seem to be falling further and further behind the spec requirements that the game assumes that you have once you reach a certain point in the storyline.

RaceRoom Racing Experience a competent simulator with decent graphics and ongoing support.  Online play is relatively well populated.  Physics are somewhat forgiving.  Sounds are loved by many.  However, the DLC system represents a clear yearly money grab with only the latest cars getting true updates.  For that reason alone (new DLC outdating old DLC purchases) I cannot recommend this game.  It gets an Uncommon rating.
-edit-
RaceRoom Racing Experience recently had an update to their triple monitor support and a physics update for GT3 cars.  With that, I gave the game a second go.  I have to admit that my impression has changed.  The physics impressed me, the graphics looked better than I remembered, and the triple monitor support (which supports screens of different sizes) is really quite amazing.  I still have reservations about their annual DLC output of various car series.  It's a system that makes prior purchases irrelevant, and that's not ok.  That being said, there are series you can buy that don't suffer the same fate.  The tracks are never outdated.  And their implementation of DLC (where you can race against other players and AI in cars you don't own from a series) is really one of the best in the industry.
Overall, I'd bump it's rating to Rare from it's previous Uncommon.  The only downsides for me now, are the annual DLC releases (updates released as full paid iterative series) and lack of structured online competition akin to iRacing.  Though they do have their competitions, which helps to some degree (though it's basically hotlapping).

The best Trading Card Game in any medium, period.
A blend of traditional TCG with features only available in the digital medium to achieve a depth of tactics and strategy that is simply unparralled. Add in that this game is ridiculously affordable for a TCG and can be played for free while still amassing a large card collection.
Magic definitely has richer, deeper, card library (as is to be expected) but in the playing of the game the tactical choices are both more numerable and more impactful. Out is the feeling of being beat by a more expensive deck or being screwed by a bad mana draw. In is the feeling that strong choices can overcome better decks or bad draws.
Hearthstone has a super polished presentation and fantasic developer but after that Infinity War has it beat on every front. So much so that there really is no reason to compare the two, it is like checkers and chess. I compare it to Hearthstone because the developer support has been Infinity Wars' biggest issue.
Infinity Wars' had a fatal flaw, however. The developers had begun a game they lacked the resources to maintain and grow. The bug list was/is extensive. Many promised features had been shelved. The game seemed to have been abandoned and the player count began to decay. I stopped playing for months at a time. I would not have recommended investing in this game at all but everything has changed.
A new partnership has been announced (information on the game's forums) and suddenly this game has surged forward again. The main bugs are being tackled and a new plan to relaunch the game is underway. Players are returning and optimism is high. This game is a gem. It is the best TCG I've played and every replacement I've looked for since has left me unfulfilled.
While the game still needs a lot of polish and improvment, the new injection of engery and resources from the developers has my hopes high. Try it for free. Play the rather basic campaign mode. Trial some of the free decks in pvp. I think a lot of you will agree:
This is the best puffy TCG ever made.

Что такое Shadow Warrior? По сути, это шутер в духе Serious Sam, Painkiller и прочих шутеров, суть которых заключается в бесконечном отстреле напирающих сил вражин.
Shadow Warrior - это:
+ Игра про крутого ниндзя, который налево и направо рубит на кровавый фарш демонов под довольно забористую и хорошую музыку.
+ Интересная система ведения боя катаной, с различными способностями, ударами и финатми.
+ Все это сопровождается обилием кровища, кишок, расчлененки, неполиткорретных шуток и черного юмора, огромного количества отсылок как к олдскульным играм подобного жанра, так и к олдовым боевикам.
+ Плюс система прокачки, благодаря которой мы учим больше приемов для нашей катаны, изучаем магию и новые смертоносные навыки, становимся сильнее и смертоноснее.
Звучит хорошо. Вот только больше хорошего я об игре сказать ничего не могу.
Ибо кроме этого у нас здесь имеется:
- Отвратительная механика стрельбы, как и все стрелковое оружие, из-за чего катана - единственное оружие в этой игре, которым можно нормально играть и убивать врагов.
- Локации очень унылы, скучны, однообразны. Абсолютные одинаковые коридоры
- Отвратительная цветовая гамма, из-за чего на экране все сливается в одну, одноцветную кашу, с миллионом засветов, вспышек, из-за чего просто не понимаешь че происходит. Такое чувство, что какой-то абсолютно мерзотнейший светофильтр врубили
- Все бои однообразны и скучны. Враги тупы, и даже на "Безумии"(4-ый уровень сложности, из 4-х доступных в начале) не представляют проблем. Бегай, руби, бегай, лечись, бегай, руби. Повторять до бесконечности.
Поймите меня правильно: я обожаю подобные шутеры. Мне очень нравится Серьезный Семен и Дум. Я люблю такие "тупые" шутаны, где необходимо толпами валить врагов. Вот только в вышеуказанных играх это интересно, приятно и круто, а здесь скучно, уныло, однообразно и неитересно. И поэтому эту игру я не прошел, и проходить не буду. I somewhat like this game, but because of the large amount of positive feedback compared to how many problems I've found in the game, I'm marking this review not-recommended. It's not that I wouldn't recommend it, it's just that this game might disappoint you.
Because of its art style, I thought that it would match it with its gameplay's genre, such as it being a 2-D puzzle platformer. And it is, but... It's also a rage game. A die-and-restart-until-you-win-in-one-run-er, with some vertical if-you-fall-you-have-to-go-back-all-the-way-up-again levels, on top of having a ton of random-obstacles-or-projectiles-which-can-only-be-dodged-after-you-die-finding-their-functions filled sections. It's not that it's bad (well, though I'd like to say that, it left me with a stale frown during the second boss fight), it's just that it doesn't match up at all with its story's theme or art style.
Oh yeah, those two parts are pretty good. You play as a highly flammable kleptomaniac who is being chased by Santa Claus and his gang of Russians through a tower filled with aliens and robots, with abilities Magneto would probably be used to make a pun with if I knew more about DC Comics or whatever. The story's alright, and its world is pretty logically put together, but it doesn't have anything too great to marvel at. Marvel. Wait a second...
Anyway, to put its presentation quick, the art style met my expectations, but the soundtrack isn't that memorable. And finally, as I said before, even though I've marked this review as not recommended, it still has its good points gameplay-wise. The mechanic to manipulate magnetic energy is really unique, and can confuse you as you forget whether blue+blue=attract or blue+red=attract, or maybe I'm just an idiot. And even though it mostly has elements from the rage-game genre, it's also a puzzle-platformer which has metroid-like elements in its level design, making it a pretty unique experience. It isn't entirely a puzzle game as its art style implied, but it's still good. That is, if you can tolerate being kicked to the beginning every time you mess up.

You need to read paragraph after paragraph of information as you explore and are given bits at a time. Now you might say. "But Damuel, what about Dark Souls? It doesn't spoon feed you the story and you would be lost without a lot of reading!". Well here's the difference. Final Fantasy gives you practically a NOVELs worth of information, and the game shoves story references down your throat left and right that will leave you absolutely confused without reading. And it's not like there's any thought, it's just that you're basically given a book that you need to have to even remotely follow along.
But how about the characters? Oh boy, Lightning is my waifu, so pretty. Shame she's an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥ for no reason, and the supporting cast isn't much better. You have Snow, your typical do-gooder, he's absent for a good portion of the game, but he's somewhat likable if perhaps a bit too generic of a "hero" type character. You have Hope, a whiny child who constantly is afraid of things and silently spits on everyone else. You have Vanille, an annoying tween girl who has been overly sexualized both in game and in the stacks of rule 34 online, possibly the most annoying character of all time in FF. Bad VO, bad script, terrible fighter, and just nothing redeeming. The two remaining characters barely have an appearance but they're decent. Sazh is amusing and an alright supporting character but he's barely ever seen. Fang is just super generic strong female character, nothing special.
The visuals were nice for its time but they're♥♥♥♥♥now. Everything is super jagged and the animations are stiff. It's not HORRIBLE, but it would have been nice to get some HD textures at least for the PC release. The CGI is nice though.
Combat system is garbage. The only practical way to fight is to use the autobattle, otherwise things take too long. Basically push A/X to win. Shifting is okay but gets VERY tiresome at times. It's basically the game's class system and you need to switch classes constantly mid fight. At times it gets frustrating to switch back and forth between every other attack. Personally I liked the old fashioned turn based fighting of the pre FF12 games.
The game is SUPER linear. A lot of the FF games are but this one takes it to the next level. The TUTORIAL is over 10 hours long. You can't change your party members (Yes, even if visually you have a crew of 5 people with you, you're forced to play with the three the game wants you to play with) or pick what classes they use until the 'tutorial' is over. What a horrible design choice.
That all being said... The game IS Final Fantasy. It has pretty CGI, the story is decent if you don't mind a TON of reading, and most of the issues gameplay wise are in comparison to the previous games. It's still a very solid JRPG for 15 bucks, though I wouldn't pay more than 10 these days for it. The game clocks in at around 20-30 hours depending on how much you're willing to grind.
Edit: I guess I should mention, the game gets A LOT better after the 'tutorial'. But it will take most people between 10-20 hours to actually get through it. And that's unacceptable. There's a good game underneath all the garbage, but we shouldn't have to play through for 10 HOURS to get to the fun stuff. The characters are more likable, the game is less linear, there's side content, and you can FINALLY play with the people you want (besides a few fights). It almost turns into a true final fantasy game.

Teslagrad is a fun action platformer with absolutely amazing artwork that makes it a joy to play and power through the minor frustrations that are present.
To elaborate, these minor frustrations were that the controls felt more complex than what I'm used to and took me a while to master. You end up getting three distinct abilities in the game, but two of those take up two buttons each (positive and negative magnetism), which ended up proving a challenge in some areas.
Part of that challenge comes from the fact that you have one life, no health bar. There are boss fights in the game, and though the first three passed by fast and easily, the last two felt rather punishing because it wasn't always clear to me how to deal with certain attack patterns and upon failing to understand them, I'd immediately have to start from the beginning.
But again, these are minor frustrations. For how frustrating having to restart a boss fight because of one single mistake could feel, they still were very fun. Especially the fourth fight was one of the most satisfying and well designed bosses I've come across in a while and kept throwing surprises at you.
There is some backtracking involved if you want to go for a 100% completion (and I would recommend you do, it's definitely worth it!), as is the norm for metroidvanias. But by the time you reach that point, you'll be able to do so very fast. Furthermore, the collectible items are hidden in a fair way - there are no walls you can unexpectedly pass through; instead clear but subtle visual cues tell you where to look or attempt to go.
Finally, I feel I should adress that I've called the game an action platformer rather than a puzzle platformer. The reason for that is that though occasionally you'll need to turn on your brain when trying to figure out how to get to places or defeat a boss, the puzzles never felt like the focus to me (unlike in games such as Braid, Fez or The Swapper) - even having figured out the solution, you still need to have the dexterity to pull it off too.
But yeah, if metroidvanias are your kinda thing, get Teslagrad. It's atmospheric and gorgeous; and though it's a bit hard at times, it's also very satisfying and fun. To some, it might feel too short, to me its length (~7 hours) felt perfect. I'll take a short game that constantly feels fresh and exciting over a game that outstays its welcome any day.

What's there to be said more about the beloved classic The Stanley Parable? NOTHING! What can I possibly add to the tower of praise this game has received since its release? NOTHING!
I read, and I watch film, to a sickening extent. Seldom do I encounter a narrative that delivers a reaction such as this. This is a story that a videogame can only tell, no other medium can do it. The story is the game-play, for once, a narrative within a videogame is the soul mechanic the player’s left to toy with. This game is like a bug in a box that you poke, in order to derive entertainment from its reactions. I guarantee you'll laugh or you'll be shocked. If you aren't, well then I believe I have done a miss-service to the game by saying that you’ll encounter either of the two emotions, thus is the human minds nature to try to suppress a feeling it's told it will feel. This game will make you feel something, make you think about something, and for once in your life you should at least feel something. This game is a statement, no matter how vulgar thoughts that word may incite, it holds truth. I believe too many times have I slit a throat, and shot someone’s brains along the ground behind them and felt nothing but "Okay now I can get to point 'X'," within a game world of course. This game showed me that I could have any emotion churned up from something other than death and violence and inane humour, because I know I will react to them, and thus I don't. As I said before, you won’t feel those feelings because you're told you will feel them, and that explains the attitude towards all excessive consumption of media. I devour as much 'media' as I can, to the point where I've become a junkie, and only that which stands out can give me a kick, give my nervous system a shimmy. This game told me to stop expecting so much and to expect a lot more, but at the same to time realise that there's only these experiences can do.

The core mechanics are simple, surfaces are invisible until you or enemies touch them, or when you squirt ink from your double jump. Also, when you die, you release a burst of ink, and previously colored surfaces remain, so death isn't so punishing (and the levels are generally pretty short). You can also wall jump, and your double jump resets when you touch a wall or the ground (but not enemies).
The levels start off as simple as possible, but they get tricky by the end. Not Meatboy level hard, but difficult enough that you feel like you've earned it when you reach the exit.
The biggest appeal of INK seems to me the aesthetic. For as bold as the colors are, I find it rather soothing, and the music is fairly relaxing too.
The game might be on the short side, depending how good you are at platformers. I managed to make it through the 75 levels in just about as many minutes, although there is replay potential, as many (most? all?) of the levels have a hidden coin to find and collect as an extra challenge beyond basic completion, and there achievements for making it through without dying.
This game is made by the makers of Diablo 1 and 2, and therefore feels very similar, but it shines above with newer graphics and game mechanics.

Fullbright has done it again.  Tacoma is utterly beautiful - not just visually but in every single part of it.  Not a single detail has gone un-thought-of in this game.  The polish is exceptional.
The story is interesting and the method of narrative is unusual and intriguing, the visual design is cohesive and enjoyable, the voice acting is excellent, the level design is absolutely top shelf stuff, the animations are filled with little organic details that make them stand out even when they're deceptively simple in design,  A tiny detail that absolutely thrilled me was the way all the characters (in their holographic ghost form even) have different body shapes!!
Sure, it's not a long game - my first playthrough (which was hardly exhaustive considering how many achievements I haven't gotten!) took about three hours.  But it's exactly the right length for what it is.  It's a self contained experience and I was not left wanting in any capacity.  If it was any longer it would be bloated with padding.
As Fullbright's second game after Gone Home, it completely lives up to expectations, and I can't wait to see what the studio does next.

This game is cool.  I really admire the clear and obvious influence of "grim n' gritty" fantasy authors like Glen Cook, Micheal Moorcock, Scott Lynch, etc on this game.  Much like the works of those writers, AoD is a refreshing alternative in a crowded genre dominated by crappy imitators of Tolkien.  For those of you familiar with tabletop RPGs, this game takes less influence from D&D, and more from RuneQuest and other BRP-games (Call of Cthulhu, Stormbringer).
Now as far as being a game goes, AoD is a mixed bag, but for something that is basically the product of one dude, it's impressive.  There are a fair amount of bugs, and if you choose to use combat, it's, well far more unpredictable then one would reasonably expect, at best.  Basically what I'm saying is that it's like an uncut diamond. In spite of those shortcomings, I really enjoyed the game. The developer has the right ideas, and I'm looking forward to his next venture.

What I dislike it the catering to specific playstyles. Their defensive playstyle and alt wincons have been attacked again and again, as has the standard control faction: Cult of Verore. I really liked Gone Home when I played it, so right off the bat I was interested to see what Fullbright would do next, so I pre-ordered Tacoma as soon as it was available.
The game play of Tacoma is pretty much identical to Gone Home, in that you are walking around the environment finding information about the situation you find yourself in. In both games you do a lot of reading and listening to audio logs. In Tacoma you have a larger cast of characters that you are watching/listening to in augmented reality with the ability to pause and rewind to move about conversations that are happening around the space.
Story wise, I preferred Gone Home as it was a more personal experience, in that you are a member of the family that the story is about. In Tacoma, you are a 3rd party that comes in after the events, and are just viewing what is happening to the characters.
You learn about the characters both through the audio logs and written logs, be it emails, private messages or notes strewn throughout their crew cabins. You never really get invested in the characters though, because you spend so little time on each one. It took me about 2.5 hours to play through the game at a leisurely pace.
The sci-fi aspect is a little weak, but to be fair to the game, it's meant to be more about the characters and how they are dealing with the situation, rather than the situation itself. But to me it doesn't really accomplish it that nearly as well as Gone Home did.
The biggest shortfall of Tacoma is the length. You don't have enough time to get to know the characters, and that is crucial for a story driven game like this. Even reading all the text, it just doesn't give you enough to really get to know the characters.
Well I guess it comes down to whether or not I would recommend it. When I started writing this review(about 40 minutes ago now, I'm a very indecisive writer) I was sure that I would come out of it recommending it, but now that I have had some time to actually think about it, I'm not sure if I can.
If you really like the genre, or even just really like Gone Home and want to see what the follow up is like, sure check it out once it goes on sale. If you have never played a game in this genre before, look elsewhere for you first foray into the so called 'walking simulator' genre.

Beautifully written and artfully constructed. From first entering Tacoma to finally leaving the station I was intrigued and immersed. The characters are engaging, each with their own tidbits of backstory, and the dialogue and story never felt forced or overdone like some other narrative games.
If a good plot and an air of intrigue are what you look for in a game, then Tacoma will fill that need very well.
Things that I wish had been improved or expanded on are the "puzzle" aspects of the game and the graphics for the holograms. The codes for some of the doors were hidden in clever ways, but these are few and far between. I wish there had been more locked areas with increasingly challenging codes for me to discover. Also, I know this is probably a petty gripe all in all, but during each AR playback I was increasingly distracted by the holograms lined-through bodies and hands. And I know if I was noticing it a lot someone else is too.
But despite these qualms I very much reccomend Tacoma, and will be replaying it many times over.

As you can see I have put in a bit of time on this game. It is fun. If you are tired of the simplicity and repetitiveness of meta card games like Hearthstone and MTG, then this might be the breath of fresh air you are looking for. Infinity Wars' mechanics are complex, it will take you a couple hours to get used to how some abilities work, and how the board layout works. The way you play and how you play are unique to IW, and I love it. I've played a lot of hearthstone and I've seen a lot of the same decks OVER AND OVER AND OVER again. This game will not do that, at least not to the extent of other games. Every strong deck archetype has a counter, and each archetype can be played in different ways.
The mental game is also unlike any other card game. Guessing what your opponent will do with what he has in play is a big part of being good at IW, and I think that is a huge plus and adds a lot to the game.
