Sparkle 2 Evo... Just a Flow clone?
Many people say and think this is a Flow clone, I personally have never played Flow, nor have I watched videos so that will not be influencing this review.
Sparkle 2 Evo is about a three hour long game, where you control a microorganism where your goal is to eat to evolve. What you evolve into depends on WHAT you eat, so eating red makes you a carnivore, blue an omnivore, and green an herbivore. Depending on which of the three you become you get special little extra stats, for example the carnivore being the fastest. What you eat ranges from bits of food floating around, to giant squids fifty times your size. Also, each animal you eat requires a specific tactic to beat, for example, using the tactic that’s used on a glass squid wouldn’t work on a skeleton, which makes the latter levels in the game more interesting, and creates some great, well thought out boss battles. There’s also an GenLab, so you can see which of the three traits you use the most, and what your current bonuses are (developers said you can use the lab to change your creature, leading to people believing you're supposed to do it in the GenLab, but they were more getting at the fact that you can change your creature based on what you eat). There’s also a competitive mode where you try to eat more than the opposing AI, fun but not too interesting.
A lot of complaints come from this game 'not looking good' or being pixelated, and not having the option to change resolutions. Well, don’t listen to those, because you can adjust resolutions, and it can look damn near perfect on the highest settings. With that having been said, the visuals are beautiful, absolutely just full of vibrant colors, and this may actually be my favorite part of this game. Various corals, and other large debris define the maps, and change depending on the depths of the levels, and location, which I think can be really good at times. The music, well, isn’t amazing. It’s not BAD, but could have used a little more variety.
Now for the problems, this game is buggy as heck. One of the more infamous glitches causes you to not be able to progress any further on a boss battle you just spent eight minutes trying to beat, forcing you to restart, and possibly having you do it a third time. Another major bug was a missing species that was required to be killed for an achievement, but recently this has been patched. The last bug I’m going to mention is when the keys stop working. Yes, they completely stop, even when you exit to the main menu and the level reloaded, they still won’t work, forcing you to shut down the game and restart it. And the biggest problem in the game, you can’t be hurt. Did a creature ten times your size just bite you? Well, better throw you up towards the surface then. This completely removes any urgency in the game, making it more boring than it should be (entertaining nonetheless).
Pros:
beautiful visuals
complex evolution system
good boss battles (sometimes boring though)
Cons:
bugs, glitches, etc.
controls are… off
your “compass” is confusing at first
cant take damage
I would recommend waiting for this game to go on sale (as it often does) if you get it.

Score (if the three mentioned bugs were removed): 7/10

It’s not that this game don’t have its merits, I see many things in its core that I really like.
It reminds me from the time I would play actual RPG with my friends, where role play mattered and the story and decisions were key to the game. This game brings a bit of that feeling back, which lacks in almost all computer RPGs.
Unfortunately it reminds also the games we played under a mean (normally unexperienced) GM, which confuses punishing with challenging, and scrapping meagre XP with accomplishment.
In my play through AoD with a cleaver silver tong scammer girl, I thought I could talk my way through anything, and it actually feels like it in some moments. Soon I started to see myself forced to learn lore and crafting, as apparently talking someone else to do her bidding didn’t occur to her, but I like mages and realise my hopes are just too high for a game... so OK.
At this point all was well, my cleaver manipulator with the knowledge of an evil genius would cross through spike pits as gentlemen would offer their own body for her to step on to protect the lady (in my imagination, as this doesn’t really happens in the game).
The first sign of trouble came with a particular fiscal feat that would require diving in putrid water. Apparently my clever Alexa Luthor would do this for a questionable man that asked. I went with the story and as it’s reasonable to expect her physical traits fell a bit short. I thought to myself “why suddenly the best solution in her mind is to do it herself?” – Brick wall. This character won’t be able to get it done.
Shortly after: another physical fit. While blinded by the “weather conditions” I couldn’t shake the feeling that this was more like a task for my minions… but hey, one cannot have everything, and she didn’t have the strength. – Brick wall.
At this point I was already questioning allot of things and looking over the internet about those same challenges, and apparently consistently players with characters based on soft skills get very frustrated whit a series of brick walls were the story seems to need the warrior stereotype. I particularly like the posts of this fellow that would argue the only solution for his problem was counter intuitive for his character, and he could not get himself to do it: like killing the golden eggs hen. I sympathise with the same hen.
Now I started looking more and more into it, and I realised the places I was looking forward to explore were locked, because somewhere 10+ game hours ago I choose the most significant option B over option A, and because of that the item for this thing that I didn’t even know existed never unlocked and never will. The dev offered an alternative, and if I only read the instructions over the internet and ignore my character’s story which I’ve been developing over all this time, I can still get through one or two of the many brick walls.
I see people saying things like: “This is a hard game, that’s why.” and “You cannot reasonably expect that any person with any set of skills can do everything.”
Well my friend, breaking rocks with a pickaxe is hard, and you don’t see people running to do it because it’s fun. Challenge is fun, when people are given the opportunity to overcome and are rewarded for that.
What is the challenge of a role playing game? To play the role through tough decisions.
This game has it sometimes, but other times it breaks it.
Regarding the second claim, that not everyone can do everything… well, obviously! That’s why most people buy their cheese at the supermarket other than make it in an old bath in the backyard shaft, and that’s also why a master manipulator with deep pockets gets people to do their bidding, instead of taking (and failing) the physical challenges themselves.
I have to mention that the most annoying thing about this game for me is the continuous claim that if you fight people, you should expect to lose. That the real world is brutal, and the odds are against you. Well, truth is that from my perspective in the game characters specialised in combat get the best rewards and bit all most significant challenges. Check the Steam achievements and you’ll find encouragement to the player to fight and kill everyone in a particular town… a town with two military factions full of soldiers. WTF?!
To be fair, the standards the devs are trying to hold themselves to is something very rare to be seen. The last I remember Fallout and Fallout 2 did it well some 20 years ago, and I'm still waiting to see it happening again.
If you are willing to endure poor graphics and text boxes, I recommend Neverwinter Nights or Knight of the Old Republic, it’s more fun than AoE.

So far this is my favourite game of 2017.
Here's why.
I feel that Hollow Knight understands the genre of metroidvania and stands true to its principles, perhaps the best of any game I've played recently. The lack of direction, absence of pointers and plot arrows, some may find frustrating and boring, for me transforms this game from a mere platformer to a real wonder of exploration. Never knowing what's beyond the door, or where this corridor leads and most importantly wondering if you even should go there removes this annoying feeling of being pandered to. Never during my time with Hollow Knight, not even once had I thought that this world was built for me to explore. It was simply there. Alien, bizarre, sometimes charming and sometimes unsettling.
The storyline, too, emerged naturally from my experience instead of being shoved down my throat by helpful NPCs and narrators. Up until very late in the game I'd been just another traveler, an adventurer, one of many. I was the protagonist of my story, sure, but not the Main Character of this universe.
It's not easy to create a living, breathing world, full of its own wonders and tragedies, the world that invites you to be a part of it, but doesn't push you into the limelight. This, I think is the main strength of Hollow Knight.
And it's accompanied by an interesting upgrade system, that allows you to mix and match various Charms, thus creating combinations of upgrades and finding synergies that work best for any given situation and your personal playstyle. As for other mechanics - they are fairly traditional for the genre: a variety of moves (dashes, jumps, etc.) that are unlocked as you explore the caverns of Hallownest and they in turn allow you to access new uncharted territories. These moves are supplemented by different attacks, both physical and magical, learned, again at various places and from different NPCs.
In other reviews I've noticed some criticism for controls in the game, them being called "clunky" or such. For me personally controls been nothing but responsive and smooth. I've been playing on keyboard, and, perhaps, the only thing that I routinely messed up was downward/upward slash, but even that, I suspect, was my own fault. Fights I've found to be quite enjoyable, although micropauses on clashes (or being hit) could be shorter as sometimes they messed with my timing.
Another commonly criticized aspect is save points, particularly the fact that they are too few and far between, thus making the "walk of shame" after dying too long and dangerous. This, I feel is a matter of taste, so I won't argue, but here's a couple of things to consider:
1) Nearly every dangerous fight in the game is either heavily signalled (e.g. a big empty chamber with doors on each side of it) or can be escaped
2) Soul (or energy or mana) can be spent to heal up between fights or even during them. And if you don't have any, nobody stops you from going back to a save point to rest and recover.
3) Aside from a couple of points Hollow Knight is a non-linear game. If you feel that you're in over your head, perhaps try turning back and exploring some other corner of the map.
4) Again, a matter of taste, but if you enjoy the combat then even retracing your steps and fighting the same enemies will be fun.
Also, true to the ideals of Dark Souls you lose all your currency when you die and to get it back you must get to your body. This, however, is not strictly necessary. First of all there are some sellable items that you do not lose on death. And second - by the end of the game I had 30+ thousands of coins with nothing to spend them on. Probably more than combined price of all the items in the game. Losing you money is really not that big of a deal. Just don't forget to spend them every once in a while. [Correction: this has been remedied by the Grimm Troupe patch that added a big money sink.]
I could sing accolades to the aesthetic, music and character designs all day, but all this you can see for yourself in trailers and gameplay. My opinion: they are gorgeous.
Bottom line is: I definitely recommend you this game if you like any of the following: platformers, free exploration, emerging lore and story, and don't mind harder combat as well as harsher punishment, Dark Souls style.

While this game suffers from mediocre graphics and a crappy user interface, it's one of the better RPGs I've played, and it's more of an RPG than most other games that claim to be in the genre, because there's more choice and freedom to play how you want to play.
The game supports three or four basic play styles (melee fighting, ranged fighting, and talking), which can be combined to some degree, and five different organizations to join, which give five different sets of quests throughout the game. The organizations are often in conflict and it's interesting to see the same events play out from other angles. This encourages and improves replayability, since you only get a piece of the truth on any given playthrough. There are also eight different backgrounds, which determine your initial start to the game, and a whole bunch of skills to specialize in, which shape your character in very different and powerful ways.
The story is ostensibly about the squabbles between three lords and four guilds in a medieval setting, but there are clues that the story is actually set far in the future after a calamity destroyed civilization. Most characters won't be able to uncover the game's backstory, but with diligence, exploration, and a lot of skill points put into lore you can discover it, adding another layer of depth to the game, giving deeper meaning to and alternate explanations for various beliefs and legends, and providing enough fun to justify another playthrough. The writing is surprisingly good, too.
The combat is challenging but fair. Bad luck can ruin your day sometimes, but by being smart and ensuring the odds are stacked as far as possible in your favor you can almost guarantee success, so you're not at the mercy of the RNG. It's important to know when
to fight, too. The really difficult fights can all be skipped, and almost all fights can be avoided if you have other skills or simply avoid the situation entirely. If you really want to win every fight, you can make a purely combat-focused character, but it's nice that there are other ways of playing.
Unfortunately, the game's user interface is pretty crappy. There aren't nearly enough keyboard shortcuts, too many repetitive clicks are needed to perform basic operations, and you'll often find yourself running around in frustration before eventually searching the web for the locations of various people because the game doesn't tell you where they are and doesn't mark them on a map. Precious few details are recorded in the in-game journal, so if you miss a bit of conversation you may again find yourself searching outside the game for clues. The game also makes it too easy to lose a battle due to a misclick, which is made more likely due to the number of clicks needed.
Despite the poor UI design, the game is technically solid. I haven't seen a crash yet, and only a few minor bugs.
Each playthrough should take about 8-12 hours (although you can do a speedrun much faster), and there's enough content to make at least three plays through the game worthwhile. There are a bunch of endings (six? eight? more?) for completionists, and they're all quite different. I haven't seen most of them, and many of them are secret, but that just means there's still more to discover!
In short, if you can look past the slightly obnoxious interface, there's a great game in here. I bought it at full price and don't regret it one bit. I also very much appreciate that they have a demo, so if you're on the fence, feel free to give the demo a try!

Sparkle 2 Evo is belonging to a series of games with Genesis and Zero, where you're taking the fate of a little sparkle in your hand. Your goal is to make him evolve and reach adulthood. To do that, your little guy can eat microelements, that will determine towards which category he will fall.
Indeed, while you don't have any control over the DNA in itself, you can choose to eat only a single kind of element or juggling between them, knowing that when you're leveling up, you can change your form and by doing so use a special ability.
You can be a carnivore (by eating red elements) with a sprint as special power, a herbivore, with the possibility of eating elements away from your mouth (for that, you should search green elements) or an omnivore, with a repulsive ability (the blue element will be your best friend).
However, through different worlds, you're not alone. You can find octopus, fishes, etc.. that you can eat. They're also belonging to each color: you will find blue, red and green fishes for example. You're generally alone in the world if you choose the casual mode and your goal is to eat one element until none is left. You can choose to continue to explore the rest of the level, which will allow you to level more.
But you can also enable the competitive mode, where other sparkles, controlled by the AI, will fight you for dominance. Your only way to win is to ensure that you ate more elements than them. When you win, you can clear the level as in the casual mode.
My great regret in that gameplay is that I don't have a real control over DNA. I can't choose the elements I really want. The only way to do it is to eat only the microelements and when you're in competitive mode, you can't really choose to avoid some elements if you don't want the AI to give you time.
Also, some enemies tend to swap layers, with a resulting chase being difficult.
The graphics are beautiful. You're really in another world, with bright colors. And the soundtrack is really relaxing.  It's fitting to that deep world.
Anyway, Sparkle 2 Evo is a game, despite its flaws, that is very entertaining. If you want a total control over your sparkle and have quests, you should orient yourself towards Genesis. If you want just a sparkle without any goal, without any worry about being carnivore/herbivore/omnivore, head for ZERO. However, Evo and Genesis are the best in the series, so, you can purchase it without any problem.

Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag doesn't really want to be an Assassin's Creed game, and I don't blame it. It seems keen to shrug off the oblique, convoluted lore surrounding the eon-long Assassins vs Templar power struggle, which managed to reach new peaks of ludicrousness even after that bit in the second game when you punch the Pope into unconsciousness in order to access an alien hologram. Black Flag stuffs all that into a box labelled 'whoops', throws it down a deep, dark hole and sends you on third-person free-running murder missions on the high seas instead. By Blackbeard's bushy eyebrows, that is a welcome move.
You are Edward Kenway, a rogue who loves money enough to leave his girlfriend in port and sail to the West Indies in search of a vast fortune. In the opening scenes he steals an Assassin's hooded garb and wristblades and accidentally falls in with a crowd of Templars, a team of comedy evil caricatures led by a bearded grand master and backed up by a plate armoured man-ogre who throws axes at people. They're searching for the Observatory, an ancient device that enables its user to see the location of anyone in the world at any time. The Templars want it because it'll make coups easier, the Assassins want it to stop the Templars, and Kenway wants it because it's probably the most valuable thing on the planet.
If that sounds a bit removed from piracy and plunder, don't worry. After the two-hour hand-holding tutorial section – mercifully shorter than in previous Assassin's Creed games – the Observatory is relegated to distant long-term objective status, and the story refocuses on the building of the pirate paradise of Nassau: a lawless little utopia maintained by a collection of criminals seeking respite from the attention of the law.
That means Kenway isn't exactly an Assassin. He has all the free-running, jumping and killing skills of the sect – a genetic bonus, it's implied – but his relationship with the series' morally ambiguous order of murder monks is fractious. That keeps the plot's severest absurdities at arm's length and lets you just be a pirate and do pirate things. Hang out with famous brigands like James Kidd. Watch affable rogue Edward Teach become an unhinged, scenery-chewing Blackbeard. Sail across the ocean, rob ships, fight the British, take sea forts for yourself, harpoon whales, explore large coastal cities such as Havana and raid ancient Aztec ruins for treasure. All this in a beautiful tropical open world that's at its glowing, hyper-detailed best on PC.
On land, much is familiar. Hubs such as Havana and Nassau are large, but there are no urban spaces to match the size and spectacle of Rome or Constantinople. A shame, certainly, but there's still a huge amount to explore in scattered settlements across Black Flag's massive archipelago. You'll sail between stilted pier towns tucked away in rocky alcoves, tropical islands sprinkled with treasure chests and larger townships like the manicured, orderly haven of Kingston. As always, you have to climb to high perches to scout sections of town, revealing chests, stores and sidequests in the area, the latter including a welcome increase in open-world assassination missions and warehouse raids. These place targets in open areas patrolled by British or Spanish forces and invite you to solve the problem creatively.
Such missions feel closer to the original vision for Assassin's Creed than the scripted story segments which, while much improved over Assassin's Creed III's restrictive and buggy offerings, are still rather over-reliant on lengthy follow tasks. To raid a warehouse, you must first scan the area for the key holder, pickpocket it off him (or rob his corpse) and then make your way to the door without being shot dead by elevated musket snipers and roaming guards. Stealth has been tightened up to make this more interesting. Pervasive jungle foliage offers constant cover and targets can be marked using Kenway's magic 'Eagle Vision' mode, which lets you track guards through walls – a serious advantage, yes, but you no longer have access to the silent, ranged instant-kill throwing knives that made similar challenges trivial in previous games.

This is absolutely one of my favorite games. The story is intricate and beautiful, the character development is very well done and has made me cry multiple times. The attention to detail makes everything even better. For instance, at one point in the game you get an ability which essentially gives you the ability to jetpack across a room, pushing gusts of air behind you. If you happen to use this ability directly above a body of water, the sound effects and art reflect the water being kicked up in the wind. Another instance of this is when you are near a battle arena, you will see corpses falling through the air and land on platforms, where they remain as you are in the area. This game takes all the good teamfighting/skirmising elements from various MOBA's and combines them in a way that makes the game action-packed and quick.
I obviously cannot comment on the balance of the game as of yet, but it does seem quite fair. The maps are small, however they allow you to out-maneuver opponents with the fog of war (which in my opinion is done very well). This lets the game not feel overbearing if you're ever in a melee vs. ranged situation.
The battlerite system is super satisfying. It gives you a good sense of growth and intensity when you get access to better rites later into the game. The best of 5 format is the best format that I would imagine for the game. Getting a reverse sweep is beautiful.
Rather than talking about cons, I would like to remind you that while I definitely advise people to purchase this game if they're a fan of the teamfighting aspect of MOBA's, that it is in early access, so bugs and minor balance issues are to be expected. I'll likely come back to discuss the cons and what can be improved with more playtime.
I really like this game and would like to see it grow, so give it a shot if you love all-out brawls.
*There needs to be more options for customising your game experience.
*The in-game ability descriptions should tell you whether an ability is a line skillshot or an area ability, just because it makes it easier to understand.
I* would personally like a clear distinction between what can and cannot go over walls in the game.
*The center orb could use a visual indicator when its about to explode (or if there is already one, make it more obvious. I haven't seen it.)
*The ability to browse through the client while in queue would be nice. You can't really do anything but look at your own characters abilities. Being able to look at other champs and open chests would be great.
*Area-cast abilities could use a max cast range indicator.
*Further steam integration (inviting, adding) would be nice
*Spectating friends could be cool. Maybe a spectate higher ranked players option?

As of the time of writing this review, this game is on update 0.9.2.
So I'll start out saying this isn't my cup of tea of a game. I'm not so into the top down, click to attack type game. I don't hate the game type but I'm not too big of a fan either. So bare with me when I say that this game is a solid 'It's OK'.
So lets start here. Gameplay-wise, it plays a lot like your regular MOBA (they really need to find a new name for those type of games). It's main difference, which is a big one, is you forget the idea of fighting smaller units and towers and skip on to the hero vs hero fights, you know one of the best parts of those games (in my opinion at least). The cooldown times are reduced quite a bit from games like Dota and the like and round are about 2 mins or so. The gameplay is fast paced and quite enjoyable because of that. Now here's where I persoanlly have an issue witht the game. It doesn't feel fast enough. I don't mean the rounds don't go by fast enough, I mean the characters themselves. They feel slow. Since the shield/dash button is on a cool down and for some characters, quite a long one, it doesn't feel like I can squeeze out of a bad situation. Even if the character does have an evasive move, it doesn't go far so the enemy is able to quickly catch up to you and start getting beat up quite badly again. Also remember how I said they're on a cooldown, even with the cooldowns being heavly reduced in comparison those MOBA type games, they're still quite long for those evasive type moves so it's you're likely going to lose quite a lot if not most of your life before you can escape.
Now with all that said, I recognise this problem as a personal one. I prefer fast evasive movements in games and this game isn't one of them. This game is more about hitting at the right time and to time your moves accordingly, which is why this game is still a good game. It's good at that. Planning out how to use your abilities at the right time and the right place is where this game shows it skill.
Gameplay is like the hero vs hero part of MOBA games and it's more about a game of timing and planning rather than evasive skills.
So I don't have too much of an issue here since I play this game pretty casually. Though I can see why others would have some issues with it. Getting into a game can take a while though this might be a issue with where I'm located. Though I think the bigger issue is the actual matchmaking for some. You can face some pretty skilled people that will just obliterate you. I don't mind it too much, since it least I get to see how skilled teams play but I can see how it would frustrate others.
From what I can tell, the characters are pretty balanced. Though I feel as though Ruh Kaan is a little in the strong side in terms of damage and health and Oldur seems to have a too little health for what he is. That could just be me though. Character design wise, I prefer the look of the females more than the males. That just seem to have more variety and color, to me. Just a small thing though.
Not a bad game but I can't say it's a game that I see myself playing hours upon hours on.

I love RPGs.  I've been playing computer RPGs since Pool of Radiance was new.  I love challenging RPGs, and I especially enjoy RPGs where communication is important to the game.  Age of Decadence purports to be a challenging, communication-heavy RPG.  It puts forward repeatedly how deadly combat is and how it should be avoided.  It then gives you no tools in which to avoid combat.  Skill points are sparse enough that you can pick one, maybe two communication skills to specialize in.  That's assuming you have no interest in crafting or lore.  It then requires a skill check of TWO skills in many conversations, making it highly unlikely you'll be successful unless you've played through to that point and rerolled a new character.  Combat skill points are equally sparse.  Guides considered "helpful" tell you to always save before combat, try the fight 10 or so times, and if you can't crack it, reroll with a different set of skills and stats.  It seeks to be bleak and ends up being frustrating.  I didn't enjoy it at all.  There are  much better options out there for your money.  Go elsewhere.

TL:DR Solid Card Game. Gameplay/mechanics are ok but somewhat overpowerd all over the place. Games can be really short cause a 40 card deck is used > faster pulls > faster good cards > faster game. So the Gameplay and Coremechanics of this game pretty much allow for the same things you would except of a cardgame. Control, aggro, ramp, graveyardaction, you want a certain heartstone/magic/yugioh deckstyle? you can build it. At first glance i really really liked this but i wondered why the games always turned out to be very short. Well only 40 cards in your deck so if your used to drafting and get your core combo going fast the game will end fast. Doesnt mean its easy to win. It's not cause its a lot more "poker"-type to play cause the turns are resolved simultanously. you might be casting destructionspells on the enemy killercard... and he just pulls it back to base the same turn. he saves his card, you get nothing for yours. Nice!
The reasons i wont be continueing playing and recommending this to any of my friends are simple. The cardart looks like the lower average user of deviantart has created it. I didnt see any card where i just zoomed in on it and was yawdropped by the art. Then there is the "animated cardgame" thing... the battlefield is a bad 3d type and the animation mostly consists of slight breathing movements or fast resovled 3 or 4 single frames. lame and also not of the epic looking kind. Also bad seems to be the way of card requisition. over the 4 hours gametime i had i managed to buy 3, yes three! cards with the influence points i got. yes i got boosters through quests but those where the starter quests. so there is no longterm benifit for this game. you just wont get cards in a good manner of time spent/card.

Mystik Belle is a really charming metroidvania/adventure with a 16-bit aesthetics. It features beautiful pixel art visuals and a nice soundtrack and charming characters. The game is somewhat short once you know what to do and though there are undertones of a fleshed out setting, the NPCs aren't featured enough to create much of an attachment.
The description doesn't lie, though it has plenty of exploration and upgrades like metroidvanias, the bulk of progress is acheived by finding the right items and taking them to the right people and places, which takes a lot of guesswork, trial and error, like classic point and click games. It is made harder by giving you a limited inventory size, which means juggling items until you have the right ones to take to the right place. A helpful tip for players: leave items you don't know how to use in easy to reach rooms, as to avoid backtracking.
The metroidvania side of the gameplay is par for the course. You have a shooting attack that upgrades as you kill enemies, and you get more skills, either for attack or movement, as you progress. One bothersome detail is that the jumps at first are just barely high enough to reach the platforms above, so it takes a lot of pixel-perfect jumps until you are given skills to navigate more comfortably.
The genre mix is a novelty that can be as amusing as it becomes bothersome, and it doesn't revolutionize anything, but overall it's a charming game that can give you some hours of fun.

So as an upgrade or expansion of Civ V, this is great, but it should have been $20-$30 tops, not $50.

Arma 2 Review:
The short; A great game, with great physics, perhaps the best for its time. Great graphics has well, night and day cycles well. Controls are a slightly confusing for some people, but can be modified and adjusted to the users liking. However for  fast for people who are willing to learn the controls are positioned quite well (Except the in-game VOIP). Game play itself is great has well. Single player has one of the best storys, with multiple endings and quite long in length (You can even finish the game early and get a "secret ending"). However the multiplayer is perhaps the best place to enjoy the game to its full. Not met a game like it ever (Except Arma 3... but thats next in the series anyway). Cant list any real flaws, at least none that i noticed, except for the steep learning curve.
Arma 2 OA adds some greater graphics, new story and new area to play around in; this is a great expansion and exactly what we needed. Furthurmore this is a great modding platform. Some of the best role play experiences i have had come from this game. The Life mode, and the DayZ mod(s) are great community produced items that have shown that giving the community the right tools, a great concept can be made.
I highly recommend this game based on the price, the mods, and the game play of the "vanilla" game. Great experience, and i hope to see you on some DayZ mods. *Hint* I am not friendly.

Mystik Belle is an indie Metroidvania/Adventure game hybrid with excellent pixel presentation.  Like most adventure games, the game is very short once you understand what to do.  Although the platforming and combat is fairly good, the controls are a little picky for the special moves, and moving around this way helps alleviate some of the boredom.
Unfortunately a few of the puzzles miss the mark a bit or involve background setpieces, and having a few red herring items and finite inventory space will tire out the fun as you head through the same corridor the umpteenth time.  Giving items to characters or asking for advice on them is a bit of a pain, and if you've just used all your items up oftentimes no one has useful advice.  Another issue is that the resolution is a bit small considering how nice and big the sprites all are.  It looks good, but it's hard to see what's ahead and Belle can neither look beyond the screen, nor can she duck which may cause some annoying deaths until you're familiar with the territory.
Despite these flaws, the dialogue, main character and setting are enjoyable enough and the game is tricky enough to keep you interested if you like the mechanics and futzing out solutions to things.  I definitely wouldn't recommend it to everyone, but there simply aren't any other games on steam quite like Mystik Belle, and if you can stomach a few nonsense puzzles most of what's here is worth it.

I want to like this game. I loved Civ 5 and for the most part, Beyond Earth plays a lot like it... Which is partially the problem. It plays like Civ 5 with less content and depth.  The new features in the game don't really do enough to make it feel any more than a mod or expansion to Civ 5.
There are only 8 factions to choose from, making it impossible to play with anymore than 8 players, even in singleplayer. You can modify the files to allow 8+ AI in singleplayer but it will only result in duplicate factions, rendering diplomacy confusing and practically unusable.
The UI is a lot less... informative than Civ 5. Many dulled, grey tones . In particular, telling factions apart on the minimap proves quite difficult with many simply appearing grey. The minimap is also way too small to make out any important details and minor feedback features such as trade route caps and "just finished building/researching" information are completely absent.
All in all, this game feels more like an unfinished expansion back or a decent mod than a quality civilization title.

This game is an interesting combination of Metroidvania and Adventures games. It has wonderful art and music, and the writing is, at least, entertaining. However it is stiffled by lackluster level design, stiff combat, and awkward controls.

Just terrible, the game is nearly unplayable in a literal sense. Any online play takes several tries to get off the ground because the game crashes constantly in multiplayer, although it is admittedly better in LAN play than over the internet.  It tends to be a toss-up whether or not the racial faction bonuses will work at any given time. The mechanics are unimaginative, with a completely uninspired tech-bubble that lets you decide exactly the way you wish your civilization to be the same as everyone else's because the techs are scattered all over the place and full of requirements from other techs placed far away on the tree. In the year 2014 there's apparently no way to make an algorithm that even attempts to balance starting conditions. In effect, it's pretty much the exact same deal as with civilization 5, although the tech bubble is less intuitive and harder to construct a proper build out of.
Barbarians, one of the most annoying and random features of civilization 5, has been given a steroid treatment so that the game can rocket into the dull trope of all alien worlds somehow inexplicably playing host to naturally bullet-resistant life-forms. Rather than being an interesting event and object of interaction with the world, the aliens pour out of nests, meaning that depending on your location they will either be an insignificant nuisance that you don't really need to take a stance on or absolutely obliterate any chance of staying competitive with anyone who was placed elsewhere on the map. Their aggression is mostly tied into the nests - if you are surrounded by them then too bad, if not then you might not even need to escort your workers and colonists to new locations. This is unmitigated by the techs for dealing with them, due to their being placed on high tiers and randomly around the tech bubble.
You're not alone in dealing with the alien threat, however. Every now and then an unafiliated outpost will land somewhere in your expansion circle, forcing you to go to war with them or 35 turns before they go away. Sometimes two outposts disagree about which one of them is going to ruin your day, and make you decide - never give you the option to tell them both to screw off. This happens at random times throughout the game, and you have no control over it. These are the exact two random events that will happen - outposts taking your spot, and aliens taking your spot. Other players may also take your spot, but that's to be expected as you can also take theirs, being that they don't fall from the sky without warning.
This game is lazy at best, more of a late beta than a full release in most of the ways that matter. If you preordered, but are intending to play with friends who did not, you can't use the bonus map types - which is pretty stupid, but the blow is softened by the fact that the new map types are basically small variations on the old ones. In their botched attempt to basically recreate Alpha Centauri, Firaxis has managed to leave out most of the interesting parts of this predecessor - the tech bubble is bad, there is no lore to speak of, the factions are bland, even the quotes are terrible - and mashed it with the worst parts of Civilization 5's engine. Just awful.

Shadow Warrior is one of those games that allow you to turn your brain off and kill things. There's no intricate plot or gameplay here, but it's a fun ride.
Unfortunately, I experienced a lot of hitching (1-2 second microfreezes), even on a beefy system. Seems to be a bug. The level design also feels unnatural -- I found myself wandering around, looking for the next item I had to touch to trigger the next bit of plot exposition.
Shadow Warrior has a unique skill system: you press some combination of keys to trigger special moves, much like in a fighting game. After each battle, you're rated on a scale of 1-5 shurikens, depending on how skillfully you fought. These are interesting systems I haven't seen in an FPS before.

Teslagrad is one of those rare gems that comes along once in a while and makes you look deeper into it's many facets.  During the first couple of minutes of play, I was severely impressed by the highly detailed art style and lovingly rendered animation.  This is, quite frankly, a great game to look at.
Gameplay wise it is a well pieced together 'gimmick' physics platformer, with the flavor this time being electromagnitivity.  Platforms and other obstacles are overcome by either positively or negatively charging elements in the world or even yourself after a certain power-up is attained.
I've always had a big soft spot for metroidvania gameplay, mostly for the exploration aspect, but most especially for the moments when you've aquirred all of the power-ups in the game and, while going through the earlier parts realize how simply things are overcame, either through the skills you've gained throughout or the power-ups you've been equipped with.
Teslagrad accomplishes this in spades, teaching you the 'hard' way how to do things; considering that you are punished for taking a single hit.  That's right, insta-kill is everywhere and it's up to you to make sure that doesn't happen.  That being said the developers do an excellent job of placing invisible checkpoints before each challenge, giving you the chance to experiment with very little annoyance of having to slug through five minutes of repetitive action.  Most of the time at least.  Bosses, on the other hand are unforgiving in that regard, often taking place over different 'phases'.  Oh, you died during the last phase?  Well you shouldn't have a problem doing the first two phases over and over again then.
At times frustrating, Teslagrad is great about the sense of satisfaction that comes with accomplishment; the feeling of finally getting through a particularily difficult skill-based challenge is a source of joy and never feels under-sold.  This isn't Dark Souls, but it isn't exactly Baby's First Platformer.
The story is told purely visually with no dialouge or narration whatsoever.  The closest clues you receive are adorable cut-out puppet theater snippets scatered throughout the tower and collectible scrolls litering the levels which require a certain amount of cunning and determination to receive.
In all, I clocked in a day's worth of gameplay from beginning to end- about the same length of Braid, which felt like a major source of inspiration.

Like with most puzzle games and especially with this game it is not clear what you can do next or where you can progress next. There are often multiple puzzles and/or paths which are blocked but only one of them can be progressed and the player has to guess which one it is. If you make a wrong guess.. well tough luck you just wasted hours of time. If you try all of them and fail at every one of them it really feels like "game over".
You will often find yourself in a situation where you wonder "Am I even supposed to complete this puzzle at this point? Have I missed items or objectives? Do I have the required tools to complete the task?" It can really leave you in a situation where you have to give up and looks at the walkthrough.
The game world and it's story are really good. I have no complaints about graphics/animation/music either. Unlike in many games they have really poured a lot of effort to make different enemies. Almost every room has unique enemies.
What I didn't like was that difficulty was more or less a joke. It's fairly easy to complete the game with less than ~30 total deaths. Most of the deaths I had were caused by an item which I willingly left behind. The world is actually also fairly small. It only feels large because puzzles require you to travel back and forth.
What really breaks the game:
-Inventory management hell:
You only have limited space in inventory and to make it worse there are a lot of items which are either junk or items which are needed only much later in the game. There is a way to automatically identify and discard junk items but it requires you to constantly travel to certain area with new items. The developers also decided to make an item which is required to be with you all the time unless you want death following you everywhere.
-Some puzzles are really frustrating:
The most frustrating puzzles require you to do the "process of elimination" which means that you have to speak at every single NPC and/or show your every item at every NPC to get clues. To make matters worse each NPC is far away from each other. There are only some teleport points in the game.
Cat + electricity puzzle really messes around with you. FIrst you think that you have to carry the cat. Then there is also that damn elevator which looks like a power generator. You also have to speak to the same NPC multiple times to get important clues.
In worm riding puzzle it's really obvious what to do and you even know where you have to go but the damn spot where you have to use the item is definitely NOT clear. There a sign which says that the worm is BEYOND that point but actually the sign is the spot where you have to use the item. To make it worse the next room contains a thing which looks like a worm but is not it.
Dynamite puzzle requires you to collect materials but you have one missing material. It is not clear that you have to speak to certain NPC to get it. There is a potential that player wastes time by searching THE WHOLE GAME WORLD just to find that material.
I can recommend this game for ~5€ but not for the current price (9,99€).

Mystik Belle is an appealing mix of Metroidvania and oldschool adventure that deserves much more attention than it's getting now.  The map design is simple but effective, the sprite artwork is beautiful and impressive, the dialogue is quirky, and it feels satisfying to play.
One element of the game that I particularly appreciated is that the adventure-esque puzzles are generally neither too obvious nor too cryptic.  At times, I got a little puzzled deciding where I needed to go next, but I never needed to resort to a walkthrough.  Everything makes sense.
I feel as if it could have used just a bit more refinement in certain areas, though.  My biggest qualm with the game might've been Belle's lack of defensive tactics.  She's not nearly small or agile enough character to avoid the barrage of attacks coming from all directions in certain situations, meaning that taking lots of damage is sometimes (seemingly) entirely unavoidable and creates some frustrating difficulty spikes, especially during later boss fights. Any sort of magic shield or dodging capabilities would have been greatly appreciated.  It also doesn't help that enemies randomly generate from the sides of the screen and sometimes hit you the moment you enter a new room.  In short, it doesn't always feel justified when you get hit.
A minor complaint that I have is that while the soundtrack is catchy and suits the mood quite well, I wish it had a bit more variety; it feels like one theme plays through the majority the game.  Item management is a hassle due to the very limited inventory space, leveling up feels like a chore until you max out, and I feel like it wouldn't have been difficult for both of those things to be set up more efficiently to keep the flow intact.
In the long run, these issues did no keep me from staying invested in the game for hours at a time until completion.  There are a lot of fun little details to it, and the whole concept is right up my alley.  For me, buying Mystik Belle was money well spent, and I could picture myself playing through it again sometime in the future.

Hollow Knight is definitely on my list of favorites. My only wish is that I could play the entire game again as if I'd never played it before. An amazing sense of progression and a gorgeous outward appearance is only the beginning of this game's successes.
Each boss battle is unique and challenging in its own way, and even manages to create a personality and backstory for a majority of them without much dialogue. I've been mezmerized by bosses' visual designs or general attitudes several times, despite the endless trouble and frustration they've caused as an enemy. I've even come to the thought that I'd like to repeat an especially difficult boss battle should it have been convenient, simply in admiration of the enrapturing atmosphere and satisfaction of defeating said boss.
Mystery shrouds the first half of the game, which is my personal favorite story element. It kept me wondering at every little foreshadowing detail and often left me in an existential daze thinking up theories about what's to come. New turns of events never failed to surprise me, either. Characters show sudden changes of heart or reveal huge details about the story or themselves. Certain events are overwhelmingly shocking and completely oppose expectation in the most glorious of ways.
This brings me to the supporting characters, all with wonderfully separate personalities and aesthetics. They each maintain an air of lightheartedness which retains sleekness, a trademark of the game's animation style. Some characters reappear periodically, while many others appear only once and still manage to provoke an entirely new set of emotions in the player.
Each area has its own unique set of mobs and a new reason to despise jumping puzzles. Subareas often lie barely out of reach as well, only to be explored when the player has the required experience. This cleverly gives reason to reexplore areas and gain new appreciation for the scale and diversity the game offers. Just when you think you've finished exploring, there's something new to visit.
All this being said, the game might not be for you if you're accustomed to extremely intense, fast-paced PvP games. If you're easily put off by frustrating or "unfair" battles, you may want to be wary as well. Otherwise, I highly recommend Hollow Knight. If you're an artist, I'm sure you can be inspired by this game in some way, as many others have been. Others of you will perhaps find a new favorite as I have.

This is not a critique, rather this review will be a love letter.
As a child I played Sonic. I played the game so much I started to imagine him running along side my school bus or my family's car while looking out the window; he would jump through trees, circle around fire hydrants. Simple childish imagination to make times of boredom fun.

A successor that feels worthy at first glance, then shows it's little shortcomings when you think things through. A mistake often made. The thinking part, that is.
As usual, if you've come to read this review, you've done some background investigation towards the game itself. So I keep those obvious details short. New aiming system, new gallery of weapons, new ways to interact, etc... You'll have read all this, and your assumption will be right.
The assumption being: This is a stellar improvement over the original. The engine looks beautiful and the weapons handle much, much better.
A lot of my Blood Money gripes have been settled.
But this is no longer a Hitman game like you're used to, in terms of Gameplay. And not always for the better.
In the past installments, you were thrown at a level, a situation if you will. And you had to figure out how to achieve your goal(s), then escape through the way you came. Everything that happened between beginning and end was up to you.
This is no longer the case. Now, you are thrown into a smaller level, where you either need to interact/sabotage something or kill someone, then escape through a designated exit into another section of the mission. Commonly, these are three parts.
As a long-time Hitman fan, this sits uneasy with me and feels less true to the Hitman spirit.
On the flip-side though, this allows new gamers to the Hitman series to easier adopt the spirit and feel of the games. In a way, train them for Blood Money or a successor that returns to the old feel.
Also, while I felt more limited in my playground, I did feel like my curiosity was still stimulated through the methods of murder available to me. The areas are still rife with typical oppertunities, relating to your targets.
You are just deprived of a large part of the exploration, finding these quirks of the targets. More often than not, the 'accident' methods are easily found and the tools are often nearby. You feel less like a detective, but still a little bit.
Storywise, the game may feel like it wants to slowly depart from the original.
47, while still cool as a cucumber most of the time, shows signs of emotion and involvement (well, at least in perspective...).
But when you sit it through, it may start to rather feel like an evolution of the story. In a sense, I think the developers are trying to open doors for the series.
Absolution will be slightly tougher to get into for long time fans. But if they can get over the big changes, you can still get a good time out of it.
For newcomers: This isn't what the Hitman series has always been about, but it's pretty close.
A 25 or 50% off will easily justify a purchase.
If you even remotely think you may like a game like this, you probably will.

This is a wonderful RPG that breaks the usual mold. As the authors note, that may mean you hate it, but I loved it. /i have played through the story 6 times so far yet I feel there is more to discover. (I did much of my play on my wife's steam account so not many hours logged here).
In AOD story is king and the what background you choose for your character will dramatically alter your play experience. You cannot under any circumstances do everything there is to do in the game in one playthrough. Each background, provided you follow through with it, will give you different experiences and opportunities. Each will be part of the same overarching narrative, but the part you play in it will vary wildly and the outcomes are pretty wide open.
Most gameplay is driven by dialog choices, so in that sense this is something like a grand choose your way adventure crossed with a more traditional RPG. You can play the game through to its conclusion without a single combat, or, you can resolve nearly every conflict with violence.  But not all paths are equal in this freedom. Choose to be an Assassin and you had best be prepared to kill. Choose the life of a merchant and you really should re-think any attempt to intimidate the local brigands.
Some reviewers complain that the gaim railroads your choices, but that is not the case. What it does is meet out consequences for your decisions and choices. If you want to sweet talk your way to greatness, invest heavily in skills and stats that support that, and then stick to that game plan. If you want to fight, you had best be the most hardened warrior you can imagine because the game is not going to cut you any slack. Every character cannot do everything. If you want to experience the full breadth of the game, you must play it more than once, choosing a different approach each time to see what can happen.
Combat is unforgiving but you can master it. The key, like other areas of the game, is specialization. Pick a fighting style and master it. Choose one of the two defenses, and any of the weapon types. Keep those capped out, learn the system, and you should do fine. All in all, it's easier to talk your way through this game than to fight, but some avenues are only open to those with the steele to master combat.
Many games promise multiple endings, and they tend to come down to some final binary choice, but AOD truly has a wide range of outcomes and combinations that will change your fate, and the fate of the world. You can choose who rules, rule yourself, destroy the wold, become a god, become a slave, and more. Looking at the achievements will give you a good idea what is possible but it won't make discovering how to achieve them any easier.
This is a game about breadth rather than length. One play through will only be a few hours (unless you spend a lot of time fighting which takes longer). But I found myself going back again and again because every play through was an opportunity to take different paths and make new discoveries. In that respect it is one of the riches RPGs I've played, and I've played a lot in the last 30 years.
Its a nice game for a short break or something like that. But if you're looking for a game for more, try Sparkle 3 - way better and more fun :))

This is one of the better RPGs I have ever played, and it isn't for everyone. Let me start with the cons:
The graphics are unpleasant. The user interface is ugly, and at times trying to work with. The combat is fundamentally unforgiving and complex (it is an utter mistake to focus on one weapon)... and escape doesn't really seem to be an option (at least, not one I could ever figure out). Markers are woefully absent from city maps -- making them a terrible chore to navigate. This game will require you to do a lot of reading, and not all pertinent text triggers a "quest".
With that said -- the game is brief (6-8 hours), and every decision you make matters in some way. There are radically different ways to approach each situation: brute force, stealth, diplomacy, technology, conspiracy, assassination. There are dead ends, but there aren't any "true" dead ends -- there's just another path that you didn't consider. After about the third play through, you begin to understand the insane richness of the world. There are so many interested parties at play, but you can never see them all at once.
In one play through, I avoided all direct combat; in another, I served a great kingdom as a solider; in another, I became a god; in another, I killed everything that claimed to be a god. Do you want to nuke a city? -- you can. Become a cyborg-lich? -- valid option. Operate as a pacifist who prevents wars from breaking out? -- you'll be complicit in some deaths, but you can. Or do you just want to become a legendary murder-ma-jig? -- oh yeah,  all options.
This work is flawed, but if you can get past those flaws -- it is nothing short of brilliant.

Combat is badly in need of balancing and the various factions really need more depth; perhaps unique units or unit enhancements. They all feel pretty much the same.
The health mechanic (aka "happiness") seems broken as well.  As your empire expands it becomes increasingly difficult to maintain a "healthy" empire.  You can mitigate this by choosing nearly every quest choice to go in that direction which then begs the question, "why have the other choices?"  It needs balancing.
On that topic, the quests are a nice idea but being given a choice of quests would be better.  As it stands, you get some significant bonuses for completing them but will fail them if not completed in time meaning your game choices are a lot more linear if you want the benefit.
In a word, the game quickly becomes - boring....
All in all, a disappointment.  Fixable; certainly but it remains to be seen how it is approached.  I expect that there will be enough negativity out there to prompt some action.

After 5 absolutely horrible horror games on Halloween this one caught my eye. I figured "meh, even if it's not horror it's still good for Halloween." Being on sale helped but honestly, I would've even bought this one at full price. I'm apparently very late to the party but that means I guess I missed most of the bugs and problems.
Mystik Belle reminds me of one of those cool-looking NeoGeo games that I'd see in magazines but knew I'd never be able to play. It's music and graphics throw back to the old days but not in the manufactured nouveau-retro way a lot of games do nowadays. The sprites and backgrounds were obviously made with attention and love. There's a lot of personality here. The areas and characters are full of tiny details which you see right from the start. Sprites are large and detailed, locations have several layers to them (the foreground layer of the lower-right area is so cool) and the customary torchlight zones are mixed with a modern effect where your fireballs also produce light. I kept shooting into the darkness to see if I could find secrets.
The story is pretty tame but still very enjoyable, with two endings (only the True ending gets a final boss, though it's more for LOLs and closure than for a suitable climax). It's easy to see both in a single playthrough. There are 8 hidden backstory notes to find (finding them all triggers the true ending) so I guess if you found them before seeing the normal ending then you might miss out? I dunno.
The dialogue is often amusing. Apparently I was playing the censored version the whole time and I didn't see an option to switch it to uncensored. If it is just a toggle that I'm missing then it would add more replay, playing again to see how dialogue changes and how the characters change because of what they say.
But apart from the main story the game has loads of bonus dialogue if you show items to NPCs. This is also often where hints can come from. There's also some subtle character stuff which some might not notice, like the identity of the masked antagonist (pay attention in the dorm and clues given when making a related item) and I always find little things like that can only be done with care and love, so including them shows a developer who worked hard on their project.
The game's fairly difficult, or maybe I'm just losing my touch with age. I was often jumping just between bullets, only to mess up a landing (memories of playing the Valis games, right there). What compounds the difficulty is that, at it's core, this is much more of an adventure game than just a metroidvania. It's not just "find item X to get to place B". You need to talk to NPCs, think about what items will need to be in your inventory if you need to combine stuff, and search the school high and low, many times over. And a lot of that happens before you have the first 3 warp rooms unlocked. So if you're not so familiar with the more-than-just-action style then you'll find yourself whittled down by enemies as you search the halls again and again.
Bosses can also get pretty rough but like most such games it's just a matter of learning what their patterns or triggers are and remembering your advanced moves might be needed to dodge some attacks.
This review is kind of stretching on so I'll end it here but I was actually very pleased with my purchase. There's a lot of love that went into Mystik Belle and I'd gladly follow more of her adventures if more get made. Good job.

Audiosurf 2 is a ride-the-music game that outdoes its predecessor in every way.
The game focuses on its one core aspect, that is allowing users to ride either their own music, or publicly available music in a variety of similar gamemodes.
Mainly Singleplayer but Multiplayer modes exist (Up to 4 without Steam Workshop)

,

Anyone wanting to listen to music and do something at the same time, or if you are in it to win it geared up for those high scores, there is something here for all. Difficulty is adjusted by both your gamemode and song intensity.

Do not purchase this game if you are looking for a game with a story, or any sort of leveling system. There is no unlockables and nothing to obtain, save for the sweet glory of Top Score.
As there is neither a story to follow, nor defined soundtrack so to speak, this is main part why one would consider buying. On its default mode, Audiosurf 2 has the player control a small, abliet fast shuttle set out on collecting all the colourful blocks and avoiding the grey ones. As the song ramps up in volume and intensity, as does the speed of the shuttle. This primarly is where the difficulty comes from. A slow trance song will be a relaxing ride; heavy deathmetal with plenty of screaming with ensure you have to focus from start to finish.
This premise plays out exactly as its predecessor, but improves upon it greatly. Whereas in the first game the edges of these cubical blocks seemed to almost seep out of the sides of their lines, alongside the ship's controls becoming janky at times where the song spiked (common in Dubstep or Opera) the sequel suffers from none of these flaws. In comparison to other audio-based games, the Audiosurf formula dominates. Up and downs go with the beats. The mechanics of the game flows through with all of its gamemodes. Aside from being a shuttle, you can also become a Sprinter jumping and sliding. In addition to this is the Steam Workshop, which adds a plethora of differing game types, allowing one to choose their style. Daily songs are something for all users to try and go for to see where a player would place compared to everyone else, each seperated by game type. This on top of allowing users to challenge friends, or when a "Dethroned" message appears when someone beats you
really adds to the thrill of trying one's best.
Comparing to the first game, Audiosurf 2 once again blows it out of the water. While the original did allow some form of customization via changing the colours depending on intensity, Audiosurf 2 takes it to a whole new level. Instead skins that can modify both the track and the shuttle allow for much greater options when choosing your song. This ties in with the Steam Workshop well, as it allows the user to have a vast number of skins ready to use with the simple push of a button. While the ingame menu isn't groundbreaking by any standard, but does make it simple and easy to use, while being non-intrusive, which can be considered a great improvement compared to mess of menus the first had.
Although it can a bit of a jumble to get to one owns songs, or connect to the internet, usually it saves the last location the user was in, saving the trouble of repeating the process. As for in-game playing, much is left to the user on what the game looks like. Despite the existence of a graphics setting, most users should be able to run the game on High or Ultra due to low setting requirements of the game.
The game serves its purpose of being able to listen to the music with great gameplay without the two getting in the way of each other. I'd personally recommend turning the sound off for collecting blocks.
The price is a bit steep for what it offers, especially considering much of its content comes from its Steam Workshop, but if you really enjoy music and you want something to do with your hands while you listen, this is it.

I just finished Mystik Belle and I have to say it was very well worth my time.
The obvious first: The graphics, animation and music are truly a treat. The same high quality from the screenshots is maintained throughout the game. The different areas are sufficiently unique and each has its own atmosphere. The soundtrack complements the game nicely.
The action is well-paced with superbly designed monsters and rewarding boss fights. The controls definitely need some getting used to and feel a bit sluggish at first, but soon enough everything falls into place.
Belle can level up, which increases hitpoints and firepower. When she dies, she is resurrected in the starting room with all items intact, but experience points reset to the beginning of the current level. So once the character levels up, that level remains fixed even after death.
Mystik Belle is sold as a Metroidvania with a point-and-click twist, the latter of which was a two edged sword for me. Belle has to find items which need to be used, either by themselves or combined with other items, to open new passages and advance the game. Since the developer wanted to reward the player for thinking about the items and paying attention to the conversations he decided to limit the inventory size, so you cannot keep all your stuff with you all the time. I kept all my belongings in one room so that I wouldn't have to go on a scavenger hunt as soon as I needed a specific item, but still I had to backtrack a lot. All in all these puzzles were not impossibly hard.
Mystik Belle was developed mainly by one person (except for the music), which I find an outstanding feat, and the game has an unbelievable level of polish for that. Metroidvania-purists may find the amount of skills to be learned somewhat limited though (one additional spell and two jump upgrades).
I finished the game in about eight hours. Visually, Mystik Belle has a lot to offer. The gameplay content I would describe as bite-sized, which I did not find particularly problematic since there are just so many things to see and explore.
There are two endings, the good one of which can be achieved by finding eight scrolls hidden throughout the map. Getting these will reward the player with an additional boss fight which, although not terribly challenging, was still exceptionally well done and gave the game a nice sense of closure.
I would definitely recommend the game.

It is the same in Black Flag. I really enjoy the sailing and ship combat, but wow coming from playing games like MGSV, The Witcher 3 and Dark Souls 3 everything on foot feels terrible. Those are all much newer games but I still enjoy the movement of AC2, Brotherhood and Revelations.
I just can't get over how bad everything on foot is. If I'm trying to chase a target I get stuck climbing every object on the left or right of the path. If I'm trying to climb the mast of a ship to cut down a flag I will either jump off to my death or get stuck running back and forth on the crossbeam of the main mast.
Stealth is hit or miss, enemies can see me from very far away but take five or more seconds to actually react. Enemies also seem to be deaf considering I can sprint up behind them without them hearing me. The combat feels like a step down from AC3, there is a counter much like in AC3, but no double counter. There is also a guard break that is required to beat some enemies.
I really wanted to like this game, the story and characters are much better then AC3, the present day/animus stuff is minimal and sailing around is a lot of fun, but everytime I desyncronize from Ed It feels more like a fault of the controls and movement mechanics and not because I made a mistake. In order to give Hitman: Absolution a fair shake, I had to get several hours into it.  After the rather superb opening sequences, the plot of the game becomes plodding at best, and detracts at worst.  And that's a damn shame because the opening to this game is absolutely compelling.
This is a top-notch stealth action game, in the lineage of Thief, with its own characteristics of course.  Cosplay is legitimately fun, and the challenge of stabbing a dude with a kitchen knife in a chef outfit and then changing into a cop's uniform to get away is thrilling.  Though dangerous, it's possible to blast your way through many areas as well.  If you care about your epeen however, you will shy away from this since it generally subtracts from your score at the end of a level.
Even so, the occasional thrill-kill is irresistible.  Quick-time melee is varied enough to be challenging (don't confuse this with a God Of War clone) and the massive variety of weapons provides GTA-esque sadistic glee.  Taking a fireman's axe to the face of a club bouncer, tossing him in a trunk, and walking away with his outfit made me giggle.
Clearly this makes me a bad person, just like Agent 47.  At least it also makes me an anti-hero, rather than merely a sociopath.  Right guys?  Guys...?

Author's Note: As of the time of writing this review, I currently have 11 hours in this game, along with a level 18 character. Any experiences past level 18 including mechanics, dungeons, raids, etc, will not be mentioned in this review.
Riders of Icarus is an MMORPG that uses the premise of being able to tame almost every non-humanoid creature in the game. Along with visuals that, by MMORPG standards, are quite appealing to the eye on max settings. RoI also has mounted combat (both ground and air).
The first thing that you will notice when creating a character in Riders of Icarus is that the 4 classes available to you are not genderlocked. The classes are the Berserker, the standard big-sword weilding psycho. The Guardian, the standard tank. The Assassin, the standard burst DPS. The Priest, the standard squishy healer, and the Wizard, the standard spell-casting DPS. All of these classes are.. Playable. Thats all that can be said really; Riders of Icarus doesn't have any new or innovative classes, but at least they work. My personal favourite class to play is the Guardian, simply because the idea of leashing my allies out of danger is a heck of a lot easier than expecting them to move on their own.
Of course though, Riders of Icarus' appeal isn't its classes; its the fact that you can tame and ride monsters into battle. Taming a monster is simple. You have a certain amount of taming points (which get reset to max every day automatically), and taming monsters uses them up. The amount of points used depends on the strength of the monster. Once you've leapt onto the monster you want to tame, the game shoves a laughably easy quick-time event in your face. Unfortunately this isn't all. Most of the time when taming a high-level monster, its all up to RNG. You can complete the quicktime event with lightning precision and still fail because the game flips you the bird. While some players may like this idea of gambling, I do not. I believe that the act of taming a monster should be based on the skill of the tamer in question. The game would benefit more, in my opinion, with a system similar to Red Dead Redemption's of taming a horse.
Another thing worth mentioning is in order to even attempt to tame a high-level monster later in the game, you'll need to craft a specific item that allows you to try which can be a bit of a hassle when you spend 10 minutes trying to scavenge the materials, then you fail taming the monster. A lot of players didn't seem to have a problem with the RNG taming, so maybe I'm just unlucky. I probably should stay away from Vegas.
Levelling up is your average MMORPG grind. Kill quests, fetch quests, talk-to-this-guy-beside-me quests, etc etc. Nothing bad, just nothing good. One problem I did have with the combat though though is, at least with flying mounts, when you are in the air and you attack a creature on the ground, the combat is glitchy as Chaser.
As soon as you attack a mob, it will run away. Not a big deal, this is realistic. If I was a simple bandit and I got an crossbow to the chest from a guy on a dragon, I'd get the hell out of there too. The
is that as soon as they go two seconds (estimate) without taking damage, THEY RETURN BACK TO THEIR STARTING POSITION. During this time they are immune to all damage, and once they get back to their position, their health resets back to full... WHAT?! I understand that this is to make it so people can't solo high-level monsters just because they're in the air, but surely there's a better, more effecient way to do this that doesn't feel clunky and immersion-breaking.
Also, there are two playstyles; tab-targeting, and action. Though really the two are exactly the same, just different camera angles. Make no mistake; both playstyles are tab-targeting
-Great visuals
-Doesn't appear to be pay to win
-No gender-locked classes
-Does not appear to be pay-to-win. (Items bought in the cash shop are either for cosmetics, or convencience. Nothing game-breaking as I've come to expect from a game published by Nexon)
-Combat (Both tab-targeting, and action) feels impactful and looks flashy
-The community seems friendly enough
-Character customization is decent
-The developers compensate players very well when unscheduled maintenance occurs
-The cutscenes, and a majority of story quests are voice acted. Some of them are better quality than others.
-There are gold sellers EVERYWHERE. Normally I don't have a problem with them. As with most F2P mmorpgs, its part of my routime to log on, block the new spammers, then move on with my life. This would work... IF RIDERS OF ICARUS HAD AN EASIER WAY TO BLOCK THEM. Right-clicking the gold-farmer's name will only bring up a Whisper window, and even if you see one out in the game, the auto-report option is about as useful as a cup made of swiss cheese since it
which every single bot is in. Seriously, this is easily my least favourite part of the game.
-Hackers. There are speed-hackers everywhere. Normally they're on at night. This doesn't really bother me since I don't do PvP, in fact its almost laughable to see some chick blinking all across the quest area like Corvo Attano. Though it gets less funny when there's an important quest-mob who gets two shotted, leaving me to wait the painstakingly long respawn timer.
-Taming is RNG-Based rather than skill based.
-Crafting has the appeal of a McDonalds cheeseburger
-You can't move when attacking.
TL;DR
I would recommend the game. It's definitely not for everybody, but it doesn't take long to download, its free, so you really don't have anything to lose. I will continue to play the game.
